items.title: The Best Gifts for Kids Are Small. Or Big. Or Lots. Or Stomp

items.author: Molly Fischer
paragraphs: When you are a kid, time can seem to organize itself around occasions for receiving treats—and, above all, presents. This is not because children are materialistic monsters (mostly) but because they have a limited ability to treat themselves. Generally speaking, an eight-year-old cannot reward herself, at the end of a tough week, by doing a little window-shopping and deciding that she deserves a cute bag, or its third-grade equivalent (glowing slime?). The calendar can become a series of buildups and letdowns around the prospect of surprise delights. This is the golden age of gift-getting. No one cares as much about presents as kids do. No pressure!

Fortunately, choosing a gift for a child comes with fewer shades of social nuance than picking something for an adult. The goal is pure pleasure, not a statement or message; the worst-case scenario is indifference or mild disappointment—not, say, horror at your fundamental misunderstanding of a long-standing personal relationship. You are going for FUN. Think about the experience of seeing the present and opening the present, and about whom the present is actually going to please.

If you are buying a present for a person who lacks object permanence, that present is for their parents. Shop with this fact in mind. Clothes are an excellent gift, in a way that they won’t be again until the child’s adolescence—here is your chance to jazz up the Center of the Universe. Buy something that’s more expensive than anyone thinking about the cost of child care could justify buying themselves, but that’s still functional enough for everyday use. No to tiny buttons, the color white, and lace; yes to $64 balloon pants. Yes to leopard-print anything. (It’ll hide stains!) Yes to seasonally appropriate comical hats ($55-$99).

Parents spend a lot of time gazing upon their babies (how would the Center of the Universe look in pink sunglasses?), and they also spend a lot of time reading to their babies, at least if they are overachieving millennials who have imbibed the requisite parenting expertise. It is important that they have books to read aloud that are not bad. My husband, a bookseller, often notes that most books are bad, and this may be doubly true for children’s books, whose brevity leads foolhardy would-be authors to underestimate the difficulty of their task. Before you give a children’s book, think: Is this book fun to read aloud? Will it be fun to read aloud twelve million times? Rhythm counts for everything, subject matter for almost nothing. Babies do not care about “art” or “science,” and you can’t make them. What you’re after here is fluid prose and pictures that contain lots of interesting items to identify and talk about. There’s a reason everyone already has “Goodnight Moon.” Instead, consider “The House in the Night,” by Susan Marie Swanson, or “All the World,” by Liz Garton Scanlon, both sold in chompable board-book editions. Richard Scarry’s “I Am a Bunny,” though not explicitly bedtime-oriented, is another durable hit. (If you want to give a new parent something to read to themselves, consider “And Now We Have Everything,” by Meaghan O’Connell, a funny and unsparing account of parenthood’s earliest days.) ($9-$40)

As for toys: true infants are scarcely capable of “play” in any sense that requires accessories or equipment; they’re still realizing that they have hands. Something with fabric that produces a crinkly sound ($10) when pawed inexpertly is pretty much the upper limit of possibility.

Not long ago, my husband and I asked our three-and-a-half-year-old what we should get his grandfather as an eightieth-birthday present. “Cars and cars and cars and cars and cars,” he replied. It was an instructive answer: the sorts of gifts that people imagine giving others are a good indication of the gifts that they themselves enjoy receiving. In general, I’m all for quality, but when attempting to please a small child there’s something to be said for quantity. Sheer, dazzling quantity: cars and cars and cars and cars and cars ($7-$30). Present them loose in a bag or in a box; remember that it’s always nice to have spares to lose, or for a visitor to take home.

By a similar token, stickers and stickers and stickers and stickers and stickers ($9-$31). The recipient can stick them on a giant roll of paper ($33) (how giant? That’s up to you), taped out on the floor. The effect is something like an off-season approximation of a sidewalk, and, your winter climate permitting, sidewalk chalk (tons of it, for $18) is another good option. And books are not excluded from the thrill of scale. Richard Scarry’s “Biggest Word Book Ever!” ($45)—about twenty-four by thirty-two inches when wide open—is irresistibly grand, full of many quintessentially busy Scarry characters, and large enough for a small reader to literally climb inside.

The appeal of something to climb inside is a valuable reminder of another language that kid gifts can speak: the charm of little. It can be fun to be small and to feel small, and this is why it is nice to build forts. Technically, doing so only requires a blanket, but you don’t need a gift guide to direct you to your linen closet. Expand your household’s fort horizons with the Nugget ($249-$299), a “play couch” made of sturdy, rearrangeable cushions that can be used to construct cozy reading corners and nooks for playing pretend. (A chair called the Smore, at $199-$239, from the same company, offers a similar concept, with a smaller footprint.)

It is also fun simply to think about small things. And so, to stock the fort’s library: the author and illustrator Phoebe Wahl produces books full of magical tiny beings, stories that are beautiful and sweet without being precious or twee. “Little Witch Hazel: A Year in the Forest” ($20) collects four stories—one for each season—about a witch who lives in a mossy stump and is small enough to ride on the back of an owl. Her friends and neighbors include the Mole Sisters, Mousepappa, and a frog named Wendell (who might plausibly have been named for Wendell Berry). Wahl’s “Backyard Fairies” ($19) depicts a kid who is sure that there are fairies just out of sight, in the woods behind her house, and tries to find them. For children inclined to such expeditions—or who just want to read in a dark spot—a camping headlamp ($35) makes an inexhaustibly useful accessory.

Becoming a parent, and shopping for a child, is a constant reminder that everything and nothing changes. I can easily recall the joy of forts; I would have loved “Backyard Fairies.” Yet certain stalwart kid pleasures have been reimagined in the intervening decades. Take training wheels and tricycles: they’re out. Now children have balance bikes, which are two-wheelers without pedals—an arrangement that supposedly makes for an easier transition to riding the real thing. Based on the anecdotal evidence of my local playground, I’m convinced. The little guys get good at gliding, fast. These new versions of that classic Big Present, a bike, can be procured from such manufacturers as Guardian ($169) and Woom ($249) (branding keyed to a target market of anxious parents).

Even crayon technology has somehow improved in the years since I was coloring. Have you tried gel crayons ($20)? Instead of hard and waxy, they’re as soft as oil pastels, but miraculously smudge-proof once dry, with colors bright and opaque enough to draw on dark construction paper. And, for kids approaching the age of phones, Tin Can ($100) has given the humble landline a contemporary reinvention: it permits calls to preselected phone numbers using home Wi-Fi, and has (yes) a cord.

When I set out to make a list of gifts for kids, there was only one thing I was sure I wanted to include. If you take nothing else from this guide, know this: a Stomp Rocket ($30) is the perfect present.

One kid can have fun with a Stomp Rocket; two kids can execute some impressive teamwork; three or four kids can share effortlessly. The learning curve is nonexistent. The payoff is immediate. The only way to improve it is to buy extra rockets ($10), which you should do. (And do not go off-brand with these—you want genuine Stomp product. Amazon imitations can get stuck on the launch tube, an unacceptable defect, and one that I discovered the hard way.) I have never seen a group of children get bored of a Stomp Rocket. I have seen a group of adults sipping early-evening drinks on a patio, idly Stomping and chatting, enjoying the beginning of a spring thaw and the return of sunlight. ♦
This article is periodically updated to reflect price changes and availability. Some items may have sold out.

items.title: Tech Gifts That Won’t Rot Their Brains
items.description: Binge-watching. Doomscrolling. Rabbit-holing. Brain-rotting. These, it seems, are the behaviors encouraged by our computers and digital devices—intoxicating masterworks of engineering that we stumble away from, glassy-eyed. It’s a sad state of affairs, especia
items.author: Joshua Rothman
paragraphs: Binge-watching. Doomscrolling. Rabbit-holing. Brain-rotting. These, it seems, are the behaviors encouraged by our computers and digital devices—intoxicating masterworks of engineering that we stumble away from, glassy-eyed. It’s a sad state of affairs, especially if, like me, you grew up in the nineteen-eighties and nineties, when digital technology was exciting and liberatory. Back then, Steve Jobs called the computer a “bicycle for the mind”; parents bought PCs hoping that their kids would become “computer whizzes.” The idea was that circuits and software could unleash our potential.

Today, of course, we associate screens with mindlessness, and computers with distraction and drudgery. But it doesn’t have to be that way. Gadgets are still great, and computers remain delightful. In fact, it’s easy to turn your personal tech dystopia into a utopia: all you have to do is shift from being a consumer to becoming a creator. We live in a golden age of digital creativity. Forget A.I.: you, yourself, can record an album from your sofa, or curate a photo-essay on the train. In that spirit, here are some of my favorite creative digital tools.

Perhaps you’ve seen, on YouTube, videos of “infinite sketchbooks”—digital drawings that can be zoomed into seemingly forever, revealing worlds within worlds. It turns out that tablets aren’t just for Netflix: even a small model, like the iPad Mini ($699), can open up onto endless vistas when it’s equipped with a digital pencil ($124) and an app like Endless Paper (free). Tablets are always getting slimmer and lighter, making them better for watching than for drawing. But turning a tablet into an ergonomic drawing surface is simple: just get a drawing board ($45)—one of those slanted wooden surfaces that illustrators use. Add a book stand and a copy of “Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain” ($24).

If a tablet is too distracting, there are other ways to make digital art. For years, I’ve been doing a lot of my writing and sketching using e-ink tablets made by reMarkable, a Norwegian company. The deluxe version, the Paper Pro ($629), has a big screen and can be expanded with a keyboard. But the Paper Pro Move ($449) is the size of a pocket notebook and lets you sketch in color. There’s no e-mail, web browsing, or social media on these—only a Kindle-esque e-ink display that feels paperlike beneath your stylus. (When my eight-year-old son and I are bored, I sometimes make sketches so that he can color them in and add to them.) I also find that writing in longhand on an e-ink device can loosen up one’s brain, and I’ve written many articles—including this one—on my reMarkable, eventually using the device’s handwriting-recognition feature to transform my scrawls into editable text. For those who like writing but want to get away from their work computer, this sort of freestanding writing device can be a godsend. The BYOK ($199) is a little portable screen that’s made entirely for writing; as its name suggests, you should bring your own keyboard, and a tiny, pleasantly clicky model like the Keychron K2 ($60) would be a good choice. The Freewrite Alpha ($349) is like a digital typewriter, and includes its own keyboard.

I was in college when the iPod appeared. In the two decades since, dedicated music players have almost completely disappeared. And yet, beneath the radar, music-making devices have proliferated. Today, there are zillions of cool little synthesizers and “grooveboxes” on the market, and they’re not at all difficult to use.

You can make beats with a Teenage Engineering Pocket Operator ($59), which is about the size of a deck of cards. You can compose lovely melodies and soundscapes with the Roland P-6 ($229), a sampler the size of a paperback book, with rechargeable batteries so that you can use it on the go. (The P-6 can be hooked up to its siblings, which include a synth, for $230, and a drum machine, also for $230, to form a synth-pop band.) Bigger units let you build whole tracks, with different parts playing in parallel. The Elektron Model:Cycles ($349) offers modern sounds and medical-device chic; the Sonicware Deconstruct ($399) lets you pretend your living room is Berghain. The most elegant grooveboxes are probably the Teenage Engineering OP-1 Field ($1,999) and OP-XY ($2,299), which are like scaled-down music studios with Apple-calibre designs and batteries that last all day; the Field is better for keyboard players, while the XY works best for purely electronic music.

A computer or a tablet can, itself, become a musical gadget, with the addition of the right piano-style keyboard. The Arturia MiniLab 3 ($119) is a compact model that connects to your computer and lets you play, compose, and record in apps like GarageBand, which contain hundreds of free synthesized instruments. You can listen through the lightweight, comfortable Koss PortaPro headphones ($50), which weigh nothing but sound gorgeous, and record your songs with a phone app like Tape It, for listening on the go. If you know a lapsed musician, any of these tools could help get them back up and running—especially in combination with a lesson or two from an online instructor. I’m hoping to learn more about my synthesizers from Jeremy, at Red Means Recording, this winter.
Photography and Filmmaking

Everyone has a smartphone, and every smartphone has a camera; this means that everyone is just a step away from becoming a hobby photographer. Doing so is partly a matter of self-perception—you have to look at your pictures with a critical, artistic eye—but it also has to do with equipment. The Canon Selphy Printer ($159), which allows you to effortlessly print four-by-six photographs at home, can help bridge the gap between taking pictures and making photographs to keep. The Aura Carver Frame ($149), which can rotate through pictures you select, creates a place for your best digital pictures to live.

Giving someone a dedicated camera is like giving them a new form of self-expression. There are all sorts of cameras, and they suit different kinds of photographers—but don’t overthink it, since people can grow into the tools they happen to have. The Insta360 Go Retro Bundle ($299) contains an action camera (great for filming daredevilry and dynamic exploits) that can also be used as a pocketable point-and-shoot. The Polaroid Now ($120) is a stylish instant camera perfect for social butterflies. The Lomography MC-A ($549) is a 35-mm. film camera with autofocus. And the Panasonic Lumix L10 ($1,498) is a discreet but powerful model with a built-in zoom lens and options for “color-grading”—that is, giving photos or footage a professional, cinematic look.

Writing, drawing, music-making—an art form that combines them all is game design. Earlier this year, I bought our family a Playdate ($229), a handheld video-game console with its own easy-to-use game-creation tool, which runs in a web browser. My son and I had fun making a little game; we even moved beyond the browser-based editor, writing our own code directly (with a little help from Claude). And we also played Big Walk ($20), an unforgettable adventure from a game studio called House House. In Big Walk, you play together but on separate screens—I used a Nintendo Switch, he used his computer—solving puzzles while communicating almost entirely through systems of symbol and gesture that you improvise. It’s a video game that brings out new aspects of your own creativity and ingenuity—a perfect example of how humanizing technology can be. ♦

items.title: Gifts for Cats (and Their Owners) That Are Worth Knocking Off the Table
items.description: Cats: what would we do without them? To the cat agnostics, not to mention the cat haters, I say: don’t answer that! (Also, what’s wrong with you?) But to the cat lovers, my intended interlocutors here, I say: no need to answer, either. We both know. A catless
items.author: Naomi Fry
paragraphs: Cats: what would we do without them? To the cat agnostics, not to mention the cat haters, I say: don’t answer that! (Also, what’s wrong with you?) But to the cat lovers, my intended interlocutors here, I say: no need to answer, either. We both know. A catless world is a terrible thing to contemplate. No lap snuggles? No headbutts? No slow blinks? No raising of the rump to welcome a wealth of scritches? No occasional, inexplicable biting? We’d truly be lost without our fuzzy, innocent but knowing friends.

A catless world would also be devoid of a whole slew of objects and accoutrements, gadgets and doodads—some meant for cats and some for the humans obsessed with them—that turn a house into a home, or, in some cases, a living room into a giant obstacle course. There are two things I can’t resist: any item that might improve or enrich my two cats’ lives in some way (even if that perceived improvement is a pathetic fallacy that exists purely in my own mind); and any item that captures, for me, the half-sweet, half-tart character of the feline species. If there’s a special cat fanatic in your life (or a special cat!), why not treat them, this holiday season, to one of the below?
Children’s Books About Cats

It’s never too early for the cat-loving parent to Stockholm syndrome their kids into becoming cat lovers, too, a process that might begin with stuffing the proverbial stocking with a nice cat-centric book. My daughter is now past the age of picture books, but one of her favorites, and mine, used to be “Rich Cat, Poor Cat” ($21), by the magnificent Bernard Waber (best known for his Lyle the Crocodile series), in which a scraggly street cat named Scat finds a home. Other picture books we never tired of were Jenni Desmond’s “Red Cat, Blue Cat” ($14), about two feline frenemies; “No Kiss for Mother” ($51), by Tomi Ungerer, in which a young kit refuses to play nice; and Judith Kerr’s Mog the Cat series ($36 for eight of the books). For the slightly older child, I’d suggest either Esther Averill’s fantastic “Jenny and the Cat Club” collection ($22), about the shy black cat Jenny Linsky and her community of cat friends in nineteen-forties Greenwich Village, or Ursula K. Le Guin’s “Catwings” series ($28), about a litter of flying cats. Finally, a book for adults that kids will also enjoy leafing through is “The Encyclopedia of Movie Cats” ($50), from A24.

The best gift for an actual cat is almost undoubtedly the gift of play. I love watching my cats go nuts for catnip, and these knitted cigarette-shaped catnip toys ($15 for three), for the bad-boy feline about town, are super cute. (For a healthier-looking playtime option, these felted vegetable toys, for $6, are also terrific.) Feather wands ($6) can help the rotund cat get her jumps in, but if she prefers a more brainteasing kind of exercise this tri-tier ball tower ($12) will keep her occupied. Finally, a clicker toy ($28) is my own cats’ personal favorite. Hours of fun following that little red dot . . . if only all of us were so easily amused.
Cat Furniture and Homeware for Cats

Let’s face it, neither a cat tree nor a scratcher is likely to stop your cat from shedding on your furniture, or destroying it (and I have the totally clawed-down Design Within Reach sofa to prove it). Still, it’s nice to make them feel like they have their own little domain, and if this domain is aesthetically pleasing, so much the better. This rustic pearwood-and-sisal cat tree-cum-scratcher (£90) will make one’s cat look like Robinson Crusoe sleeping in a tree; this fun cherry-shaped cat tree ($136) is very Claes Oldenburg; and this mid-century-modern scratching chair ($47) will class up any joint. A plush window perch ($23) will allow a bored house cat a view of the outdoors. (I always think of this kind of contraption as a public service, since there’s nothing that makes my heart beat faster than spotting an indoor cat lounging on one while walking down the street.) And, perhaps most useful, this techy litter robot ($599) will keep one’s home odor-free.
Cat-Themed Clothes, Accessories, and Homeware

I know, I know. Feline-themed clothing and paraphernalia can easily veer corny or “crazy cat lady,” but there’s some cool stuff out there that avoids these pitfalls. I, for one, always enjoy a good vintage Kliban shirt ($48). This nineteen-seventies Danish cat tapestry ($404) is giving Ingmar Bergman’s “Scenes from a Marriage” décor (in a good way), and drinking coffee out of this William Steig New Yorker-cover cat mug ($24) could turn a terrible morning into a good one. The cat bus from Miyazaki’s “My Neighbor Totoro” always gives me a warm, happy feeling, so falling asleep in a room illuminated by this night light ($55) seems very soothing. Another famous cartoon cat that I’m obsessed with is, of course, Garfield, and this vintage ceramic figurine ($35) takes me straight back to 1981.

There’s never enough support for the people and organizations that are helping to save cats from the mean streets of America’s cities. I live in Brooklyn, and I adopted my extremely soft black-and-white cat, Gully, from Bushwick Street Cats, a nonprofit doing fantastic work with stray cats in the area. (They also helped neuter my other cat, the grumpy but loving Gingy.) Two other great organizations near me are Flatbush Cats and Brooklyn Animal Action. I can’t imagine a nicer gift than making a donation in someone’s name to one of these charities, or the cat charity of your choice, wherever you live.
And . . . a Bone for the Dog Lovers

Believe it or not, I love dogs, too (though maybe not as passionately as I love cats), so I was delighted to take my editor’s note and add a few choice finds for our canine friends. Since my knowledge of dogs is much less intimate, however, I solicited the assistance of two friends. Susan Korn, who owns both an accessories brand called Susan Alexandra and a gentle senior chihuahua named Pigeon, makes fabulous hand-beaded leashes ($155) and collars ($98). Pigeon, meanwhile, recommends this dog shampoo ($98) and this human-grade dog food (a basic plan starts at roughly $1 per meal). My friend Claire Jarvis has recently found herself the owner of a large, Marmaduke-like setter named Frankie, who’s been enjoying this wand toy ($32) and this harness ($40). He’ll also “walk on water” for these freeze-dried elk treats ($30). ♦

items.title: After a Record Loss, Leopold Aschenbrenner Is Still Betting Everything on A.I.
items.description: Leopold Aschenbrenner, the twenty-five-year-old manager of Situational Awareness LP, a San Francisco hedge fund, has crammed a lot into a quarter century. Born in Germany, he matriculated at Columbia University as a fifteen-year-old. There, he read the great b
items.author: Stephen Witt
paragraphs: Leopold Aschenbrenner, the twenty-five-year-old manager of Situational Awareness LP, a San Francisco hedge fund, has crammed a lot into a quarter century. Born in Germany, he matriculated at Columbia University as a fifteen-year-old. There, he read the great books and joined the debate society. A forty-four-page economics paper he wrote at seventeen was considered Ph.D.-quality work by leading figures in the field. Aschenbrenner graduated, at nineteen, as the school’s valedictorian, and went to seek his fortune in Silicon Valley, where he witnessed, encouraged, and perhaps triggered an ongoing series of spectacular explosions: financial, social, technological, and more.

From late 2024 to mid-2026, Situational Awareness reported returns of more than a thousand per cent, mostly through investments in the A.I. industry. Then, this summer, it blew up, suffering one of the largest trading losses in American stock-market history. About two-thirds of its value was wiped out—but such was the magnitude of Aschenbrenner’s previous gains that Situational Awareness’s returns were still positive for the year.

I met with Aschenbrenner recently at his firm’s offices, near San Francisco’s South Park. The neighborhood was cozy, and I imagined viewing it from an isometric 2-D perspective, as in a world-building game, with little pawns zipping around on e-scooters and the latest trillion-dollar idea indicated by the appearance of an exclamation mark over someone’s head. It was Election Day, but no one in the cafés surrounding the park seemed to notice. The talk was of money—who got in early and who was oversubscribed, who was entering stealth mode and who was exiting it, who got what in the cap table and who missed out. All this was interrupted by little sips of espresso from biodegradable cups.

Situational Awareness’s offices are large and airy; after clearing three security checks, I was seated across from Aschenbrenner at a twenty-two-foot-long conference table. He is tall and a little gangly, with facial features that seem to have been exaggerated for emphasis. His nose and ears are large, his mouth toothy and wide, and he wears his dark-blond hair in a part.

Conversation with Aschenbrenner resembles a formal lecture; you expect, at the end, to be graded on your understanding of what he’s said. When he’s making an especially salient point, his eyebrows raise suggestively above his pale-blue eyes. “We live in a slightly more anarchic world than I expected,” he told me.

Aschenbrenner’s big idea is that the world has not yet grasped the implications of the A.I. revolution. “Next year—that is, calendar year 2027—we will see A.I. accelerate between two and five times faster than anything we have seen so far,” he said. “Next year is the last year that anything in modern life still feels a little normal.” Aschenbrenner has held this view for some time, having explained his insights in 2024, in a long essay titled “Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead.” He predicted that by 2027 spending on A.I. infrastructure would rival the entire U.S. defense budget, that A.I. companies would find themselves targeted by Chinese spies, that traditional software firms would struggle as A.I. automated their work, and that A.I. would outperform even Ph.D.s at intellectual tasks.

All this has occurred, and what in financial circles has become known as the “Leopold trade”—buying shares in data-center suppliers and betting against vulnerable software stocks—has been profitable. And yet Aschenbrenner’s most striking prediction has not yet come to pass: that A.I. itself will automate A.I. research, leading to an explosion in superintelligence. It was maybe for this reason, even as he was being forced to liquidate most of his holdings this summer, that Aschenbrenner fought so hard to hold on to Situational Awareness’s most prized asset: an early stake in Anthropic, whose I.P.O. occurred last week, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion. Aschenbrenner is happy with his investment, but when we met he added a caveat. “This period is also their twilight,” he said, of Anthropic’s employees. “In two or three years, most of these people won’t be useful as researchers.”

Aschenbrenner was born in Berlin in November, 2001. His parents, both physicians, had grown up on opposite sides of the Wall. When Aschenbrenner was six, his mother got a job at Yale, and the family moved to Connecticut for a short time. He began to learn English, and when he returned to Germany he studied at an English-language international school. Today, Aschenbrenner speaks English without any trace of an accent. “I don’t even think in German anymore,” he said.

Aschenbrenner excelled in school and skipped several grades. At fourteen, he published his first scientific paper, after developing a machine-learning app to analyze air pollution. He arrived at Columbia in 2017. “I wanted a classical liberal education,” he said.

Aschenbrenner participated in the school’s effective-altruism society, along with a friend he knew through competitive Rubik’s Cube solving. (The effective-altruism movement promotes a rigorous, evidence-based approach to long-term human welfare.) In 2019, he began circulating a math-heavy economics white paper titled “Existential Risk and Growth,” which argued that humans were living in a unique “time of perils,” with the destructive power of new technology outpacing our ability to control it. The paper caught the attention of Tyler Cowen, a polymathic economics professor who, since 2003, has posted to “Marginal Revolution,” his influential blog, more than thirty thousand times. Cowen invited Aschenbrenner to a conference near Washington, D.C., where he told him he was one of the most promising young economics scholars he’d ever met. He then discouraged him from becoming a professional economist. “He felt the field had become somewhat decadent,” Aschenbrenner said.

Cowen introduced him to other conference attendees, whom Aschenbrenner described as “young weirdos.” Aschenbrenner began to move through this and other esoteric intellectual networks. In addition to Cowen’s weirdos, there were the weirdos in Patrick Collison’s progress-studies community, in the Bay Area, and the weirdos of the Future of Humanity Institute, at Oxford University. (Aschenbrenner eventually moved away from effective altruism; he later described it as a “defective religion.”) The talk in these circles was of the coming revolution in machine superintelligence, and their debates were about when it would arrive, who would build it, and what risks it posed to humanity. To discipline these discussions, which could easily spiral into dorm-room bullshitting, participants encouraged one another to back their positions with real-money bets.

While visiting Oxford in 2021, Aschenbrenner went on a lunch date with Avital Balwit, another weirdo with a strong interest in A.I. Balwit, who’d grown up in Portland, Oregon, came from a family of literary intellectuals; her mother was a poet and an essayist. Balwit had green eyes and short blond hair, and was a couple of years older than Aschenbrenner. Given that she travelled in the same circles, it seemed likely that they would have run into each other eventually. Or, as Aschenbrenner put it, “it seems overdetermined that I met my wife.”

Soon the two were living in adjacent apartments in the Bay Area—Aschenbrenner had turned down an offer from Yale Law School, and Balwit had turned down a Rhodes Scholarship. “She grew up in a family where going to Oxford was probably the greatest dream one could have,” Aschenbrenner said. “But I think she realized, and I realized, that this A.I. stuff was happening. You could spend three years at Oxford doing a D.Phil. in some random thing, but the most important thing in the world is happening here—and you had to be a part of that.”

At Situational Awareness, employees use A.I. more or less continuously. Some oversee “agent swarms,” which consist of hundreds of A.I. agents operating in tandem. Rogue swarms can hack out of their digital containers and take over other computers, but, when used properly, agents are extremely useful tools. “We have two guys who maybe between them do the work of sixty software engineers,” Aschenbrenner said. “One person on our team spent two million dollars on tokens last month.” (Tokens are the building blocks of A.I. output.)

Aschenbrenner believes that agent swarms will soon perform most white-collar work. He said that Anthropic, which deploys agent swarms internally, hires few entry-level software engineers. Across the industry, even job postings for mid-level software workers are disappearing. “With agent swarms, small numbers of people will get tremendous leverage,” he told me. “Eventually, they will do everything. Or not eventually—pretty soon.”

To some extent, I share Aschenbrenner’s view about the looming job apocalypse; when I first used ChatGPT, in 2022, I was convinced that it would take my job within six months. But, four years later, I am as busy as I have ever been. When I told Aschenbrenner this, he grew excited, sprang from his chair, and grabbed a dry-erase marker. It was time to whiteboard.

In mauve-colored ink, Aschenbrenner drew an x-axis and a y-axis. Then he drew an exponential curve, which trended upward until it hit an inflection point, after which it dropped straight down. “Human capital in the age of A.I. looks like this,” he said.

He pointed to the middle of the curve. His mother-in-law, the writer Devon Balwit, was currently here, he said. Publishing in small literary magazines, she had earned essentially nothing from poetry for most of her life; she made money teaching English as a second language. But recently she’d been contracted by an A.I.-training firm to critique poetry that L.L.M.s were writing, in order to make it sound more human. She is paid more than a hundred dollars an hour to do this, which makes her one of the best-paid poetry critics alive. (She also critiques A.I.-written essays.) “But that’s a temporary phenomenon!” Aschenbrenner said. He gestured to the line plunging down. “Once the A.I. learns poetry, that job will disappear.”

Aschenbrenner shares office space with his friend Dwarkesh Patel, whose technology podcast is required listening in Silicon Valley. Patel is a sort of anti-Joe Rogan—his interviews are known for their depth and for his thoughtful, penetrating questions. (Before interviewing the C.T.O. of Intel, Patel memorized the layout of a silicon transistor.) Aschenbrenner and Patel met as teen-agers, in Tyler Cowen’s circle. Even then, Aschenbrenner was talking about the technological singularity, which could occur when A.I. learns to make itself smarter, triggering a runaway cycle of self-improvement. “In every conversation I’ve had with him, and with other people, the main topic is just how we make sure we’re prepared for superintelligence,” Patel said.

The two also share office space with another friend, Dylan Patel, who is not related to Dwarkesh but is his roommate. Dylan runs SemiAnalysis, which began, in 2020, as a one-man trade newsletter for the semiconductor industry and now has revenues of more than a hundred million dollars a year from selling research on and analysis of A.I. hardware to investors, including Aschenbrenner. Naturally, both Dylan and Aschenbrenner have appeared on Dwarkesh’s podcast, and Dwarkesh attributes a portion of Aschenbrenner’s success to the value of Dylan’s research. (“Why is Leopold the only person using your spreadsheets to make outrageous money?” Dwarkesh asked during Dylan’s appearance in March.) Aschenbrenner, in turn, jokingly takes credit for Dwarkesh’s podcasting success. “There was a period where his podcast sucked, because he and I weren’t talking as much,” Aschenbrenner said.

This endearing if slightly obnoxious fraternity was like a post-college clique you might find anywhere—but the three men had strategically situated themselves in the middle of the A.I. revolution. Anthropic’s headquarters were about a mile away; OpenAI’s were about a mile and a half in the opposite direction. Everything that mattered happened in between.

Aschenbrenner talks quickly, and, in the parlance of Silicon Valley, his signal-to-noise ratio is high. At one point in our conversation—Aschenbrenner was comparing A.I. to jet-engine companies—my focus drifted to the neighborhood outside, which, long ago, had been a hangout for sailors and merchant mariners. I started to think about historical maritime trade hubs: Amsterdam, Calcutta, Singapore. When my attention returned, Aschenbrenner was in fact discussing the importance of location. “San Francisco is like a small college town,” he said. “But if you aren’t here—literally here—you’re downstream of it all.”

In San Francisco, Aschenbrenner began working for the philanthropic-investment arm of FTX, Sam Bankman-Fried’s short-lived cryptocurrency platform, as part of a four-person team. Balwit worked there, too. The two were not involved with trading; instead, they directed money to causes they found important, including A.I. safety, pandemic prevention, and Dwarkesh Patel’s podcast. They visited Bankman-Fried in the Bahamas, where he was living, but jointly resigned on November 11, 2022, the day FTX filed for bankruptcy. Bankman-Fried is now serving a long prison sentence for misappropriating customer funds. “I didn’t know Sam Bankman-Fried was a fraud, but I knew S.B.F.,” Aschenbrenner has said. “I knew he was extremely risk-taking. I knew he was narcissistic. He didn’t tolerate disagreement well.”

Some months later, Aschenbrenner was hired at OpenAI. He worked on the company’s superalignment team, a small but influential group of about twenty people. Their assignment was to protect humanity from runaway superintelligence, but Aschenbrenner grew increasingly worried that OpenAI was becoming a target for Chinese espionage, which he compared to Soviet infiltration of the U.S. nuclear program. He warned his superiors but felt they didn’t take him seriously, so, in late 2023, he sent a memo to members of OpenAI’s board about the threat, going over the head of Sam Altman, the company’s C.E.O. Aschenbrenner was fired in April, 2024, with OpenAI saying that he’d leaked confidential information. He has claimed that the material was a brainstorming document, and that he followed standard practices when sharing it with external researchers. He maintains that his firing was an act of retaliation. (A spokesperson for OpenAI said, “Leopold was not fired for raising security concerns, internally or with our board.”)

Scott Aaronson, a computer scientist who also worked on the superalignment team, wasn’t convinced that Aschenbrenner had done anything wrong. OpenAI had an ethos of information sharing, Aaronson said, and he felt that Aschenbrenner was trying to work within it. “OpenAI was extremely explicit when it was founded that ‘We are not a traditional company,’ ” he told me. “But them being a traditional company has won out.” A few weeks after Aschenbrenner was fired, the superalignment team was dissolved.

Undeterred, Aschenbrenner raised money for a new idea, which would be something like a think tank inside a hedge fund. “This investment firm will be kind of like a brain trust on A.I.,” he said. Backed by high-profile investors, including Patrick and John Collison, the founders of the payment-processing firm Stripe, the fund launched in late 2024, with more than a hundred million dollars in capital. Aschenbrenner named it Situational Awareness, a term that researchers use to describe A.I.s that can recognize their own surroundings. Across a hundred and sixty-five pages, his essay of the same name, which he’d posted earlier that year, had argued that financial markets were underestimating the degree to which artificial intelligence would change the world. “Before long, the world will wake up,” Aschenbrenner had written. “But right now, there are perhaps a few hundred people, most of them in San Francisco and the AI labs, that have situational awareness.”

Long essays about the future of A.I. were by this point commonplace. The usual response to them, Aaronson told me, was “Who is this weird nerd?” But Aschenbrenner’s essay had gone viral, with commentators praising its prose and its clarity of thought. (Ivanka Trump posted a link to it on social media.) “He agreed with the rationalists, insofar as they say that almost the entire world is asleep,” Aaronson said, of Aschenbrenner. “But then, rather than looking to slow down, he draws the opposite conclusion, which is that we have to race ahead and beat China.”

Situational Awareness—the hedge fund—began aggressively investing in line with this theme. At first, Aschenbrenner was printing money. Situational Awareness bought stakes in power companies, reasoning that the data-center build-out would constrain the electrical grid, and in makers of memory chips, in anticipation of a squeeze on supply. At the same time, the fund bet against software venders like Adobe, assuming that A.I. would put pressure on their businesses. These trades were successful, and soon other hedge funds were taking similar positions.

In early 2025, the Chinese A.I. developer DeepSeek sparked a temporary market panic when it unveiled a model that it claimed had a startlingly low training cost, causing investors to question whether all those data centers would be necessary. But Aschenbrenner, along with his investment partner, Carl Shulman, had already analyzed what might happen if more efficient models became available, and concluded that lower training costs would actually increase data-center demand. They regarded the panic as a buying opportunity. Situational Awareness increased its holdings, and the market soon rebounded. An analyst at another major technology fund reportedly reassured colleagues with the words “Leopold says it’s fine.”

Aschenbrenner grew popular on Wall Street, and was a featured speaker at a Goldman Sachs investment conference in March, 2025. He also began to rely on leverage: borrowing money to increase the size of his positions. The practice substantially boosted the fund’s returns, but it left Aschenbrenner with little margin for error. Still, he was able to attract capital from some of Wall Street’s best financiers. “Asset allocators said, ‘Hey, I think this violates my rule-of-thumb approaches, but you know what? The kid’s making money,’ ” Rich Falk-Wallace, a former portfolio manager at Citadel, Ken Griffin’s hedge fund, told me. “ ‘Who am I to say that I know better?’ ”

It was around then that Aschenbrenner invested in Anthropic. The company was holding a private financing round to raise money, much of which went toward computing infrastructure. Aschenbrenner appeared to have an inside track, as many of his friends from OpenAI’s shuttered superalignment group had defected to Anthropic. Also, his girlfriend worked there.

Balwit had joined Anthropic a few months before Aschenbrenner started at OpenAI. But she was a less contentious co-worker than Aschenbrenner, and soon she began to serve as chief of staff to Dario Amodei, the company’s C.E.O. Although OpenAI seemed to have an unassailable lead in the race to artificial superintelligence, Aschenbrenner believed that Anthropic could catch up. “We thought the most important thing was talent,” he said. “Anthropic had more of it, and was five times cheaper.”

The Anthropic fund-raising round was oversubscribed—investors wanted more shares than were available. When this happens, companies can choose their owners. Discussions about share allocations can grow contentious as founders huddle around a spreadsheet to determine who gets what. (A fraction of a percentage point might be a billion-dollar payday down the road.) Political considerations can play a role in these allocations, but Aschenbrenner denied that his connections helped him secure a stake.

When the investment round closed, in March of 2025, Anthropic was valued at about sixty billion dollars. Then Claude Code, the company’s coding assistant, became popular, and engineers started to simply tell agents what to do. “I really am mostly programming in English now, a bit sheepishly telling the LLM what code to write,” the A.I. pioneer Andrej Karpathy wrote, terming the practice “vibe coding.” Anthropic projected that Claude Code would generate billions in revenue, and in another oversubscribed funding round, in May, 2026, Situational Awareness was once again allocated shares—but this time Anthropic was valued at nearly a trillion dollars.

Meanwhile, Situational Awareness was generating spectacular returns in publicly traded stocks of companies that sold the picks and shovels enabling the A.I. gold rush. By mid-2026, the fund had about forty billion dollars under management. With leverage, it was actually pushing a hundred billion dollars around, and its moves were becoming noticeable to other market participants.

Aschenbrenner is close to his family, and he has two younger sisters who are still in school. I asked him what he thought they should study, given his belief that human intellectual labor would shortly be made obsolete. “I tell them to study the classics,” he said. At Columbia, Aschenbrenner had enjoyed his courses on political economy the most. He especially admired Edmund Burke, the eighteenth-century Anglo-Irish parliamentarian who believed that a just society was the product of centuries of accumulated experience. Nine years before Napoleon took power, Burke had predicted that the French Revolution would end with a military strongman in control. Aschenbrenner fears similar outcomes from A.I. “I’m a Burkean,” he said. “Soon we’ll have robot factories building robot factories. I wonder what Burke would make of that?”

Aschenbrenner predicts that, within a few years, annual G.D.P. growth will exceed ten per cent. He also believes that the race to superintelligence will provoke a great-power conflict between the U.S. and China—and that it is critical to the future of democracy, and of humanity, that the U.S. win this race. He remains especially concerned about the security inside frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, which he maintains are being targeted by Chinese spies. He is also worried about the practices of the chipmaker Nvidia. “It’s crazy to ship chips to China,” Aschenbrenner told me. (Earlier this year, Donald Trump lifted certain restrictions on exporting advanced hardware to China.) “It’s like shipping enriched uranium to the Soviet Union before we built the bomb.”

Aschenbrenner is so thoroughly assimilated to American culture that it is easy to forget he is a foreigner. Occasionally, though, his European side comes through. “He has a strange allergy to anything that’s not German food,” Dwarkesh Patel said. Aschenbrenner is also obsessed with German history. He likes to discuss the causes of the First and Second World Wars, and the life of Frederick the Great. “He just kind of understands how important it is that free societies win,” Patel said.

One of Aschenbrenner’s influences is his great-grandmother, who is in her early nineties. Aschenbrenner listed the events she’d witnessed in her life: Nazi rule, the aftermath of the Dresden firebombing, Soviet occupation, the Stasi imprisoning her son, the fall of Communism. “This sense of history,” Aschenbrenner said. “This sense of turbulence. I think this turbulence will return.”

This summer, on July 29th, David Mann, a New York investor, was in a cab to LaGuardia Airport when he received an unexpected call. The person on the phone represented Situational Awareness, and was wondering if Mann was interested in purchasing a discounted stake in Anthropic. The deal, the caller said, would have to be completed overnight.

Mann, who has spent more than twenty-five years on Wall Street, understood at once what was going on. “Aschenbrenner was being forced to sell,” he told the Wall Street Journal. “He needed the money and was sounding people out.”

In the first half of the year, hardware stocks had gone berserk. Data centers were buying up the flash-memory supply, prompting a squeeze in what had previously been a boring commodity. The retail price of even a removable flash-memory card—the kind used in a digital camera—more than doubled, and the stock price of Sandisk, a flash-memory manufacturer, went up eightfold.

Situational Awareness had bought into Sandisk early. By the middle of the year, it held more than five billion dollars’ worth of Sandisk stock, and was reporting over-all returns of more than four hundred per cent for the first part of the year. As the stock went up, he kept buying more.

By July, investors were growing concerned that the shortage of flash memory would be followed by a glut, as so often happens in commodity markets. The price of Sandisk and other data-center-related stocks started to fall. Aschenbrenner saw the dip as a buying opportunity, as he had with DeepSeek. This time, though, the prices didn’t recover.

Compounding Aschenbrenner’s concerns was his growing market visibility. Every quarter, Situational Awareness was required to file a Form 13F, a public report that showed the stocks it owned. Aschenbrenner began to feel that his specific positions were being targeted by short sellers: that his cards were showing. “This guy’s in the Journal—let me just pull up his 13F,” Falk-Wallace said. “He could have easily become a target, even without anybody having any specialized knowledge.”

Meanwhile, software stocks were recovering. One company that took a beating earlier in the year was the consultancy Accenture, which provides software services to businesses. Investors worried that it would be vibe-coded out of existence. But Accenture proved unexpectedly resilient. On July 24th, Aschenbrenner sent a letter to his investors, who by this point included not just Wall Street veterans but also the endowment of the University of Virginia. In the letter, Aschenbrenner argued that, despite market swings, current conditions offered some of the best investment opportunities he’d seen in more than a year, and invited investors to add capital. But Sandisk kept going down, and software stocks kept going up.

As Aschenbrenner’s positions moved against him, Situational Awareness’s brokers started issuing margin calls, forcing the fund to either post more collateral or sell positions at a substantial loss. By the time Mann received the call about the Anthropic shares, Situational Awareness was in danger of being wiped out entirely—or, as Aschenbrenner put it, suffering “permanent capital impairment.”

In addition to Mann, Situational Awareness offered its stake in Anthropic to a consortium of investors led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital. The consortium worked overnight to structure the deal, and by the morning of July 30th the terms were prepared. But, shortly before the contract was scheduled to be signed, Aschenbrenner reversed course and announced that he was keeping the Anthropic stake. Instead, he was selling the bulk of his public-stock portfolio—Sandisk and all—to Citadel, Griffin’s hedge fund, at a ten-per-cent discount to market prices. After the transaction was completed, Situational Awareness informed its investors that, in the month of July, it had lost an estimated thirty billion dollars—the single biggest drawdown in hedge-fund history.

Just a day later, on August 1st, Aschenbrenner got married. He and Balwit had been planning their wedding for months—the theme was “European Garden, except on the verge of the singularity.” The event was preceded by a small conference on topics including the future of A.I., complete with lightning rounds and breakout sessions. “Debating what will happen in the future is our job,” Aschenbrenner said, of his and Balwit’s friends. “It’s also all of our main hobby.” The ceremony took place at an estate in Carmel Valley, with about a hundred and fifty guests in attendance; Ross Douthat, then an opinion columnist for the Times, was the officiant. (Douthat had befriended Aschenbrenner after reading “Situational Awareness.”) Dwarkesh Patel, one of the groomsmen, was surprised by how unaffected Aschenbrenner seemed by the previous week’s events. Aschenbrenner is a remarkably resilient person, he told me—he hadn’t seemed affected when he’d been fired by OpenAI, either. Later, at the reception, Patel gave a toast. “Leopold was supposed to find an engagement ring worth three months’ salary, but he couldn’t find anything that big,” he said. Referring to the hedge fund’s reversal, he quipped,“So he found another way to show her how much she means to him.”

In the aftermath of the liquidation, Falk-Wallace, who now runs a software company called Arcana, decided to reconstruct Situational Awareness’s portfolio, using a combination of public filings, Aschenbrenner’s statements, and a little guesswork. He found that Aschenbrenner was an excellent stock picker. “The hard thing to do in the A.I. thesis was predicting what part of the supply chain would be the next narrative that everyone would freak out about,” Falk-Wallace told me. “He nailed that.”

But Situational Awareness also took on more risk than any hedge fund Falk-Wallace had ever seen. Such funds can “hedge” exposure by balancing long positions against short ones. The resulting risk is sometimes calculated using a measure called “vol,” or implied volatility. The typical fund runs at about five per cent vol; a very aggressive fund might run at thirty. Situational Awareness, he estimated, was somewhere close to a hundred per cent. Plus, the hardware and software trades were inversely correlated, meaning that, if one side of the portfolio failed, the other side probably would, too. “He wasn’t truly hedged at all,” Falk-Wallace said.
My meeting with Aschenbrenner took place shortly after he returned from his honeymoon to Italy. “My wife is great,” Aschenbrenner said, smiling. “We went to the Dolomites.

items.title: A Thanksgiving Tradition of Rewatching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz”
items.description: To my mind, one of the single greatest live performances one can see exists midway through the concert film “The Last Waltz.” Directed by Martin Scorsese, it documents the final concert of the Band, on Thanksgiving Day, 1976, at Bill Graham’s Winterland Ballro
items.author: Hanif Abdurraqib
paragraphs: To my mind, one of the single greatest live performances one can see exists midway through the concert film “The Last Waltz.” Directed by Martin Scorsese, it documents the final concert of the Band, on Thanksgiving Day, 1976, at Bill Graham’s Winterland Ballroom, in San Francisco. The performance is from after the concert was filmed, when Scorsese shot for multiple days at a studio soundstage on the M-G-M lot, capturing the Band playing their most famous song, “The Weight,” alongside the Staple Singers. The soundstage is, aesthetically, a sharp departure from the Winterland stage. The lighting is sparse, with a red-orange hue shooting across an otherwise black backdrop, slightly tinting everyone it falls upon in a way that makes them look as if they are bathing in a final gasp of sunlight before nightfall. The group trades verses of the iconic song with the Staples Singers. Levon Helm takes one, Pops Staples takes the next, Rick Danko takes another, and Mavis gets a verse—Mavis sings her brief verse with an air of delight and revelation, as if she’s enjoying a meal made by someone she loves. She comes back in the song’s final verse, and by the closing moments she’s in full gospel mode, clapping her hands into the microphone, overcome, reaching into the open mouth of the folk song and pulling a bit of God from beneath its tongue—a bit of God which, in the case of “The Weight,” is never hard to find.

The concert recorded in “The Last Waltz” is marking its fiftieth anniversary this Thanksgiving. For almost half of that time, I have had a tradition of watching the film every year on Thanksgiving Eve. Like most of my traditions, this one began when the thought of solitude became unbearable, which, at nineteen years old, was almost always. At that age, doing anything with anyone seemed better than doing something I loved alone. In college I was among the misfits, the people in my dorm who either couldn’t go home for Thanksgiving or wouldn’t: the ones who lived too far away to travel back for both Thanksgiving and Christmas; the ones who’d been dropped off on campus earlier that fall by parents who didn’t even bother to get out of the car; or those, like me, whose families didn’t care much about gathering for this holiday or any other.

There were about nine of us left over, and we had the run of the dorm, which had a large television and a new DVD player. There was a Blockbuster within walking distance, and I knew that none of us wanted to be alone for the holiday in the large, echoing dorm building, thinking about those whom we missed or were too mad at to miss. And so I rented the newly released “Last Waltz” anniversary DVD and ordered some pizza, and that Wednesday night all nine of us crammed into the TV room and watched it together. It was my first time seeing the film in full. We laughed at the interviews and scenes interwoven among the concert performances: Danko, Richard Manuel, and Robbie Robertson talking about how, in the early days, the Band would wear massive overcoats and steal food from the supermarket on the road. In one scene, a clearly drunk Danko plays “Old Time Religion” on the fiddle with a small black hat resting atop his head. As we got deeper into the film, many of my comrades fell asleep, but I realized that I didn’t need the screening to be a group activity. The film was teeming with companionship—Neil Young bouncing over to Robertson and Danko to share a microphone at the end of a stunning rendition of “Helpless,” or the Band’s first leader, Ronnie Hawkins, shouting at his old backing band as if they were still his backing band and not veteran headliners themselves. The film itself was an antidote to loneliness, a vision of a life lived well.

I am more rigorous about my “Last Waltz” tradition than I am about most other rituals. I have watched the movie every year since that first time, and always alone. I generally commit myself to not being on the road for the holiday, but in the rare times when I have been, I’ve closed myself off in whatever hotel room I’m staying in and found a way to stream the movie on the hotel TV. I have not, since that first college viewing, been interested in sharing the experience with others. I am especially not interested in serving as a tour guide for someone who has never seen the film, even if this is antithetical to my usual impulse of finding someone, anyone, to share the things that excite or bewilder me. I only watch the movie once per year, on the day before Thanksgiving. It is a foolish superstition, but one that I stick to.

“The Last Waltz” manifests itself to me differently every year. The film ages and I age alongside it, and in the process I find new moments of tenderness, or old moments of tenderness that have tuned themselves to aches in my heart that hadn’t existed the last time I watched. Take, for example, the aforementioned performance of Young’s “Helpless.” Some viewers tend to focus—foolishly, I might add—on the clearly dazed onstage presence of Young as an example of the not so subtle drug use happening off camera. This kind of pearl-clutching seems to risk emphasizing the very ordinary at the expense of the extraordinary, which, in this case, is a moment when Joni Mitchell starts singing from a hidden perch backstage, invisible to the audience except as a shadow underneath the curtain. Onstage, Young, Robertson, and Danko (who do know that Joni is there, and have situated her there specifically for this moment) playfully look to the heavens, as if to say, The angels are here, among us.

“Helpless” is, broadly, a song about reaching through the devastating and overgrown acres of memory. If I were to sit beside you watching this scene I would ask about people you miss: what their singing voices sounded like, if you can remember; how long they’ve been gone and at what point their voices began to fade in your mind into intermittent static. For me, there is a new voice that begins to fade every year. Someone who has died, or otherwise left. The symphony of their living becomes first flimsy, and then gone. I like to imagine the moment that the audience watching the Band could hear a voice they loved but couldn’t see where it was coming from—the split second, before logic kicked in, where they did think that something was falling upon them from the same heaven their beloveds were in.

In its best moments, “The Last Waltz” highlights the affection and camaraderie among the bandmates and their peers, which means that much of the friction that is known to have existed within the group at the time is barely visible, especially if one doesn’t know what to look for. By 1976, Robertson was done with being on the road. The Band had spent more than fifteen years touring non-stop, first as the backing band for Hawkins, then backing Bob Dylan, and then on their own. The other members of the Band didn’t want the show to stop as Robertson did, and so humming underneath their farewell concert was the drama of one member walking out on his own. The Band, sans Robertson, reformed and started touring again in 1983, but the tensions continued and grew, to the point where, when the Band was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1994, with Robertson joining them, Helm stayed home. But even knowing all of this, you might watch “The Last Waltz” and forget the grievances. There is a moment, in one of the interstitial storytelling scenes, when Helm lights a match, mid-sentence, and holds it toward Robertson’s cigarette before he lights his own, before Robertson could even gesture to ask. When the group performs “Who Do You Love” with Hawkins, and he playfully storms offstage, leaving the Band to find their own close to the song, Robertson and Helm momentarily look at each other, laughing, perhaps remembering what it was to be young and briefly lost.

At the same time, it’s become clearer to me as I’ve aged that a central engine of “The Last Waltz” is grief. There’s a scene that takes place after the concert ends, when Martin Scorsese goes to visit Danko in Shangri-La, their Malibu clubhouse and studio. After a brief tour of the space, Danko sits down at a control board, and Scorsese asks him what he’s been doing since “The Last Waltz.” Danko reaches for a wide-brimmed hat, puts it on his head, and asks his engineer to press play on a song. As the first notes of his then new solo song “Sip the Wine” come through the studio speakers, Danko responds, “Just making music, you know . . . trying to stay busy. It’s healthy.” As the song continues to play, Danko leans back in his chair and smiles at Scorsese, as if he knows he’s done something miraculous. But then he turns back to the control board, his hat obscuring most of his face, and as the camera zooms in it becomes evident that his smile is gone, his self-satisfaction suddenly wrecked by an understanding that he was doing a significant thing alone. Danko is my favorite of the Band’s vocalists. Everything he sang sounds like pleading, mourning, suffering, like the stakes couldn’t be higher. Every note sounds as if he was watching the final threads of a memory slip through his fingers. But the scene might be heartbreaking only because of what I know of its aftermath. Manuel would die less than eight years later, by suicide. Danko’s first son would die, after a night of binge drinking, three years after that. The Band’s remaining members would face dwindling popularity in the eighties, playing smaller venues with far less fanfare. At that moment in “The Last Waltz,” playing a new song for Scorsese, Danko looks as if he’s already mourning the future his dream won’t survive in.

Helm, though, played until he was damn near gone. One of the disconnects between him and Robertson was that Robertson seemed to view being on the road and the stage as a hazard to his life, whereas Helm could not imagine a worthwhile life without it. In one of his last shows before his death, in 2012, from throat cancer, he sang a cover of Ralph Stanley’s “Gloryland,” which is a song about leaving the earth behind. In “Gloryland,” there are no undertakers because no one dies. There are no doctors because no one falls ill. Your earthly pain won’t be making the trip, and you have friends already in Gloryland—the one who hung himself in a motel room, the one who sang like his heart was a hundred puzzle pieces from a hundred different boxes until it gave out on him way too young, the one who took too much of something just the one day. During his life’s final act, Helm performed the generous gesture of singing about where he believed he was going, and where he believed they’d be going one day, too. The song insists that we are all spending a lifetime travelling toward another lifetime, and death is the door we have to slip through.

I would like to believe in the place that Helm is singing about. You don’t have to be who you were. Whatever haunted you once doesn’t need to haunt you always. Because my “Last Waltz” tradition was born out of isolation, I decided along the way that it had to be defined by isolation. This year, however, I am spending Thanksgiving week with my fiancée, and I have limited ability (or desire) to close myself off in a room for a couple of hours. She’s never seen the film, and knows very little about it beyond the fact that I watch it every year. And so, for the first time since I was nineteen years old in a mostly abandoned college dorm, I am going to watch it alongside someone else. You don’t have to be who you were. ♦

items.title: ‘Is James Bond Conservative?’ Trump Asks Natalie Harp to Find Out
items.description: Donald Trump loves inserting himself into major pop-culture controversies. And at one point, he had a lot of thoughts about Robert Pattinson. Over a four-week period in late 2012, he tweeted about the Twilight heartthrob’s relationship with Kristen Stewart an
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump loves inserting himself into major pop-culture controversies. And at one point, he had a lot of thoughts about Robert Pattinson. Over a four-week period in late 2012, he tweeted about the Twilight heartthrob’s relationship with Kristen Stewart an incredible 11 times, urging him not to take back his co-star because “She cheated on him like a dog & will do it again–just watch. He can do much better!”

So it was a bit surprising that Trump did not immediately weigh in when Pattinson was announced as the next James Bond earlier this month. Now he has finally done so, and it seems his opinion hinged on whether RPatz is MAGA-friendly.
The New York Post asked Trump about the next 007 at an Oval Office interview on Tuesday. Before he answered, Trump sent his top aide, Natalie Harp, on an important mission:
“Is James Bond conservative? Natalie,” he called through the open door of the Oval Office.
Harp rushed in from her desk in the outer Oval, with printouts about Pattinson in hand, and gave them to Trump.
Harp told Trump, “He’s been good.” He responded, “I always like people that like me.”
Then Trump looked through the stack of printed-out articles, and read the first of his iconic Pattinson tweets aloud:
One of the printed-out articles was Trump’s tweet from 2012 where he gave Pattinson relationship advice.
“Robert Pattinson should not take back Kristen Stewart. She cheated on him like a dog & will do it again — just watch,” the president said, reading his tweet aloud.
He then added: “This was a long time ago” …
Laying aside his 2012 tweet, Trump went on to flip through the clips about him and Pattinson.
“That’s cute. He says nice things,” he said.

It is unclear which RPatz comments Trump found “nice.” The actor, who is British, has never shared his political views publicly. He has said he considered becoming a political speechwriter when he was young, but “I’m quite apolitical, weirdly. I like the game.”

Pattinson has discussed Trump’s tweets about him, but his remarks weren’t exactly positive. In a 2017 Daily Beast interview, he called them a “bizarre curiosity.” That same year, he offered these existential musings when Entertainment Weekly inquired about the new U.S. president’s apparent obsession with him:

I think there’s so many different levels of it. Your identity exists on many different planes at the same time, and they all can be quite different from each other. When he said that, it didn’t really mean anything. But I guess now I’m sort of thinking, like, “Well, I guess that is related to me.” But how does that fit in with all the other things going on in my life? And sometimes you think, “Can I use this in my acting? Or should I be putting it away?” It’s kind of interesting, I guess. I don’t know — this could be why people get annoyed with me.
Whatever Harp showed Trump, he took it as a compliment. “He looks nice,” the president said of Pattinson. “You know, I wish him luck.”
