- Trump Shouts About Corrupt Huang Intervention From the Rooftops
- Melania: The Series Is Deleted Scenes Hiding Under a Trench Coat

items.title: Washington’s War Over Nvidia and Jensen Huang
items.description: In a social-media post Monday, Hillary Clinton helpfully identified four potential buckets of scandals surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s extraordinary intervention to restore him as CEO: national security, corruption, insider trading,
items.author: Nate Weisberg
paragraphs: In a social-media post Monday, Hillary Clinton helpfully identified four potential buckets of scandals surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s extraordinary intervention to restore him as CEO: national security, corruption, insider trading, and market manipulation. It isn’t difficult to find possible examples of each. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and whose company allegedly diverted restricted American chips to China, fits the national-security category. For corruption, consider Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees chip-export restrictions even as his former (now his sons’) investment firm has financial interests in overseas data centers that could give Chinese companies access to American computing power. Insider trading encompasses questions about Trump’s own Nvidia stock purchases and whether anyone traded on advance knowledge of his intervention. And market manipulation? The president personally persuaded Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, sending the company’s shares soaring. “If it’s ‘super intelligence,’ call it Supergate,” Clinton wrote.

Clumsy coinage aside, the Nvidia mess is only getting started. This is a cascading, open-ended scandal that encompasses aspects of nearly every past Trump administration imbroglio. Three separate House committees and one Senate committee are set to call Huang as a witness next week alone.

The Huang Affair is unusual in its size and scope, and it can be difficult to discern the actual stakes beneath the sex, spies, and stock-market gyrations. That’s in part because the standard political battle lines are scrambled. Some Republicans, including J.D. Vance, are cheering the president for overruling a corporate board’s judgment about who should run its company. Others, particularly those pushing for tougher restrictions on China, are openly defying him — or at least Nvidia’s board. Many Democrats find themselves aligned with those Republican hawks on China policy, though they disagree among themselves about how far to go. Neither party affiliation nor conventional ideology offers much guidance about who stands where.

Almost everyone in government wants America to maintain its AI lead over China, whether for economic or military advantage or both. Since 2022, Washington has restricted exports of advanced American AI chips and the equipment needed to manufacture them, though the rules have changed repeatedly. And while Nvidia’s most powerful processors remain off-limits, advanced American chips have nevertheless made their way into China through intermediaries in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. (Megaspeed, the company founded by Jensen Huang’s ex-paramour, is one of the firms suspected of facilitating those diversions.)

Huang has long argued, both publicly and in the president’s ear, that the best way to beat China is to keep its developers dependent on American technology. Ease restrictions, let Chinese companies buy Nvidia chips and build their systems around Nvidia software, and they will have less incentive to develop competing products. Cut them off, and Washington will merely accelerate China’s technological independence. Trump has been very receptive, allowing licensed sales of advanced Nvidia chips under an arrangement involving a 25 percent cut for the treasury. (Another scandal: It remains unclear to what extent Nvidia managed to pocket the government’s levy through its third-party diversion.)

“It was a seductive argument that Nvidia was presenting,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a national-security analyst at the Foundation for American Innovation, told me, “and it really gained some currency.” But China is already investing heavily in developing its own semiconductors, Fedasiuk and others argue, and American chips could help it develop more sophisticated military and intelligence capabilities in the meantime. They don’t think keeping China dependent on American technology in the short term is worth supplying it with the computing power it needs to compete with America in the long term.

Huang’s case for relaxing controls has powerful fans in the White House, but faces a bipartisan wall on Capitol Hill. Most lawmakers in both parties want to keep America’s most advanced chips out of Chinese hands, but they disagree about how much older technology Beijing should be allowed to buy. Ro Khanna, the Silicon Valley Democrat who serves as the top Democrat on the House committee focused on China, has said he is open to selling Beijing advanced chips once America establishes a sufficient technological lead. His position is more accommodating than that of Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren or the committee’s Republican chairman, John Moolenaar, both of whom oppose the sales outright.
The Fight in the Trump Administration

The chip question has divided Trump’s camp. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who doubles as national security adviser, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed for broader restrictions on Chinese access to American computing power, including through overseas data centers. Lutnick resisted, reportedly fearing a confrontation with Beijing. According to Axios, Trump approved enforcement action three times, only for Lutnick to stall. Rubio also circulated an intelligence memo months ago warning about Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

The scandal and Huang’s ouster seemed to remove the most influential advocate in Trump’s ear for looser export controls. Last week, the Commerce Department issued a rule, written “by and at the direction of the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council,” meant to stop Chinese companies from using American AI chips remotely through data centers in other countries. And on Monday, Commerce finally blacklisted Megaspeed. But Trump also put Huang right back in charge the same day, dealing a blow to hawks who seemed to have gained the upper hand. The factions are already sniping anonymously. A source close to Rubio called the reinstatement (which has no constituency outside of Wall Street, Silicon Valley, and China) a “big win” for Vance, Axios reported.

Not many are convinced the administration did its homework before vouching for Huang. Representative Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, is still trying to understand the government’s assurances that Huang posed no national-security risk. At a recent meeting of the Gang of Eight — lawmakers privy to top-level classified information — neither the CIA director nor the director of national intelligence could tell him whether the FBI had opened a counterintelligence investigation into Alice Huang, or whether she had knowingly worked for Chinese intelligence. A subsequent briefing was indefinitely delayed, and Himes still hasn’t seen Rubio’s memo.

“We’re being kept completely in the dark,” Himes told me Monday. “It would appear that the New York Times and any number of other journalists know a lot more than the Gang of Eight did.” Himes had no reason to believe Jensen Huang knowingly participated in espionage — “That would surprise me” — but doubted Trump had “invested the time and energy to really assure himself that Jensen Huang is not a security risk.”
The Coming Fight in Congress

In the meantime, there is broad bipartisan agreement that China should not gain access to America’s most powerful processors. But lawmakers disagree about how far Nvidia’s product line restrictions should extend, how to enforce them, and how much discretion to leave the president.

Warren and Republican Senator Jim Banks have sponsored the AI OVERWATCH Act, which would preserve restrictions on the most advanced chips while giving Congress greater oversight of licenses for less powerful ones. Other lawmakers are focused less on deciding which chips can be sold than on preventing Chinese companies from getting around the existing rules. Republican Senator Tom Cotton’s Chip Security Act would require measures to verify where restricted processors end up. The MATCH Act, sponsored in the Senate by Republicans Jim Risch and Pete Ricketts and Democrat Andy Kim, would pressure American allies to restrict the equipment China needs to manufacture advanced semiconductors. And legislation sponsored by Republican Dave McCormick and Democrat Ron Wyden would strengthen controls on Chinese firms renting American computing power abroad. The first three have been included in the Senate’s proposed defense authorization bill, though their fate remains uncertain.

Still, rescuing Huang did not necessarily mean rescuing his preferred China policy. “The export controls aren’t going anywhere,” Gavin Fry, another analyst at the Foundation for American Innovation, told me. Lawmakers on the relevant committees still appeared determined to act, regardless of Huang’s return. “The last kind of check to Nvidia’s influence here is Congress,” he said.

That creates an awkward situation for Republican lawmakers, who are considerably more comfortable criticizing Nvidia than criticizing the president who rescued its CEO. Senator Josh Hawley told me last week that he was glad Huang had been removed, but after Trump reversed the decision, Hawley’s office did not respond to my several requests for comment. Senator John Curtis demanded to know which government officials had reassured Nvidia’s board about Huang’s security risk, without mentioning the president who already had taken credit for it.

Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego, who has discussed chip restrictions privately with Republican colleagues, expects them to find a way around that problem. “You’re talking to a lot of future presidential primary candidates; they want his support,” he told me. “They won’t attack the president personally because he still owns the Republican Party.” But opposing his preferred policies was another matter. “If you’re asking them to go on TV to, you know, shake their fist and swear damnation to the president, that’s not going to happen,” Gallego said. “But will they find their courage in legislation? I think that’s more likely to happen.”

Gallego also wants the incoming Democratic Congress to investigate the decisions behind Nvidia’s sales. “We want to see exactly what happened with the shipments of the chips, who ordered them, who approved them on the White House side,” he said. “Was the president directly involved? Who else was directly involved? How much did Jensen know about Megaspeed?”

Other Democrats have their own investigations in mind. The Foreign Relations Committee in the Senate wants answers about the administration’s handling of intelligence warnings. Representative Jamie Raskin is examining whether Lutnick’s family financial interests influenced export enforcement, while Senator Ron Wyden has scrutinized the administration’s arrangement to collect revenue from chip sales.

Chris Van Hollen wants to go further still. At an emergency press conference Monday, the Maryland senator, who is challenging Chuck Schumer for Democratic leader, called Huang’s reinstatement “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He supports tighter chip restrictions, but also wants independent safety evaluations of advanced AI systems, stronger liability rules, protections against passing data-center electricity costs to consumers, and a congressional committee to examine the technology’s broader effects.

It also isn’t clear how much the new majority can actually do. Subpoenas can pry loose the documents Gallego wants and put Huang and Lutnick under oath, but legislation is another matter: Democrats won’t have the two-thirds majorities needed to override a veto. Their best shot at writing export controls into law is to attach them to must-pass bills Trump can’t afford to veto, which is exactly what the hawks are trying to do now with the defense bill. And the most consequential chip legislation may be settled before Democrats take power at all. Negotiators are deciding during the lame-duck session which export control proposals survive in the final defense bill, and House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “a developing consensus” for limiting China’s access to advanced chips.

But the hawks have been here before. Last December, a similar export control measure designed to give American companies first dibs on advanced AI chips was left out of the final defense bill after Huang lobbied Trump and lawmakers in person and the White House pushed to drop it.

It was another reminder that Trump has never been as tough on China as he pretends to be — a point underlined in bold by the events of the last week. When it’s a contest between protecting national security or propping up the stock market while rescuing a powerful man accused of sexual impropriety, it’s no mystery which side Trump will choose.
- Pushing Medicare for All a Choice, Not a Mandate, for Democrats
- ‘Is James Bond Conservative?’ Trump Asks Natalie Harp to Find Out
