items.title: GTAVI: An exclusive deep dive into the video game of the decade
items.description: This story is taken from the autumn 2026 issue of Dazed, which is on sale internationally from September 10. Pre-order a copy of the magazine here.
paragraphs: This story is taken from the autumn 2026 issue of Dazed, which is on sale internationally from September 10. Pre-order a copy of the magazine here.

On the sweltering Leonida Keys, sweat slicks the skin of two lovers on the run as they toast new beginnings, watching the sun set over the water. A breeze blows through their hair, and you can almost feel the condensation dripping from the cold beer bottles in their hands; in the background, locals gather on the weatherbeaten dock, indifferent to the story unfolding between the outlaws. Elsewhere, a few miles north, tanned bodies of all shapes and sizes swarm the sand on Vice Beach. Further north still, locals are caked in mud, kicked up from the back of a dirt bike or spattered on a stars-and-stripes bikini. And as night falls back in Vice City, sweaty crowds surge to deafening hip-hop beats, spilling out from clubs on to the neon-lit streets.

It’s been 13 years since Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto V, one of the most acclaimed – and controversial – video games of all time. And it’s been roughly the same amount of time since work began on its sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, which transports the action from San Andreas (closely inspired by real-life southern California) to Leonida (based on Florida). That’s more than a decade of anticipation, meaning there’s “unprecedented pressure” on the follow-up to meet expectations, as Rob Nelson, head of development and co-studio head at Rockstar North, tells Dazed: “However, I don’t know that any amount of external pressure could compare with the pressure we put on ourselves as a team.”

If you accept that video games are an artform, then Rockstar Games has produced two of the most significant works of the 21st century so far: GTAV and the western-themed adventure Red Dead Redemption 2. The numbers speak for themselves: in 2013, the former broke the record for the fastest-selling entertainment product of all time, earning a billion dollars in just three days – more than any book or Hollywood film. Five years later, RDR2 took the second spot. But the latter also came with a gear shift. While GTA satirised modern life with wacky characters, high-octane car chases and explosive gunfights, RDR2 was hailed as one of the most realistic and immersive games to date, with a slower, more emotional tone suited to its storyline.

GTAVI promises something in between the two. The open-world game is set in the same fictionalised US that serves as the backdrop for the rest of the series, with all the weapons and supercars you’d expect, but the world is more grounded and reactive than before – gone are the days when you could traverse the city like a god. Now, players’ actions have consequences. Walk down the street with a rifle, and the city will have something to say about it. More and more, the games are converging on real life, and non-player characters (NPCs) are acting... well, less like NPCs than ever. For some gamers, there’s a fear that what GTAVI gains in immersion, it loses in the chaos and anarchy that have been part of the series’ DNA since the outset, but for Rockstar, the goal is to create a world of total immersion, which reacts more realistically than ever to what you choose to make of it.

“We look back at our previous games with a critical eye and see where we want to evolve based on what we didn’t do as well as we would have liked to, either because we didn’t have the time, resources or technological capabilities, or in some cases things we just didn’t do as well or consider as fully as we could have,” says Nelson. “A lot of what we do is very iterative – we adjust a lot of things by feel based on what is working and what isn’t.”

The story has evolved, too, with higher stakes and characters grounded in all aspects of the world they inhabit. Players step into the shoes of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos – an ex-military drug runner and a fighter fresh out of prison, respectively – and can choose to either play as a couple, or go off and cause chaos independently. This marks the first time that a GTA game has featured a playable couple in the lead role, which makes for some unique scenarios: on the way to a job, for example, players can cruise along the highway as Jason, or swap to Lucia in the passenger seat to scroll on the in-game phone. (Yes, there are working social media feeds – what satirical take on 2020s America would be complete without them?) When the job inevitably goes wrong and spirals into a car chase, the fluid system enables players to take the wheel in one moment, then fire on pursuers out of the passenger window the next. And afterwards, when it’s all blown over, they can skim across the waves on a jetski, admiring the Leonida seascape and leaping dolphins with their arms wrapped around their partner’s waist.

True romance like Jason and Lucia’s usually takes a back seat in GTA games, which, when it comes to matters of love and sex, are more commonly associated with strip clubs and underground sex work. But GTAVI is very consciously staged as “a Bonnie and Clyde-type narrative”, says Rupert Humphries, senior vice president of narrative at Rockstar. The trailers alone feature a slew of intimate cutscenes from Jason and Lucia’s own fugitive tale, which showcase the special attention that Rockstar’s art and technology teams have paid to how bodies look and feel – a hand on a ribcage, hips swinging on a packed dancefloor. For some gamers, the story might even serve as one of their earliest encounters with a romantic (albeit crime-ridden) relationship, where their choices can have repercussions that cut much deeper than Rockstar’s previous titles or “honour” systems that reward conscientious game playing.

“The thing we love about this medium is the way these characters aren’t empty avatars that you can do whatever you want with... Their story becomes a journey you share with them” – Rob Nelson, head of development and co-studio head at Rockstar North

Lucia is also the first fully fleshed-out female lead in a mainline GTA game. Before her, it’s male protagonists all the way down, dating back to 1999. (Grand Theft Auto’s 1997 debut featured a 50-50 split of male and female protagonists.) Previous instalments, including GTAV, drew criticism for misogynistic themes and underdeveloped female characters, but the series has evolved, and hopes to attract more female gamers to its previously male-heavy player base. In Lucia and Jason, they have created characters with rich, complex identities, while still leaving ample room for players to make them their own. “The thing we love about this medium is the way these characters aren’t empty avatars that you can do whatever you want with,” says Nelson. “Their story becomes a journey you share with them.”

The joy of GTA is as much about what players do with the moments in between story beats, though. And Rockstar offers what has been – up until now – as close to true freedom as you’re going to get within the confines of a virtual world. “We want to enable as much self-expression as possible,” says Nelson, “without losing the essence of the characters.” Take GTAV’s version of 2010s Los Angeles, for example: you could rampage through the streets with an assault rifle or a tank, cruise by the Pacific in an open-top car blasting Frank Ocean, or even relax with a round of golf. RDR2 pushed things further: between shootouts, the player-controlled protagonist Arthur Morgan could retreat into the wild to fish, hunt big game and make a campfire under the geographically accurate stars, or lose time drinking and gambling in remote frontier towns. Come down out of the mountains a few in-game weeks later, and he’d have grown a long beard and a mane of hair, and visibly lost some weight (or gained it, depending on your skill with a bow and arrow). Bar fights, meanwhile, would leave him bruised and scarred.

GTAVI marks the return, and expansion, of these interactive systems that alter the protagonists’ bodies. Food affects Jason and Lucia’s weight, while exercising visibly builds and tones their muscles. And, if you end up spending a long time away from your bed, on the run from police or on a multi-day bender, their features are going to pay the price for that as well. The effect is a bit like The Picture of Dorian Gray – only, instead of your soul being recorded on a spooky painting in the attic, your habits and sins are written on to the faces and bodies of the game’s avatars. This kind of interactivity is unique to video games, shaping the virtual world and the player’s responses to it in turn. Between visual feedback mechanisms, deep relationship mechanics and the heightened realism of the world they inhabit, people might even think twice about going on the arcade-style rampages of GTA games gone by, once they land in Leonida.

“We will meet with ex-criminals, law enforcement, club promoters, gun dealers and anyone notorious or influential who’ll take our calls. We hang out, get a feeling for the place, listen to the stories...” – Rupert Humphries, senior vice president of narrative at Rockstar

Vice City, the heart of GTAVI’s Leonida, is based on Miami. This means players can expect encounters with virtual iterations of Florida Man, the cultural archetype-turned-meme known IRL for wrangling alligators, drunken antics and literal grand theft auto. But these outsized characters are just one bizarre facet of a world built with “an open mind, a genuine appreciation and a deep curiosity” towards the culture it’s based on, says GTAVI game writer Michael Wiafe. “It’s easy to go in with a cynical view and say, ‘Well that’s weird, put it in the game,’ but we couldn’t just stop there. We have to bring a sense of discovery to the players too, not just repeat cliches that already exist.” To do that requires years of on-the-ground exploration: various groups of Rockstar employees have visited Miami and its surrounding areas over the last decade, and there is a dedicated research team embedded in the city. “That firsthand context helped us understand the visual markers and nuances that define the identities we wanted to represent,” explains Jamie-Lee Lloyd, senior art director for characters, “while filtering them through the unique lens of GTA and the stories we wanted to tell.”

Humphries agrees that these experiences are essential, noting that a majority of the game’s characters are born out of this research, which includes meeting real people who call the state home. “We will meet with ex-criminals, law enforcement, club promoters, gun dealers and anyone notorious or influential who’ll take our calls,” he adds. “We hang out, get a feeling for the place, listen to the stories, cross-reference that with books and journalism, and try to get to the heart of which characters will bring the city we are creating to life.”

In GTAVI, this cast includes various criminals, from old-school drug runner Brian Heder and his conspiracy-obsessed associate, Cal Hampton, to suave bank robber Raul Bautista. Elsewhere, the lines are blurrier. Vice City legend Boobie Ike oversees a private empire including the Jack of Hearts strip club (a GTA staple) and a music studio, overseen by the young, opportunistic Dre’Quan Priest. “We love Miami music, particularly Miami bass, going through to more recent Miami artists like Kodak Black and Sexyy Red,” says Humphries. “We were also really interested in how the hip-hop scene in Miami exists in house parties in Overtown, clubs like Booby Trap on the River, and then high-end places on South Beach where bottles can cost thousands of dollars. We needed characters who could take us through those worlds.” In the years since the release of the last game, the music industry has witnessed a shift in focus towards female artists, as represented in the game’s rising stars Real Dimez, whose journey can be traced via in-game viral social media posts.
“[GTA VI’s] brands reflect the aspirations, aesthetics and lifestyles of the people that inhabit our world’s spaces” – Stu Petri, vice president of 2D/UI design

With characters like these, anchored in a specific place and time, is there a risk of tipping back into reductive Miami parodies, especially given the game’s long lifespan? If today we look back on GTAV’s hipsters and geeky tech bros as a kind of 2010s time capsule, what kinds of cultural archetypes will we look back on when we revisit GTAVI in another 13 years, and will they remain true to how we experience them in the present day? The artists, writers and developers at Rockstar are conscious of the tightrope they’re walking. Take Stu Petri, vice president of 2D/UI design, who has overseen much of the careful world-building in GTAVI, including the many in-game products, brands, shops and campaigns that bear more than a passing resemblance to their real-life counterparts. “Our vision is to build a vibrant, believable culture,” he says, meaning that every brand, from fashion label to car company, has to feel like more than just a one-off joke, as if it actually exists and serves a real purpose in Leonida’s cultural ecosystem. “These brands reflect the aspirations, aesthetics and lifestyles of the people that inhabit our world’s spaces.” Drop into the game as Jason or Lucia, and they come to reflect your inner life as well, lending an extra layer of meaning to each haircut or outfit choice.

The potential to explore a diversity of cultures and lifestyles is partly why the series ended up circling back to Vice City and the state of Leonida in the first place, Nelson suggests: “Florida and Miami have perhaps one of the most diverse and interesting populations in the world.” Few know this better than Miami-based stylist Jillian Carr, who has worked with Rockstar since 2023, designing an in-game “fashion ecosystem” that aims to reflect all the nuances of “taste, lifestyle, affluence and individuality” that are displayed in the city, and in America as a whole. “Vice City is built around vanity,” says Carr. “Between social media, celebrity culture and a constant flow of tourists, appearances carry significant weight, and trend cycles turn over quickly.” This brings us back to the background NPCs. Young and old, tall or short, tattooed, pierced or modified with plastic surgery, wearing throwback Hawaiian shirts, sharp suits, luxury fashion or muddy combat gear, the bodies and clothes of the virtual masses are also far more varied than in previous games, and more tailored to their local environments, from Vice City’s Little Cuba to the wilderness of Mount Kalaga national park.

“To bring that diversity to life in-game, we developed new tools and pipelines that enabled us to build the most detailed and varied character population we’ve ever created,” says Lloyd. But ultimately, he adds, making that population feel authentic comes from more than appearance alone. “It’s the combination of how a character looks, moves, interacts and expresses themselves, brought together through collaboration across multiple teams.” Wiafe hopes that all of these systems working together deliver “a landscape that players feel they’ve been dropped into and are made to endlessly roam around in.”

“Vice City is built around vanity. Between social media, celebrity culture and a constant flow of tourists, appearances carry significant weight, and trend cycles turn over quickly” – Jillian Carr, stylist

To pull off the technical and cultural feats required to build a world of the scale, depth and interactivity of GTAVI, the Rockstar team has more than doubled in size since the release of Red Dead Redemption 2. It has offices around the world, with one branch in LA dedicated almost solely to the world of in-game pedestrians (NPCs). More than 50 real street artists were brought in to design murals in places like Vice City’s Stockyard (based on Wynwood, Miami). The team that deals with vehicle handling is made up of literal race-car drivers.

Again, it all adds up to a lot of pressure, and not only because the investment of time, money and effort is on a par with several wonders of the world – at the time of writing, there’s an online rumour that the game cost more to build than the Burj Khalifa in Dubai. But also because, if all goes well, this is a work of art that people could spend the next decade with... at least. “It is a lot of pressure internally and externally, but that pressure is ultimately a privilege we know we are fortunate to have,” says Nelson. “All we want to do is deliver for our audience.”

This story is taken from the autumn 2026 issue of Dazed, which is on sale internationally from September 10. Pre-order a copy of the magazine here. Grand Theft Auto VI is out on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

items.title: How Matières Fécales won over the fashion establishment
items.description: When a pair of bare, mutant feet emerge on a runway – supported by ten-inch spears of flesh bursting from their heels – people tend to sit up and pay attention. That’s what happened at Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran’s first-ever catwalk show, Non-
paragraphs: When a pair of bare, mutant feet emerge on a runway – supported by ten-inch spears of flesh bursting from their heels – people tend to sit up and pay attention. That’s what happened at Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran’s first-ever catwalk show, Non-Human, staged in October 2018 at the Mandrake Hotel in London. Known jointly as Matières Fécales, the designers had until then been posting images of their alienoid, DIY garments to Instagram, augmenting their strangeness with SFX and image-editing. In otherworldly regalia, Dalton was often seen with flesh-toned stilts extending from her heels, her feet digitally distorted to resemble a pair of en-pointe skin shoes. On the catwalk, the pair actualised the illusion they’d been teasing for years. Made from silicone and moulded to Dalton’s feet, the first physical version of the shoes shifted their online fantasy into material reality.

The heels – thigh-high streaks of alien eroticism – acted as an entryway into the world of Matières Fécales. The Canadian duo, who are partners in both fashion and life, had been purveyors of extreme clubwear since 2015, selling mid-priced designs on an uber-popular Depop page – but the moment exposed Dalton and Bhaskaran to an even broader audience.

Years later, when I meet Dalton and Bhaskaran in person, there are no feats of anatomical impossibility. The sense of immediate, physical discomfort that dominated those early shows has melted into something more luxury-minded, even as it retains its transgressive edge. Though Dalton’s look is disarmingly businesslike – a shin-length wool dress in a mid-grey twill – her signature shaved head, full-coverage white make-up and soaring, curved heels are enough to offset any assumptions of normalcy. Bhaskaran is dressed, more casually, in cargo shorts, a camouflage cut-off tee and leather platform boots. Today, he’s forgone his usual dramatic eye make-up for arching black sunglasses. His own shaved head is covered by a baseball cap that reads PAINSLUT.

The time is 11am and we’re in Rose Bakery, a sparsely decorated café on the ground floor of Dover Street Market Paris, where their studio has been based since early 2025. It’s the final day of the A/W26 couture season, and the temperature outside is searingly hot. Dalton excuses herself to procure a peppermint tea, and returns on the phone, her brow pinched in concentration. “Oui… oui…. oui…,” she repeats, hurriedly.

“I’m so sorry,” she says when the call finishes. “When we did our first show, Law Roach sent Steven a message about the wedding dress I wore at the end. He said, ‘Can you save this? There’s something special we have to do with it.’”

The pair have been in and out of fittings with Zendaya since March 2025, when Roach decided to use the look as the final, showstopping gown for The Odyssey press tour. Dalton was on the phone arranging shipping to New York, the last hurdle in an arduous 18-month journey – fitting, given the film’s subject matter. Five days after our conversation in Rose Bakery, Zendaya arrives at the premiere in a pleated white gown sprouting floor-length angel wings – the final look from their A/W25 show. It’s a major fashion moment that further confirms their status as a brand to be reckoned with. Before this, the pair had already collaborated with Demi Moore, Chappell Roan and Lady Gaga. They also designed Gabbriette’s “distorted Cinderella” dress for her wedding to The 1975 frontman Matty Healy in July – their first foray into bridal wear. “Anything custom goes through us,” says Bhaskaran. “We start by asking, ‘Would this person protect us on the street if we were being harassed?’”

Our meeting also takes place the day after Kylie Jenner’s Dunkin’ ad drops. In the glossy commercial, Jenner introduces a line of “King Kylie” beverages while wearing a satin pink skirt suit from Matières Fécales S/S26. “She bought that,” Dalton responds offhandedly. “I didn’t send that.” I mention that the pairing did seem out of step with their usual custom clients. “No, she purchased it,” Dalton reconfirms. “Also, you can see she’s removed the shoulder pads. She took it and remade it, actually–”
“Anything custom goes through us. We start by asking, ‘Would this person protect us on the street if we were being harassed?’” – Steven Raj Bhaskaran
“Which I love!” Bhaskaran interjects, quickly.
“Yeah, it’s chill,” claims Dalton in return.
“What’s amazing is that we’re a real brand, selling luxury clothes that are beautiful and desirable,” says Bhaskaran, diplomatically. “People can embody it the way they want to embody it.”

Alongside outfitting global stars, another defining moment was the pair’s A/W26 show, their third on the official Paris Fashion Week schedule. Titled The One Percent, the collection was an incisive send-up of the filthy rich, designed to spark conversation about wealth inequality. Featuring menacing businessmen and women with blood on their hands (which were actually the crimson palms of leather gloves), A/W26 was an exploration of the one per cent’s endless quest for immortality. Dior’s New Look silhouette was “fecalised” with jutting shoulders and frayed hems; cadaverous socialites were blinded by money masks or had their wrists bound with pearls; Alexis Stone transformed into “Catwoman” Jocelyn Wildenstein to parody an obsession with plastic surgery, while “longevity advocate” Bryan Johnson appeared in the final section of the show, his presence symbolising the pernicious hunt for eternal youth. Alongside the satirical overtones, the show demonstrated Dalton and Bhaskaran’s skills as genuine couturiers who know how to advance their vision beyond the “outsider” aesthetic that has come to define them.

Though Matières Fécales are technically an emerging brand, for the last ten years they have been the poster children for subversive beauty and outsider fashion. The One Percent, with its vast, shaggy greatcoats and couture-grade gowns, was a declaration that Dalton and Bhaskaran’s provocative vision – and what they represent as people – had outgrown the confines of online notoriety, ready for a much grander stage. Still, the collection’s commentary on extreme wealth inequality had its detractors – mostly from those who took exception to the idea that fashion designers, who operate within a largely elitist industry, should have the temerity to make such a critique. Dalton manoeuvres the potential hypocrisies by drawing a parallel to the art world. “It relates back to, ‘Do you see fashion as art?’ In art you can make a statement like that, but in fashion it’s like, ‘Oh, you can’t do that,’” she says, reminding us that “a painting is worth more than a dress. Art is a business, too.”

Actor Sarah Paulson drew a similar parallel. When the 2026 Met Gala proposed that “Fashion Is Art”, Paulson responded with a shredded ball gown and dollar bill mask from The One Percent collection. Her thinly veiled commentary on the Gala’s billionaire backers didn’t go unnoticed, but many saw an irony in the stunt – she was attending the same event they were, after all. “I understood that, I guess,” concedes Dalton, in response to the criticism. “To clarify, she didn’t buy the dress; we loaned that – there were a lot of articles like, ‘She spent $100k on her seat! She spent another $100k on her dress!’,” which, ultimately, was not true. “The only way to deconstruct and reconstruct dynamics is from within,” says Bhaskaran. So was the dress taking direct aim at Jeff Bezos and Amazon’s involvement in the Gala? “Of course!” they say in unison. “But it goes beyond the Met Gala,” says Bhaskaran. “It’s how we see life.”

The seed that Matières Fécales sprang from was planted 12 years ago, when Dalton and Bhaskaran met at LaSalle College in Montreal. Bhaskaran, a lower-income student in combat boots and a Beth Ditto T-shirt, encountered Dalton for the first time in a fashion illustration class. “I came in late and saw Hannah sandwiched between two other girls. You were wearing a pussy-bow blouse” – he says, turning towards her – “and you had a below-the-knee pleated skirt. And Tory Burch flats.” Bhaskaran’s curiosity was piqued; Dalton, with her long, mousy hair, seemed prissy in comparison to himself. “There was a little bit of bitterness,” he recounts. “Seeing someone like Hannah physically represent a symbol of privilege, of acceptance and normality – it was a confrontational feeling.”

When discussing her upbringing, Dalton is upfront about the advantages she enjoyed. Born in New Zealand in 1995, Dalton and her family moved to Montreal when she was just six months old, following her father’s work. “Because my dad was a diplomat, I had a wide set of privileges – going to private school and being in a circle of elite people in Westmount.” Though she was obsessed with fashion as a child, when she was 17 this love was put to the test by the collapse of the Rana Plaza factory in Bangladesh. “That burst my bubble, to know that there was suffering happening through something I would purchase at Abercrombie…” she says, trailing off. “From that moment I decided not to buy fast fashion any more.” (The name Matières Fécales was later born from this same feeling – Dalton and Bhaskaran both agreed that the fashion industry was “shit”.)
“I never wanted to be seen or noticed. I just wanted to blend in and get through it” – Hannah Rose Dalton

Dalton continued to pursue garment-making, but with sustainability as a driving force. She began experimenting with her clothes, making pieces out of newspaper and other found materials. “I was very prim and proper,” she says of her childhood style, which Bhaskaran compares to Blair Waldorf from Gossip Girl. “I was literally making my school uniform, but out of recycled materials.” Though she had begun to create for herself, fashion had yet to assume the identity-making function it would later in life. “I never wanted to be seen or noticed. I just wanted to blend in and get through it.”

Bhaskaran’s path to fashion school was markedly different. Born in Montreal in 1993, to a Guyanese mother and Sri Lankan father, his family relocated to Guyana after the death of his maternal grandmother, when he was just six months old. But their family life was further upended following the revelation that his father had had a child with another woman. For three years, Bhaskaran’s father, who was often violent, forced them all to live together. “My dad was abusing [my mother] and forcing her to live with this woman that he cheated on her with,” he recalls. “They were all sleeping in the same bed. It was the craziest environment.” Bhaskaran’s mother eventually escaped the grasp of her husband, fleeing to New York to seek refuge with her sister. “I still remember my mom abandoning us when I was three.”

Four years later, by which time Bhaskaran was seven and his sister ten, their mother returned to Guyana and took them back to Montreal. Bhaskaran’s father made his fortune through nefarious means, which allowed his children to attend private schools, but left them in extreme poverty when they returned to Montreal. “I was very cocky, very arrogant,” remembers Bhaskaran, moving on to his fashion school days, during which he attended underground raves with his boyfriend and dabbled in illegal substances. “I always came in late. I had issues [with the teacher] because I sort of drew better than he did, so I would redraw things that he would do.” To improve his standing in class, Bhaskaran befriended teacher’s pet Dalton – here’s a person who would let me copy their notes!, he thought. The friendship they struck up soon developed into something more than a platonic bond.

The word that Dalton and Bhaskaran use the most, by a wide margin, to describe the start of their romantic relationship is “confusing”. “I never had a boyfriend or girlfriend, so I’d never experienced falling in love with somebody, which was confusing,” remembers Dalton. “When our friendship blossomed into our relationship, it was very confusing for both of us,” recalls Bhaskaran. “It was confusing for you, who had spent so much of your life trying to be gay, and convincing your mom that it’s OK to be gay,” continues Dalton, who adds that their relationship is “beyond sexuality – it’s love.”

It’s a kind of partnership that might remind you of Rick Owens and Michèle Lamy, who have played a pivotal role in the Matières Fécales story. In 2018, Owens cold-emailed the pair after reading an interview with them in The New York Times. Dinner in Paris soon followed, and Owens vowed to look after them, taking on a mentor’s role. Dalton and Bhaskaran quickly became part of Owens’ world, modelling in his shows and becoming “unofficial ambassadors” for the brand. “It became an amazing moment for them also,” says Dalton, “because we’re from a different generation, but still committed to the same philosophies of beauty and human transformation.”

But in 2022, Dalton and Bhaskaran were forced to put their brand on hold after moving to Paris and experiencing the competitive nature of the industry. A chance encounter with Adrian Joffe, the Dover Street Market and Comme des Garçons president, backstage at a Madonna concert, would change that. The duo later pitched to him an upscale Matières Fécales, harnessing the raw energy of their Depop days but focused on the luxury market. “Then he ghosted us for four months,” Dalton says with a laugh. “Four months of standby.” When Joffe finally did respond, the pair were DJing at Lamy’s 80th birthday in Venice. His text read: “let’s do this”.
“We’re, like, popular today” – Steven Raj Bhaskaran

Outside of these relationships, their own network had also been taking shape. “It was so exhilarating, being a part of their world,” says Chadd Curry, a performance artist who walked in that first show at the Mandrake Hotel. While at high school in Montreal, Bhaskaran discovered Curry on the street style blog Lookbook.nu, when Curry was a Rick Owens sales clerk in chalky white make-up and Edwardian attire. The mutual admiration blossomed into a years-long online friendship between the trio, but it wasn’t until the S/S19 runway that they met in the flesh. Curry wore a minidress fashioned from aluminium office blinds, fitted directly to his body before the show. He was one figure in a wider creative circle that’s now central to Matières Fécales’ shows, alongside DJ Lewis G Burton, performance artist Gena Marvin, drag queen Dragoness Lola von Flame and cult model Debra Shaw.

This creative vision, bolstered by the stewardship of Owens, Lamy and Joffe, has burst open the doors of possibility. Today, Dalton and Bhaskaran are beacons of attention for fashion’s top set. Lady Amanda Harlech, the stylist, consultant and former Lagerfeld muse, approaches our table to introduce herself. She’s prepping for a “Narnia shoot” and just needs to let them know she’s pulled one of their pieces. Konstantinos Katalakinos, the husband of Jean Paul Gaultier, later arrives to bemoan their absence from the label’s couture show a day earlier (“I’ve been so busy, but looking from afar and sending good vibes,” Dalton offers as consolation). Joffe also bounces into frame, inviting us all upstairs to his office once the interview has concluded. “We’re, like, popular today,” laughs Bhaskaran.

As they sit across from me, one might assume that the pair’s bright and warm demeanours are antithetical to their visual aesthetic. But, really, the essence of Matières Fécales wills you to understand the very opposite, to unlearn the prejudice that difference – sometimes even extreme difference – is something to be shunned. Handling scrutiny of their image has become second nature to Dalton and Bhaskaran, ever since the pair shaved their heads in university, an act of defiance against what they saw as a toxically normative world. What constitutes “normal” is a question that is repeated multiple times in our conversation. “Before we met each other, we were very normal, and we felt suffocated in that,” says Bhaskaran, who describes a hypothetical stylist who might take one of their dresses, “strip it back and put it on somebody who looks super normal.” But what does that look like to them? “Normal is someone who is naturally beautiful, but relies on that,” says Bhaskaran. “In fashion that’s sort of the norm. We like to push that even further – but our standards of normality are quite far out.”

items.title: New York designer Briah Artemis is spilling her guts
items.description: The fashion brand Briah Artemis first crashed into the collective consciousness last year, at the start of the second consecutive Brat Summer. Charli xcx had been invited to play Coachella and needed an outfit for the afterparty. “Chris’s team reached out abou
paragraphs: The fashion brand Briah Artemis first crashed into the collective consciousness last year, at the start of the second consecutive Brat Summer. Charli xcx had been invited to play Coachella and needed an outfit for the afterparty. “Chris’s team reached out about my SS25 collection, which explored different ideas of success,” says designer Briah Taubman, recalling when Charli’s stylist Chris Horan first contacted her. The collection’s focus on the aesthetics of achievement – all pageant sashes and ironic rosettes – was a fitting comment on Charli’s narrative at the time: the overlooked artiste who’d finally hit the big leagues. Despite the uber-success of her sixth studio album, Charli was booked as a support act on the Coachella line-up, rather than a headline slot. “After discussing different ideas with them, I thought of personalising my ‘Miss Universe’ sash dress for her,” says Taubman. “I’m a huge Charli fan, so when they suggested ‘Miss Should Be Headliner’, I thought it was hilarious.”

As you might remember, the tongue-in-cheek slogan led to a Twitter storm-in-a-teacup. Fans of Green Day, the real headliners of Saturday night’s bill, were incensed by Charli’s apparent diss, while Tré Cool, the band’s drummer, responded with a parody of Taubman’s outfit, creating a makeshift sash out of toilet paper scrawled with the phrase ‘Actual Headliner’. “I honestly loved the storm,” says Taubman. “I always want my pieces to start a conversation. To be a talking point in the cultural zeitgeist felt like a pinch-me moment.”

For SS27, Taubman returns with the latest collection from Briah Artemis. Inspired by a visit to the butchers, Taubman became fixated on the meaning of the phrase “spill your guts”. “Ruminating on gutted animals, I fell down a rabbit hole of late 19th century and early 20th century butchers’ uniforms,” she tells me. In the collection, layered tank tops are criss-crossed with straps for a workwear vibe, protective blouson jackets are paired with thick leather gloves, while the extra wide plackets of sheer separates are buttoned all the way to the top. These mostly utilitarian garments are complicated by the presence of heavy fringe throughout the collection, which realistically would be a nightmare addition to any uniform. “It felt like the perfect conduit for exploring emotional armour,” explains Taubman. The fringe, acting as the proverbial guts, spills from the familiar-looking clothes to create a visual and emotional fault line. “The collection holds this tension by pairing buttoned-up layers with fringe and ripped transparent taffeta,” says Taubman.

Before designing for Charli xcx, Taubman was an alumnus of Parsons’ class of 2021. During her time at university she’d interned with brands like Anna Sui, Eckhaus Latta, Proenza Schouler and even a stint at Dazed Media, carrying out various design and styling jobs on the side of her studies. Briah Artemis, the brand, was officially launched in 2025, starting life with just Taubman and one intern working after hours in her apartment. “That collection led to work with creatives I’d long admired, like photographer Drew Jarrett,” remembers Taubman. The designer’s first collection with a full production was SS26, its accompanying campaign shot by Hart Leshkina. “Creating my own brand has always been my dream. After countless jobs styling and executing the vision of other people, I realised there was something deeply missing,” says Taubman. “Despite the difficulty of being an emerging designer, once I saw my first piece come to life on set, there was no doubt that this is what I’m meant to be doing.”

Taubman wanted to pursue a career as a designer from an early age. “I was a quiet kid, and clothes always energised me creatively because of the ability to express myself tacitly,” she says. Though art was her first creative outlet (she’s classically trained as a painter), Taubman realised as a teenager that the process no longer served her and turned to fashion instead, inspired by designers like Helmut Lang and Nicolas Ghesquiere at Balenciaga. “When I was 14 I had the opportunity to spend summers in NYC, staying with my grandma and interning at fashion houses,” she recalls. The name of the brand also has a familial link: Artemis, Taubman’s middle name, is an ode to her great-grandfather Arthur, who passed just before she was born. “Although I was bullied for the name in middle school, I came to learn more about who Artemis was, the Greek goddess of the hunt,” she says. “Her name and story aligned with my own and served as a reminder of strength and tenacity.”

items.title: Ozuna y el Arte de Reinventar a su Yo de Antes
items.description: Dos guitarras, un amplificador y una voz melódica. El ensayo se ejecutaba como preparativo para la próxima gira y de pronto, el silencio se apoderó de la sala. Los acordes de “Una Aventura” comenzaron y en automático la gente empezó a grabar. “¿Qué está pasand
items.author: Ricardo Diaz
paragraphs: Dos guitarras, un amplificador y una voz melódica. El ensayo se ejecutaba como preparativo para la próxima gira y de pronto, el silencio se apoderó de la sala. Los acordes de “Una Aventura” comenzaron y en automático la gente empezó a grabar. “¿Qué está pasando? ¿Por qué graban esto? ” Ozuna asimiló que el peso de la conexión en vivo, es lo más grande que tiene un artista.

Ozuna, está de vuelta: más honesto, más romántico, más él. En realidad, el boricua nunca se fue pero ahora augura una nueva etapa musical. Su ambición por incorporar más instrumentos musicales, su impacto en la moda y la intención de volver a su sonido de origen, lo sitúan en esta nueva temporada.
Hace unos días compartiste en redes un video de ti cantando en un minimarket. Tu carrera aún no despegaba y simulabas con un micrófono desconectado. ¿Qué estaba viviendo el Ozuna de antes?

En ese video había incertidumbre y para mí, la música era solamente un hobby. Yo tenía un oficio principal y no me gustaba que la gente supiera que yo cantaba, pero a la vez no me molestaba que me escucharan, si lo llegaban a hacer. Algo bien raro en mí.

Estaba feliz en ese momento, tal como lo estoy ahora. Sigo siendo la misma persona: me levanto tarde, llego tarde - se ríe. Creo que es bien especial cuando no cambias tu esencia, sobre todo en la música: en tus letras, en el ritmo, en tu estilo. Creo que como artistas a veces experimentamos tanto, que nos olvidamos de lo que le gustaba al público originalmente.
Hablando de orígenes y tras más de una década de carrera, decides volver a ellos con tu nueva música. ¿Aún lidias con incertidumbre o ansiedad cuando tienes un nuevo lanzamiento?

No, nunca lidio con nervios o ansiedad cuando saco música. Yo desconozco lo que es una pérdida, lo que es un hit. Si la canción funciona o no funciona, me da igual porque yo las hice todas con mucho amor.

Lo que sí puedo notar ahora es que los temas que escribo yo, son los que más conectan. Es algo bien raro porque mi público sí se da cuenta cuando colaboro con amigos y ahora con “Una Aventura” y “Mi Yo De Antes” percibo que mucha gente se está identificando. El saber que yo las escribí al 100% es muy satisfactorio.
Todo artista evoluciona y con él, los temas de sus canciones. Ahora que vuelves a enfocarte en la escritura ¿de qué te gusta hablar?

Algo que tengo bien claro es que mis letras siempre son auténticas, sea el tema que sea. “El Farsante” o “Se Preparó” son canciones muy exitosas y aunque a lo mejor el público masculino no es tan amante de las letras románticas o de las que hacen llorar, ya que no nos gusta hablar de eso, volver al reggaetón romántico es lo que quiero.

Desde septiembre a enero me senté a escribir mucha música, más de lo normal. Ya tengo un proyecto, aún no te puedo decir si va a ser un disco, pero va a tener colaboraciones y va a llevar esa esencia romántica que siempre he tenido.
“Mi Yo de Antes” en vivo con músicos y con un arreglo más íntimo fue algo totalmente diferente a lo que normalmente haces ¿Te ves haciendo un compilado así?

Sí, me gustaría hacer un disco 100% hecho por músicos, crear ritmos que no vienen de una computadora. Creo que mi próxima producción va a ser un álbum completamente de arreglos musicales. Va a ser especial porque sé que hacer esto toma mucha dedicación y disciplina, implica cosas de las cuales nosotros no estamos acostumbrados.

El estilo de Ozuna siempre ha sido un reflejo del movimiento urbano. El año pasado te vimos modelando en el Paris Fashion Week con el diseñador Willy Chavarría. Tras esa experiencia ¿cómo conectas con la moda en tu vida diaria?

Creo que la moda y la música van de la mano desde el día uno en mi carrera. Es un elemento bien importante. Me acuerdo que en 2017 usaba mucho skinny jeans, ahora estamos con los pantalones un poco más baggy y más cortos.

Willy Chavarria me dio una bonita experiencia, me encanta modelar. La gente siempre busca las marcas grandes pero a mí me gusta ver a las que están empezando, lo que viene. De hecho, voy a regresar el próximo año con mi nuevo proyecto con la visión que tienen estos diseñadores emergentes.

Además, estoy creando mi propia marca que se llama “Los Purple Homies”, la cual me ha ayudado a aprender muchas cosas: desde el fitting hasta cómo coser. Prácticamente estoy en una universidad de la moda para poder ejecutar mi propia marca.
¿Iniciar “Una Aventura World Tour” representa una nueva temporada en tu carrera?
Sí, es una época de disfrutar lo que estoy haciendo. Tras tantos años dándole a lo mismo, a veces uno dice: párate, déjame quitarme ese chip que tengo de querer competir y solo trabajar.

Ahora le cogí amor al estudio otra vez, a hacer música. Eso me tomó uno o dos años. No estoy compitiendo ni demostrándole nada a nadie, porque Ozuna es Ozuna. Estoy disfrutando a mi familia, a mis compañeros de trabajo, todo al máximo… al final eso es lo más importante de un proyecto.
La música urbana ha cambiado cómo es que el mundo percibe a la música latina. ¿Qué te gustaría que las futuras generaciones entiendan sobre estas raíces al escuchar tu música?

Siento que el reggaetón en un momento dado, fue subestimado por muchas cosas que se estaban haciendo. A lo mejor no está en el top global de Spotify, pero no todo necesita estarlo para ser bueno. Por ejemplo, cuando Michael Jackson despegó, no había Spotify. Él fue el número uno.

Yo creo que el reggaetón viene más del underground, del baile. No pertenece a ninguna lista, pertenece a la cultura. Estoy seguro que las próximas generaciones lo van a seguir haciendo y reivindicando. Al final del día, el reggaetón sigue vivo, sigue activo, sigue dando hits.
Ozuna arrancó su gira internacional “Aventura World Tour” y recorrerá Europa y Latinoamérica desde junio a diciembre del 2026.

items.title: De pionero a ícono musical: Arcángel cumple 20 años siendo La 8va Maravilla
items.description: En su momento más lúcido, Arcángel celebra 20 años de trayectoria musical con su más reciente álbum “La 8va Maravilla” rindiéndole homenaje a su pasado, presente y futuro. El compilado incluye colaboraciones con Ricky Martin, Daddy Yankee, Beéle, Grupo Firme,
items.author: Ricardo Diaz
paragraphs: En su momento más lúcido, Arcángel celebra 20 años de trayectoria musical con su más reciente álbum “La 8va Maravilla” rindiéndole homenaje a su pasado, presente y futuro. El compilado incluye colaboraciones con Ricky Martin, Daddy Yankee, Beéle, Grupo Firme, Sech, Kapo y su propio hijo.

Con la mente iluminada y un corazón sobreviviente, Arcángel se reinventa una vez más para celebrar el camino recorrido. Siendo pionero del trap en español y una de las figuras que moldeó el reggaetón en sus inicios, Austin Agustín Santos, mejor conocido como Arcángel, le recuerda al mundo que hoy está vigente y de pie tras dos décadas de carrera.

Desde el calor de la costa este y la euforia de arranque de año, nos conectamos con Arcángel para platicar de “La 8va Maravilla”: un álbum que no solamente construyó en un momento de nitidez mental y recuperación física tras una operación, sino que puso en perspectiva su legado como artista puertorriqueño.

Y es que Arcángel y la convencionalidad no van de la mano: esculpir 20 piezas requirió horas de creatividad, introspección y talento. Honrando el título del álbum, y su propio apodo, el boricua viajó el mundo entero para visitar las grandes obras que han forjado la identidadhumana.

Un recorrido de 18 días para visitar las 7 Maravillas del Mundo, seguramente imprimió una perspectiva muy única a “La 8va Maravilla”. Al estar frente a éstas ¿qué pensamientos te cruzaban sobre tu propio recorrido musical?
Para serte sincero, yo soy un tipo al que le gusta leer y estudiar mucho. Yo ya sabía la historia de cada una de las Maravillas, pero solamente había podido visitar una: el Coliseo Romano.

En cuanto a lo musical, cada vez que iba a un lugar, siempre se me ocurría sumarle algo a los temas que ya tenía. Me inspiraron para darles un upgrade a las canciones del disco y como ese viaje lo hicimos en octubre, nos dio tiempo de editar el álbum para sacarlo en enero.

El compilado está lleno de contrastes musicales y me parece que hay un diálogo entre quien eras cuando empezaste en el trap y quien eres ahora: más abierto al pop y la electrónica. Si esos dos “tú” se sentaran a hablar ¿en qué estarían de acuerdo y en qué chocarían?
Yo creo que estarían de acuerdo en todo y no chocarían en nada, porque esa es la esencia de Arcángel. Mi primer disco se llamó “La Maravilla” y cuenta exactamente lo mismo que este último álbum.

Arcángel domina muy bien todas las ramas dentro de la música urbana: ya sea pop, techno, rock, baladas, etc. El primer trap en español de la historia lo hice yo en 2006, llamado “El Pistolón” con Yaga y Mackie; también con “Chica Virtual” tengo que ver, este fue un gran tema de techno en español. Así que no, no creo que ninguno de mis alter ego chocarían.
Ahora que tocas el tema de las baladas, “La 8va Maravilla” está bañado de romantiqueo. ¿Crees que el reggaetón se ha vuelto más romántico de lo que era antes?

Cuando yo inicié ya existía R.K.M & Ken-Y, ellos tenían la exclusividad de lo que era el reggaetón romántico. Yo no te puedo decir que el género ha tomado algún rumbo en específico porque hay artistas que se dedican a hacer ciertas ramas.

Lo que sí creo, es que el género se ha vuelto más comercial. Por ejemplo, hay artistas muy buenos que hacen “malianteo”, que es el reggaetón callejero, pero la gente no los conoce porque ese es el tipo de música que no suele ser nominada a ningún premio. Creo que ya no se reconoce al reggaetón de mata: hubo que fusionarlo con otros ritmos y cambiar la letra para que pudiera ser tomado en consideración.

Como dices, hay cantantes que son icónos de ciertos géneros y en “Lluvia” invitaste a Ricky Martin. ¿Cómo fue encontrarte creativamente con alguien que públicamente has dicho que admiras y que desde otro género también ha representado a Puerto Rico a nivel global?
Mira, cuando tú trabajas con una persona talentosa, no es difícil tener química, musicalmente hablando. El respeto entre nosotros es mutuo y la admiración es recíproca.

Este tema yo ya lo había grabado completamente y cuando estábamos produciendo la canción, dije “esta parte está como para Ricky Martin”. Lo tiré así al aire y mi manejador es bien amigo del mejor amigo de él, así que hizo las movidas pertinentes para mostrarle el tema a Ricky. A él le gustó y dos días después nos invitó a su casa para conocernos personalmente. Ahí me dijo que le encantó y lo demás es historia.

Si hay algo que dominas es producir en el estudio y otra colaboración con la que quizás este proceso fue distinto, es la que hiciste con tu hijo Austin San en “Historia” y “Me Dañas La Mente”. ¿Qué fue lo más inesperado que descubriste en él como artista durante estas sesiones?

Mi hijo está metido en los escenarios y estudios de música desde que nació: incluso yo le cambié los pañales dentro de un estudio, ha ido conmigo alrededor del mundo, estado en diferentes camerinos y en distintas bases desde siempre.

A los 14 años, él me dijo que quería ser cantante y yo le dije que terminara de ser niño primero, que no tenía ninguna necesidad. En realidad a mí no me sorprende nada de él porque lo conozco muy bien. Incluso el tema “Me Dañas La Mente” era una canción suya.

Cuando estábamos produciendo el álbum, me hacía falta un featuring y uno de mis ingenieros me dijo que metiera a Austincito. Yo lo vi perfecto porque amo a mi hijo y es mi sangre. Si yo colaboro con personas que no son nada mío ¿por qué no hacerlo con alguien que vino de mí?

Desde que Daddy Yankee regresó, ha tenido escasas colaboraciones y “Di Amén” es una de ellas. Más allá de lo musical, este tema tiene un peso simbólico muy importante: dos grandes exponentes del reggaetón hablando de fe y de espiritualidad. ¿Qué significa para ti este mensaje en esta etapa de tu carrera?
Para mí es una de las cuestiones más importantes del disco porque si tú haces una producción de 18 o 20 temas ¿por qué no puedes dedicarle uno al ser que nos lo dio todo?

Este fue uno de los tracks que mientras estábamos produciendo, yo escuchaba la voz de Daddy Yankee todo el tiempo. Dije “tiene que ser él". Nosotros tenemos amistad con su relacionista público y de hecho, Daddy es vecino de mi casa en Puerto Rico desde hace 15 años.

Con él estuvimos distanciados unos cuantos años, pero luego nos sentábamos, hablábamos, nos dejamos sentir. Y obvio, en el nombre de Dios todo es posible, estamos rindiéndole respeto, brindándole honor a quien merece todo.

No podemos dejar de hablar de las colaboraciones sin tocar una de las más originales. Se dice que el productor Edgar Barrera te propuso unir talento con Grupo Firme en “Cuánto Cuesta”. ¿Con qué te quedas de esa semana que pasaste al lado de Eduin Caz y el grupo en México?

Me quedo con todo. Esa semana fue espectacular, maravillosa. Me quedo con las ciudades que visité, el tequila, la comida, las personas, los escenarios y con todas las experiencias que viví esa semana.

Mira, que yo he estado en todos lados y he compartido con mucha gente, de verdad que con Grupo Firme es con quienes mejor la he pasado. La energía con ellos nunca baja. Cuando comparto con buenos artistas y a la misma vez son buenas personas, yo me quedo con todo.

Hablando justamente de gente talentosa, tú has sido clave en el camino para muchos artistas del género urbano, entre ellos Bad Bunny. Fuiste de los primeros en creer en su música ¿qué sientes al verlo hoy en este punto de su carrera y qué fue lo primero que viste en él?

Desde que lo conocí lo que más me gustó fue personalidad, aparte de la gran música que hace, porque es un visionario. Él era algo que le hacía falta al reggaetón. En una escena en donde reina el machismo y todo el mundo quiere ser “el más”, llegó un niño que no es de la calle, que no le interesa hablar de ella, que tiene valores como ser humano y que además es muy educado.

Benito se ha atrevido a hacer lo que nadie había hecho. Él está logrando cosas, no solamente para él, sino para todos nosotros que somos parte del mismo género y que representamos el mismo lugar del que él viene.

Haber estado en el Super Bowl como un artista 100% hispano, está pavimentando el camino para futuras generaciones y abriéndoles paso gracias a las puertas que está derrumbando. Tenía que ser él el primero que lo hiciera. Yo me siento bien contento, bien feliz. Siento que cada éxito que logra, me alegro como si fuera mío. Está demostrando que sí se puede lo que muchos de nosotros veíamos como imposible.

“Lúcido” y “Vigente” son temas que conmemoran tu historia y todo lo que implica mantenerse relevante durante estos 20 años. Cuando miras ese camino ¿cuál sientes que ha sido tu mayor propósito dentro del género?
Mi propósito ha sido inspirar nuevas generaciones a que continúen con este tipo de música, ya que los géneros que no producen nuevos talentos, mueren.

Hace 21 años, yo era el artista más nuevo que había en el 2005. Imagínate, si después de mí no hubiesen existido nuevas generaciones, el género ya hubiera desaparecido. Pienso que el futuro de cada género musical, descansa en los hombros de los artistas nuevos.

En el último tema del compilado también hablas de quién eres ahora y de un cierre de capítulo. Al mismo tiempo vas a recibir el “Icon Award” en “Premios Lo Nuestro” y con todo esto ocurriendo ¿cómo se ve el próximo capítulo para ti?

Volvemos a lo básico. Dentro del nuevo capítulo, venimos con el próximo álbum que va a ser de reggaetón. Siento que, como te digo, yo soy un híbrido dentro de la música urbana: navego muy bien todas las aguas, todos los estilos. Ahora quiero darle al reggaetón callejero de Puerto Rico.

Me gustaría sacar dos álbumes más este año. Se acerca la saga de “El Regreso de Los Favoritos” Volumen 3, en donde colaboro con un montón de artistas y no necesariamente todos son mainstream. Hay muchos que sí son estrellas, pero para que el género continúe su camino, incluyo a artistas que hay que apoyarlos para que el mundo los escuche, puedan salir de Puerto Rico y sigan representándonos.

Por otro lado, en 2019 saqué “Historias de un Capricornio” y me gustaría hacer una parte dos. Voy a empezar a trabajar en ambos álbumes simultáneamente, yo suelo hacer mucho eso porque el estudio es mi segunda casa.

También estamos por arrancar la gira de “La 8va Maravilla” y tenemos como cuatro o cinco videos que todavía no hemos soltado: el de la canción “Chula” junto a Beéle, “Historia”, “Lúcido” el cual lo grabamos durante nuestro recorrido por las Siete Maravillas y el video con mi hijo Austin San.
Arcángel celebra 20 años de carrera, 20 años de éxitos y aprendizajes y nosotros con él, un legado irrepetible en la historia y la cultura de la música urbana.
