items.title: Ingrid Bergman and Roberto Rossellini: The Affair That Outraged America
items.description: The whole situation had become such a mess that their marriage had to take place by proxy, through lawyers thousands of miles away. The romance between actor Ingrid Bergman and director Roberto Rossellini was one of the great scandals of the 20th century. They
items.author: Raquel Piñeiro
paragraphs: The whole situation had become such a mess that their marriage had to take place by proxy, through lawyers thousands of miles away. The romance between actor Ingrid Bergman and director Roberto Rossellini was one of the great scandals of the 20th century. They were two married people who had fallen in love and embarked on an adulterous relationship—nothing that hadn’t been seen before, especially in the film industry—but something about their particular situation sparked a wave of international outrage with an intensity that’s rarely seen. There were condemnations from the Vatican, proclamations from the US Senate, insults of every kind, and an avid and destructive interest from the press and the public. There were also some glorious moments, erupting volcanoes, and even plates of spaghetti used as weapons.

This now legendary letter above has become part of film history. It’s no surprise that two artistic sensibilities of the caliber of Bergman and Rossellini would connect through the latter’s films—masterpieces of Italian neorealism that Bergman connected with emotionally and intellectually. “The realism and simplicity of Open City were heart-shocking,” she recalls in Ingrid Bergman: My Story. “No one looked like an actor, and no one talked like an actor. There was darkness and shadows, and sometimes you couldn’t even see it. But that’s the way it is in life…. You can’t always see and hear, but you know that something almost beyond understanding is going on.” Bergman left the movie theater where she had just seen the film on a spring night in 1948 deeply moved. She didn’t know it, but her life had just changed forever.

The world 80 years ago was very different from today, of course, and the actor had a hard time tracking down the director. When she finally did locate him, they began an exchange of letters filled with deep admiration, during which they agreed to collaborate on a screenplay that Rossellini was working on which would eventually become the film Stromboli. The involvement of someone as famous and talented as Bergman should have, in theory, made it easier for Rossellini to raise funds for another film. She was Sweden’s most successful export since Greta Garbo, the Ilsa of Casablanca, and an Oscar winner for her performance in Gaslight. She was admired worldwide for her naturalness and beauty. She was so popular that there was even a reported surge in women choosing to become nuns after the release of another film she starred in, The Bells of St. Mary’s, much to the chagrin of many parents. For his part, Rossellini might not have been well-known in the US, but his revolutionary ability to capture the realities of life on film had earned him a Palme d’Or at Cannes and the admiration of cineasts. He had also starred in various encounters with Italy’s fledgling paparazzi. Married for over a decade, he maintained a relationship that was an open secret, with his lover and muse, the spectacular actor Anna Magnani. Together they were a tumultuous and popular couple—that is, until Bergman appeared on the scene via her letter.

Their relationship was long limited to correspondence, but there was clearly some passion in those letters because, upon arriving at the Hotel Luna Convento in Amalfi with Magnani, Rossellini requested that any telegram or letter from England be delivered to him with the utmost discretion. (Bergman was, at the time, shooting Under Capricorn at the Elstree Studios outside London.) The staff assumed this didn’t apply to his well-known partner, and when they were in the hotel dining room, a waiter approached him and said, in full view of Magnani, “I was instructed that if a telegram arrived for you from England, I should give it to you in private. Here you go.” Magnani had already begun to hear rumors about the relationship between Rossellini and the famous Swedish actor, whom he was said to be planning to offer a role that had been written specifically for her. “Now, is this all right—eh, Roberto?” she asked kindly as she served herself more spaghetti with tomato sauce. “Ah, yes, yes, grazie,” he replied distractedly.
“Good. Here, you can have it,” and she tossed the heap of spaghetti straight into Rossellini’s face.

Magnani’s intuitions were right. When Bergman first arrived in Rome to then travel through the south of the country on her way to Stromboli, the island in the Aeolian archipelago where the film was to be shot, she and Rossellini became lovers: “I fell in love with him because he was so unique. I’d never met anyone like him, so free. He brought new dimensions to life, new boundaries, new emotions, and new horizons. And he gave me a courage I’d never known before.” She had been married for over 10 years to Petter Lindström, a doctor who was her first love, but she hadn’t been happy for a long time—neither in her relationship nor in Hollywood. In fact, she’d earlier asked him for a divorce; he refused to grant it, and since they had a young daughter, Pia, and their cohabitation was proceeding smoothly enough, they continued to live together under the same roof. In the eyes of the world, they were still husband and wife. But shortly before meeting Rossellini, Bergman had had a romance with another tormented artistic figure, the photographer Robert Capa. Since that affair had no major consequences, Lindström turned a blind eye. The story with Rossellini would be completely different. He represented a way out of a marriage and an industry in which she felt trapped. “I think I was just waiting for someone to come along and help me out of that marriage because I didn’t have the strength to go. That was over three years before I met Roberto Rossellini.” What she didn’t realize was how much her decision would turn her world upside down.

Italy would be a revelation for Bergman. Rossellini introduced her to his circle of friends, including figures such as Federico Fellini, and served as the best possible guide on her journey to Naples, Amalfi, Sorrento, and Messina. In Amalfi, the actress decided that this was more than just a passing fling; it was a love intense enough for her to end her marriage and leave the United States. She wrote to Lindström from the very same Hotel Luna Convento where Magnani and Rossellini had their confrontation, telling him that she had fallen in love and was staying in Italy. He refused to accept the news, and his denial would give rise to much of the drama that was about to unfold.

Meanwhile, the new happy couple drove along the country’s roads, which still bore the visible scars of World War II, through one of the most spectacular landscapes on earth. Everywhere the film crew went, crowds cheered them, delighted that the world’s most famous actor had decided to make a movie in their country. At one of the simple hotels where they stayed, Bergman had to leave her room to use a bathroom on a hallway. Fans cheered her on both on her way there and back.

It soon became clear that their partnership was more than just a creative one. Life magazine photographed them holding hands, and the images went around the world. By the time they arrived on the small island of Stromboli, the shoot, with its many ordinary people recruited to perform in the film, was swamped by press from all over the world eager to capture images of the lovers at the foot of the island’s volcano. The role of a refugee who agrees to a loveless marriage in order to be released from an internment camp and then ends up trapped in an unfamiliar world that is as oppressive as the one she escaped came naturally to Bergman. It reflected her emotional state: She was caught between the joy of being in love, the guilt of leaving her husband, and the doubts and pain regarding her 10-year-old daughter, Pia, who remained in the United States. In Ingrid Bergman: My Story, Bergman recounts, “It was absolute hell. I cried so much that I thought there couldn’t be any tears left. I felt the newspapers were right. I’d abandoned my husband and child. I was an awful woman.”

There are images from the shoot in which Bergman is seen in close-up, and behind her are several women in mourning, an oppressive and threatening presence. They evoke exactly what happened to her. The world exploded in anger against its once favorite star. She was portrayed as a lost woman, if not a whore, and an insult to every sense of propriety. Much of the intensity of the reaction was related to Bergman’s previous popularity and her nearly flawless, pristine image. She was seen as an embodiment of a strict Lutheran morality, a sincere and honest woman. (Lindström would later say she was, in fact, a heavy drinker and smoker, promiscuous, and cared only about her career, not her family.) That this almost angelic figure would give up everything to run off with an unattractive, tempestuous Italian director seemed like an unfathomable mistake. Added to this was the intrigue that she was now his new muse, following the landmark films shot with Magnani. And there was also, of course, Pia’s complicated situation. Rossellini prevented Bergman from returning to the United States, fearful that if she went, she wouldn’t come back to Italy, while Lindström refused to let their daughter travel to Italy. The divorce and custody battle became bitter, filled with mutual accusations and animosity. As a result, mother and daughter went two years without seeing each other. And then, after that, another six. This is how Pia, the main casualty of this love story, would recall those times: “I stayed with him [her father], and my mother left. She was offered a dramatic life, full of excitement, with romantic, wonderful love affairs. It was magnificent for her. But not what came of it. I didn’t experience the splendid side of the situation. In other words, I was left behind. That’s why I see things differently. I was part of what was left behind.”

As if there weren’t enough elements to this scandal already, it soon emerged that Bergman was pregnant. Senator Edwin C. Johnson referred to her in the Senate as “a powerful influence for evil.” Some of her friends, however, came to her defense. In 1961, she told Lillian Ross of The New Yorker: “When I gave birth to little Roberto, the whole world started to throw stones at me. But I knew I had friends when I received a letter from Ernest Hemingway saying he wanted to be the baby’s godfather. And when I came to New York to accept the New York Film Critics award for Anastasia, Hemingway said, ‘I’ll come with you and punch the first one in the nose who says anything bad to you.’”

The night Ingrid went into labor coincided with the Italian premiere of Volcano, a film with a plot similar to Stromboli—created by Anna Magnani to compete with her ex’s film and directed by a German émigré to the United States, William Dieterle. Midway through the screening, the press began to leave the theater upon learning that Bergman had gone into labor and been admitted to a clinic. Magnani resigned herself to the situation, knowing that her film could not compete with Bergman’s baby in terms of media interest. Volcano was a critical and commercial failure. And so, in 1950, the boy, whom they named Robertino, was born. The press hounded the hospital relentlessly: One photographer passed off his pregnant wife as a woman in labor by adding padding to her belly; another crawled through a drainpipe to reach the actor’s balcony; others tried to bribe nuns at the hospital with a million lire; and still others, resigned to not being able to get a photo, created montages with Bergman’s and Rossellini’s faces and published them.

The baby’s birth presented a tricky situation. Legally, Lindström could have claimed custody because his divorce from Bergman hadn’t been finalized, which infuriated Rossellini, so they registered the child under Rossellini’s name and that of a “mother whose identity would be revealed later.” Eventually Lindström’s and Bergman’s divorce would be finalized in a Mexican court, where Bergman also decided to get married to Rossellini by proxy. A producer and a lawyer, friends of the couple, stood in for each of them while, on the outskirts of Rome, the real couple stopped into a small church near the Via Appia. “I knelt down and Roberto held my hand and then we went home and told all our friends that now we were married and drank Champagne.”

The couple settled in an apartment on Viale Bruno Buozzi in Rome and spent their summers in Santa Marinella, a town on the coast about an hour by train from the capital. After years speaking a mix of broken English and French, Bergman managed to learn Italian. The twins, Isotta Ingrid and Isabella, were born in June 1952, and the young family enjoyed a period of intense happiness. But their challenges were not over yet, of course. Bergman’s eldest daughter was becoming a teenager and her relationship with her mother was conducted solely through letters. Living with Rossellini wasn’t easy either. At the height of the tension with Lindström, the director had threatened to kill himself by either shooting himself or crashing one of his sports cars into a tree. Moreover, he was jealous, domineering (he let Bergman work only with him), and at times violent. This was all behavior that Bergman appeared to excuse as simply part of his Italian temper. This is how she describes one episode: “Things were flying through the air, I rush up and I took him in my arms and I started to say…and bang, he threw me against the wall so hard I almost broke in pieces. Well, I mean, I couldn’t do anything. Even to get near him was to risk your life.”

And then there was the matter of money. Rossellini, who had grown up in affluence, was used to living the high life, but every single movie he made with Bergman was a commercial failure. In 1956, director Jean Renoir approached Bergman to offer her a role in Elena and Her Men. Rossellini admired Renoir so much that he allowed his wife to work on the film, which finally put an end to the frustrating professional slump she had been stuck in for years. After that, she was offered the lead role in a French adaptation of Robert Anderson’s Tea and Sympathy. This is how Bergman recounts what happened: “Tea and Sympathy is the story of a young boarding-school boy who is afraid he is homosexual. Roberto was always disturbed by any sort of homosexuality. When I wanted to send Robertino to a Swiss or English boarding school, he blew up. ‘What!’ he screamed, ‘That’s where it all starts, in those boarding schools.’…The whole theme was too distasteful to him. It wasn’t the writing or the writer; he just hated the general theme. He also hated the fact that in the play I was going to prove to this boy that he wasn’t a homosexual, lead him into sex. The whole part disturbed Roberto immensely.”

Rossellini tried to forbid his wife from performing in the play, but she ignored him, arguing that she had signed a contract and that she loved the script. He fought back by emphasizing that people would laugh at her and that it would be a flop. On opening night, he snapped at her, “Be prepared when the first intermission comes for half of them to walk out.”

That’s not what happened. She was greeted with a thunderous ovation. “The house went wild. You couldn’t stop them. They were standing up and screaming, standing up and applauding, and the ‘bravos’ never stopped. Then I took my solo bow in the center of the stage, and as I bent over, I turned my head and looked at Roberto. Our eyes met. We looked straight at each other. I knew then my marriage was over even though we might stay together.”

He, for his part, stated: “I separated from Ingrid Bergman because it was impossible for me to continue. We loved each other very much; we had three children…she could return to the industry, but I didn’t feel comfortable in the role of the man whose wife brings home the money. We decided to separate, and that’s why I went to India, as far away from her as possible.” In India, Rossellini began a romance with the wife of his film’s producer, Sonali Dasgupta. Bergman wasn’t outraged when she found out; instead, she calmly proposed a divorce. He insisted on two conditions: that the children never travel to the United States and that Bergman never remarry. She laughed at the absurdity of the requests and refused, saying, “That was just Roberto.” (Shortly thereafter, she began a relationship with the Swedish theater producer Lars Schmidt, whom she married in 1958.)

The custody battle over the Rossellini children was also contentious, almost as much as the one involving Pia. There were mutual accusations of kidnapping and bad faith, and in the end, Bergman ceded custody to Rossellini. The children split their time between Rome and Paris, and Bergman frequently traveled to both cities to be with her children. The couple never completely drifted apart; they remained connected by Isabella’s health issues, including a back operation that nearly left her paraplegic, and the emotional bond that tied them together.

The world changed very quickly, and the former persona non grata won her second Oscar in 1957 for her role in Anastasia, which was accepted on her behalf by her friend Cary Grant. Bergman heard the news on the radio while taking a bath at her hotel in Paris, where she was staying while performing in Tea and Sympathy. She cried tears of joy in front of her son, Robertino, and soon returned to the United States to resume filming. Her rehabilitation within the industry was complete. She became one of the most respected names in cinema across various countries and languages—a living legend. In 1972, an apology was read into the Congressional Record for the attack against Bergman that had taken place in 1950. At the time she stated, “When I left for Italy, there was a senator in Washington who made a speech against me, and he ended by saying that out of Hollywood’s ashes will grow a better Hollywood.” Bergman didn’t realize her mistake, saying “Hollywood’s ashes” instead of “the ashes of Ingrid Bergman” until she later heard a recording of her comments. She laughed and laughed. “A line I had been waiting 22 years to deliver, and I mess it up!”

Vengeance was never a part of Anna Magnani’s plans after her separation from Rossellini, beyond that infamous plate of pasta. She continued her career working with Italy’s top directors and even won an Oscar a year before Bergman won her second statuette. When she was diagnosed with cancer, Rossellini sent her flowers despite the years that had passed. She wrote to him asking him to come see her, and from then on they saw each other regularly. Bergman recalls, “When I found out, I called her to tell her I was happy about what she was doing. The circle had closed: She had the man she had loved above all others close to her again.” When Magnani died in 1973, Rossellini agreed to have her buried in his family crypt, and she still rests there alongside him. (He died in 1977.)
Petter Lindström remarried in 1956 to Dr. Agnes Ronavec, with whom he had four more children. He continued his career as a renowned brain surgeon and died in 2000 at the age of 93.

Over time, Bergman would also be reunited with Pia after many years apart. At age 20, following a failed marriage, the young woman—feeling lost and unsure of what to do with her life—moved to Paris to live with her mother and Lars Schmidt. “I came to see Mom in a new light and fell in love with her. Few young women have such an extraordinary, cheerful, fun-loving mother—always ready to go out and do things, see this or that, go to the movies and the theater, dine out, run around, get up early, and go shopping. She had boundless energy. It was amazing.” Shortly after that, the grandmother of her half-siblings—Isotta Ingrid, Isabella (who would go on to become an acclaimed actor), and Robertino—passed away. Pia decided to go to Rome without speaking a word of Italian and take charge of the household, with a cook and a governess, to get to know them as well as find herself. “That way I’d be doing something and mattering to someone. I spent three years with them. Mom sent me money; I paid the salaries and took my siblings to the dentist, horseback riding, and to their lessons. It was a wonderful experience that, in a way, I needed. I didn’t have a specific place in the world; I couldn’t imagine a profession I felt called to; I felt lost. I needed to put down roots, find a place to live, convince myself that I was useful, help someone, and do something that wasn’t just for the sake of doing it.” Rossellini would visit them at lunchtime, talk on the phone about business, movies, and money, and leave after giving everyone a kiss. Pia continued: “I liked Italy. I was happy to be there. I was glad to have met them and to get to know Roberto firsthand, without relying on other people’s opinions or ideas about what he was like; I’m glad to have met Sonali and everyone else, because it helped me observe and understand everything that was happening, to get a sense of how things had come to be.”

Bergman concludes in her biography: “Someone wrote somewhere about my life with Roberto that I had found a world that for me was probably better than most of us ever attain. And that is true. I did have marvelous happiness with Roberto as well as deep troubles. But trouble is part of one’s life. If you have never had any trouble, if you have never cried, if you have never been really miserable and thought that you could not go on, what kind of understanding would you have for other people who are in trouble?…I think a person who is always happy would be a big bore. And Roberto was never a bore.”
Originally published in Vanity Fair España.

items.title: The 21 Best Thanksgiving Movies to Stream Right Now
items.description: Sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course. But while there might not be a feast’s worth of Thanksgiving movies, there is undoubtedly a
items.author: Savannah Walsh
paragraphs: Sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course. But while there might not be a feast’s worth of Thanksgiving movies, there is undoubtedly an appetite for Thanksgiving fare in film. Look no further than the inclusion of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Miracle on 34th Street or Wednesday Adams’s sinister (if historically-accurate) re-enactment in Addams Family Values for proof that audiences love turkey’s least favorite holiday. Of course, Thanksgiving tends to get a better treatment on TV, inspiring canonical episodes of Gossip Girl, Friends, Master of None, and, of course, A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving.

Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater. Here’s to finding post-meal common ground with one of the titles on this list.
Planes, Trains and Automobiles

This isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing. You know the story: Steve Martin’s uptight marketing executive, Neal, just wants to travel from New York to Chicago for turkey with his family. His plans for an uneventful trip are foiled again and again by John Candy’s boisterous shower-ring salesman, Del, who’s eager to make friends with Neal during their wayward journey. We will never look at pillows—or rental car agents—the same way again.

Don’t let the word Christmas in the title scare you away. This 2016 ensemble comedy starring Danny Glover, Kimberly Elise, Mo’Nique, and Gabrielle Union has undeniable Thanksgiving vibes. Produced by Will Packer and originally sold to Universal Pictures under the title A Meyers Thanksgiving, Almost Christmas follows the dysfunctional Meyers family as the family patriarch, Walter Meyers (Glover), tries to get through his first holiday season after the death of his wife. While it isn’t exactly about Thanksgiving per se, most of the best moments in Almost Christmas—including Elise chasing Romany Malco away from the table with a shotgun, or the whole table having to pretend to like Mo’Nique’s terrible food—take place during large family gatherings around the dinner table. What could be more Thanksgiving-coded than that? With an all-star cast of Black actors that also includes J.B. Smoove, Nicole Ari Parker, Omar Epps, and Gladys Knight, Almost Christmas feels like a homecoming full of your favorite uncles and aunties. And, to be fair, isn’t Thanksgiving almost Christmas?

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting carved up in this holiday slasher. Starring Patrick Dempsey and Tik Toker turned recording artist turned film actress Addison Rae, Thanksgiving begins with a Black Friday sale gone horribly awry in Plymouth, Massachusetts, leading to the death of multiple customers. The following year, a murderous slasher wearing a John Carver mask is wreaking havoc in Plymouth, and targeting Rae’s Gaby and her friends. If you’re not feeling warm and gooey on over the holiday, you might want to throw on Thanksgiving and watch Rae and Dempsey’s Sheriff Eric Newton try and track down and escape the clutches of a grisly murderer.

In Jodie Foster’s comedy, Holly Hunter plays Claudia Larson, who returns home for Thanksgiving after losing her job and learning that her daughter (My So-Called Life–era Claire Danes) plans to spend the holiday with a boyfriend. The family she returns to is filled with colorful performances from Anne Bancroft and Charles Durning as her eclectic parents, Robert Downey Jr. as her misanthrope brother, and Dylan McDermott as a semi-mysterious dinner guest.

Fantastic Mr. Fox isn’t technically about Thanksgiving, or even really about humans. And yet, Wes Anderson’s 2009 stop-motion film, featuring the voices of George Clooney and Meryl Streep, has been labeled a Thanksgiving must-watch. Perhaps that’s because the film, based on Roald Dahl’s classic children’s novel, is all about animals trying to escape the tyranny of farmers—something every turkey not lucky enough to be pardoned by the president wishes it could do around Thanksgiving time. Beyond the war between animals and farmers, Anderson’s rustic color palette filled with burnt orange—and the massive feast that brings a diverse array of animals around a dinner table after they successfully joined forces to steal food from their nemeses—are full of the spirit of Thanksgiving.

At times, the titular April’s (Katie Holmes) fate feels as if it rests on whether she’ll successfully cook a turkey in her crowded Lower East Side apartment. As April prepares to host her suburban Pennsylvania family, the high-stakes nature of spending a day hunkered down with relatives—played by Patricia Clarkson, Oliver Platt, Alison Pill, and John Gallagher Jr.—rushes in.

Sometimes getting families together over the holidays is fraught. In this 1997 moody drama directed by Ang Lee, two affluent Connecticut families unravel over Thanksgiving break as their secrets come to lights. The ensemble cast includes stalwart actors Kevin Kline, Joan Allen, Sigourney Weaver as messy parents, and, at that point, up and comers, Tobey Maguire, Elijah Wood, and Christina Ricci as their even more troubled teens. The Ice Storm, which won best screenplay at Cannes Film Festival, is rife with adultery, substance abuse, as well as surprising turns from a host of talented actors and a sharp early film from one of cinema’s most celebrated directors.
A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving

Nothing feels more nostalgic during Thanksgiving than watching Snoopy whip up a makeshift meal with jelly beans, popcorn, and mountains of buttered toast for all of his Peanuts pals. And Vince Guraldi’s timeless score makes for a perfect soundtrack to your own festivities.

A Thanksgiving flashback provides key context for the complicated dynamics amongst this group of recently-reunited college friends, played by Glenn Close, Kevin Kline, Jeff Goldblum, Mary Kay Place, and William Hurt. Lawrence Kasdan’s film earned three Oscar nominations, including best picture, original screenplay, and supporting actress for Close.

While not a Thanksgiving-themed film, protagonist Nola Darling (Tracy Camilla Johns) invites all three of her potential suitors to a tense dinner on that very holiday, making her memorable decision between them from her head-of-the-table vantage point. This was most of the world’s introduction to Spike Lee, both as an actor and director, and the electricity is still palpable. And if you’ve gotta have more? You can always stream the 2017 Netflix original series of the same name, starring Lee and DeWanda Wise as Nola Darling.

Rian Johnson’s whodunnit has all the trappings of a Thanksgiving movie, without ever mentioning the holiday. There’s family infighting, Chris Evans in a cable-knit sweater, foggy fall weather, and even a political allegory about the treatment of people of color. Also not about Thanksgiving, but worthy viewing for the full family: Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery, which hit theaters last November.

The same year that Merriam-Webster acknowledged Instagram captions everywhere by adding “Friendsgiving” to the dictionary, a movie of the same name was released. True to its titular tradition, a group of friends convenes for a meal that inevitably devolves into chaos.

While not an outright Thanksgiving movie, 1997’s ensemble dramedy contains some of the most sumptuous shots of food ever committed to film. After the death of their family matriarch, a group of disparate relatives must put aside their differences and reconvene for a weekly Sunday dinner. Starring Vivica A. Fox, Vanessa Williams, and Nia Long, Soul Food captures the bonding powers that plates of cornbread, catfish, and collard greens can bring.

This 1976 best picture Oscar winner stars Sylvester Stallone as the eponymous down-on-his-luck boxer, whose fate begins to change with the meeting of his future wife, Adrian (Talia Shire). “To you, it’s Thanksgiving. To me, it’s Thursday,” Rocky tells Adrian as he whisks her away from a disastrous family feast minutes after her brother Paulie (Burt Young) hurls her turkey into the nearby alley. As fans of the franchise, which has debuted several films over the Thanksgiving holiday, know, their Thanksgiving meet-cute will stand the test of time.

Thanksgiving isn’t always about bickering with your blood relatives. Spend Thanksgiving with Instant Family, which stars Mark Wahlberg and Rose Byrne as Pete and Ellie Wagner, an unwitting couple who, overnight, become parents to three foster children. Their decision to become parents happens over a tense Thanksgiving dinner where Ellie’s family shares they don’t think that Pete and Ellie were ever really cut out to be parents. In an effort to prove them wrong, the Wagners wind up biting off more than they bargained for as they become foster parents to three children, the eldest played by Madame Web star Isabela Merced.

Before Greta Gerwig forced Noah Baumbach to write Barbie with her, there was Mistress America. Written by the real-life couple who helmed the billion dollar blockbuster, this 2015 Sundance favorite centers on the unlikely friendship between Lola Kirke’s Tracy, a first-year college student alone in New York, and Gerwig’s Brooke, the Times Square-living twentysomething who will soon become her stepsister. Conflict between the pair gets resolved on Thanksgiving at New York City’s Veselka, a Ukrainian institution where pierogis stand in for the traditional bird.

Greta Gerwig must really love Thanksgiving. The auteur’s Oscar-nominated take on the Louisa May Alcott classic is brimming with cozy, Thanksgiving-esque vibes. Set largely in the weeks before Christmas, the March sisters (Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Eliza Scanlen, and Florence Pugh) and matriarch (Laura Dern) battle wits, trot through the snow, and stage living room plays in a film that feels reminiscent of many a-family gatherings.

“First, let’s give thanks to our families not being here. It’s always easier without the family,” Adam Sandler’s George Simmons, a stand-up comedian who has been newly diagnosed with cancer, says to a group of new friends. In Judd Apatow’s 2009 dramedy, George attempts to revamp his fledgling career in the eleventh hour with the help of aspiring comic Ira Wright (Seth Rogen). At one point, he joins the younger talent’s friendsgiving festivities, where the table is surrounded by stars including Jonah Hill, Jason Schwartzman, Aubrey Plaza, and Bo Burnham.

In one of the newer entries to the turkey day canon, Stephen Karam adapts his 2015 Pulitzer finalist play of the same name, exploring the long-held resentments and deeply-rooted admiration that live in an East Coast family. Jayne Houdyshell reprises her Tony-winning role as Deirdre alongside a stacked ensemble, including Richard Jenkins, June Squibb, Beanie Feldstein, Steven Yeun, and Amy Schumer, all gathered in a drab Chinatown apartment for Thanksgiving.

Prisoners finds Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal teaming up to find a pair of missing girls who were abducted after Thanksgiving dinner in Conyers, Pennsylvania. EGOT recipient Viola Davis also stars in the thriller as the mother of one of the kidnapped girls. Directed by Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, Prisoners is an unconventional and unsettling Thanksgiving film.

Another unconventional choice, Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man is arguably the only superhero movie that doubles as a Thanksgiving movie. While the central action follows Tobey Maguire’s Peter Parker, there’s a pivotal scene set at Thanksgiving dinner that directly follows a heated battle between Spider-Man and the Green Goblin (a.k.a Norman Osborne, played by Willem Dafoe.) Parker and Osborne have Thanksgiving dinner together with MJ (Kirsten Dunst), Harry Osborne (James Franco), and Aunt May (Rosemary Harris). During the meal, Osborne comes to the stunning realization that Peter Parker is, in fact, Spider-Man. Others have already made the case that the first Spider-Man film deserves to be included in the Thanksgiving canon. The way Dafoe carves the turkey is also both sinister and iconic, as is Maguire apologizing for his tardiness because he “had to beat an old lady with a stick to get these cranberries.”
All products featured on Vanity Fair are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

items.title: This Year, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Is Doing Broadway a Little Differently
items.description: This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a big change:
items.author: Chris Murphy
paragraphs: This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a big change: While in the past, viewers would enjoy five or so of the best performances from the current Broadway season, this year, there’s only one big Broadway number. But don’t fret, theater folk. For the milestone occasion of the parade’s 100th anniversary, the powers that be at NBC and Macy’s have put a new spin on their tried-and-true formula, gathering the Broadway community for one supersized performance, featuring more shows and performers than ever before.

The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway shows: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.

The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous. Kitt is no stranger to writing a big production number, having cowritten the Tony Awards opening number “Bigger!,” performed by host Neil Patrick Harris with lyrics by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2013, among other ambitious musical endeavors. Despite his previous experience, a 10-minute, nine-show medley presented a unique set of challenges the composer had yet to tackle.

A total of 133 people are performing in the medley—114 Broadway cast members, 17 dancers, a child actor, and Hough. On top of that, more than 125 other Broadway professionals—including stage managers, wardrobe supervisors, and hair and makeup teams—are on site to facilitate the production, bringing the total number of people involved to well over 250.

“Most important to me in doing something like this—to celebrate this community, this beautiful community that I’m so lucky to be a part of,” Kitt tells me. “Everyone who’s participating, you want them to feel happy and excited about what they’re doing.”

A little over a month ago, Kitt and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby got to work figuring out how to make a cohesive musical number out of nine very different shows. He wrote the first draft of the arrangement over the course of a few days. “It was way too long,” he says. That might be because Kitt had to figure out how to connect these disparate shows musically while also finding room for Easter eggs for theater fans: musical nods to shows that might not otherwise be featured in the medley, including Anything Goes, The Music Man, A Chorus Line, and Kitt’s personal favorite, Into the Woods, whose music kicks things off.

“Into the Woods was one of those shows that made me want to write for the theater,” he tells me. “The downbeat of the prologue is one of the most beautiful musical gestures; every time I hear it, I get goosebumps. So that was really special and important for me to get to plug into, and there are so many others.”

Surprisingly, it will be Kitt’s first time attending the parade in person. “The parade has meant so much to me,” he says. “I’ve watched it for years. I’ve taped it. I’m lucky enough to have shows that have been a part of it. I think that celebrating that relationship and celebrating the history of Broadway and being able to spotlight so many important shows and artists just feels very exciting and gratifying.”

“I’m a tiny little person, but I love to do really big things,” says O’Gleby. A former performer on the West End, O’Gleby moved to the States almost two decades ago to pursue a career as a Broadway performer, dancing in revivals of Brigadoon and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. Now she choreographs Broadway productions like Shucked and, most recently, Pink’s widely celebrated Tony Awards opening number. Given her Broadway bona fides, she’s also intimately familiar with the magic of the parade. “I was lucky to perform on the parade as a Broadway girl and the associate choreographer and dance captain on shows that I was in,” she says. “It was so wonderfully American.”

The first of two rehearsals took place Friday afternoon at Pier59 Studios at Chelsea Piers. Around 4 p.m., as the sun began to set over the Hudson River, Broadway performers from different shows practiced the medley. O’Gleby, wearing silver leather pants and clutching a God mic, was charged with organizing the chaos and managing the more than 100 Broadway performers in the room. Standing offstage between a broomstick and a red Les Mis flag, I could still see traces of green makeup on the face of Wicked’s current Elphaba, Keri René Fuller. Most of the performers gathered had a show of their own to perform in just a few hours, but that didn’t stop them from giving it their all in rehearsal, onstage and off, cheering the other productions along as each got its moment in the spotlight.

Case in point: At the end of the rehearsal, the whole room erupted into cheers for the original cast members from Rent—including original Angel, Tony winner Wilson Jermaine Heredia, and original Joanne, Fredi Walker—who are gathering to perform “Seasons of Love” in the parade. (During the rehearsal, Aladdin’s current Genie, Sherri Shepherd, couldn’t help but mouth along to the words of the seminal song.) “It was that moment of why we’re a part of this community,” O’Gleby says, nearly choking up. “Everyone in the room—stage managers, costume, I mean everybody in the room—the way they were applauding these original cast members and what they gave to all of us as a community, really all over the world, it was incredible.”

At the second rehearsal, on Monday night outside on 34th Street beneath Macy’s giant turkey, the mood remained high even as the temperatures dropped. By 11 p.m., performers were bundled in winter jackets, sweatshirts, and leg warmers, with their character shoes still on. They hugged one another for warmth and jumped up and down, kicking their feet to stay loose between setups. Margaret Cho, who stars as the Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show, danced “The Time Warp” with her Chihuahua, Lucia, tucked into a pouch in her jacket, the dog’s head peeking out.

For O’Gleby, a smooth Monday-night rehearsal means setting each show up for success come Saturday morning and making sure all nine shows are “represented in the most powerful and clear storytelling way that we can,” she says. “This is a huge moment for these shows to sell lots of tickets so everyone gets to keep making their magic every night. And so it’s important to me that each team gets to communicate what they need and what they think would really make their show shine.”

On Wednesday afternoon, Macy's announced that “after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” a disappointing piece of news for those who build their holiday around the annual event.

This is only the fourth time in history that the parade hasn't been held on Thanksgiving: In 1942, 1943, and 1944 it was canceled completely as its trademark giant balloons were repurposed as part of the World War II effort. Compared to those years, a move to Saturday seems manageable, O’Gleby says. “The weather will be what it will be, but we will delight in that and deliver the best."

items.title: Lucia’s Rise: ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Forces Gamers to Grow Up—and Punishes Them With Narrative Consequences If They Refuse
items.description: For the last 25 years, nearly every noxious gamer stereotype had a home in Grand Theft Auto. Juvenile, sexist, crass, embarrassing—people could accuse the games of being these things because the allegations were, in part, true. Beginning with 2001’s Grand Thef
items.author: Joshua Rivera
paragraphs: For the last 25 years, nearly every noxious gamer stereotype had a home in Grand Theft Auto. Juvenile, sexist, crass, embarrassing—people could accuse the games of being these things because the allegations were, in part, true. Beginning with 2001’s Grand Theft Auto III, the series began giving players the freedom to wreak havoc across satirical renditions of US cities. It was an amazing technical feat that only grew more impressive with each subsequent Grand Theft Auto game—and harder to appreciate the more those cities were filled with dick jokes and sex workers.
This, for the most part, suited Grand Theft Auto’s publisher just fine. What business did the company have calling itself Rockstar Games if it cared what a bunch of prudes thought?
But with Grand Theft Auto VI, something has changed. And the game’s staggering launch-day revenue—$3.79 billion—suggests that this change was a welcome one.

Rockstar has executed an astonishing about-face in Grand Theft Auto VI, choosing to build a game around a couple depicted with aching sincerity—from their car-boosting meet-cute to the desperate stickups they commit, with the player’s help. Jason Duval (played by Dylan Rourke) and Lucia Caminos (Manni L. Perez) are a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, out of options and on the run, hoping they can land a score big enough to turn things around.

This earnestness is new for Grand Theft Auto, which historically has had a deep love for pushing buttons. (Its sister series, the Western Red Dead Redemption, has less of a problem with heart-on-the-sleeve storytelling.) Lucia, especially, is new. She’s the first woman you can play as in the series, and by the transitive property, she’s also the first woman that Grand Theft Auto has ever had to take seriously. Doing so changes the entire shape of the series.

Until now, Grand Theft Auto has never really thought much of women. True, the games have never thought much of anyone; Rockstar traffics in a nihilistic comedy that lies somewhere between South Park and a Verhoeven film, a dim view of the United States where everyone sucks. But women, usually, have sucked the most. They’ve been the butts of countless jokes; in the Grand Theft Auto universe, they’ve been nags and drags and sex workers secondary to the men that the games were about. Grand Theft Auto III, a game that barely has a plot, begins with main character Clyde’s girlfriend betraying him after a heist, shooting him and calling him “small time” before running off with the take. It doesn’t get much better from there.

So yes: Lucia is a huge pivot for the series, especially because Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t trust players with her right away. After a brief prologue in which a desperate stickup goes wrong, Lucia is sent to jail and players begin the game as her boyfriend Jason Duval. In addition to doing odd jobs for a small-time crime boss (Stephen Root) and hanging out with your pal (Bobby Moynihan), players have to choose: Are they going to be a good boyfriend? Rockstar Games know they might be making a big ask of their audience, so they slow-roll it. Before Lucia gets out of jail, the game suggests to the player, maybe fix the stairs? Or get a haircut? Buy her a necklace?

In the days since the game came out, many have noted how amusing it is that Grand Theft Auto VI has made caring about your girlfriend one of its first challenges. The game’s “Lucia will appreciate this” notification is its first viral meme, and the source of both incel crashouts (“woke slop … so obvious it was made by women”) and earnest appreciation. (One of the first clips to spread online was of streamer Stable Ronaldo painting Jason and Lucia's bedroom one color before recoiling in horror: What if she hates that shade?)

Lucia is a destabilizing event not just for gamers, but for Grand Theft Auto—a damning yet fascinating example of gaming culture’s priorities on its biggest stage. GTA has always been a series of warring ambitions: violent Rube Goldberg machine, Karl Ove Knausgaard–esque obsession with quotidian details, and thrilling Hollywood blockbuster all in one. These disparate aims are often in conflict with one another, and one way to read the series’ heretofore exclusively male focus is as an attempt to thread this needle. By tossing all of its commentary under the carpet of “satire," Rockstar can also use a veneer of meanness to argue that the games’ misogyny is actually an intentional lambasting, much like everything else in GTA.

But taking a woman seriously, and making her colead with a male character, requires an entire rethinking of what Grand Theft Auto is. “It’s a product of the story we’re trying to tell,” Grand Theft Auto VI codirector Rob Nelson said when asked by The Guardian if this is the first Grand Theft Auto to encourage empathy from players. “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.”

This is an extremely roundabout way of saying that, in this Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar asks gamers to grow up—and punishes them with narrative consequences if they don’t take the game up on the offer.

The funny thing about Grand Theft Auto VI’s gamified empathy is that, like everything else in a video game, it has to teach the player how to accomplish that goal. The game does this through prompting players to do chores, but also through Jason’s characterization. Throughout the game, Rockstar has to convey what its writers believe a well-adjusted man looks like—or at least what constitutes a man well-adjusted enough to earn the respect of a woman like Lucia, who walks out on him when he tries to exclude her from some of his more dangerous criminal activities.

To that end, there are an abundance of moments in the game where Jason demonstrates the virtues of being respectful and maintaining boundaries, several of which are a departure from GTA series norms. There are no sex workers in the game anymore (though there are strip clubs). While Jason and Lucia can break up depending on the player’s choices, there are no other options for committed or casual romance.

The money you steal is ostensibly for Jason and Lucia to use together: so they can get away and start over with their young son, who’s currently entrusted to a relative. Casual conversations between strangers players meet on the road make Jason’s respectful nature both a point and a punchline. There’s one man who’s looking for his missing wife after a night of partying. When he starts to brag about her sexual dexterity, Jason interjects to say, “Hey. Let’s draw a line, bud.”

In some ways, this is all rather embarrassing—though in a different way than the weapons-grade sexism of Grand Theft Autos past. One ought to feel a twinge of shame while marveling at any entertainment franchise for including a woman. Yet Grand Theft Auto VI is being graded on a curve. It has a near-perfect Metacritic score in large part for its depiction of Lucia, and for Jason’s relationship to her. The context speaks to a state of arrested development, both in Grand Theft Auto and in big-budget games writ large.

None of this changes the fact that Lucia really is one of the most well-realized video game characters in a digital city unlike any other. But perhaps her inclusion is less an apology for GTA’s past, and more of a concession to how out of step the series had become with the culture. Because if you’re meant to have empathy for one character, the natural next question is, “Well, what about everyone else?"

Rockstar’s maniacal pursuit of verisimilitude goes a long way here. The game’s animations are so realistic that in GTA VI, shooting unarmed civilians is legitimately unsettling. It’s also disincentivized by a “criminal profile” rating that will mark your character “irredeemable” if you engage in too much wanton violence. (This is not a “game over”—it merely locks players out of achieving a happy ending unless they restart from before their murder spree.) These sorts of limits have become another reliable source of outrage directed at the game, with rage baiters drumming up controversy over Rockstar’s decision to, for example, not permit players to shoot up a nightclub.

This is the tricky reality of encouraging empathy for “those who want to,” as Nelson put it. Rockstar has certain intentions, but so do players—and managing both is the great challenge of making any video game. Empathy is a shock to GTA’s system and to the audience alike.

Replicating humanity with computer software is a daunting and costly task, and one that only Rockstar seems to have the limitless resources to pursue. Those resources—the luxury to work as long as necessary to complete Grand Theft Auto VI, and the obscene amount of money it cost (our only solid figure is “less than $1.5 billion”)—are rapidly dwindling in the video game business, as all available tech funding is vacuumed up by AI companies and private equity loots what’s left. Grand Theft Auto VI may very well be one of one: the most expensive game ever and the last of its kind, the peak of Rockstar’s ambition and also of every big-budget video game. Here, at the end of everything, the biggest of video games has finally decided that it’s time to try empathy. And for a woman, even, should gamers choose (and not all will).

It’s a bit of an indictment of the billion-dollar video game industry that the most expensive game in history is also the first major game to commit to a realistic heterosexual relationship. Grand Theft Auto VI deserves many of the accolades it instantly garnered upon release, but the nature of its accomplishment is not yet fully understood. It’s possible that what Rockstar has built is less a monument to video games’ potential than a magnificent funeral pyre, a testament to how things might’ve turned out if Rockstar’s priorities—and those of everyone chasing after its vision of what video games could be—were just a little bit different.

items.title: Behold, the Most Disastrous Thanksgivings in Sitcom History
items.description: Ah, Thanksgiving. A time for family; a time for food; a time for trying very hard not to overdo it on the Xanax. While we love the holiday, this is a safe space: we can also admit it’s kind of stressful, right?
items.author: Laura Bradley
paragraphs: Ah, Thanksgiving. A time for family; a time for food; a time for trying very hard not to overdo it on the Xanax. While we love the holiday, this is a safe space: we can also admit it’s kind of stressful, right?

But never fear: your lamest Thanksgiving will never compare to the disasters we’ve seen on some of our favorite sitcoms. Because even if you burn every item on the table, we’re guessing you still won’t have to utter the words, “As God is my witness, I thought turkeys could fly.”
Friends, “The One Where Ross Got High”

This episode might be better remembered as “The One Where Rachel Makes a Trifle That Is Also Shepherd’s Pie.” A runner-up from the Thanksgiving-loving sitcom: “The One with All the Thanksgivings,” which gave birth to this iconic image:
Full House, “The Miracle of Thanksgiving”

The Tanners’ first Thanksgiving dinner without the girls’ mother does not exactly go as planned. D.J. forgets to defrost the turkey, and in their efforts to cover her mistake, the men of the house accidentally set fire to the poor bird. Stephanie drops the pumpkin pie. All is lost—until Danny reminds D.J. that her mom would be proud of her for pulling everyone together for a home-cooked meal.
Cheers, “Thanksgiving Orphans”

This is yet another episode in which an undercooked turkey poses a dilemma. The Cheers patrons gather together, since they have no one else to spend Thanksgiving with—but as the gang waits for food, everyone gets testy. The result? The beginnings of a food fight. Diane, in peak form, scolds everyone for being so childish—until Sam hurls some cranberry sauce her way, at which point the battle takes off. The bright side? By the time the war is over, the turkey is ready.
WKRP in Cincinnati, “Turkeys Away”

Mr. Carlson’s idea for a promotional turkey give-away turns disastrous thanks to one major oversight. His idea: give away live turkeys by dropping them out of a helicopter. The problem: turkeys are flightless birds. After Les recounts the horrors he witnessed on the ground, Mr. Carlson delivers one of the best lines in TV history: “As God is my witness, I thought turkeys could fly.”
Seinfeld, “The Mom & Pop Store”

As with most Seinfeld episodes, there are a lot of threads going on here at once. The important one in this case? Jerry crashes a Thanksgiving party, where he accidentally knocks a trophy off the window ledge and damages a Macy’s Thanskgiving Day Parade Woody Woodpecker balloon below.
The Bob Newhart Show, “Over the River and Through the Woods”

An oldie but a goodie: when Bob’s patient expresses anxiety about the holidays, Bob decides it’s best not to leave town—but his wife, Emily, does so anyway, leaving him alone. So he invites the patient, Elliot Carlin, to his house for the holiday, along with one of his associates. They all get drunk, exposing the fact that even the usually straight-laced Bob has a sillier side. Oh, and as you might expect, none of them has a clue how to cook a turkey either. Bob sums up the episode pretty well when he says, “I knew it was going to be bad, but I didn’t know it was going to be this bad this early!”
The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, “There’s the Rub”

This one’s a two-parter in which Will accidentally lands Uncle Phil in jail. No big deal! Turns out, the massage parlor where Will takes Phil in the hopes of healing his injured back is not just any massage parlor. The police burst in after the women offer the two more than just a massage. Thankfully, Phil is able to spring them loose just in time, by laying down the law as only Uncle Phil can.

items.title: Anthony Ippolito Is a Knockout
items.description: Anthony Ippolito Is a Knockout
items.author: Matt Dillon
paragraphs: Anthony Ippolito Is a Knockout

Anthony Ippolito is so good as Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky that within the first few minutes you forget you’re watching someone else. He has the voice, the swagger, the chip on the shoulder, and even the famously droopy face. A baseball player who once dreamed of playing pro, the New York native came up through walk-on parts and a Netflix high school drama, then played Al Pacino in The Offer, a dress rehearsal for this. Directed by Peter Farrelly, the movie follows a broke 29-year-old Stallone, writing a script about a scrappy boxer and then refusing to sell it unless he got to play the lead. The rest is Hollywood history. Here, he talks with Matt Dillon, who plays Stallone’s father in the film, about Brando, painting, and the real Sly.
MONDAY 6 PM OCTOBER 26, 2026 LOS ANGELES
MATT DILLON: So how are you feeling?
ANTHONY IPPOLITO: Honestly, I’m a little tired. How are you?
DILLON: Tired, man. I sometimes feel like it’s all changed so much. The original Rocky came out 50 years ago, but it’s been in the zeitgeist for so long. You knew about Rocky?
DILLON: You weren’t born when it came out, and then there were all those sequels, but you knew about it.

DILLON: It’s crazy how long it’s been since then. If you went back to 1976 when they made Rocky, and you said, “They’re going to make a movie about the making of a 50-year-old movie,” that would’ve put you back to 1926. So it would’ve been a silent movie, right?
IPPOLITO: Oh my gosh, it would’ve been.
DILLON: It’s so crazy to think of that. A few years after Rocky came out I became an actor. I started acting at 14. When did you start?
IPPOLITO: I was doing commercial auditions when I was a little kid, but I started taking it more seriously when I was around 17. When did you start taking it more seriously?

DILLON: I never had any desire to be an actor. It took me a long time to figure out what made me gravitate toward it. There were two things: my curiosity and my imagination. It wasn’t because I needed to be a performer. And if we look at Rocky, a similar thing happened to me as a kid. I remember watching that black-and-white TV in my mother’s kitchen and thinking, “Who is that guy?” It was you, because you were so brilliant in this thing.
DILLON: You really are. You really became him, and not as a caricature. What do you think you would’ve done if you didn’t become an actor?

IPPOLITO: That’s a tough question. Maybe a psychologist. In a lot of ways it’s pretty closely related to acting, and that’s fascinating. I would hate to do a job where I wasn’t following any curiosity. There’s this Picasso quote, “Never permit a dichotomy to rule over your life, making you hate what you do, so you can have fun in your free time.”

DILLON: I like that. Like Bukowski said, “Find what you love and let it kill you.” But you do a lot of things, man. You’re not just an actor. I sense that in talking to you. You didn’t become an actor because you were an exhibitionist or you needed to be a performer. It was something else.

IPPOLITO: Yeah. I’m glad you mentioned Bukowski because I love him and I admire so much of his style, which I also see in your style. Growing up as an actor, I felt like I was living a double life because nobody around me was an actor. I went to a normal public high school. Acting encourages a certain self-awareness and introspection that’s incredibly useful for a young man growing up.

DILLON: You became Sly and then you became Rocky as Sly, right? It’s got to be tricky playing somebody we all know. I love that this thing kicks off early on, establishing his physical challenges with his face, et cetera, and you’re playing with that.
IPPOLITO: Well, you played Brando [in Being Maria], and I can’t not bring that up. You got to give me something about that.

DILLON: The beautiful thing about playing somebody like Brando, or in this case Sylvester Stallone, is that they exist, so there’s a wealth of material to work from. Brando revealed so much about himself. You can’t get away from it, but that’s part of the fun. There were times when I was watching the film where I did really feel like I was watching Sylvester Stallone.
DILLON: You pulled that off. You approached it from the inside. Not an impersonation.

IPPOLITO: That’s a question I was asked a couple times recently. Is that something you were asked about with Brando? Were you worried because he’s someone who has had so many people do their version? You bring such a groundedness to it. I’d imagine that there’s no other way to do it, because Last Tango [in Paris] feels so grounded. It almost feels documentary-esque.

DILLON: It really changed everything, his performance, because it was very personal. He was revealing so much of himself in Last Tango in Paris. I remember [Bernardo] Bertolucci says, “Well, you put up the mask again, Marlon. Drop the mask.” Bertolucci wanted him to lose that, and he did, and that’s what’s powerful. He did it right after he did The Godfather, but you would’ve thought it was before.
IPPOLITO: Wow. You would’ve thought that, because he looks a certain age in The Godfather, which is so convincing.

DILLON: One is a very contained, structured performance and the other is an open exposure. I just had to say yes. When I made my first film, the director, Jonathan Kaplan, used to call me Marlon as a joke, because he got pissed off when I improvised. He laughed about it all the time. Then I would go too far, and he’d say, “Cut the bullshit, Marlon.”
DILLON: I was studying Brando movies by the time I was a teenager, so he was with me in the way Rocky was with me.
IPPOLITO: He’s in the pantheon of the greatest of all time. Even Stallone pulled from Brando. He based a lot of Rocky on Terry Malloy in On the Waterfront.
DILLON: I remember when we did the reading, I looked at you across the room and went, “Okay, we’re in good shape.” The writing’s good, and that makes a big difference.
IPPOLITO: The writing’s really good. Peter Gamble’s able to capture so many things that parallel the original film.
DILLON: Yeah, his writing was authentic. When did you first see Rocky?
IPPOLITO: Oh, man. I was a little kid. I don’t remember the first time, honestly. I saw the sixth one in the theater.
DILLON: You saw Rocky VI in the theater?
DILLON: Listen, you saw more than I did. I never saw six.
DILLON: I think I saw two. Of course, I saw one so many times. Back then, the movie theaters hadn’t all been turned into cineplexes. It was the only movie playing.

DILLON: I probably saw it five or six times. I remember seeing several movies like that, where it was the only movie playing in the theater at the time. You couldn’t say, “Oh, I saw that one, now I’ll go see this other one.”
IPPOLITO: Yeah. Now there’s 10 or 20 playing at the same time.

DILLON: At least people are going back to the movies. I liked watching it again because this is a good movie for now, in a way. There was a sense of community back then. People actually showing up at people’s houses, people knocking on people’s doors, talking to each other, picking up the phone. People are doing less and less of that.
IPPOLITO: Yeah. Another thing that’s very uncommon today is Stallone writing the script long-hand. He wrote it with a Bic pen.
DILLON: So am I. We have the worst penmanship.
DILLON: I also know you’re a painter, and you’re a good one.

DILLON: Thank you, brother. I can draw a little bit, I can paint a little bit. I can’t draw like other people, but you know what? I had terrible penmanship, and lefties were cursed with that, but we have other things. Sly’s a lefty.
DILLON: I played Bukowski’s alter ego in this movie called Factotum They had me writing all the time, and he was not left-handed.
DILLON: Does Rocky Balboa fight as a southpaw? I’m trying to remember.
IPPOLITO: He does, and it’s pivotal. But in the second one, he switches. He goes right-handed because he hurt his eye.
DILLON: What did trainers say to you about that? Not that you’re really fighting in these scenes, but Kevin Rooney trained me a little bit for this thing I did for HBO. I was playing a ’30s boxer.
DILLON: I said, “I’m a southpaw, is that an advantage?” And he said, “No, it’s really not. It just makes for a more awkward fight.” I guess the advantage is you can switch it up a little.
IPPOLITO: It throws people off a little.
DILLON: Did you meet Sylvester after you were cast?
IPPOLITO: I met him only a month before we started.

IPPOLITO: He was great. I was nervous to meet him, but thankfully he was an open book, willing to share a ton of what it was like for him. He was in a dark period before Rocky, so I felt privileged to hear about it from him directly. He also talked about how he learned by being an usher. His version of film school was sitting in the theater every day, watching the same movie 10 times with 10 different audiences and seeing how everyone reacted. That was huge, plus the relationship he had with his father, and the facial paralysis, and the toll that took on him throughout his childhood.
DILLON: He’s a really good writer, man. Did he talk much about his writing?

IPPOLITO: Yeah, and about the other writers who inspired him. He’s a big fan of Edgar Allan Poe. He spoke about how he approached it from a very raw perspective and understood the common man very well. He explored ordinary people in difficult circumstances because he could relate.
DILLON: He does have that gift of storytelling.
DILLON: Did you like working with Peter? I remember that dinner scene when he had a new idea and threw it out at you.
DILLON: I love that. Let’s see what happens, right? Did you enjoy that?

IPPOLITO: I really did. The trick is being ready for new ideas, because you want everything to be fresh. Sometimes you come in with a couple of ideas, but to have an endless well of ideas coming out of Peter— he’s never going to miss a moment. The other night, he said, “If anybody has an idea of how to make this movie better, let me know and I’ll consider it.”
DILLON: He’s great. I felt that spirit on the set. If you had to meet any historical figure or old actor and sit down and talk to him, who would it be?
DILLON: Thank you for mentioning him. You like Bruno Ganz?
IPPOLITO: Yeah. I know you got the opportunity to work with him.

DILLON: Bruno Ganz was a great actor. I did his last film. Sadly, he passed away. When I was very young, I was doing a comedy thing up in Massachusetts, and I saw him in Black and White Like Day and Night, a film about a chess player who goes mad. At the time, that was my favorite movie I’d ever seen. I’m glad you mentioned him, man.
IPPOLITO: He seems like a sweet soul.
DILLON: Yeah, he really was.
IPPOLITO: How about you? Who would you pick?
IPPOLITO: That’s a good call. Why?
DILLON: He didn’t seem to care that much. He was at ease with himself. I guess it really is that simple.
DILLON: So how are you doing with the painting, man?
IPPOLITO: I’m still doing it. We’ve been bouncing around a little bit.
DILLON: I haven’t had time myself, really.
IPPOLITO: You ever paint lying down?

DILLON: No, man. I’m not an anti-painter. My friend says I am an anti-painter, but I’m, as my friend would say, too loose. My whole objective is to make my paintings as loose as those little doodles I do in a restaurant. But my father was a classical portrait painter and all that. Have you studied?
IPPOLITO: Just self-taught.
DILLON: It’s in the blood sometimes. Did you have it in your family?
IPPOLITO: Yeah, my grandfather did a lot of watercolor stuff.
IPPOLITO: In terms of painters, are there a few you really like?

DILLON: I always go back to Georg Baselitz. I like a lot of German expressionism, like [Emil] Nolde. Recently, I was looking at the works of [Jannis] Kounellis. He was Greek, but he was part of the Arte Povera movement in Italy.
DILLON: He was very much a painter, among other things. Who do you like?

IPPOLITO: I like all sorts of stuff, but I really like Eugène Carrière. I got to see some of his work recently in a museum and it was beautiful. It’s very loose and wispy. Everything seems like it’s in a dream. All his work feels like it’s emerging through a fog. Obviously I really like Francis Bacon. That’s powerful stuff, but it’s very dark.
IPPOLITO: There’s tons. Norman Rockwell.
DILLON: His work is soulful. I’m a big Norman Rockwell fan. He actually went to my high school.

DILLON: I always got a kick out of that. He was like me: he didn’t finish. He got in some kind of situation there, but I always thought that was funny because he had this wholesome pure image, but back then it was, “You’re never going to amount to anything, Rockwell. Now get the hell out of here. You’re banished from the school.”
IPPOLITO: Every artist has been shunned in one way or another.
IPPOLITO: He’s very cinematic. He’s great. But anyway, I think we’re—
DILLON: You’ve been talking enough today.
IPPOLITO: You’ve talked too.
DILLON: I have, but not as much as you, man. Hey, brother. Listen, good stuff. Let’s do it again.
Hair: Sonny Molina at Streeters.
Skin Prep: Karina Milan at Twenty-Four Eleven.
Set Design: Peter Klein at 11th House Agency.
Market Director: Nicholson Baird.
Photography Assistant: Soren Demas.
Set Design Assistant: Levi Wolf.
