items.title: Jesse Rutherford Is Performative and He’s Okay With That
items.description: Jesse Rutherford Is Performative and He’s Okay With That
items.author: Ary Russell
paragraphs: Jesse Rutherford Is Performative and He’s Okay With That

Jesse Rutherford is very self-aware. He knows he can be performative, and he also knows that you can’t get enough of it. Shortly after forming in 2011 and releasing their debut record I Love You., The Neighbourhood became the soundtrack to the coming of age of moody Tumblr youth across the globe. And despite cool kids’ attempts at keeping their favorite indie band their little secret, the group ended up with one of the highest-streamed songs in Spotify history with “Sweater Weather,” holding a whopping 5 billion plays. Even after going on hiatus for five years, the band’s popularity never dwindled. If anything, it only made way for a growing number of album deep cuts to become TikTok fan favorites.

Then, in November 2025, they returned with their newest album, (((((ultraSOUND))))), and a hankering to get back on the road. Since March of this year, they’ve been trekking from continent to continent for their Wourld Tour, the band’s most expansive endeavor to date. Before The Neighbourhood’s sold-out show at Barclays Center on Saturday, I met up with Rutherford and his dog, Anthony, backstage to chat about mourning 2011 Instagram, embracing fan nostalgia, and why getting the band back together feels like falling in love all over again.
SATURDAY 5:11 PM NOVEMBER 21, 2026 NEW YORK CITY
ARY RUSSELL: All right, so I’m here with—
JESSE RUTHERFORD: Jesse from The Neighbourhood.
RUSSELL: How’s New York been treating you? Did you land today?
RUTHERFORD: Well, we didn’t land. We drove in. So we got here from Detroit two days ago. I’ve just been chilling. I love it here. It’s probably my second favorite place on earth.
RUSSELL: What’s the first?
RUTHERFORD: I mean, home. I do love L.A.
RUSSELL: Have you watched the show? Is it accurate?
RUTHERFORD: It’s so accurate that it makes people like me uncomfortable. But I think it’s really good.
RUSSELL: Can you do a cameo? You’re so L.A.
RUTHERFORD: I mean, if they’re going to ask me, that’s on them.
RUSSELL: Rachel Sennott, if you’re reading this–
RUTHERFORD: I did meet Rachel Sennott and she was really sweet.
RUSSELL: When you come to New York, do you get the opportunity to explore? Do you have any spots you always go to?

RUTHERFORD: Probably pretty basic spots. I’m actually staying in Brooklyn this time and that’s a new experience for me, which I know I’m so late to the game. You could look at me and be like, “I bet I know where this guy goes.”
RUSSELL: I’ll admit I’m a Bronx girl, so some parts of the trendy Lower East Side vibes are off my radar.
RUTHERFORD: You’re way out of my league.

RUSSELL: Come to the Bronx. If you’re with me, you’ll be fine. I don’t want to get too much into the early days because everyone that’s going to be reading this knows about you. But there’s one thing that I haven’t been able to get out of my head that I really hope you can answer. Why’d you decide to use British spelling when you were naming the band?
RUTHERFORD: Because the American one was taken. But I really like that we did that and I’m just a cornball, so I love being able to say, “Can’t do it without U” kind of thing. [Laughs]

RUSSELL: That is so “millennial optimism” core. Also, to be honest, it’s better SEO because if you have a band that’s called The Neighborhood and someone looks it up, no shade, but a gajillion things are going to pop up.
RUTHERFORD: Bro, even with the U in it, for many years, it was a pretty hard band to search.
RUTHERFORD: It’s true. I mean, hey, we’ve been very blessed. And now if you search The Neighbourhood spelled that way, at least on my Google, it’ll come up.
RUSSELL: When you were first starting the band, what were your first impressions of everyone?

RUTHERFORD: Well, we were all friends before we even started the band. I probably had some sort of a man crush on all of them at some point in time. I met Brandon [Alexander Fried, drummer] first, we went to high school together. I was tapping on my desk playing a drum beat, and when I stopped from the back of the classroom, he hit a fill on his desk and I turned around, and I saw him, and that was the first time I ever laid eyes on Brandon.
RUSSELL: Love at first sight.

RUTHERFORD: Yes, and then the other three boys I met all together. They were like The Three Musketeers. So they were a couple years younger and I had just kind of seen them around at shows because we all played in the local music scene, hardcore metal music. I remember seeing Zach [Abels, guitarist] and being like, “Who’s he?” Because he just looked hot and had good style. Then we eventually became friends and the first day we ever hung out, it was immediate and we never left each other’s side from that moment.
RUSSELL: I don’t know if they’ve ever told you, but what would you guess were their first impressions of you?

RUTHERFORD: I was always opinionated, because I would do my own thing and have my own little style and shit. So in my little town, it was kind of like, “What’s this guy’s deal?” I got bullied for sure, but I kind of got away with just being my own character. So Brandon just took me for who I am. The other boys knew me from another band that I was in. They were a little younger and I was a little older and my band was doing pretty okay in town. I mean, it was just local.
RUSSELL: No, local bands are sick.
RUTHERFORD: Of course. And so I don’t know how cool they thought I was, but they definitely knew me.
RUSSELL: How did you feel being a local celebrity, people knowing who you were, knowing your music?

RUTHERFORD: It went in waves because when they first met me and I was playing in bands, there was a moment where I felt a lot of love and a lot of respect from the others and I definitely felt good and confident. Then I stopped making that kind of music and I started rapping.
RUSSELL: Oh, I’ve heard this.
RUTHERFORD: And it went full opposite. I mean, that’s when I went through the most bullying and harassing and it got pretty brutal at times.
RUSSELL: Did you get beat up or something?
RUTHERFORD: Kind of. Somebody spit on me once, really vile things.
RUSSELL: Oh my god, that’s one of the worst things you could do to someone.

RUTHERFORD: Pretty degrading. I’m not going to say I deserved it, but that’s just what came along with trying something different in the area that I grew up in. I mean, I grew up in a suburb. Maybe it’s changed a little bit in the past few years, but I think the intro to a lot of young people making music is making rap music on Garage Band and putting it on SoundCloud. Everybody, no matter where you’re from, what you look like, that ended up being kind of the gateway music genre. I was just a little bit early at the time. Yeah, so I was clowned on, but I mean, it was corny.

RUSSELL: I mean, it builds character in a way. There are certain stars now who are very unprepared for the level of criticism that you’re going to get online. And to have that as a trial run to see if you can handle it is really important.
RUTHERFORD: It’s a blessing.

RUSSELL: I hear a lot of stories about artists who feel like they had to leave home in order to get the impetus to pursue that creative endeavor. Outside of the fact that California is a music mecca, why do you think it was so important for you to stay?

RUTHERFORD: Oh, good question. Hold on, I never thought about this. I guess the simple reasons, family and friends. I get to travel for this job, and every time I get back to L.A., I’m pretty stoked. It feels very natural there for me. It was funny because during the fires, it was scary. We were actually making a record at the time and I remember we came back and the sky was all fucked up. We all were talking in the studio and I was like, “I don’t know, should we get out of here and go somewhere else?” And we were all kind of just like, “Nope.”
RUSSELL: “We need each other.”
RUTHERFORD: “Fuck our lungs, I guess. We’re just going to keep rocking here.”
RUSSELL: So you could never see yourself being bi-coastal?
RUSSELL: Where would you be bi-coastally?
RUTHERFORD: Here. [Rutherford’s dog, Anthony, sits in Russell’s lap] What are you doing? Oh, he’s trying to cuddle up.
RUSSELL: Oh my god, I’m winning at life right now.
RUTHERFORD: Honestly, more than ever, I’m pretty serious about getting a place here again.

RUSSELL: Do it. Get an apartment in the Bronx. [Laughs] So it’s been 15 years since you formed the band. What is something that you miss about 2011 and what’s something you were so happy to leave behind?

RUTHERFORD: Well, it was a different political climate. I mean, it was probably a trick, but I really liked the trick and the illusion that things felt better. Our radars weren’t broken yet, and we’re all fucked up now. Everything is just entertainment now. Everything is just on the same platform and I’m competing with a model and a politician all at the same time.
RUSSELL: And it’s the attention economy.
RUTHERFORD: I do like TikTok a lot, but social media back then, I was having more fun for sure. Early Instagram—bomb.
RUSSELL: When it was casual. That’s what the kids say, right?

RUTHERFORD: It was creative and it wasn’t maybe as serious. I always took it pretty seriously. I’m a MySpace kid, so I grew up creating my layout and customizing everything, and I really liked that part of it. The Facebook era was so boring to me, so I was so excited when Instagram came and it was like there was a style to it.
RUSSELL: Well, now we have dumps. But at the time, you could only post one photo and one caption. It’d be a stupid little selfie, but we were together in that.
RUSSELL: You were talking about the political climate and the very daunting attention economy. Does that existentialism ever bleed into your music?

RUTHERFORD: It’s always present in my mind and there’s definitely songs that are directly about it. I don’t think people would know, but the minute I would tell you, you would listen to it and go, “Oh my god, that is what it’s about.” But that’s part of how I like to write too, where I assume everybody thinks every song I write is about a girl. They’re not, but it’s all up for interpretation and that’s fine.
RUSSELL: Is there a specific song that you can point to?

RUTHERFORD: Well, I hate saying this because people should have their own interpretation of it, but I’m also just going to be honest with you, “Here We Go Again” on Chip Chrome [& The Mono-Tones], the deluxe, that song is about my feelings as far as–

RUSSELL: How fucked we are. So you were obviously on hiatus as a band. When you came back on this tour and released a new album, there was obviously a huge wave of fans in deep nostalgia. Was it intimidating to come back and want to put forth new music knowing that there are going to be people that are nostalgic for what you guys were before?

RUTHERFORD: I was ready for it at that time. As this year has progressed and as we’re almost at the end of this tour, I’ve been saying to the guys, “Okay, this was the nostalgia run and next year we could move forward a little bit.” That being said, I’ve got to be real, we’ve been doing this for 15 years. We’re very lucky to still be here and very lucky that people know any of our songs, let alone as many as they do. Do you know how fun it is to sing a song and everybody’s singing it back to you? It’s the most lit shit ever. We still have more to offer. The next record will be something different because now we’re back, and we’re comfortable again doing all this shit—the playing, the photos, the interviews, the performing, the writing, whatever, all of it.
RUSSELL: Are you guys working on new music now?

RUSSELL: Exclusive. I’m so excited for that. So I’m obsessed with the track run of the album (((((ultraSOUND))))). “Start” feels like a dam breaking where immediately it’s like you’re hit with this wave of instrumentation, which is fitting for coming back from a hiatus. And then when it ends with “Stupid Boy,” it feels like a downward spiral, like we’re ending something. Can you walk me through how you decided the tracklist and what order it was going to go in?

RUTHERFORD: Well, “Start,” there were conversations about it. I would always be like, “Bro, I’m sorry. Just take the song off if we’re not going to put it at the very beginning.” It’s the only way it could work, or at the end, but that would’ve been too obvious. We’re pretty conscious of the tracklist, mainly just on a vibe and feeling and usually what songs we think—Well, I can’t even say that because whatever ends up on the record, all of us vouch for. And because of the way things have gone historically, we never know what people are going to like. Fucking never. We’ve tried to call the single and we’re wrong almost every time. So who knew “Zombie” was going to be a standout track?
RUSSELL: I’m always someone for the deep cut. I mean, I love singles, but maybe it’s the inner pretentiousness of—
RUTHERFORD: Being a discoverer?
RUSSELL: When you started this band, you were in your early 20s and now, not to call your age out, you’re in your mid-30s.
RUTHERFORD: I am. It’s official.
RUSSELL: Coming back on tour, in what ways does it feel like a return to boyhood with the band?

RUTHERFORD: I mean, I get to be like Peter Pan. We do get to be like boys out here and it’s brought us together again. We’re really close with each other and you don’t really have the choice when you’re traveling and you’re essentially married to the people you’re working with and you’re mixing friendship, and creativity, and business, and all these things. It can get complicated. We’ve always put our relationship first. When you’re making music with people, it’s super intimate. That crush that I had on everybody early on feels very back to me.

RUSSELL: Something that’s interesting that you do is when you sing fan favorite, “Baby Came Home 2/Valentines” and you’ll change the lyrics. Is that pre-written? How do you decide what show is going to get the new version?
RUTHERFORD: No, I got to cut that shit out though.
RUSSELL: Why? Everyone loves it.

RUTHERFORD: Because I have said some shit and kind of crashed out. Now, no matter what I say, people are like, “Oh, it’s about this.” And I’m like, “Oh, fuck. No, it’s not.” But I get it, and that’s on me to be responsible, I guess. But bro, I’m just feeling it and probably just being performative. I’m literally performing.
RUSSELL: News flash: performing man is performative. [Laughs]

RUTHERFORD: I’m just in it and freestyling shit. A lot of the time, there’s really not that much thought behind it, which again is why I should probably chill because people have their interpretations of it and then it does affect my life because I wake up the next morning and I see people posing like, “He’s doing it again.” I’m like, “No, that was not ‘doing it again.’” But okay, I understand.

RUSSELL: Lesson learned. So I love your new song, “Why’d You Have To Leave?” It’s melancholy and yearning, just how I like my Christmas music. So my final question is: what do you want for Christmas this year? Don’t say world peace.

RUTHERFORD: I got a house recently, and I’ve never been a host and I love being able to have people over. I’m trying to get better at cooking. I made meatballs last year and that was pretty bomb, but I think I could do it better.
RUSSELL: So get Jesse Rutherford a cookbook for Christmas?
RUTHERFORD: There you go. Yeah, that’s a better answer.
RUSSELL: [To Anthony] Do you want to sign off? Bark bark?

items.title: Geena Meszaros and Ethel Cain Bond Over Having No Eyebrows
items.description: The Body’s Geena Meszaros and Ethel Cain Bond Over Having No Eyebrows
items.author: Ethel Cain
paragraphs: The Body’s Geena Meszaros and Ethel Cain Bond Over Having No Eyebrows

What do you get when you mix one part Sissy Spacek in Carrie, one part cult leader, and one part Dance Moms? The answer could only be Geena Meszaros’s character Lisbeth in the new hit Netflix show The Body. Just don’t call her evil. While the actor knows it’s easy to dismiss the uprooted teen as a bad seed, what with the whole covering up a teammate’s drug overdose and whipping the rest of her dance troupe into a religious psychosis thing, at the end of the day, Lisbeth’s still just a girl who wants to feel loved and included by her peers, and that desire can drive you to do some pretty crazy things.

That outsider’s need to belong is a quality Ethel Cain resonated with in Lisbeth from the jump, and what made the musician want to call up Meszaros to find out more about her process of transforming into this disciple of god-cum-wannabe Regina George. Together, the pair discussed unlikable characters, fan theories, and why having no brows is a canon event in every hot girl’s life.
THURSDAY 2PM NOVEMBER 19, 2026 LOS ANGELES
ETHEL CAIN: Hi, Geena. How are you? Nice to meet you.
MESZAROS: I’m good. Thank you for doing this.

CAIN: Of course. It’s such an honor. I literally just watched the show three days ago and I posted about it on Tumblr, and then my manager texted me the next morning and was like, “Do you want to do this?” I was like, “Absolutely. Are you kidding?”
MESZAROS: I know. Everyone’s been sending me your review.
CAIN: I finished it at 4:00 in the morning and I got on and I was like, “Oh, my god. I’m obsessed with this.”
CAIN: So it’s such an honor. I’m so excited to chit-chat about it.

CAIN: I guess I’ll start with the first question that popped into my head. I feel like there’s been such a thing in the past few years where people say, “Y’all always say that you want a weird girl, but y’all can’t even handle so-and-so.” And I feel like Lisbeth falls into that so, so well. I searched The Body on Tumblr and I was reading everybody’s posts about it, and I think so many people were trying to put Lisbeth in a box. But she’s so complex, and probably the most complex character on the show. So I was going to ask, do you feel like people are handling her with the level of nuance that maybe you portrayed her with? Do you feel like people are getting what you were putting down for her?

MESZAROS: I think they’re finally starting to. I think the first people that watched the show, they had an idea already of what they thought she was. It’s been really interesting actually how many people cannot separate me, Geena, from Lisbeth.

MESZAROS: But I think the cool people that matter can see her nuances. But I’m surprised. I really empathized with her all the way through. Even in her more questionable moments, I still didn’t find it that hard to empathize with her. I think as more people watch it, hopefully more people will get her.
CAIN: I was really fascinated by how many people were either like, “I hate her. She’s such a villain,” or like, “Oh, she did nothing wrong. She was just misunderstood.”

MESZAROS: The crazy theories, like that she’s drugging people. I’m like, “Where are you pulling that from? That’s insane.” But I take it as a compliment when they’re like, “She’s pure evil. I hate her.” It is really funny to me though that I’ve never been compared to you in my entire life, and then suddenly without eyebrows I am.

CAIN: I will say though, I’ve seen a couple pictures of me where the light hits my eyebrows, which I pluck very thin, and I do look like I have no eyebrows. So I can understand the confusion. But I really resonated with the response to Lisbeth because when I was creating Ethel Cain, in my head, she was so much more of—not a villain, but she was a little, fucked up character. And so many people I think were kind of doing the opposite where they were projecting this sanctified—

CAIN: Purity victim on it. I was like, she goes through a lot of bad stuff, but she’s also this homeschooled girl who wants to be included to the point that it makes her go a little crazy. She’s very aggro and very weird. People talk so much about wanting complex characters, but then they can only really comprehend a perfect character who hasn’t done anything wrong, or this is a villain and we have to hate her. It’s like there’s really no space for truly weird girls.
MESZAROS: Even just normal humans who are in the gray area.
CAIN: Literally, which is most of us.

CAIN: But so many people rely on these archetypes like, “You’re a good person, you’re a bad person,” and it’s always been fascinating to watch that lack of nuance when we’re dealing with characters, especially characters who are as nuanced as Lisbeth. I haven’t seen a character like her on TV or in a movie in a while.

MESZAROS: Me neither. I was so excited to play her because she never accepts being a victim. I feel like anytime people are maybe rude to her or she’s being bullied or whatever, she just flips it on them.
MESZAROS: Exactly. I respect Lisbeth, honestly.

CAIN: Did the character come to you in that way, or did she come to you maybe a little differently and then you shaped her into your own? Do you feel like she changed a lot over the initial reading of the script to your performance of her?

MESZAROS: Definitely. Well, I didn’t get to see the script when I was auditioning. I only had the sides, and for some reason she was just really funny to me, and I guess nobody else thought she was funny. Once I got the role and I learned more about her, I actually listened to a lot of your music. Obviously behind the scenes, she’s very much a preacher’s daughter, but she definitely evolved and I didn’t get the later scripts for a while where she’s doing more questionable things. So it was actually quite easy to keep the empathy for her all the way through. I can’t grasp the people who think she’s purely evil. As far as villains go, she’s really not that bad. They cannot handle anything.

CAIN: I was reading in an interview this morning while I was eating breakfast that you were talking about how much you loved playing her to be so flawed and you enjoyed creating this girl who has all of her deeply rooted reasons for why she is the way she is, but ultimately, she does do a lot of bad things. And I was going to ask, as you progress through your acting career, is there any kind of archetype of character you think you’d really love to sink your teeth into playing, whether it’s a young adult heroine or a Clarice from Silence of the Lambs?

MESZAROS: I mean, yes and yes. I think with acting, I need to play a complicated character. My parents divorced when I was a baby, and they both really villainized each other growing up. I think that I just understand gray areas really well, and I feel like I can bring something genuine to those characters. But then at the same time, I’m like, “What if I did something totally different? What if I was so likable and just shoved that right down people’s throats and then they were all confused?” That could be fun. But I’m actually scared of watching horror because it really sticks with me.
CAIN: Really? That’s so interesting.

MESZAROS: But it’s what I want to do. I get way too caught up in it, and I can’t stop thinking about it. But I like the impact that they have, and I think they have the best female characters in horror.
CAIN: Oh, yeah. That actually leads perfectly into my next question. Did you find yourself dwelling on Lisbeth a lot even when you weren’t filming?

MESZAROS: She fully possessed me, even just my body language. I’m already very awkward and wormy, but I exaggerated it a bit with her and now it’s stuck in me. Maybe it’s just the real me actually feeling comfortable too.
CAIN: You’re channeling each other.

MESZAROS: Yeah. But on the weekends, going grocery shopping and stuff, and people would always look at me a bit weird. Without the eyebrows, and normally I just kind of dress like a homeless person, I think they were a little bit alarmed. But I really don’t think the eyebrows are that scary.
CAIN: They’re really not. I had no eyebrows for three years when I was younger.
MESZAROS: I’m not the first person to have no eyebrows.
CAIN: Literally, I feel like the no eyebrows is kind of a canon event when you’re a hot girl.
MESZAROS: You have to. Now, I’m like, “I want to play something where I have to shave my head.” I would love to do a crazy transformation.
CAIN: That’d be really sick. So you’re Canadian and you filmed in Canada, correct?
CAIN: Is it far from where you’re from?
MESZAROS: Where I live is further west. It’s kind of above Montana, I guess.

MESZAROS: Alberta. And then Toronto’s on the other side of Canada. So it was much different because Calgary’s not a huge city like that. It’s more spread out, a lot of suburbs. Then Toronto was a big, busy city.
CAIN: Yeah. I’ve only been to Vancouver and Toronto. I finished Preacher’s Daughter in Toronto.

CAIN: But my next question is, in that first episode where Lisbeth is talking to Anya by the fire, she mentions how her dad talks about the religious experiences and how she feels like dancing is part of that. So I was going to ask if on a meta level you feel that way about acting. Does it feel like a performance that you do, or does it feel like something heavier and more spiritual?

MESZAROS: It definitely is a spiritual thing for me. I know when a project’s right for me in my gut, and I felt that way about Lisbeth right away. I go into a vessel mode, which maybe is not healthy. But it’s also kind of the opposite for me where, instead of putting on a performance, I feel like I can unmask in a way and just be free to do anything without any judgment because it’s not me doing it, you know?
MESZAROS: It’s cathartic almost, but I feel like I really absorb the character. So it would be cool to play someone that was a real person that existed.
CAIN: Maybe it’ll find you at the right time.
MESZAROS: I feel like it will. This role kind of just found me also. It really emphasized my belief that things will find you when they’re meant for you.
CAIN: Absolutely. I remember there was this interview with Brian Cox, who played the father in Succession. I don’t know if you watched Succession.
CAIN: I surprisingly really liked that show. That’s not my usual TV show, but I really liked it.
MESZAROS: What is your usual TV show? What do you like watching?
CAIN: I just watch a lot of horror.
MESZAROS: That makes sense.
CAIN: I love to watch a drama. I love to watch stuff that’s really—I don’t want to say gruesome, but I like gritty.

CAIN: I was honestly surprised because The Body is not my usual show. I’m very picky about campiness, and I think The Body is the best version of it, and I got immediately hooked on it. But what Brian Cox said in this interview was I think somebody else in the show was going on and on about method acting, and then he roasted his co-star and was like, “Acting is acting. You show up and you do the job and then you go home.” And I don’t act, but I think maybe some actors have that kind of mindset of you just show up, and you say your lines, and you give a good performance. But I feel like if I got into acting, I would want to be consumed by the role.

CAIN: I mean, I felt so consumed by Ethel Cain when I was making the albums, and I moved to Alabama, and lived in this little house in the middle of nowhere. It was so fun to be completely taken over.
MESZAROS: That’s really cool.
CAIN: It’s very spiritual.
CAIN: Acting just looks like it feels good to do. You disappear into it.

MESZAROS: I took acting classes, and they just didn’t work for me. I find if I’m in my head too much and thinking too much, I’ll do the work ahead of time, and then it’s kind of like, “Okay, now I am her.” I don’t even know how to explain my process really.
CAIN: No, I get it. I feel like the only way I’m able to work is when I’m on autopilot, because if I think about what I’m doing, the whole thing just falls apart.
MESZAROS: And you have to stay human. If you’re thinking too hard about it, it’s just not human anymore.
CAIN: Yeah, I agree. Do you have a favorite scene that y’all filmed? Maybe one that you feel like encapsulates Lisbeth’s character the best?

MESZAROS: I did really love the scene in the first episode at the fire pit with Anya. I feel like she’s being so honest there. And maybe she loses her way, but I think that really is the core of Lisbeth. Her whole idea of religion was just pulled out from under her, and I feel like when you don’t have any sort of belief in anything bigger than yourself, you get so lost and you do crazy things. I think it shows her heart is not evil and black and empty.
CAIN: One thing I think The Body does well is—I’m kind of reluctant to call anyone a protagonist or an antagonist because I think everybody is.

CAIN: Even among those of us who like to exist in the gray area, your brain still wants to do that kind of categorizing thing. I was like, “Okay, Anya’s kind of neutral, Elise is maybe the antagonist, and Lisbeth is the protagonist.” Then, as the show progressed, it was like episode three or four where I started to be like, “Wait. Is Lisbeth getting set up to be the bad guy?” I was so confused by the dynamics that kept shifting. Then by episode eight, I said to my sister, “Anya is so trifling. I cannot believe her.”
MESZAROS: I’m thinking Anya’s the real villain.
MESZAROS: You’re watching it correctly. But they really wanted it to be like that. There are no clear boundaries around anything, and it’s really your own interpretation.

CAIN: Do you feel like there is a moment in the show where Lisbeth goes from being the outcast girl who just wants to be friends with these girls? Is there a specific moment where she switches and goes, “I can get what I want, and I can pull a fast one on these girls, and I can be in control”?

MESZAROS: That’s such a good question. I do think there is maybe the catalyst shift for her when she’s in the car with Anya and Anya suddenly needs her help. I think she’s kind of clocking like, “Oh, this girl actually doesn’t have it all together, and I can bring something to the table here.” But I really don’t think that she has a master plan. At the start, she’s really observant and hypervigilant and sees when things could go wrong, and protects herself by flipping the table a little bit. She’s clearly a little power hungry later on, but I think that car scene is a big thing for her where she’s like, “Oh, I actually do have some power here.”

CAIN: I really do feel like she didn’t have a master plan. She would see an opening and think, “I can take this.” It’s fascinating to watch her roll with the punches and become more confident as her power grows over the show and realize what she’s capable of.
CAIN: All that to say, it was such an interesting nuanced performance, and I was really fascinated, and also so flattered, to have our darling characters compared in some way there.
MESZAROS: People are going to die at this interview.
CAIN: I think Lisbeth and Ethel Cain would get along very, very well.
MESZAROS: Me too. Season two, you’re in the show as Ethel.

CAIN: Yeah, I’m the ghost of her. She’s like 15 years dead at that point and Lisbeth starts seeing her in visions. Anyway, hopefully this will just be the first of many chats. Hopefully our paths will cross again at some point.
MESZAROS: This is the highlight of my whole entire life.
CAIN: I’m so happy and honored. Yeah, like I said, hopefully we’ll get to chat again in the future.

items.title: Ziwe Presents
items.description: The comedian surrounds herself with this season’s finest gifts.
items.author: Interview
paragraphs: The comedian surrounds herself with this season’s finest gifts.
World peace, thanks for asking.
What books are you gifting this season?
Parable of the Sower by Octavia E. Butler, Beloved by Toni Morrison, Between the World and Me by Ta-Nehisi Coates, and my book, Black Friend.
Malcolm X, Dr. Strangelove, Network, Triangle of Sadness, and Election.
What’s your favorite Robert Pattinson role?
I’m a Robert Pattinson traditionalist. I love Good Time, I love Twilight.
What wellness trend needs to die?
The idea that wellness is a trend. Health is wealth. Hashtag!
What’s the greatest length you’ll go to for beauty?
I get chemical peels twice a year. It makes my face shed like a lizard, but my skin looks like a baby.
How do you sleep at night?
What would you ask Santa if he came on your show?
How much do the elves get paid? They should unionize. Know that the elves have representation and an ally in me.
Can you have your cake and eat it too?
Whatever carries the most food. But if you’re talking about in bed, I’m tiny. So, big spoon.
What was the worst gift you ever received from a partner?
One partner gave me dog supplies. I love my dog, but I don’t believe a dog’s gift should supersede my gift. But who’s going to complain about free stuff.
What’s the best way to train a pet?
How do you know when it’s time to log off ?
It’s always time to log off.

items.title: This Shygirl Playlist Gets Us in Our Feelings
items.description: This Shygirl Playlist Gets Us in Our Feelings
items.author: James Bunting
paragraphs: This Shygirl Playlist Gets Us in Our Feelings

Somewhere between the feeling of Tokyo drifting on a freeway and free-floating in space lies SHYGIRL’s music. We first spoke with the British singer slash DJ back in 2024 when she crafted us the ultimate night out playlist amid the release of her EP Club Shy, and now we’re back for a second helping. This time around, her new album SWALLOW! is less focused on the party girl side of things and more on the mature, vulnerable, and complex woman she’s become. SHYGIRL’s music is growing up with her, with lyrics dedicated to themes of personal growth and falling in love. As her hypnotic beats interwoven with ambient layers plays, we find ourselves lost in the SHYGIRL multiverse. —ISABELLA SOCCI
What’s your favorite song on SWALLOW!?
It changes all the time. They’re all different parts of me, so choosing one feels a bit like choosing a favorite version of myself. Depends who I am that day.
Don’t make me choose! I love them both for different reasons. The UK knows where I come from, but there’s something about the energy in America that’s completely infectious.
Bluetooth or wired headphones?
Which side of TikTok or Instagram Reels are you on?
Definitely more of a Reels girl.
How do you unwind after a show?

I think people assume I’m always ready for the afterparty, but sometimes I just want to be somewhere quiet with people I love. There’s something quite nice about coming down from all that energy and just being myself again.
I don’t smoke, so I’d leave.
What are you ordering to the studio?
An Aperol Spritz, obviously.
What’s been the most challenging part about making this album?

Learning to take my time. I’m naturally quite impatient and I’m used to working instinctively, but I wanted this album to exist beyond one moment or one feeling. I started making it when I was in a really happy place, and I wanted to give myself the space to explore that properly rather than rush to finish something. I think another challenge has been allowing myself to be more vulnerable. People often have quite a fixed idea of who I am or what my music represents, and I wanted to explore parts of myself that maybe haven’t always been as visible. Sometimes the hardest thing is allowing yourself to be understood in a different way.
Both! I use one for listening to albums and the other for making my own playlists. Different purposes, different moods.
What made you decide to drop SWALLOW! now?

I started making this record at the end of 2023, around the time I turned 30 and fell in love. I was in a really good place and wanted to make something that reflected that. It’s probably the most emotionally open I’ve ever been in my music. I didn’t want to rush it. I wanted to live with those feelings and allow the music to evolve alongside me. It feels like the right time now because I’m ready to share that side of myself.
What’s your cry in the car song?
What’s your least favorite song to perform?
I don’t think there’s one I dislike, but my relationship with songs changes over time. Some songs take on a completely different meaning when you’re performing them years after writing them.
What’s the one genre you just can’t get into?

I don’t really believe in limiting myself by genre. I’ve always listened to everything, and I think the most exciting music happens when you stop worrying about what category something belongs to. If it makes me feel something, I’m interested.
Who’s an artist you’d drop everything to collaborate with?
What does the future of SHYGIRL look like?

Hopefully, something even I can’t predict. I’ve never wanted to be tied to one version of myself. Every project has been an opportunity to explore something different and I think SWALLOW! has opened up even more possibilities for me creatively. I want to keep making things that excite me, challenge me, and allow me to connect with people in different ways. I don’t think I’ve even scratched the surface of what I want to do.

items.title: Watch Goo Goo Dolls’ Complete NFL Halftime Show
items.description: It’s a Black Friday miracle. After NBC angered fans by not showing the entire halftime performance by the Goo Goo Dolls during the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills game on Thursday night, the Bills dropped the band’s complete set online.
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: It’s a Black Friday miracle. After NBC angered fans by not showing the entire halftime performance by the Goo Goo Dolls during the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills game on Thursday night, the Bills dropped the band’s complete set online.

For their 10-plus-minute performance at Highmark Stadium in Buffalo, the Goo Goo Dolls played “Iris,” “Broadway,” and “Slide.” Instead of airing the entire thing, NBC opted to let Mike Tomlin and Mike Tirico chew the fat about Aaron Rodgers, much to the annoyance of many viewers.

Fans in attendance at the game praised the rainy performance, with some going so far as to call it “one of the greatest shows ever.” NBC ended up running only about 30 seconds of the band’s set on their broadcast. One fan wrote, “Aaron Rodgers ruins one last thing as NBC airs Tomlin interview instead of Goo Goo Dolls concert.”
Steven Van Zandt wrote on X, “They are a great band. That was badly handled and disrespectful.”

Goo Goo Dolls were one of several artists performing across NFL halftime shows on Thanksgiving. Earlier in the evening, Wu-Tang Clan took the stage in Detroit at Ford Field during the Chicago Bears match-up against the Detroit Lions.

The New York hip-hop group, joined by Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith on drums, kicked it off with “Triumph” from their 1997 album Wu-Tang Forever. The rappers also showcased a medley that included “C.R.E.A.M,” “Da Mystery of Chessboxin,” and “Bring Da Ruckus.” Notably, Ol’ Dirty Bastard’s son Young Dirty Bastard performed his father’s lines off 1995 single “Shimmy Shimmy Ya.”

Later, Miranda Lambert showcased a medley of her hits during the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles game at AT&T Stadium in Dallas. The Grammy-winning singer took the stage to perform “Snakeskin Boots” (sorry, no Ella Langley cameo), “Kerosene,” “Gunpowder & Lead,” “Mama’s Broken Heart,” and “Little Red Wagon.”

items.title: Amelia Dimoldenberg Tears Up in Final Episode of ‘Chicken Shop Date’
items.description: Don’t cry because it’s over. Amelia Dimoldenberg aired the emotional final episode of her long-running YouTube interview series Chicken Shop Date, concluding the show by wiping away a few genuine tears.
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Don’t cry because it’s over. Amelia Dimoldenberg aired the emotional final episode of her long-running YouTube interview series Chicken Shop Date, concluding the show by wiping away a few genuine tears.

Instead of enlisting a celebrity to join her on the series, Dimoldenberg opted to make acclaimed Belgian relationship therapist Esther Perel her guest for the finale. “For my final date, I wanted to do something different,” the host shared on social media. “I wanted to end Chicken Shop Date by showing another side of myself, in the most truthful way I could think of.”
For the episode, Dimoldenberg shed her usual persona and got real with Perel, explaining why she had decided to bring the show to its conclusion.

“I think I have to end the show to meet somebody,” Dimoldenberg told Perel. She added, “I definitely would love to meet someone that wasn’t a celebrity, if I’m being honest. It seems very intense to go out with a celebrity.”
Perel encouraged Dimoldenberg to imagine she is having a conversation with Chicken Shop Date itself, which leads to an emotional monologue and a tearful farewell.

“Thank you for allowing me to be where I am today,” Dimoldenberg told Perel as the show. “I’ve learned so much. I’ve grown up so much and I’ve had so much fun. But I feel now trapped in a cage of my own making and I’m ready to try something else. I never thought I would be able to say goodbye. I thought you would be part of my life forever.”
She added, “It was quite a shock to realize that doesn’t need to be the case. And now I feel kind of liberated in the farewell, in thinking there could be another path.”

Since 2014, Chicken Shop Date has shown the British hostess going on “dates” (read: cringy interviews) with Daniel Kaluuya, Ed Sheeran, Charli XCX, Phoebe Bridgers, Cher, Billie Eilish, Sabrina Carpenter, and many other celebrities. In September, she announced this would be the last season.

“I never thought I’d stop Chicken Shop Date,” Dimoldenberg wrote. “I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it’s now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one.”

“To me, the show is my very own romcom and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch,” she continued. “I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes.”

items.title: Kate Middleton Reflects on ‘Lonely’ Cancer Journey in ‘Heal’ Documentary Clip
items.description: Kate Middleton shared footage from her upcoming documentary, Heal, which sheds light on how she dealt with her cancer diagnosis.
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Kate Middleton shared footage from her upcoming documentary, Heal, which sheds light on how she dealt with her cancer diagnosis.

In the clip, shared on the Prince and Princess of Wales’ Instagram account on Friday, the royal says in a voiceover, “Navigating cancer or any longterm illness is a lonely road. But it’s clear we’re not carry life’s challenges alone. My illness has brought me alongside so many others navigating their own journeys too. This has become so much more than a personal or solitary experience, but really a collective one.”

Middleton can then be seen joining a cancer support group, Shine Cancer Support. “Genuinely, meeting you all here today really means a lot to me because it’s just lovely to be able to share my personal experience, but also hear your stories and be able to connect with others who’ve gone through something similar,” she tells her fellow group members.
She adds, “I haven’t really explored this outside my family walls, really. So thank you for allowing me the time to do that and the open space to explore that. I really appreciate it, so thank you.”

Heal: A Princess of Wales Story will air Nov. 30 on NBC, a day after it premieres on the BBC. The documentary follows Middleton as she reflects on her cancer battle while completing the Three Peaks Challenge — climbing the tallest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in the span of 24 hours — this past June in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, the hospital where she was treated; proceeds from the distribution of Heal will also benefit Royal Marsden.

The news of Middleton’s initial diagnosis was disclosed to the public in March 2024, following an abdominal surgery in January. In a video statement, Middleton said, “At the time, it was thought that my condition was non-cancerous,” referring to her surgery. “The surgery was successful, however, tests after the operation on cancer had been present,” she added.

By September 2024, the Princess of Wales revealed that she had completed the treatment. “The cancer journey is complex, scary, and unpredictable for everyone, especially those closest to you,” Middleton wrote at the time. “With humility, it also brings you face to face with your own vulnerabilities in a way you have never considered before, and with that, a new perspective on everything.”
In January 2025, Middleton announced, “It is a relief to now be in remission and I remain focused on recovery.”

items.title: Former Buzzcocks Drummer Phil Barker Dead at 65
items.description: Phil Barker, drummer for British punk rock band the Buzzcocks from 1992 through 2006, died on Nov. 21 at age 65 on the Isle of Wight, England. His death following a battle with an unspecified form of cancer was announced by the band on Nov. 26.
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Phil Barker, drummer for British punk rock band the Buzzcocks from 1992 through 2006, died on Nov. 21 at age 65 on the Isle of Wight, England. His death following a battle with an unspecified form of cancer was announced by the band on Nov. 26.

“We’re saddened by the news of the passing of our longtime drummer Phil Barker,” the band wrote on their website. “He died peacefully in his sleep on Saturday, November 21, 2026 on the Isle of Wight, after a five-year battle with cancer. He is survived by Deb, his wife of 26 years.”

They continued, “Phil joined the band alongside bassist and childhood friend Tony Barber in 1992, backing Pete Shelley and Steve Diggle. He was integral to our success throughout that era, and left the band in early 2006. Just good memories. He will be missed.”

The Buzzcocks were founded in 1976 by Pete Shelley and Howard Devoto, who left the band sthe following year. The group released three albums before disbanding in 1981. They reformed in 1989 and released their fourth album, Trade Test Transmissions, in 1993. It was during this era that Barker joined the lineup as drummer alongside bassist Tony Barber. He collaborated on five albums with the group prior to Shelley’s death in 2018.

Diggle paid tribute to Barker on social media, writing, “I’m remembering the good times Phil and you were a great Drummer. Thinking of you Debbie and family. Tonight we play st Petersburg Florida and I will dedicate songs and the whole show to you Phil.”

During his career, Barker also recorded with Slaughter Joe and The Modern Folk Quintet, occasionally working under the alias Phil Phuture. During the 1980s, he played with Lack of Knowledge. More recently, he performed with Crass vocalist Steve Ignorant in Stratford Mercenaries and punk band Dirt. The Buzzcocks have continued releasing music and touring since Shelley’s death. Barker left the group in 2006.

Local record shop Triple A Records paid tribute to Barker on Facebook. “We’re very sad to hear our brilliant friend Philip Barker has passed away,” they wrote. “Phil drummed on our favourite Buzzcocks records and was a keen and generous supporter of the shop. We’ll be playing some of his music today as we think about his cheery visits. RIP mate x.”

items.title: Watch ‘Sesame Street’ Pay Homage to Mariah Carey’s ‘All I Want for Christmas Is You’
items.description: Mariah Carey‘s 1994 hit “All I Want for Christmas Is You” is the gift that keeps on giving. This year, the characters from Sesame Street paid tribute to the holiday tune with their own whimsical version, titled “All I Want for Christmas Is U.”
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Mariah Carey‘s 1994 hit “All I Want for Christmas Is You” is the gift that keeps on giving. This year, the characters from Sesame Street paid tribute to the holiday tune with their own whimsical version, titled “All I Want for Christmas Is U.”
In the clip, shared today, Abby Cadabby, Grover, Elmo, and Cookie Monster sing about the all-important letter “U,” which is their top wish this Christmas.

“If we had no U for Christmas, there’d be no U words you see,” the colorful muppet sing. “We could not unwrap the presents underneath the Christmas tree/ Without words that start with U, the holiday would not feel right/ We couldn’t even untie ribbons/ Or untangle Christmas lights/ Want to unbox Christmas but we can’t/ Won’t you help us understand/ Don’t know what we’ll do/ All we need for Christmas is U!”

Carey’s hit typically returns to the top of the Billboard Hot 100 each year. The song has topped the Hot 100 for 22 weeks since it first reached the spot on the Dec. 19, 2019. This year, however, Carey has seen some competition from Ella Langley, who took the record for chart-topping appearances in September when “Choosin’ Texas” scored its 23rd week at No. 1 on the Hot 100.

Carey, the undisputed queen of Christmas, kicked off her holiday season on Nov. 1, which means there’s still time for her record to prevail. And this year, her festivities even include a Santa-themed Barbie doll.
Sesame Street debuted its 57th season on Monday, Nov. 23. It’s available to watch via Netflix and PBS Kids.

items.title: The 6 Movies You Shouldn’t Miss on HBO Max This Month
items.description: As the year winds down, the saga of HBO Max continues to be one of the most unusual on streaming. On the one hand, it’s been embroiled in WBD-Paramount-Skydance merger nonsense, but it also remains arguably the best non-Criterion streaming service when it come
items.author: Brian Tallerico
paragraphs: As the year winds down, the saga of HBO Max continues to be one of the most unusual on streaming. On the one hand, it’s been embroiled in WBD-Paramount-Skydance merger nonsense, but it also remains arguably the best non-Criterion streaming service when it comes to classic movies. And for more recent stuff, it’s the exclusive home of new A24 releases (including one of the company’s most underrated this month), and of course it has HBO Originals, including a searing doc that just premiered. Is it the best streaming service? The diversity of the few entries below certainly makes a case.

One of Cameron Crowe’s best films has grown into something of a punch line (“Show me the money,” “You had me at hello,” everything that cute kid says), but it’s actually a character-driven romantic comedy that holds up incredibly well a quarter-century later. Tom Cruise plays the title character, a sports agent who is pushed into starting his own agency while he falls in love with a single mother, played by Renée Zellweger. It’s sweet, smart, and funny. ➽ Streaming now.
National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation
Director: Jeremiah Chechik

A movie so funny that it can be watched any time of year, this family favorite was the second sequel to the classic Vacation. Chevy Chase returns as Clark Griswold, who suffers a wave of setbacks around Christmas, from annoying relatives to problematic lights to a boss who ends up taking him for granted. There’s a reason this is the Vacation movie that has been the most watched since the franchise became popular, especially during the holidays, when it leads a wave of classic Christmas flicks now on HBO Max. ➽ Streaming now.
Rise of the Planet of the Apes

Any list of the best modern action trilogies needs to include the rebooted Planet of the Apes series that started with this excellent blockbuster over a decade ago. James Franco plays a man who raises a genetically engineered chimpanzee named Caesar (Andy Serkis, who gives an all-timer mo-cap performance), who starts the revolution of the primates over their human captors. It’s a phenomenal movie. Both excellent sequels are also on HBO Max, along with 2024’s Kingdom, a restart of the series. ➽ Streaming now.

HBO Max added a bunch of horror movies in October and November, and this is easily one of the best, an essential genre flick that changed everything when it dropped almost three decades ago. Reinventing the slasher genre, Wes Craven and Kevin Williamson crafted a brilliant mystery that owes as much to Agatha Christie as it does Jason Voorhees. It’s a perfect horror flick, one that launched a franchise still rolling today. ➽ Streaming now.

The director of Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie had two movies this year worth a look. The second was this comedy biopic that takes two chapters from Anthony Bourdain’s Kitchen Confidential and brings them to vibrant life thanks to lived-in performances from Dominic Sessa, Emilia Jones, Leo Woodall, and Antonio Banderas. It’s a memorable coming-of-age story because we know where this coming would lead. ➽ Streaming now.

A critical hit at festivals like Sundance, this powerful doc was buried in an underpromoted HBO premiere on a Tuesday night in November. Dig it out to watch the moving story of the Harlem Park Three, a trio of young men convicted of a murder they did not commit. A meeting with the witness that falsely put them away for decades makes for one of the most emotionally powerful nonfiction segments in any film this year. ➽ Streaming now.
