items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Recap: Dead Girl Walking
items.description: Here’s how you know I’m not watching screeners ahead: Last week, I confidently guessed that Hannah was at the door when we ended on a cliffhanger, completely ignoring the fact that Mia’s return had already been spoiled by the season trailer. (Look, she could h
items.author: Louis Peitzman
paragraphs: Here’s how you know I’m not watching screeners ahead: Last week, I confidently guessed that Hannah was at the door when we ended on a cliffhanger, completely ignoring the fact that Mia’s return had already been spoiled by the season trailer. (Look, she could have been a ghost, okay?) It’s a little deflating, but I should make it clear that my disappointment with the reveal — despite my love for Krysten Ritter! — is not why I’m declaring this the weakest episode of the reboot so far. “Out of the Past” is a confusing and largely repetitive hour that does little to move the plot forward. At the halfway point of an oddly aimless season, the last thing Dexter: Resurrection should be doing is spinning its wheels.

But back to that cliffhanger. When Mia was found hanged in her cell last season, I assumed she’d been taken off the board for good, and given Dexter’s shock, so did he. Nevertheless, here she is in the flesh, explaining that Charley helped fake her death by bribing the coroner and orchestrating an escape. “Charley spared me because I had morals,” Mia says. At one point, Lady Vengeance did target rapists and murderers exclusively, and while we know she’d since moved on to innocent victims, Ms. Brown apparently missed the memo. That’s all in the past, though. “I want to get back to my roots, to when my kills had purpose,” Mia tells Dexter, and who better to teach her than the Bay Harbor Butcher? Yes, Charley didn’t just resurrect Mia — she also told her the truth about “Red,” and sent her Dex’s way.

I need to take a moment here to acknowledge how little sense this makes. If Mia got her start killing bad guys, what does she need to learn from Dexter? And why would he even entertain the idea of working with a woman who blinds men and tortures them to death? We’ll later learn how little Dex actually trusts Mia, but we see him and Harry debating whether or not she deserves a second chance, which means that on some level, he’s sincerely considering making her his protégé. To do so, he’ll need to teach her the Code — and lay down some ground rules. Dexter says they’ll have to keep things professional and not get “entangled,” which is a polite way of saying “naked.” “We’re too.. combustible,” he explains. As much as I enjoy Ritter and her performance as Mia, she has the unfortunate disadvantage of returning to the show after some explosive chemistry between Michael C. Hall and Uma Thurman. That’s a tough act to follow, and it makes the alleged sparks between Dexter and Mia much less convincing.

The two begin stalking their target: the New York Ripper. (I really don’t think Dex needs any help taking down an elderly man in a wheelchair, but hey, Mia’s already in town.) “Framt’s exactly the kind of pervert I would have taken out when I first started,” she says as they eye him from across the street. Of course, they still have to vet him to make sure he fits the Code, and because Dexter has already done his fanboy shtick with Framt, Mia steps in for a one-on-one with the Ripper. The show at least acknowledges that she’s a well-known serial killer who everyone thinks is dead, but I don’t buy that she could simply brush off her resemblance to Lady Vengeance. Krysten Ritter has a very distinctive face! Whoever Framt thinks Mia is, it takes all of two minutes before he shares that if he were the Ripper, she would be too old for him. “But if you have a daughter…” he suggests. Okay, yes, they can go ahead and kill this guy — if they can get to him first, that is. As Dexter and Mia continue to track Framt, they see Sam McCormick, the father of a Ripper victim, open fire on their target.

Turns out he’s a terrible shot and only manages to graze Framt’s leg (which, of course, he can’t even feel). But this is still a problem for New York’s finest, who continue to be in their flop era. Before taking matters into his own hands, Sam had gone to Detective Wallace for help, only to learn that she was no longer working the Ripper case. When he later shoots himself at his daughter’s grave, that’s another life that weighs on Wallace. And now, adding insult to injury, Framt is requesting 24-hour police protection. Meanwhile, Harrison and Fiona are called away to a murder scene. While securing the perimeter, Harrison stumbles on a bullet casing with fingerprints belonging to Nicky Nine-Fingers, a suspect in mob killings the cops have been trying to lock up for years. Now, Harrison has finally delivered the evidence that could nail him … and then the bullet goes missing. They’re back to square one, with the rookie cop forced to take the blame. As I said, flop era — and I haven’t even mentioned the NYPD’s complete lack of progress in the FBK case. No wonder Harrison is Team Let Dexter Cook.

Back at Dex’s apartment, Dexter and Mia drink red wine while looking at his blood slides, which is like third base for serial killers. They lean in to kiss but get interrupted by Harrison, who has apparently forgotten how to knock. (It does amuse me that Dexter appears to live in a sitcom apartment, where someone is constantly barging in without notice.) Harrison does have useful intel, at least — Framt’s police protection starts tomorrow, so if Dex and Mia are going to kill him, they’re going to have to do it now-ish. And no more almost kissing!

Dexter takes his new protégé to an abandoned subway station with a retired train car to transform into a kill room for Framt, a former MTA employee. As they deck the halls with plastic wrap, Dexter’s voiceover muses, “Even if this all ends tonight, there’s something nice about working with a partner, if not in life, then at least in crime.” It strikes me as woefully naïve, especially when Mia asks if she can have a little torture as a treat. Dex reminds her that they don’t want to become like the monsters they target. “Is this how Harry felt instilling the Code in me, channeling my energies for good?” he wonders. As soon as Dexter lets Mia get a closer look at his etorphine needle, I find myself yelling at the screen, because of course she immediately injects him with it. “Did you think I would ever let you get away with it?” she hisses. And then, perhaps just as obviously, Dex injects Mia with the real etorphine needle and knocks her out. He always knew it was going to go down like this.

I hate to be the logic police, I really do, but I have some more questions. If Dexter was always preparing for Mia to turn on him, why was he talking to Harry about taking her under his wing? Why was he, mere moments ago, reflecting wistfully on the meaning of teaching Mia the Code? In addition to being a retread of the “Dexter takes on a protégé” storyline that we’ve seen in multiple seasons past, I can’t get over how much of this episode is an attempt to misdirect the audience. Sure, I suppose Dex wanted to believe Mia could redeem herself while simultaneously prepping for her inevitable heel turn, but it reads more like trying to pull a fast one on viewers.

Strapped to the kill table, Mia reveals that she knows Dexter framed her for a murder his son committed, because Charley told her. “Charley’s the bad guy here,” Mia insists. “She played us against each other.” True as that may be, when Mia shares that she was going to lure Harrison to the kill room and torture him to death while Dexter watched, it’s clear she is also the bad guy. I have to say, I don’t buy the Charley twist either, and no, that’s not just my sadness about the ship being over (R.I.P. Dexley!). From the moment we met her, Charley’s disgust for serial killers has never felt like a put-on, so the idea that she’d ally herself with torture-fiend Mia doesn’t quite track. Regardless, the partnership is dunzo, as Dex plunges a knife into Mia’s heart. “Final rule of the code,” he says. “Don’t get emotionally involved.” The moment might hit harder if Mia had been back for more than an episode of mild flirtation.

While The National’s “About Today” plays, Dexter heads out on the Slice of Life Too to dispose of Mia’s body. When her phone rings from inside a trash bag, he sees that it’s Charley calling. “Hello, Mia,” she says as he picks up. “Is it done?” Dexter isn’t just angry about Charley turning on him — his feelings are hurt, and to make matters worse, she immediately clocks it. Charley calmly explains that she’s still making amends. “I simply thought Mia was the lesser of two evils,” she says. Again: huh? Whether or not she approves of Dex’s methods, he gets rid of serial killers, the very people Charley wants disposed of. If Mia had killed Dexter, she would have gone on killing true innocents, and she would only be able to do that because she got sprung from prison. Wouldn’t Charley have had those deaths on her conscience, too? I guess it’s a moot point. Dexter warns Charley that he’ll kill her if he ever sees her again, dashing any hopes that the rest of this season would focus on his revenge. But if Mia’s return wasn’t designed to set him on a new mission, where do we go from here?

• More questions, sorry. Did Charley fake Mia’s death behind Prater’s back? And when exactly did she clue her in on the Bay Harbor Butcher’s true identity? And why didn’t she seem more prepared for the possibility of Dexter winning? I realize I’m being extra nitpicky this episode, but Charley is methodical, and this plot felt sloppy.

• Speaking of which, Dex was being so careless with Mia, though given how he handled Al, that’s not surprising. Presenting your knives to a woman you’re pretty sure might want to kill you? Come on now.

• It’s an episode light on FBK, who I wish were emerging as a more defined antagonist by now. His big scene has him visiting a priest for confession. “Have you been paying attention to what is happening out there?” he demands. “Nobody cares. And if God does exist, he doesn’t give a fuck either.” Fair enough!

• Is Fiona working for the mob? At the crime scene, Harrison sees her getting yelled at by a guy who looks like a made man (not to stereotype!). Later, we learn that she’s the one who pocketed the missing bullet casing. I don’t think Fiona is a crooked cop — maybe she borrowed money from the wrong person?
• “What the hell did we do before Ring cameras?” Harrison asks. “Welcome to the world of living in a surveillance state,” Fiona says. For copaganda, this show is pretty progressive!
• Wallace assigns Harrison to Framt protection duty, then gives him her cell number so he can keep her in the loop. Looks like she’s found a way around being off the Ripper case.

• In the interest of ending on a positive note, I’m loving all the deep Dexter lore this season. In this episode alone, we get flashbacks to Lila starting a fire, Dexter knocking Rita’s abusive ex unconscious, and Dex murdering pedophile choirmaster Mike Donovan, his very first kill on the series.

items.title: Yellowjackets Recap: Reality Bites
items.description: You think a 19-month stint in the wilderness is hard? Try returning from the horrors of a cutthroat cannibal cult, only to have a mom on your case and a curfew to uphold.
items.author: Erin Qualey
paragraphs: You think a 19-month stint in the wilderness is hard? Try returning from the horrors of a cutthroat cannibal cult, only to have a mom on your case and a curfew to uphold.

A curfew isn’t actually stopping any of the Yellowjackets from doing whatever they want, but most of the survivors’ mothers are hovering like they might lose their kids again at any moment. Who can blame them? It surely feels like a miracle that their children have returned after all this time, and there’s certainly no normal way to welcome your trauma-stricken teen back to society. “Human Interest” shows us the variety of different ways that the mothers of Wiskayok are attempting to reconcile their own feelings while trying to help their kids readjust.

As per usual, Lottie’s parents are entirely unsure of what to do with her. When she won’t get out of the car upon returning home — she stays in there for days, maybe? — Lottie’s mom eventually comes down and gently coaxes her out, telling her that whatever she experienced will fade with time. Lottie doesn’t want things to fade. So, her response is to dutifully go to bed, wake up in the middle of the night, and climb out onto her rooftop in an attempt to commune with the elusive “It”. She is devastated that she can’t feel “It” anymore, which is probably due to a combination of not being in the wilderness, continuing to be unmedicated … and the fact that “It” might not actually exist. (We’re still in limbo on the whole supernatural presence thing, but in my opinion, it’s more compelling if the whole “nefarious forces in the wilderness” call was coming from inside the house the entire time.)

Untreated mental-health issues notwithstanding, the other Yellowjackets are having various adjustment issues as well. Van’s mother seems to have experienced an epiphany since her daughter disappeared. Instead of sinking deeper into her alcoholism when the plane crashed, she got sober, got a job (with dental insurance!), and started recording every episode of The X-Files for her beloved missing daughter. It’s sweet, if a bit of a stretch for a character we last saw catatonic on her couch when Van needed a ride to the airport, but hey, we get the luminous Molly Ringwald out of the deal, and Van doesn’t have to return to maternal neglect like poor Natalie does. Van is concerned about her relationship with Tai, though, and so she calls her in an attempt to rekindle what they had in the woods.

Tai has also been basking in the glow of her parents’ love. They got her “welcome home” presents and even put up a banner to celebrate her return, but they’re a little confused about why their daughter might want to become a vegetarian. Tai’s parents aren’t really concerned about what happened to her “out there,” because they’re pretty much only focused on her excelling at everything and living an outwardly perfect life. This guise of perfection is why Tai is already considering her Howard admission offer, mere days after returning from one of the most traumatizing ordeals anyone could ever experience, and why she pretty much rejects Van’s eager admission of love on the phone. It’s heartbreaking, especially because Tai uses a line from Ghost to basically ghost her wilderness wife.

Perhaps because she’s the most outwardly together Yellowjacket, Tai appears to be the most popular survivor, as she also gets a visit from Akilah later that night. Akilah’s parents are the opposite of Tai’s, as they’re asking a lot of questions, and Akilah doesn’t have answers. She doesn’t know if she can keep up the ruse, which brings into question exactly why teen Melissa felt the need to fake her own death. In the present-day timeline, adult Melissa tells her interviewer that she wanted to flee from the press, but when she mentions the grief she harbors for her parents and her brother, her need for escape feels more dire than that. Do the Yellowjackets kill Akilah because they feared she couldn’t keep their secrets? Is that why Melissa fled?

We get brief glimpses of the rest of the Yellowjackets with their moms: Natalie’s mom is completely checked out, Travis’s mom tends to a shrine on the wall, and Misty’s parents have turned her room into a bonus room of sorts. But we spend the most time with Shauna and her mother.

Shauna’s mom is awkward and somewhat self-centered, just like her daughter. When Shauna comes home, her room is exactly as she left it, complete with all-caps “FUCK YOU” Lite-Brite art in the corner. There’s also a giant Reality Bites poster on the wall, which she soon tears down in a fit after angrily confronting some pictures of Jackie on her mirror. Reality after the wilderness does, indeed, bite for Shauna because she can’t take bites out of her friends to distract from her inner pain anymore. Too soon?

That afternoon, after Jeff avoids Shauna at the grocery store, her mom confronts her about the cheating — she read her journals when she thought she was dead — and Shauna gets angry. Then, when her mom starts babbling about being a mother, Shauna full-on attacks her, twisting her hair back and pulling her to the floor. Shauna is shocked that her first instinct was to go feral on her own mom, but she shakes it off pretty quickly. With all the overt references to Shauna’s complicated feelings about losing her and Jeff’s baby in the wilderness, it sure seems like she’s willing to do whatever it takes in order to have another chance at having that baby. We know that Shauna tells Jeff about her wilderness stillbirth at some point in time, but does she tell him in order to guilt him into being with her? It’s certainly possible. This girl is no stranger to manipulation.

After the altercation with her mother, Shauna stalks Jeff down to the apartment he shares with Randy. He doesn’t really want to let her in, but she brushes her way through the door and quickly intimidates Randy into leaving. It’s very clear that Jeff does not want Shauna in his life, or even in his apartment. They briefly talk about Jackie, and then Shauna makes her move, culminating in the most pathetic hand job ever. Jeff comes almost immediately and then starts sobbing, his naked butt bobbing up and down as he flees the couch and runs away from Shauna for the second time that day.

In the present-day timeline, Shauna once again stalks Jeff, this time at his place of work. She’s annoyed that he’s doing well for once, pissed that he’s cut her off financially, angry about his shirtless commercials (damn, Jeff), and actively scares off a flirty customer. Civilians are straight-up scared of Shauna now, and I’m here for it.

Jeff, however, is not here for it anymore. He once loved Shauna — maybe he still does — but now that he’s had time to confront the realities of their marriage, he’s realizing that she always breaks things and he always swoops in to put them back together. She might actually be a curse. It’s no coincidence that the furniture store is doing well for the first time ever; it’s because Shauna’s relentless negativity isn’t weighing Jeff down anymore.

Adult Shauna is getting more unhinged by the minute, and it’s always entertaining to watch her lose her mind. In the best sequence of the episode, she answers an ad to beat a dude up for a thousand bucks. She comes in, right hook blazing, but when he tries to set some terms — maybe they could cuddle, or she could draw him a bath afterwards? — she balks. They chat for a bit, and she discovers he’s a divorce lawyer, which is convenient because Jeff ends up asking for a divorce.

Really, nothing is going right for Shauna. Her husband wants a divorce, her daughter won’t speak to her, and her mortal enemy just moved in next door to her. Oh, yes, Melissa. Well, I’m sorry to report that Melissa’s storyline is really only interesting because of the power of Hilary Swank. The casting on this show has always been A+, but the adult narrative has always been a bit lacking, and the shoehorning of Melissa into the adult timeline is awkward at best, even if it does provide a few LOLs (mostly courtesy of Misty).

We see Melissa and her wife Alex give an interview for a local news station in their new home. Melissa explains that she ran away to get away from the press, and that it was just a wonderful coincidence that Alex happened to be the daughter of the woman who ended up saving the Yellowjackets. (Sure, Jan.) The only reason this interview works at all is that we see Tai, Shauna, and Misty snarkily commenting on it from next door. “She’s the first Yellowjacket to tell her story in 25 years, and she doesn’t know not to end her sentence with a preposition,” is a particularly funny burn from Misty. The women congregate out front to take a picture together, and then Melissa returns home, Alex threatening her with bodily harm if anything happens to their daughter, Lilah.

Tai, Misty, and Shauna wouldn’t hurt a child … would they? I don’t think so. But they did hurt one another quite a lot when they were basically children themselves. To complete Shauna’s downfall in all three acts, she’s beaten to an absolute pulp by the rest of the survivors in the wilderness timeline. Once Hannah and Misty reveal that Natalie is attempting to call for help, Shauna’s hold over the group is broken. Britt, Gen, and Robin — the resident redshirts of the series — finally get to do something as they start pummeling Shauna into the dirt. Others, including Melissa, Van, and Misty, jump in as well, until Tai begs them all off.

Shauna reels from the beating, and Tai steps up as the new (if yet unofficial) queen bee. She orders the girls to throw Shauna and Lottie in the pit in order to keep Shauna safe from the group and Lottie safe from herself. Shauna, for her part, is absolutely terrified to go home. “We’re so totally fucked!” she screams into the sky as all the survivors start to contemplate what a homecoming might really look like after all they’ve done.
• “I know what the fucking internet is, Randy.”
• Shauna’s Reality Bites poster just reminded me that it’s kind of a bummer that ‘90s queen Winona Ryder never made it onto the show. Or Jeanine Garofolo, for that matter.
• In the ‘90s timeline, we hear a crack on the radio that the girls might have eaten one another while they were out there. Did someone see or hear something? Or is this just wild speculation?

• One thing that keeps popping up for me is that three of the four surviving Yellowjackets are mothers, but we only know for sure that Shauna has been pregnant and given birth. I don’t know what this means, but my brain keeps returning to it.

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Season-Finale Recap: Taking the Cake
items.description: This season has brought a lot of changes. Obviously, Nigella Lawson has been a delightful new addition to the tent, pulling a bit of focus away from Paul Hollywood, and when he mentioned bitter caramel being a bad thing, and she said, “Oh, you and your sweet t
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: This season has brought a lot of changes. Obviously, Nigella Lawson has been a delightful new addition to the tent, pulling a bit of focus away from Paul Hollywood, and when he mentioned bitter caramel being a bad thing, and she said, “Oh, you and your sweet tooth,” while putting a condescending arm around him, I crème diplomatted in my pants. Also, aside from the first episode, we never got any of those punny introductions with Matt Lucas dressed up like a cow for some reason that we used to have to endure before every episode. I also can’t remember a bond between two bakers like the one between Moyin and Connie, a thread throughout the entire series; that’s the kind of good-hearted humanity Baking Show has espoused for almost two decades.

Those were all the good new things, but we also need to talk about the bad new things, which include a few disasters. There was the Bread Week where absolutely no one triumphed in any of the challenges. There were also a couple of technicals where people weren’t making the same thing, which seems antithetical to the very nature of the challenge, and a few others, like the millionaire’s shortbreads during Caramel Week, that looked like so many dogs’ dinners. I’m afraid that we’re going to have to add this finale to the pile of terrible new things this season. Let’s be clear: Moyin didn’t win for his showstopper; he won for his signature bake. Tom had a screw-up in the signature that is one of the worst things we’ve seen on the show, and certainly in the finale. And the technical, once again, no one really triumphed.

All season, some commenters (and others on the internet) have wondered if this year’s crop of bakers were a bit substandard. All season, I thought that couldn’t be true, that it must be the fault of production, that they were making the challenges too hard or not giving them enough time. I always wanted to give them the benefit of the doubt because they delivered some masterpieces. But when the whole season starts to feel like a series of mishaps, can that all be production’s fault? I’m not sure, but I hope the Baking Show team looks at what happened this season and takes away a lesson or two.

The signature is to make a citrus celebration cake, which seems like a fine and easily accomplished challenge. As I said before, Moyin’s layers of lemon chiffon cake with raspberry compote, lemon curd, Swiss meringue buttercream, and candied peel look like something that would be on the cover of a cookbook or in one of those spinning displays of cakes in a diner that your mother would never let you order. Paul says it’s absolute perfection, inside and out, and Nigella says the sponge is tender and perfectly balanced. This is the cake that wins the finale because it was the only thing all episode that I looked at and thought, There is no way I could ever bake this.

To be fair to Mo, his lemon cake, which he also made in week one, with strawberry and passionfruit curd, looked absolutely stunning with strawberries and curd decorating the top. Nigella says the cakes are absolutely delicious, but both judges agree that it’s more about the passionfruit than the citrus that is supposed to be the star.

Tom serves up something that looks like, well … I have a confession to make. This episode aired the day after Thanksgiving, and this Turkey Day I decided to do some baking of my own and made my grandmother’s apple pie recipe, one that I’ve made many times before. As I was pulling it out of the oven, my husband distracted me, and I dropped the pie right onto the oven door; the cake plate broke, and I then had to use a pizza board to try to get the remaining pie and pan off of the oven door without burning myself or making a mess in the oven, since I needed to make a turkey later that afternoon. I tell you my own story of baking disaster because that is just what Tom’s cake looked like. It was like a desiccated corpse similar to the idea of what it should have been, but in a big fat pile of goo. Both Tom and I made a rookie mistake; mine was dropping it, just like Molly did in the premiere, and his was decorating a cake that was still too warm. After a season of watching Tom succeed spectacularly so often but also seeing him let his ambition get the better of him just as many times, sadly, he went out on a bad note. Once the judges confronted this cake, I knew his chances at winning were over.

The technical is to make crème brûlée donuts. I’m going to say something possibly controversial, but I have never had a good donut in the U.K. I’m sure they’re out there somewhere (at the Dunkin’ they recently opened in Soho, probably), but they’ve all been too dense, overly filled, and not at all the light, fluffy sort that are scattered all over America. If you are a British donut maker who can prove me wrong, DM me for my address because there is nothing I would like more than boxes and boxes of delicious donuts showing up at my doorstep.

Because of this, I was not at all surprised when Mo’s donuts were lumpier than a bad beanbag chair, Moyin’s were coated in sugar for some reason, and most of them look like they could have a cameo on the next season of Heated Rivalry, not as the ripped players but as the hockey pucks. Tom does manage to win, with Mo coming in second and Moyin coming in third.

The showstopper is to make an “edible landscape” of a British landmark using two different kinds of baking skills. This is the kind of construction challenge this show loves, and I find it a bit tedious, but at this stage of the competition everyone should be able to pull it off. When they all bring up what are essentially their final exams, I want them all to be good, to show just why these are the people to make it into the final. I want the show quite literally stopped. Not a single one of them did this.

Mo decides to make the Bull Ring, the site of an ancient market in his native Birmingham. He is making a famous hyper-modern Selfridges that opened in 2004 and is covered with a billion silver balls, as well as St. Martin’s Church from the 1870s. The church looks rudimentary, like any structure that you would make in your first gingerbread-making class, and the Selfridges doesn’t at all capture the look or spirit of the building. While Mo’s gingerbread for his church is lackluster, the judges say his vanilla cake with coffee and mascarpone crème is a marvel. “Every bite gives me a shiver of delight,” Nigella says. Yes, that is what we want from a finale, but the challenge is to make a thing. Does he lose points because it does not look like the thing he was trying to make but also doesn’t look like any other thing?

Tom, as ever, gives himself far too much to do with his version of Shibden Hall, a stately home in Halifax. He makes the house itself out of gingerbread, the garden out of lemon sponge with raspberry cheesecake filling, and a pond that is secretly a key lime pie. (Does that mean it’s a low-key lime pie?) Tom’s biggest problem is that he dropped the nougatine for his roof just like I dropped my pie, but luckily it was the back half, so the judges never had to know. It’s like the opposite of a mullet: business in the front and nothing in the back. To me, it looked the best with some cool icing on the front of the house and grass and flowers making the cake stand out. While his biscuits are a bit underbaked, both judges love his pie and the cake, and Paul says it would be a nice cake on its own. Then they make up something about how it wasn’t cohesive, that it didn’t conjure up a landscape. What? It sure looked like a complete vision to me. Mo’s were two separate buildings that look nothing like each other and didn’t even look like the buildings, but that is a landscape, and Tom’s wasn’t? Make it make sense.

I think they had to disparage Tom’s because otherwise it would be hard to give Moyin the crown based on his rendition of Queen Elizabeth Park, the East London location of the London Olympic Games back in 2012. The Olympic stadium looks like this. Moyin made it look like a series of nougatine triangles pointing to the sky to look like a crown. The Orbit Tower (which is also the world’s tallest slide) looks like this. Moyin made it look like a bunch of red lumps. When he brings it up, Paul states the obvious and says it looks nothing like Olympic Park. However, since it all stands on one big cake that he baked, they say this counts as a cohesive landscape. Okay, so is the most important part of this challenge for it all to be on the same cake even if it doesn’t look like anything at all? I don’t get the criterion at all.

They both love the choux buns that are supposed to be Orbit; they’re great, and they like the nougatine stadium, though Paul gets in another dig about how it could be Stonehenge or anything really. The worst part is they say the cake that is supposedly the foundation for this being a cohesive landscape is gross and wet because he put too much cream and compote on his lemon chiffon sponges (the same he made in his transcendent signature) and it ended up too gloopy.

So what can the judges do when they have Mo’s showstopper that tastes great but looks rudimentary, Tom’s which looks good and tastes good but he served up a sponge diarrhea in the signature, and Moyin’s which looks like nothing, doesn’t taste great, but he’s had a great run up to the finale and made the best cake of the whole season previously the next day? Well, they give it to Moyin, who was the only solid choice to win.

Outside of the tent, when they give him the trophy, his family loses their minds, chants his name, and carry him on their shoulders. It was a great moment of celebration and made me happy because, from what we saw this season, any of these three young men deserved to win, so why shouldn’t it be him? And then Connie came and hugged him, and he picked her up and spun her around in the air. “I told you, I told you, I told you,” she shouted to him over the roar of the crowd. “This was yours to have. I’m so proud of you.” I started to tear up a little bit (just like when I dropped my pie in the oven), and I forgot about cakes and landmarks and technicals and bread week. I forgot about biscuits and sponges and craquelin and proving drawers and crumbs. I just thought about these two people, these twelve people, this whole nation, this whole world brought together by people and their triumphs, and that, at the end of the day, is enough.

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Season-Finale Recap: Let the Liars Dance
items.description: You know you’re watching a season finale because “Twelfth Night” starts with a wedding and ends with a gasp. Not a sex gasp, although there is definitely that in this episode, but an oh-they-finally-did-it gasp. Also, maybe two important people die? A lot is g
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: You know you’re watching a season finale because “Twelfth Night” starts with a wedding and ends with a gasp. Not a sex gasp, although there is definitely that in this episode, but an oh-they-finally-did-it gasp. Also, maybe two important people die? A lot is going down in this Blood of My Blood episode, and for most of it our people are in kind of freaky-deaky masks.

Let’s start with Brian and Ellen’s wedding because aside from maybe Maura and Dougal falling in love, this might be the one lovely thing this bleak, bleak season has brought us. So yes, Jamie’s parents finally, officially get married. In the ruins of what will one day be Lallybroch, no less! Ellen is in her mother’s gown and wears her mother’s ring (Colum sent them over as a peace offering of sorts). Mrs. Fitz and Ned and Murtagh are all there to bear witness. Brian says, “In darkness, in death, in oblivion, I’d know you,” to Ellen, and like, where did this guy come from? I know they were not giving out Kings of Soul-Stirring Romance lessons at Castle Leathers, okay?

The whole thing’s a refreshing change of pace for this show, although weirdly, they don’t show us Mr. and Mrs. Fraser’s wedding night. Just kidding! This is an Outlander series. They basically only have weddings on this show to get to the wedding-night sex. So yes, we spend some time with the happy couple alone in their little house. Ellen gets a sheet-clutching orgasm as a wedding gift from her husband, which is nice.

But the romance can only last for so long — we have a Twelfth Night masquerade to attend where basically everyone hates each other. The only main cast member not headed to the party is Julia, who, instead, is running for her life. Just to remind you where we’re at with Julia: Lovat has decided he’d like to marry Uncle Grant’s sister Margaret because, well, because he sucks. The problem, of course, is that divorcing Julia would be too much of a scandal, and it’s the world’s worst-kept secret that Lovat is planning on killing his current wife, and everyone is kind of like, Okay, dude, you do you. Except Julia and Henry, of course. In a letter, Henry confirms Lovat and Grant’s plan and tells her not to attend the party. Instead, he’ll sneak away during the festivities and come for Julia and baby William. If he doesn’t show by sunrise, he wants her to meet him at the stones.

Now, this would be all well and good, but Julia telling Lovat that she can’t go to the masquerade anymore because she’s not feeling well plays exactly into his whole “gotta find a way to secretly kill my wife” plan. He makes some ominous comments about the place they’re moving into now that his titles have been restored, having a “new lady,” gives her a creepy kiss on the hand, and then orders Balloch to take Julia to see a doctor right away, which Julia and Davina realize is code for “it’s murdering time.” Knowing they’re running out of time, the two women share a tearful goodbye, and Julia takes off on horseback, and Balloch chases after her. The show obviously wants us to think she’s racing off with William slung across her chest, but let’s be for real, there’s no way she could move that quickly with that baby on top of her. If you came to that same conclusion, you probably had a good idea where this was all headed from the jump.

Meanwhile, everyone who’s anyone arrives at the masquerade. No one seems particularly jazzed to be there except Jocasta, who, although she’s there with Hugh, whom she fucking hates, is using the evening for a little bit of fun before she’s locked down into a terrible marriage again. It’s wild that none of her siblings come to chat with her about, I don’t know, her husband suddenly dying and her immediately agreeing to marry the guy’s cousin, but they do not. Not even Ellen! They mostly stick to snide comments about how drunk she’s getting. Jocasta does get named the Lady of Misrule and is given the power to make people kiss and stuff, and I guess that’s nice for a widow. Her power over the party does not lead to getting Murtagh to confess he’s secretly in love with her like she clearly hopes, but if this woman could just chill for like three months, he could process the fact that he killed that guy and lost his great love in one fell swoop. Jocasta is so thirsty.

Nevertheless, Jocasta’s rule about no lying aloud lest ye be cursed for a year and/or have to dance for everyone does embolden a few guests to tell it like it is. This includes Uncle Grant, who, you’ll remember, swore last week that he was going to finally get his revenge for Malcolm’s death. First, he approaches Colum and Dougal and goes off about being slighted by them, his own kin now, for not being invited to Ellen and Brian’s wedding. When Maura intervenes and explains that they weren’t even invited, Uncle Grant doesn’t much care. All he wants to know is if some vows were possibly exchanged prior to what was supposed to be Ellen and Malcolm’s wedding day. And he also wants to make sure Dougal knows that he thinks Lord Grey should’ve killed him. In-laws are so sweet sometimes!

Uncle Grant moves on to Brian and Ellen, although Brian clocks what is about to happen and gets Ellen out of there before Grant can lay into her. He takes the brunt of it instead. When Uncle Grant asks Brian if Ellen had anything to do with Malcolm’s death, Brian continues to tell the story they’ve been trying to sell from the beginning, which is that Malcolm was drunk and died from his own dagger. But no one believes this story, and Brian knows that Grant knows who is to blame. Grant walks off, but when relaying the story to Murtagh, Brian knows it was too easy an end to that conversation and that Uncle Grant is coming for him.

And he’s exactly right! First, he goes to tell Lovat that he’s going to murder Lovat’s son, and he wants his blessing, and since Lovat is a dope, he believes Grant is talking about killing Ellen, and we all know how on board with murdering people’s wives Lovat is; He wishes Grant luck in his endeavor. Grant then pulls Henry and Arch aside: Henry will murder Brian Fraser before sunrise in order to finally prove his loyalty, and if he does, Grant will release him from his bond of service. If he doesn’t, well, Grant isn’t explicit, but the last bladier did wind up with his head on a pike, so Henry can make an educated guess. Henry is forced to wear Grant’s mask so that it looks like the laird of Clan Grant is getting justice — don’t worry, Henry calls Grant a coward to his face for this move, but that doesn’t exactly help with the whole head-on-a-pike situation. And so Henry, dressed as Uncle Grant, follows Brian out into the big maze under the fireworks to do his boss’s bidding.

But come on, friends! Do you think Henry is really going to murder Brian? He knows him! He knows Julia cares about him! Also, Henry isn’t super into murdering. Especially not at masquerades. He does track Brian down, but quickly reveals who he is under the mask, warns him about Grant’s vendetta, and gets Brian safely out of the party. For reasons I’ll never understand, Henry proceeds to put Uncle Grant’s mask back on and turn back into the maze where he is immediately met with … Lord Lovat and his gun. Lovat bumped into Murtagh, who went on and on about needing to protect Brian now that Grant has him marked for death and realized what he had encouraged Grant to do just moments ago. The one time in his life when Lovat decides to be an actual father to Brian leaves Henry with a gunshot wound to the abdomen. Lovat thinks he’s killing Grant, although I doubt he’d be that upset to know who he really attacked. The last we see of Henry, Arch Bug has him loaded in the back of a cart, and he’s racing down the road to find help, but things don’t look great for our time traveler. That’s a lot of blood!

And what of Julia? During her attempted escape, she winds up falling off her horse and starts running. Balloch catches up to her just as she realizes her only option to stay out of his grasp is, well, it’s jumping down into an extremely rocky waterfall. Which she does! And she winds up on top of those aforementioned rocks. Now, I don’t know how a person survives a fall like that, but it seems as though there’s still some life in Julia yet because, last we see her, Balloch carries her to the doors of a monastery, where one of the monks knows him by name, and he asks him to give Julia sanctuary. Was Balloch going to save Julia this whole time? All that running for nothing!

Both Henry and Julia are at death’s door at the moment, but what of baby William? If you guessed that during that tearful good-bye between Julia and Davina, Julia handed over her child to keep him from Balloch, you were right! Davina took William directly to the stones to wait for his parents, but when the sun rises and neither of them has shown up, Davina only has one place to go. She bursts through the doors of Lallybroch and tearfully tells Brian and Ellen that she had nowhere else to safely bring William but to them. And there it is, folks. From the moment Julia secretly gave her son the name William in season one, we were left wondering if this could possibly mean that all along Jamie’s late brother William could actually be Claire’s brother, sent to hide out with Brian and Ellen. It looks like that is exactly where Blood of My Blood is taking us. Sure, there will be a lot of explaining Brian and Ellen have to do to make people buy that this kid is theirs, but Brian did say he owed Henry one after he saved his life in that maze. There are lots of pressing questions to be answered if this Outlander prequel gets a third season, but top of mind for me personally is, uhhh, what the hell does this mean for the fates of William’s parents?

• Hey, it was kind of nice to see Ellen and Colum begin to entertain the idea of thinking about mending their relationship. Now that Colum is stewing in his shame and grief, he does seem ready to atone for his sins when it comes to his sister, but for Ellen it will take more convincing. Still, I doubt she’ll go through with her plans of permanent no contact.

• Blood of My Blood giveth and Blood of My Blood taketh away. After a season building up the Dougal-Maura love story, we are reminded that Maura thinks Ellen is to blame for her brother’s death, and she is never going to get over that. When she defends her uncle and tells Dougal that if they find out for sure that Ellen killed Malcolm, she would damn her soul to hell, Dougal is aghast. Seems like this might be a tough thing to come back from.
• At one point during the masquerade, things get very Eyes Wide Shut, and it is glorious. I mean, Ned furiously making out with that cute guy? Get yours, Ned!

Dolly Parton will be honored with a special musical tribute at this year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, which celebrates its historic 100th edition on Saturday after being postponed from Thanksgiving Day due to weather conditions.

Tony-nominated Broadway star Megan Hilty will lead the tribute to the country music icon, who died in August at age 80. The performance is among several high-profile musical numbers planned for the milestone celebration, alongside appearances from RAYE, Teddy Swims, Megan Moroney, Queen Latifah and “KPop Demon Hunters” breakout EJAE.

The 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will air Saturday, Nov. 28, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones on NBC and Telemundo, with an encore presentation on NBC at 2 p.m. ET/PT. Those without cable can stream the festivities live on Peacock, in addition to a variety of live TV streaming services that carry NBC, including DirecTV, Hulu + Live TV and Sling TV in select markets.
“Today” show personalities Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker will return to host the Emmy-winning telecast.

The parade’s 100th edition coincides with NBC’s own centennial anniversary, marking a particularly significant year for the network. More than 11,000 volunteers and participants will descend on Manhattan for Thursday’s festivities, which will span 2.5 miles from the Upper West Side to Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square. In a nod to the anniversary, Macy’s has assembled a record 100 inflatable creations, including new balloons depicting Bluey, Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey Mouse and Snoopy’s Joe Cool alter ego. The parade will also bring back balloons designed by some of the art world’s biggest names, including Tim Burton, Keith Haring, Jeff Koons and Yayoi Kusama.

Hollywood will be well represented among this year’s new floats, too, including a Hogwarts-themed creation from HBO. A commemorative Macy’s All Stars float will bring together familiar characters from throughout the parade’s history, from Bugs Bunny and Scooby-Doo to Sonic the Hedgehog.

Broadway, a fixture of the annual telecast, will get an expanded showcase this year. A 10-minute musical medley introduced by Julianne Hough will bring together performers from nine productions, including “Hamilton,” “Wicked,” “Rent,” “Chicago,” “The Book of Mormon,” “Aladdin,” “Schmigadoon!,” “The Lost Boys” and “The Rocky Horror Show.”

Other musical performers on this year’s roster include Natasha Bedingfield, Jimmy Fallon and the Roots, Keke Palmer, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Leslie Odom Jr., Anthony Ramos, Indigo Girls, DEVO, Smash Mouth and K-pop boy band RIIZE. The Radio City Rockettes will also return before Santa Claus closes out the festivities.
Stream the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade live on Peacock, or watch for free with an eligible streaming trial through DirecTV.

items.title: Thanksgiving Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Rules With $11.6 Million, ‘Focker-in-Law’ Follows With $7.7 Million
items.description: As people traveled back home for Thanksgiving, a lot of moviegoers made a stop at Panem to return to the world of “The Hunger Games.” The new prequel, “Sunrise on the Reaping,” ruled the Thanksgiving box office with $11.6 million on Thursday.
items.author: Jordan Moreau
paragraphs: As people traveled back home for Thanksgiving, a lot of moviegoers made a stop at Panem to return to the world of “The Hunger Games.” The new prequel, “Sunrise on the Reaping,” ruled the Thanksgiving box office with $11.6 million on Thursday.

Lionsgate’s latest entry in the YA action franchise will dominate the box office for the second week in a row. It’s on track to make $85 million over the five-day Thanksgiving break, bringing its domestic total to $233 million. Original “Hunger Games” stars Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson (who appear in a cameo) let a new generation take the spotlight in this prequel, which focuses on a younger version of Harrelson’s character Haymitch as he enters the 50th Games. The cast includes Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Kiernan Culkin, Glenn Close and more.

Another entry in a long-standing franchise, Universal’s comedy “Focker-in-Law,” came in second place with $7.7 million on Thursday. It will beat out this week’s fellow newcomer, Disney’s original animated movie “Hexed,” and end the five-day frame with an estimated $40 million. Ariana Grande joins the Focker family fun in the new movie, which brings back Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Owen Wilson and Blythe Danner.

“Hexed,” starring Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster, made $4.5 million on Thanksgiving, putting it at third place. It’s projected to make $34.4 million over the five-day weekend. Steinfeld stars as a teenage witch who discovers her powers and gets transported to a world of magic in Disney’s latest animated offering.

Elsewhere at the box office, Paramount and Johnny Depp’s “Ebenezer” is coming in at fourth place with an estimated $13 million through Sunday, and Amazon MGM’s “I Play Rocky” is on track for fifth place with $8.8 million over the same time. Netflix’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” starring Brad Pitt, is only releasing in Imax screens and projected to make $3.5 million in its first five days.

items.title: Record Store Day Co-Founder on How Black Friday Evolved Into a Major Holiday for Vinyl Hounds, and What Will Fly Off the Shelves This Year
items.description: In April of this year, the 19th installment of Record Store Day was the event’s most successful ever, but Nov. 27 brings another opportunity for music junkies to get their vinyl on: Record Store Day Black Friday.
items.author: Andrea Dresdale
paragraphs: In April of this year, the 19th installment of Record Store Day was the event’s most successful ever, but Nov. 27 brings another opportunity for music junkies to get their vinyl on: Record Store Day Black Friday.

While the O.G. Record Store Day was conceived as a general celebration of independent record stores, and features limited-edition, in-store only releases, the Black Friday edition exists for a different reason: to give those indie stores a slice of the “biggest shopping day of the year” pie. That’s also why the vinyl releases you’ll find making their debuts on Black Friday are more likely to remain there for the rest of the holiday season, and why many stores will make them available on their websites starting on Saturday the 28th.

The concept of hyping local independent record stores as a must for holiday shopping may sound rather obvious, but RSD co-founder Michael Kurtz says that, at first, he was opposed to the idea, which his wife came up with.

“I was not on board with it,” he admits. “My initial response at the time was, ‘Ah, that’s for big-box stores and selling cheap toasters and stuff.’” But eventually, he came around, thinking they could do “a little bit smaller version” for the holidays. RSD Black Friday does feature fewer releases overall, but its main goal is to get customers through the door. “Most record stores do about two months’ worth of business” that day, Kurtz says.

For Black Friday, Kurtz says what you’ll find in the racks is largely thanks to what he calls a “Secret Squirrel group” of about 20 record store owners nationwide, who help winnow down the overwhelming numbers of releases pitched by artists and record labels.

“They’ve been around forever; they run iconic record stores,” Kurtz explains of this crate-digging cabal. “And I go to them and say, ‘Hey, do you think record stores would want to have this?’ Because Black Friday is not the same as Record Store Day. It’s not supposed to be just a limited thing only. It’s also supposed to be things that record stores want to have in their bins year-round.”

But what’s true for both events is that they feature releases from a dizzying array of artists across multiple genres. That big tent approach, Kurtz reveals, was inspired by Metallica bassist Robert Trujillo, who early on convinced Kurtz to do a vinyl release by iconic jazz bassist Jaco Pastorius.
“It went to No. 1 on Billboard‘s jazz chart,” Kurtz recalls. “And that made us rethink: ‘Oh, geez, we could do jazz records, we could do bluegrass records, we could do soul records, R&B, funk.”

Of course, rock in its various forms is still a huge focus of both Record Store Day and RSD Black Friday, but in recent years, pop artists have climbed on board the vinyl train en masse, resulting in a surprising boom in customers who are too young to even remember a world where vinyl was once the only option.

Kurtz says, “The majority of people who come to Record Store Day now and participate are younger than the age of 35, and slightly more female than male.” Of course, you can credit the biggest pop star in the world for that.

While Kurtz says Billie Eilish’s 7-inch releases for RSD “sort of cracked the door open” for that demographic, he notes, “It got blown wide open with Taylor Swift. When she did her ‘Long Pond Studio Sessions’ record with us exclusively for record stores [in 2023], it changed everything.” That album became the first Record Store Day exclusive release ever to hit the top 10 of theBillboard200, proving that brand-new releases on vinyl could do just as well as streaming titles.

For RSD Black Friday 2026, Kurtz predicts that it’ll be Noah Kahan’s vinyls getting the youth through the door. “He’s got a special 7-inch that was done just for record stores that’s very very cool: It’s tied in with the ‘Hunger Games’ soundtrack,” says Kurtz, referring to “Draw You Out,” Kahan’s contribution to “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping – The Album.” “And then he’s also got an additional record that’ll be highly sought after.” That would be “The Last of the Bugs,” which collects the four tracks Kahan added to the expanded edition of his album”The Great Divide.”

Kurtz is also excited about a Bruce Springsteen live box set, the American version of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul LP on gold vinyl, a live album by Billy Joel, a disc of the Doors’ studio sessions and a 2-LP set by Ween “for all the pot smokers out there.”

He also predicts the Miles Davis, Jerry Garcia Band and Grateful Dead releases will be popular, as well as the original, previously unreleased version of Joan Jett’s “I Love Rock & Roll” album and not one but three albums by Japanese guitar virtuoso Masayoshi Takanaka.
Kurtz says he doesn’t even mind that many of those younger customers are buying vinyl not to play, but to display.

“Y’know, I was originally freaked out about that because I’m a music person, but I kind of get it,” he tells me. “Like, I will get the Beatles’ ‘Rubber Soul’ reissue this year and I probably will never open it. I just want it because it’s so beautiful, and to know that I have one of 15,000 copies that will ever be printed … I want to keep it pristine.”

Despite admitting to being “completely anxiety-ridden” each year over how successful each Record Store Day event will be, Kurtz is looking forward to the event’s 20th anniversary next year. He and co-founder Carrie Colliton would love to mark the milestone with live performances and some kind of art installation featuring past Record Store Day releases. (A copy of each of those limited releases is currently stored in a warehouse in Raleigh, North Carolina, in case you might want to pull off the vinyl equivalent of robbing Fort Knox.) But for right now, Kurtz notes, those plans are “dreams right now. They’re not reality.”

Still, the failure he fears is unlikely. Nearly 20 years into an event which has helped drive pop culture back to the vinyl age, Kurtz says there’s no sign of its popularity tapering off. As he notes, “demand for [vinyl] and the excitement around it is completely still there – even more so, I think.” But, he acknowledges, “The only thing that’s a bit alarming is how expensive it’s becoming” – a reflection of the rising cost of shipping due to increases in gas and diesel.

“It’s stunning for me as a person who’s ridden this tiger called Record Store Day for almost 20 years to see it from the beginning: When we first started we were the only ones doing new vinyl, and in the used bins you could find [high quality copies of] Led Zeppelin or the Beatles or Pink Floyd for $3, $5 — those days are over.”

Kurtz says it was interesting working with shops in the early days, and still can be today — because they’re independent in all sorts of ways, including what they prefer to emphasize in their stores and sometimes think RSD should focus on as a whole.

“The most difficult thing about putting it together was working with record store owners, because they’re a very creative bunch,” he says. “They’re very different; they’re not people who typically play by the rules. They like to do things their way. So to try to get them all together to do this was very difficult.” He adds, “I was in London once and there was a record store owner who just just raked me over the coals because we’d done the Taylor Swift record. I was like, ‘What records do you like?’ He’s like, ‘Yes, Black Sabbath, Deep Purple …’ and I said, ‘OK I get it. That’s what you love and what you’re passionate about, but there’s another generation.’ And so it’s working with them and not alienating them, because sometimes I do that by accident.”

items.title: NBC Pulls Spot Advocating for End of U.S. Military Aid to Israel, Will Review Approval Procedures After Outcry
items.description: NBC has pulled an ad from a Middle East advocacy organization that calls for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel. The network will review its ad approval procedures after criticism from the Simon Wiesenthal Center and other organizations.
items.author: Cynthia Littleton
paragraphs: NBC has pulled an ad from a Middle East advocacy organization that calls for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel. The network will review its ad approval procedures after criticism from the Simon Wiesenthal Center and other organizations.

The spot, purchased by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, pushes for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. The spot titled “Every Three Seconds” ran Nov. 25 on NBC in primetime during the network’s “Saturday Night Live” Thanksgiving special.

The ad makes a jarring juxtaposition between the suffering in Gaza and scenes of a typical American preteen girl doing chores and odd jobs to save money for a bicycle amid tough economic times. Just as the American girl brings her jar full of money into a bike shop, the spot cuts to a scene of a girl standing in a pile of rubble in Gaza. As the camera pans back, the girl is revealed to be leaning on a crutch, having lost one of her lower legs. The spot tells viewers that “Every three seconds” the U.S. sends about $400 million in military aid to Israel under a long-term deal set to expire in 2028.
NBC’s top brass were unaware of the spot before it aired. As a result, there will be a review of the network’s ad approval processes, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Jim Berk, CEO of the Wiesenthal Center, issued a lengthy statement on Thursday questioning NBC’s decision to air the ad during an “SNL” entertainment special in primetime. He pointed to the ad’s potential to fuel hostility against Israel and Jews.

“The advertisement’s imagery, an American child’s hardship set against the anguish of a child in Gaza, offers viewers a seductive but unsubstantiated narrative: that the struggles of American families are somehow bound up with U.S. support for Israel,” Berk stated. “In collapsing a complex foreign policy into a single, emotionally charged image, it erases the deeper realities, including the imperative to protect Israeli lives and the very existence of the country itself. By manipulating emotion and stripping it of context, this ad seeks to become a catalyst for hostility. … Without scrutiny, insinuations and half-truths are allowed to seep into the consciousness of millions, unchallenged and unchecked. Turning children’s suffering into a prop for political theater is an unacceptable manipulation.”

The Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project did not immediately respond to a request for comment on NBC’s decision. It’s unclear how many more times the spot had been scheduled to run on NBCUniversal platforms. According to the organization’s website, IMEU “was founded in 2005 by a group of concerned Americans who want to foster an increased understanding among Americans about Palestine and the Palestinians.”

items.title: Denis Villeneuve Was ‘Deeply Disappointed’ When Disney Put ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ on Same Release Date as ‘Dune 3’: ‘I Hope We Will Survive’
items.description: Denis Villeneuve is not exactly thrilled that “Dune: Part Three” will be going head to head with “Avengers: Doomsday” at the box office.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Denis Villeneuve is not exactly thrilled that “Dune: Part Three” will be going head to head with “Avengers: Doomsday” at the box office.

Both blockbusters will hit theaters on Dec. 18, paving the way for a huge box office event similar to “Barbenheimer,” with people already coining it “Dunesday.” It will likely be a great weekend for cinema with many fans opting to see both movies, but Villeneuve admitted in a new interview with Time magazine that he does have his concerns.

“Listen, I will be honest. The first ‘Dune’ came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us,” the director said. “Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy.”

For the third and final “Dune” film, Villeneuve was looking forward to breathing a sigh of relief: “Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release,” he remembers thinking. “Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth.”

The Marvel tentpole was originally set to release on May 1, 2026, but was delayed last year to Dec. 18, the same date “Dune 3” already held. The last “Avengers” movie, 2019’s “Endgame,” still ranks as the highest-grossing movie of all time with $2.94 billion worldwide.

“I was deeply disappointed,” Villeneuve said of the shift. “But we had committed to this date, to Imax. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. ‘Dune’ is not a mammoth like the ‘Avengers,’ but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive.”
Disney did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

However, Villeneuve is trying to stay optimistic. “It could be one of the biggest box office weekends of all time because of both movies,” he concluded. “Am I in competition with the ‘Avengers’? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.”

Besides, the director is sure to have another box office juggernaut (or three) on his hands with the new James Bond movie, starring Robert Pattinson as 007. Though the Time interview took place before Pattinson’s casting was announced, Villeneuve teased: “I don’t sleep a lot right now because it’s like I have electricity in my veins thinking about this new project. It is so different.”

He added that he doesn’t see himself changing the world of Bond too much. “I love traditions. I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache. I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today,” he said. “I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film. Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure.”
Read Villeneuve’s full Time magazine interview here.
