That means you can get the ribbed-cotton-blend set in the polka-dot design or the breezy solid blue for under $100.
New! You can now save this product for later.

The retailer also has PJs available in cotton poplin and flannel for men, women, and kids, all up to half off. We’re just one month away from everyone wearing their matching pajamas around the Christmas tree, which means now is a good time to actually get them — for you and your loved ones.

Want a few more options? We browsed the web for more pajamas up to 60 percent off. The Gap has cotton separates to mix and match, while Cozy Earth, Old Navy, and Abercrombie have super-cute patterns as low as $25. I also recommend Lunya’s best-selling washable silk options and J.Crew’s cotton set.
For every other deal, head over to our list of the best Black Friday deals.

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: The Shane Gillis Experience
items.description: A couple of months ago, when comedian Shane Gillis hosted Saturday Night Live, he said in his opening monologue that women dress like “whores” at the gym. An outrage cycle ensued — Dan Levy called him a misogynist, former SNL star Ego Nwodim responded with a g
items.author: Grace Brassel; Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: A couple of months ago, when comedian Shane Gillis hosted Saturday Night Live, he said in his opening monologue that women dress like “whores” at the gym. An outrage cycle ensued — Dan Levy called him a misogynist, former SNL star Ego Nwodim responded with a gym selfie — but I wasn’t the least bit surprised. Until last August, I was in a yearlong relationship with Shane, and his comments didn’t faze me. After our time together, how do I think he feels about women? He doesn’t like them much.

In May 2024, I was having the time of my life. I had just moved out of my mom’s house into my first real apartment in Hoboken with a roommate I loved. I was working full-time as a social-media manager for an eyewear brand and had started to build a TikTok following of my own. It felt like everything I wanted my early 20s to be.

On the recommendation of a friend, my roommate and I decided to watch Tires on Netflix. I had never heard of Shane Gillis — I didn’t even know about his world record for fastest hiring and firing at Saturday Night Live — but I thought he seemed so charismatic on the show. I’ve always dated big Irish guys, and here was this big Irish guy with blue eyes and a sense of humor on my TV screen. On Tires, the workplace comedy he created about a family auto shop, Shane plays the lazy sidekick cousin of the store manager, also named Shane. For the first time ever, I decided to DM a famous person on Instagram.

“Hey, if you’re ever in New York, let’s go on an adventure,” I wrote to him, not expecting anything. He replied alarmingly fast, telling me to give him my phone number. My roommate and I were jumping up and down in our tiny apartment. The guy from the TV wanted my number!

Soon, we started texting, which turned into daily phone calls, which turned into an invitation to meet in person in Austin. I was too afraid to tell my mom that I was being flown out to a city by a celebrity 12 years my senior, so I told her I was going on a business trip.

I felt incredibly anxious about going to Austin, but Shane assuaged all that. He got me a room at the Four Seasons and promised that if we didn’t hit it off, I could just consider it a free vacation. For our first real date, I went to watch him perform at the Mothership, Joe Rogan’s comedy club. The audience full of men was losing their minds when he walked onstage; he was the golden boy of comedy, and I was impressed. Backstage, I met Rogan for the first time (three apples tall, by the way), and he gave me an overly assertive Donald Trump handshake and asked my opinion on trans people.

That weirdness aside, the rest of the weekend was a dream. Shane was rich, he had a cool car, and his house was lined floor to ceiling with awards. He thought I was beautiful and treated me with care. He said all the right things, and I would later tell my mom that he was the most liberal man I had ever dated. (This is now a hilarious sentiment to me.) His world was so fast and extravagant. I was just happy to be part of it. By the time I left Austin, we were official.

For our second date, I was his plus-one to Christian McCaffrey and Olivia Culpo’s wedding. When Shane bought me an $800 dress, I literally fell to my knees. “Wow, you’re really grateful,” he told me. “That’s really nice.”

Two months later, Shane was getting ready to move to Philadelphia for a few months to write the new season of Tires. He asked me to join him. My best friend is a Realtor in Philly, and he used her to get us a comically large, $20,000-a-month brutalist apartment. Once we started living together, it was a nonstop party — Eagles games, long nights of drinking, hanging out with celebrities. Wash, rinse, repeat. It became harder and harder to work my day job as a social-media manager, so Shane told me I should just quit. He would take care of me, and I would take care of him. He made it seem like the most plausible option.
Little did I know I had actually just accepted a different full-time position, one that had a high rate of burnout and no chance for upward mobility: Shane Gillis’s stay-at-home girlfriend.

I soon started to notice that Shane’s life had no structure. He slept in, he played his college-football video game, and he drank every night. I have ADHD, which I’ve always been ashamed of, and have had to work to keep my life in order. And here was a man who was successful despite living like a frat boy. At the time, I found this unironically inspiring.

My friends started to miss me, and I missed them. They would come down to visit, and Shane would take us out to do something fun, swiftly winning them over. My friends cheered me on, viewing this new world as a wild and thrilling detour from our typical nine-to-five routines. I felt plucked out of my ordinary existence like some kind of chosen one, dropped straight into the orbit of the coolest guy with the flashiest life. It felt like a dream. I was so excited for my and Shane’s life together that I didn’t even notice my agency was slipping through my fingers.

Tires shot in West Chester, Pennsylvania, so obviously I was going to move to West Chester, Pennsylvania. We found a beautiful 19th-century farmhouse and it was almost as if the setting inspired Shane to create a new image of me. I felt like I was turning into a 25-year-old housewife, someone who cooked, cleaned, did the laundry, and waited for her man to come home from a long day at work. I never said I was capable of all that, but it felt like an expectation. When things weren’t exactly to his liking, he would tell me that I wasn’t “being good.” You know, the way you would talk to a dog.

There were so many red flags I ignored about Shane because I really did love him. In our time together, Shane would often say something remarkably cruel and then play it off like a joke. He did it with me, he does it with his friends, and I saw him do it with his colleagues. I felt like being able to handle it made me the Wild Shane Tamer. I saw him as my best friend, so I didn’t think too much about it when he spent thousands of dollars at O.J. Simpson’s estate sale because it was “funny” or when he came to the defense of a country star after we watched him yell at his team and girlfriend backstage. When he was mad at me, he would withhold touch and call me greedy or put pillows in between us in the bed to show how much he didn’t want to be near me. I was walking on eggshells so often that they began to feel like regular hardwood.

About five months into the relationship, people began to worry about me. I was alone at home all day while Shane was shooting with no friends or family nearby. I started gaining weight from all the drinking we were doing, and I dyed my blonde hair brown on a whim. My friends jokingly asked if I was experiencing psychosis. I didn’t have a good answer for them. One day, our landlord, an older woman, took me out to lunch and asked me what my plan was. “I’m going to take care of the house, be Shane’s girlfriend, and support him,” I told her. We barely knew each other, and I could tell she was disappointed in that answer. “You can’t give up,” she told me. “You can’t just be his girlfriend.”

During our time in West Chester, Shane started getting really mean. I heard him calling other women whores around me, so I started dressing more conservatively. He thought I didn’t do enough around the house, and tasked me with throwing a big Halloween party so that I would “get to work.” After we got into a fight about whether or not I could wear a costume that was revealing, I gave up and agreed to be some kind of vampire whose whole body was covered. I wanted the party to be perfect, since he said that Bradley Cooper and Gigi Hadid would be there. They weren’t.

I cried every day. I would call my mom in tears, telling her that I didn’t know if I was meant for this life. My six-month free trial of Sweet Shane Gillis had run out, and it was time for me to start paying. We already had made plans to move to Austin together in January 2025, which my mom thought was a bad idea. On a visit to West Chester, she pulled Shane aside and told him the move was not going to be good for me. She told him I was lonely and upset and he wasn’t doing anything to help me. His response was “She will be fine.”

I was not fine. In fact, things only got worse once we moved to Austin, a city where I knew absolutely no one. Two weeks later, he told me that he was leaving to go to the Super Bowl and that there was no ticket for me. When I checked Instagram the day of the game, it hurt to see him hanging out with his friends and his team but not me. I had no friends, really nothing to my life there, and I felt like he had just ditched me to go party with celebrities. I played it cool and then privately sobbed in the guest bedroom.

My birthday is March 1, the same day he hosted SNL that year. I understood that he’d be busy on my actual birthday, so I went to SNL with him and lightheartedly asked what we’d be doing next week to celebrate. “You’re lucky I’m even fucking inviting you to this,” he told me in a faux “I’m just joking but maybe not” tone. But his wins were mine, and I was more than happy to celebrate him. If you listen to his monologue from that night, you can actually hear me laughing louder and harder than anyone else in the audience.

Once, I misplaced Shane’s AmEx while my friends were visiting us in Austin, and I had a panic attack about telling him. My friends didn’t understand why I was so afraid and were reasonably freaked out by my quick shift in demeanor. After I found the card, I pulled myself together, but my friends told Shane I’d been upset. “Grace, what do you mean? I wouldn’t care,” he responded, sounding unexpectedly compassionate.

Things came to a head on the Fourth of July. Two days before, he’d told me that I was “so fucking depressed” and had “no motivation.” His friends were in the house, and I worried that they had all heard what he’d said. In a way, he was right. I had spent May and June constantly sleeping. My body was so inflamed that I began to think I had a chronic illness. I began to ask myself, Who am I, and what do I do if this life is slowly killing me?

For the Fourth, Shane decided he wanted to rent a boat on Lake Travis and drink with his friends all day. Everyone came back to our house afterward to keep the party going. (By that, I mean grown men willingly sat around watching Shane play a video game.) I asked for his phone to put on some music, and after I’d chosen a song, my intuition told me to go through his texts. I scrolled, looking for a woman’s name. It didn’t take long to find one.

Valerie, I’ll call her. I had met her before. She’d been really cold to me at one of Shane’s recent shows, which I now realize was because I had cockblocked her from having sex with my boyfriend. Shane had texted her, “I should have had sex with you, I was being gay.” (He’s not exactly a poet.) The time he “should have had sex” with her was Super Bowl weekend — the one I wasn’t invited to. I scrolled and realized they had been sexting for months and had probably had in-person encounters as well. The floor seemed to give way beneath my feet.

I dragged two women I thought were my friends — both girlfriends of Shane’s friends — out to the backyard to tell them what I had found. As I lay down in the sharp, fake Texan grass, my whole world crashing down around me, I felt a disconnect. I thought these were my close friends, but it seemed like they were feigning empathy as I bawled my eyes out. I had no idea just how disposable I was; they would ghost me months later. Who even were these people? They now felt like strangers. The girls told me I shouldn’t say anything to Shane and should wait to do so until I calmed down. In theory, I agreed with them. But the dam had broken, and a year’s worth of dormant rage was flowing out of me.

“Who’s Valerie!” I yelled, barging into the living room from outside. Shane pretended he didn’t know who I was talking about and fiddled with the Xbox controller as his friends shuffled out of our house. I ran into the bathroom, where I punched a hole through the wall like a hormonal teenage boy. (Not as hard as you might think, considering our McMansion was basically made of papier-mâché.)

I am not entirely proud of how I acted in this moment. I threw my phone. I threw a chair. I was not myself, but then I hadn’t been myself in months. I didn’t even hear my own voice in my head anymore. It was always Shane’s. Every action was filtered through thoughts of him: What would Shane think? Will Shane get mad at me for this? Finally, I snapped. It was the first time I ever felt like I had any sense of control in the relationship.

The next day, he came into our bedroom with an apology matcha. “I read the messages, they were really bad. Sorry,” he said. I chucked the matcha at the wall. I asked him why he would cheat on me. “Because I’m an insecure faggot,” he screamed. This mean, successful man ripped the mask off his own face, exposing a small and guilty child.

In August, we started the process of breaking up. It dragged on forever, and we even got back together briefly a couple months later. One day, he said we could never really mend things because I had committed the cardinal sin when you’re dealing with a narcissist: telling people how he treated me.

In an effort to get him and his fans off my back, I went on an hourlong podcast, where I vowed to say only nice things about him. This worked for a while. But his fans were still obsessed with me. Throughout our relationship, they loved to comment on every one of my posts, calling me a gold-digging whore. I’m way too type B to have a villainous plan to use a guy for his money, but I appreciated being considered calculated enough to do that. After we broke up, it felt like every white man age 18 to 40 in America had daggers on me. They would recognize me out in public and shout degrading things at me. It came to a climax when I was recognized and shoved into a table at a bar in West Village, leaving a nasty bruise on my hip bone. When I told Shane about it, he said to stop telling him stuff like that or he would block me. Validating my experience would mean facing the reality that he has a toxic fan base and the only one to blame is himself.

For the past year, I have been in weekly therapy, working to deprogram myself from the relationship. What I’ve learned is that while my experience may seem exceptional because it involved private jet rides and hanging out with celebrities, how Shane made me feel could not be more textbook. Men like him exist in every tax bracket. They put you on a pedestal, kick it out from under you, and tell you it was your fault you fell. I spent so much time trying to understand what happened only to realize the answer is actually kind of boring. Guys like that are insecure, and instead of choosing to be better men, they take their shortcomings out on everyone else around them. These days, his once-looming presence has shrunk down to that of a buzzing gnat. When I happen to see him onscreen or his fans send me hate comments in my DMs, I repeat a sentiment I learned in therapy: They know the entertainer. I knew the man.

People were rightly pissed off about Shane’s SNL monologue, but the only thing that really shocked me was that the rest of the monologue seemed lazy too. Seeing the outrage provided me with some kind of closure. I posted a video of my own workout routine and called it a “Full Body Workout for Hoes.” The top comment on TikTok reads, “I can only imagine how awful he was in private, thinking of you and your healing.” He had flown too close to the sun, and people were finally seeing the man I knew. I had spent so long protecting this part of my life, afraid to speak publicly about it, and then he just did it himself. Finally, some initiative.
In response to a detailed request for comment, Gillis replied, “Grace and I had some good times together. Breakups are tough, and I wish her the best.”

items.title: 26 Times Women's Sports Made History In 2026
items.description: 26 Times Women's Sports Made History In 2026
items.author: Frankie de la Cretaz
paragraphs: 26 Times Women's Sports Made History In 2026
Shattered records, new leagues, landmark victories — what can't these athletes do?

It seems like every year is deemed the “biggest” year for women’s sports, and 2026 is no different. As increased interest and money pour into everything from major pro leagues like the WNBA and Professional Women’s Hockey League (PWHL), to smaller ones like the Athletes Unlimited Softball League, women athletes continue to show that the investment is well-deserved.

Surprise, surprise: It turns out that when women are properly funded and supported, they are capable of greatness that many (sexist) people thought impossible. Records aren’t just being broken on the field — they’re also getting smashed at the negotiating table, in the stands, and on TV screens. For every on-court achievement an athlete like A’ja Wilson or Trinity Rodman notches, there are also labor victories secured, attendance records broken, and sportsmanship displayed (both in the gay way and the not-gay way).
In such an eventful year, it can be hard to know which moments stood out above the rest, but we’ve got you. Below, here are the 26 moments that defined women’s sports in 2026.
Jan. 22 — Trinity Rodman signed a record-breaking contract

At the start of the 2026 season, soccer phenom Trinity Rodman’s future with the NWSL was uncertain. She was in negotiations with the Washington Spirit, where she’d spent the entirety of her professional career. Ultimately, Rodman secured a three-year deal at $2 million annually, making her the highest-paid player in both league history and women’s soccer internationally.
Jan. 30 — Marina Mabrey dropped 47 points in Unrivaled in front of a sold-out crowd

Unrivaled, the 3x3 league founded by WNBA stars Breanna Stewart and Napheesa Collier, had a big year. They added two teams (bringing the total to eight) and went on tour for the first time, selling out the Barclays Center in Brooklyn and the Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philly. But perhaps the biggest highlight was Marina Mabrey’s 47-point game, which broke the league scoring record. She made over 64% of her shots that night, hitting 10 threes — a feat that’s even more impressive considering Unrivaled’s shorter games. She used the attention to promote her “crash out jar,” a self-imposed accountability tool. Each time she curses or has an angry outburst on the court, she has to pay. She donated the money to organizations helping immigrant communities impacted by the ICE occupation in Minneapolis. Mabrey was far from the biggest name in the superstar-filled league, but she sure made the biggest splash.
Feb. 1 - July 4 — Nikki Hiltz dominated the mile in track and field

Nikki Hiltz is best known for the 1500m but over the last few seasons, they’ve been making a name for themselves in another distance: the mile. Thanks to their signature kick (the finish of a race), Hiltz was able to win two of the most prestigious mile races this past season: the Wanamaker Mile indoors in February, and the Prefontaine Classic Bill Bowerman Mile outdoors in July. The latter victory saw them break the venue record at Hayward Field in Oregon, and beat Kenya’s Faith Kipyegon, who is considered one of the most dominant middle-distance runners of this generation.
Feb. 18 — Mikaela Shiffrin won Olympic gold in women’s slalom

Mikaela Shiffrin arrived in Milano Cortina with both nothing and everything to prove. Even though she already had four Olympic medals and a jaw-dropping record of 108 World Cup victories, her struggles at the 2022 Winter Olympics loomed large over her legacy. Many people thought her career was done. Shiffrin knew it wasn’t. She returned for the 2026 Games, where she won gold — with the 1.5-second gap between her and the second-place finisher being the largest margin in Olympic alpine skiing since 1998.
Feb. 19 — Alysa Liu earned an Olympic gold medal in figure skating — her way

One of the first truly feel-good sports stories of 2026 happened at the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics in February. American figure skater Alysa Liu shocked the world by winning gold in the women’s singles event. Liu had taken two years off from skating following the 2022 Olympics, saying that she had lost her joy for the sport after spending her entire life focused on a singular goal. She returned on her own terms, refusing to let anyone tell her what she could or couldn’t eat or how she had to train. The result was a magical performance that earned her both a gold medal and countless admirers.
Feb. 19 — Team USA elevated women's hockey to new heights

The U.S. women’s national hockey team defeated Canada to win gold in Milano Cortina, adding another chapter to what some consider to be the biggest rivalry in all of sports. It was the first Olympic Games since the PWHL launched and the event showcased a ton of the league’s players on an international stage. For perhaps the first time, U.S. women’s hockey found the limelight. Interest in the sport surged, with ticket sales jumping nearly 42%.
March 14 - 28 — A brand-new NWSL team broke the league’s attendance record

The NWSL fielded two new expansion teams for the 2026 season, Boston Legacy FC and Denver Summit FC, the first additions since the Utah Royals in 2024. Both teams set attendance records at their home openers, with the Legacy drawing over 30,000 fans to its first game at Gillette Stadium, making it the highest-attended game in league history. Just two weeks later, the Summit broke that record with over 63,000 fans at Empower Field at Mile High.
March 18 — WNBA players signed a historic collective bargaining agreement

Ahead of the 2026 season, all eyes were on the WNBA. Coming off record-breaking viewership and attendance numbers, the Women’s National Basketball Players’ Association was seeking a new collective bargaining agreement with the league. Players stood their ground through nearly five months of negotiation and numerous inadequate offers from the league. After extended deadlines, threats of a work stoppage, and countless hours around a conference table, the players came away with the biggest labor win for pro women athletes in history. They secured higher salaries, better benefits, and payments for retired players, among other boons.
April 5 — UCLA women's basketball won its first NCAA championship

In pursuit of the title, the UCLA Bruins went up against the dynasty that is coach Dawn Staley’s University of South Carolina Gamecocks. USC had won the NCAA women’s championship in 2017, 2022, and 2024, and made it to the Final Four each of the past six seasons. The Bruins, meanwhile, had never won an NCAA national championship. After an undefeated regular season led by a powerhouse group of seniors including Lauren Betts, Kiki Rice, Charlisse Leger-Walker, and Gabriela Jaquez, they notched a decisive victory over the Gamecocks, winning 79-51 and bringing home the championship trophy.
May - August — Women’s Elite Rugby players stood with their trans teammates

Shortly before the start of Women’s Elite Rugby’s second season, the fledgling league dropped a bombshell: trans women were no longer allowed to play. This news came as a shock, as multiple trans women had been on rosters for the inaugural season and women’s rugby was widely considered to be one of the most inclusive sports. But many of the remaining players refused to be silent about the way their teammates had been treated. Throughout the season, athletes protested in a variety of ways, from organizing legal aid for trans teammates who had been kicked off their teams to creating a player petition opposing the exclusionary policy (more than half the league signed) and encouraging a fan boycott of the league. While the policy has not been changed, WER athletes’ solidarity with their banned colleagues was one of the few bright spots for trans athletes this year.
May 6 — Rachel Entrekin won the Cocodona 250

The Cocodona 250 is not for the weak. The ultramarathon covers roughly 250 miles in Arizona, traversing remote desert landscapes, hills, and valleys, all while climbing at a grueling altitude. Rachel Entrekin won the 2026 race while setting a new overall course record — including beating the men’s all-time high.
May 20 — The Montreal Victoire became the first Canadian team to win the PWHL’s Walter Cup

Before the PWHL was founded in 2023, pro women’s hockey in North America consisted of a bunch of short-lived leagues that almost always had teams from both the U.S. and Canada. When all these independent bodies came together to launch one pro league, the founders were clear that there would be proportionate representation for both countries. It launched with three teams from each country; the first round of expansion in 2025 added one more team per nation.

The Minnesota Frost won the title in 2024 and 2025, but for a league that has gone out of its way to ensure Canadian and American teams are equally represented, it was time for a new champion. The Finals guaranteed there would be, with a series between the Montreal Victoire and the Ottawa Charge. Ultimately, the Victoire were decisively victorious, 4-0.
May 21 - July 3 — Kelsey Pfendler shattered records while rowing from California to Hawaii

In July, Kelsey Pfendler made history when she became the first American woman to complete a solo row across the mid-Pacific Ocean. Pfendler left from Monterey, California, and, after 44 days at sea, she arrived in Honolulu, Hawaii. Her goal had been to become the first American woman, the youngest woman, and the fastest woman to complete the over 2,400-mile journey, but she accomplished even more than that: She outpaced every man who attempted the same route, and she didn’t just edge out the previous best times — she shattered them. The existing women’s record had been 86 days, while the men’s record was 52.
May 25 - Sept. 19 — Carissa Moore made her comeback in surfing

Carissa Moore is a five-time surfing world champion and the first Olympic gold medalist in the sport. In 2011, when she won her first world championship, she was just 18 years old — the youngest person to ever win the title. The American athlete dominated the sport for over a decade until she decided to step away to start a family in 2024. Late last year, she announced her return to the World Surf League tour with a wildcard entry, saying that she had no expectations of returning to the highs she had achieved pre-pregnancy; she just wanted to show women, including her daughter, that they can keep chasing their dreams, “even as life evolves.”

It turns out she had set her goals too low. In May she won the New Zealand Pro, and by August she had taken over the world’s No. 1 ranking on the Championship Tour. In September, she positioned herself as a World Champion contender by qualifying for the WSL’s postseason. She’s currently ranked second heading into the season finale at the Lexus Pipe Masters event in December.
June 6 — Janja Garnbret became the first woman to climb Bibliographie

Slovenian rock climber Janja Garnbret made history when she became the first woman to climb Bibliographie, a 115-foot route on a limestone cliff in Céüse, France. Bibliographie is categorized as a 9b+ climb, which is the second most difficult grade in sport climbing. She chose to focus on the route, which only five men had completed before, after she lost motivation following the 2024 Paris Olympics. It took 21 sessions over two years. “Usually, in the past, if I couldn’t do a route in two to three tries, I would walk away and never come back,” Garnbret said. “But this route required me to be a different climber. To commit, to be patient — the challenge was mostly mental.”
July 16 - 19 — Flavor Flav threw a weekend-long party for U.S. women Olympic and Paralympic medalists

We wouldn’t ordinarily highlight a man in a women’s sports lineup, but Flavor Flav’s unwavering support has truly earned him a spot. The rapper and former reality TV star hopped on the women’s sports bandwagon ahead of the 2024 Olympics when he signed a five-year contract to be the U.S. women’s water polo team’s official hype man (yes, that’s his actual title). He took his role abroad to the 2026 Milano Cortina games to support the bobsleigh and skeleton teams, and was outraged when the U.S. women’s hockey team didn’t receive an invite to the White House even though the men did. To right the wrong, he decided to host SHE Weekend in Las Vegas this past July, celebrating all the U.S. women Olympic and Paralympic medalists. There was a parade, a concert, and a full weekend of events. That’s real allyship.
July 28 - Aug. 16 — The Malawi women’s soccer team had the most impressive underdog story of the year

In an appearance that ESPN dubbed “the most remarkable [run] by an international team in a major tournament ever,” Malawi women’s soccer’s debut at the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) was unprecedented. Heading into the tournament, the team was ranked 32nd in Africa, and they were set to face 10-time WAFCON champions Nigeria in their first match. Not only did Malawi beat the powerhouse Nigerian team, but they made it all the way to the championship match against Morocco. Led by the Chawinga sisters, Temwa and Tabitha, this small country with virtually no international soccer footprint took the world by storm and qualified for the 2027 Women’s World Cup for the first time ever.
Aug. 1 — Pro women’s baseball returned to the U.S. after 72 years

For the first time since 1954, a mainstream professional women’s baseball league took the field in the United States. Playing at a centralized location in Springfield, Illinois, the four founding teams of the WPBL — the San Francisco Firebells, Los Angeles Queens, New York Heights, and Boston Hunters — picked up the torch from the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League players who came before them.

AAGPBL player Maybelle Blair, 99, was on hand to throw out the ceremonial first pitch from her wheelchair and meet the league’s mascot — a giant version of Maybelle herself. At the end of it all, the Los Angeles Queens were crowned the first-ever league champions, and Queens third baseman Ashton Lansdell was announced as the WPBL’s first signing for the 2027 season.
August - November — WNBA and NWSL fans clapped back at transphobia

During an election year in which trans athletes became a political lightning rod, anti-trans groups tried to bring the controversy to major pro women’s sports. But longtime fans of leagues like the WNBA and NWSL refused to let a few bad actors ruin their welcoming, inclusive culture. In Brooklyn, a Trans Joy Rally stomped out the noise of a small group of anti-trans protesters. And in Portland, Oregon, and Seattle, supporters of the Thorns and Reign used trans flags to cover up hateful signs in the stands, ensuring that the trans community knew it was loved.
Sept. 3 - 9 — Megan Eckert made ultrarunning history (again)

In the sport of ultrarunning, no American can touch Megan Eckert. After setting the American women’s record last year at the world championships in France, she decided that wasn’t good enough for her. In September, she entered the Global Organization of Multi-Day Ultramarathoners Six-Day World Championship in Hungary, where she ran 636.482 miles in six days, beating both her own record from last year (603.155 miles) and the American men’s record that had been in place since 2015 (606.243).
Sept. 13 — Team USA won its fifth consecutive Women's Basketball World Cup

While much of the world watched the men’s World Cup, real ball knowers were locked in to the FIBA women’s basketball World Cup in September. A meeting of international superstars, the final game came down to the United States and France. Both teams were stacked with WNBA talent but ultimately, the U.S. was victorious for the fifth straight time, defeating the French national team 97-79. It was the fourth World Cup victory for tournament MVP Breanna Stewart, while younger talent like Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers secured their first world championship.
Sept. 24 — The Connecticut Sun's “Sunset Season” came to a close

The Connecticut Sun played its final WNBA season in 2026, as the team was sold to an ownership group in Houston to become the revived Houston Comets. Despite a difficult season for a young team plagued by injuries, the franchise went out on a high note. They won their final game against the Toronto Tempo, 95-81, in front of a sold-out hometown crowd of passionate fans. And while losing the first Native-owned team in pro sports is unfortunate, the so-called “Sunset Season” allowed the franchise to honor its legends like Alyssa Thomas and Jonquel Jones, and provided the fans with a collective opportunity to mourn and say goodbye to the beloved Sun.
Oct. 5 — A'ja Wilson won her 5th WNBA MVP

A’ja Wilson can’t stop proving that she is the women’s basketball GOAT. This year saw her collect her fifth WNBA Most Valuable Player award. She’s now the first player in WNBA history to do so, joining the ranks of Michael Jordan, Bill Russell, and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar as the only players in pro basketball history with five or more wins.
Oct. 23 - Nov. 12 — The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders and AUSL unionized

Labor victories swept women’s sports in 2026. With record-setting investment, it was only a matter of time before athletes demanded their fair share of the pie. The Netflix show America’s Sweethearts drastically changed the game for the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, creating over $50 million in brand value for DCC. And while they secured a historic 400% pay raise after the second season of the show in 2025, DCC announced in October of this year that they were unionizing, and that the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association (DCCA) had been recognized by the NFL franchise.

Just a week later, pro softball players announced their own intention to unionize, forming the Athletes Unlimited Softball League Players Association (AUSLPA). Less than a month later, their union was officially recognized by their league. The softball union came after an eight-figure investment last year from Major League Baseball into the Athletes Unlimited Softball League (AUSL).
Oct. 31 — Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship in their second season

The 2026 WNBA season came to the most exciting finish possible: two teams that had never won a championship before faced off in the Finals and went to (the league’s first ever!) Game 7. The Golden State Valkyries defeated the Atlanta Dream to win the championship in just their second season, making them the fastest expansion team in pro sports history to do so. And perhaps the best part is that they did it with a roster of players who were often overlooked by other teams, led by veteran Gabby Williams, whose rallying cry of “for the gays!” made the Chase Center (also known as “Ballhalla”) the most inclusive arena in the league.
Nov. 10 — After making a major splash, the PWHL debuted four new expansion teams

The PWHL’s third season set records left and right. Hot off their gold medal at the Winter Olympics and riding the wave of mainstream interest in hockey thanks to Heated Rivalry, the league’s attendance surpassed 1 million fans. The “Takeover Tour” visited 16 cities and sold out arenas in Seattle and Boston. After fielding the league’s first two expansion teams in Seattle and Vancouver, they announced four new teams for the 2026-27 season, debuting the names and logos for the Detroit Clutch, Hamilton Havoc, Vegas Vanguards, and San Jose Sea Lions. When the puck drops next month, there will be 12 teams in the league.

items.title: Lea Michele’s Favorite At-Home Spa Essential Is From Duane Reade
items.description: Lea Michele’s Postshow Routine Is A Master Class In Winding Down
items.author: Leigh Scheps
paragraphs: Lea Michele’s Postshow Routine Is A Master Class In Winding Down
The Broadway star on her Kiehl’s campaign, closet meditation, and beauty must-haves.

Lea Michele is rethinking wellness. “I just saw this interview that Alanis Morissette did, and she said she doesn’t believe in wellness — she believes in wholeness. And I really love that concept now,” she tells me over Zoom. “Wholeness has always been something that I make a priority, and it helps me be a better wife, mother, and performer.”

It’s a philosophy that makes sense for someone whose recent schedule has included a sold-out concert at New York’s Beacon Theater with former Chess costar Aaron Tveit, a guest-starring role on CBS’ Elsbeth, and a new holiday campaign with Kiehl’s. The morning after the concert, Michele was still riding high. “It really was such an epic day,” she says. “I think it was the first time I was returning to television in many years — maybe 10.”

Between late-night performances and morning school drop-offs, Michele prioritizes small moments of self-care. “I take care of my body and my voice in the same way that an athlete would if they were going to go and play a game,” she says.
Ahead, the Broadway star opens up about her postshow beauty routine, the makeup products she keeps in her purse, and the rituals that help her unwind.
What was your favorite moment from the concert?

I love watching Aaron perform. His rendition of “Without You” and “Glory” from Rent — I just fangirl out. I got to do “Nobody’s Side,” and I was flipping my hair around and rocking out with our amazing guitarist Aurélien [Budynek]. It’s obviously not stuff that you get to do onstage every night when you’re on Broadway.
What does your postshow self-care routine look like?

Number one, I always wash my face. Something I’m obsessed with is cleaning my cell phone and my sunglasses with alcohol at the end of the night. I take a nice shower. Last night, I made myself some sourdough toast, got into bed, checked a couple of text messages, took my little magnesium tea, and went to sleep.
After performing and spending hours in makeup, what are the little things you do to reset?

I think everything starts from within. It’s very hard to get good sleep with two children, but I really try to prioritize it. I have my Hatch light by my bedside, and it goes off at 9:30 p.m. with this warm red light and meditative music that reminds me it’s time to wind down.
I try to drink a ton of water and just take good care of myself. I sit and meditate on the floor in my closet with my red light. It’s one of my favorite little weird private habits.
I have so many wellness things in my house. I have my HigherDOSE [infrared sauna blanket] — I try to do that every day if I can.
What’s one beauty product you always have on you?
I’ve been a fan of Kiehl’s for so many years. I love their body moisturizer. It’s something that I always keep on me, even in my purse, to help my dry skin get through the horrible changing weather.
What does your makeup routine look like for school drop-offs or running around the neighborhood?

I’ll use a foundation, powder, a really nice cream blush, some mascara, a little eyebrow pencil, and some lip gloss. I like the brands Gucci Westman and Saie. I have one blush brush, and it makes getting ready so quick and so easy now.
What’s one beauty ritual that feels like a luxury to you that you do for yourself, not because you have an on-camera appearance or performance?
Getting a lymphatic massage is such a great reset. It’s something that I used to do only for red carpets, but now I do them for myself.

I also love a good bath. I go to Duane Reade, get a bag of Epsom salt, dump it in with a couple drops of lavender oil, and I feel like I’m at a spa. I light a little candle, pour myself a cup of tea, and it feels just as good as any luxury spa.
Last night, you sang “Move On” from Sunday in the Park With George and said it was “a look into the future.” What did you mean by that?

I think what I’ve learned over the past couple of years on Broadway is just how much my joy for what I do is growing and growing and growing. I might not have the opportunity now to play some of the younger ingenue roles, but I think that there are still so many amazing roles that are out there and in store for me. I can’t wait to play them all.
You could play The Nanny. Perfect role for you.
Oh my God, you’re not the first person to tell me that.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: The 10 Best New Books Of November
items.description: With Thanksgiving fast approaching, the hustle and bustle of planning menus, booking travel, and feasting with your family can feel overwhelming. But what’s better than taking some “me time” with a good read?
items.author: Sophie Fishman
paragraphs: With Thanksgiving fast approaching, the hustle and bustle of planning menus, booking travel, and feasting with your family can feel overwhelming. But what’s better than taking some “me time” with a good read?

Fans of literary fiction have plenty to enjoy. Louise Kennedy, author of the critically acclaimed Troubles-era novel Trespasses, returns with Stations, a novel that charts a friendship over 25 years. Kit de Waal’s latest novel, Sweet Pea, celebrates the small moments of love and kindness that make up a human life.

Over on the sports-romance front, things are heating up. For anyone with a Las Vegas Grand Prix-sized hole in their heart, Crash Into You, Simone Soltani’s forbidden F1 romance, is sure to get your engines revving. And if you’re still riding the high of the Valkyries’ win, Zakiya N. Jamal’s fake-dating WNBA romance will keep you in the spirit.
Whether you’re cooking a turkey or just ordering takeout, here are Bustle’s best books of November.
Stations by Louise Kennedy

Out Nov. 3. In a small town in County Kildare, Ireland, two outsiders become fast friends. Red is from an influential family with a proclivity for trouble and Róisín’s family has recently relocated from the north amid The Troubles. Ultimately, the pair’s connection wanes when an incident sends Red running for England. Years later, visiting her estranged father and his new family in London, Róisín reunites with Red in an attempt to restore what they once shared.
How to be Less Useful by Priyanka Mattoo

Out Nov. 3. In a culture obsessed with efficiency, author-filmmaker Priyanka Mattoo dares to ask a radical question: What if we relaxed? It’s part memoir, part self-help, as the author/filmmaker documents how she unwound her identity from people-pleasing and perfectionism, learned to be more present, and ultimately, actually enjoyed the life she’d once painstakingly optimized.
Clear Water by Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes

Out Nov. 3. Recently divorced Alma Figueroa said she would never return to her hometown, Brewer, Wisconsin, but something has pulled her back. All over town in the woods and on roads, locals have been seeing girls dressed in white who disappear without a trace. Perplexingly, none of these girls match the description of the young women who have gone missing in years past. As Alma begins investigating, she begins to uncover answers to questions around her sister Kayla’s death years before.

Out Nov. 3. An immigrant to the United Kingdom from St. Kitts, 29-year-old Paulette is on the precipice of the life she’s always wanted: a stable job; a marriage with her long-term partner, Denton; and a baby. When a sudden tragedy strikes, grief-stricken Paulette has a child, Bird, with Denton’s best friend. Later, as a single mother, a child the same age as her son unexpectedly enters her life — one who calls her sweet pea, just like her grandmother in St. Kitts used to do.
Crash Into You by Simone Soltani

Out Nov. 10. Formula 1 driver Zaid Yousef is finally getting back to the races after last season’s catastrophic injury. Ava Farahani is also looking for her place in the world, as rumors in the press have forced her to leave her job in F1 marketing. Although the two have admired one another from a distance over the years, they know a connection would be forbidden — Ava is the daughter of the principal of Zaid’s rival team. But when an unexpected preseason encounter leads to a positive pregnancy test, the two decide to take it on together.
Mr. Disappear by Virginia Trench

Out Nov. 10. Online dating catfisher Mr. Disappear has ruined the lives of countless victims, gaining their trust before disappearing with everything they own. After connecting on a True Crime sub-Reddit, three women from three different walks of life join forces to take him down once and for all.

Out Nov. 17. On an island off the coast of Bangladesh, a group of children bear witness to their mothers being bought and sold by a brutal madam named Amma, knowing that one day, they will succumb to the same fate. When a new woman, Kusum, is trafficked to the island by her own family, the girls watch as their mothers — initially skeptical of her beauty and education — come to respect her unrelenting spirit and fierce resistance. Led by Kusum, the women incite a revolution that will change all of their lives forever. Uprising is a finalist for the Orwell Prize for Political Fiction.
Two Can Play That Game by Zakiya N. Jamal

Out Nov. 17. Sex-positive influencer Chelsea has never been a sports fan, but an encounter with Adrienne “AD” Daniels, the 6-foot-4 star of the New York Rebels, might change her mind. AD, for their part, has never been able to commit to a relationship. With their reputation putting brand deals in jeopardy, they make a proposition: Chelsea should pretend to be their girlfriend for the remainder of the season. When Chelsea and AD’s fake connection starts feeling real while convincing fans and friends alike of their romance, it puts into question everything they’ve worked to build.

Out Nov. 17. When Jack Chen, the eldest son of two caterers, lands a prestigious internship at tech company K.O. Systems, he’s prepared to do whatever it takes to succeed. Then his world shifts when he strikes up a friendship with fellow intern, Jack Owens, the son of the company’s billionaire founder. As the pressures of the competitive environment build around them, however, their relationship morphs into something far more ruthless.
Long Wave by Daisy Johnson

Out Nov. 24. As a toddler, Ori was found alone and stranded on a remote English island. Growing up, she was kept in the dark about her earliest years. Now, decades later, she’s given birth to her own child and is increasingly plagued by a deep-seated sense of doubt. Unraveling and losing touch with her surroundings, Ori spends her sleepless nights traveling back to the island through her memories in search of her mother.

items.title: Exclusive: Antonia Thomas Opens Up About Filming ‘Dig,’ Your New Feel-Good TV Show
items.description: Never has the workplace comedy looked so aspirational as it does in Peacock’s Dig. Co-created by Parks and Recreation’s Amy Poehler and Michael Schur — and based on Kate Myers’ novel Excavations — the new Peacock series (out now) takes place at an archaeologic
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: Never has the workplace comedy looked so aspirational as it does in Peacock’s Dig. Co-created by Parks and Recreation’s Amy Poehler and Michael Schur — and based on Kate Myers’ novel Excavations — the new Peacock series (out now) takes place at an archaeological dig in Greece. Sure, it’s dirty and sweaty, and plenty goes wrong. But it’s also a place where four women unearth a surprising friendship and a career-making discovery they’d like to keep secret from their overbearing boss.

Antonia Thomas plays Clare, a buttoned-up conservator planning her wedding, but coming to terms with the fact that her perfectly curated life isn’t totally serving her. As the actor tells Bustle, the real love story is the one between the colleagues — brought to life by Poehler, Thomas, Geraldine Viswanathan, and Fina Strazza.

“They’re all doing their own thing,” Thomas says over Zoom from a cottage in the English countryside, where she was celebrating her 40th birthday in early November. “They’re all completely different, and they’re all at different phases of their lives, but all realizing that they’re questioning where they are and not sure if what they’re doing is the right thing. It’s just really beautifully written in that they all manage to learn something from one another.”

Thomas is learning a lot about herself too. The Good Doctor and Misfits alum has been flexing new acting muscles over the past year, genre-hopping from vacation drama Two Weeks in August to detective series Tommy & Tuppence. In Dig, she continues to prove her versatility.

“That kind of comedy world was something new for me, and that was a challenge,” Thomas says. “It just feels like an exciting jumping-off point where I’m like, ‘OK, I want to take on more things that I don’t know yet how to do.’”
Below, Thomas opens up about karaoke with the cast, her hopes for a second season, and what’s next.
Your chemistry as a cast is amazing. Can you tell me about a time behind the scenes that you felt that energy?

At the beginning of the series, we’re introduced relatively separately [on screen] — so it was a while before we all got to be together as girls. That happened for the first time at the dig site, and we were looking down at the statue like, “Oh, my God.” This unlikely girl gang.

And then, at the very end of the shoot, we were in Italy, all staying in the same hotel, and we got to meet for dinners. The hotel had this amazing piano player, and we ended up doing karaoke with him. It was this beautiful old masseria, and we were the only ones there. And he only had the songs he knew how to play, so we all managed to find one and blasted it out. I did Tina Turner’s “Simply the Best.”
What did you envision Clare’s relationship with Gary to be up to this point? It feels like she’s been taking a path in life that’s very “don’t rock the boat, don’t do anything crazy.”

Clare’s big emotional arc is realizing that she doesn’t need to please her mother, and her engagement to Gary is very much a product of going, “I’m at the stage in my life where I really ‘should’ be married now. I should have kids. I should be... whatever.” And Gary’s there in the place where she spends a lot of time, because she does want to work on the dig site. And so she’s like, “That guy will do. He’s nice. I can mold him.” He’s a lovely guy. He’s just not really right for her.
It was so nice that Clare stands up to her mom. Can you talk about that mother-daughter dynamic?

Oh, my God, it was so fun. Noma [Dumezweni] is the most incredible actress, and I have been such a fan of her work from afar for a really long time. We have a lot of friends in common from the British scene. Instantly on meeting, we were chatting, chatting, chatting. We both had a really clear idea of what their lives had looked like — which is, she thinks she’s being a good mum by setting her daughter on the right track. But she’s just so preoccupied with the world that they live in and what everybody thinks that she’s never made room to actually listen. She still loves her daughter. She’s probably not going to change as a person, but she can learn to loosen that up a little bit.
I love that at the end Clare’s like, “I’m going to India. No itinerary.” Is there a time that you’ve done that?

This industry can be a little bit like that. Sometimes you get opportunities, and you’re like, “There’s the safe choice, and then there’s the one that really scares me, and I don’t know if I can do it — but I’m just going to do it anyway.” That choice of going for the path less trodden, not playing the role that you know you can do, I try to apply that to my job.
Is there a specific genre or role that you imagine?

For me, it’s all about the writing — if the character is well-drawn and interesting. I’d love to do a really serious piece of drama. I’d also like to do something quite genre-y. I love a really good intellectual horror or a thriller. But really, I’m open to any challenge.
Should there be a Season 2, what would you love to see for Clare?
There’s so much fun to find in the nuance of this female friendship, and where that can go. Seeing them leaning into the new freedom of the choices that they’ve made would be really interesting.

I would love to see Clare really letting loose. The comedy of her trying to do that and embrace it, versus her personality, and trying to find that sweet spot of what feels true to her, would be really fun to watch.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: 'Heated Rivalry’ Is Actually A Holiday Show
items.description: Sometimes, the best holiday entertainment isn’t expressly festive. Maybe it’s just a cozy vibe you want to curl up with, or a crowd-pleasing popcorn flick your entire family can agree on. Or perhaps it’s something that makes you nostalgic for the year you spen
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: Sometimes, the best holiday entertainment isn’t expressly festive. Maybe it’s just a cozy vibe you want to curl up with, or a crowd-pleasing popcorn flick your entire family can agree on. Or perhaps it’s something that makes you nostalgic for the year you spent every Friday from Thanksgiving through Christmas watching two beautiful hockey players go from on-the-ice enemies and secret lovers to passionate, life-altering soulmates.

Yes, somehow it’s practically been one year since Heated Rivalry premiered on Nov. 28. And there’s no better way to celebrate than by welcoming the streaming phenomenon, based on Rachel Reid’s hit Game Changers novels, into your canon of go-to seasonal viewing.

Not that you haven’t already rewatched it a lot. But if you find yourself yearning for that first blush of Shane and Ilya’s love story, well, that makes sense! After all, our cultural obsession with Heated Rivalry was largely forged during the holidays.

You might remember kicking your feet watching Shane and Ilya’s first charged conversation in the gym (you know the scene), cozied up with Thanksgiving leftovers and Black Friday scores. Maybe you strung up lights while jamming to Scott and Kip’s de facto anthem, “I’ll Believe in Anything.” And no matter what you gave or received, there’s a good chance Shane and Ilya’s cottage escape was the gift that brought you the most butterflies last year.

Even Reid knew by the end of the holidays that Heated Rivalry was... a big deal. As she recently told Bustle, the realization came when Andy Cohen and Anderson Cooper decided which characters they were most like while hosting New Year’s Eve for CNN: “I thought, ‘This is really, really surreal. They’re talking about my characters by name, and everybody knows who they’re talking about.’”

This time of year is all about gratitude and reflection, and there’s something special about honoring a piece of pop culture that was (and is!) a bright light in your life. While Heated Rivalry is a steamy love story, it’s also an ode to the surprising ways our loved ones can show up for us — see Shane and his mom’s beautiful heart-to-heart at the cottage — which is perennially one of those big things we pine for at the holidays.

Even without a Santa hat in sight (save that for the reported Heated Rivalry Christmas movie), the show offers all the warmth and comfort you could crave from holiday viewing. Not to mention an affirming reminder to seize hope and courage in the new year — think of Ilya’s moving line, “I’m coming to the cottage.” What’s your metaphorical cottage in 2027? Run there!
