items.title: My grandparents’ music drove me mad. Now it carries me home
items.description: Chatter floats around me and smoke rises from the bonfire. It is a warm August night in the Philadelphia suburbs, and one of my friends slowly taps the darbuka under his arm. Then he sings Umm Kulthum’s ‘Alf Leila Wa Leila’ (‘A Thousand and One Nights’). One a
items.author: Elissa Odeh
paragraphs: Chatter floats around me and smoke rises from the bonfire. It is a warm August night in the Philadelphia suburbs, and one of my friends slowly taps the darbuka under his arm. Then he sings Umm Kulthum’s ‘Alf Leila Wa Leila’ (‘A Thousand and One Nights’). One after another, we join in, singing along to what I once considered the epitome of old people’s music:
The night and its sky, its stars and its moon, its moon and its awakening,
and you and me, my own love, my own life.
The next line comes to me instinctively. I’m singing in ecstasy, as my parents used to on our night rides. I laugh to myself as I watch my friends sway in their seats.

I’m back at my grandparents’ house in the Palestinian town of Beit Sahour. After playing in their yard until sunset, my cousins and I would gather on their bed, where Teta would turn down Umm Kulthum on the television to tell us the story of the Elderly Woman and her Cow while slicing apples. Now and then, I’d glance at the flickering black-and-white screen to see the audience clap, sway and cry out in a state of tarab, surrendering to what they called ‘her grandeur’. She would finish a stanza, and the audience would erupt in applause, calling out Azama ala azama, ya Sit! (‘Greatness upon greatness, oh lady!’), waiting for her to sing again.

They were out of their minds, I thought. Why such reverence for an Egyptian woman with dark sunglasses, a silk handkerchief draped over her hand, standing on a stage for hours accompanied by a full orchestra, repeating almost the same lyrics relentlessly?

Morning came and so did Fairuz. I woke up to my grandfather’s voice calling me. Eyes half-open, I put on my school uniform and ran down the stairs to my grandparents’ house, the scent of Arabic coffee rising from the stove. My Teta was in the backyard. She embraced me with her flour-dusted hands, then continued kneading the dough, humming along with the voice on the radio:
I write your name, my love, on the old poplar trees.
You write my name on the sand of the road.
Tomorrow winter will come on wounded stories,
your name shall remain, and my name shall be erased.

Fairuz, again. I expressed my dismay at the music choice, only to hear Teta’s monologue on the renowned Lebanese vocalist, the great ‘Bird of the East’, and the horrific possibility of a morning without her songs. I sighed and accepted my fate. I rolled my eyes and tapped my foot, taking a bite of Teta’s bread and waiting to be saved by my ride to school.

Naively, I had forgotten that my suffering would not end. It felt like an epidemic when Fairuz’s voice trailed from Teta’s radio to Amo Essam’s van. Oblivious to my frustration, with a cigarette between his teeth, he would sing along:
The people have asked me about you, my darling.
They’ve written letters and the wind took them.
It’s not easy for me to sing, my darling,
when for the first time, we are not together.

We left Beit Sahour when I was 15 for a ‘better life’, my father said – one where his kids’ futures would not be restricted by political turmoil and economic instability, but filled with security, opportunity and dignity that presumably awaited us in the West. So, in the summer of 2017, we packed our bags, gathering whatever crumbs of our life in Beit Sahour we could carry, and headed for the United States.

Philadelphia was beautiful – tall buildings and ancient architecture, enormous roads, and cheesesteak shops around every other corner. As we explored the suburbs for a place to settle, we drove past rows of identical houses with gable roofs, vast stretches of lawn and fast-food chains. Walmart was a sensational experience. It was our family’s picnic destination for the first few weekends in the US. I couldn’t believe there was a store with gardening tools, clothes, groceries and toys, all under one roof. There seemed to be infinite choices for everything – milk, bread and even eggs: cage-free, organic, conventional, and free-range. I had no clue what any of it meant. It was just eggs.

The mornings were quiet. I started eating a blueberry muffin on my way to school. I sat alone on the bus, where the speakers blasted country music. I had nothing to say to the bus driver. I searched for an English equivalent of Ya’tik Al Afiye. But my tongue was tied, and I settled for ‘Thank you.’
My ears searched for Arabic across campus. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me

Amid the white American student body, my frizzy hair, bushy brows and distinctive nose made me conspicuous. Although students invited me to join their table, I sometimes chose to eat lunch alone, especially when I had a za’tar mankoushe – flatbread with dried crushed thyme and olive oil. I dreaded explaining that, no, I was not having marijuana for lunch.

I was not necessarily left out – kids liked to sit with me and ask me about my life in Palestine – but I always felt like an exotic creature among them. I couldn’t follow their conversations and cultural references. Listening to Taylor Swift, watching American TV or wearing flannels with miniskirts never quite made me feel that I belonged. Back with my family, I would exhale a long breath of Arabic phrases, exhausted from a seven-hour shift of imitating an American accent.

In college, I gravitated toward Arabs wherever I found them – and I was determined to find them. My ears searched for Arabic across campus, and when I detected it, I was filled with such giddiness that I ran to introduce myself. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me. For the first time in my life, my closest friends were Jordanian, Lebanese, Syrian and Egyptian. We ate za’tar mankoushe together, argued over who made the best shawarma, laughed at the differences between our accents and traded stories about our homelands.

In each conversation, we searched for fragments of our old lives we still longed for: tea with our grandparents, soccer in the streets with the neighbours, the small corner stores in our neighbourhoods that sold cigarette-shaped candy. We remembered our elders’ obsession with listening to Fairuz in the morning and Umm Kulthum at night – and our irritation whenever they did.

I lost Teta and Sedo a few years later. I watched my father mourn both of his parents as he said goodbye to them over video calls, and we livestreamed their funerals on Facebook. Overcome with grief, I played Fairuz:
And I’d write you on a paper so I won’t say, I can’t say.
If only you are not leaving, if only you stay, stay forever.
I listened to the songs that my Teta played every morning, the ones I couldn’t wait to escape.

Fairuz’s voice carried me back to my grandparents’ backyard, where Teta hummed along to the radio as her hands kneaded the dough. Lemons dangled from the tree above her. Coffee brewed on the stove as she handed me a cup of mint tea and a piece of freshly baked bread. Then Sedo would greet me with my nickname: Ahlan wa Sahlan, Alooseh, habibet Sedo.
Welcome, Alooseh, Sedo’s dear one.
I had become the person I used to roll my eyes at. In the diaspora, I found my way back to Umm Kulthum and Fairuz. What once belonged to my elders had quietly become my own.
I look around at my friends. We are singing the songs we once thought belonged to our grandparents

As a little girl I used to fall asleep on chairs at weddings, only to open my eyes to find my parents and grandparents, my uncles and their wives, holding hands and leaning into each other singing along to Umm Kulthum’s ‘Alf Leila Wa Leila’, more enchanted with every stanza – and perhaps a little more in love.
Now, with my fair share of love, longing and heartbreak over men, I find my yearning reflected in Umm Kulthum’s songs.
At my friend’s engagement last winter, three generations sang along to Umm Kulthum. With eyes closed and glasses raised, hands swaying and some crying out ‘Allah’, we were in a state of tarab.
Back at the bonfire, I look around at my friends. Some had left home at a young age; others know it only through their parents. We are singing the songs we once thought belonged to our grandparents:
Let’s live in the eyes of the night,
and we tell the sun, come, come,
after a year, not before a year.
This is a beautiful night of love,
worth a thousand nights and a night,
a thousand nights and a night.

After playing in their yard until sunset, my cousins and I would gather on their bed, where Teta would turn down Umm Kulthum on the television to tell us the story of the Elderly Woman and her Cow while slicing apples. Now and then, I’d glance at the flickering black-and-white screen to see the audience clap, sway and cry out in a state of tarab, surrendering to what they called ‘her grandeur’. She would finish a stanza, and the audience would erupt in applause, calling out Azama ala azama, ya Sit! (‘Greatness upon greatness, oh lady!’), waiting for her to sing again.

They were out of their minds, I thought. Why such reverence for an Egyptian woman with dark sunglasses, a silk handkerchief draped over her hand, standing on a stage for hours accompanied by a full orchestra, repeating almost the same lyrics relentlessly?

Morning came and so did Fairuz. I woke up to my grandfather’s voice calling me. Eyes half-open, I put on my school uniform and ran down the stairs to my grandparents’ house, the scent of Arabic coffee rising from the stove. My Teta was in the backyard. She embraced me with her flour-dusted hands, then continued kneading the dough, humming along with the voice on the radio:
I write your name, my love, on the old poplar trees.
You write my name on the sand of the road.
Tomorrow winter will come on wounded stories,
your name shall remain, and my name shall be erased.

Fairuz, again. I expressed my dismay at the music choice, only to hear Teta’s monologue on the renowned Lebanese vocalist, the great ‘Bird of the East’, and the horrific possibility of a morning without her songs. I sighed and accepted my fate. I rolled my eyes and tapped my foot, taking a bite of Teta’s bread and waiting to be saved by my ride to school.

Naively, I had forgotten that my suffering would not end. It felt like an epidemic when Fairuz’s voice trailed from Teta’s radio to Amo Essam’s van. Oblivious to my frustration, with a cigarette between his teeth, he would sing along:
The people have asked me about you, my darling.
They’ve written letters and the wind took them.
It’s not easy for me to sing, my darling,
when for the first time, we are not together.

We left Beit Sahour when I was 15 for a ‘better life’, my father said – one where his kids’ futures would not be restricted by political turmoil and economic instability, but filled with security, opportunity and dignity that presumably awaited us in the West. So, in the summer of 2017, we packed our bags, gathering whatever crumbs of our life in Beit Sahour we could carry, and headed for the United States.

Philadelphia was beautiful – tall buildings and ancient architecture, enormous roads, and cheesesteak shops around every other corner. As we explored the suburbs for a place to settle, we drove past rows of identical houses with gable roofs, vast stretches of lawn and fast-food chains. Walmart was a sensational experience. It was our family’s picnic destination for the first few weekends in the US. I couldn’t believe there was a store with gardening tools, clothes, groceries and toys, all under one roof. There seemed to be infinite choices for everything – milk, bread and even eggs: cage-free, organic, conventional, and free-range. I had no clue what any of it meant. It was just eggs.

The mornings were quiet. I started eating a blueberry muffin on my way to school. I sat alone on the bus, where the speakers blasted country music. I had nothing to say to the bus driver. I searched for an English equivalent of Ya’tik Al Afiye. But my tongue was tied, and I settled for ‘Thank you.’
My ears searched for Arabic across campus. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me

Amid the white American student body, my frizzy hair, bushy brows and distinctive nose made me conspicuous. Although students invited me to join their table, I sometimes chose to eat lunch alone, especially when I had a za’tar mankoushe – flatbread with dried crushed thyme and olive oil. I dreaded explaining that, no, I was not having marijuana for lunch.

I was not necessarily left out – kids liked to sit with me and ask me about my life in Palestine – but I always felt like an exotic creature among them. I couldn’t follow their conversations and cultural references. Listening to Taylor Swift, watching American TV or wearing flannels with miniskirts never quite made me feel that I belonged. Back with my family, I would exhale a long breath of Arabic phrases, exhausted from a seven-hour shift of imitating an American accent.

In college, I gravitated toward Arabs wherever I found them – and I was determined to find them. My ears searched for Arabic across campus, and when I detected it, I was filled with such giddiness that I ran to introduce myself. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me. For the first time in my life, my closest friends were Jordanian, Lebanese, Syrian and Egyptian. We ate za’tar mankoushe together, argued over who made the best shawarma, laughed at the differences between our accents and traded stories about our homelands.

In each conversation, we searched for fragments of our old lives we still longed for: tea with our grandparents, soccer in the streets with the neighbours, the small corner stores in our neighbourhoods that sold cigarette-shaped candy. We remembered our elders’ obsession with listening to Fairuz in the morning and Umm Kulthum at night – and our irritation whenever they did.

I lost Teta and Sedo a few years later. I watched my father mourn both of his parents as he said goodbye to them over video calls, and we livestreamed their funerals on Facebook. Overcome with grief, I played Fairuz:
And I’d write you on a paper so I won’t say, I can’t say.
If only you are not leaving, if only you stay, stay forever.
I listened to the songs that my Teta played every morning, the ones I couldn’t wait to escape.

Fairuz’s voice carried me back to my grandparents’ backyard, where Teta hummed along to the radio as her hands kneaded the dough. Lemons dangled from the tree above her. Coffee brewed on the stove as she handed me a cup of mint tea and a piece of freshly baked bread. Then Sedo would greet me with my nickname: Ahlan wa Sahlan, Alooseh, habibet Sedo.
Welcome, Alooseh, Sedo’s dear one.
I had become the person I used to roll my eyes at. In the diaspora, I found my way back to Umm Kulthum and Fairuz. What once belonged to my elders had quietly become my own.
I look around at my friends. We are singing the songs we once thought belonged to our grandparents

As a little girl I used to fall asleep on chairs at weddings, only to open my eyes to find my parents and grandparents, my uncles and their wives, holding hands and leaning into each other singing along to Umm Kulthum’s ‘Alf Leila Wa Leila’, more enchanted with every stanza – and perhaps a little more in love.
Now, with my fair share of love, longing and heartbreak over men, I find my yearning reflected in Umm Kulthum’s songs.
At my friend’s engagement last winter, three generations sang along to Umm Kulthum. With eyes closed and glasses raised, hands swaying and some crying out ‘Allah’, we were in a state of tarab.
Back at the bonfire, I look around at my friends. Some had left home at a young age; others know it only through their parents. We are singing the songs we once thought belonged to our grandparents:
Let’s live in the eyes of the night,
and we tell the sun, come, come,
after a year, not before a year.
This is a beautiful night of love,
worth a thousand nights and a night,
a thousand nights and a night.

items.title: What exile was like for the first people called ‘refugees’
items.description: One dark night in 1683, a 19-year-old girl from the small town of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, not far from Grenoble in southeastern France, approached the fire in the hearth of her family home. This was a time of high religious tension in France, and Blanche Ga
items.author: Nora Baker
paragraphs: One dark night in 1683, a 19-year-old girl from the small town of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, not far from Grenoble in southeastern France, approached the fire in the hearth of her family home. This was a time of high religious tension in France, and Blanche Gamond’s Protestant family had been forced to host soldiers in their house whose goal it was to intimidate them into converting to Catholicism. They were not alone in being subjected to this treatment, known as the dragonnades policy, which had been instigated by Louis XIV’s government two years earlier. Over the course of the Sun King’s reign, anti-Protestant measures continually increased. These included restrictions on when and how Protestants could hold funerals, and prohibitions against Protestant women working as midwives; conversions to the religion were also forbidden.

Gamond had heard of Antoine Chamier, a man in the nearby town of Montélimar, being broken on the wheel for his refusal to renounce his religious beliefs. She admired Chamier’s steadfastness, and wanted to prove to herself that she, too, could endure great suffering for her faith. In approaching the fire, her aim was to test herself, and to prove that she was strong enough to withstand the pain. But Gamond could not do this. ‘As soon as my fingers began to burn,’ she wrote (my translation), ‘I would immediately withdraw my hand.’ This was no casual test of strength, however, and Gamond was devastated by her inability to tolerate the heat.

Though many people today don’t associate exile with western Europeans, the experiences of French Protestants in the early modern period were often fraught with uncertainty and suffering. They departed their homeland in search of security and stability elsewhere, and they often established large communities in the lands in which they settled, with churches catering to their diaspora. When leaving France, they often brought skills in fields such as silk-weaving or watchmaking with them, resulting in what some commentators have labelled as a ‘brain drain’ in their home kingdom.

So, while it may be difficult for those of us who have grown up in stable or safe countries without persecution, and who are part of a majority, to comprehend Gamond’s conviction and the danger with which it was associated, these were very common experiences for many people in history. Today, as well as in the past, humans tend to want to see ourselves as part of something bigger than us, a grand cause, something that will survive us, a religion or a nation or a cause – and many have sacrificed for the values or ideals they believe it represents.

As for how it occurred to Gamond to briefly burn her hand, it seems likely that she was inspired by the story of Thomas Bilney, a 16th-century Englishman who tested himself in much the same way the night before he was to be burnt at the stake. Though Bilney also initially instinctively retracted his hand when the flame tickled his fingers, the second time he attempted this feat, he succeeded in withstanding the heat for a couple of seconds. Bilney’s story featured in a popular martyrology (a collection of martyr stories) owned by many Protestant families in 17th-century France. The tales of those who remained firm in their faith against all odds – even in the face of torture or death – were designed to be inspiring, to provide comfort to readers through examples of those who had calmly met their end.

But these stories could also be sources of pressure, as we can see in Gamond’s account. Frustrated that she couldn’t properly emulate the martyrs of old, she frequently pleaded with God to make her better, more pious, less attached to the world and to herself: ‘My God, make it so that I love neither the world, nor the things in it, give me the grace … to renounce myself.’ This desire to be detached from worldly concerns was a common theme in medieval and early modern Christianity, and even in the earlier traditions of classical antiquity: it is often known as contemptus mundi, or ‘contempt for the world’. In making these appeals to God, Gamond was drawing on language that she had likely picked up from pastors and religious services, employing it in order to try to cope with a period of stress and uncertainty.

In 1685, rights previously granted to French Protestants – or Huguenots, as they were also known – were stripped back through the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, an event often simply called the Revocation. Persecution of this group grew so intense that many sought to leave their homeland. Historians estimate that around 200,000 Huguenots left France in the wake of the oppression. This exodus became known as the Refuge, and it was, in fact, as a result of this upheaval that the word ‘refugee’ entered the English language – from the French ‘réfugié’.

Of course, there was nothing new in history about populations being uprooted – the Huguenots, themselves, took inspiration from the story of the Babylonian exile of the Jews in the Bible. And, indeed, previous generations of French Protestants had also settled far from France, in bids to escape the Wars of Religion (1562-98). But the post-Revocation Huguenots were perhaps among the first groups of people to seek shelter in foreign climes after the Thirty Years’ War (1618-48) had helped plant the seeds for the development of the modern nation-state. The idea that a state might be intrinsically associated with a particular ethnic group living within its borders would remain in flux for many years before further solidifying amid the Romantic nationalism of the 19th century – however, the 1648 Peace of Westphalia was among the factors that helped lay the groundwork for this idea to take hold, through its assertion of the principle of territorial sovereignty.
Gamond sought to steel herself against physical pain, whereas Cabrit removed himself from harm’s way

Huguenots have furthermore been labelled ‘modern’ refugees by scholars such as John Hintermaier due to their propensity to appeal to the altruistic sentiments and economic concerns of those in their host nations, rather than seeking support based on religious affinity alone. The achievements of many Huguenots and their descendants in the textile industries and trade networks of their host nations have led to the community garnering praise as an example of successful integration. However, the path to a stable and secure future in a new land did not always run smooth. Another Huguenot, the minister Jacques Cabrit, initially moved to London, but wrote that people there ‘recognised from our mannerisms and our clothes that we were French, and we were subject to verbal and sometimes physical abuse’ (my translation).

Cabrit and his friends were, nonetheless, prepared to settle in England, until they heard rumours that King James II was planning to persecute Protestants in much the same way as Louis XIV had done in France. The threat of such an attack against their religion proved too much to bear, and on 1 March 1688, just a few months before the English king was overthrown, Cabrit set off again, eventually settling in Prussia. It may seem, then, that religious matters were more central to Cabrit’s identity than national affiliation, if it was those rumours that proved to be the last straw for him rather than actual instances of xenophobia.

But we can reflect on the role that fear can play in already tense environments. Cabrit, by leaving England, and Gamond, by trying to burn herself, both acted in the ways they felt would best protect them, in the face of an uncertain future. In this context, Gamond sought to steel herself against physical pain, whereas Cabrit removed himself from harm’s way.

Cabrit’s account also provides us with a reflection on how cultural differences can affect the expression of emotions. While employed as a French tutor in the home of an aged professor in Frankfurt an der Oder in Prussia, Cabrit witnessed the death of the elderly man. He was later stunned by the widow’s calm response to the news of her husband’s death:

She listened to me with the greatest sangfroid in the world, which surprised me immensely, as I expected her sobs to make the air shake, as that is what women in the Languedoc do in such circumstances.

Though Cabrit was taken aback by this reaction, he did write that he admired the woman’s ‘stoicism’. This was just one of the clashes between cultural expectations and reality that he was to experience while adapting to life in German-speaking lands. We know that different cultural traditions value emotions, and their expression, differently, as scholars such as Barbara H Rosenwein have shown. It would appear that, in the Languedoc context – at least, according to Cabrit – women were expected to be highly vocal, and even clamorous, in the expression of their grief. It may have been that these raw evocations of pain were viewed as more authentic, signs of a close bond with the deceased. The Frankfurt an der Oder widow’s response, on the other hand, suggests a cultural context where measured reactions were valued, even amid difficult circumstances.

Eventually, Cabrit succeeded in settling down and living a relatively normal life in Cottbus, near Potsdam, in what is now eastern Germany. The same cannot be said for Gamond, who died in Zurich aged just 53. Imprisoned following an initial attempt to escape from France, she eventually managed to cross the border into Switzerland in 1688. Records show that she and her father requested alms in order to survive, and it is thought that the tragic and extremely pious image she painted of herself in her memoir was played up so as to attract sympathy and, thus, monetary assistance. And yet, there is also raw emotion to be seen in her words. While describing a deeply painful operation on her leg, Gamond wrote that she could not bring herself to give further detail: ‘[My quill] falls from my hand, and this sad memory makes me shed so many tears that I could [not] continue anymore [to endure] the horrible pains that I felt.’ The page on which these words are written in the manuscript is blotchy, in a way that might lead us to speculate over the presence of centuries-old tear stains. Whether or not tears are indeed the cause of the smeared writing cannot be determined, but one thing is certain: even after establishing oneself in exile, past pains and anxieties could continue to echo in early modern refugee lives.

While Cabrit and Gamond each ultimately led very different lives, both of their experiences were profoundly shaped by the persecution that their community faced. Both sought to carve out spaces for themselves within their religious and social community following their departure from their homeland, Gamond through writing and circulating an autobiographical account of her experiences, Cabrit mostly through pastoral work. Both leaned heavily on their networks for support, contacting family members, friends of friends and distant relatives in times of need. This experience of reaching out to others was shared by many other members of the Huguenot diaspora, and we can see from their stories that it was often thanks to being able to build on existing connections that refugees were able to thrive in new lands – though this was not always easy or even possible, as Gamond’s challenging experience in the Swiss cantons shows. While popular narratives about Huguenot trajectories often focus on the community’s economic and social success following their settling in new lands, we should not overlook the pain associated with being uprooted from one’s home that was experienced by many of these refugees. What they managed to achieve in spite of these difficulties is a testament to their resilience.

items.title: The streets of Karachi scared me less than home did
items.description: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watch
items.author: Sadia Khatri
paragraphs: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watched me drive away – to another part of the city, where my childhood best friend Aesha and I had found an apartment for ourselves.

Salute to the girls who do this here, in Karachi: live outside of blood, family, marriage or whatever patriarchal bargain most women in my city use to seek their freedom. Anam was the first girl I saw who did this – who did not transfer, like property, from her father’s house to a husband’s, but instead lived with two others in this sprawling city of at least 20 million, but very likely more, home to every ethnic and religious group in Pakistan. Its indigenous communities were historically fisherfolk, pastoralists, and Sindhi and Baloch people, but modern Karachi was founded and funded by Sindhi Hindus and Parsis and Gujaratis. Post-partition, it became home to Muhajirs, who migrated from India, as well as millions of Pashtuns from northern Pakistan and Afghanistan. In the city’s mix are also migrants from Punjab and Balochistan, Burma and Bangladesh. Every kind of population has laid its stake to the city, so why not single women?

We might be one of the tiniest populations in Karachi’s history to fight for our right to the city. A friend from Bangalore visited and, after we’d walked the old streets of Kharadar and the shiny roads of Clifton, she said, baffled: ‘And I thought we in India had few women on the streets.’ Where were the akeli women? She meant unaccompanied women – not the rich-girl variety who outsource their lives to drivers and guards who shuttle them around the city in protective containers, but middle-class girls like us.

‘My family lives in another city,’ I’d told my landlord, nervously avoiding his gaze. In Karachi, respectable girls did this only under the pretext of majboori – some justifiable excuse grounded in necessity, like working or studying away from home. Otherwise, only sex workers and trans women typically broke away from their families to live an unconventional life, one far more difficult than mine. Turned out he hardly cared. The apartment was cheap and, given the neighbourhood it was in – Badar Commercial, an unruly stretch in an otherwise upscale residential part of town, where the lane was not well kept and the building did not have a lock – he wasn’t looking for respectability points. Most others, landlords and landladies alike, had looked at me and said: ‘Families only.’ They did not want to hand over their apartment to two girls, all akeli, all alone, by themselves. Potential blemishes. Danger.

When we moved into the building at Badar, we anticipated all kinds of eyes. The apartment opposite ours was a lawyer’s office, or posed as one. Upstairs lived a gruff old uncle, a retired policeman who fought with everyone and threatened to call the cops after arguments. All day, he slept with the rooftop keys, effectively controlling access to the building’s water tanks.

The two apartments below us belonged to a family that had bought both units and broken down the middle wall. There were lots of women and children and a little dog. The ‘man of the house’ was a 21-year-old boy, evidently a drug addict who was usually found by the entrance staircase, getting high and holding a gun. His 20-year-old wife, a decade younger than us, was friendly. She asked us how we managed, all akelay. Again that word. We got into the habit of saying: ‘Yes, God knows how we manage, all akelay, all saath saath.’ Alone-together.
Since she’d been over a few times, we told her that the gun made us feel queasy. Could her husband please put it away? Very calmly, she replied: ‘He has never pointed it at you, has he?’
The neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely

Our balcony faced the balcony of the building opposite ours. The grilles were close enough to talk to the person on the other side. We knew these neighbours only at this elevation: it was the COVID-19 pandemic era, so everyone was stuck inside. WhatsApp numbers were exchanged; regretted it instantly. Uncle A had an on-again, off-again relationship with his wife, which meant he sometimes rang me up in the middle of the night, sobbing. Aunty B, wonderful to chat with during the day, was obsessed with jinns at night. She loved sending us links to YouTube videos where such supernatural beings were summoned into a courtroom, and she wanted to know if we, too, had ever seen one.

Badar Commercial – with its cast of characters all breaking the codes of Pakistani respectability in some way – got used to us faster than we got used to it. But the neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely. We sometimes dressed respectably – shalwar kameez and saris – whereas other times I walked around Badar in knee-length shorts and tank tops. We spoke English but also Urdu, Kutchi and Memoni; one of us was a teacher and the other a psychologist, but was that really all we did? And were we really Muslim? Often, at home, or grocery shopping, or having chai at the streetside dhaba, or tea-shop, someone would ask: Hindu? Christian? Foreign?

This inability to categorise us reached its pinnacle after a Qawwali night at our apartment – a Sufi music performance. A neighbour who had invited himself midway through the performance after hearing it from his window later asked us with utter confusion: ‘Are you Sunni or Shia?’
We said: ‘It’s hard to explain…’
He leaned in uncomfortably close and whispered: ‘You are the Illuminati?’

Some men assumed we were sex workers and showed up at our door. This might have been my father’s deepest fear: if my family discovered I lived akelay, they’d think me a loose woman, and him a dishonourable man who could not keep his property in line. My extended family continued to believe I still lived with my parents. If an uncle visited, he was told I was out of town. ‘Sadia goes to Hyderabad a lot,’ my relatives noted.

Our time in that apartment was spent, really, undoing our lives. Aesha and I came from families where a room of your own was a luxury only richer relatives afforded their children. Until I was 16, I shared a room with my parents and four siblings; after that, there were two rooms, one for my parents and one for us. Now, Aesha and I each had a room, with a door we could close behind us and let nothing in for a while. At first, I did not know what to do with the emptiness. Just me and my friend, and a feeling of being untethered, unpropertied. We wanted others to feel it too, so our home was always filled with friends and women and anyone who needed a place to crash.

We set up the space with what little we had. Our mothers donated precious items from their kitchens. (When she came over, I introduced ammi to the neighbourhood women – trying to prove, I think, that it was possible to not live a double life, to have both my freedom and my mother by my side.) Our friends gave us our first furniture: a floor rug, a cupboard. We raised and killed too many plants, and washed our clothes by hand or sent them home when the water was out again. We learned to interact with the city in ways we never had before: comparing the vegetable vendors’ rates and learning who had been taking advantage of us, becoming experts at shortcuts on foot, especially during the rain, and knowing where to find rickshaws at 6 pm versus 9 pm.
For the first time, I prayed under the open sky while the city raged around me

Karachi is a logistical nightmare for anyone who lives here – and none of its systems are designed to include women in their public unfolding. Every bank vendor and dhaba server and home electrician is a man. This was another city that opened up to us: of everyday upkeep and haggling and bills. In this city, we learned to be less afraid of the men we had been taught to be suspicious of our whole lives: the electrician boys, the plumber uncles, the carpenter brothers. While any kind of man can turn uncomfortably friendly at a moment’s notice, there’s a way both patriarchy and capitalism benefit by insisting that the working-class man is the biggest threat to a woman’s safety. Under this ruse, the ‘good’ men in my life can surveil and control my movements, while a whole world of centrally airconditioned, securitised and gatekept enterprises can capitalise on this idea of keeping out the riff-raff.

In Badar Commercial, this lie came further undone. Plumber #1 was younger than us, fascinated by our women-only lives, and before leaving would help himself to swigs of whatever alcohol we had left over. Electrician uncle was popular among all the single girlies and slowly taught us how to drill the walls and reinstall ceiling fans. Plumber #2 was of a more conservative bent, refusing to look us straight in the eye but kindly and non-patronisingly telling us we had burned, nay destroyed, our new water heater.

At the roadside dhabas where I read books and people-watched, I often met men not from my world. M J, a rickshaw-wallah, learned my daily routines and routes, and knew exactly which friend lived where, and where I went and what I bought. I, in turn, learned about his life, one among thousands of Pashtuns who migrate from the northwest to seek a better life here. He had two jobs, sent money home to a family he maybe saw once a year, yet made less than our monthly rent. M J was beloved by everyone he met, punctual to a fault, and smoked two packs a day. He said: ‘Sadi, if you weren’t a girl, I’d invite you to Ludo nights with the boys.’ We went everywhere in his grand rickshaw that he’d decorated himself, every inch of it shiny and tasselled. I loved sitting amid all those colours. For the first time, with him, I prayed under the open sky in Karachi, touched the grass with my forehead while the city raged around me. We were by the sea; he rolled out his janamaz to pray and offered that yes, I could do it too if I wanted, why not?

I think we got away with living in that apartment because it was in a seedy neighbourhood where everyone knew everyone’s shit but collectively agreed not to meddle unless things got really out of hand. In close quarters, noise is not contained. Everyone knew when Uncle A and his wife were fighting, or whose side Aunty B took when her sons clashed over the eaten biryani. And when the retired officer upstairs sent cops after the drug-boy on the first floor, the whole neighbourhood knew, because men with guns were banging on our doors at 3 am.

There were conflicting accounts. One neighbour said the boy downstairs sold ice, others said he consumed it, yes, but did not sell. Everyone agreed he was high out of his mind when, middle of the day, in our tiny alley, he pointed his gun to the third floor where the police uncle lived and fired four times.
It was difficult to get to sleep; our bodies now jumped at the slightest noise
‘Motherfucker, wait,’ said the shaking retired cop from his balcony. ‘Motherfucker, you just wait, I’m gon get you fucked up.’
All this was relayed to me via WhatsApp by my best friend, who was watching it unfold. ‘Maybe don’t come home tonight,’ she texted me.

By that night, the boy had fled the scene, and police uncle was having it out in the alley with the boy’s wife. A chair was hurled, unclear who hurled it upon whom, and a few nights later, men with guns were at our door. When the story was pieced together over the following days, it was already too late: fear had lodged itself in our bodies; we now jumped at the slightest noise.
‘No one will enter your house just like that,’ the grocery store uncle said.
‘But if they come back…?’ I asked him.
‘That ice-boy needs to go,’ he said. ‘If nowhere else then to rehab.’
‘But his wife is pregnant,’ I said, and realised how deep I was in Badar Commercial gossip and lore.

Something I learned living alone-together in Badar Commercial, and that I want younger women to know, is that we are actually never guaranteed safety. Therefore, one way to collect the guts and energy to move out of your parents’ home and make a life alone in this city is to realise that the question is not whether we are safe but what the cost is, the violent cost, of trying to live a full life in this city and world.

At Badar, the cost for me was estrangement from my relatives, especially my aunts whom I loved but who knew nothing about my feminist life anymore. The other cost was a new edginess – always alert for the 3 am bang on the door. Then there were the men who tailed me while I cycled, who lurked outside our building, the officer who showed up with my full name at my door, who wanted me to know he knew I lived here.

Still, none of the fear these men instilled in us came close to the body-wreckage from the violence and betrayal we had known inside our own homes. Under our family’s so-called protection, we were surveilled and shamed in the same breath. Men, assigned as our guardians and teachers, hurt us. In my case, it was my cousin and my music teacher. The worst part was having to continue showing them respect. That kind of lying festers inside the body, when everyone knows that danger for women is two feet away, at home. It’s a trap to think we have ever overcome danger. As a result, I have spent my life watching men’s gazes for that livewire glint. The ones on the street I can usually recognise and quickly counter. The home gaze is tricker because I cannot anticipate when and where it might suddenly appear.

As the streets got to know me and I them, some knots in my body loosened, knots that had to do with the entanglement of class and gender politics, of who is portrayed as a threat versus where the actual danger lies. Other un-knottings had to do with feeling free in practice, not just theory, cycling around Badar in shorts and shalwar kameez.
I told my aunts the truth about my life. What was the point of all this public and street freedom if nothing changed in the hardest of spaces: at home?

As the knots loosened, other cities opened within us. A parent’s death; a friend’s secret abortion; walking away from a marriage; walking towards ourselves. We learned that it is possible to live within four walls that hold our grief, not just cause it – that can take it all, and more and more and more. I’d spent my 20s chasing freedom in the streets because I’d never imagined an inner space – the apartment, my room, but really, a space within – that could feel like home, where you don’t feel trapped or sealed or estranged. This indoor city opens up what you can do with your body in the cities outside, so that one day, in that same Badar Commercial, I chased a man away with a chappal because he was following me. I chased him away, wielding that slipper with a confidence that came from having lived in Badar for three years now. How familiar the streets felt; how I knew that they would not betray me.
Another time, however, I ran home breathless and called M J for help, worried I had been followed home. Limits of bravery differ day by day.
‘I’m coming to pick you up,’ he said. ‘Let’s get you some air by the sea.’

items.title: All our models of how the mind functions are missing something
items.description: Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some sta
items.author: David Colaço; Philipp Haueis
paragraphs: Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.
So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.
A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.

So the metabolic constraints on physical systems like brains cannot be ignored when modelling the mind. This means rethinking our stance towards views like multiple realisability and medium independence. Rather than taking them to be firm metaphysical commitments, we should think of them as working hypotheses: great starting points, but open to revision after new research.

Recently, the philosophers Mazviita Chirimuuta, Corey Maley and Rosa Cao have each argued that information-processing in brains depends on signal amplitudes, metabolic molecules and energy supply. This suggests a tight link between mind and metabolism, but it does not decisively rule out multiple realisability or medium independence. Instead, it shows that studying brain metabolism can test how much these hypotheses help us understand the mind. Looking at metabolism is therefore important, even if future science finds out that there is no one-to-one relation between mind and brain, that minds can exist in silicon, or that body and environment are essential for cognition.
Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime

The past 25 years have seen great advances in our understanding of brain metabolism, providing us with a wealth of material for studying metabolic constraints on the mind. We now have detailed energy budgets: the brain devotes about 16 per cent of its energy to generating action potentials, 44 per cent to transmitting these signals chemically at the synapse, and 40 per cent to maintaining and repairing neuron cells. This means that only 60 per cent of brain energy is for signalling, while the rest is spent keeping the neural machinery from falling apart. According to a 2015 paper by the neuroscientists Elisabeth Engl and David Attwell, energy for maintenance and repair ‘must contribute to limiting the cognitive abilities of the brain because the total energy use of the brain constrains the temporal rate at which information can be encoded and processed.’ But budgets like this are too coarse on their own to serve as constraints, especially when modelling individual cognitive capacities. Numerical costs of information-processing, by contrast, are more specific. According to one study by the theoretical neuroscientist Jan Karbowski and colleagues, storing one bit of information in the synapse costs about 500,000 ATP (the ‘fuel’ of the cell).

Return to the example of memory. How can metabolism help us assess whether a model of memory is plausible? The dominant theoretical framework in neuroscience is that memory is stored in synapses: the junctions where signals pass from one neuron another. When a new memory is formed, the synapses change, affecting the signals that are transmitted. One such change is known as ‘Hebbian learning’, named for the neuropsychologist Donald Hebb, whose work is summed up in the slogan (not his) ‘neurons that fire together, wire together’.

Models are useful when they solve a theory’s problems, and the synaptic theory has two big ones. The first, often called interference, is that synapses that change easily are good at storing new memories but bad at keeping old ones. Almost any change in neural firing alters a synapse’s molecular makeup slightly. But then how do new memories keep from overwriting old ones? The second problem is called turnover. Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime. In order to stay alive, neurons must constantly rebuild their decaying parts. A neuron is like Otto Neurath’s ship, rebuilt plank by plank at sea. How does information survive in a system whose every part is being replaced?

In 2016, Stefano Fusi and Marcus Benna published a mathematical model to solve the interference problem. It asks us to imagine the synaptic memory process as a set of beakers – each standing for a chemical process at the synapse – filled with liquid and connected by tubes. The level in the first beaker is the synapse’s strength: adding liquid strengthens it, and removing liquid weakens it. ‘Over time,’ Benna explained in an interview, ‘the resulting flow of liquid will diffuse across the other beakers, corresponding to the long-term storage of memories.’ Because those deeper beakers fill and drain more slowly, they hold a trace of past changes and keep drawing the first beaker back towards its old level. New memories form quickly; old ones fade only slowly, as the levels even out.

However, metabolic constraints render this solution implausible. The beaker model describes a system in which biochemical processes in the synapse even out over time: liquid can flow one way or the other, but it ultimately reaches equilibrium. In biology, settling into equilibrium means death. As the physicist Erwin Schrödinger put it: ‘Living matter evades the decay to equilibrium.’ Neurons must take in and expel ions and molecules to stay alive. A neuron that reaches equilibrium loses its organisation and can no longer perform functions such as storing memories at the synapse. Treating metabolism as a constraint shows us that a linear beaker model does not solve the problem of forming new synaptic memories and keeping old ones. This consequence is easy to miss if modellers do not consider the relevance of metabolism.

Metabolism itself, though, points to a better model. Karbowski has developed a model of synaptic memory in which metabolism takes centre stage. Because living systems are never at equilibrium, he builds his model with the mathematics of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Unlike the beaker model, this framework describes the resting state of the synapse as not being in equilibrium with its environment, and thus capable of storing memories.
Holding on to old memories costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep them while laying down new ones

The model links biochemical processes at the synapse in cycles rather than in linear sequences (as in the beaker model). ATP powers transitions between states in the cycle, so metabolism is built into the model directly. These transitions represent how the synapse strengthens or weakens to store or erase memories. Because the state changes in the cycle have different rates, they never reach equilibrium. The synapse can form new memories and keep them over time without dying.

Karbowski then combines the cyclic model with the numerical costs of information-processing (such as the ATP cost per bit of memory storage). His calculations show that encoding new memories is energetically cheap, and so is, under certain conditions, storing them for a long time. That may explain why interference doesn’t erase long-lasting memories: holding on to them costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep old memories while laying down new ones. The same picture suggests an answer to the turnover problem: if a memory is held in a state that the synapse actively maintains, rather than in any particular molecules, it can outlast the molecules themselves, much as Neurath’s ship stays afloat precisely because it is constantly being rebuilt.

A second example of how metabolism can inform models comes from research on mental effort. When you start work in the morning, you feel fresh. But as the day grinds on and you’re writing your 700th email and attending your fifth meeting, tasks that were easy become gruelling. This is the cost of mental effort. How can mental effort be modelled? One possibility is the ego depletion model, developed by the psychologist Roy Baumeister and colleagues. It posits that performing effortful tasks depends on a finite resource: glucose in the brain. The decrease in performance is explained by the decrease of the resource.

But the model has been challenged on empirical grounds, such as difficulties with replicating its findings. As a result, researchers such as Robert Kurzban and colleagues have turned towards computational models of mental effort, in which the brain calculates the benefits and costs of staying on task versus switching to another activity. Proponents conclude that computational models are superior, and that metabolism is not relevant to model mental effort.

Yet the opposition between resource models such as ego depletion and computational models of mental effort is false. Ego depletion was undone partly by metabolic evidence: the brain’s glucose use barely changes during demanding tasks, far too little for an afternoon of self-control to run it down. That is metabolism doing just what we have described, ruling out a model the brain could not run. And computational models face metabolic questions of their own, because weighing the costs and benefits of staying on task is itself work that must be paid for. Neuroscientists such as Amitai Shenhav, Matthew Botvinick and Clay Holroyd believe this computational process takes place in a brain area known as the anterior cingulate cortex. We can use evidence about available energy to assess whether models of this process are feasible.

Some researchers already integrate metabolism into their models of mental effort. Alexandre Zénon and colleagues, for instance, posit that effortful tasks require the brain to process more information and therefore use slightly more energy. Since its energy budget has a hard upper limit, the brain needs to spend less energy on other tasks. Zénon and his team explicitly link metabolism to our subjective feeling of effort, which might reflect how fast metabolic changes build up during demanding tasks. Fatigue, in turn, might reflect our expectation that these changes will continue.

Likewise, Holroyd’s ‘controllosphere’ model starts from the theory of how the brain controls behaviour and draws on empirical findings that sustained mental effort produces waste in neurons. On this model, the feeling of effort is a signal to the brain to stop tasks that require high control, so that waste can be cleared before causing damage. Research on mental effort shows that including metabolism into models of the mind is not a mere theoretical possibility. It is already a practical reality.

Attention to metabolism and energy use can improve more than just our knowledge of biological organisms. It can also help our understanding of artificial neural networks at the heart of dramatic advances in artificial intelligence. While the speed of development is new, the link between AI and the brain is old, going back to the first neural network model in 1943, from pioneers such as Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, or ‘the perceptron’ of Frank Rosenblatt in 1958. Recent advances like LLMs (large language models) reignited existential questions about whether AI is really intelligent, or even conscious. Metabolism and energy use should inform how we approach these questions.

The relationship between AI and energy use is largely uncharted territory, and a metabolically informed perspective suggests where to start looking. Hyperscale data centres use a lot of energy, far beyond the 20 watts the human brain runs on. Yet in philosophy and cognitive science, views like medium independence lead scholars to think of AI in abstract, formal terms: while the physical basis of an AI system may vary, the computation, so the thought goes, is the same. This focus on abstract computation leads philosophers such as Luke Kersten and Leonard Dung to argue that AI systems could, in principle, duplicate human minds. But, in brains, energy constraints help determine which computations are performed in the first place. If the same holds for artificial systems, then whether a chip and a brain are running ‘the same’ computation cannot simply be assumed. It has to be found out.
Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows

Our research belongs to a growing discussion of energy use and its role in modelling both brains and AI systems. For example, Cao and the neuroscientist Daniel Yamins have studied how AI models implement a highly abstract version of the mechanism that brains use to respond to novel visual stimuli. Cao and Yamins recognise that brains and engineered AI face different energy constraints, yet they consider energetics only abstractly, in terms of efficiency and optimisation. We propose instead to rethink energy use in AI from the bottom up. How an AI system uses energy is a modelling problem, which depends on scale, training data and details of grid infrastructure, just as the brain’s energy use depends on the details of its metabolism. This crucial parallel between studying brains and AI systems is missed when we focus on task optimisation alone. Modelling AI energy use informs how and when energetic differences lead to computational, perhaps even cognitive, differences.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows. AI energy use is a practical problem that the study of metabolism can help tackle. Cognitive scientists such as Megan Peters are already looking to the brain to improve energy efficiency in AI. These projects highlight the practical benefits that come from studying brain metabolism for engineering projects like AI model building. They also have theoretical benefits: projects that include energy use serve as tests of philosophical positions like medium independence.

When it comes to figuring out how to model minds, it is time that researchers take a ‘metabolic turn’, to quote our colleague Patrick McGivern. Taking seriously how systems use energy and regulate themselves gives us new ways of addressing the toughest questions that we face in making sense of the mind.

items.title: A new answer to why there is something rather than nothing
items.description: Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the issue in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when
items.author: Andrew T Brenner
paragraphs: Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the issue in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when properly considered. This very obvious fact about the world – that things exist – can shift from seeming mundane and trivial to very surprising, even downright weird. Ludwig Wittgenstein expressed this astonishment when he wrote in his Tractatus (1921): ‘Not how the world is, is the mystical, but that it is.’ Arthur Schopenhauer in 1818 called the question ‘an unfathomable and always disquieting riddle’. And the Rigveda, one of the world’s oldest surviving religious texts, suggests that even the ‘overseer’ (adhyakṣaḥ) of the cosmos might not know the answer. Sheer existence is baffling.

Philosophers continue to discuss the question today, but there isn’t any consensus about the answer. Some have suggested that it’s the sort of question that couldn’t possibly have an answer. In 1973, the German philosopher Carl Hempel wrote:

But what kind of an answer would be appropriate? What seems to be wanted is an explanatory account which does not assume the existence of something or other. But such an account, I would submit, is a logical impossibility … No theory, no conceptual scheme, can explain the existence of anything without assuming the existence of something.

His idea is that if you were trying to explain why, for instance, any penguins at all exist, then you couldn’t appeal to a penguin in your explanation – after all, that penguin is one of the things you are trying to explain. Similarly, if we’re looking for an explanation for why anything at all exists, then our explanation cannot appeal to an existing thing, since that existing thing is one of the things we are trying to explain. But Hempel thinks that there couldn’t possibly be any other sort of explanation for why anything exists, since any explanation for why something exists has to appeal to some other existing thing.

One response to Hempel’s concern is to go ahead and do what he claimed can’t possibly be done: offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, an explanation that ‘does not assume the existence of something’. Many philosophers have attempted to do just that. But there is something wrong with these explanations.

Why might we expect there to be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing in the first place? Leibniz thought there must be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing because, as he put it, nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. It is this thought that lies behind much of the astonishment people have expressed at the fact that there is something rather than nothing.

A world in which nothing exists is how we should expect the world to be if it takes what would, by our usual criteria, be its most probable state. What I have in mind here is Ockham’s Razor. Simpler accounts of the world are more likely to be correct than complex ones. For example, consider all the traits shared among the species alive today. Whales and humans have similar bone structures, despite the fact that they live in very different environments. One of Charles Darwin’s key insights was that, while it might conceivably have been true that a creator just happened to want these various species to have similar traits, despite their different environments and lifestyles, it is so much simpler to suppose that they share those traits because those traits are derived from a common ancestor. And the simplicity itself of that explanation gives us an excellent reason to think that the common traits are derived from a common ancestor. We constantly rely on the assumption that the simplest account of the world compatible with our evidence is most likely to be correct. This is something we do in science as well as in everyday life.

Many of the proposed explanations for why there is something rather than nothing that have been offered in the past do not address the apparent fact that nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. The proposed explanations say that there is such-and-such a reason for why there is something rather than nothing, but they do nothing to address the thought that we should antecedently expect there to be nothing because, if there had been nothing, then reality would have been so much simpler.
There would have been a whole lot of non-ontological truths even if nothing had existed

What I’d like to do here is kill two birds with one stone: to offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, which simultaneously dissolves the suspicion that nothing would have been so much simpler than something. This also happens to be, as far as I can tell, a new explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, and new explanations are hard to come by given the antiquity of the question.

I would like to start with the important insight that there are truths that are not truths about existing things. Since they are not truths about existing things, we’ll call them ‘non-ontological’ truths. Contrast these with ‘ontological’ truths – truths that are about existing things, like the truth that Earth orbits the Sun, or that there are more trees in the world than there are dogs. The observation that there are non-ontological truths is an insight expressed by other philosophers puzzled by the question of why there is something rather than nothing. For example, in a number of publications, the philosopher John Leslie has argued that there is something rather than nothing simply because it is good for there to be something rather than nothing. Setting aside whether this is a successful explanation, note that it appeals to a non-ontological truth: even if there was nothing, then there would have still been the truth that reality was less good than it could have been. And that does seem plausible.
Once we notice that there are non-ontological truths, we can see on reflection that there would have been a whole lot of them even if nothing had existed. Here are a few examples:

- Negative existential truths, ie, truths regarding that which does not exist. A possible world in which nothing exists would have to have lots of these truths! This doesn’t exist, that doesn’t exist, and so on.
- Truths regarding what is possible and impossible. Even if nothing existed, it would still be possible for dogs to exist, and impossible for square circles to exist.

- Truths of logic. Even if nothing existed, we would still have what logicians call modus ponens, the logical rule that says that, if A is true, and it’s also true that if A is true then B is true, then B is true.

- Mathematical truths. Even if nothing existed, it would still be true that 2+3=5. Regardless of the existence of numbers or any other mathematical objects, it would still be true that if you’ve got two things, and you add to them three things, you’ll end up with five things.

- Moral truths. Even if nothing existed, all sorts of actions would still be morally better or worse than other actions. Even though Ewoks don’t exist, it’s still true that it would be wrong to pinch their fur. In fact, even if nothing existed, it would still be wrong to pinch Ewoks.

Again, these are just a few examples. I could list many others. Admittedly, it’s mysterious how we know about these non-ontological truths. Since they don’t concern existing things, it’s surprising that our cognitive faculties can ‘get a grip’ on them, in the way that they can get a grip on objects with which we can interact (eg, the dog in front of me that I can see with my eyes and pet with my hand).
There can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be

An immediate objection is that if there were truly nothing then there would not be any non-ontological truths either. A truly empty world would have nothing at all, including truths of any sort. The philosopher Tyron Goldschmidt expresses this thought when he writes in The Puzzle of Existence (2013) that the question of why any beings at all exist is:

the broadest question of all … The question amounts to a question about why any world obtains. After all, worlds are ways things could be, and without any ways or things – beings broadly construed – there can be no world.

But I don’t think this is right. This view assumes that, in asking why anything at all exists, we are asking why there are any truths at all (in Goldschmidt’s terms, ‘why any world obtains’). That is not what we are asking. We are looking for an explanation for existence specifically. We are not asking why there are truths rather than no truths. That would, as Goldschmidt himself notes, be a confused question to ask, since there isn’t any alternative to there being truths, not even an impossible alternative. ‘A situation in which nothing is true’ doesn’t describe a situation, not even an impossible situation, since descriptions of a situation tell us what is or would be true were that situation to happen. With the concept of non-ontological truths, we can also see that there can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be. In those empty worlds there would be truths, but no things.

Many non-ontological truths would still be true even if nothing existed because they are necessarily true, if true at all. For example, recall modus ponens. That logical rule couldn’t help but be true, whether or not anything exists. The same holds for many of the other non-ontological truths, such as truths regarding what is possible and impossible, mathematical truths, and moral truths.

Some of these non-ontological truths are more controversial than others. But you don’t have to buy into every non-ontological truth to see that a possible world in which nothing exists would be more complex than it seems at first glance. When we think of complexity we normally think of the complexity of things and their properties and behaviours. But there is this whole other sort of complexity that is more abstract: complexity with respect to non-ontological truths.

Even if a possible world in which nothing exists might be more complex than we initially thought, it doesn’t follow that Leibniz was wrong when he said that it is simpler for nothing to exist than for something to exist. After all, you might think that if something exists this would leave us with all those non-ontological truths cited above as well as ontological truths about the things that exist. But postulating something new can simplify our overall picture of reality if the new thing can explain a great deal that would otherwise remain unexplained.

A possible world in which something exists may very well simplify matters if one or more of the existing things could explain why the non-ontological truths are true. This is similar to how Darwin simplified our account of biological reality by postulating the existence of something we didn’t previously believe in: a common ancestor. So if something of the right sort exists, this might make reality simpler than if nothing at all exists, if the existing thing can explain why many of the non-ontological truths are true. The simpler that existing thing is, and the wider the range of non-ontological truths it can explain, the simpler our overall account of reality will be. But what sort of existing thing might do the trick? Three possibilities naturally suggest themselves, though I don’t claim that these three options are exhaustive.

First, God is a natural candidate. Here I have in mind the sort of God we find in the world’s major monotheistic religions, all-powerful, all-knowing and so on. The feature of theism most important for our purposes is the idea that God’s nature and decisions are supposed to ultimately explain many aspects of reality. It is God’s status as reality’s explanatory bedrock that makes God a natural candidate for explaining various non-ontological truths. For example, if there is a God, then God’s decisions would explain various negative existential truths. Mechagodzilla doesn’t exist because Mechagodzilla just isn’t one of the things God wanted to create, or allow to be created.

Divine command theorists such as William of Ockham (of Ockham’s Razor fame) explain moral truths in terms of God’s commands – an act is good or bad because God commands it to be. René Descartes notoriously claimed that God decrees which logical and mathematical truths are true. These truths could not be otherwise – they are necessary – but that too is only because God decided they can’t be otherwise. There is also a case to be made that God is a particularly simple being. If that’s right, then our overall account of reality might end up being simple if God explains why many non-ontological truths are true. There is the traditional doctrine of divine simplicity, endorsed by prominent Jewish thinkers such as Maimonides, Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas, and Islamic thinkers such as Ibn Sina. According to this view, there are no distinctions at all within God, either between God’s attributes, or between God and God’s attributes. Over the past several decades, the philosopher Richard Swinburne has argued in detail for a more modest way of understanding the idea that God is a very simple being, and so theism is a very simple hypothesis. The basic idea, which I don’t have the space to discuss in detail, is that many of God’s attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, etc) are ultimately derivable from one or two of God’s attributes, and those attributes fit together in a neat and tidy manner.

Here is a second option if the God explanation doesn’t appeal. Many of the non-ontological truths might be explained by a natural (that is, non-supernatural) object that explains why the Universe has many of the properties it has. Suppose that the Universe originated in a cosmic singularity, an object of infinite density. The state of the initial singularity would, given how the laws of nature dictate the Universe evolves over time, explain why various negative existential truths are true. This is because the Universe’s initial conditions plus the laws will result in the Universe’s history taking one course rather than another, one that either does or does not include the existence of various particular things in it. Even non-deterministic laws may dictate that the existence of certain things is very improbable, given the Universe’s initial conditions.
The actual world, though filled with existing things, may for all we know be the simplest possible world

Some philosophers think that truths regarding what is possible and impossible in the broadest sense are also explained by the properties had by an initial singularity. The idea is that what’s possible and impossible is grounded in which states of the Universe can result from the evolution of the initial singularity, given how the laws of nature say the Universe will evolve over time. If some state of the Universe can in principle result from the initial singularity and the laws, then it’s possible, but if it can’t result then it is strictly impossible, as impossible as a round square. In fact, on this view that’s what makes round squares impossible. But would an initial singularity give us a particularly simple explanation for various non-ontological truths?
