And people say Ridley Scott’s film is not historically correct but I was struck by certain images that turn up in it – the guillotine, the pyramid, Joaquin Phoenix’s flattering hat – they stick in the mind. I actually don’t care about story. What I care about is how it looks – in a painting, the surface, the quality of the line, the quality of the paint, the juxtaposition of images, the difference of scale, the contrast, whether it’s alive or dead or dreary or dull. When I was a child, my mother used to tell me that appearance doesn’t matter. I often do the opposite of what I’m told, because actually I think appearance does matter. Look at a tree – velvety, dignified, beautiful. A lot of people went off beauty. They don’t talk about beauty and painting, they talk about energy, confrontation, event, meaning – they talk about context. Beauty has gone out the window but it’s always there in the natural world. As an artist it’s enough to deal with how things look.”

Rose Wylie is speaking from her home in rural Kent – a house and studio filled with the Royal Academician’s monumental paintings and a garden abundant in chaotic beauty. Now 91, Wylie paused her career as an artist to raise her three children, resuming when they were grown and she had graduated from the Royal College of Art in London, aged 47. She hit her stride in her seventies, when she found international acclaim. As a mother, she channelled her desire to create beautiful things into the “soups, jam, clothes, curtains and Christmas cards” she made, and as an artist she draws on the material she encounters in everyday life and the media – celebrities, sport, childhood memories, anime, art history. Vivid scenes from films she watches at home – Kill Bill, Thelma & Louise, Napoleon – have also made their way onto her large-scale canvases, in an ongoing series of paintings she calls Film Notes. Earlier this year, Wylie made history as the first woman painter to have a major solo exhibition in the Main Galleries of the Royal Academy of Arts in London.

items.title: Cartier Legends from Louis XIV to Elizabeth Taylor
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Alexander Fury
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:

Big stones have been a big deal at Cartier for, basically, the entire 179-year history of the house. Jewellery is all about rocks, typically the larger and more exceptional the better. Indeed, in French there is a distinction made linguistically – bijoux is the term for jewellery pieces without valuable stones, while joaillerie is reserved for those framing precious gems. As a high joaillier par excellence, Cartier has been responsible for setting (and resetting) stones that truly qualify as legendary across its lifespan.

How about the Taylor-Burton diamond – a gargantuan 69.42-carat pear-cut stone bought in a fevered auction by Cartier in October 1969? The very next day, the actor Richard Burton – an unsuccessful bidder – purchased the jewel for his wife at the time, Elizabeth Taylor, for a reported $1.1 million. It was immediately rechristened with their names. Or maybe the Bérénice emerald, a hexagonal jewel of more than 141 carats, which likely originated during the 17th-century reign of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, fashioned into a Cartier necklace with pearls, enamel and white diamonds in 1925? Or, indeed, the Hope diamond, probably the most famous gemstone in the world, a deep blue jewel of 45.52 carats, first sold to Louis XIV in 1668 as Le bleu de France, its ownership and nomenclature passing to the Dutch Hope banking family after the French Revolution. It was bought in 1909, reset, and resold two years later by Pierre Cartier at Cartier New York. By that point, the gem had shifted from famous to infamous, with specious stories of its “curse” proliferating, involving shipwrecks and suicide, murder and misery, as well as a revolutionary mob reputedly tearing the French aristocrat the Princesse de Lamballe limb from limb after she wore it. The gem has been held, without nefarious incident, in the Smithsonian Institution since 1958, with an estimated value today of a quarter of a billion dollars.

Stones have always been the big news in high jewellery, singular creations that surpass their mere mineral origin, around which pieces are devised to showcase their extraordinary size, weight and clarity. “The design is at the service of the stones,” is how Pierre Rainero, the house’s director of image, style and heritage, sums up Cartier’s approach. His extensive history with the company goes back to 1984: today, he oversees the Cartier Collection – the brand’s private museum archive of more than 3,500 historic pieces – as well as guiding the house’s designers in the creation of new pieces. It has been argued that his cross-departmental duties mean he embodies the jeweller’s past, present and future. He’s a rock at Cartier – even his first name can be translated from the French to mean stone. “Our culture is the one of stones. It’s really our essence.” The challenge in these kinds of joaillerie creations is to effectively make the metal ‘vanish’ – which is why Louis Cartier first started to use platinum extensively at the turn of the 20th century, its whiteness intended to make it “almost invisible” next to the sparkle of diamonds. Cartier terms its construction methodology fil couteau, or knife’s edge, metal deep-set for security and stability but as ribbon-fine as possible. To borrow more French terminology, in essence this is savoir-faire in the service of se faire avoir – know-how on the one hand and to be fooled on the other. Cartier pieces often seem to consist of gems floating impossibly or improbably, magically melded without fixture, anchored somehow on the body, allowing the stones to sing.

That idea is key to Cartier’s latest annual high jewellery collection, titled Le Chœur des Pierres, which translates as “the choir of stones”. It’s apt – the collection this time comprises more than 125 one-of-a-kind pieces, necessitating almost 85,000 hours of design and craftsmanship across Cartier’s Paris ateliers. The translation, in Rainero’s mind, is fluid – again, harking back to French, chœur is pronounced with a hard k, the same as cœur, meaning heart. “And that notion of heart can be the facts about the stone itself, but also the intrinsic power each stone wields. And of course, the chorus – meaning putting different stones all together at the service of each of them.” This is also only the first chapter of a three-part collection that will total 250 items, making up the maison’s largest high jewellery collection to date.

Cartier doesn’t even begin to conceive of such one-off pieces without first sourcing the impressive and unique stones they are made for. Those are placed on waxed paper – better to maintain the condition of the gems – and designs are devised around them, whether abstract or figurative. While this is how Cartier always creates high jewellery, this collection is based on the juxtaposition and interplay of stones, rather than a specific thematic. Cartier’s menagerie of animals is present – pavé-set panthers and tigers as impressively scaled necklaces – as well as the carved, riotously mixed gemstones dubbed Tutti Frutti that the house has proposed for over a hundred years. But this time the focus is unequivocally on gems.

And even if none of the specific stones celebrated this time come with centuries-deep cultural histories, a built-in curse or romantic provenance, they are superlative: a 5.24-carat cushion-cut ruby from Mozambique is embedded in a ring conceived as a bejewelled corolla; an 11.60-carat oval diamond the colour of champagne, a gemological rarity in weight and hue, is showcased on an architectonic white gold mount; 13 Zambian emerald beads totalling 63.62 carats are suspended from a necklace of contrasting angular diamonds set in platinum, the design tipped with a pair of nearly matched ellipsoid emeralds the size of olives.

The collection itself creates harmonies – occasionally dissonance – between those different jewels. Stones are sometimes chosen to frame or offset others, with white diamonds habitually used around coloured stones not due to their preciousness, but for their light-reflective qualities, a Cartier hallmark. In this collection, topazes are tonally contrasted with garnets and yellow and orange diamonds, while a bed of white diamonds may emphasise, say, the presence of six remarkable pink stones from a now-closed mine in the remote north of Western Australia. Colour is important – especially trademark Cartier tones like the deep scarlet of rubies (the colour of Cartier packaging and awnings), or the contrast between emerald, onyx and diamond, which has been a design signature since the teens of the last century. “I would say colour is too simple,” Rainero says. “It’s more than one colour. Even if we are talking about an emerald, the emerald can offer many different nuances when we look at it according to the light and according to the cut.” That said, Cartier does not see its role as one of transforming stones, but rather to bring out a hidden inner presence, an inherent natural quality embedded within.

Rainero’s position means he isn’t just looking forward but, inevitably, backwards. He’s considering contemporary creations adding to a future patrimony of Cartier even before they’re fully fashioned – especially these unique items, each destined for a distinct client. “I always think, when we have a new project, about an evaluation 10 or 20 years from now,” he says. “What will it represent in the future in the entire history of jewellery, in the entire history of the evolution of a Cartier style?” He thinks. “In French, we use that phrase, ‘the intelligence of the hands’. It’s about that. I think it’s very interesting to challenge that idea, that these marvels challenge the human possibilities.”

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

items.title: Ten cool new CD players provide the path to audiophile heaven at home
items.description: Maybe you never let your CD collection go, or perhaps you’ve started to rebuild a curated set of classic albums that streaming services just don’t seem to do justice to. Whatever your motivation for getting on board the CD revival train, one of these ten conte
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Maybe you never let your CD collection go, or perhaps you’ve started to rebuild a curated set of classic albums that streaming services just don’t seem to do justice to. Whatever your motivation for getting on board the CD revival train, one of these ten contemporary players will help you get back to the original digital source.

Arcam has a new flagship CD player, the CD25. Shown here partnered with the A50 Signature Class G Integrated Amplifier, the CD25 builds on the company’s four decades of experience building digital audio systems. The slender system has gently rounded edges, a black fascia containing the display, and dual-mono digital-to-analogue converters, one for each channel.

Quad’s 3CDT player is now available in a new satin black finish with a green illumination, a classic colourway for this 90-year-old British audio brand. Paired with the Quad 3 integrated amplifier, the 3CDT (a transport only, with no onboard amplification) follows the company’s purist approach. In addition to conventional CDs, the 3CDT is compatible with CD-R, CD-RW and data CDs, and a variety of audio file formats, including FLAC, WAV, WMA, and MP3.

The newest model in Musical Fidelity’s B-Line of high-end audio products, the B1xcd is a purist’s CD player that pairs well with the company’s B1xi integrated amplifier. You won’t find any extraneous features other than a straightforward front-loading CD player with an LCD display and analogue and digital outputs.
£549, details at MusicalFidelity.com. Stockists at henleyaudio.co.uk

Released as part of the venerable audio company’s Classic Series, the new C 569 from NAD joins the C 359S streaming amplifier to create a simple, no nonsense home system that follows a set of enduring design principles. That means push-button design, a modestly sized screen and stripped-back design.
Fitzwilliam Connect Amp + CD

If space is at a premium, consider the new Fitzwilliam Connect Amp + CD from Majority Audio. Although it the same form factor as a traditional stackable hi-fi component, the new model not only incorporates a 200W Texas Instruments amplifier but also has onboardDAB/DAB+ and FM radio and a USB slot, alongside a conventional CD drawer.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The new DP11 CD player from FiiO has a compact, desktop-sized footprint. Finished in retro silver, the DP11 can not only drive a pair of headphones but also includes a USB-C socket that lets you rip CDs straight to a thumb drive.
Eversolo DMP-A8 Master Gen 2

Another all-in-one solution, this time from Eversolo. The DMP-A8 is not only a network music player, high-resolution DAC and analogue preamplifier, but it also comes with a CD playback system with a top-loading mechanism. Thanks to the unit’s impressive connectivity, album information comes up on the large 8.6-inch touchscreen panel, while there’s support for Qobuz Connect, TIDAL Connect and Spotify Connect. An internal SSD can be added if you want to keep your ripped music all in one place.

Marantz’s latest CD player is the CD 70, launched alongside the Model 70 integrated amplifier. The CD 70 also comes with its own headphone amplifier, as the ability to play files back from USB. It’s available in classic black or a silver and gold finish.

The Shanling CD-S100 offers multiple features in addition to straightforward CD playback. The Chinese brand has created a full-size player that also serves as a DAC for phone and computer audio, thanks to the ability to receive and output music over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and USB.

Visually and physically hefty (over 25kg), the new Luxman D-100 Centennial is a CD player of exceptional robustness, stability and quality of componentry. Thick-gauge aluminium and steel give this model its gravitas, along with handmade circuitry and a high-resolution OLED display. Created to celebrate the centenary of the Japanese manufacturer, no expense has been spared.

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: These are the films not to miss at London’s 20th Fashion in Film Festival
items.description: ‘It’s just a number, isn’t it?’ remarks the art historian and Central Saint Martins tutor Marketa Uhlirova, contemplating what it means for Fashion in Film Festival to be turning 20. ‘But it felt like a good excuse to pause, look back and think about what come
items.author: Zoe Whitfield
paragraphs: ‘It’s just a number, isn’t it?’ remarks the art historian and Central Saint Martins tutor Marketa Uhlirova, contemplating what it means for Fashion in Film Festival to be turning 20. ‘But it felt like a good excuse to pause, look back and think about what comes next. What’s changed? What are we doing now, and is it still relevant?’ This year’s programme, titled ‘The Party and the Guests’ and running between 28 November through 7 December 2026 across several London venues, has been devised to be both a celebratory occasion and a moment for reflection.

Indeed, that William Klein’s Who Are You, Polly Maggoo? is screening at the 2026 edition takes the festival right back to the beginning: It was after watching the 1966 fashion mockumentary, twice (once in English with poor visuals and a second time in French with a sharper picture), at the invitation of the late Roger K Burton – the stylist and archivist with whom Uhlirova co-founded the festival alongside Christel Tsilibaris – that the idea for some kind of event recontextualising cinema’s sartorial leanings originated. ‘When you say “fashion and film”, people tend to imagine Blow-Up or The Devil Wears Prada, but we wanted to open that up,’ explains Uhlirova. ‘The aim for the festival is and was always to investigate something, rather than show the already familiar.

‘Christel and I both came from curating contemporary art, so our minds veered towards curating an exhibition, but in cinemas,’ she continues. ‘Most people involved in exhibiting film called themselves programmers then, but we saw curating and programming as quite distinct. For us, curating meant digging into archives for the unknown, finding unexpected connections between films, and proposing concepts beyond the usual frameworks of auteur or genre-based seasons. We were trying to rethink how we understand the relationship between fashion and film – a relationship between two art forms, two industries and two cultures that constantly interact.’

The very first festival, which Klein would subsequently attend, was called ‘Between Stigma and Enigma’ and examined the ambiguous attitudes cinema holds towards fashion; last year’s programme meanwhile, curated with Wallpaper* contributing editor Dal Chodha, took nature as its starting point, surveyed under the banner ‘Grounded’. This year the team have borrowed the moniker of Czech filmmaker Jan Němec’s twice-banned 1966 political satire, reinterpreting the ‘guests’ of the title to honour the ongoing conversation and contributions of previous collaborators. As such, it’s a programme focused not on any one theme, but rather indebted to the touchstones of curation that have come to shape Fashion in Film Festival.

Exploring punk, forgotten French fashion, early motion picture and the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival – via rare screenings, live music, discussions and new commissions – ‘The Party and the Guests’ features in its line-up Jarvis Cocker, Caroline Evans, Ahmir ‘Questlove’ Thompson, Émile Reynaud and John Maybury, among many others. Below, Uhlirova shares and discusses five of her must-sees.
Animated into Being: First Dressed Bodies in Motion

‘This programme is a bit of an experiment. I wanted to look at how the very first bodies in moving images were dressed. Film history has largely been written with an emphasis on technology and medium-specific innovation. It has focused on cinema emerging from animation and photography, and on various chemical and technological advances. I’m asking a different question: how are these bodies dressed, and what does that tell us about the beginnings of moving images? There are recurring ways of staging bodies, and dress plays a part in those, even before films explicitly take it as their subject. As a historian of visual culture, I’ve always been puzzled by how, in the 2000s, everyone seemed to think fashion film was this new phenomenon. That’s bollocks: fashion has been part of moving images from the very beginning – you just have to know where to look.’
Sunday 6 December 2026, 2pm, Ciné Lumière. Book here.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
Who Are You, Polly Maggoo? (1966)

‘Polly Maggoo was the film we started with, so holds a lot of memories. The film wasn’t officially out on DVD back in 2005, so we first watched it on two bootleg copies that our co-founder Roger K Burton had got hold of. One day he said, “You should come over and let’s watch a film together.” We ended up watching it twice: one copy had a good image but was entirely in French (and our French was quite poor then), the other was in English, but the image was terrible. Still, we were intrigued and thought it would be interesting to organise something around fashion and film – this was, in fact, Roger's idea, one he generously sent me away with. That’s really how it all started. The project grew into a film programme, which then became a festival. Miraculously, William Klein agreed to come to the screening. Christel and I were only just starting and we were really naïve – it didn’t occur to us that his visit to London might attract quite a bit of press attention.’
Sunday 6 December 2026, 3.30pm, Ciné Lumière. Book here.
Resistance, Connection, Enclosure: John Maybury in the 1980s

‘John Maybury is someone I’ve had my eye on for a long time – though I was mainly familiar with his music videos and his collaborations with fashion designers. We’re screening four of his films, ending with one he made for Rifat Ozbek, to replace his live fashion show for S/S 1990. But the programme as you see it was sparked by a chance conversation with the film scholar Juan A Suárez, who came to London to research his new project on queer memory in the 1980s, which also included Maybury’s shorts. Within five seconds of his mentioning this, we agreed he would curate a programme. It is entirely his selection; we just agreed he would focus it on fashion and the way Maybury works with the surfaces of images as well as textiles. This is quite typical for the way we work: the curation is often somewhat open-ended, and shaped organically through many different encounters and conversations. We’re actually publishing a booklet featuring Sophia Buck’s interview with Maybury about his fashion films for Rifat Ozbek. Sophia is one of this season’s co-organisers, and the interview grew out of Suárez’s programme.’
Saturday 28 November 2026, 8pm, Institute of Contemporary Art (ICA), Cinema 1. Book here.
Top Ten Designers in Paris (1980)

‘Top Ten Designers in Paris is a really interesting piece of cultural history. It was made by a collective called Soft Ware Productions in 1979 and released in 1980 – though it was shown only a couple of times before disappearing into the archive. The six collaborators, including the experimental filmmaker Vivian Ostrovsky, decided to go to Paris to film the fashion shows. They felt fashion was an interesting subject and that hardly anyone was showing it on film. There were of course earlier television formats like Dim Dam Dom and Videofashion, but this film was produced in a different spirit. It has a more introspective tone and gives the collections more space than television allowed. It is interspersed with designer interviews – but also lovely shots of Paris, which give it another dimension that places fashion within the life of the city in a really beautiful way. I was intrigued to discover two or three designers I’d never even heard of, including France Andrevie. Working on fashion, it’s not often you come across historical names that are completely new to you.’
Screening 1, Saturday 5 December 2026, 3.50pm, Ciné Lumière. Screening 2, Monday 7 December 2026, 7.50pm, Ciné Lumière. Book here.

‘My final highlight is, inevitably, Protéa at the Barbican, with live narration by Jarvis Cocker, a string trio from the Elysian Collective and Foley artists Franziska and Matthias Radcliffe. Protéa is a resourceful action heroine from 1913, arguably cinema’s first female spy, who moves from one disguise to another on a secret mission. What’s brilliant is that we actually watch her transform: the film draws our attention to the art of disguise as a visible passage from one identity to another. In this, the film still draws on the earlier tradition of trick film, but it also feels very quirky and contemporary. Our team was blown away that Cocker accepted the invitation to do a live narration – and, in fact, to go much further, inviting his own guests to help bring the film to life in a completely new and unexpected way. We can’t wait.’
Sunday 29 November 2026, 3pm, Barbican, Cinema 1. Book here.

Zoe Whitfield is a London-based writer whose work spans contemporary culture, fashion, art and photography. She has written extensively for international titles including Interview, AnOther, i-D, Dazed and CNN Style, among others.

items.title: Brit Awards 2027 reveal trophy design by Rachel Whiteread
items.description: The Brit Awards 2027 will take place at Manchester's Co-Op Live on 27 February, and British artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for the trophy.
items.author: Rosa Bertoli
paragraphs: The Brit Awards 2027 will take place at Manchester's Co-Op Live on 27 February, and British artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for the trophy.

A pioneering artist whose work sheds light on the objects that recur in our daily lives, Whiteread's work is based on familiar forms, repetition and memory. Casting everyday objects and architectural elements in a range of materials including plaster, concrete, resin, rubber and metal, she brings to the fore what is often unseen.
With her Brit trophy design, Whiteread joins a roster of celebrated creatives who have shaped the awards over the years, including Yinka Ilori, Es Devlin, Zaha Hadid and Tracey Emin.
Brit Awards 2027: trophy by Rachel Whiteread

Every year, the trophy features a novel interpretation of a stylised Britannia statue, and Whiteread's vision included 'exposing the interior of the statue, as an artist would do with their music,' she explains.

In her design for the trophy, the chrome surface is interrupted by the black holes, the hole being a recurring motif across the artist's oeuvre, as she has used it as a device to explore negative space in photography and sculpture. In 2014, she was invited to leave her mark on the London Tube map, and took a similar approach where the holes formed part of a trompe l'oeil layer that revealed the map below.

Whiteread was the first woman to be awarded the Turner Prize, 1993, and again in 1997 she became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale. Her body of work includes some major public commissions including the Holocaust Memorial / Nameless Library in Vienna, a reinforced-concrete bunker that commemorates the 65,000 Austrian Jews murdered in the Holocaust, and a permanent concrete cast of a Nissen hut in Dalby Forest, commissioned on the centenary of the First World War and honouring the labourers and prisoners of war who lived and worked in the forest.

'Art and culture are under very real threat, so I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists – whether from music or the visual arts,' she said.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

'I accepted the invitation to design next year’s Brit Award trophy, as I saw this as a natural extension of my work – to continue to celebrate and recognise British art and creativity, and to have an opportunity to apply my own perspective within such an iconic British cultural institution,' she added.

Rosa Bertoli was born in Udine, Italy, and now lives in London. Since 2014, she has been the Design Editor of Wallpaper*, where she oversees design content for the print and online editions, as well as special editorial projects. Through her role at Wallpaper*, she has written extensively about all areas of design. Rosa has been speaker and moderator for various design talks and conferences including London Craft Week, Maison & Objet, The Italian Cultural Institute (London), Clippings, Zaha Hadid Design, Kartell and Frieze Art Fair. Rosa has been on judging panels for the Chart Architecture Award, the Dutch Design Awards and the DesignGuild Marks. She has written for numerous English and Italian language publications, and worked as a content and communication consultant for fashion and design brands.

items.title: ‘Aluminum gave us lots of freedom’: jeweller Cora Sheibani reveals new pieces
items.description: ‘201’ is the name of a new jewellery series by Cora Sheibani. Currently counting six pieces, the collection marks a debut for the jeweller: it’s the first time that she has worked with aluminium. Creating in the metal has allowed Sheibani to consider new shape
items.author: Felix Bischof
paragraphs: ‘201’ is the name of a new jewellery series by Cora Sheibani. Currently counting six pieces, the collection marks a debut for the jeweller: it’s the first time that she has worked with aluminium. Creating in the metal has allowed Sheibani to consider new shapes, volumes and dimensions. ‘What was fantastic about sculpting in aluminium was that we could make really large shapes, and have a lot of freedom to make things because aluminum is not that expensive and [it's] relatively soft, so it’s quite easy to mill,’ says Sheibani, who in 2026 exhibited her work at TEFAF Maastricht for the first time. She is scheduled to return to the specialist fair for its March 2027 edition.

It was 201 years ago that aluminum was first isolated, hence Sheibani’s choice of collection title. In her creations, which include a selection of earrings, a pendant, a double yin and yang clip, and a jabot pin, Sheibani matches raw, anodised aluminium with gemstones in soft pastel shades. Her designs are made by hand in Switzerland; once perfected, an aluminum twin of a wax prototype is made slowly through milling and carving.

Aluminium is soft, corrosion-resistant and malleable; it was another characteristic of the modern metal that had a design impact on Sheibani’s pieces: as aluminium can’t be soldered, separate elements were joined using fastenings and screws, each from gold. ‘It’s been great fun!’ Sheibani says of her experience.
Jewellery can be viewed by appointment at Cora Sheibani's London, Mayfair showroom.

items.title: Meet the Royal Designers for Industry 2026 – shaping landscapes, Paddington Bear and more
items.description: The Royal Designers for Industry were announced on 26 November 2026 in a ceremony in London, and this year's cohort includes landscape architect Bridget Baines, product and interaction designer Durrell Bishop, multidisciplinary designer and creative director H
items.author: Rosa Bertoli
paragraphs: The Royal Designers for Industry were announced on 26 November 2026 in a ceremony in London, and this year's cohort includes landscape architect Bridget Baines, product and interaction designer Durrell Bishop, multidisciplinary designer and creative director Harris Elliott, illustrator and ceramicist Laura Carlin, costume and creature designer Tahra Zafar and Honorary Royal Designer Eelco Hooftman, a landscape architect who co-founded Gross.Max with Baines in 1995.

The UK's highest design accolade, the Royal Designer for Industry (RDI) prize was established in 1936 and is only bestowed upon 200 members at any given time. The new cohort joins a network that currently includes James Dyson, Sir Paul Smith, Es Devlin and Dame Zandra Rhodes, among others.
Meet the Royal Designers for Industry 2026

With their multidisciplinary representation, this year's new Royal Designers for Industry reflect the boundless creativity of design as a profession. 'These six appointments are a wonderful reminder of the sheer breadth of design today,' comments Catherine Joyce, programme manager at the Royal Society of Arts, the body that established the prize nine decades ago.

'Ninety years on, the Royal Designers are still looking forward: this year’s appointments show how far design now reaches, from public landscapes and picture books to exhibitions, the stage and the objects we use every day,' echoes Johanna Gibbons RDI, Keeper of the Faculty of Royal Designers for Industry.

'Their work is joyful, and it is serious about making life better. That is what unites Royal Designers across the decades: a living entanglement of disciplines that, with the RSA Fellowship, is a profound force for good.'
Bridget Baines and Eelco Hooftman

Bridget Baines and Eelco Hooftman are co-founders of Gross.Max, a landscape architecture practice whose mission is focused on radically transforming public spaces globally. 'Our projects are based on thorough understanding of – and reflection upon – site and context,' they share. Their projects include a sensitive landscaping approach to London's Potters Field Park, with the aim of 'reconciling different user groups such as residents, workers, visitors and tourists on a relatively small and intensely used space', and the masterplanning of the waterfront area of Greenwich Peninsula.

One of contemporary design's most future-forward creative voices, Durrell Bishop's work balances aesthetics, behaviour, systems and the ways in which technology can enable humans. Among his projects is the Marble Answering Machine, a 1992 project which, a statement accompanying the award notes, 'helped change how we think about interacting with technology'.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

A multi-disciplinary artist and cultural curator, Harris Elliott describes his work as 'alchemising beauty and counterculture into narratives; visual poetry that anchors us into the slipstream of popularism with disruptive elegance.' In his practice, he brings together fashion, art, exhibitions and cultural storytelling, and his projects include ‘The Missing Thread’ at Somerset House, chronicling the untold history of Black British fashion.

An illustrator and ceramicist celebrated for her distinctive storytelling and imaginative ceramic works, Laura Carlin is known for her children's books including London: A History and What is a Sculpture? The brilliance of her work lies in her ability to inject visual poetry into scenes of everyday life.

Olivier Award-winning costume and creature designer Tahra Zafar brought Paddington Bear on stage, and among her achievements is the creation of 23,000 costumes for the London 2012 Olympic and Paralympic ceremonies. Her work combines design, craft, storytelling and an ability to convey emotion through transforming mundane objects.

Rosa Bertoli was born in Udine, Italy, and now lives in London. Since 2014, she has been the Design Editor of Wallpaper*, where she oversees design content for the print and online editions, as well as special editorial projects. Through her role at Wallpaper*, she has written extensively about all areas of design. Rosa has been speaker and moderator for various design talks and conferences including London Craft Week, Maison & Objet, The Italian Cultural Institute (London), Clippings, Zaha Hadid Design, Kartell and Frieze Art Fair. Rosa has been on judging panels for the Chart Architecture Award, the Dutch Design Awards and the DesignGuild Marks. She has written for numerous English and Italian language publications, and worked as a content and communication consultant for fashion and design brands.

Memberships allow us to invest back into our editorial production as an independent publisher, free from commercial pressure. Your support means we can keep bringing you new stories and publications inspired by our community.
Members are the first to receive each issue of Apartamento magazine, delivered straight from the printer to your doorstep! All magazines are shipped express with tracking.

Apartamento was founded in Barcelona in 2008. Its namesake magazine, published twice yearly and widely considered one of the most influential interiors publications of the past two decades, is rooted in how people actually live: the spaces they inhabit, the food they cook, the work they make, and the conviction with which they build their lives. Known for its unfiltered, human approach, each issue brings long-form conversations with artists, writers, designers, and thinkers across disciplines, accompanied by photography that unsettles conventional categories.

The values of the magazine extend beyond print. Through events, collaborations, exhibitions, design objects, and a growing body of short and documentary films, Apartamento builds community in real spaces around the world.

Since 2015, Apartamento has published books across a range of formats: monographs, cookbooks, photobooks, architecture series, artist books, and even a graphic novel. The publishing programme extends the editorial curiosity of the magazine into longer, more sustained forms, spanning art, design, architecture, food, and visual culture.

Members receive each issue of Apartamento magazine at a special 20% discount, plus unlimited access to our digital archive—including every interview, essay, and story ever published in our previous issues. In addition, members receive an automatic 10% discount in our Shop, as well as a free Apartamento Tote Bag and one 60-day trial for MUBI.

Current issues of Apartamento magazine tend to sell out quickly, and all earlier issues are sold out and can be hard to find. Our digital archive preserves each and every issue of the magazine on our website, a place where members can read every interview, essay, and story ever published!
The exact cost of shipping each issue express to your home is calculated at check out, according to the competive rates our courier partners offer us.

items.title: Apartamento Magazine Issue #38
items.description: In issue #38 of Apartamento magazine, isolation becomes grounds for imagination, encouraging the possibility of creating the worlds we want.
paragraphs: In issue #38 of Apartamento magazine, isolation becomes grounds for imagination, encouraging the possibility of creating the worlds we want.

On the cover, American artist Dozie Kanu, winner of the Hublot Design Prize, talks with writer Camille Okhio in the home and studio he has made in the Portuguese countryside of Azoia de Cima. Photographed by José Pedro Cortes, the story follows what took his practice from New York to Portugal, how ambition has emerged from his Nigerian heritage, and the existential pressures of Blackness. Dozie candidly recounts how his live/work space once caught fire just before a photoshoot with furniture company Knoll.

In Paris, Playboy author and provocateur to the French literati Constance Debré speaks with contributing editor Jina Khayyer about the contradictions of love and desire, and boredom as ‘a state where you develop the freedom to invent things’. Photographed by Osma Harvilahti, she shows us her minimalist apartment, which has no full bath, proving that showers don’t need to be in the privacy of the home.

Featuring: Dozie Kanu, Constance Debré, Anupama Kundoo, Julian Schnabel, Dave Baby, Peaches, Joey Arias, Martine Syms, Gerard Malanga, Rodney Mullen, Filip Pągowski, Go Hasegawa, Darina Allen, and Muller Van Severen.
Plus: Peter Hanley’s ‘The Culinary Academy of the Pyrenees’ with illustrations by Oscar Grønner, an ode to Inge Mahn by Anna Herms, and ‘Wei Xing Doesn’t Skate’, an essay by Jocko Weyland.
Members have unlimited access to the entire Apartamento magazine digital archive!

items.title: HOLIDAY GIFT SET #1
items.description: Don't miss out on our Bar Brutal T-Shirt!
paragraphs: Don't miss out on our Bar Brutal T-Shirt!

What we talk about when we talk about Bar Brutal: This is a portrait of one of the world’s best-loved drinking holes and its formative role in the natural wine movement, a two-way symbiosis from Barcelona to the world. Emerging in 2013, Brutal is the place where a legendary cast of winemakers, sommeliers, chefs, musicians, and wanton drinkers have all converged in the feeling that something was taking shape there between the never-ending party and an intimate knowledge of the wines. The book combines multiple, intersecting strands that veer between structure and chaos, reflecting the bar’s own underlying methodology. At the centre of the work is Bar Brutal’s first official cookbook, featuring 26 recipes, while collage sections merge archival imagery with the stories—or revelations—of 80-odd contributors, including Stefano Colombo, Joan Ramón Escoda, Christian Tschida, Nuria Renom, John Wurdeman, Thierry Puzelat, LCD Soundsystem, Peggy Gou, 2manydjs, Gilles Peterson, Aziz Ansari, Alice Feiring, and many more. Photo essays by Adrià Cañameras, Nacho Alegre, and Yago Castromil document the dinners, wines, people, and spaces that bring the place alive by day and night, while four written chapters anchor the story in time and place, tracing the bar’s evolution. Brought together by Madeleine Willis, former Apartamento editor and long-time Brutal regular, the work reflects the same energy that Brutal has injected into Barcelona and the wide world of wine since 2013 and celebrates over a decade of happy, chaotic, expansive service.

Bar Brutal was founded in 2013 by Max and Stefano Colombo, supremely generous hosts and restaurateurs; Joan Valencia, co-owner of the wine distributor Cuvée 3000; and Joan Ramón Escoda, a forerunner of natural winemaking in Catalunya. Since then it’s become a globally recognised epicentre for the natural wine movement—offering countless drinkers an entry point into this world and, just as importantly, providing a space for winemakers, sommeliers, and all ‘wine people’ to exchange experiences, agricultural knowledge, and a specific language and camaraderie before moving off again to help spread the word.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: June 3, 2026
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking.

items.title: HOLIDAY GIFT SET #2
items.description: Essential: A Design Guide for Life by acclaimed Spanish designer Miguel Milá (1931–2024) is a braided narrative weaving artist manifesto with family history with notes on living and living well. Originally published in Spanish as Lo esencial to much success in
paragraphs: Essential: A Design Guide for Life by acclaimed Spanish designer Miguel Milá (1931–2024) is a braided narrative weaving artist manifesto with family history with notes on living and living well. Originally published in Spanish as Lo esencial to much success in 2019 and translated into English by the award-winning Valerie Miles, Essential is the very first volume in our new series of reading books, focusing on the ideas and reflections of renowned creatives. While books in praise of his work abound, including Apartamento’s own Miguel Milá: A Life in Design, this unique volume is the first devoted to his design philosophy in his own words.

Miguel Milá (1931–2024) first began designing his own furniture and lamps out of an organic necessity to create what he could not find at a time before ‘industrial design’ as we know it today even existed. Among his many honours, Milá was awarded the National Design Award (in its first edition, jointly with André Ricard), and the Compasso d’Oro International Award from the Italian Industrial Design Association. He was a six-time winner of Barcelona’s Association of Industrial Design ADI-FAD award and was bestowed the Gold Medal of the City of Barcelona posthumously in recognition of his unparalleled contributions to the world of design.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: November 20, 2025
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking
Delivery time: 2-4 days from the shipping confirmation

The Unimportance of Form and Other Arguments gathers the early writings of British designer Jasper Morrison, written between 1984 and 2002 and collected and edited by industrial designer Sina Sohrab. Published together here for the first time, these texts map the formation of ideas that would come to define his practice: the responsibilities of design, the value of usefulness, and the quiet authority of ordinary things. From autobiographical manifestos and his 1985 RCA thesis to later essays, musings, and even notes for an unfinished novel, this compendium of 31 texts captures the honing of a lifelong argument about what design is—and what it should be. Taking its title from his 1991 essay The Unimportance of Form, one of his most searching critiques of the designer’s role, the book offers rare access to the early thinking of one of design’s most influential figures, from ideas behind objects not yet iconic to reflections on his expanding relationship with the industry. Celebrated for objects that feel as though they were always meant to exist, Jasper is also a sharp, sceptical, and often humorous writer. A longtime contributor to the Apartamento world—including The Hard Life Notebook (2016) and his introduction to Miguel Milá: A Life in Design—this volume provides a singular glimpse into the formative ideas that would shape a remarkable career.

Jasper Morrison is a British designer known for furniture, lighting, tableware, and everyday objects that fit seamlessly into daily life. Born in London in 1959, he studied at Kingston Polytechnic, the Royal College of Art, and Berlin’s HdK, and founded his Office for Design in 1986. He made his name with works such as Thinking Man’s Chair (1985) and the Plywood Chair (1988), and has gone on to design furniture and products for companies including Vitra, Flos, Cappellini, Muji, Alessi, and many others. Morrison co-curated the influential Super Normal exhibition in 2006 with Naoto Fukasawa, which became a defining moment in his practice. Alongside a canon of published books, including A World Without Words, The Good Life, and Super Normal, his contributions to design have earned him membership in the Royal Designers for Industry, a Compasso d’Oro, and a CBE.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: April 8, 2026
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking.
Delivery time: 2–4 days from the shipping confirmation.

The third in our reading series, Written at Night is the fragmented autobiography of Ettore Sottsass, one of the most seminal figures of 20th-century radical design. Originally written in Italian and published posthumously in 2010 as Scritto di notte, it now arrives in English for the first time, translated by one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English, Alastair McEwen.

As he recounts his upbringing in Trento and Turin, his conscription in WWII, his Milan debut, his dance with poverty, and his travels—from Cuba with Hemingway to a snowy Italian night drive with Ginsberg to the fever of India—Written at Night begins as a slow tide into the mind of one of radical design’s greatest figures, only to sweep you up in its storm. Digging through the debris of memory, he finds the precious metals of people and places, so that what he’s writing in the dark is a sweeping blueprint of love, lust, and survival. In his attempts to start from childhood and climb forwards, Sottsass produces a piece of art in and of itself—self-interrupting, self-critical, self-affirming, self-annihilating.
Written at Night joins our growing reading book series, following Essential and The Unimportance of Form.

Ettore Sottsass (1917–2007) was an Austrian-born Italian postmodernist designer and architect, considered one of the most seminal figures in 20th design, and hailed for co-founding the design collective known as the Memphis Group. Considered a polymath by many, he moved freely between furniture, glass, lamps, jewellery, objects for the home and office, as well as the design of many buildings and interiors, magazines, and publications. Alongside a significant canon of published books, his contribution to design has earned him four Compassi d’Oro. His works are exhibited in the permanent collections of museums around the world, such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Centre Pompidou in Paris, and the Victoria & Albert Museum in London.

Alastair McEwen is considered to be one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English. To date, he has published over 100 book-length translations, essays, articles, and poems, plus several feature film scripts and operatic librettos. He has translated some of the most important Italian writers of our time: Umberto Eco, Roberto Calasso, Antonio Tabucchi, Fleur Jaeggy, Alessandro Baricco, Aldo Busi, and many others.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: November 16, 2026

items.title: HOLIDAY GIFT SET #3
items.description: Peluquería is the first book dedicated to late Spanish photographer Ouka Leele’s formative years in Barcelona and her portraits of the city’s underground scene. Widely celebrated as a key figure of the Movida Madrileña, Leele settled in Barcelona one year befo
paragraphs: Peluquería is the first book dedicated to late Spanish photographer Ouka Leele’s formative years in Barcelona and her portraits of the city’s underground scene. Widely celebrated as a key figure of the Movida Madrileña, Leele settled in Barcelona one year before the country’s official turn to democracy. The improvised ‘hair salon’ referred to by the series’ title gathers legends of the counterculture movement at this moment of extraordinary freedom, marked by the playful, defiant objects on their heads. Peluquería’s electric colours, unique for the era, are achieved through Leele’s innovative use of watercolours, which she painted onto her black-and-white prints by hand. Original sketches that inspired the series, as well as previously unpublished writings by Leele are presented alongside contact sheets newly unveiled by the artist’s archive. Reflections by Javier Mariscal, one of the first artists photographed for Peluquería, and Rossy de Palma, an icon of Spanish cinema, honour Leele’s poetic vision, while essays by Pepe Ribas and Elisa Medde mine the radical landscape that informed Leele’s early work.

Ouka Leele (1957–2022), born Bárbara Allende Gil de Biedma, is a Spanish photographer and a fixture of the Movida Madrileña. She is renowned for the distinct visual language she pioneered with her work, beginning with the Peluquería series, in which she transformed black-and-white prints by painting them with vivid watercolours. She was awarded the 2004 Culture Prize by the Community of Madrid and the Spanish National Photography Prize in 2005.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: November 23, 2026
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking.
Delivery time: 2–4 days from the shipping confirmation.

Between 1999 and 2006, before fast fashion and social media changed the world forever, Kyoichi Tsuzuki published 87 instalments of his Happy Victims series in the fashion magazine Ryuko Tsushin. In cramped quarters across Tokyo, these anonymous disciples joyously detailed the ritual and the sacrifice of their brand-name obsessions. A Buddhist monk with a Comme des Garçons shopping habit, an Alexander McQueen collector listening to neighbours through paper-thin walls—photographed at home, their collections before them, Kyoichi’s anti-heroes exist in parallel to the fashion universe of fame, fantasy, and glamour. Happy Victims was first published in book form in 2008. Long out of print, this edition follows Apartamento’s reissue of Kyoichi’s earlier seminal work, Tokyo Style. The new hardcover design comes with an updated foreword by the author, Japanese photographer Kyoichi Tsuzuki, and an introduction by Isabella Burley of Climax Books.

While the cover and belly band have been completely reworked, in collaboration with designer Han Gao, the book’s interior maintains a simple, documental format: one happy victim per spread, Kyoichi’s photos supplemented by a short commentary on the individual and his or her daily schedule. Not typically members of the leisure class, the goths, Lolitas, and stringent Margiela fans must also go to work and find time to care for their clothes.

A Tokyo native, Kyoichi Tsuzuki is an award-winning photographer and a former editor at such iconic publications as Popeye and Brutus. He received the 1996 Ihei Kimura Award for his first photography exhibition, Roadside Japan, and has since shown work at the White Cube Gallery, London, MUDAM Luxembourg, Galerie Da-End, and more. Kyoichi is also the author of Tokyo Style, a cult classic reissued by Apartamento in 2024.

Isabella Burley founded Climax Books in London in 2020 as a home for rare editions, adding a New York outpost in 2024. At 17, she started on the shop floor of Dover Street Market with Comme des Garçons, then later served as editor-in-chief for Dazed & Confused from 2015 to 2021. Additional appointments include Helmut Lang and Acne Studios.
‘A grail for obsessive little fashion freaks everywhere’. —Los Angeles Times

‘[T]here is something deeply poignant about portraits of people whose modestly proportioned living spaces are dominated by their treasured fashion archives, and who are often making many sacrifices in other areas of their lives to acquire new items’. —AnOther
‘Happy Victims…remains one of the clearest visual records of how branding, personal identity, and private living space intersect’. —Yokogao Magazine
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: July 8, 2025

Birds of Paradise is a vibrant photobook by Spanish artist Ángela Suárez which explores the brave and bold hair colours found on walks around the photographer’s homeland and beyond. Inspired by her love of Spanish fashion and portraiture photography combined with her genuine surprise when she first took notice of the phenomenon, this collection marks an awakening of awareness and crystallises Ángela’s obsession in printed images. What began as a personal project of Spain street photography grew as Ángela began to share the work on social media, and it bloomed into a community-sourced record of electric blues, cotton-candy pinks, hazard oranges, and a rainbow of hues in between. Birds of Paradise is a casual documentary of eccentricity, an homage to what might inspire us when we take the time to notice the wild personalities around us.

Ángela Suárez’s work operates at the intersection of portrait, art, fashion, and architectural photography. She is the author of Blurry Days/Sharp Nights and Good Intentions, and her practice also includes collaborations with brands such as Loewe, Dior, Uniqlo, and Self Service. In 2022, she participated in the exhibition Madrid Diversa, curated by the Madrid City Council at CentroCentro, and in 2024, her work was recognised with the Photovogue Global Talent Open Call (Milan) award. Ángela’s latest group exhibition, Spirit, opened in November 2024 at Domicile Gallery (Tokyo), reaffirming her presence in the international contemporary art scene.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: November 12, 2025
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking
Delivery time: 2-4 days from the shipping confirmation

items.title: ADRIEN BRODY
items.description: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star
paragraphs: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star

Twenty-two years after he became the youngest ever winner of a best actor Oscar, for ‘The Pianist’, Adrien Brody has gone and done it again, this time taking home an Academy Award for his deeply moving performance as Hungarian architect László Toth in ‘The Brutalist’. What makes it all the more remarkable is that only a few years ago Adrien had all but given up acting. The awards are much deserved, of course. Adrien, 52, is an intense and uniquely gifted actor, which also makes him entertaining company. He doesn’t do things in half measures. He’s all in, all the time, and not afraid to speak his mind. In the following story Adrien engages in some energetic verbal ping-pong and gets dressed up in fashion by his friend Thom Browne. It captures some of the essence of what makes him such an incredible performer.
From Fantastic Man n° 40 – 2025
Photography by ILYA LIPKIN

The instant Adrien Brody sweeps into the room, he begins to express what I will soon come to think of as his resting affect: a kind of intense but fuzzy gratitude. “I just got back from London yesterday night,” he tells me. “Feeling very blessed with all the love that’s been coming my way. It’s a really special moment. It really is.” Maybe it’s just for now, in these hectic weeks promoting ‘The Brutalist’ ahead of the Academy Awards, but it’s with words like these that Brody seems at his most comfortable, and throughout our conversation he will periodically return to similar sentiments, restating and expanding upon them with evident sincerity.

With other kinds of words, though, it will often come to feel as though there are fault lines everywhere. Seconds after this initial declaration, I ask Brody – my question intended as little more than small talk to fill the empty space between us as we greet each other and take our seats – whether it feels like he’s being carried away in a whirlwind. He responds – not just in his words but in his body language too – as though he’s being somehow misunderstood or as though something wonderful is at risk of being spoiled.

“No, it’s not that at all,” he says, correcting me firmly. “No, my feet are on the ground. I’m ultra-present. I’m ultra-present and able to reciprocate the love. It’s different. Being older gives you a degree of perspective. It’s been a very long time since I’ve had an opportunity to do the work that I’m yearning to do. And the work is completed. So this is just something magical.”

Brody will prove to be engaging, fascinating company, and a man with plenty to say. In our conversation there will also be moments where he exudes a sense – verbally, but also through a repertoire of expressions that seem to hover between saddened and harried – that the world doesn’t quite get him.

What I then find myself wondering is whether such a sensibility might be a consequence of setbacks and reversals he has faced along his idiosyncratic chosen path, or whether it’s such a sensibility which sends you down that path in the first place. Conversely, I also find myself wondering whether it’s exactly this kind of off-kilter mindset which, when everything comes together in just the right way, somehow fuels Brody’s singular ability to inhabit and transmit a role like ‘The Brutalist’s’ László Toth with such compelling, all-consuming mastery.

It was back in 2019 when Adrien Brody was first given the script of ‘The Brutalist’, the expansive tale of a visionary Hungarian architect who escapes the Holocaust and makes his way to America, where he finds a new life – one of opportunity, but also one with horrors all of its own. Brody read it in the apartment he and his partner, fashion designer Georgina Chapman, then had in Manhattan. “I found myself very moved by the writing and the breadth of the storytelling, the complexity, the flaws of the character,” he remembers. “The opportunity for me to play someone that is experiencing so much and contending so much in life [was] wonderful. And I did consider parallels of László’s lived experience with my mother’s and my grandparents’ journey.” Brody’s mother, whose maternal grandparents were rounded up and taken to Auschwitz, survived the war in Budapest. She escaped in 1956, at the age of 13, buried under corn in a horse-drawn cart as she and her parents crossed the Austrian border. In New York, Brody grew up around his Hungarian grandparents. “So that, too, definitely is evident to me in reading it – saying: ‘Wow, I’m quite right to play this character.’”

After reading, Brody met with the director, Brady Corbet, who had written the script with his professional and personal partner, the filmmaker and actor Mona Fastvold, for brunch downtown. “A very long meeting – conversed a lot about lots of things,” Brody recalls.
