YORKE: Artist’s own clothing.

items.title: The 200 Best Songs of the 1990s
items.description: The Nineties music explosion was a golden age. Whatever style of music rings your bells, it was booming in the Nineties — from grunge to gangsta rap, from country to techno, from riot-grrrl punk to TRL teen-pop. It was the age of Lollapalooza and Lilith Fair,
items.author: Rob Sheffield
paragraphs: The Nineties music explosion was a golden age. Whatever style of music rings your bells, it was booming in the Nineties — from grunge to gangsta rap, from country to techno, from riot-grrrl punk to TRL teen-pop. It was the age of Lollapalooza and Lilith Fair, Kurt and Courtney, Biggie and Tupac, Beavis and Butt-Head. Fans were devouring music—paying actual money for CDs! in record stores! — on a level never seen before or since. We felt stupid and contagious. It was the most gloriously chaotic era for music ever — which is why so many fans revere as the greatest.

So let’s break it down: the 200 best songs of the Nineties. The hits, the misses, the deep cults, the fan favorites. A mix tape of pop classics, rockers, rappers, soul divas, disco jams, country twangers, punk ragers, dance-floor anthems, karaoke standards. There’s all-time legends and one-hit wonders. But only one song per artist, or half the list would be Missy Elliott.

This list has so many legends: Nirvana, Biggie, Prince, Madonna, the Wu-Tang Clan, Radiohead, Oasis, Jay-Z, OutKast, Garth, Whitney, Alanis, Aaliyah. There’s rising pop stars ready to conquer the next century, like Beyoncé and Britney; there’s also grizzled vets like Bob Dylan and Neil Young, refusing to fade away. There’s New Jack Swing, Britpop, trip-hop, shoegaze, ska, goth, rave. And Cher, obviously.

Some of these Nineties songs remain famous around the world. You hear them at weddings, parties, clubs, the karaoke bar. Others make people run and scream in terror. Some are cult classics that only the hardcore fans know. Every fan would make a different list — that’s the whole greatness of it. There’s no way one list could sum up such a bountiful decade
But all 200 of these tunes reflect the beauty, the brilliance, the weirdness of Nineties music. Slip this mix tape into your boombox, crank up the volume, and press play.
Photographs in Illustration:

Paul Natkin/Wire Image; Al Pereira/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images; Paul Bergen/Redferns/Getty Images; Dave Hogan/Getty Images; Brian Rasic/Getty Images; Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic; Steve Granitz/WireImage; Gie Knaeps/Getty Images; Ron Davis/Getty Images; Tim Mosenfelder/Getty Images; Lester Cohen/Getty Images; Steve Eichner/Getty Images; Frank Micelotta/Getty Images; Chris Walter/WireImage
- Digital Underground, ‘The Humpty Dance’ (1990)

The Bay Area rap crew Digital Underground kicked off the Nineties with that rarest of pop treasures — the song that absolutely everybody loves. “The Humpty Dance” was the summer jam of 1990, as the late great Shock G turned into his crazed alter ego Humpty Hump. His motto: “I’m a freak! I like the girls with the boom! I once got busy in a Burger King bathroom!”  As Shock G said, “I wanted to bring the gap between Prince and hip-hop.” Digital Underground were a free-spirited collective where the freaks were definitely welcome. (Tupac got his start as a member.)  “The Humpty Dance” remains a timeless dance-floor banger—and the perfect song to get this party started right. R.I.P., Humpty Hump. All over America, Burger King employees are still mopping up after you.

- The Divinyls, ‘I Touch Myself’ (1990) A brazen Australian punk queen and her shy guitar boy, after nearly a decade of small-time scuffling, finally conquer America with “I Touch Myself,” the most shamelessly sticky-fingered ode to solo sex to ever hit the Top Ten. Every other autoerotic jam out there sounded coy and simpy compared to this, especially since Christina Amphlett sings it with all her vixen energy. (Somehow “Shock the Monkey” never hit like this.) “I like double entendres,” she said, but come on — “I Touch Myself” barely counts as half an entendre, which is why it’s brilliant.

- Third Eye Blind, ‘Semi Charmed Life’ (1997) Third Eye Blind’s hits always stood out because of Stephan Jenkins’ sore thumb of a voice — sharp, pushy, adenoidal, so bitchy you wondered if he was kidding, except he never was. But his narcissistic flash was a breath of fresh air, as rock radio recovered from its Her Placenta Falls To the Floor phase. In “Semi-Charmed Life,” he’s bedeviled by a woman who just uses him for his body (a frequent Stephan Jenkins dilemma, at least in his songs) and leaves him doing way too many drugs (ditto), to that “doo doo doo” chorus.

- Deee-Lite, ‘Groove Is In The Heart’ (1990) New York club-kid DJ culture, translated into a Saturday-morning kiddie cartoon? This groove really is in the heart, as Lady Miss Kier holds court alongside her Ukrainian DJ (Dimitry) and a Japanese art student (Towa Tei), meeting up to form their own world clique. This party has everything: a very young Q-Tip rapping in a “Hendrix haze,” Bootsy Collins on bass (“Dig!”), soul horns from the legends Maceo Parker and Fred Wesley, a jazz bassline sampled from Herbie Hancock, hooks swiped from Dr. Seuss and the Beatles. But Deee-Lite turn their global collage aesthetic into a surefire floor-filler.

- Seal, ‘Kiss From a Rose’ (1995) Remember those weekends when your mom would lock herself in the bathroom for “Bible study” after asking to borrow some AA batteries? It was all Seal’s fault. This man was the smoothest of romantic balladeers, and he proves it in “Kiss from a Rose.” The words make absolutely no sense at all (“Did you know when it snows, my eyes become large?” No, Seal, in fact we did not) but he turns anything he sings into pillow talk. You can hear how hard he works at singing the word “baaay-baaay” exactly like George Michael in “Faith,” and these are the tiny details classic slow jams are made of.
- Keith Murray: The Most Beautifullest Thing In This World (1994)

Few songs capture the blissed-out poetics of hip-hop circa 1994 like the greatest hit by Keith Murray, from Long Island’s Def Squad, one of the coolest MCs. “The Most Beautifullest Thing In This World” is laid-back, cozy like a blanket, as Murray kicks it in the basement with Erick Sermon and Redman, getting interplanetarian like Doctor Who.

- Magnetic Fields, ‘All My Litttle Words’ (1999) Stephin Merritt burrowed through the Nineties, making his name as one of the most clever songwriters around. But he took everyone by surprise with his triple-disc opus 69 Love Songs. He’d already crafted so many gems with the Magnetic Fields, Future Bible Heroes, and the 6ths. (Their 1995 Wasps’ Nests is a real spinner, especially when Barbara Manning sings “San Diego Zoo.”) “All My Little Words” is his most exquisitely despondent ballad with singer LD Beghtol lamenting, “I could make you fly away, but I could never make you stay.” Even the banjo sounds miserable.

- The Verve, ‘Bittersweet Symphony’ (1997) The Verve’s Richard Ashcroft was born to be a rock star: 40 percent lips, 40 percent cheekbones, 20 percent shades, until he opened his mouth and became 100 percent poetic pretensions. In the great tradition of English bands, the Verve hated each other so much they broke up every time they made an album. “Bittersweet Symphony” is their classic, with Mad Richard at his most shamanic. They famously lost the rights by sampling an orchestral remake of the Rolling Stones’ “The Last Time.” (A gospel standard the Stones had no business claiming as an original in the first place.) But “Bittersweet Symphony” was the hit that made them international superstars. Naturally, they immediately broke up.
- Sir Mix-A-Lot, ‘Baby Got Back’ (1992) Butt of course. At the height of the “never trust a big butt and a smile” era, Sir Mix-A-Lot was there to remind us all to always — always — trust butt.

- Pam Tillis, ‘Cleopatra, Queen of Denial’ (1992) Pam Tillis was one of the era’s unforgettable country voices, with classics like “Maybe It Was Memphis” and “Spilled Perfume,” giving us so many poignant ballads. This is NOT one of them. “Cleopatra, Queen of Denial” is a high-water mark of the Nineties Hot Country line-dance boom, with the great Nashville goofball song title of the decade. (A close second: Mark Chesnutt’s “Bubba Shot the Jukebox.”) “He’s probably stuck in traffic/He’ll be here in a little while / Just call me Cleopatra, everybody, because I’m the Queen of Denial.”

- Stardust, ‘Music Sounds Better With You’ (1998) A landmark of French filter-house, not to mention a prime Nile Rodgers rip from an era full of them. Daft Punk’s Thomas Bangalter (he’s the robot on the left, or maybe the one on the right, who knows) did this one-off collabo with a couple of club confreres, bouncing the simple refrain off an energy-flash guitar lick (sampled from a Chaka Khan record) to the break of dawn.
- Hi-Five, ‘I Can’t Wait Another Minute’ (1991)

The ultimate New Jack Swing smooch ballad. The early Nineties were a golden age for teen R&B slow jams, from smoothies like Mint Condition or Color Me Badd. The Waco, Texas boys in Hi-Five were the deep South’s answer to New Edition, with hits such as “I Like the Way (The Kissing Game).” But “I Can’t Wait Another Minute” is prom perfection, as the boys harmonize to pour their hearts out, before the clock ticks down to curfew.

- The Spinanes, ‘Hawaiian Baby’ (1993) A haunting love story, from the Spinanes’ guitar poet Rebecca Gates, one of the era’s sharpest indie-rock storytellers. Gates sings about a romance from the past, going through old photos, postcards, love letters. She plays an old mix tape, remembering how much you loved that song by the Verlaines. But even though she knows the relationship didn’t work — “it’s my heart and it doesn’t fit yours” — the memory of that song won’t leave her alone. “Hawaiian Baby” is a springtime song for sure — every April I lose at least one day disappearing into this tune.

- Ghostface Killah feat. Mary J. Blige, ‘All That I Got Is You’ (1996) A Wu-Tang family affair: Ghostface gives it up to his mama with a gospel choir and a string section. “All That I Got Is You” is a vulnerable confession amid the bravado of Ironman, as Ghost looks back on the struggle of growing up in the desperate poverty of the Staten Island projects, where he had to “pluck roaches out of the cereal box” and wonder why he was ever born at all. Mary J. Blige sweetens the song in the voice of the angel showing him the way forward.

- The Offspring, ‘Self Esteem’ (1994) Just another bunch of Orange County punk dudes going megaplatinum with a ditty about masochism. The Offspring had quite a run of grunge bangers after emerging from the SoCal hardcore scene, with “Come Out and Play (Keep ‘Em Separated)” and “Why Don’t You Get a Job?” But “Self Esteem” is their funniest and best, with the quintessential Nineties proverb, “I might be dumb but I’m not a dweeb.” It’s still a timely sentiment — unless you ARE a dumb dweeb, in which case you’re probably the guy in this song.
- Supergrass, ‘Alright’ (1995) Trying to pick just one song from the Clueless soundtrack? That’s as useless as searching for meaning in a Pauly Shore movie.

- Ricky Martin, ‘Livin’ La Vida Loca’ (1999) The former Menudo stud shook his bon-bon to the electric-salsa sleaze of “Livin’ La Vida Loca,” falling under the spell of a mocha seductress with devil-red lips. Ricky’s popularity took a tumble after his disastrous dance with President George W. Bush, but he hung in there, eventually came out, and got his shot at redemption in American Crime Story: The Assassination of Gianni Versace.

- The B-52s, ‘Roam’ (1990) Kate Pierson and Cindy Wilson take it hip to hip, rocketing through the wilderness. The B-52s looked like a thing of the past, after the death of their guitar savant Ricky Wilson, but the Georgia new wavers took their grief and danced this mess around, when Cosmic Thing blew up as their surprise comeback hit. “Roam” feels like an elegy for Ricky, but it soars like an invitation to a Southern road trip, as Kate and Cindy go for a spin down the dirty back roads of their memories.

- Paperclip People, ‘Throw’ (1994) A Detroit techno classic from the legend Carl Craig, one of dance music’s most innovative minds. “Throw” is a classic from his alter ego Paperclip People, with disco vocals distorted into the stratosphere, eerie robot synths, planet-rocking bass throb. LCD Soundsystem do a bang-up version of “Throw” live. Carl Craig learned to play guitar at 15, as he said, “because I wanted to be Prince.” But then he heard his lifelong heroes Kraftwerk. “I threw all that Prince shit out the window. I wanted to be Kraftwerk.” “Throw” came from touring England with fellow Detroit techno pioneers Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, inspired by the raves.“ I put out ‘Throw’ in 1994,” Craig recalled. “I played it on acetate at a small club and the floor jumped. That was how it all started.”
- Dump, ‘International Airport’ (1995)

A buried treasure from Dump — the sound of a sad guitar boy in his room, pouring his heart into his 4-track. He plays a bittersweet melody on his guitar, stretching it out, letting it build for 10, 11, 12 minutes of achingly plaintive rock shimmer, with a Brian Wilson sense of pathos. Then he signs off with a coda where he warbles a few lines about flying away and waving goodbye. The boy is James McNew, bassist for Yo La Tengo, but auteur behind excellent Dump records like this 10-inch vinyl EP, or his Prince covers album The Skinny Motherfucker with the High Voice. The Nineties underground was full of DIY songwriters like this, making their music not to get rich or popular or even heard, but just to get their feelings down on tape for a few minutes. “International Airport” might be the most obscure song on this list, but once heard, it’s in your soul forever.

- LL Cool J, ‘Doin’ It’ (1996) Ten years after his debut, Ladies Loved Cool James more than ever. In “Doin’ It,” he represents Queens, she was raised out in Brooklyn, but neither of them is getting any sleep. LL brings in his fellow Eighties O.G. rapper LeShaun to reprise her “doin’ it, doin’ it, doin’ it well” hook, for one of the Nineties’ friendliest sex songs. Uncle L was already a rap veteran heading into the 1990s — he began the decade proclaiming, “Don’t call it a comeback!” But when he dropped “Doin’ It” in 1996, it was downright shocking how he’d managed to stay on top for so long without ever going stale. He calls this hit his personal favorite — as he recently said, “I think the beat, the lyric, the flow, the collaboration, the moment, the visual — it’s perfect.”

- Luna, ‘Chinatown’ (1995) New York guitar aesthetes Luna spent the decade making one expert dream-pop record after another, to the point where they made everyone else in the rock game look a little thick. Dean Wareham spun his witty vignettes of romantic obsessives lost in the big city, in albums like Penthouse and Pup Tent. (“It’s no fun reading fortune cookies to yourself,” so true.) In “Chinatown” he’s going home alone, after another wasted night of fancy drinks and lucky toasts, over the sleek Velvets-meet-Television guitars.
- Wreckx N Effect, ‘Rump Shaker’ (1992) All they wanna do is zoom-a-zoom zoom-zoom and a boom-boom, over those Teddy Riley beats.
- Everything But The Girl, ‘Missing (Todd Terry Remix)’ (1994)

Everything But the Girl started in the Eighties as a moody New Wave duo, a married couple with a taste for cocktail jazz and bossa nova. But they grew up with a bang in the Nineties, with the acoustic folk-soul breakthrough Amplified Heart. Then things got weird: “Missing” blew up into a left-field pop hit, in a dance remix by Todd Terry. EBTG kept exploring club beats on Walking Wounded and Temperamental, but “Missing” is their deepest cry from the heart, as Tracey Thorn and Ben Watt grieve over a loss that won’t heal.

- Fatboy Slim, ‘Praise You’ (1998) A true only-in-the-Nineties hit, from the moment when electronica went populist. An English techno DJ digs up an obscure hippie-gospel hook, then bombards it with go-go breakbeats and computer blurps and Nashville honky-tonk piano. Result? A pop smash everybody and their mother loves. Norman Cook, a.k.a Fatboy Slim, mixed a whole armful of rare wax — most prominently, Camille Yarborough’s voice—into a song that sounded at home in a club, a minivan, a day-care center, a druggy rave, or a dollar-an-hour Internet café. It summed up the genre briefly dubbed “big beat,” one of the most useless names any genre has ever had. At other points in history, “Praise You” would have been considered a weird little art project. But in the anything-goes Nineties, it was pure pop for all people.
- Cornershop, ‘6 A.M. Jullandar Shere’ (1995)

Cornershop took the guitar drone of the Velvet Underground somewhere new in this uplifting processional hymn, sung entirely in Punjabi. Tjinder Singh and his brother Avtar were London guys with Indian parents, taking their band name from the English stereotype of Indian immigrants managing convenience stores. (They even put out their DIY debut on “curry-colored” vinyl.) “Jullander Shere” is a guitar groove mixing up sitar, tablas, a stoner electro-rave vibe, devotional vocals, for six jubilant minutes. (Very rough translation: “Brothers and sisters, we are speaking of the true path!”) Cornershop went on to have hits like “Brimful of Asha,” working that same groove.

- Onyx, ‘Slam’ (1993) Hey ho, let’s go: “Slam” is one big mosh pit of grimy Queens hip-hop and hardcore punk, with a room full of crowd-surfing, body-smashing, slap-happy hooligans. “We wanted to bring slam dancing to rap,” Onyx’s Fredro Starr said. “Believe it or not, Nirvana was a big influence on us. Red Hot Chili Peppers too.” The baldhead rappers got massive with this jock jam, from their well-titled Bacdafucup. Their awesomely tone-deaf singing has a jolly all-in-together-now spirit, even if Onyx were out of their minds on acid when they recorded it.
- Utah Saints, ‘Something Good’ (1992)

In the wide-open days of the Nineties, practically anything could explode into a hit, no matter how bizarre. Exhibit A: the English techno duo Utah Saints, who scored a global arena-rave smash with “Something Good.” At first, they’re shouting their remarkably silly name. (“Utah Saints! U-U-U-Utah Saints!”) But the disco beats build until they get to the climax — a sample of Kate Bush singing exactly one line, from her hit “Cloudbursting”: “Ooooooh, I just KNOW that something good is gonna happen!” They warp her voice, looping the line over and over until it turns into a glow-stick mantra. By the end, the idea of turning Kate Bush into a disco diva sounds like a stroke of genius, taking her to wuthering new heights.  “Something Good” snagged more airplay in the 1990s than all of her actual music combined, yet nobody was mad at it. No wonder Kate herself loved it.

- Selena, ‘Fotos Y Recuerdos’ (1994) The Tejano queen became a permanent pop legend even though her life ended tragically too soon, at her musical peak. “Fotos y Recuerdos” shows off her eclectic style — a Spanish-language cumbia version of the Pretenders’s new wave nugget “Back on the Chain Gang.” It was Top Five on the Billboard Latin charts the week Selena died, becoming her first posthumous Number One.

- Usher, ‘You Make Me Wanna…’ (1997) Usher, still in his teens, makes his big move with his breakthrough hit, agonizing over a love triangle, torn apart by doubt and guilt. “You Make Me Wanna…” introduced Usher as we’ve known him ever since.

- Suede, ‘The Drowners’ (1993) Suede helped kick off the Britpop explosion, which gave us a sizable percentage of the decade’s kickiest guitar bands, with champs like Pulp, Blur, Elastica, Oasis, Placebo, the Auteurs, but also fondly remembered fly-by-nighters like Shed Seven, Gene, and Menswe@r. It couldn’t have happened without Suede, who threw down the gauntlet for everyone with their debut single “The Drowners.” The London boys turn their Bowie/Roxy obsessions into a glam-trash manifesto, with hair-flopping madman Brett Anderson yelping, “We kiss in his room to a popular tune!”
- Deborah Cox, ‘Nobody’s Supposed to Be Here’ (1998)

People were just starting to say “empowerment” as the Nineties began and sick of it by Y2K, but the concept was pretty much defined by Nineties R&B radio. Case in point: Deborah Cox’s “Nobody’s Supposed To Be Here,” a rainy-day jam about a woman who’s gotten burned too many times but dares to try again. (“How…did…you…GET here?” Damn.) First it was a blockbuster ballad, then got remixed into a disco hit — both versions killed. When Angela Bassett directed her Lifetime biopic about Whitney Houston, Ms. Cox had the honor of singing Whitney’s vocals.

- Paul McCartney, ‘Calico Skies’ (1997) Paul got his mojo in the Nineties — he stopped aiming for mainstream pop hits, and started trusting his eccentric muse again. “Calico Skies” is a poignant acoustic ballad from Flaming Pie, with finger-picking straight from the White Album. It feels like a love song to Linda under the shadow of mortality, with Paul vowing, “I’ll hold you for the rest of my life,” just a year before she passed away from cancer. “Calico Skies” was one of the songs played at her memorial service, in Paul’s string arrangement for the Brodsky Quartet.

- Tori Amos, ‘Cornflake Girl’ (1994) Tori Amos came on like one of rock’s truest rock eccentrics — she aspired to be as huge as Zeppelin or the Stones, straddling her piano bench. “Cornflake Girl” was her parable of growing up in America, set amid the cryptic battle of Cornflake Girls vs. Raisin Girls, with Tori gulping, “Rabbit, where’d you put the keys, girl?” The success of “Cornflake Girl” put Amos in a position where she was primed for mainstream stardom — all she had to do was, you know, maybe tone it down a notch? Needless to say, that’s when she entered her “breast-feeding a pig in the album photos” era.
- Mya, ‘It’s All About Me’ (1998)

A psychedelic R&B slow jam from Mya, the D.C. ingenue who spent her nineteenth summer in the Top Ten with her very first single, “It’s All About Me.” Mya sings uncannily like Prince’s feminine alter ego Camille, her voice lost in dubbed-out reverb, with help from Dru Hill’s Sisqo (pre-“Thong Song”) and producer Darryl Pearson, as she kicks her groovy sexual politics: “Tonight it’s about me, me, me, me, me / Forget about you, you, you, you, you.”

- Smash Mouth, ‘All Star’ (1998) Yep, what a concept. The San Jose golf bros in Smash Mouth might have looked like a one-shot fluke after their 1997 hit “Walkin’ on the Sun,” but “All Star” was a jock-rock pep talk, as the late Steve Harwell reminds us all that you’ll never shine if you don’t glow.

- FreakNasty, ‘Da Dip’ (1996) “Da Dip” was one of the Dirty South’s easiest dance crazes: “I put my hand up on your hip/ When I dip, you dip, we dip!” Even Cardi B busted these New Orleans moves in “Bodak Yellow.” The B-side was called “Bump That Rump.”

- Wilson Phillips, ‘You Won’t See Me Cry’ (1992) And now, dear reader, I fear it’s time for some tough love. As we used to say back in the Nineties, this is a “care-frontation.” You probably believe “Hold On” is the best Wilson Phillips song, right? So wrong. So tragically wrong. That’s fine for the locals, but true Wilson Phillips aficionados prize their real masterpiece, “You Won’t See Me Cry,” the over-the-top tearjerker ballad from their underrated 1992 follow-up album, complete with a flaming candelabra of a sax solo. For Carnie, Wendy, and Chynna, it’s their “Wouldn’t It Be Nice?”

- Ivy, ‘I’ve Got a Feeling’ (1998) L’amour, c’est bleu. A bittersweet guitar-chime gem from one of the decade’s great cult indie-pop records, Ivy’s Apartment Life, whose mood is captured by the cover photo of a mod French girl putting on her makeup — glossy yet introspective. The dream-team trio features the late Adam Schlesinger (moonlighting from Fountains of Wayne), Andy Chase and chanteuse Dominique Durand, whose Parisienne accent adds that touch of tres tragique to their young-adult romantic malaise. “I’ve Got a Feeling” made a memorable appearance in the first episode of Felicity, but a melody this great would make an impression anywhere. If you’re living your life without this song, you’re blowing it big-time.

- Superchunk, ‘Slack Motherfucker’ (1990) The Chapel Hill scruffers Superchunk let out a rebel yell for Gen X kids with the day-job blues, for their wonderfully snotty breakthrough single — a punk rock “Take This Job and Shove It.” Mac McCaughan wrote it about an annoying co-worker at the copy shop. (Google “copy shops” — they were such a thing.) “Slack Motherfucker” sounded like a one-shot, but as it happened, Superchunk turned into one of the era’s most enduringly brilliant guitar bands, still going strong. A dumb Nineties joke: Why did the indie rocker cry? She moved to Chapel Hill and saw a sign that said “Merge Left.”

- Chumbawamba, ‘Tubthumping’ (1997) An anarchist punk anthem about fighting the power? A common-as-muck English working-class drinking song? A bizarro but beautiful fluke of a pop hit that never fails to light up any room? Guilty on all charges. “Tubthumping” remains a song for those days when you get knocked down, but you get up again.

- Belle and Sebastian, ‘Me And The Major’ (1996) The Glasgow cardigan kids won a worldwide audience without even trying. “Me and the Major” is a highlight of their breakthrough album If You’re Feeling Sinister, bristling with bookish wit, as Stuart Murdoch sings about a strange cross-generational friendship with an older guy who seems exotic to him. (“He remembers all the punks and the hippies too / And he remembers Roxy Music in ’72.”) But for Belle and Sebastian, this was just the beginning.

- P.M. Dawn, ‘Set Adrift on Memory Bliss’ (1991) The New Jersey duo P. M. Dawn had their own style of dreamy hip-hop reveries, aiming to sound soft and tender. “Set Adrift on Memory Bliss” turned into a startling Number One hit, with that jaw-dropping Spandau Ballet sample. The song mixed up Native Tongues-style hip-hop, New Romantic synth-pop, and goth melodrama. P.M. Dawn rejected rap cliches about gender roles, and paid the price for it, which might be why they’re so underrated now. But “Set Adrift” is a tribute to Prince Be’s omnivore imagination as well as his gentle warmth.

- Sebadoh, ‘Brand New Love’ (1992) Sebadoh were an archetypal Nineties cult band — the guys who sang the tongue-in-cheek anthem “Gimme Indie Rock!” (Sample verse: “Milk that sound, blow your load / Further than you ever thought it would go / Four stars in the Rolling Stone!”) But in “Brand New Love,” the punk wolfboys take a bold step into full-fledged human-hood with a ballad about opening your bitter little world to scary new feelings and smiling back at that girl across the room and starting a mosh pit in your heart. An inspiring noise from their album Smash Your Head On The Punk Rock, building from acoustic folk to screaming feedback. Words to live by: “If you need a different face / It’s definite time to destroy this place.”

- Mary J. Blige, ‘My Life’ (1994) No holleration or hateration here, just the Queen of Hip-Hop Soul with a song in the key of her life, revealing her vulnerable side over the jazziest of grooves, promising herself that she’s on her way to finally see the sunshine.

- Lois, ‘Capital A’ (1996) If you made a rainy-day mix tape in the Nineties, you had to include at least one Lois song. With her acoustic guitar, tea cup and wry grin, Lois Maffeo came on as indie rock’s wiseass auntie, on classics like Strumpet and Infinity Plus, dueting with members of Bratmobile and Fugazi as well as her friend Elliott Smith. Lois had an Olympia band called “Courtney Love,” which seemed like a clever idea until somebody else got famous using that name. But “Capital A” is a lost Nineties classic of heart-shredding romance, about two scared kids looking up at the sky, holding hands, hoping this night never ends.

- White Town, ‘Your Woman’ (1996) One of the era’s shrewdest one-hit wonders — one of the things that made it so shrewd was the way White Town refused to flog it into more. Jyoti Mishra was a longtime indie-rock dude, an Anglo-Indian guitarist from the twee scene, but here he warps into an Eighties New Wave diva, He adopts a femme voice to sneer at an ex, sniffling, “So much for all your highbrow Marxist ways,” looping a 1930s jazz-horns sample into a synth-pop taunt.

- Roxanne Shanté, ‘Brothers Ain’t Shit’ (1990) The self-proclaimed “Bad Sister” from Queensbridge, Shante became a rap legend with the Juice Crew, alongside Big Daddy Kane, Biz Markie, and Marley Marl. But in “Brothers Ain’t Shit,” she chooses violence with her nastiest dis record ever. Shante has choice words for men who approach her on the street (“I know your number / You got an ‘Ass, Gas, or Grass’ sticker on your bumper”) and suggests revenge techniques for ex-girlfriends done wrong. Given hip-hop gender politics, it’s no surprise Dre and Snoop had their answer record “Bitches Ain’t Shit” onThe Chronic before Shante got to release “Brothers Ain’t Shit” on an album of her own, but even they couldn’t top the original.

- The Mountain Goats, ‘The Recognition Scene’ (1995) When the Mountain Goats first appeared, nobody knew John Darnielle’s name, or what a role his songs would play in our lives over the coming decades. Nobody would have guessed he’d become an award-winning novelist, or a star with a TikTok mega-hit about hoping your spouse dies. He was just another basement busker with a guitar, pressing “record” on his boombox because his friends were smart enough to screen out his calls. But goddamn, his songs. Take “The Recognition Scene,” from Sweden, the tale of an outlaw couple robbing candy stores on a road trip. “We had hot caramel sticking to our teeth / The only love I’ve ever known, burning underneath.” Make no mistake: if Darnielle stopped here, we’d still revere his name today.
- Mandy Moore, ‘Candy’ (1999) You know who you are. Your love’s as sweet as candy. I’ll be forever yours. Love always, Mandy.

items.title: The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time
items.description: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks. So we’ve updated the list. We kept the update light; the 2021 list covered many decades of popular music, and was the result of a vote among more than 300 artists, writers, producers and industry figures; this update covers three years, from 2021 to early 2024.

In 2004, Rolling Stone published its list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. It’s one of the most widely read stories in our history, viewed hundreds of millions of times on this site. But a lot has changed since 2004; back then the iPod was relatively new, and Billie Eilish was three years old. So we’ve decided to give the list a total reboot. To create the new version of the RS 500 we convened a poll of more than 250 artists, musicians, and producers — from Angelique Kidjo to Zedd, Sam Smith to Megan Thee Stallion, M. Ward to Bill Ward — as well as figures from the music industry and leading critics and journalists. They each sent in a ranked list of their top 50 songs, and we tabulated the results.

Nearly 4,000 songs received votes. Where the 2004 version of the list was dominated by early rock and soul, the new edition contains more hip-hop, modern country, indie rock, Latin pop, reggae, and R&B. More than half the songs here weren’t present on the old list, including a third of the Top 100. The result is a more expansive, inclusive vision of pop, music that keeps rewriting its history with every beat.

- Harry Styles, ‘As It Was’ The lead single from Harry Styles’ third album balances its agitated inner monologue, where the shape-shifting pop star picks at the details of a relationship in crisis, with spun-sugar synths that give cover to his torment. From its playful opening — Styles’ goddaughter Ruby giggling “Go on, Harry, we want to say goodnight to you!” — to its singsong bridge, during which Styles’ thoughts are ping-ponging around his head at “high-speed internet” velocities, “As It Was” paints an unusually vivid picture. Everything might seem fine on first glance, but it all becomes more troubling (“What kind of pills are you on?”) with each repeated glimpse.

- Townes Van Zandt, ‘Pancho and Lefty’ An epic story-song about a bandit and the friend who betrays him, “Pancho and Lefty” became a country hit thanks to Willie Nelson and Merle Haggard’s 1983 duet. But it’s the songwriter’s own forlorn reading, on 1972’s The Late Great Townes Van Zandt, that best conveys the doomed fates of the main characters. It begins with what might be one of the most descriptive opening verses in the country-folk canon: “Living on the road my friend/was gonna keep you free and clean/now you wear your skin like iron/your breath as hard as kerosene.” “It’s hard to take credit for the writing,” Van Zandt said in 1984, “because it came from out of the blue.”

- Lizzo, ‘Truth Hurts’ “That song is my life and its words are my truth,” Lizzo wrote at the time. She had to tack on a writing credit to British singer Mina Lioness, who had tweeted its iconic line “I just took a DNA test, turns out I’m 100 percent that bitch,” but the power of this gale-force breakup banger was pure Lizzo, uproariously swaggering and endearingly soulful. “Truth Hurts” was originally released in 2017, but the song got a big boost two years later, when Gina Rodriguez day-drunkenly sang it in the Netflix show Someone Great, and it became Lizzo’s signature hit.

- Harry Nilsson, ‘Without You’ “We did it because my career was on the wane and we wanted something to make a hit,” Harry Nilsson bluntly told an interviewer when asked why he covered Badfinger’s near-despondent ballad: “I heard it and searched through every Beatles album for two and a half weeks, trying to find out which one of their tunes it was.” Producer Richard Perry agreed, piling on the strings to showcase Nilsson’s desperate lunge of a vocal. Both were right — the song went to Number One and earned a Grammy nomination for Record of the Year.

- Carly Simon, ‘You’re So Vain’ The holy mother of all diss tracks, “You’re So Vain” contains one of the most enduring musical mysteries of all time. Just who is so vain that he probably thinks the song is about him? Simon previously revealed that actor Warren Beatty inspired the second verse of the song (“Oh, you had me several years ago/When I was still naive”), but speculation abounds regarding the other man (or men) behind the ire. Either way, the track — boasting omnipresent Seventies arranger Paul Buckmaster’s orchestration and Mick Jagger’s background vocals — is pure soft-rock fire.

- Cyndi Lauper, ‘Time After Time’ Cyndi Lauper was nervous about “Time After Time” — the aching ballad she wrote in the studio with keyboardist Rob Hyman to finish off her blockbuster solo debut, She’s So Unusual. “I asked them to please not put ‘Time After Time’ out as the first single,” Lauper said. “People would never have accepted me. If you do a ballad first, and then a rocker, that doesn’t work.” Her instincts were right: Following the jaunty “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” “Time” became her first Number One.

- The Pixies, ‘Where Is My Mind?’ No song typifies the freakish pop instincts that made the Pixies stand out in a sea of gloomy Reagan-era bands better than “Where Is My Mind?” Joey Santiago’s lead guitar is catchier than most Top 40 hooks, and by the time Fight Club made this song iconic a decade after its release, it had already formed part of the DNA of countless alternative-radio hits in the years between, from Nirvana to Korn. When an interviewer in 1988 asked about his unique ability to crank out great songs, Black Francis’ answer was typically cryptic: “It’s nice to have space. How much can one brain deal with?”

- Kanye West, ‘Stronger’ Explaining the tighter, broader-reaching songs on his third album, Graduation, Kanye West said, “I applied a lot of the things I learned on tour [in 2006] with U2 and the Rolling Stones, about songs that rock stadiums. And they worked!” West found the inspiration for his most grandiose statement to date from Daft Punk’s “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger,” which he sampled and reshaped. West is a big fan of the French duo: “These guys really stick with the whole not-showing-their-faces thing. Just amazing discipline — that’s straight martial-arts status.”

- Miles Davis, ‘So What’ It’s likely that no song on this list has soundtracked more dinner parties than Kind of Blue’s warm, welcoming first track. But at the time it was a jarring departure, trading bebop chord changes for a more open-ended modal style. According to pianist Bill Evans, the trumpeter worked up his material just hours before recording dates, but the all-star band here sounds like it’s been living with “So What” for years: Saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley turn in solos that have since become as iconic as any in jazz history, and the rhythm section of Evans, bassist Paul Chambers, and drummer Jimmy Cobb swings like it’s dancing on air.

- Bad Bunny, ‘Titi Me Pregunto’ “Tití Me Preguntó” is a showcase for Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny’s unbridled creativity and eccentric pop genius, mixing frantic dembow beats, a classy sample by bachata master Anthony Santos, and a coda with a dash of Latin psychedelia to the global mainstream. He does it all with panache and a healthy sense of humor. Using the archetype of the concerned Latin American aunt asking about her nephew’s potential girlfriends as a starting point, he launches into a hilarious tirade of salacious puns to a bouncy party vibe that — in typical Bad Bunny fashion — unexpectedly morphs into moody self-reflection.

- Lil Nas X, ‘Old Town Road’ Montero Hill was an Atlanta college dropout sleeping on his sister’s couch and looking to break into music when he came across a track he liked by a Dutch 19-year-old called YoungKio that was based around a banjo sample from a Nine Inch Nails track. “I was picturing, like, a loner cowboy runaway,” he told Rolling Stone. Within a year “Old Town Road” was the longest-running Number One song of all time, seeming to sum up eons of American cross-cultural love and theft in just one minute and 53 seconds.

- The Breeders, ‘Cannonball’ Notified by fax that her services in the Pixies were no longer required, Kim Deal called up her twin sister, Kelley, to be her new guitarist (never mind that she didn’t know how to play guitar) and had the last laugh when this absurdist gem became an MTV phenomenon in 1993. “When people were talking about the Breeders being a one-off,” Kelley told Rolling Stone, “I was like ‘No, actually … the Pixies are a side project.'” A little over a year later, the Breeders were on an extended break of their own, but the effortlessly fun trampoline bounce of “Cannonball” is one for all time.

- The Weeknd, ‘House of Balloons’ Far from the international superstar he’d become, Toronto singer-songwriter Abel Tesfaye didn’t even send out photos or do any interviews when he released the first Weeknd album. “The whole ‘enigmatic artist’ thing, I just ran with it,” he said. “No one could find pictures of me. It reminded me of some villain shit.” But the title track of House of Balloons nevertheless set the course for his career, both thematically — drugs and sex, meet depression — and musically, with its sample of Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “Happy House” announcing a new direction for R&B.

- Solange, ‘Cranes in the Sky’ In an interview with her sister Beyoncé, R&B innovator Solange Knowles described how this song was inspired, in part, by overzealous real estate development she noticed around Miami: “This idea of building up, up, up that was going on in our country at the time, all of this excessive building, and not really dealing with what was in front of us.” She turned the metaphor inward to examine her own feelings about change, self-doubt, and aspiration, finishing the song years after it was originally conceived with producer Raphael Saadiq to create a lavish moment of neo-soul introspection.

- Lil Wayne, ‘A Milli’ Producer Bangladesh looped the opening chords from Gladys Knight and the Pips’ “Don’t Burn Down the Bridge,” then segued to a drill-like volley of trap drums. He gave the beat to his friend Shanell — a onetime R&B singer on Wayne’s Young Money Entertainment — to pass along. Wayne initially had grand plans for “A Milli”: He wanted to use the instrumental as skits for rappers like Tyga, Hurricane Chris, Corey Gunz, and Lil Mama. In the end, though, “A Milli” is just Weezy solo, blacking out in the booth and dazzling everyone who hears him.

- Azealia Banks, ‘212’ In 2011, Azealia Banks was a teenage rapper-singer whose clear talent yielded a development deal with XL Recordings but little else. “She had been working on a collection of tracks and there was one Dutch house-sounding one that was just absolutely insane,” producer Jacques Greene recalled. Banks freestyled ferociously about her New York hometown and, uh, cunnilingus over the jittery beats of Belgian house duo’s Lazy Jay’s “Float My Boat.” Initially released in 2011 as a viral track, “212” was a hip-house banger that earned Banks a deal with Interscope and served notice that this uninhibited provocateur would not be constrained.

- Weezer, ‘Buddy Holly’ Never has geek been so chic as in Weezer’s 1994 breakout single, “Buddy Holly.” Written for frontman Rivers Cuomo’s girlfriend, the poppy ode to nerdy romance was almost left off the band’s self-titled debut, also known as the Blue Album, due to Cuomo and now-ex-member Matt Sharp’s reticence. “We had the sense that it could be taken as a novelty song, and people aren’t going to take the album seriously,” Sharp told Rolling Stone. After producer Ric Ocasek heard the receptionist at the recording studio humming it, he insisted they keep it in.

- The Four Tops, ‘I Can’t Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)’ One of Motown’s most rousing anthems, “I Can’t Help Myself” was inspired by songwriter Lamont Dozier’s grandfather, who’d call the women his hairdresser wife fixed up “sugar pie” and “honey bunch.” During the recording, engineer Harold Taylor recalled, “People were banging on the door of the studio; they were so ecstatic about what they heard.” Nevertheless, Levi Stubbs asked Brian Holland if he could do another take. Holland promised him they’d do it soon — and Stubbs’ first pass hit Number One.

- Lady Gaga, ‘Bad Romance’ Shortly after Gaga had established herself as a star, she catapulted to a next level of weirdness with this Nadir “RedOne” Khayat production, which drew upon the electronic music Gaga had been inundated with while touring Europe. “I want the deepest, darkest, sickest parts of you that you are afraid to share with anyone because I love you that much” is how she summed up the idea behind the song. Fittingly, she debuted the hit-to-be at Alexander McQueen’s show at Paris Fashion Week.

- Robert Johnson, ‘Cross Road Blues’ The primal terror in the Mississippi bluesman’s voice, and his mystifying slide guitar playing, transfixed the Sixties generation of British rockers: “I could take the music only in very small measures because it was so intense,” said Eric Clapton. Recorded during a session at a San Antonio hotel room in 1936, two years before Johnson was murdered at 27, “Cross Road Blues” is a mythmaking statement of spiritual desolation and scorched-earth betrayal — even if the legend that it’s about Johnson selling his soul to the devil in exchange for his monster guitar chops is, as far as we know, apocryphal.

- Biz Markie, ‘Just a Friend’ Nobody beats the Biz (1964-2021), an impossibly good-natured DJ, rapper, producer, human beatboxer, and hip-hop personality who broke big with this ode to the friend zone off his second album. Built on a fat beat, plinking piano, and his charmingly off-key singing, “Just a Friend” interpolates Freddie Scott’s 1968 song “(You) Got What I Need” as Biz warbles about a love that will never come to pass. It was based on real life. As he told Rolling Stone in 2000, “I was talking to this girl from L.A., and every time I called her, this dude was at her house, and she’d say, ‘Oh, he’s just a friend.’ I hated that.”

- Santana, ‘Oye Como Va’ Growing up in San Francisco, Carlos Santana was shaped by the city’s psychedelic explosion. “You cannot take LSD and not find your voice,” he once claimed, “because there is nowhere to hide.” And while his early heroes were bluesmen, he changed history with this foundational Latin-rock reworking of a 1962 salsa number by Cuban percussionist Tito Puente. Santana kept the original’s cha-cha pulse but replaced its horns with Greg Rolie’s organ and Carlos’ lysergic guitar flares. Said Puente years later, “He put our music, Latin rock, around the world, man.”

- Juvenile feat. Lil Wayne and Mannie Fresh, ‘Back That Azz Up’ In the late Nineties, Mannie Fresh’s diamond-sharp productions for Cash Money Records helped put New Orleans in the center of the hip-hop map. The title of this hit was so reminiscent of local artist DJ Jubilee’s single “Back That Thang Up” that Jubilee sued (unsuccessfully) for infringement, and the beat rode the “Triggerman” rhythm that is foundational to New Orleans bounce. Juvenile freestyled his best shit-talking bounce rhymes, and Lil Wayne shut it down with a “drop it like it’s hot” hook. As Mannie said, “[He] immediately was just like, ‘Shit, I’m getting a piece of this.’”

- The Go-Gos, ‘Our Lips Are Sealed’ The radiant first hit of the Go-Go’s was influenced, according to writer Jane Wiedlin, by “the Buzzcocks and Sixties girl-group stuff.” It was also inspired by a clandestine relationship she was having with Terry Hall, of U.K. ska group the Specials, who got a co-writing credit because Wiedlin based the lyrics on some poetry he’d written her in a letter. “It was pretty personal,” Wiedlin recalled. “I mean he had a fiancee at the time — nowadays I wouldn’t touch that with a 10-foot pole, but I was 19, and I was like ‘fiancee shmiancee.’”

- Kris Kristofferson, ‘Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down’ The desolation of spirit in Kris Kristofferson’s “Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down” is so heavy, so apparent, that it’s almost hard to listen to. But that despair is exactly what drew Johnny Cash to sing it on his TV variety show in 1970. Kristofferson cut his own stunning studio version that same year for his debut album, Kristofferson. Cash’s interpretation, more shuffling and accessible, is the one most listeners turn to, but listen to them back-to-back if you can, and marvel at how Kristofferson’s lyrics about being hung over, alone, and desperate shake your soul.

- Janet Jackson, ‘Rhythm Nation’ Jackson’s socially conscious Number Two hit came together late in the sessions for her blockbuster LP Rhythm Nation 1814. Co-producer Jimmy Jam recalled being in the studio and “switching between MTV and CNN. Watching music videos on one side and watching atrocities on the other. Somehow they all merged together. The idea for ‘Rhythm Nation’ was you can dance, but we can also do something more intelligent.” When Jam heard Sly and the Family Stone’s “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)” at a restaurant, he raced to the studio to sample it.

- Curtis Mayfield, ‘Move On Up’ Mayfield’s irresistible “Move On Up” was politically empowering, morally demanding, and effortlessly propulsive, powered by swinging horns and tangy congas — the nine-minute LP version, with its powerful drum break, laid a foundation for disco and hip-hop alike. Mayfield’s message was just as steadfast: that pride and dignity were paramount for Black America to rise. “I’m not trying to say anything to make you think, ‘Well, this is the way, this is the only way,'” Mayfield said. “I’m trying to cover the whole subject.”

- Tammy Wynette, ‘Stand by Your Man’ From the start, this pledge of wifely devotion, the first song Wynette ever co-wrote, was a cultural lightning rod. Feminists recoiled from its pledge of unquestioning fidelity in the Seventies, and Hillary Clinton defined herself a modern woman by slamming the song during Bill Clinton’s first presidential run. But the recording itself steamrolls over ideological objections, as the catch in Wynette’s voice on the verses gives way to a vocal swell that rises to meet the epic sweep of Billy Sherrill’s production.

- Peter Gabriel, ‘Solsbury Hill’ Shortly after Gabriel quit Genesis in 1975, he climbed to the top of Little Solsbury Hill in Somerset, England, to reflect on his life-changing decision. It inspired his debut solo song, in which he explained to fans why he felt the need to go out on his own. Musically, it was a departure too, a pastoral tune with a 12-string acoustic guitar lead that was pointedly different from Genesis’ prog-rock. The song has since become ubiquitous in movies and film trailers. “Maybe I’ve let it go too much,” he admitted to Rolling Stone in 2011.

- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.title: Southern Charm Recap: Easter Islands
items.description: Oh, these boys and their homes. Craig is in the backyard rescuing bees while there is still a full cavern in the ceiling of his living room. Shep is turning his rental property into a more “grown-up home” while there are dorm posters on the walls, countless tr
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Oh, these boys and their homes. Craig is in the backyard rescuing bees while there is still a full cavern in the ceiling of his living room. Shep is turning his rental property into a more “grown-up home” while there are dorm posters on the walls, countless trucker hats with various booze-brand logos, and piles of shirts with the shaka on them taller than most Duke fraternity pledges. Austen has decided to redo his bathroom, and when Rodrigo shows up to display some tile combinations, his face glazes over like the “Hot Now” sign is on at the Krispy Kreme. It’s not like the girls are any better. Molly finally has a big old house, but it’s still full of boxes, mess, and pets, and she can’t find her most prized possession: the weave she had to wear on America’s Next Top Model.

The worst, however, is Miss Pat’s house now that it is in Whitney’s control. She fired the last butler because he kept melting phones in the oven, and now someone has to answer the door and no one can figure out how. She might have hired a private chef, but she’s serving up Easter luncheon buffet style. A buffet? At Miss Pat’s? Excuse me? That’s like going to Jean-Georges and they give you a McDonald’s hash brown in a paper bag. Then, once everyone is seated, suitably waiting for the host, there aren’t any napkins for these people. The standards are slipping. What’s next? A white refrigerator?

We’re talking all about their houses because not a lot happened during this episode. Shep met with his mom, and she hates his new beard, probably because it looks as scraggly as the dead bushes outside of his adult home. Venita’s mother came to visit her and told her what all of us at home are thinking: that she shouldn’t ruin her friendship with Whitner trying to make something romantic happen because he doesn’t seem that interested. Venita’s mother, Vi, tries to have a deeper conversation, but Venita says that she can’t because her mother wouldn’t let her discuss serious topics when she was a kid. Girl, meet your mom halfway. She just gave you some great dating advice; why not throw her a little bone?

Whitner has a phone call with Allie, who texted him that their date was off after she talked to Salley and the girls at the pool party, and they freaked out when she said that Whitner slept with a close friend of hers. I’m sorry, but this is the right call. Whitner says that it’s a “bad look and poorly timed.” Um, dude. Once you have shown interest in her, there is no suitable time to fuck one of her close friends. Not before the date, not after, and not even after you break up. Once you have picked someone in the friend group, everyone else is off-limits. Even Samantha Jones knows that, and she once masturbated to the sounds of her neighbors having sex.

Allie is nonplussed that he says the issue is the timing. She says, “Why couldn’t you just keep it in your pants?” Oh, Allie. Why are you asking existential questions? That’s like asking what our purpose on this earth is. That’s like asking why God lets bad things happen to good people. That’s like asking why, oh why, did they cancel the gorgeous reboot of Ladies of London after only one season? There are some things that are unknowable, and it’s much easier to just accept the reality that no man will ever keep it in his pants than imagine a universe where they don’t. When Whitner talks all this through with Molly, he says that he and Allie weren’t dating, that he owed her nothing. “Bad look, yes. Morally questionable, no,” he says in confessional. Dude, that is not the bar you are trying to clear here. This isn’t about morals; it’s about making a good impression on a woman you are trying to date. Sleeping with her good friend is probably the worst thing you could do, short of sharting on her white sofa. That impression says that he is not to be trusted, and she is right for not trusting him.

Patricia has Austen, Craig, Shep, Madison, Salley, and her extra E over for Easter (ahem) buffet. Whitney is there serving drinks and dressed not as the butler in a Grey Poupon ad or the car that pulls up to the butler or even the glove box in the car, but as the bottle of mustard. This is brand synergy at its finest. Salley shows up wearing another shawl. What is wrong with her? Does she think that she’s constantly in a cathedral? Why are her shoulders constantly covered these days? At least this time it seems like she can move them past her waist without her C-cups totally falling out onto Miss Pat’s bunny-themed centerpiece.

Salley does bring up the comment that Austen told her that Allie made about the most attractive thing about him is that he hadn’t slept with her yet. He says he doesn’t remember telling her that, and he says that she did ask if they slept together, and he said “no,” and she was like, “Phew, thank God.” Madison and Salley act as if that is totally different and, well, they’re kinda right. Even if it’s phrased more lightly, it’s still basically like, “Thank God you haven’t tainted yourself with Salley.” Either way, Salley and Austen are both entirely unreliable narrators. I’m sure what Allie said was somewhere in the middle, and now Austen is trying to make it sound sweeter than it was, and Salley is trying to make it sound more sinister so that they can both serve their own purposes. The bottom line is that these two are terrible for each other and should stay away. Shep, however, lays the blame squarely at both of their feet. He says that he couldn’t be clearer to Salley that he’s not interested; however, he also keeps texting her and hanging out with her and getting her even more confused.

Shep and Austen have their own issues. Austen is pissed that Shep talked to Allie about their relationship and made it sound like he broke up with her because she wouldn’t sleep with him. When Shep won’t take any blame, Austen tells him that he started it by even bringing up their relationship, which he shouldn’t have done. Shep then tells Austen he started it by going out on dates with her. Dude. Really? That’s like blaming a murder victim because they bothered to be born. It doesn’t work like that. Shep tells Austen that he always thinks he’s a victim, which isn’t entirely wrong, but in this instance, Austen is right. They all complain that the hardest part about dating in Charleston (and I wonder if they mean on the show) is that the pool is small and everyone is always up in their business. Then why is Shep committing this cardinal sin? Why is each relationship a little bit like this fight, where the two keep pounding the table to make their points? Each coupling is like a shock wave, each one hitting the community like fists on wood so that the bunny perilously placed in the center of Miss Pat’s table gets more and more askew, a little bit uglier, a little bit more bent out of shape until there is nothing in the world that will set it square again.

items.author: Christina Grace Tucker
paragraphs: Well, folks, I got got! I was certain that the SUV that flipped was Kane, or Lincoln, hell, even Jed himself. And I gotta say, I find Sophie’s impulse to walk to the crash bonkers, because I am personally hitting the gas. Well, no, I would probably be throwing up or wheezing and crying. Either way, nothing would compel me to go look, but thank God they did! How else would we discover the victim is, in fact, NADIA!

I am heartbroken, but I don’t really have time to sit with it, because now it’s time to be fully horrified, as Margo and Sophie … hmm, how to put it? Encourage Nadia’s death? Allow her to choke on her own blood? It’s, like, deeply upsetting to watch, and it’s even worse because Nadia is still with it enough to beg for help. I don’t like it! I wanted Callie and Nadia to be a team for good against these insane blondes! Back at Sophie’s, Margo pivots to “we did nothing wrong,” which is objectively not true! But Sophie is manic, so she goes with it. All they have to do is destroy the laptop and it will be like it never happened! Okay!

Jonny comes home to Callie and drops the news about Nadia on her. His explanation is very coplike of him, describing the details of what happened clearly and slowly, ending with Nadia’s death. Callie’s reaction? Well, it made me cry every single time I watched it! Granted, I am watching this in circumstances that are almost too on the nose to be believed, so maybe that is coloring my perspective. Either way, my heart is breaking for Callie! She deserved to find love with a messy coastal-elite dyke who wore leather and manipulated people with ease. Justice for Callie!

Margo makes her way home to Jed, semi-contrite about blowing off her security detail. She wants to make this work, she really does! It’s just that, well, Lincoln Trout is kind of a murderer, and she thinks Jed needs to cut ties with him ASAP. After hearing about Jai-Yi, Jed agrees to look into it, but it’s clear he is still quite pissed at Margo. Meanwhile, Sophie is dealing with Graham, who has since had the locks to their home changed. Oh, and he’s going for full custody of Jack. I hate to agree with this man and his mustache, but Sophie is not really giving the vibe of a woman who should be in charge of a child right now. It is kind of a normal reaction to being threatened with murder! He didn’t really need to add insult to injury by reminding her she is jobless and broke, with only a ridiculous sports car to her name, but he did.

My poor girl Callie is sitting on the couch in a grief daze as the ladies of Married Justice chatter around her about the show. Who is gonna produce it now? How are they gonna get famous? I know they don’t know about Nadia and Callie, but their dismissal of her death is quite cruel! And to pour salt on the wound, here comes Margo in a bonkers fur, bearing grief flowers and a smug smile. Kinda wild of her, but I get that people would think it was weird if she didn’t show up. Callie is furious and wonders aloud about how strange it is that Margo was the last person to see both Brad and Nadia alive. Strange indeed! Margo fires back that Brad never was the same after Callie killed his mother, and Callie leaps up, ready to brawl. Ever the head bitch in charge, Margo gathers the rest of the girls to leave Callie to mourn her “very special relationship.” Y’all, am I rooting for Callie now? Has Margo lost my goodwill?

Well, she’s certainly lost Callie’s, who storms into Jonny’s office and lays the whole thing out. Nadia had information on Margo proving she killed Abby Jackson, and if Jonny just checks Nadia’s laptop, he’ll see it’s all there. But no laptop was found at the scene, so Callie confesses that she loved Nadia and begs Jonny to really look into Margo. He knows Nadia loved Callie, too, and promises to do his best. These two are by far and away the best duo; I love them so much!

At Banks’ campaign headquarters, Jed demands that Lincoln Trout put his stupid phone away and tell him why he killed Jai-Yi. The thing is, Lincoln Trout has the president on the phone for Jed. Well now! What’s a little murder if the man can provide such access? This is basically what he tells Margo, though he does also make the good point that Margo isn’t really the one who should go around accusing people of murder. Jed got me there, too, like there is no real reason that I should want Lincoln Trout to go to jail and not Margo. She killed two teenagers! Much to reflect on there, I think!

How is the Blonde Duo From Hell gonna get out of this one? Well, Sophie has one idea that kind of makes sense: Margo can tell the truth about her abortion and tank Jed’s campaign. Once that’s over, everything will go back to normal, and the two of them can be together. I gotta say, nothing about Jed makes me think he would take kindly to his campaign being torched, and certainly Lincoln Trout would not. But they seem to think this will work, and to them I say: Good luck, babes!

Wanda has been having a nice little streak of good luck! Her man is home from the hospital and she has a cleaned-up file of the 911 call Margo placed. You might remember that Sophie confessing to murder is on that call? So Wanda comes flying into the station, fairly vibrating with joy to report this news to Jonny. On top of everything Callie has already told him, this is just too much to ignore. He calls Callie to let her know she was right again (good boy!) and that he’s bringing Margo in for a proper questioning. Hell yeah, Jonny! Way to stand up for what’s right!

… Almost. He manages to stand up to Jed for a bit, insisting that he will be taking Margo to the police station to ask her some questions about Sophie, Kyle, and Abby Jackson. Jed simply cannot have this right now, not on the day he is announcing he’s been endorsed by the president! So he does what he always does: dangles power Jonny can’t resist right in front of him. DAMN YOU, JONNY! CALLIE NEEDS SOMEONE ON HER SIDE RIGHT NOW!

High off her victory and certain Jonny is on her side, Wanda drops by Sophie’s house to tell her she has her fuckin’ number. Sophie isn’t under arrest, but she does have a court order to stay in town. What else is Sophie to do but call Margo to panic? Alas, Margo can’t talk right now because she is en route to the press conference with Jed, and he has some things to say. He makes her admit she killed Abby Jackson before telling her that he cleaned up the whole mess with Jonny. Jed has protected Margo once again, and in return, he needs her to shape up and act right. No more Sophie, because she’s going to jail for murder, and Margo will be the good wife she pretends to be on TV. After Jed announces his endorsement, Margo shocks everyone and grabs the mic. She wants to tell a story no one has heard before. Oh my God, is she actually going to drop the abortion and blow up this campaign?

No! Well, kind of no? She does drop the abortion, but instead of fucking the campaign, she actually builds it up. Yes, she had an abortion, but thanks to the love of the Lord God and her husband, she is a new and changed woman! And if they elect Jed to the governor’s mansion, he’ll redeem the whole damn state. Meanwhile, Sophie is watching in her house, screaming and tearing apart everything she owns. Yeah, that’s the logical response here.

Callie can’t believe her luck! Margo admitted the abortion on national TV; now all they gotta do is round her up! Wait, why isn’t Jonny out there rounding her up? Because he’s got power to dangle for her too! Maybe she’d like to be attorney general? Hold up, didn’t Callie say she’s never even taken the bar? How is that gonna work? Is Jed the Redeemer that powerful? Let’s hope so, because Wanda is pissed. She really thought Jonny was gonna do the right thing this time, and she cannot believe how wrong she was. Walter, her rock, has her back. If she wants to tell the state troopers or the FBI or even CNN, he’s gonna stand beside her. Sweet! Even sweeter: the big kiss Wanda lays on him! Happy for them, but this show is NOT about straight people, so let’s move along!

Once again, an angry woman comes roaring up Margo’s driveway, but this time it is Sophie. Jed kindly agrees to let them have one last good-bye. Huge of him, to be honest. Margo tells Sophie that the only reason she agreed to Jed’s terms was to keep Sophie out of jail. “You for me.” Hmm, that seems pretty selfless for Margo Banks, doesn’t it? Sophie seems to think so and has one final request. If she can’t have Margo, then she will settle for $10 million. And if Margo doesn’t get it to her, she just happens to have a recording of Margo admitting that she killed Abby. Margo is grudgingly impressed, but warns Sophie there is no coming back from this. Maybe there isn’t — but Sophie doesn’t care anymore. DAMN.

TWO YEARS LATER? We see a rich-looking Sophie saunter into a bar with an almost comically long blowout and request a Watenshi gin martini. As I just spent a summer bartending, so I can tell you that brand of gin retails for like $3,000. Okay, Miss Thang! As she waits for her drink, she watches in rage as Governor Jed Banks signs a bill that will allow anyone to deny LGBTQ+ folks if they want, with Margo at his side. “Hypocritical cunt,” Sophie mutters, then her phone rings. Heavy breathing and whimpering, before we cut to Margo, once again covered in blood. Then it cuts to credits. Look, if we get a season three, you know where I’ll be!
