- The Hunting Wives Recap: No More Scissor Sisters

items.title: The Hunting Wives Recap: An Act of Margo Banks
items.description: That Lincoln Trout is no good! We are treated to a flashback from eight months ago, where we learn just how far he is willing to go for this job. He lures the other candidate for the Jed Banks gig back to his hotel room, before tying him up and leaving him to
items.author: Christina Grace Tucker
paragraphs: That Lincoln Trout is no good! We are treated to a flashback from eight months ago, where we learn just how far he is willing to go for this job. He lures the other candidate for the Jed Banks gig back to his hotel room, before tying him up and leaving him to choke on the sock that Lincoln stuffed in his mouth. Lincoln swoops into his job interview and manages to convince the man in charge that he is right for this. Yeah, this is definitely the guy who hired a 24/7 killer/bodyguard for Margo. Bad sign!

Sophie is desperate for info and desperate to talk to Margo. So desperate, in fact, that she comes knocking on Nadia’s door. Callie answers and tells Sophie they are filming confessionals tomorrow, but that’s all. Despite Sophie’s many pleas for more information, Callie hits her with a “best of luck,” and a door closes in her face. Devastating! But iconic!

C&N Private Eye is far too busy cracking this case to worry about SOPHIE, please. When Callie comes back, Nadia has just gotten off the phone, linking another piece of evidence, this time the gun used to kill Abby, to Kyle, Margo’s brother. Nadia is ready to confront Margo TOMORROW at the confessional shoot, but Callie needs to think. She had feelings for Margo once — can she really condemn a woman she cared about to the clink?

Jail might sound good to Margo right now, actually! She’s in a different kind of jail, one where all she is allowed to do is go to campaign events and hang out in the house. They won’t even let her have a phone, but she is Margo fucking Banks after all, and gets around that by setting up a hair appointment in her name under Sophie’s number. When the salon calls to confirm, Sophie knows where to go. Their plan works, and Sophie is even able to smuggle Margo a burner phone. Damn, when push comes to shove, Sophie locks the fuck in, huh? But how the hell are they going to get Margo out of this? Jed is the problem, so they need leverage on Jed. Sophie’s eyes light up, and she has a solution. She’ll give Old Eye Patch a call and buy his file of Jed blackmail material! Brilliant thinking! She sets up a meeting, but someone has already beaten her to it. Goddamn it!

After getting pressure from Callie and Wanda, Jonny finally comes to the Banks’ with the news of Kyle’s death. He wants to confirm this terrible news with DNA, and even though Margo is boo-hooing with the best of them, Jonny doesn’t seem to be buying it. Jed doesn’t NEED this right now, damn it, but for the first time, Johnny throws his weight around. He’s got a man shot thanks to all this mess, so he’d like to figure out what’s going on. Margo uses this time to duck into the bathroom to call Sophie. The dangerous duo is panicked, especially when Sophie admits she didn’t get anything out of the eyepatch man. Margo is the one who realizes that Jai-Yi must have gotten to them after she got sacked by Lincoln Trout. Thankfully, Jai-Yi’s love for midday cardio is no match for Sophie’s love of stalking, and Sophie manages to get her to agree to a deal. One million dollars, split between Sophie and Jai-Yi. Of course, Jai-Yi immediately goes home and calls Lincoln Trout, ready to flip for higher pay. Oh girl, I fear you might be making the highest payment there is, with this one.

Callie is still not sure what to do about Margo, so she heads to see the Reverend in the hospital to talk about faith and guidance. The Rev is quite disillusioned at this point with the whole thing. I mean, I get it, but you know, sir, you could have tried one time to get your son real tangible help? The fact that he will have the bullet his son shot him with lodged in his chest for the rest of his life is kind of a bummer; I get that. He’s having a real crisis of faith, but it’s helping Callie realize something. None of this was an act of God or a divine punishment. This was an act of Margo Banks.

The wool is gone from Callie’s eyes, and she heads back to the hotel, ready to put Margo in the slammer. Nadia wants one piece of evidence they can startle her with, one bit of proof she can’t deny. Luckily, Callie has just the thing: photos of Margo and Brad on the very night of the murder. She confesses she took them while lurking in the bushes like a stalker, and it’s clear that she’s worried Nadia is gonna be like “see you later you absolute FREAK,” but Nadia warps her in a hug instead. I am rooting for these two, sue me!!!

Callie and Nadia welcome Margo to the confessional shoot like it’s gonna be just the best time ever. And you know what, maybe for them it will be? Nadia softballs her for like one second before leaping to questions Margo refuses to answer, no matter how hard Nadia pushes. So she drops the big one, throwing the photos up on her laptop screen and throwing them in Margo’s face. To credit, Margo doesn’t blink. She tries to say that Callie is a stalker and unwell, but when Nadia doesn’t back down, she folds. Props to Nadia for being the first person to say that Brad was a BOY she was sleeping with! Nadia is really confident and aggressive, talking to a woman who she thinks is a murderer and one we KNOW is a murderer, twice over! Margo uses her early end time to slip out of her shadow’s sight, disappearing into the woods in a shot that did actually make me lol.

Sophie has been tracking Jai-Yi down to see why she blew off their meeting. Once again, she is able to locate her apartment building, and oh my gosh, what does she walk in on but Jai-Yi being KILLED by Lincoln Trout and his security killer! She manages to get the hell outta there by the skin of her teeth, and picks up Margo from the woods somehow? Thankfully, it gives them a moment to catch up. Yeah, Nadia knows everything, from Abby to Brad, and yes, Lincoln is a stone-cold freak and killer. Oh, and there is a car following them! Fun! Thanks to Sophie’s new car, she’s able to pull a move that sends the hulking SUV flipping over them and crashing dramatically on the pavement. Will our intrepid duo pull it off? Could it be that they are free?

• Certain that their John Doe is Kyle Burkett, Wanda gets permission to run down the numbers of the cell phones in the location his truck was found. Sophie comes right on up, but so do three others, and Jonny wants her to run through them all before zeroing in on Sophie.
• Jai-Yi’s response to Sophie asking where the file is. “You think I carry it around in my purse like a fucking tampon?”

items.title: ‘A Girl Unknown,’ ‘Crawling Into Myself,’ ‘Concrete Land’ Take Main Prizes at Doha Film Festival
items.description: Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown,” Asmahan Bkerat’s “Concrete Land” and Hamad Al-Fayhani’s “Crawling Into Myself” won the top prizes at the sophomore edition of the revamped Doha Film Festival, which took place between Nov. 19-27 in the Qatari capital.
items.author: Rafa Sales Ross
paragraphs: Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown,” Asmahan Bkerat’s “Concrete Land” and Hamad Al-Fayhani’s “Crawling Into Myself” won the top prizes at the sophomore edition of the revamped Doha Film Festival, which took place between Nov. 19-27 in the Qatari capital.

The Doha Film Festival has transformed the Doha Film Institute’s existing Ajyal Film Festival, dedicated to youth and family-friendly cinema, into a more ambitious international event for a broader audience. Prizes totaled over $300,000 across four competition strands: international feature film competition, short film competition, the Ajyal film competition (judged by the festival’s youth jury), and the Made in Qatar competition, dedicated to projects made in Qatar regardless of the director’s provenance.

“A Girl Unknown,” which won Best Narrative Feature in International Competition, trails a young Chinese girl passed between three families between the ages of 6 and 18; “Crawling Into Myself,” the winner of the Made in Qatar competition, tells the story of a man grappling with a rare illness that erases his facial features. “Concrete Land,” the Best Documentary in International Competition, is a multi-generational portrait of a mixed-race family fighting displacement and hostility in Jordan.

Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, festival director and CEO of the Doha Film Institute, said: “Tonight, as we celebrate the winners of the 2026 Doha Film Festival, we celebrate far more than cinematic achievement. We recognize the power of stories to transcend borders, challenge perspectives and bring the experiences of people and communities into the global conversation.”
The festival director added that the Doha Film Institute “believes that important voices deserve to be seen, heard and recognized.”

“The Doha Film Festival exists to provide that platform—bringing together filmmakers and audiences from across the world, championing bold and independent storytelling, and creating space for stories that might otherwise go untold,” she added. “The films we honor tonight remind us that cinema is not simply a reflection of the world we live in; it is a force that can shape how we understand it, connect with one another and imagine a more empathetic future.”

This year’s jury at the Qatari festival was presided over by Japanese director Naomi Kawase, who chose the winners alongside French Tunisian actor Adam Bessa, Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha, Italian documentary filmmaker Gianfranco Rosi and award-winning Palestinian filmmaker and artist Kamal Aljafari.

The short film competition jury was presided over by French Moroccan producer Karim Aitouna, who was joined by Malaysian filmmaker Amanda Nell Eu, and Swiss-Rwandan actress and filmmaker Kayije Kagame. The Made in Qatar jury was led by Lebanese actress and filmmaker Yumna Marwan along with Qatari filmmaker Al Johara Al Thani and Palestinian Belgian filmmaker and producer Naël Khleifi.

The ceremony, which was hosted by Sudanese filmmaker and presenter Amjad Al-Nour, was attended by names such as Elia Suleiman, Brigitte Lacombe and Ahmed Al Baker. Other notable guests included H.E. Sheikha Al-Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, chairperson of DFI; H.E. Sheikh Dr. Abdulla bin Ali Al Thani, managing director and vice chairman of the board of directors of Qatar Leadership Centre; Hamad Omar Al-Mannai, chief executive officer of Media City Qatar; and Eng. Abdulaziz Ali Al Mawlawi, chief executive officer of Visit Qatar.

Earlier in the week, the festival delivered a successful industry sidebar, the Doha Industry Days. The three-day event was attended by some 450 prominent executives from 38 countries. Speakers included “Squid Game” creator Hwang Dong-hyuk, “Avengers” director Joe Russo, Omar Sy and Noomi Rapace. The buzzy Industry Days saw the announcement of several projects, including a Neon-backed biopic titled “Caesar” about Syrian military officer Farid Al-Madhhan and two other biopics, one on Egyptian music star Mohamed Mounir and the other on Lebanese pop star Fadel Shaker.
See full list of winners below:
International feature film competition
- Special Mention: “9 Temples to Heaven” by Sompot Chidgasornpongse
- Best Performance: Josette Kwanya from “House of the Wind,” directed by Auguste Bernard Kouemo Yanghu (awarded posthumously)
- Best Artistic Achievement in Documentary: “Bardi” by Tala Hadid
- Best Artistic Achievement in Narrative: “Filipiñana” by Rafael Manuel
- Best Documentary: “Concrete Land” by Asmahan Bkerat
- Best Narrative: “A Girl Unknown” by Zou Jing
- FIPRESCI Prize: “Concrete Land” by Asmahan Bkerat
International Short Film Competition
- Special Mention: “Nothing Happens After Your Absence” by Ibrahim Omar
- Best Performance: Damián López for his performance in “For the Opponents”
- Best Director: Maryam Tafakory for “Ghazal-e Sorkh”
- Best Film: “Whispers of a Burning Scent” by Mo Harawe
- Special Mention: “Ghafleh” by Tony El Ghazal
- Abdulaziz Jassim Award for Best Performance: “Amneh Aldam for Light to Ashes” by Nadia Al-Khater
- Best Director: Sebastian Delascasas for “In the Silence After”
- Best Film: “Crawling Into Myself” by Hamad Al-Fayhani
Ajyal Film Competition (winners were selected by an international youth jury aged 16-25)
- Best Short Film: “We Were Here” by Pranav Bhasin
- Best Feature Film: “We Are Aliens” by Kohei Kadowaki
“Jodari Meno” by Jamal Rashid Alkhanji

items.title: Monica Bellucci on Challenging Hollywood Ageism in James Bond, Working With Mel Gibson and the Power of Onscreen Nudity: ‘It’s Like a Costume That Brings a Role to Life’
items.description: Monica Bellucci, the glamorous Italian star who broke through internationally with “Malena” and “Irreversible,” was 50 when she made James Bond history as the oldest woman to play a Bond girl in Sam Mendes’ “Spectre.”
items.author: Elsa Keslassy; Anna Tingley
paragraphs: Monica Bellucci, the glamorous Italian star who broke through internationally with “Malena” and “Irreversible,” was 50 when she made James Bond history as the oldest woman to play a Bond girl in Sam Mendes’ “Spectre.”
But rather than marking the twilight of her career as a Hollywood sex symbol, the movie ushered in a new chapter for Bellucci whose career has been enjoying a second wind in recent years.

During a candid, wide-ranging masterclass moderated by Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival, Bellucci recalled that Mendes really “wanted to show a mature woman, and I thought it was a beautiful idea.” “He told me, ‘Listen, I have a strong and unusual role that’s going to be surprising, a little revolutionary,” she said. “I was 50, and I had never seen a 50-year-old Bond woman. So I think I’m the oldest James Bond woman, lady or girl that we’ve ever seen,” Bellucci said with a laugh in front of a huge crowd of locals and film students who queued for over two hours to get in.
Ultimately, “Spectre” and Emir Kusturica’s “On the Milky Road,” in which she starred opposite the Serbian filmmaker, came at a pivotal moment in her life.
“Suddenly, I had two very strong roles. Those two films helped me get through the transition of turning 50, which wasn’t easy for an actress,” she said.

Bellucci, whose body of work has largely been shaped by celebrated male auteurs — from Francis Ford Coppola to Giuseppe Tornatore, Gaspar Noé and David Lynch — also noted that she has enjoyed working with more female directors in recent years. She cited Alice Rohrwacher with her Cannes-prizewinning “The Wonders,” Rebecca Miller with “The Private Lives of Pippa Lee,” Kaouther Ben Hania with “The Man Who Sold His Skin” and Léa Mysius’ “Birthday Girl,” which competed at this year’s Cannes.

“When I was younger, there weren’t as many female directors as there are today. It’s new to have so many female directors, screenwriters and even technicians on a set, so many women. We’re witnessing something completely new,” she said.

“It’s another way of telling stories, sometimes another vision. And between women, sometimes there’s this ‘je ne sais quoi,’ as we say in France. Suddenly, we look at each other and, without words, we express ourselves and we understand each other. So I also really like working with women whenever possible.”
Bellucci said the roles she is being offered have also evolved as she’s gotten older, allowing her to explore facets of herself that she couldn’t have accessed earlier in her career.

“Our body is our working instrument. So the instrument changes and, consequently, the roles change. It’s another part of ourselves that’s expressing itself,” she said. “As we get older, we also gain experience, and we have another way of telling the story of life.”

Bellucci, who made her debut on stage in 2019 with the solo show “Maria Callas: Letters and Memoirs” — which she toured in different countries and played in French, Italian and English — said she felt lucky that “times have changed and there’s a lot of respect for women in cinema.”

“In the ’40s, ’50s and ’60s, it was very difficult for a woman over 40 to have a career, even if she was very talented and still had everything it took. And today that has changed.” She cited Susan Sarandon, Judi Dench, Jamie Lee Curtis and Meryl Streep as actors who have paved the way for women to continue playing compelling roles as they age. “There are magnificent actresses who are absolutely fearless,” she said, singling out Streep. “She’s so fearless and she’s incredible. There are several actresses who are free in that sense.”

Bellucci also reminisced about her defining role in Giuseppe Tornatore’s 2000 drama “Malena,” which earned two Oscar nominations. Bellucci plays a young woman whose beauty triggers desire and eventually violence in a small Sicilian town during World War II.

Bellucci, who says she was already a film buff from a young age “watching three films a day,” had met the Oscar-winning director of “Cinema Paradiso” during her modeling years in Italy and worked with him on a commercial for Dolce & Gabbana. Four years later, while Bellucci was shooting “Under Suspicion” with Gene Hackman and Morgan Freeman, Tornatore called to offer her the lead role which he wrote for her.

“The script was already very powerful because it tells the story of women living in a man’s world, the difficulty of those relationships, the violence. It’s about a woman who finds herself alone in a man’s world and has to deal with it. Ultimately, it’s still a very contemporary film,” she said.

At the time, Bellucci had already broken through in France with “L’Appartment,” starring opposite Vincent Cassel, and “Malena” represented a daring role which required a great deal of nudity and some intimate scenes with a teenage actor. She said approached these scenes “very naturally.”

“I came from fashion, so I had a freedom with my body that came from the work I had done before,” Bellucci said. “Even today, I think nudity can serve to bring a character to life. When I see films like ‘Anora’ or ‘Poor Things,’ these are films where the actresses’ bodies are very important in bringing the characters to life.”
“When you play a role, if nudity is part of that role, it’s simply a working tool. It’s not a way of exposing yourself. In fact, it’s like a costume that brings a role to life.”
During the conversation, Bellucci also talked about her experience shooting Mel Gibson’s highly controversial blockbuster “The Passion of the Christ,” in which she portrayed Mary Magdalene.

“I had another action film at the same time, and I chose ‘The Passion of the Christ’ because I wanted to work with Mel Gibson. I’d seen films of his that I liked, and it was an experience I wanted to have.”
She said she had no regrets about making the 2004 biblical epic, which sparked controversy over its graphic violence and portrayal of Jewish figures, and went on to gross over $611 million worldwide.
“I think every time a film sparks a discussion, it means it was important to make it. Because discussing and exchanging ideas — that’s the power of cinema,” she said.

She said she approached the role Mary Magdalene as “a simple, human woman who experiences something greater than herself, something she can’t really explain. There is a form of spirituality in everyone.” Although the film didn’t bring her closer to her Catholic upbringing, she said she felt “there is never anything bad in religions. It’s the political use of religion that is dangerous.”

Bellucci also praised Gibson for being “really incredible with actors on set” and revealed she had talked to him about the two-part follow up, “The Resurrection of the Christ,” which he’s currently filming. “Yes, we spoke,” she said of the sequel, adding: “I think he’s a great director.”

During the masterclass, Bellucci also revisited the memorable scene in “The Matrix Reloaded” in which her character, Persephone, demands that Neo — played by Keanu Reeves — kiss her as if he were kissing Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) in exchange for her help.
Asked whether she had to do numerous takes of the kissing scene with Keanu Reeves, Bellucci quipped, “It’s not tiring, is it? You can do it.”
“He’s someone who is very gentle, respectful. We met on ‘Dracula’ and saw each other again years later on ‘The Matrix,’“ she said of Reeves.
Despite landing supporting roles in several Hollywood movies at the height of her international breakthrough, Bellucci said she never felt the desire to relocate to the U.S.

“I like America. I love all these possibilities, all this energy, the possibility of making big films as well as independent films. And I like going there. But I feel profoundly European. I live between Paris and Rome, and I love that,” she said.

“The more time passes, the more I realize that I adore my profession and I still have that passion. But I also love the real things in my life. I love having my friends, I love my family. I also love having a kind of everyday life, something that keeps me connected to something real,” she said. “I like cinema, but I prefer life.”

Among her more recent Hollywood outings was Tim Burton’s “Beetlejuice Beetlejuice,” in which she plays Delores, Beetlejuice’s vengeful, soul-sucking ex-wife who comes back from the dead to hunt him down.

Bellucci said Burton’s drawings of Delores helped her envision the character. “He expresses so many things through his drawings and he had made a magnificent drawing of this character. I was already really inspired by that,” she said.

“With all her scars, Delores is a bit of a parody of existence, a metaphor for life,” she said, adding that the role necessitated three hours of makeup every day. “We all have scars. We have to face them, continue to live with them and move forward.” Speaking of the scene in which she reassembles her body, she said “there were special effects, but it was also a bit like a a macabre dance.”
Bellucci, who also worked with Ben Hania and Moroccan-Belgian directing duo Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah on “Seven Dogs,” was also upbeat about the new generation of Arab filmmakers.

“There’s a lot happening. This festival is proof of that, isn’t it? All these first and second films, these incredible young filmmakers, beautiful films like ‘Adam’ and ‘The Blue Caftan.’ Beautiful things are reaching international audiences, the Cannes Film Festival and beyond. Long live cinema!“

She concluded the masterclass with a rallying cry for the moviegoing experience. “I hope cinema will never disappear because I truly believe in cinema as one of the cultural elements that are essential to humanity,” she said.

items.title: The 25 Best New York Movies of All Time, Ranked
items.description: Hollywood has always been synonymous with the movies, but film history buffs know that American cinema really started in New York — or, if you want to get picky, just across the Hudson River at Thomas Edison’s lab in New Jersey, where the Kinetoscope was inven
items.author: David Rooney; Jon Frosch; Jordan Mintzer; Leslie Felperin
paragraphs: Hollywood has always been synonymous with the movies, but film history buffs know that American cinema really started in New York — or, if you want to get picky, just across the Hudson River at Thomas Edison’s lab in New Jersey, where the Kinetoscope was invented.

One of the first narrative motion pictures, Edwin S. Porter’s The Great Train Robbery (1903), was shot partly at Edison’s studios in Manhattan. The earliest works of D.W. Griffith were also made in Manhattan, until Biograph built a bigger stage in the Bronx. “King of Comedy” Mack Sennett, who launched Charlie Chaplin’s career, started off at Biograph as well.

In other words, New York was Hollywood before Hollywood was Hollywood, and even if the studios soon moved west (although Netflix is now headed back east with its ginormous new facility in Jersey), the city has remained an ideal backdrop for some of the greatest films ever made, many directed by native New Yorkers. Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Spike Lee, Woody Allen, Sidney Lumet and John Cassavetes were all either born or grew up in one of the five boroughs. They shot some of their best work there, eschewing L.A. sunshine for the vibrance and grit of the Big Apple, which has no equal anywhere on earth.

To celebrate the release of three true-blooded NYC movies — Club Kid, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York and Queens boy James Gray’s latest crime drama, Paper Tiger (in addition to fabulous doc Once Upon a Time in Harlem) — THR critics have compiled and ranked a list of the 25 best films taking place in the city. To say there were more options than we had room for is an understatement; we started with a “shortlist” of around 100 titles we love or like, then debated and whittled down from there.

We’d like to think you can trust us — two of us are NYC-born-and-raised, one from Manhattan, one from Queens; one of us is a longtime transplant (25 years in Chelsea and counting); and one of us is a Californian with deep family roots in Brooklyn.

Our list could have consisted exclusively of works by the directors name-checked three paragraphs above, so we decided to limit the count to one film per filmmaker. We excluded documentaries (Welfare, On the Bowery and Paris Is Burning would have staked strong claims). And while we adore the classics that have stood the test of time, we also wanted to make room for some more recent films that are plugged in to the city’s ever-evolving set of joys and challenges.

There are countless beloved mainstream hits featuring NYC in significant ways — Tootsie, Kramer vs. Kramer, Ghost, Splash, Big, When Harry Met Sally, Ghostbusters, Moonstruck, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, Working Girl, The Devil Wears Prada … we could go on. Those aren’t on our list, not because we don’t have affection for them (we do!), but because there were other titles we found more interesting, more distinctive in their use of the city as a setting and, in many cases, really a character in and of itself.

Some of our selections exude sheer energy. Others are marked by solitude and despair, chaos and murder, because New York is a town that has broken many a soul. Brooklyn-born Jay-Z may have said it best in “Empire State of Mind,” undoubtedly the NYC anthem of our time: “Eight million stories out there in the naked city; it’s a pity half of y’all won’t make it.”

That lyric references Jules Dassin’s 1948 noir The Naked City, one of 10 honorable mentions — films that could have made the list if we had finalized it another day. The others: All That Jazz, Escape From New York, Girlfriends, It Should Happen to You, Klute, Marty Supreme, Midnight Cowboy, Saturday Night Fever and Tiny Furniture.
And here are our 25 favorites.

- ‘A Thousand and One’ (2023) Set against the background of rapidly gentrifying 1990s New York — Brooklyn and Harlem in particular — debuting director A.V. Rockwell’s atmospherically charged Sundance winner gives Teyana Taylor a powerhouse showcase as Inez, a hair stylist and single mother fresh from a stint at Rikers and determined to get her 6-year-old boy out of the foster care system by whatever means necessary. Tracing a decade-plus in the marginalized lives of the mother and son, this moving character study watches Inez evolve from youthful bravado to hard-won self-possession. It also acutely observes painful rips in the fabric of New York City life for the economically disadvantaged and racial minorities, under the aggressive policies of Rudy Giuliani’s mayoral administration and on through the rampant development and discriminatory policing of the Bloomberg years.

- ‘Two Lovers’ (2008) Queens native James Gray made a trio of dark and eloquent outer-borough thrillers (Little Odessa, The Yards, We Own the Night) before switching gears with this romantic drama set in Brighton Beach — about as far as you can get from Manhattan without officially leaving New York City. The neighborhood’s windswept boardwalks and beaches are a perfect backdrop for a searing study of desire, in which a 30-something homebody (Joaquin Phoenix) is caught between two women: the nice local Jewish girl (Vinessa Shaw) that his parents want him to marry and the bewitching blond shiksa (Gwyneth Paltrow) that he spies on, Rear Window-style, from across the courtyard of their apartment building. With a mastery of tone and an eye for authentic detail, Gray turns the setup for a zany rom-com into an arrestingly intimate tale of longing anchored by three great performances. Set to the swooning arias of Puccini and Mascagni, the film takes on the emotional proportions of a small-scale Brooklyn opera by the final act.

- ‘Raising Victor Vargas’ (2002) Peter Sollett’s film is not only a radiant and delicate indie rom-com/coming-of-ager, in which a 16-year-old self-styled lothario (Victor Rasuk) learns to be worthy of his guarded, regally dignified crush (Judy Marte). It’s also an indelible portrait of the Lower East Side’s Dominican community that vividly captures the romantic glow and sweaty, sensual restlessness of summer in the city. From the cacophony of a public pool on a scorching day, to the cramped apartment where the protagonist spars with his siblings and grandma, to tender close-ups of the teenage characters seducing, rebuffing, confronting and then tentatively yielding to each other, it’s a modest movie that nonetheless brims with authentic New York swagger and soul.

- ‘Love Is Strange’ (2014) Revolving around a longtime gay couple (John Lithgow and Alfred Molina at their rumpled best) forced to sell their West Village apartment — and make less-than-ideal sleeping arrangements — when one of them is fired from his job, Ira Sachs’ understated heartbreaker is also an ode to the glories, aggravations and absurdities of life in the city. Lovingly shot and precisely observed, the film is imbued with a weary affection for a metropolis that’s changed in cruel ways but retains its inexorable pull on the eccentric, creative people who call it home — and go to often logic-defying lengths to do so. This is a movie that grasps the socioeconomic and logistical challenges of 21st century New York City (from daunting subsidized housing applications to the awkwardness of hosting guests in small apartments), folding them into an achingly wise story about loss, legacy and the imperfect ways we love one another, in life and beyond.

- ‘The Taking of Pelham One Two Three’ (1974) Made in an era when hijacking planes was a frequent occurrence, Joseph Sargent’s raw and riveting adaptation of a novel by John Godey (real name Morton Freedgood) revolves around an almost ridiculous premise: Bad guys hijack a subway car and threaten to kill one passenger per minute if the city doesn’t cough up $1 million in used bills within an hour. But the bad guys weren’t counting on the perspicacity of Transit Police Lieutenant Zachary Garber (Walter Matthau at his most deliciously Matthau-ian), among others. The dialogue’s abundant racism hasn’t aged well, and the command center’s walls of blinking Christmas light bulbs look absurdly quaint. But there’s real, palpable New York City grit in the movie — literally so, in the grimy tunnels used as locations standing in for the 28th Street station, where the titular 6 train stops while negotiations proceed over walkie-talkies between Matthau’s officer and the lead hijacker (a silken Robert Shaw). Watch and marvel at how fast the cops get across lower Manhattan traffic in order to hit the deadline.

- ‘Crossing Delancey’ (1988) Before the Lower East Side became an overpriced haven for hipsters, fashionistas and finance bros, its streets were lined with modest mom-and-pop businesses, many of them run by Jewish New Yorkers whose families had settled there at the turn of the 19th century. The last remnants of that Manhattan shtetl are lovingly portrayed in Joan Micklin Silver’s charming rom-com, which follows a bookshop employee (Amy Irving) and a pickle vendor (Peter Riegert) who can’t manage to hook up despite the pair of matchmaking bubbes trying to get them together. Adapted by Susan Sandler from her own play, the film captures a vibrant pre-Giuliani-era LES, in which working- and middle-class 30-somethings could still afford to pay the rent and, perhaps, fall in love. (Micklin Silver’s memorable debut, Hester Street, depicts the very same neighborhood back in 1896, when Jewish immigrants were first building a community that has all but disappeared by now.)

- ‘Frances Ha’ (2012) The fact that Noah Baumbach’s sharp, affectionate portrait of a very modern millennial woman (Greta Gerwig, also co-writer) is filmed in knowingly retro black-and-white is just one of its many charming contradictions, along with the way its sketch-comedy randomness builds to a perfect, cohesive ending. The monochrome palette also signifies that this is a particular kind of New York movie, harking back to screwball comedies and vintage Woody Allen. The city is a playground for the not-quite-grown-up heroine, and Baumbach and Gerwig punctuate Frances’ odyssey through it with title cards noting each address she comes to rest at — from the Prospect Park digs she starts out sharing with her bestie (Mickey Sumner) to the room in a Chinatown walk-up that she rents from more moneyed hipsters (Adam Driver, Michael Zegen) and beyond. Frances, a disorganized dancer struggling to find her footing in the performance world, literally prances and pirouettes through city streets in immaculately edited montages cut to pop classics like David Bowie’s “Modern Love.” You can’t help but fall in love with her at least a bit, as well as seeing how clearly Frances’ journey augurs Gerwig’s own eventual transition from ingenue to confident writer-director.

- ‘Margaret’ (2011) While Spike Lee’s The 25th Hour captured the rage and chaos of post-9/11 New York, the film that best channeled that period’s deep-seated malaise was Kenneth Lonergan’s maligned, underseen, then critically resurrected coming-of-age drama Margaret. For this epically intimate story of a teenage girl (played by a remarkable Anna Paquin) whose life is upended after she witnesses a fatal bus accident, Bronx-born Lonergan chose to stage the action on the Upper West Side, populating his film with well-educated, upper-middle-class Manhattanites facing the consequences of a gruesome death that could have perhaps been avoided. Shot in 2005 but then mired in legal and editing-room disputes for years, the film only hit theatres in 2011, by which time many New Yorkers had tried to put Sept. 11 behind them. More than a decade later, Margaret remains a rich and unsettling portrait of a time when the city suddenly lost its mojo — a sentiment echoed by the film’s 17-year-old heroine, who can’t shake off her sense of guilt, or the feeling that the world has suddenly fallen to pieces.

- ‘On the Town’ (1949) This exhilarating post-World War II MGM classic musical is packed with top-name talents both in front of and behind the camera. Co-star Gene Kelly choreographed it and co-directed with Stanley Donen, the first of many fruitful collabs between the two. Meanwhile, Kelly is one of a trio of male leads, alongside Frank Sinatra and Broadway star Jules Munshin, who play three sailors maximizing their fun on a 24-hour shore leave. The lads link up via a series of very New York encounters with three women (or “goyles”): a horny cab driver (Betty Garrett), an anthropologist (super-hoofer Ann Miller) and an aspiring model-dancer (Vera-Ellen). Kelly and Donen insisted that they film on location at least a little bit, which means the cityscape of 1949 Columbus Circle is on full display, as are other locales. The city’s eternally changing nature forms a key component of the plot, toasted in songs like “New York, New York” and “Come Up to My Place,” wherein Sinatra’s character keeps asking to visit long-gone tourist attractions. Now the then-modish spots they do visit seem just as antiquated and historical as the Hippodrome.

- ‘Desperately Seeking Susan’ (1985) A good chunk of Susan Seidelman’s delightful screwball mistaken-identity comedy unfolds in bougie Fort Lee, New Jersey. But the movie’s punk heart beats loudest in downtown New York, where Roberta, a bored housewife played by Rosanna Arquette, gets a bump on the head in Battery Park and becomes convinced she’s Susan, a bohemian scenester played by Madonna in her first and best major screen role. The pop star was still in her ascendance when the film was shot, her signature sense of style informing the character and becoming influential in ’80s fashion.

Locations featured include the former cult East Village vintage clothing store Love Saves the Day, the Bleecker Street Cinema and hot night spot Danceteria, while Washington Heights’ Audubon Ballroom stood in for fictional dive Magic Club (John Turturro plays the emcee). And Seidelman peppered the cast with downtown artists including Rockets Redglare, Annie Golden, John Lurie, Ann Magnuson and Shirley Stoler, and included a cameo from the adult triplets whose astonishing history was recounted in 2018 doc Three Identical Strangers. The Village Voice personal ads play a significant role, but MVP is Laurie Metcalf, in sublimely acerbic form as Roberta’s judgy sister-in-law.

- ‘Parting Glances’ (1986) This funny and achingly felt film is an artifact of the times, as one of the first to engage with AIDS and its impact (writer-director Bill Sherwood himself died of the disease four years after this, his only feature-length work, was released). But it’s also an admirably expansive snapshot of New York life on a broader scale. At the center, there’s a love triangle of sorts, between couple Michael (Richard Ganoung) and Robert (John Bloger) and Michael’s rock-musician ex Nick (an inconceivably young Steve Buscemi), who is HIV positive. The night before Michael leaves for a six-month work assignment in Africa, he and Robert attend a dinner party thrown by a married man and woman with their own sexual secrets and then another soiree downtown hosted by their artist friend (Kathy Kinney).

Sherwood and his cast limn these different milieus with the lightest of brushstrokes, bringing in a galaxy of vividly realized characters to populate the overlapping realms. This is a scruffy New York on the back foot in the era of Mayor Ed Koch, seething with anger and creativity that’s not yet been priced out by Wall Street money.

- ‘The Apartment’ (1960) A razor-sharp depiction of the kind of soul-crushing corporate culture and patriarchal entitlement that decades later would become the language of Mad Men, Billy Wilder’s evergreen 1960 romantic comedy is shot through with an expressive vein of melancholy. Jack Lemmon stars as Baxter, an insurance clerk who mistakenly believes career advancement will be his reward for handing over the key to his Upper West Side apartment multiple nights a week to married company executives in need of a place to carouse with their mistresses. Among them is Fred MacMurray’s head of personnel, whose affair with elevator operator Fran Kubelik — one of Shirley MacLaine’s most cherished performances — hits a bump when she attempts suicide with an overdose of sleeping pills in Baxter’s apartment. While much of the shoot took place on a Hollywood studio lot, this is a quintessential NYC movie, from its portrayal of the midcentury workplace grind to its tender insights into urban solitude, notably in Baxter’s line from the exquisite closing scene: “I used to live like Robinson Crusoe. I mean shipwrecked among 8 million people.”

- ‘Shadows’ (1959) What Jean-Luc Godard’s first feature, Breathless, was to New Wave-era Paris, John Cassavetes’ jazzy and downbeat Shadows was to Beat-era New York City. Both were made in the late ’50s and both broke directing norms, helping launch movements — the Nouvelle Vague in France, independent filmmaking in the U.S. — that changed the face of cinema. But whereas Godard’s film was a tongue-in-cheek homage to film noir and Hollywood, Cassavetes’ hip, deeply felt drama tackled tensions in a city divided along racial lines, even if it wasn’t technically segregated. The project stemmed from theater workshops the actor-director conducted with aspiring young talents in Manhattan, and that improvised approach lent it a striking realism compared to most American films of the time. Shadows still resonates powerfully through its honest portrait of three Black siblings — two of them light-skinned — trying to make it as musicians and writers in New York, which also means trying to overcome biases that were prevalent back then and haven’t yet been definitively erased.

- ‘The French Connection’ (1971) Big Apple realtors like to claim “location is everything” while selling overpriced, closet-sized apartments to folks dying to live in one of the city’s coveted ZIP codes. Such a tagline could also be applied to William Friedkin’s heart-pounding NYC cop thriller, which set a standard for action flicks that has rarely been equaled ever since the film triumphed at the box office and Oscars more than 50 years ago. Friedkin broke lots of rules — as well as several laws — during the shoot, sending stunt drivers down pedestrian-lined Brooklyn streets or bribing an MTA official for a mind-boggling subway chase toward the end of the movie. The result was a sustained game of cat and mouse that literally hits the ground running and never lets up until the credits roll. By then, we’ve raced through three out of five boroughs in a pursuit that feels both visceral and existential, making us question whether the movie’s obsessive pair of NYPD detectives (a never-better Gene Hackman and Roy Scheider) have been chasing phantoms the entire time.

- ‘The Godfather Part II’ (1974) Of the many qualities that contributed to the immense success of The Godfather, the authenticity of its setting is seldom mentioned. And yet unlike most mob movies before it, Francis Ford Coppola’s crime classic was shot entirely on location in New York City (except for sequences set in L.A. and Sicily), lending it a verisimilitude that made the travails of the Corleone clan feel both real and Shakespearean. Working with twice the budget and the full blessing of Paramount, Coppola went bigger and broader for the film’s brilliant sequel, hopping across several continents and time periods for a three-plus-hour epic set simultaneously in the 1950s and the 1920s. For the latter part, which traces the rise of Vito Corleone (Robert De Niro) from Sicilian immigrant to all-powerful Don, the director — along with DP Gordon Willis and production designer Dean Tavoularis — took several streets on Manhattan’s East Village through a time warp. The result was a stunning re-creation of classic Little Italy, as well as one of cinema’s great murder scenes.

- ‘All About Eve’ (1950) One of the all-time great movies about New York City as the nation’s vibrant theater hub, Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s delectably witty 1950 backstage drama left such a mark that calling someone “an Eve Harrington” — after the rapacious title character played by Anne Baxter — remains widely understood code for the kind of ruthlessly ambitious upstart who would step over your corpse to climb the ladder. Insinuating herself into the life of Broadway legend Margo Channing, one of Bette Davis’ defining roles, Eve poses as the meekest, most devoted of fans while plotting each maneuver that gets her closer to becoming a grand leading lady of the stage. She’s the ultimate protégée as predator. In the bright lights of Broadway, the stage-door alleys, sophisticated cocktail parties and self-congratulatory awards ceremonies, the film captures a moment when New York theater was considered the epicenter of American culture. For those of us who chose a career as critics, it also has the magnificent George Sanders as Addison DeWitt, a viper-tongued drama critic with make-or-break influence, whose perceptiveness allows him to see through Eve and exert control over her, even as he helps clear her path to stardom.

- ‘Sweet Smell of Success’ (1957) No movie nails the boozy, sophisticated and sinister ambiance of post-war midtown Manhattan like Alexander Mackendrick’s scathing New York noir. Inspired by the antics of legendary gossip columnist Walter Winchell and publicist Irving Hoffman (who wrote regularly for The Hollywood Reporter), this sharp-tongued look at journalism, celebrity, cutthroat competition and backstabbing New Yawkas features a murderers’ row of talent both in front of and behind the camera: stars Tony Curtis and Burt Lancaster; writers Clifford Odets and Ernest Lehman; a score by Elmer Bernstein; and cinematography by the great James Wong Howe, who captures the city — mostly Times Square and its surroundings — in vibrant chiaroscuro black-and-white. Famous for its machine gun one-liners, delivered like disses in a rap battle a few decades before New York would invent hip-hop, the film is best summed up by what Lancaster’s J.J. Hunsecker says before he climbs into a cab after another night of making and breaking people with the stroke of his pen: “I love this dirty town.”

- ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’ (1961) Is there a more iconic New York movie moment than Audrey Hepburn’s Holly Golightly, resplendent in a black Givenchy evening gown, stepping out of a yellow cab onto Fifth Avenue in the early morning hours, sipping takeout coffee and nibbling on a Danish while gazing at the window displays of the famed jewelry emporium? Blake Edwards’ 1961 film of the Truman Capote novel shows its age in Mickey Rooney’s cartoonish ethnic stereotype as Holly’s Japanese photographer neighbor Mr. Yunioshi. But it nonetheless remains an enchanting portrait — both cynically transactional and romantic — of the city as a sanctuary for a self-invented social butterfly living off wealthy men and a handsome young aspiring writer reliant on the “patronage” of a well-heeled woman (all hail Patricia Neal). The boozy party in Holly’s East 71st Street brownstone is one for the ages, eventually shut down by cops, but not before willowy model Mag Wildwood crashes drunkenly to the floor like a felled tree.

- ‘Taxi Driver’ (1976) Beyond Woody Allen, there’s perhaps no director more synonymous with the Big Apple than Martin Scorsese, who was born in Queens and grew up in Little Italy — a neighborhood that would shape him as an artist and serve as a backdrop for his earliest features. Several Scorsese flicks (Mean Streets, Raging Bull, After Hours, Goodfellas, The Age of Innocence) could easily have made our list, but the one that feels the most indelibly New York-y of them all is Taxi Driver. This may be because the movie nearly plays like a documentary, bringing to deeply unsettling life the grimy, horny, crime-ridden streets of Times Square, Hell’s Kitchen and other Manhattan enclaves during the dog days of the 1970s — when the Daily News famously quipped that President Gerald Ford had told the city to “drop dead.” But Taxi Driver is as much a N.Y. of the mind as it is of the eye, channeling the inner solitude of its antihero, Travis Bickle, a perennial outsider who lives by night in a town that never sleeps, viewing it as either fantasy or hellscape from the safety of his cab.

- ‘Rear Window’ (1954) Anyone who has lived in a Manhattan courtyard apartment block or has a clear view into homes across the street knows the unplanned voyeuristic pleasures of catching neighbors doing weird shit. In the case of Alfred Hitchcock’s riveting murder mystery — among the filmmaker’s very best — James Stewart’s Jeff is the observer, a photojournalist immobilized by a busted leg who becomes convinced that a lugubrious-looking traveling salesman in the building opposite his Greenwich Village home has killed his bedridden wife. Unable to convince his detective pal of foul play, Jeff enlists his wisecracking home nurse, Stella (peak Thelma Ritter), and glamorous model girlfriend, Lisa (Grace Kelly, dripping couture), in his amateur sleuthing. Shot almost entirely inside and through the windows of Jeff’s apartment, the movie makes masterful use of subjective camera. It also vividly evokes the kind of sweltering heat wave — without air-conditioning — that might make any New Yorker contemplate murder.

- ‘Dog Day Afternoon’ (1975) With the Godfather trilogy, The Panic in Needle Park, Serpico, Cruising and Carlito’s Way, among others, Al Pacino almost merits his own personal NYC movie ranking. Unforgettably paired here with John Cazale — one of just five features in the brief but blazing career of the great character actor, who died at 42 — they play Sonny and Sal, inexperienced crooks attempting in 1972 to rob the First Brooklyn Savings Bank, in part to pay for the gender-affirming surgery of Sonny’s lover, Leon. Sidney Lumet’s gritty thriller is steeped in the kind of unbearably tense, restless pressure-cooker atmosphere that’s typical of a scorching New York City summer. Based on a real-life heist-and-hostage situation, the film unfolds with both irreverent humor and searing compassion as the naïve would-be robbers watch the situation spiral out of control over the course of eight sweaty hours, becoming a media circus that builds to preordained tragedy at Kennedy airport. Standouts among the deep bench of outstanding supporting players are Charles Durning as the cops’ empathetic primary negotiator, Susan Peretz as Sonny’s emotionally volatile wife and Chris Sarandon as Leon, his eyes brimming with raw pain and exhaustion through a semi-improvised farewell phone call.

- ‘Rosemary’s Baby’ (1968) Many of us would love a spacious two-bedroom Upper West Side apartment — but maybe not the one where Mia Farrow’s title character, an expectant mother, lives with her husband, a theater actor struggling to get a foothold on Broadway (played with an incremental drip of subtle menace by John Cassavetes). Then there’s the neighbor (the inimitable Ruth Gordon), a seemingly benign eccentric who’s a tad too solicitous to be genuine. While the exteriors of Roman Polanski’s ageless psychological chiller were filmed at the famed Dakota Apartments facing Central Park, interiors were shot on Paramount soundstages in Los Angeles. But this enthrallingly insidious tale of women’s bodily autonomy, paranoia, lapsed-Catholic hysteria and Satanism lives and breathes residential Manhattan — namely, the unsettling side of apartment-building living, in close proximity to complete strangers. The film includes a nail-biting scene in which pregnant Rosemary wanders through oncoming midtown traffic in a daze, captured by Polanski himself with a handheld camera since no crewmembers were willing to risk their lives on a busy street not closed off for shooting.

- ‘West Side Story’ (1961) Robert Wise and Jerome Robbins’ outstanding, canonical movie musical — a grafting of Romeo and Juliet onto a pre-gentrification Upper West Side — improves on the 1957 Broadway hit right off the bat: The exhilaratingly staged “Prologue” and “Jet Song” use aerial footage of 1961 New York, coming down to land just north of the San Juan Hill area (now Lincoln Square), where the Sharks and Jets express their enmity with finger clicks and elegant jetés through eerily empty streets. The romantic tragedy at the film’s center is timeless, but this West Side Story also bottles up a stylized version of the period’s working-class New York culture and ethnic strife (Puerto Ricans versus mainland-born whites) with warmth, emotion and wit — the latter expressed particularly well through Stephen Sondheim’s droll lyrics for numbers like “Gee, Officer Krupke” (“I’m depraved on account I’m deprived!”). Even the soundstage sets evoke the stark lines and scruffy textures of that midcentury concrete landscape.

- ‘Annie Hall’ (1977) Does the still-contested cancellation of Woody Allen mean we can’t continue to love Annie Hall? Of all his movies, losing this one would hurt the most. Manhattan, as the name suggests, might be his most echt New York film, but the Allen character’s deeply icky romance with Mariel Hemingway’s high schooler is a punch-bowl turd you can’t ignore. Annie Hall, in which Allen’s Alvy Singer is in love with a woman nearly his own age — an indelible, never-more-charming Diane Keaton — is every bit as much a mash note to the city as it is to the characters’ relationship, which Alvy likens to a shark that must keep moving lest it die. The metropolis we see here, full of real residents’ favorite spots, is never at risk of ceasing its perpetual motion, its constant churn of characters and kookiness becoming part of the film’s laugh-laced, bittersweet momentum. Where else could you pull Marshall McLuhan out of nowhere to solve an argument in a line to buy movie tickets? Sure, it’s a gag, but it’s rooted in a deeper truth — that that sort of thing could only happen in New York. items.title: New ‘Hunger Games’ Movie on the Way? Lionsgate Film Chief Shares Latest on Franchise’s Future
items.description: The Hunger Games franchise has whetted appetites for more films, given the success of its latest title.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: The Hunger Games franchise has whetted appetites for more films, given the success of its latest title.

Lionsgate released The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping over the weekend, with the movie grossing a commanding $119.3 million from 4,018 North American locations to open in first place at the box office. The feature adaptation of author Suzanne Collins‘ 2025 prequel novel notched a better opening frame than the two most recent entries in the six-film series that kicked off with 2012’s Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games.

During a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter to celebrate the success of Sunrise on the Reaping, Lionsgate Motion Picture Group chair Adam Fogelson emphasizes that the studio would love to collaborate again with Collins on another project in the franchise. Director Francis Lawrence‘s latest movie stars Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, portrayed in the first four films by Woody Harrelson. The $150 million-budgeted feature is set 24 years before the events of Collins’ original 2008 book.

“We have complete respect for Suzanne as the architect,” Fogelson says. “I have told her that, if and when she is ready for me to read something else, I will drop everything and go anywhere in the world to get to read it. And I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call.”

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had a far bigger impact at the box office than the 2023 prequel film The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which starred Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer. Centering on the backstory for villainous President Snow — portrayed in the new movie by Ralph Fiennes — Songbirds and Snakes opened to $44 million domestically before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million.

“All of us understood that the story that Suzanne wanted to tell on Songbirds was a challenging one and that she was inspired to tell it,” Fogelson explains. “She did it in an extraordinary way. Clearly, the movie worked really well for the audience that saw it, but the origin story of the villain — with no grand Hunger Games spectacle at the center of the story — is a challenging ask.”

He continues, “But we are in very regular, very authentic dialogue with this giant fan base, and we had plenty of indications that a story like this one could relight the fire in an exceptional way. It’s why we chose to invest the way that we did, both in the production plan and in the casting. And so, we were confident that there were plenty of signals that, if you gave the audience a story like this one, they were ready to return in big numbers.”

As far as what a potential sequel movie could entail, Fogelson notes that the franchise’s supporters have offered suggestions about potentially fertile storytelling opportunities within the dystopian world. The Sunrise on the Reaping book sold 1.5 million copies in its first week, making it the biggest launch among Collins’ titles in the series.

“The fan base have definitely let us all know that there are other stories they would be thrilled to both read and watch,” says Fogelson. “We’ll see if any of them spark Suzanne to go ahead and write them.”

The exec pointed out that each major character reveal during the film’s New York premiere was met with feverish cheers from the audience. The new movie’s expansive cast includes Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke and Whitney Peak.

“It starts with the fact that Suzanne decided to tell a story that the audience had clearly been desperate for — anchored by a character that the audience both loved and was fascinated to learn more about — and then the filmmaking team and the production group at the studio partnered to cast and make an exceptional version of that story,” Fogelson says. “This is one of the most exceptionally put-together casts I’ve ever been a part of.”

The streaming business is in flux, and Black Friday deals can help explain it.

It’s not hyperbole: Netflix stock has been cut in half from its all-time high. Bundles are proliferating. And Skydance CEO David Ellison has made it clear that a merger of HBO Max and Paramount+ is a question of when, not if.

Black Friday streaming deals are an annual tradition at this point, but given the state of the business, they can also shed light on how the entertainment giants behind them are thinking about the future of their products.

Netflix, for example, is the lone streamer not offering a Black Friday deal (at least as of writing). In fact, it has never offered a discount, underscoring its place in the streaming ecosystem as the unambiguous market leader: There’s no need to entice subscribers with a discount when you already have the market hooked.

HBO Max and Paramount+ are offering very different types of deals, even as their parent company Skydance, is actively preparing for a discount bundle set for early next year, and with a full merger of the services following later on

HBO Max is offering an aggressive 50 percent discount on its ad-supported tier, charging $5.49 per month for a full year. Paramount+, meanwhile, is offering both its premium and standard plans for $2.99 per month, albeit only for the first two months.

With the bundle imminent and a merger coming (expect Paramount+’s tech stack to win out over HBO Max’s), the Black Friday deals are a last gasp before what is expected to be an aggressive discount campaign early next year.
The biggest new streamer to launch in the last year, Fox One, is offering a steep 75 percent discount, $5 for the first month, before it reverts back to $20 in month two.
Peacock, meanwhile, is offering generous discounts on both its select and premium plans, selling them for $2.99 and $8.99 per month for the first three months.

The Paramount+, Fox One and Peacock deals are, conspicuously, time-limited, and that timing coincides with the heart of the NFL season. Subscribers will get hooked right as the NFL playoffs begin, with NBC, CBS and Fox (and their respective streamers) all holding those rights.

Disney, which has been leaning into bundles, is offering a year of Disney+ and Hulu for $5 per month, hoping to get viewers hooked on its two entertainment platforms (ESPN is the other) ahead of a full sunset of the Hulu standalone app (it is expected to continue as a standalone service within Disney+).

Apple TV, which is still trying to gain the scale that many of the other services already have, is offering an aggressive discount of over 50 percent, selling six months of the services for $6.99 per month, down from its typical price of $14.99 per month.

And niche streamers are being more aggressive: Look at Starz, which is offering an astonishing deal: $11.99 for 12 months, putting the price at under $1 per month when buying the annual plan (a more modest discount is available on monthly plans), underscoring how it needs to gain scale, and fast. Crunchyroll, Sony’s anime-focused streamer, is also offering discounts of over 50 percent for six months, ranging from $3.99 for its base tier to $8.99 for its ultimate tier.

Streaming is in a new phase, where consolidation and bundles are the norm, and the status quo of today won’t be so in a year. It’s a world where creative discounting may be required, even if the long-term strategy prefers profits over subscriber progress.

And it’s a world where Netflix, the king of the crop, still feels as though it has no need to offer discounts of any sort. After all, when you have won the subscription streaming war, it’s better to keep those margins intact.

items.title: The Dark Side of the Moon Was the Brightest Part of 2026
items.description: Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. Tha
items.author: Brendan I Koerner
paragraphs: Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. That mindset is a big reason why the crew of NASA’s Artemis II was so oblivious to their celebrity as they circumnavigated the moon in April. It wasn’t until the seventh day of their nearly 10-day journey that they began to realize their exploits were causing a massive stir back home.

“We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew. “And that’s when we all heard, one after another: ‘Hey, this is really resonating on the planet in a way that you’re going to be shocked by.’”

Hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth. Nearly 150 million people had watched the mission’s key moments on NASA’s online platforms, which included feeds with near-constant access to the interior of the Orion spacecraft. The buzz around the mission harkened back to the glory days of American spaceflight, when people would gather around TV sets to marvel at astronauts floating outside their capsules or bounding around the moon.

The romantic spirit of the Artemis program’s long-term objective certainly helped: People are alive to the dream of a moon base that’s meant to serve our species’ idealistic aspirations rather than be a zillionaire’s private plaything. Artemis II supported that noble mission by putting the Orion’s life-support, navigation, and piloting systems through their paces. But fans were also drawn to the crew’s infectious energy. There was palpable chemistry between Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman, all of whom exuded pure joy and wonder as they dealt with the minutiae of life aboard a multibillion-dollar vehicle traveling as fast as 25,000 miles per hour.

“It was not a natural thing for us,” admits Hansen. “You have four type-A personalities who are willing to strap themselves to a rocket and go to the moon. We were doing stuff for the first time, and it was not uncommon for us to have four different opinions.” When the astronauts began to notice that interpersonal friction was becoming problematic during training, they enlisted the aid of professionals. During a September 2024 training trip to Iceland, the crew spent two extra days in conversations and teamwork exercises organized by Rick Rochelle, a renowned leadership guru. Once the Artemis II schedule was firmed up, the crew made a pact: Launch as friends, land as friends.

Their historic flight past the far side of the moon marked the apex of that friendship. They were more than 250,000 miles away from Earth. The planet looked no bigger than a fingernail sliver—“just this lifeboat hanging undisturbingly in the universe,” Koch would later say during the crew’s first public remarks after touchdown. “You look at it, and you just kind of shake your head,” says Hansen. “How can we do anything other than lift one another up and try to make life better for one another?”

Then that “tiny Earth” vanished as the spacecraft went behind the moon, and the crew spent 40 minutes out of radio contact. They carved out a few seconds to toast each other with maple cookies—carefully, to keep crumbs from floating free in zero gravity. They also selected a crater to name for Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll, who died of cancer in 2020. Soon after they reemerged from total isolation, they came together in an ecstatic, four-person embrace. “I knew right there that we were going to be bound together for life,” Wiseman says.

There were plenty of lowlights during the mission, too. Some lint got trapped in the primary urine vent line, Wiseman says, “so we had to go to a backup method of urination, which for the men wasn’t bad, but for the woman wasn’t great.” Another hiccup involved a smoke detector that erroneously went off while the spacecraft was still 80,000 miles from home, leading to 15 minutes of intense anxiety.

None of the Artemis II crew members are likely to return to space: Hansen, Glover, and Wiseman have all moved on from astronaut life, and Koch transitioned into a leadership role at NASA. Their new, less stressful lives should give them ample opportunity to cheer on Artemis III, tentatively scheduled to launch in summer 2027—an event that may once again remind us that we’re all part of a shared story far bigger than ourselves.
What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

items.title: 82 Best Beauty Gifts to Buy On Sale This Black Friday
