items.author: Jason Zengerle
paragraphs: One evening in early October, the Secretary of the Treasury, Scott Bessent, sat in an empty meeting room in the Hershey Lodge, a chocolate-themed resort and convention center in central Pennsylvania. He was waiting to speak to seventeen hundred people attending the annual dinner of the state’s chamber of commerce. The comedian Kevin Hart had warmed up the crowd with a story about a trip he’d taken to Dubai with the rapper Ludacris, during which he fed a sheikh’s pet liger. Now Bret Michaels, the lead singer of the glam-rock band Poison, was onstage recalling his teen-age years in nearby Mechanicsburg. If Bessent was concerned that these would be tough acts to follow, he didn’t let on. He has encountered plenty of new things as a Cabinet member in Donald Trump’s second Administration. “I’d never danced with Nicki Minaj before, either,” he said, referring to a TikTok video he had made with the hip-hop star a few months earlier.

Bessent would seem an unlikely denizen of Trumpworld. He amassed much of his fortune—he’s currently worth an estimated six hundred million dollars—as a money manager for the billionaire investor and liberal bogeyman George Soros, and he likes to say that had he not gone into finance he would have been a college professor. He and his husband, John Freeman, a former New York City prosecutor, have earned plaudits from preservationists for their painstaking restorations of historic homes, including a pink mansion overlooking Charleston Harbor, in Bessent’s home state of South Carolina. “What are the chances?” Sean Patrick Maloney, a former Democratic congressman from New York, who’s been friends with Bessent for decades, told me. “A gay guy with money loves beautiful homes!”

Some of Trump’s supporters were initially skeptical of Bessent; Elon Musk branded him a “business-as-usual choice” for Treasury Secretary. But, in the past two years, Bessent has become one of the most consequential figures in the Trump Administration. A former White House official called him “the smartest person in the Administration, by far.” Jason Miller, a longtime Trump adviser, said, of the Treasury Secretary, “There’s no other person whose name comes up more often for V.P. in ’28.” Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist, went further: “If Scott Bessent wanted it, I think he could be the Republican nominee in 2028.”

In the run-up to the midterms, Susie Wiles, then the White House chief of staff, oversaw an unofficial Cabinet competition that awarded each member points for visiting swing states and competitive congressional districts. Bessent was a top performer. Past Treasury Secretaries have generally tried to avoid overt politicking, but Bessent was, presumably, the member of the Administration best equipped to address the issue that most dogged Republicans this fall: the economy. He was also the most willing to hit the hustings on his own. Many Cabinet members racked up points by accompanying Trump on his campaign travels, often hitching a ride with the President on Air Force One. But Bessent, Wiles told me, “knows that’s not what’s most helpful. What’s most helpful is to go ahead and speak to the crowd and see voters. If you travel with the President, that doesn’t happen.”

That afternoon, Bessent had been in Harrisburg with Scott Perry, a six-term Republican congressman, to promote Trump Accounts—the tax-free investment plans for American children which were established in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill. “These children will be able to watch the Trump Accounts compound in real time, from a couple of thousand dollars in kindergarten to an estimated half a million by the age of retirement,” Bessent told a crowd in the rotunda of the state capitol. He called Perry, who, in 2020, had played a central role in attempting to overturn the results of the Presidential election, “one of the most effective members in all of Congress.”

Bessent, who is sixty-four, with combed-back silver hair and rimless glasses, is barrel-chested and six feet three. He carries himself in a way—throwing back his shoulders when he walks, sitting ramrod straight—that can make him seem even larger. One Trump adviser described him to me as “an alpha operator”; another said, “He’s very smooth, very patrician, all that, but he won’t take anybody’s crap.”

In Hershey, Bessent was eager to argue with anyone who thought that the economy was in bad shape. “The economy is good,” he told me. The only problem, he said, was energy prices, which were carrying over to interest rates—and the only reason energy prices were high was the war in Iran, which was both temporary and necessary. “Gas could be at at least six or eight dollars if the Iranians had a nuclear weapon,” he said. Otherwise, “there is no number in the economy that is bad. If I had a dashboard, there’s nothing on the dashboard that would worry me. It’s just the opposite. Things are accelerating.”

Bessent was aware that this was not the opinion of most Americans, who, polls showed, believed that not just gasoline but also grocery and health-care prices were too high and that wages were too low. The same polls showed that most Americans laid the blame for this situation on Trump, whose approval ratings were mired in the mid-thirties. “What I’m not going to do is say the American people don’t know how they feel,” Bessent told me. “But the data suggest otherwise. Like, there is revealed preference and stated preference.”

The revealed preference, Bessent said, could be found in data from credit-card companies, which showed strong consumer spending and no increase in delinquencies. Reports from retail banks like Bank of America, meanwhile, showed that “their working-class clients have more money coming into their accounts.” I asked what he and the rest of the Administration needed to do for revealed preference and stated preference to align. “I think it’s just time,” he said.

A day earlier, the Times had reported that a top official in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had admitted that his country’s economy was in dire straits. “Even the I.R.G.C. guy who was in charge of torturing and killing civilians came out and said that they’re fucked,” Bessent told me. In August, Bessent had seemed to take charge of the conflict in Iran by announcing Operation Economic Outcast, an aggressive sanctions campaign that replaced the military one. I asked Bessent what his timeline was for the Iranians to give up and accede to Trump’s demands. “I don’t have to have a timeline,” he said. “I just have to squeeze them more and more every day.”

Bessent pulled a pen from the inside pocket of his suit jacket and grabbed a paper napkin that was lying next to his four mobile phones on a table. “Do you remember what a decay curve looks like?” he asked. He drew a horizontal line that slanted downward before abruptly plummeting, a graphic representation of Hemingway’s old saw about how someone goes bankrupt: gradually, then suddenly. At some point, Bessent said, the situation in Iran would “go like that.” He jabbed a finger at the vertical line. “If you think about it, what happens on November 3rd?” he added, invoking the midterm elections. “The Iranians lose all their leverage.”

I said that that fact was probably cold comfort to the imperilled House Republicans he and Trump had been campaigning for—many of whom, including Perry, would go on to lose their jobs in the midterms. Bessent was unsympathetic. “Well, which is more important?” he shot back. “Getting rid of the Iranian threat? Or holding the House?”

The Treasury Secretary’s office occupies the southwest corner of the third floor of the Treasury Building. Previously, it provided an enviable view of the South Portico of the White House and the Washington Monument. But this fall the sights were largely obscured by a giant crane and other construction equipment, as crews worked twenty hours a day to build Trump’s ballroom. During one of my visits, Bessent gestured toward a window. “The big, beautiful ballroom is just big,” he said. “It’s not beautiful yet.”

Not that Bessent has much time to enjoy the view. In addition to overseeing the President’s economic policy and formulating and executing much of the Administration’s approach to Iran, he is largely responsible for managing the United States’ relationship with China. He ran the nominating process that resulted in Kevin Warsh’s appointment as Federal Reserve chairman, and, since the departure of Trump’s Senate-confirmed I.R.S. commissioner, who was made the Ambassador to Iceland in August, 2025, Bessent has been in charge of the tax agency. In September, Trump asked Bessent to take the lead on A.I. issues as the Administration’s new “Super Intelligence” czar. Bessent declined, and the job went instead to the director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton. Bessent took a seat on the Administration’s new Super Intelligence Force, under Clayton’s leadership. “The impact without the responsibility,” Bessent said, of his A.I. assignment. “It’s the D.C. way.”

Steven Mnuchin, the Treasury Secretary during the first Trump Administration, was viewed as a loyal and competent technocrat. But though he was well liked on Wall Street and on Capitol Hill, he could frustrate other Trump officials—including, at times, the President—with his refusal to pursue a broader, more aggressive agenda. “Mnuchin was not MAGA at all,” a former Treasury Department official told me. “It wasn’t that he didn’t agree with the President. He did. But, culturally, it was just not his ethos.” Bessent, on the other hand, has displayed none of Mnuchin’s reticence. Jamieson Greer, the U.S. Trade Representative, said, “In the past, when you might have had one of those neoliberal-style Treasury Secretaries, they would have been the first to be, like, ‘No, don’t do this. The sky is falling. The other countries will say mean things about us.’ Scott doesn’t care about other countries saying mean things about us.” Another Administration official told me, “He’s willing to get down in the mud and fight.”

Before Bessent’s confirmation hearings, a Trump official gave him a pep talk, saying, “Just remember, you know more about the economy in your pinkie than every single person who’s on that dais.” Bessent seems to have taken that advice to heart. During a Senate Finance Committee hearing, in June, he accused the Oregon senator Ron Wyden, the committee’s ranking Democrat, of criticizing Trump’s “anti-weaponization” fund—a $1.776-billion settlement with the I.R.S. which would have disbursed payments to Trump allies who claimed that the Biden Administration politically targeted them—“in an attempt to cover up his son having an investment meeting with Jeffrey Epstein.” This was a reference to Justice Department e-mails showing that Wyden’s son Adam had met with Epstein in 2016 to discuss Epstein potentially investing in his hedge fund, ADW Capital, which had a stake in the parent company of the strip-club chain Rick’s Cabaret. Bessent remarked, “Did your son and Jeffrey Epstein talk about pole dancing as he begged him for money using your limited credibility?”

Last month, in a letter responding to the Democratic Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, who had requested information about what the Trump Administration was doing to lower borrowing costs, Bessent wrote that the request “adds to the mounting body of evidence of your complete paucity of knowledge about financial markets” and offered Warren “a Foreign Exchange for Dummies tutorial.” Warren has long been a favorite target for Trump—he calls her Pocahontas, a mocking reference to a controversy over the extent of her Native American heritage. In a handwritten addendum, Bessent wished Warren “Happy Indigenous Peoples’ Day in advance.”

Civilians sometimes wind up in Bessent’s crosshairs. Last December, while the Secretary was having dinner at a Brazilian-Italian restaurant in Washington, hecklers from the left-wing group Code Pink showed up and accused him of being responsible for the deaths of six hundred thousand people around the world through the Administration’s economic sanctions. Bessent blamed the restaurant owner for not removing the protesters, and spit in his food before storming out. After a recent visit to a D.C. coffee bar with his teen-age daughter, he complained that customers seemed displeased by his presence. “There was some old hag who had to keep taking photos,” he recalled.

Even members of the Trump Administration have been subject to Bessent’s wrath. In the early days of Trump’s second term, when Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency were taking a chainsaw to the federal bureaucracy, Musk installed as acting I.R.S. commissioner a senior official who had publicly accused the Biden Administration of slow-walking an investigation into Hunter Biden’s taxes. Bessent confronted Musk about the move in the Oval Office. The two exchanged “fuck you”s before the argument spilled out into the hallway, where, according to Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, in their book “Regime Change,” Bessent taunted Musk about his unrealized expectations for DOGE. “Elon, are the savings two trillion?” Bessent prodded. “One trillion? A hundred billion?” In response, Musk threw a shoulder into Bessent’s torso.

A few months later, during a dinner for top Administration officials at Executive Branch, an exclusive Georgetown club co-founded by Donald Trump, Jr., Bessent objected to the presence of Bill Pulte, the Federal Housing Finance Agency director, who, Bessent had heard, was bad-mouthing him to the President. “Why the fuck are you talking to the President about me? Fuck you,” Bessent reportedly told Pulte. “I’m gonna punch you in your fucking face.” (Later, during testimony before the Senate Finance Committee, Bessent partially disputed this report, saying, “I actually said I was going to kick his ass.”)

Bessent maintains that the stories about his temper are overblown. “I would say that I have great equanimity, and that people are startled when you get the occasional rupture,” he told me. If anything, the episodes have raised his standing in the White House. “It’s so Trumpy,” a former Administration official said. “ ‘If you push me, I’ll push you back harder.’ ” Another Trump adviser regarded Bessent’s occasional outbursts as a sign of his integrity: “He’s a straight shooter. You don’t have to wonder, ‘Oh, what’s he really thinking? Is he trying to fuck me?’ He’s not gonna hide it. You know where you stand with him.”

Indeed, the Trump Administration has sought to take advantage of Bessent’s tough-guy approach. Last year, when a group of House Republicans from New Jersey and New York were threatening to derail Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill by holding out for a higher limit on the state and local tax deductions, the White House sent Bessent to Capitol Hill to take over the negotiations. At one point, he reached across the table and pulled the Administration’s term sheet toward him. “Guys, I think we’ve entered the valley of stupidity here,” he told the members. A former White House official recalled hearing from one of the holdouts that “everybody’s sphincter tightened at once.” The former official added, “It was just the absolute perfect negotiating gambit, and it went over in the room like a nuclear bomb.” After a brief break, the Republicans took the deal.

The first time I met with Bessent, in his office, he made a point of showing me the family Bible that he was sworn in on. It was printed in 1779, he noted, and some of it was in French. Bessent is a descendant of two of the most prominent and affluent families in the South Carolina Lowcountry. One set of his ancestors, the Horrys, were French Huguenots who arrived at Charles Towne Landing in 1680. The other set, the Bessents, came to South Carolina from Barbados in 1672, lured by the prospect of larger plantations. Bessent takes obvious pride in this heritage: Trump’s official statement announcing his nomination noted that Bessent was “a member of the French Huguenot Church of Charleston, where his family were founding members in the 1680s.” His Secret Service code name is Swamp Fox, the nickname of the South Carolina Revolutionary War hero Francis Marion, in whose unit Bessent’s great-great-great-great-great-grandfather fought.

Despite this prestigious lineage, Bessent’s childhood was not without hardship. The oldest of three children, he grew up in Little River, a small town north of Myrtle Beach. His mother, Barbara, was a fashionable chain-smoker with a fondness for vodka Martinis. His father, Homer, was a real-estate developer who claimed to own the largest collection of science-fiction books in the state. When Bessent was six years old, Homer, who had a drinking problem, contracted tuberculosis. That same year, Bessent’s great-grandmother died, and Homer and Barbara had to sell her home, where they and six generations of Bessents before them had lived. The family was forced to move into the guest cottage of Barbara’s parents’ house. “I had what I hoped then would be the worst year of my life,” Bessent told me.

Two years later, Homer’s real-estate business went bust, and he declared bankruptcy. Bessent, at the age of nine, started taking jobs—busing tables, putting up umbrellas at a beach club—to try to help with his family’s finances. “My dad made a lot of bad financial choices,” he said, during an appearance on Tucker Carlson’s podcast last year. “So when I was born—first six, seven, eight years—we were affluent. He lost everything. So I’ve seen what that’s like. I’ve seen both sides.”

Homer and Barbara couldn’t afford to send Bessent to boarding school, as they had originally planned, so he attended a public high school, where he played basketball, finished first in South Carolina’s Model U.N. competition, and, as a senior, was voted Most Likely to Succeed. He received an appointment to the Naval Academy but decided not to attend because of the military’s ban on gay service members. Instead, he went to Yale. In New Haven, Bessent leaned into his Southern identity, subjecting classmates to lectures about his home state’s palmetto-and-crescent-moon flag and marvelling in a Yale Daily News column that he “somehow survived” the city’s “lack of cornbread, grits, and stock car racing.” When Ronald Reagan visited New Haven a month before the 1980 Presidential election, Bessent was one of five students who showed up to meet him.

In his junior year, Bessent, who hoped to become a journalist, ran for editor-in-chief of the Daily News. “He was qualified,” an editor who participated in the election recalled. “But certainly no one’s first choice.” Bessent lost and was devastated by the outcome. “I kind of locked myself in my room for a month,” he later said. He walked away from the consolation prize of news editor and quit the paper, abandoning journalism altogether.

Instead, he set his sights on Wall Street—specifically money management, which he thought would offer a relatively gay-friendly path in finance. In trading or investment banking, he explained, firms controlled who got which accounts and the sizes of employees’ annual bonuses. “I’d actually heard what friends of mine said: ‘Oh, well, you didn’t think you were going to get the same bonus as Bob? He has a family,’ ” Bessent told me. But, in money management, “it’s just your scorecard.”

In November, 1991, Bessent was a few months into a job as an analyst in the New York office of Soros Fund Management when the hedge fund’s chief investment officer, Stanley Druckenmiller, called him into his office. S.F.M.’s European portfolio manager in London had made a bad bet on some German stocks, and George Soros was going to fire him. Would Bessent be willing to go to London and babysit the European portfolio? “Just stay there until we find a high-powered European guy to take over,” Bessent recalled Druckenmiller telling him. Three days later, Bessent was in England. The firm put him up in the mother-in-law flat attached to Soros’s house in Onslow Gardens, which came with the perk of being able to use Soros’s domestic staff.

As part of his new remit, Bessent studied the United Kingdom’s volatile housing sector, which had just experienced a boom in homeownership thanks to Margaret Thatcher’s privatization program. But, unlike in the U.S., almost all home mortgages in the U.K. had adjustable rates. After a few months in London, Bessent learned that Druckenmiller was considering shorting the pound—borrowing large quantities of it to purchase other currencies in the hope that a swing in exchange rates would yield a profit. He told Druckenmiller that the U.K.’s adjustable-rate mortgages would make it politically difficult for the Bank of England to deter currency speculators; raising interest rates to make short selling more expensive would also increase mortgage costs for millions of British homeowners. As Bessent later explained, “The Bank of England could punish us and raise rates up to fifteen per cent to try to make us go away, but they would be bankrupting all the new Tory homeowners who they needed to vote for them.”

Soros liked the idea of shorting the pound so much that S.F.M. invested ten billion dollars in the position. On September 16th, a day that came to be known in England as Black Wednesday, the bet paid off: after a series of interest-rate hikes failed to stabilize the pound, the British Prime Minister, John Major, pulled the currency out of the European exchange. S.F.M. made around a billion dollars in profit. “Scott gave Stan the conviction to do it, and then George pushed Stan to get bigger,” Michael Oliver Weinberg, a Soros portfolio manager, said. “It was a great synergy.” After Black Wednesday, Soros and Druckenmiller left the firm’s European portfolio in Bessent’s hands. “Scott was like a son to them,” Weinberg said.

Although S.F.M. was becoming one of the world’s most successful hedge funds—between 1989 and 1998, its assets grew from a billion dollars to twenty-two billion dollars—the firm’s offices near Carnegie Hall remained spartan, with duct tape holding together patches of pink carpeting. Soros himself promoted a culture of thrift, flying commercial, even to Russia on Aeroflot. He was deeply influenced by the philosopher Karl Popper—who posited, among other things, that a scientific theory cannot be proven with absolute certainty—and viewed investing as more of an intellectual endeavor than a financial one. He also believed that if you were confident in a position it was your duty to be as aggressive as possible. One of the fund’s mottoes was “It takes courage to be a pig.”

Years later, during a series of interviews with the journalist Chrystia Freeland, who was writing a biography of Soros, Bessent marvelled at Soros’s work ethic, his genius, and his attunement to the market. “George is like a big cat, like a panther walking through the jungle,” he told Freeland. “And he can hear every twig.” But it wasn’t Bessent’s appreciation of Soros’s financial acumen that stood out. As Freeland told me, “Of all the people I talked to about George, Scott was one of the most positive about his human characteristics. If ten is ‘This guy is Mother Teresa’ and one is ‘This guy is Mephistopheles,’ Scott was an eight—and a lot of people were fours.”

Since entering the Trump Administration, however, Bessent hasn’t been so effusive about his old boss. At this year’s World Economic Forum, in Davos, he took a gratuitous shot at Soros’s son Alex, who now handles his father’s philanthropic and political efforts. Alex had been photographed in Davos with the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, who, during a speech accusing European leaders of failing to stand up to Trump, had brandished a pair of kneepads bearing an ersatz Trump signature. In a press conference, Bessent said that Newsom was in Davos “with his billionaire sugar daddy Alex Soros” and quipped, “If he brought the kneepads, maybe that was for his meeting with Alex Soros.” Later, in an off-the-record comment to a reporter, he joked that Newsom’s kneepads still had Soros’s “cum” on them.

Bessent told me that, when he started at S.F.M., George Soros’s political views weren’t necessarily out of line with his own. The animating idea of Soros’s philanthropic group, the Open Society Foundations, Bessent said, “was to bring down the Iron Curtain. And it worked.” But during George W. Bush’s Presidency their politics began to diverge. “A lot of people have asked me, ‘When did George get so political?’ ” Bessent said. “I think something snapped under Dubya, because I remember at one point, when it was Dubya versus Kerry, he said, ‘Oh, I think I should go to Ohio to campaign for Kerry.’ I said, ‘George, I would just send more money.’ I would not say that self-realization is his strong suit.”

Bessent also claimed that the press had overstated his relationship with Soros, saying that he’d always been closer to Druckenmiller. “Stan was kind of like the Pope,” he said. “You didn’t really speak with George.” Bessent left S.F.M. for a time in the two-thousands to launch his own hedge fund and to teach economic history at Yale, but he returned to S.F.M., as chief investment officer, in 2011. He recalled telling Soros, “I’m going to do what I want to do, and, if the performance is bad or you’re not happy with me, you can fire me, but you can’t tell me what to do in the portfolio.”

By 2015, Bessent said, Soros “was starting to renege on his word,” letting his political views influence financial decisions, such as trying to get Bessent to take positions designed to protect the eurozone. “I think it’s a real challenge when you get older to be able to maintain a positive attitude,” Bessent said. “So he had gone into doomerism.” That same year, Bessent announced that he was leaving S.F.M. and starting his own hedge fund, Key Square Group, with a two-billion-dollar investment from Soros. Bessent said that he and Soros haven’t spoken in a decade.

Last year, at the Allen & Company Sun Valley Conference, an annual gathering of the world’s business élite, in Idaho, Bessent was asked to compare his current boss with his old one. He said that Soros and Trump were “the same animal”—both had an “incredible propensity to take risks” and “incredible survival skills.” When I asked him the same question, earlier this fall, he was less equivocal. “To George, everybody’s a stock,” Bessent told me. “You’re either going up or down. Not very sentimental.” He went on, “The President has much more empathy than George. The President is friends with people for twenty or thirty or sixty years.”

In the spring of 2023, Jason Miller, the longtime Trump adviser, got a call from Steve Bannon. “Steve just said, ‘Hey, there’s this guy you’ve got to meet. He’s going to be the absolute perfect Secretary of Treasury for the President,’ ” Miller recalled. “That’s how he introduced Scott.”

Bessent wasn’t obvious MAGA material. During the 2000 Presidential campaign, he and his partner at the time, Will Trinkle, hosted a fund-raiser for Al Gore at their home in East Hampton. “Our issue was equality, and Democrats were best on that issue,” Trinkle said. After Bessent and Trinkle broke up, in 2004, Bessent tilted his political giving toward the G.O.P., supporting establishment Republicans, including Paul Ryan and Mitch McConnell. During the 2016 G.O.P. Presidential primary, he gave two hundred thousand dollars to the super PAC of the anti-Trump Ohio governor, John Kasich. (The donation prompted Ted Cruz’s super PAC to run attack ads accusing Kasich of accepting “hundreds of thousands of dollars from George Soros.”)

For many years, Bessent’s economic views were those of a conventional Wall Street Republican. He told Steven Drobny, the author of the 2006 book “Inside the House of Money,” that “no one in the United States realized what a favor Mexico was doing us” with NAFTA by providing the U.S. with “cheap labor.” But Bessent told me that in the two-thousands he began to depart from the Wall Street consensus about who was—and wasn’t—benefitting from free trade. On trips back to South Carolina, he said, he was “seeing the whole textile industry get wiped out,” while on visits to China he’d hear about new manufacturing hubs with nicknames like Sock City and Underwear City. He recalled learning at the Shanghai Auto Show that a Chinese car company had produced “an exact copy” of a Buick model that was popular in China and thinking, “G.M.’s fucked.”

After reading Charles Murray’s 2012 book, “Coming Apart: The State of White America, 1960-2010,” which argued that the education gap between white élites and white working-class Americans amounted to a kind of caste system, Bessent became concerned about the “self-sorting at Ivy League schools.” Two Uber rides he and his husband took in the summer of 2016, to and from an expensive Charleston restaurant, were also influential. Both drivers, a groundskeeper at the Citadel and an elementary-school teacher, told Bessent that they were driving for Uber because they couldn’t “make ends meet.” Trump had just secured the Republican Presidential nomination, and Bessent began to think that he had a real chance of winning. “And then, also, Brexit happened,” he said. “I sensed a big mood shift in the country.”

After the election, Bessent adjusted his stock positions in the expectation that the market would climb during Trump’s tenure, which, after a brief dip, it did. Soros, by contrast, bet on a sustained market plunge and reportedly lost nearly a billion dollars in the weeks after Trump’s victory. During the transition, Bessent donated a million dollars to Trump’s inaugural committee.

Less than a year later, Bannon—who’d recently been fired from the White House after a brief, tumultuous tenure as Trump’s chief strategist—was giving a paid speech at a conference in Hong Kong. At the event’s dinner, he struck up a conversation with a man sitting beside him. It was Bessent, who

items.title: The Death Penalty Is on Life Support
items.description: Earlier this month, California governor Gavin Newsom dramatically announced he was commuting all death sentences in the state (548 of them) to life without the possibility of parole. Opposition to the death penalty was by no means a new stance for Newsom, and
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Earlier this month, California governor Gavin Newsom dramatically announced he was commuting all death sentences in the state (548 of them) to life without the possibility of parole. Opposition to the death penalty was by no means a new stance for Newsom, and as he pointed out in his announcement, the state has observed a “de facto moratorium on executions … since 2006, the last year California executed anyone.” But since death sentences have continued, California has “the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.” Newsom acknowledged the legislature has the exclusive power to entirely abolish capital punishment in California, but his mass commutation made that step a lot more likely than before.
Predictably, Donald Trump seized on Newsom’s action in one of his first domestic-policy pronouncements following his party’s historic midterm election debacle, as CNN reported:
During a speech at the Justice Department, Trump called it “one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen” and denounced the prisoners as “Newsom’s monsters.”

“What happened to you, what happened to all of us, should not be allowed to stand,” Trump said to several families of inmates’ victims who were in attendance. “Newsom, a terrible governor in so many other ways, came along and stole away the only closure those families might ever have.”

Nobody, but nobody, loves old-school law-and-order politics as much as the 47th president does, particularly when he’s offered a chance to bash one of his political enemies. He was probably delighted to get back onto the firm ground of retributive justice after floundering so badly in recent months in responding to Americans’ concerns over living costs, artificial intelligence, and his war of choice against Iran. And he’s doubtless aware that keeping and selectively imposing the death penalty has been a political winner for conservatives for many years and a stumbling block for liberals.
But is it still? Perhaps not so much anymore. Gallup reported just a few days after Newsom’s mass commutation:

Forty-nine percent of U.S. adults are in favor of the death penalty for convicted murderers, and 45% are opposed. While statistically similar to last year’s 52%, the latest update marks the first time support has been below the majority level since 1971, when it was also at 49%. The last time support was lower than now was in 1966, when a record-low 42% favored the death penalty. The high point for support was 80% in 1994.
As with so many other issues, attitudes toward capital punishment are polarized by partisan affiliation, but a downward trend in support for the death penalty is universal:
Today, 28% of Democrats are in favor of the death penalty, a decline of 28 percentage points from 2000 and 47 points from their 1994 record high.
Among independents, the change has been smaller, including drops of 18 points since 2000 and 29 points since 1994, to 50% today.

Republicans’ opinions of the death penalty have been more stable over time, although the 73% in favor this year is one of the lowest Gallup has measured for the group. Typically, Republican support has been around 80% since the 1990s.

Why is support for capital punishment declining? There are two very notable reasons. America is in the midst of a historic decline in violent-crime rates (after a brief upward blip during the COVID-19 pandemic). It’s no coincidence that the spike in support for the death penalty coincided with a historic rise in crime rates. But a second reason is growing public awareness that executions are administered unevenly, even arbitrarily, and to a distressing extent ineffectively. The last big drop in support for the death penalty, in the 1960s, was in part driven by publicity over the vast racial and economic disparities in who did and didn’t face the executioner, a reality that led the U.S. Supreme Court in 1972 to suspend capital punishment until state laws and sentencing guidelines had been reformed (the suspension was lifted four years later). Similarly, bad publicity over botched executions via lethal injection (notably the recent failure by Tennessee to put Christa Pike to death) and wildly varying rates of executions in different jurisdictions has troubled many Americans who might in theory support capital punishment as a last resort in cases of heinous crimes. As The Wall Street Journal reported last month, the death penalty has been a regional phenomenon for a long time:
Most executions since 1977 have occurred in the South. Six states — Texas, Florida, Oklahoma, Virginia, Missouri and Alabama — account for 70% of the 1,685 executions in that span.
Virginia and 10 others states have abolished the death penalty in the past 20 years, and 32 states haven’t executed anyone in at least a decade.

It may not be entirely coincidental that Newsom’s mass commutation occurred smack in the middle of a national backlash (even in the Deep South) to Trump’s policies and the atavistic cultural views he has championed. Newsom is widely expected to run for president in 2028; his position on capital punishment isn’t especially controversial among the Democrats who may determine his fate in the presidential primaries. And support for the death penalty may no longer be a cultural validator for Democrats, as it was in 1992 when then-Governor Bill Clinton proceeded with the execution of Ricky Ray Rector in the midst of a successful presidential campaign, helping prove he was a “different kind of Democrat.” Indeed, religion-based objections to capital punishment (the Catholic Church, for example, has opposed it categorically since 2017) could give opposition to the practice a tinge of moral rigor.

So Trump may be doing Newsom a favor by demagoguing the issue so visibly just as the 2028 circus is beginning. More generally, if crime rates keep going down, the death penalty may soon be on life support.

items.title: Your Favorite Economist’s Favorite Economist
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Alex Bronzini-Vender
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Sometime in 2009, a few chapters of an unpublished book began making the rounds inside the Treasury Department. The small group coordinating the government’s emergency response was putting in 80-hour weeks, their inboxes stuffed with postmortems of the financial crisis. “You didn’t have time to read everything,” says Morgan Ricks, who was on that team. Most of what he did manage to look at proved unhelpful, offering only “a vague conception of systemic risk.” But these chapters were different. “You would read them,” Ricks tells me, “and a light bulb would go off.”

Their author was Perry Mehrling, then an economics professor at Barnard College. He rarely published in the profession’s top journals, spending much of his career studying the history of economics — a specialty that, as Ricks puts it, has never held “a central place in the pantheon of economic thought.” In fact, when Mehrling’s work first landed in his inbox, Ricks “had never heard his name.” But when Mehrling died last month at 67, he’d become famous in his own way, mourned by traders and regulators, financial journalists and podcasters, democratic socialists and unapologetic capitalists alike. Tyler Cowen, the libertarian economist, said he was a “big fan” of Mehrling’s work; the left-leaning Columbia historian Adam Tooze praised Mehrling’s “exceptional clarity”; The Economist suggested the professor’s unfinished manuscript might join the “shelf of monetary classics.”

What did this unlikely coalition see in Mehrling? Mostly, a usable picture of the economy, one the late professor called the “Money View.” Mehrling thought the standard approaches in both academic economics and finance were missing something fundamental. Economists, he said, saw “a world of commodity production and exchange,” of goods being made and traded. Theorists of finance saw “a world of asset pricing,” of figuring out what stocks and bonds are worth. Both assumed traders would never struggle to access cash, treating money as a convenient medium of exchange but nothing more. Mehrling’s “Money View” began from a different premise: The most important action in the economy isn’t the flow of goods or the pricing of assets, but everyone’s daily, existential struggle to pay their bills on time.

Before the 2008 crash, economists had largely lost interest in how actual financial institutions worked, preferring to build models of the economy from mathematical first principles instead. The resulting equations were internally consistent, sure, but built on assumptions so extreme that they had little to say about how people acted in the real world. When the crash came, it blindsided most of the discipline. But not Mehrling. “He was way ahead of the economics profession,” Ricks says, “and he understood it better than virtually any policymakers, including those at the Federal Reserve.”

Mehrling had spent his career stubbornly ignoring the trends in his field. Instead, he studied markets like an anthropologist. An undergraduate in one of Mehrling’s courses might be assigned the Financial Times, or asked to read Marcia Stigum’s The Money Market, the thick handbook traders kept on their desks. “In some sense,” he told his students, “what this course is all about is teaching you to read the Financial Times … and translate it into English.”

Studying how banks and businesses actually operated gave Mehrling a very different view of the financial system. We tend to picture the global economy as a collection of national economies, each churning out piles of goods and services. As Mehrling saw it, though, the economy isn’t just about physical stuff, and it certainly isn’t sliced up by anything as quaint as national borders. It’s better understood as a single web of payments and IOUs crisscrossing the world with little regard for where one country ends and another begins. Some of these IOUs are relatively small: Your rent comes due once a month; your boss has to make payroll every two weeks. On a vastly larger scale, banks fund themselves partly by borrowing huge sums overnight. Each morning they have to pay those sums back, usually by taking out new loans. Every day, the system has to settle up; usually, it does.

When the economy is humming along, people “will take all kinds of funny pieces of paper as payment,” says Thomas Ferguson, a longtime friend of Mehrling’s and the research director at the Institute for New Economic Thinking (INET), which supported his work. Usually, nobody thinks about it. During periods of panic, though, everyone does. And what Mehrling called the “hierarchy of money” — the pecking order of which promises count as money and to what extent — suddenly becomes all-important.

This is roughly what happened during the financial crisis. Over the previous three decades, a huge market for short-term IOUs had taken hold, spanning overnight loans, short-term corporate debt, and shares in money-market funds. Investors treated these IOUs as virtually as good as bank deposits. Still, many of those instruments depended, one way or another, on home mortgages. When banks borrowed cash overnight, for instance, they sometimes handed over bonds made of bad housing debt as a guarantee that they would pay it back. Firms like Lehman Brothers, loaded up on subprime home loans, issued other IOUs, like corporate debt. Once homeowners began defaulting, short-term lenders couldn’t tell which firms were still sound, so they stopped lending to all of them. That was a disaster for the big banks, which relied on freshly borrowed money to meet their obligations each day. When they tried to sell assets to raise cash — scrambling up the “hierarchy of money”— they discovered that everyone else was doing the same. Prices plunged, nearly bringing down the financial system.

When subprime mortgage losses first began roiling the financial system in 2007, the Federal Reserve mostly lent cash to struggling banks against their shaky assets. But the problem, as Mehrling saw it, was that no one would buy enough of those IOUs, so their prices kept falling. The central bank, Mehrling believed, would need to become the “dealer of last resort,” stepping in as the buyer itself. After Lehman collapsed in 2008, the Fed took up exactly this role, buying up troubled securities in bulk — and not just at home. European megabanks had bought the same shaky mortgage bonds with borrowed money, so the Fed needed to save them, too. After all, the system Mehrling described didn’t look like a classroom globe, neatly divided into countries with their own currencies, GDPs, and trade balances. It looked more like the route map in the back of an inflight magazine, with arcs of dollar debt and credit looping from hub to hub.

Mehrling had a knack for making complicated things sound simple. Loans, he insisted, are promises like any other. “The commitments we make to one another,” he wrote, “form the very fabric of the society in which we live.” Marriage is like that, he added, and so is credit. Mehrling, as Ferguson puts it, “was casting a lot of light on how markets were actually working.” Ricks, for one, came away from Mehrling with a new way of thinking about his job. “It wasn’t until I had read Perry’s work,” he tells me, “that I was able to say: Financial instability is a problem of monetary system design.”

In hindsight, all this sounds rather strange. Mainstream economists had been working with models that left out finance? A few now claim they never did. But this is mostly “revisionist history,” Ricks says. Mehrling’s ideas have become so widely accepted that “some people who have been around for a long time pretend that they had understood this all along.” Whether they cite him directly or not, central bankers and newsletter writers alike now see the economy the way Mehrling did. “Once you start thinking that way,” says J.W. Mason, an economist at John Jay College, “it’s kind of everywhere. It’s all around you.”

Mehrling graduated from Harvard in 1981, at the tail end of another revolution in macroeconomics. Out of practical necessity, an older generation of economists had paid close attention to banks and money markets. In the 1960s, the Fed didn’t simply announce a target for short-term interest rates, as it does today. Instead, it bought and sold government securities to control how much cash banks had on hand to lend and capped the interest they could pay depositors. How those moves affected the economy depended upon how savers responded to them, so economists needed to pay close attention to their behavior. That approach worked well enough until the 1970s, when the economy stopped behaving the way the conventional models said it should.

Prices would rise when unemployment fell, economists thought, because more spenders were competing for the same pile of goods. After the 1973 oil embargo, though, inflation and joblessness surged at the same time, and the formulas economists used to forecast the economy no longer worked. According to the University of Chicago economist Robert Lucas, these old equations shared a fatal flaw: Models built on past data couldn’t anticipate how people would change their behavior once they came to expect inflation.

The discipline chose to start from scratch. Casting aside the mess of real-world observation, Lucas persuaded much of the field to rebuild macroeconomics from mathematical first principles, borrowing a framework devised in the 1950s by the economists Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu. “Lucas’s critiques of the existing models were very good,” the longtime Bank of England adviser Charles Goodhart tells me. But the assumptions he put in their place, Goodhart says, “were faulty.” They’ve done “a lot of damage.”

The profession long claimed that a market economy could coordinate itself since prices would adjust until every good offered for sale could find a willing buyer. In the 1950s, Arrow and Debreu proved mathematically that such a set of prices could exist. The world they modeled, though, was a bizarre one. Every economic contract across all of time would be struck on day one, covering every conceivable contingency (say, a binding agreement to buy an umbrella next Tuesday if it rains). Every promise, moreover, would be honored to the letter.

Arrow himself, Goodhart tells me, “would never actually have believed that this was realistic.” For one, this was a world with no need for cash, which people hold because they can’t be sure strangers will honor their IOUs. As the British economist Frank Hahn complained in a 1981 lecture, the “best developed model of the economy” couldn’t explain why money existed at all. Lucas’s approach caught on anyway, Goodhart says, “because it was technically elegant, because it was mathematically attractive, and because it was new.”

Mehrling learned the new math as well as anyone. Before beginning his doctorate, he earned a master’s with distinction in econometrics and mathematical economics from the London School of Economics. But it was at LSE, he recalled in a 2022 interview, that the economist Douglas Gale mentioned that all of this meant “money” remained “a big unsolved problem in economics.” (In models like these, Goodhart and three coauthors wrote in 2016, “the whole financial sector could be eliminated.”)

Back at Harvard for his Ph.D., Mehrling used those questions to begin piecing together what he’d later call the Money View. Hunting for an alternative to the reigning orthodoxies, Mehrling turned to an older tradition of thinkers, from Walter Bagehot to Hyman Minsky, who recognized that capitalism runs on credit, and that credit is inherently unstable. In a modern economy, banks, businesses, and households all have bills coming due on a fixed schedule — and when credit dries up without warning, they can’t just borrow more to cover the tab. Where Arrow and Debreu had assumed promises would always be kept, Mehrling insisted that even the most solemn vows could be violated. That was what made his work so useful. Once you accept that “people don’t know everything about everything,” Goodhart says, “one’s access to money actually becomes enormously important.”

Mehrling joined the faculty at Barnard in 1987. In Morningside Heights, his insistence on the “money problem” didn’t win him many allies. Columbia’s monetary economists “weren’t comfortable having him in their seminars,” Ferguson says. “Most of the profession,” he says, “really didn’t like him.” Mehrling “recognized he was quite isolated.” He complained about it, Ferguson tells me, “but he didn’t think he was missing a lot either.” In any case, Mehrling didn’t think of himself as a rebel. He considered himself an heir to Charles Kindleberger, a longtime MIT professor and the onetime president of the American Economic Association. “He couldn’t quite conceptualize himself as an outsider,” says Nathan Tankus, who was friendly with Mehrling and is the author of the popular left-wing finance newsletter Notes on the Crises.

Mehrling mostly kept to his books, writing intellectual biographies of earlier economists. “The only allies he had,” says Jay Pocklington, who runs INET’s Young Scholars Initiative and worked alongside Mehrling for more than a decade, “were the dead people.” In his taped Barnard lectures, though, Mehrling comes across as anything but aggrieved. “I don’t feel alone at all,” he once assured his students, adding that he had “all these ancestors” — the economists and bankers he’d written about. Standing up to “the bullying that’s so commonplace in economics” took “a sense of self-respect and toughness,” Tooze tells me; Mehrling was “a prideful man in a very positive sense.” In person, that pride could take some getting used to. “It was always the Perry Show,” Mason tells me. Some found that off-putting, but Mason never minded. “It was so honest,” Mason says. “Perry was just so delighted with whatever idea he’d come up with.”

After the financial crisis hit, Mehrling had even less reason to care about his colleagues uptown. Downtown, traders began reading him; in Washington, so did officials at the Treasury. In his 50s, Mehrling went from the margins of the profession to the center of the action, writing for the Financial Times, presenting his work to the Fed, and eventually consulting for Credit Suisse and BlackRock. Years later, in his 2018 history of the crisis, Crashed, Tooze would credit Mehrling as perhaps the first outside commentator to grasp the significance of the Fed’s emergency dollar loans to foreign central banks.

There’s an old line, usually credited to Brian Eno, that hardly anyone bought the first Velvet Underground album but everyone who did started a band. “Perry is a very apt equivalent to that in financial economics,” says Joe Weisenthal, a cohost of Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast. In 2013, Columbia and INET put Merhling’s Barnard course, Economics of Money and Banking, online for free. On Columbia’s YouTube channel, the first installment stands at about 40,000 views. Some banks now assign the course to junior hires, says Pocklington, and some central banks use it to train staff. Wall Street strategists apply Mehrling’s ideas, and so do socialist bloggers. “Regardless of what your point of view is,” Weisenthal says, “Perry taught a lot of people to pay attention to these interlocking webs of financial obligations.” He was “the hidden king,” Tooze says, of the “monetary theory underground.”

Mehrling was no radical. He was more interested in how the system worked, Pocklington tells me, than in regulating or changing it. Even so, many of Mehrling’s most devoted followers were on the left. For those approaching the economy from a “left-wing or radical position,” Tooze tells me, Mehrling’s appeal “was the sense, really, that when you were listening to him, you were actually hearing how the system worked.” There’s a running joke that socialists’ favorite newspaper is the Financial Times, because the investors who read it concur that personality politics are mostly theater, and money and markets run the world. As Tankus puts it to me, encountering Mehrling “was like, what if the Financial Times part of the ‘socialists read the Financial Times’ meme were a real person and a serious scholar?” Mehrling’s loyal following among bankers and traders could have been a liability in radical circles. In fact, Tooze says, “the endorsement by Wall Street made him all the more interesting to people on the left.”

Mehrling mostly left his students to draw their own conclusions. As he argued, the financial sector survives its crises only because a public institution, the Fed, stands behind it. Was that an indictment of the whole arrangement — what Bernie Sanders in September 2008 called “socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor”? Mehrling didn’t think so; to him, this was simply the price of keeping a modern, prosperous economy running. But it’s hard to miss the implication that America’s financial elite have amassed their staggering fortunes knowing that the public will catch them if they fall.

Perhaps some of Mehrling’s relative obscurity stems from the reality that, when times are good, we can afford to ignore his work. “Everyone always really pays attention to things like financial market plumbing when something breaks,” Weisenthal says, as in 2008 or during the bond-market selloff of March 2020. “Most of the time, they don’t think about it.” Even now, his ideas are rarely taught by academic economists. In economics, students “are really encouraged to think about a world where money is unimportant,” Mason says. Mehrling’s followers, Pocklington notes, mostly went into finance and government “rather than infiltrate the academy.”

Among legal scholars who study financial stability, Ricks says, Mehrling’s approach is “definitely not heterodox anymore.” The Fed has come around, too. For years after 2008, it resisted casting itself as a “dealer of last resort,” refusing to spell out how and when it would intervene to stabilize the financial system. Then the pandemic-induced panic of March 2020 made the question unavoidable, and the following year, the Fed established a permanent facility to backstop the market for overnight loans.

Before long, we may have another chance to watch Mehrling’s theories play out again. If you want to know where financial crises break out, Mehrling contended, watch who owes what to whom, and when. Lately, there’s one obvious place to begin. This year alone, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle have sold more than $370 billion in bonds — roughly a fifth of all investment-grade U.S. corporate bond issuance — much of it to erect the data centers powering the AI boom. The chips humming inside those warehouses may quickly become obsolete, but the debts incurred to buy them must still be paid on time.

Will this particular bet go sour? Nobody truly knows. Maybe AI will turn wildly profitable in time and the hyperscalers will pay off their loans without incident. Or maybe the financial system will buckle somewhere else entirely. (Mehrling had his eye on stablecoins, warning that these dollar-pegged cryptocurrencies could easily collapse if too many holders sold at once.) But, sooner or later, Weisenthal tells me, “there will be another crisis.” When it comes, we’ll need a way to make sense of the system. So, he says, we’ll “revisit the works of Perry Mehrling.”

items.title: 11 Insights From Our New Profile of Jared Kushner
items.description: We’ve published a sweeping profile of Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his go-to diplomats for no less than three separate wars. Andrew Rice spent months reporting the story, including having several conversations with Kushner. Below are
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: We’ve published a sweeping profile of Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his go-to diplomats for no less than three separate wars. Andrew Rice spent months reporting the story, including having several conversations with Kushner. Below are 11 highlights, including Kushner’s thoughts on Israel, mixing business and diplomacy, the forthcoming probes by congressional Democrats, and playing video games with MBS.
He sees no problem mixing diplomacy and business
Kushner’s day job is running Affinity Partners, a private-equity firm with more than $6 billion in assets that “does business in some of the same countries where he practices diplomacy.”

“The accumulation of more wealth is not my top objective,” he tells me. He says he could be making more money if he weren’t giving his time away, and his standard answer to critics is to challenge them to find any instance when he acted contrary to American interests. “Having the resources that I need to live my life makes me more independent to pursue the things that I want to pursue,” Kushner says. “I’ve been doing this for ten years, and my business has been an objectively successful business. My diplomacy’s been successful diplomacy. Nobody’s ever identified any case where I’ve done one thing to benefit the other.”
Kushner also told Rice he’s all in when tackling each of the wars:

“I’m a fairly all-in personality, so when I’m in something, it consumes all of me,” Kushner says as he drives. “It takes a big toll on me to do one of these, let alone three.” Crisis No. 1 is Gaza, which Kushner took on last year by inserting himself into the middle of cease-fire negotiations between Hamas and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “Not only getting the war stopped — getting all the hostages home, getting the bodies of the hostages home. It was a crazy operation,” he says. “Bibi didn’t think we could do it.” Since then, Kushner has been working on the future of Palestine — without much substantive input, critics say, from actual Palestinians — while also trying to resolve crisis No. 2, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and navigating crisis No. 3, Trump’s war of choice with Iran.
“Fixing Iran-U.S. relations, that’s something that has been broken for 50 years, so it’s not like there’s a precedent for success,” Kushner tells me.
He thinks Israel took the wrong path after the October 7 attack

“I feel like the fork in the road,” Kushner tells me, “is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status.”
“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role”

He says he has not raised any funds since Trump’s reelection. But earlier this year, the New York Times reported that Affinity was exploring the possibility of starting a second fund with new capital from the Middle East. Kushner claims Affinity ceased to consider that “the instant the actions in Iran began.”

“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role,” Kushner says when I talk to him at his office. He claims that for the past year, he has hardly been involved in managing his fund at all, a decision he portrays as a costly diversion from his original plan. “I started a business when I left government. I focused on that business. I worked really, really hard. I did a good job with that business. Circumstances changed, where my father-in-law became president again. I intended to stay out but got pulled back in.”
On life in in the “Billionaire Bunker” of Indian Creek, Florida

When I visit on a weekday morning, the house is quiet and sunbathed. Through the glass double doors of the living room, I can see a backyard pool and a thatch-roofed sukkah the family has erected for the holiday season. Beyond that stands a large covered patio with a grill for alfresco dining and a gym with weight machines and a sauna. (“Set the cold plunge at 42 degrees, and just go for it,” Kushner says. “After that, the day’s easy.”) A boat is docked at the rear of the property. The boys fish, and Ivanka likes to paddleboard. It’s a good life, and their market timing was impeccable. Since they purchased on the island, they’ve acquired new neighbors, including Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg.

“Now it’s become a place for immortals, but we were some of the last mortals to be able to buy there,” Kushner says. He has served as a member of the Indian Creek Village council, and the family recently was accepted into the island’s country club after a cooling period on the wait list. To some of their old friends in New York, it looked like they were retreating to a temporary place of exile, but Kushner doesn’t look at the island as an Elba. It’s become his family’s home. “A narrative people were writing is that we were running away from New York, but we didn’t view it like that,” Kushner says. “We viewed it like we were running toward the lives we wanted to live. We stopped giving a shit what other people say, and we just started living for ourselves.”
He won’t say if he opposed the Iran war

“Look, you can’t rerun the simulation. So you learn from what’s occurred. I think there’s been a lot that’s been achieved. Our job is to engage and try to create the best deal possible for the president.”
He’d rather “suffer” than publicly distance himself from Trump

On January 6, 2021, Kushner was flying home from Saudi Arabia, where he had been attending an economic summit, when he learned that rioters had broken into the Capitol. Although he has never stated unequivocally that Trump lost the election, Kushner had concluded weeks before that any effort to overturn it was hopeless. He left it to Rudy Giuliani and others to pursue legal challenges. Still, after his plane landed, Kushner went to the White House to support Ivanka, who has since said she was trying to persuade her father to call on his supporters to disperse. While Kushner would personally condemn the attack as “wrong and unlawful,” he never uttered a critical word about Trump himself. “You’ll never, ever read a public thing where I distance myself from him,” Kushner says to me one morning in July. “I won’t do that. I’d rather suffer.”
He also said all you can do is surf Trump’s waves:

During the first term, Kushner would sometimes advise colleagues not to try to control Trump — he makes the waves, Kushner says, and you can only try to surf them. He swears he didn’t want to get pulled back into the water. When pressed, Kushner concedes that he may be excited to exercise power, but he claims he doesn’t want it for its own sake — rather, he wants the power to do good in the world.
Trump is a “very special” everything

“Look, he keeps everyone off balance — at this point, I accept that,” Kushner tells me. “I think he’s got a very special deal instinct, and he’s a very special politician and a very special leader and a very special boss and a very special father-in-law. So you kind of buy the package, and it’s not my job to say, ‘Oh, do this’ or ‘Don’t do this.’ I think you have to follow his instincts and then use his instincts to try and take advantage of whatever uncertainty he wants to create.”
Jamie Raskin says the subpoenas are definitely coming

Jamie Raskin, the incoming chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, tells me he will use his subpoena power to examine (among other things) the allegations in Cole’s book. “If the key policy person in the Trump administration on Middle East issues is in business with foreign powers that are deeply invested in those issues and has been for essentially a decade, then we need to know about that,” Raskin says. “Either he’s being unfairly maligned or he’s a billion-dollar bagman for the Trump family.” And even if there were no secret bank accounts, Raskin adds, it’s undisputed that Kushner has profited from the legal investment in Affinity. “He keeps wanting to have it both ways. The whole point of conflict-of-interest laws and the Emoluments Clause is that if you represent the U.S., you owe 100 percent undivided loyalty to the United States.”

Kushner claims he is willing to entertain “serious questions” about his alleged conflicts of interest if the Democrats in Congress really have any to ask. But, he adds, “if they want to do political theater, then we’ll engage accordingly.” His definition of theater seems expansive enough to rule out any substantive cooperation with the legislative branch if it tries to examine his quasi-governmental role and anything he has done overseas.
And he claimed he was unfazed at the prospect of Democratic oversight
“I sleep well at night because I know what the laws are, I know what the rules are, and I don’t come close to violating them.”
Tony Blair thinks Kushner is “probably the best natural political mind I have come across”

“I actually say to people he is probably the best natural political mind I have come across,” says Blair. “And I have come across quite a few.” The accords demonstrated not just the value of Kushner’s relationships but his willingness to go big, Blair tells me. “One of the things he is extremely good at is that when a problem is in quite a narrow compass and there is a blockage, he creates an enlargement of the matrix of issues to be decided that allows you then to unlock the problem.”
He used to play League of Legends with Mohammed bin Salman

He bonded with MBS at one of the crown prince’s estates in the desert, staying up all night and watching the sun rise over a fire. Kushner was impressed with his vision for modernizing Saudi Arabia and his willingness to spend his oil money on transformative projects. When they weren’t together, Kushner and MBS would talk and text on WhatsApp. MBS loves video games, and sometimes they’d play together. (“League of Legends,” Kushner specifies. “He’s a big League player.”) When MBS was implicated in the grisly assassination of a Washington-based dissident, Kushner refused calls to repudiate him. “It’s a real friendship,” Kushner says.

items.title: Why are so many young women getting obsessed with creatine?
items.description: Campbell Gulbrandsen, a fashion assistant living in New York City, says she was on the creatine wave “before it got super popular” online. The 24-year-old first heard about creatine on social media, where it was being promoted by fitness influencers doing high
paragraphs: Campbell Gulbrandsen, a fashion assistant living in New York City, says she was on the creatine wave “before it got super popular” online. The 24-year-old first heard about creatine on social media, where it was being promoted by fitness influencers doing highly demanding sports, like bodybuilding and marathon training. But it wasn’t until she saw it being taken by more casual exercisers – the Pilates princesses – that she decided to give it a try. The brand she opted for was Arrae, which sells creatine in gummy form. “The branding definitely roped me in,” says Gulbrandsen. “They’re cute flavours and the whole thing is that it tastes good … It’s very female-oriented.”

Once primarily advertised with blocky typefaces and images of men with bulging muscles, creatine supplements, which have existed since the 90s, have recently shifted their focus to female consumers. That’s been made obvious through a shift in the supplement’s visual identity, with Goop-esque, pastel-coloured options like Midi, Flo and Cymbiotika entering the market. Alongside the sleek new branding, the nature of the products has changed too. Not a fan of giant tubs of powder? You can now chew your creatine in the form of gummies, drink it from squeezable packets, or slap it on via topical patches. Within the past year, the supplement’s aesthetic facelift has been accompanied by a swell of social media content, in which UGC wellness creators rattle off everything creatine has done for them, from toning their muscles to alleviating their brain fog.

The rebrand isn’t subtle. New female-centred brands, like Fit Girl Creatine, are continuing to enter the market. “What we wanted women to feel when they first saw it was that it was something they could see themselves using right away,” says creative director Olivia Vlachos, whose agency has led the new product’s marketing and design. The supplement, which launches early next year, comes in hot pink sachets and flavours like pink lemonade. “Branding is how someone encounters a product,” says Vlachos. “If you’re walking down the aisle at Erewhon, are you going to pick it up?”

The marketing efforts are working. Searches for “creatine monohydrate for women” are up 190 per cent compared to this time last year, according to Google Trends, and on Amazon, sales within the creatine subcategory have surged 90 per cent over the last 12 months, according to SmartScout marketplace data. With creatine market size projected to reach $8.7 billion by 2033, growing at nearly three times the rate of the global dietary supplements market, the numbers are clear – the boom is real. But what exactly is behind it?

Answering that question requires an understanding of where creatine comes from, and what it can and can’t do. Creatine is a compound that comes from amino acids and supplies energy to the muscles. “[It’s] something that our bodies naturally make from three amino acids, and it’s mainly created in our liver and kidneys,” says Yasi Ansari, a sports dietitian based in California. “Having more creatine in our muscles can allow us to do more short and intense work in the gym, on the field, on the court, and over time, this results in more gains in our strength and our muscle,” she adds.

While creatine has long been taken to build muscle, more and more people are now reaching for the supplement to promote brain health. But is there any validity to these claims? Experts believe it’s too soon to say. Although a few small studies have shown that large doses of creatine can slightly increase brain activity, the research isn’t conclusive, and, as Ansari says, “the jury’s still out” on the supplement’s cognitive benefits.

On social media, however, the concept of creatine’s brain-boosting abilities has gained traction, making it one popular reason people are clicking “add to cart”. Hana El Sherif, a 25-year-old finance associate, for example, began taking creatine after a friend told her it could help with sleep and cognitive function. “One thing I liked about creatine is that it almost felt like a multivitamin,” says El Sherif. “It ticks so many boxes, and you get all these benefits you otherwise would have to get from four or five supplements.”

Grace McHugh, a 24-year-old living in New York City, also started taking creatine because of its potential cognitive benefits. Her primary reason, though, was for marathon training. Though her college boyfriend took creatine every day, it was female influencers who got her to start – she decided on the brand Promix after reading a profile on the brand’s founder, an extreme athlete turned wellness entrepreneur. “I do think there’s an increased interest among women,” says McHugh.

“In the 2010s, it was all about women trying to lose as much weight as possible. Then, we saw a complete shift in how women think about workouts, as muscle mass became something that people started to value more”

There is clearly a connection between the rise of creatine and the fact that, in recent years, more women have taken an interest in building strength. “In the 2010s, it was all about women trying to lose as much weight as possible,” says brand strategist Katie Klencheski, whose marketing agency SMAKK Studios specialises in health and wellness. “Then, we saw a complete shift in how women think about workouts, as muscle mass became something that people started to value more.”

It’s true that the popularity of strength training, which can be especially beneficial as we enter menopause and lose bone density, has been on the rise among women. But aside from increased awareness about menopause, Klencheski also points to the explosion of GLP-1s, which can cause muscle loss, as a reason for the current preoccupation with strength. “You have a lot of people on GLP-1s who are barely eating any food, and the muscle wasting thing is a very real concern,” says Klencheski. “A lot of people are looking for ways to stop that.”

Aside from eye-catching packaging, brands are partnering with influencers and UGC creators to spread the good news of creatine to the masses. As with other supplements, though, this can get murky because, as Klencheski notes, the regulatory system around this content is “a little bit like the Wild West”. In the US, supplement companies can make certain claims about how a product affects the structure or function of the body, provided those claims are substantiated and not misleading, but they cannot market supplements as diagnosing, treating, curing or preventing disease.

The lack of regulation of the supplement market is especially important to keep in mind when it comes to creatine, given that much of its current online buzz is being fuelled by creators using language like “body-changing” to promote its powers. “Everyone thinks they’re going to take creatine and magically transform their body solely from the supplement,” says Anna Hellickson, a 23-year-old living in Los Angeles. Hellickson started taking creatine in March, but, sceptical of the gummies and drinks she saw marketed towards women online, opted for an old-school unflavoured version. “I don’t need the fun version, just the benefits,” she says.

Though the irresponsible claims by influencers don’t negate the fact that creatine has legitimate, science-backed benefits, Ansari says that it “cannot be a substitute for good nutrition”. While some of the online commentary has veered into problematic territory, many women feel that the overall movement is still about getting stronger rather than shrinking, which is a step in the right direction. “We’ve been in this skinny trend for a good amount of time now, and I think that creatine is helping propel this next stage of body image norms,” says Hellickson. “Strength is coming back.”

Still, it's not exactly the case that the creatine boom is the antithesis of diet culture. While creatine may have once been viewed as something for more extreme fitness enthusiasts, in a health landscape where DIY peptide stacking has become normalised, it’s perhaps not surprising that there’s a new sense of openness around the supplement. And with that openness, or “white space,” as a marketer would call it, comes a readiness for the wellness industry to do what it’s always done: sell, sell, sell.

items.title: The wellness industry wants to sell you your attention back
items.description: Rebecca Gruwell’s “low cortisol night routine” includes drinking a cup of Trader Joe’s sleep tea, spritzing her pillow with magnesium spray and applying “low tox” (that’s non-toxic) skin care, all before her Hatch alarm clock has struck 10pm. About a month ago
paragraphs: Rebecca Gruwell’s “low cortisol night routine” includes drinking a cup of Trader Joe’s sleep tea, spritzing her pillow with magnesium spray and applying “low tox” (that’s non-toxic) skin care, all before her Hatch alarm clock has struck 10pm. About a month ago, Gruwell, a lifestyle content creator based in Tampa, Florida, added something new to the lineup: an “anti-blue light brain stack.” Inspired by the recent brainstacking trend on social media, the 24-year-old created her own analogue activity stack – one that includes playing Sudoku, writing in a gratitude journal, and reading her Bible – in an attempt to cut back on doomscrolling before bed. For Gruwell, unplugging has become an integral part of her wellness routine.

Gruwell is of course not the only one attempting to cut back on screen time. As Big Tech sinks its claws deeper into our lives, it seems that everywhere you look, there are examples of our desire to unplug. Searches for Brick surged 250 per cent in the past year; dumb phones are back and, in a new survey by wellness app publisher Rocapine, cutting screen time outranked smoking and alcohol reduction among Americans’ wellness goals. While the idea of what makes one “well” has evolved and been debated ad nauseam in the past few decades, today, a consensus appears to be emerging: getting well, in 2026, means getting offline.

Our exasperation over losing hours a day to our phones has led to myriad methods for unplugging – from brainstacking to phone-free cold plunge spas to a litany of social media-blocking apps. However, this is nothing new. While today’s tech anxieties are centred on the rise of AI and “addicting” short-form content, people have been in a panic over technology for over a century. In 1926, newspapers fretted that radio was “keeping children and their parents up late nights, wearing down their vitality for lack of sleep and making laggards out of them at school.” In 1941, American paediatrician Mary Preston studied hundreds of six- to 16-year-olds and concluded that more than half were severely addicted to radio crime dramas. Preston observed that many children consumed these dramas “much as a chronic alcoholic does drink”.

While it’s true that tech anxiety isn’t entirely new, there are now increasingly niche ways it’s manifesting in the wellness industry. Take Steppin, a social media-blocking app that, by syncing with an iPhone’s Health app, requires users to walk in order to earn more screen time. The app, where the default setting equates 100 steps to one minute of screen time, was founded by serial entrepreneur Paul English, who also co-founded the travel search engine Kayak back in the 2000s. The idea for Steppin was born during a family road trip through Spain, where, at one point on the drive from Madrid to Toledo, everyone in the van had their heads down, looking at their screens. “I laughed and said, ‘This is crazy. We’re in Spain, in this countryside that we’ve never been to before, and we’re looking at our phones. How pathetic are we?’” English says.

The entrepreneur, whose venture group also developed the AI-powered food and habit-tracking app Wellagram, is a big believer in “the quantified self,” a cultural phenomenon rooted in the concept of “self-knowledge through numbers.” It’s a movement that’s become increasingly embedded in wellness – and, by extension, popular culture – in recent years, making it unsurprising that the same logic is now being applied to efforts to spend less time online. “You can only improve something if you measure it,” says English, who credits Steppin with both raising his step count and curbing his social media addiction. “An hour I used to spend on Twitter or TikTok, I now have to do other things… It’s been delicious to have something that gives me that much time back.”

Other screen time-reducing apps like PhoneLess, the self-proclaimed “Strava for screen time,” are tapping into the accountability partner approach often associated with fitness challenges. Diego Garrido and Daniel Suriol, two of the app’s founders, are climbers, and noticed that it was much easier to motivate themselves to get to the climbing gym if they knew the other was there waiting for them.
