They applied that same thinking to PhoneLess, which allows your friends to see what your screen time is in real time, therefore enabling them to call you out on it. “We saw that all the solutions on the market were individual, basically becoming a battle between you and your phone,” says Suriol. “It’s highly likely that your willpower is weaker than the algorithms of your phone, so we think this accountability and social power is needed.”

On social media, it’s even become a flex to post your unplugging behaviours, whether that means bricking your phone, printing out articles rather than reading them on your phone, or other de-rotting methods. In April, Lissa, a 22-year-old living in London, spent a week trying to “un-rot” her brain, an experience she shared with her TikTok followers. “I didn’t expect it to blow up as much as it did,” she says. The goal of sharing, according to the creator, was to hopefully inspire others, as a YouTube video about digital detoxes partially inspired her own unplugging. In real life, Lissa’s detox did indeed earn her respect from her friends, who told her they’d never be able to do the same. And as for her screen time now? “I can’t lie, it’s gotten a lot worse,” she confesses.

For small business owners in the wellness space, such as Kat Smith, owner of Offline Wellness Club, branding something as “offline” has proven to be a powerful marketing tactic. The Calgary-based business, born out of Smith and her co-founder’s burnout from working in finance, first began as a run club in 2022. Though there were plenty of run clubs in the city at the time, theirs blew up, something Smith attributes in part to including “offline” in the name. “The [interest] was so inflated, and I think that the branding and messaging had something to do with it,” says Smith. “People are attracted to ‘offline’ as a movement.” Today, the club has evolved into a cold plunge and sauna studio, where phones are discouraged. Alongside bathing suits and locally made candles, baseball caps that read “Offline” and Bloom devices, Brick-esque social media-blocking cards, are sold in the studio’s gift shop.

Still, with technology being an intrinsic part of how many of us make money, going offline – and caring for your own mental and physical health by doing so – is beginning to feel like a privilege not everyone can afford. Chloe Madison, a 25-year-old based in Ontario, for example, was told by her naturopath and doctor that her health issues were rooted in stress, something she says stems from her work. Her job? Freelance content creation for weddings and brands. “For myself, it’s a business sacrifice,” Madison says of unplugging. “It’s definitely become a luxury to be able to take time offline.”

If the pursuit of “getting well” already felt exhausting, the pursuit of getting offline, the latest wellness flex, feels closer to impossible. Still, that doesn’t mean it’s not worth trying – especially since reducing screen time has been linked to improvements in mental health , and you don’t need to buy anything to do it. In addition to getting eight hours of sleep and drinking three litres of water a day, one of Madison’s wellness goals this year has been spending her weekends offline. She’s unplugging the old-fashioned way: simply leaving her phone at home. While a trip to the farmers’ market used to mean taking lots of photos and videos, she now spends those errands phoneless. “There’s so much more to life than this digital world we’re all living in,” she says.

items.title: Help! I’m obsessed with trying to look like my boyfriend’s ex
items.description: My ex-situationship’s ex-girlfriend paid me a visit in a dream a couple of weeks ago. She was all smooth, creamy skin and cascades of blonde waves, like some sort of Botticelli angel. She reached forward to hug me, and then I woke up. That was weird, I thought
paragraphs: My ex-situationship’s ex-girlfriend paid me a visit in a dream a couple of weeks ago. She was all smooth, creamy skin and cascades of blonde waves, like some sort of Botticelli angel. She reached forward to hug me, and then I woke up. That was weird, I thought. Followed closely by, God, she is just so beautiful.

The term ‘parasocial’ was coined in the 50s, describing the illusion of intimacy audiences felt with television personalities. In the decades since, the definition has stretched to cover podcast hosts and influencers; public figures in the contemporary media ecosystem. However, through the invasive nature of social media, we have developed a far more claustrophobic phenomenon: the ability to construct unreciprocated fascinations with people on the immediate periphery of our lives, fuelled by access to trivial specifics. And no target is more compelling, or more haunted, than the ex that came before.

Many come to social media in search of aesthetic inspiration, coaxed into buying affiliate-link lip oils or emulating a specific actor’s wardrobe. But what happens when we decide we want to look like our partners’ exes?

Martha*, 23, who works in events in Cardiff, remembers the moment her comparison turned physical. “This is pretty mortifying to admit, but I got my smiley pierced because the guy I was trying to pursue at the time’s ex had hers done,” she explains. In hindsight, she was attempting to embody what she assumed was his romantic blueprint – a shortcut to securing his devotion. “The worst part is that the piercing fell out on our first date after a kiss, so it ended up closing up anyway. Looking back on the relationship, that must have been some kind of universe-level warning sign.”

Similarly, Ruby*, a 26-year-old working in marketing, revealed that when she first started dating her partner, she quickly became obsessed with looking at his ex-girlfriend’s Instagram profile. “She still had old photos of them together on her account, and that sort of morbid curiosity drew me in at first.” Eventually, that curiosity led to an unconscious identity shift. “Before I even realised what I was doing, I dyed my hair black, just like hers. I don’t remember making the active choice to copy her, but looking back, it was definitely because I had been comparing myself to her so much that she became this image of what I thought was attractive to him.”

For others, the emulation that begins as beauty and style inspiration can expand into an entire lifestyle. Chloe*, 27, a stylist working in London, found herself restructuring her identity around her current partner’s long-term ex. “I began checking her Instagram from a burner account. She had this outdoorsy, ‘granola’ aesthetic. Lots of climbing photos, natural linen, zero make-up. That sort of vibe,” Chloe says. “My style has always been a bit extra. But I convinced myself that maybe I was too high-maintenance for what he really wanted. I bought a pair of Salomon shoes, stopped wearing foundation and convinced him to go on a weekend hiking trip to the Lake District.”

The breaking point came midway up a trail in Cumbria. “I was standing drenched in rain, watching my partner trek ahead of me,” she says. “He turned around, looked at me struggling, and said, ‘You know, you really don't have to force yourself to do things like this if you don’t enjoy them.’ I realised how silly I was being. Trying to perform the identity of a woman he’d already left behind, to prove I was worthy of staying.”

Leo*, 27, a bar manager from Manchester, started tweaking his appearance after discovering photos of his boyfriend’s ex. “My boyfriend’s ex had this rugged, bearded, hyper-masculine look, while I’d always been clean-shaven,” Leo says. “I started feeling like I was too boyish, like I lacked the presence my partner secretly wanted. I stopped shaving and spent months trying to grow out a moustache and stubble. It looked completely wrong on me.”

What Martha, Ruby, Chloe and Leo describe is an attempt to reverse-engineer desire. When we enter a new relationship, we are naturally eager for clues about what our partner values. Before smartphones, an ex was a ghost. Maybe a name mentioned in passing, or a stray photograph in a box under the bed. Now, we can view their holiday photos, track their style evolution, listen to their playlists, and deduce our own perceived inadequacies across grids.

In psychology, this obsession with a partner’s past is termed retroactive jealousy. A 2018 study found that digital platforms can intensify jealousy around a partner’s past by making that history more visible and accessible.

The fixation is accelerated by platform architecture. Social media platforms thrive on categorising human beings into neat aesthetic archetypes. So when an ex fits neatly into one of these visual boxes, the algorithm rewards curiosity. Click on their profile enough times, and your Explore page begins feeding you hair tutorials and make-up guides that align with their specific look. The platform becomes an accomplice, obscuring the line between your authentic taste and your fixation.

The problem with emulating an ex’s look is that it operates on a fundamental misunderstanding of why relationships end and why new ones begin. Relationships rarely fail because someone’s hair was the wrong shade or because they lacked a specific piercing. Yet, because physical appearance is one of the few things social media allows us to measure with precision, we treat beauty as the primary variable.

The impulse to look like the person who came before you is rarely about them at all. It reveals your own tender, human desire to feel chosen. But trying to secure love by wearing someone else's aesthetic is like trying to get into a house using a key cut for a different lock. The trick is to wake up, acknowledge their unique beauty, and step out into the day wearing your own face.

items.title: UK nightlife is addicted to rules
items.description: It’s midnight on a Friday and I’ve finally made it into central London nightclub Fabric. After queuing for nearly an hour, followed by my boxers being meticulously fondled by a security guard I can only imagine was trained by the TSA, I am met with one final b
paragraphs: It’s midnight on a Friday and I’ve finally made it into central London nightclub Fabric. After queuing for nearly an hour, followed by my boxers being meticulously fondled by a security guard I can only imagine was trained by the TSA, I am met with one final barrier: a doorman holding a roll of stickers. “We have a no photos policy here, so I’m just going to pop this sticker over your phone camera,” he tells me, wearing an unnerving, almost apologetic smile. It’s as if he is expecting me to say: Thank you, stranger, for saving me from my dirty phone-addicted self. Instead, all I can think is: Great, now my iPhone is covered in a sticky residue that will make every photo I take look shit for the next two months.

Everyone in nightlife seems to be obsessed with phones right now. Soho nightclub lost recently built a mythical reputation for locking phones in a prison-style magnetic pouch in order to – in the words of their ‘founder’ – save us from our tech overlords. New Peckham haunt Palais threatens immediate removal if dancers are caught taking photos on the dancefloor. Even cult-favourite festival We Out Here joined in on the fun this year, launching a new secret stage that required people to queue blindly behind a hole in a fence – which all felt rather exhilarating until I was met with a sign at the front of the line: no photos allowed.

Of course, no one likes being surrounded by phones on a night out. They’re patently bad vibes, and recent research suggests that they have made young people more self-conscious and less likely to let loose on the dancefloor. But when I’m instructed to lock away my phone for my own good by a security guard who treats everyone as guilty by default, it feels uncomfortably paternalistic. Nowadays, UK nightlife feels more focused on telling me what I can’t do than what I can.

This smartphone witch hunt is just one example of an increasingly rules-based approach to UK nightlife. Over the past year, we’ve seen events for men over six foot, events for people over 21, events where cups are leased under a convoluted deposit scheme that no one ever, truly, understands ... the list goes on. But it wasn’t always like this. Once upon a time, the UK was home to the world’s first rave movement – the so-called ‘second summer of love’ in the late 80s in which young people flocked to anarchic free parties in the British countryside, seeking refuge from the era’s Thatcherite conservatism in a nightlife movement made for the people, by the people. This utopian dream was crushed with unprecedented force and legal pressure during the 90s – a process that continues right up to this day, with recent updates to the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 now classifying an illegal rave as a gathering of just 20 people. (France, meanwhile, introduced similarly heavy-handed regulations this year).

Granted, some rules are good. Nightlife’s recent obsession with phone use can be traced all the way back to pioneering Berlin nightclub Ostgut (now known as Berghain), a landmark haven of queer expression at the turn of the century which was one of the first venues to ban photography in order to protect its community. Elsewhere, in 2022, the UK’s own “intentional nightlife” platform Pxssy Palace defended their decision to charge cis white men up to six times more than LGBTQ+ and PoC attendees in order to “respond to the unfair economic imbalance that exists within our society”. On a different beat, Portugal-based festival Waking Life enforces a range of sustainability and anti-littering rules to protect its idyllic site for future generations. All of these feel like justifiable nightlife rules: ones that are intended to protect their community, safeguard its future or address wider systemic imbalances.

But when lifted out of these communities and enforced as a means of making a nightclub seem more interesting (after all, Berghain’s infamous rules are today more understood in terms of exclusivity than in protecting queer expression), rules begin to feel a little dystopian. At its widest level, it’s comparable to the ‘social contract’ on which modern society is based – the idea that, by agreeing to certain rules like not stealing or killing other people, the collective as a whole are better off. In recent years, nightlife rules have multiplied, but have they really been for the better?

The other week, I found myself being forcefully removed – along with the 50-year-old man I was borrowing a lighter from – from a pub smoking area because he had accidentally brought a pint outside. Glass, it turns out, is a material that grown adults are incapable of holding after 7 pm – one of many British smoking area regulations that also require us to huddle within tiny, fenced-off areas on the street, and to constantly be subject to an angry security guard yelling at us to either hurry up or pack closer together so that other revellers can enjoy their yard time, too. As my unwitting co-conspirator and I were marched shamefully back into the pub that night, he turned to me and sighed: “People used to trust each other more back in the day, now it’s all…” He pointed his finger and scrunched up his eyes.

Trust seems to be the crux of this issue. Earlier this year I rolled a joint on a literal cliff face at Solstice Festival in remote, northern Finland. There were no searches upon entry and security barely bothered me apart from to warn of muddy paths. The year before, I cycled – along with thousands of others – in the pitch black along Amsterdam canals back from legendary electronic music festival Dekmantel. It was quite literally the only way to get to and from the event, and, in lieu of security holding my hand the entire way, I relied on the crowd to find my way home. These are two of the best festivals on Earth but, in both cases, I was struck by the realisation that they would never be allowed to run with such freedoms in the UK. There, the organisers seemed to trust attendees not to yeet themselves off a cliff or into a canal, and I, in turn, trusted in the festival, invested my time and money – and didn’t yeet myself off a cliff or into a canal.

It’s this mutual trust that we seem to have lost here in the UK. Fabric is, more often than not, mid. lost, while in a cool venue, is plagued by existential questions of who it is actually for beyond the vague premise of banning phones and ‘Making Nightlife Great Again’. And We Out Here’s secret stage, I regret to report, was largely devoid of phones – not because people identified with the rules, but because the stage was kind of boring and people milled about there for an average of about five minutes before fucking off. Perhaps, instead of putting all their efforts into locking up phones and policing fun, UK nightlife would be better off if we started thinking about building spaces actually worth sacrificing our freedoms for. Or, better yet, a night so good that I forget I have a phone to begin with. After all, that’s what we all want, right?

items.title: Fact, Fiction, and Fraud in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’
items.description: Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s new limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you an
items.author: Julia Black
paragraphs: Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s new limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew. The show, which follows the stunning multibillion-dollar collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, starts off a bit slow, but accelerates episode by episode until its high-octane finale.

I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere. Some of that company’s founders and employees share similar intellectual roots to The Altruist’s protagonists; watching its fictionalized Caroline Ellison, in particular, justify astoundingly reckless behavior with her system of mathematical-optimization-of-everything felt uncannily like watching frontier labs proceed with a seemingly inexplicable appetite for risk.

The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies. (According to people involved with the project, the working title for the project was Untitled Love Story.) But as with any fictionalized account, the series takes some liberties with the characters and plot. If you’re anything like me, you want to know what exactly is fact, and what is fiction.

I spoke with Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, two of the reporters who exposed the FTX fiasco in real time, and who consulted on the series. “When Jen and I started working with Graham Moore, the showrunner, he made it really clear that he wanted this to be very character driven. Nobody wants an eight-hour lecture on how the blockchain works,” Dugan tells me.

“The bones of the show are rooted in reality,” says Wieczner. Understanding these flawed and complicated characters helps explain “how one decision leads to another decision and a small oopsies turns into a multibillion-dollar fraud and this huge criminal conspiracy.”

Even if there’s a little fiction in the nitty-gritty, Dugan says that there is one overarching truth he hopes the series will reveal: “That even the prettiest ideas still have to turn into reality through imperfect people, and those imperfect people will end up making mistakes that they cannot foresee.” Here’s what the show ripped from real life—and where it took some creative license.
CAROLINE ELLISON WROTE SEXY HARRY POTTER FAN FICTION

Not quite. In the first episode, Caroline is humiliated when her raunchy writing titled “A Ride on Draco’s Nimbus” surfaces online. And while it’s true that Ellison was a huge Harry Potter fan, there is no evidence she wrote erotic fan fiction herself. Instead, this plot point is likely gesturing toward Ellison’s 2010s-era Tumblr, which was called WorldOptimisation—a reference to a 660,000-word-long work of Harry Potter fan fiction by Silicon Valley philosopher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky’s work popularized the kind of mathematically strategic thinking Ellison applies to love and business alike.
SAM TRABUCCO’S “INFINITE MONEY HACK”

In episode six, Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther) makes the mistake of introducing Sam and Caroline to a hack that proves irresistible: FTX can mint its own coin, FTT, and then allow its crypto trading firm, Alameda, to take out large loans using off-market FTT as collateral. Alameda can then use those loans to place highly leveraged, incredibly risky bets on FTX—which in turn increases the value of FTT. (TL;DR: it’s a perfect loop.) Appalling as it sounds, in real life, this practice is more or less exactly what brought SBF’s empire tumbling down.

“One of the things that led to the FTX bank run,” explains Wieczner, “was the leaked balance sheet that showed that much of FTX and Alameda’s holdings were in FTT, which was FTX’s own coin. So that if that went to zero, it was like a house of cards and things just would’ve fallen apart. And that’s why you see at the end why is everything is falling…you have that kind of death spiral effect.”

As for Trabucco, he and his yacht (yes, it was really named Soak My Deck) didn’t get off unscathed. Trabucco didn’t face criminal charges, but was forced to liquidate many of his assets in order to help return about $80 million to defrauded investors.
CAROLINE ELLISON WAS INTO POLYAMORY

True. Caroline chronicled some of her adventures in nonmonogamy on her since-deleted Tumblr. She once wrote, “The only acceptable style of poly is best characterized as something like ‘imperial Chinese harem.’”
SBF’S ANTHROPIC INVESTMENT

Real! In the final episode of the series, SBF presents a last-ditch plan: He wants to repurpose his early stake in Anthropic to cover the losses of billions of dollars in customer funds. Indeed, FTX did use $500 million in customer funds to purchase a 13.5% stake in Anthropic’s Series B in late 2021. Of course, Sam’s plan did not pass muster. Yet if it had, he’d have been in the clear. After the company’s IPO last week, Alameda’s stake would be worth about $35 billion, according to The New York Times—enough to solve the disgraced firm’s liquidity issues several times over. Oh well.
CAROLINE ELLISON CONFESSED IN FRONT OF HER STAFF

True. In the penultimate episode, a visibly cracking Caroline delivers a halting confession amidst fits of nervous giggles to a shocked staff, telling them that she knew about FTX’s shortfall of user funds that would add up to more than $8 billion. I was sure this scene had been invented, but lo and behold: Ellison did admit that she had been aware of the inappropriate transfers between the two firms at a December 2022 all-staff meeting. You can even listen to the leaked recording online.
CAROLINE ELLISON BEARS MORE RESPONSIBILITY THAN SBF

I felt the show tilted towards placing the blame on Ellison, who is portrayed as incorrigibly risk-addicted and the muse behind SBF’s worst decisions. Constance Wang, who is played in the series by Madison Hu, is just one of the former FTX employees who found the show misrepresentative. In a lengthy X post, she rebutted its narrative: Ellison, said Hu, “wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.”

items.title: Meet the Biggest Ralph Lauren Fan in France
items.description: Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon
items.author: Pierre Groppo
paragraphs: Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing company and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

At his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He shows me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

But how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image issues. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he says with a laugh.

His connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

As retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a New York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

One might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

He quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of New England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”

If the self-made New Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

items.title: Are the World’s Top Literary Scholars Being Targeted by a Chinese Spy Op?
items.description: Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was thrilled when she got the email inviting her to be an honorary fellow at the International Institute of Literature & Arts. She had never heard of IILA, but she recognized several prestigious names
items.author: Clara Molot
paragraphs: Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was thrilled when she got the email inviting her to be an honorary fellow at the International Institute of Literature & Arts. She had never heard of IILA, but she recognized several prestigious names of fellow big-time literature professors who were listed among its fellows. “I saw Gayatri Spivak and Homi Bhabha, Franco Moretti, and I was like, Oh, finally,” she says.

The letter, signed by one Julian Lee “on behalf of the Secretariat” of IILA, invited Newell to join highly esteemed literature scholars at the Ivies, Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge. Newell, who has taught world and African literature at Yale for more than a decade, had been inducted into other prestigious societies with many of these same scholars, such as the British Academy.

This one, it seemed, came without strings. “There are no fees or membership dues,” read the letter. “Participation in award reviews, academic meetings, and consultation will be arranged with you in advance and subject to your availability.”

It seemed like a no-brainer. They’d also given her an award, and she even decided to accept an offer to join IILA’s academic committee. Yale was pleased for her too. The English department posted an announcement congratulating her on receiving the award.
Then she started to see red flags.
Soon, Newell says, she was listed among IILA’s leadership, even though she’d only agreed to be a committee member. “Please will you remove my name,” she wrote in an email to Lee.

Her concerns compounded when she received a draft of IILA’s bulletin, featuring a perplexingly poorly written biography—not what one would expect from a fancy literary academy. “Please delete my profile from the Bulletin,” Newell asked Lee, “as it contains too many errors for circulation, and is very poorly written.”

While the institute’s membership ranks included many of Newell’s high-profile peers, there were also a number of names on the list that seemed a bit random. Pat Barker, a novelist rather than a scholar, seemed out of place among the critics and theorists. There were, however, about half a dozen Chinese professors (including one who had already died).

“I’ve always been a bit of a doubting Thomas,” Newell wrote in an email to a colleague on the list who confirmed that she, too, had accepted the fellowship despite not knowing who was behind it. “I’m starting to wonder what’s going on and whether we’ve been somehow flattered into something that doesn’t exist!” Newell wrote.

That’s when Newell, who was my professor when I was a Yale undergraduate, decided to reach out to me about “a fake academic institute that has sucked in numerous very high-profile professors.” This was a couple of weeks ago, right after the news broke of Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman US authorities believed to be a Chinese spy. It made sense what China would want from Huang, the CEO of the powerful AI chip maker Nvidia, but could world literature professors really be a target? I started digging, which led me down a rabbit hole that included an entire constellation of shadow academies that former national security officials say have real potential to be part of a Chinese intelligence operation.

The website for IILA, which claims to be based in California, appears to have been registered in China. An IT specialist who reviewed the website for Vanity Fair assessed that it was built using artificial intelligence and riddled with glitches and broken links. The file name of the site’s logo is the Chinese word for “picture.” Registration records list the owner’s location as the Hubei province in central China, whose capital is Wuhan. But a data bug in the site’s administrative code suggests that the computer being used to post news on the site is not in China, but likely in Southeast Asia. The bug leaks the computer’s time zone with every new post saved through the site’s form, and every post carries a UTC+7 offset—the time zone for Bangkok, as well as Hanoi, Jakarta, and Phnom Penh.

Every edit also carries a second fingerprint: The computer saving the changes has an internal clock that runs a few seconds fast. That consistent drift shows that the same machine has been used for every post, which suggests that a single person could be updating the site.

Though IILA says on its website that it is a 501(c)(3), the IRS has no record of it, and it has no California registration. Instead, Colorado records list an “International Institute of Literature and Arts” as a nonprofit corporation registered in August 2025 at the address of a virtual mailbox service in Denver. It’s had a “delinquent” status since late August. (A local Denver newspaper ran a story in May asking why “over 12,000 different businesses all use” this same address.)

Several of the other organizations that use that same Colorado address, including the National Academy of Artificial Intelligence, the International Institute of Film Science & Arts, and the International Institute of Engineering Psychology (IIEP), were the subject of a Nature investigation in September. Nature’s reporting found that these organizations boasted high-ranking academics as their members, oftentimes without their knowledge or consent. According to Nature, the name most frequently associated with these organizations was Michael Chu, whose Chinese name, Chaoyang Zhu, is also listed as the incorporator of IILA in public records.

Chu’s name was previously listed on IILA’s website where Julian Lee’s name now appears, and his biography, according to another now deleted webpage, recovered through the Wayback Machine, includes a stint at another fake university that appears to belong to the same network, the City University of Colorado.

In response to a request for comment, IILA’s secretariat sent VF a series of unsigned emails, the first of which said the organization’s Colorado address was just an “early transitional filing point” and that a move to a “new regional and national headquarters is currently underway.” The “delinquent” status, they wrote, merely “reflects an administrative transition delay between entities.”
Another email stated that “we don’t know” about the other Chu-linked organizations mentioned in Nature’s report or why they all shared the same address.
“What’s the matter with Michael Chu? He is not working here at present. I can’t contact him at present,” the secretariat wrote, before passing along Chu’s email.

Chu swiftly responded to Vanity Fair in both Chinese and English to “prevent misunderstandings.” “I have no contact with the Chinese government at present” and “I am not related to IILA at present, and I am not responsible for any work of IILA,” Chu wrote. He then went on to speculate about the questions regarding IILA’s legitimacy: “IILA is an organization registered according to law, but because the previous registered agency company said that there was a problem with the agency address, it needs to be re-registered. This may be the reason why some people think IILA is illegal.”

“I think the supervision of the media is good and necessary, but we can’t use the power of the media to deliberately hinder normal academic exchanges,” posited Chu regarding the Nature article, which he says “many professors” he works with called “inexplicable and absurd."
Nature did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.
Asked to comment on IILA's connection with China, a Chinese embassy spokesperson said, “I am not familiar with the specific situation you mentioned."

Last month, César Pablo Domínguez Prieto, a professor of comparative literature at the University of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, found himself going down a similar rabbit hole after he was invited by IILA to give a talk for an online seminar series titled “New Directions in World and Comparative Literature” and promised an “Outstanding Speaker Award.”

“This solicitation prompted me to review their platform, where I discovered that the names and academic credentials of several of you are currently listed on their website,” Prieto wrote in an email to a group of his peers, which included Cornell’s Jonathan Dwight Culler, Harvard’s David Damrosch, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Wang Ning. “The list includes other colleagues with whom I’m not acquainted.”
Suspicious of the site and the invitation, Prieto dug further, finding those same public records that revealed Zhu’s name and the Colorado delinquent status.

Damrosch, a professor of world and comparative literature, was horrified to learn that his name was still being used by IILA without his “knowledge or permission.” He says he had written to them weeks ago asking for his name to be removed, with no result. (It has since been removed.)

“I suspect it is organized by the Chinese to place Chinese scholars in the company of distinguished Western scholars, but it is all a bit of a mystery,” Culler, a professor of English and comparative literature, tells me.
“I checked, and you’re right! I am a fellow there,” Moretti, a literary scholar, responded when I asked if he knowingly accepted the fellowship from IILA.

Yale has since deleted its announcement of Newell’s honorary IILA fellowship amid her concerns about the academy’s legitimacy. Shanghai Jiao Tong University, however, proudly displays comparative literature professor Wang Ning’s honor on its website, congratulating him on his fellowship and on receiving “the Global Laureate Award in Literature and Cultural Theory.” A magazine sponsored and supervised by the Chinese National Academy of Arts under the Ministry of Culture and Tourism similarly applauded Wang’s IILA award in October.

“This organization’s business model relies on unilaterally placing the names of highly respected scholars—such as yourselves—on their website without informed or explicit consent, while using targeted invitations for seminar series like the one I received as a fishing hook,” Prieto alleged in the email to his colleagues. “They use your collective prestige to look legitimate, allowing them to target early-career researchers and charge them annual membership fees ranging from $95 to $175 USD for worthless certificates.” (The membership pricing that previously appeared on IILA’s website has apparently been removed.)

Prieto’s assessment of what might be driving this scam was in line with Nature’s reporting: While the journal said it “has not identified anyone who has admitted paying for” any awards or titles from the academic societies, sources interviewed for that article theorized that they are designed to attract younger professors in China who might be willing to pay to be in the company of more highly esteemed academics.
But experts who spoke to Vanity Fair suggested there might be something else more nefarious at play.

Jeff Fields, a fellow at the UC Berkeley Institute for Security and Governance who spent more than 20 years with the FBI, most recently as the assistant special agent in charge of counterintelligence at the FBI’s San Francisco field office, says he’s familiar with this type of scheme.
“One of the things they like to do,” Fields says of the Chinese government, “is to fabricate these associations that they then use to leverage for more sophisticated operations.”

He has seen Chinese intelligence play such a long game, that it will spend years exaggerating or inventing affiliations in case it ever needs them, whether to lend someone credibility or to reach a particular target. If an agent later wants to get close to a professor who is friends with a certain researcher, for instance, the initial connections are already in place.

Jake Braun, who served as the White House’s acting principal deputy national cyber director under Joe Biden, agrees with Fields’s analysis, citing what’s known as the “thousand grains of sand” theory of Chinese intelligence. Because of its massive population, China has the ability to deploy an extraordinary number of people in its information-gathering techniques. Some might not necessarily be intelligence officers, he says, but each one can collect a single “grain of sand” of intelligence, which, when put together, works as an extremely powerful and effective intelligence apparatus.

Newell says that she was prompted on IILA’s website to create an account using her email address and a password, though once she was logged in, the website appeared entirely the same. Neither Fields nor Braun seemed terribly concerned about the possibility that those passwords could be used by whoever was behind the website to try to hack into the professors’ university accounts or emails.

What’s more likely, says Braun, is that in addition to the long game of network-building for future intelligence operations, IILA may also double as a platform to lend credibility to misinformation and disinformation campaigns by associating them with reputable scholars—another tactic he’s seen used before to influence narratives about China at the West’s foremost universities.

The Chinese professors listed as IILA fellows primarily come from three public, and therefore government-funded, universities, all in Shanghai: Fudan University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), and Shanghai University. In July 2026, the US Department of Defense added Fudan University and SJTU to a list of academic and research institutions deemed “a concern to national security.”

SJTU had already come under scrutiny following a 2023 incident in which five Chinese students enrolled in its joint program with the University of Michigan allegedly photographed military exercises at a National Guard training facility in the state. The students were charged in October 2024 with making false statements and related offenses, months after they left the country following graduation, according to the federal complaint. Three months later, the university announced the termination of its two-decade partnership with SJTU, citing national security concerns. (The partnership is still featured on SJTU’s website, however.)

Fudan University, meanwhile, was involved in the recent high-profile spying case of former Federal Reserve employee John Rodgers, who allegedly funneled classified government information to a spy he met at a conference in China. Rodgers would later send sensitive information to a Fudan professor and become a teacher there himself after leaving the Fed. (In July, he was sentenced to 38 months in federal prison for making false statements to federal investigators about sharing restricted Federal Reserve information with Chinese intelligence operatives.)
Still, Damrosch notes that those schools are also home to the leading literature programs in China, so their inclusion on the list does make sense from an academic perspective.

Because of their positions at public universities in China, some of the professors listed alongside Newell and her colleagues on IILA’s list of fellows also have ties to the Chinese Communist Party. Wang, for example, is the dean of SJTU’s Institute of Arts and Humanities, which houses a research hub, jointly established by Shanghai’s municipal CCP publicity department, focused on China’s international image. And, in 2023, he spearheaded the launch of a new cultural research center at SJTU dedicated to China’s “united front” work, which the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission has described as being used “to co-opt and neutralize sources of potential opposition to the policies and authority of its ruling Chinese Communist Party.”

When I reach out to Wang, he is eager to talk, noting that he knows “Vanity Fair is a prestigious popular journal in the United States.” We meet over Zoom, which he joins from an empty room in Beijing with one overhead light.

He tells me he received Prieto’s email, but he believes his colleague is mistaken and feels certain that IILA is legitimate. Wang insists that the members he has nominated from his own university were not asked to pay any fee. He says he’s communicated with both Michael Chu and Julian Lee, and that he doesn’t actually think it matters that he’s never met them. What affords the academy authenticity, says Wang, is its members and their own accomplishments, which are real and impressive—on that part, at least, everyone is in agreement.

“Oh, please let them be Chinese spies, please,” Newell says of IILA’s leadership. “That would be one of the best things ever in my whole life.” She finds the whole thing very amusing, needing to pause in the middle of our interview for a laugh break.

“I love the idea of fooling top academics,” says Newell. “I think it’s hilarious that we’re so famous, that our egos…the fact that none of us questioned getting awards and fellowships and we’re all so eagerly accepting them and letting our universities know how clever we are…I mean, it’s hilarious, and pathetic, and it says so much about the profession.”

items.title: Karon Davis is Recasting Art History
items.description: Karon Davis is Recasting Art History
items.author: Thelma Golden
paragraphs: Karon Davis is Recasting Art History

Karon Davis thinks of her sculptures as actors. Having grown up in a family of dancers and performers and gone on to study film at USC, the artist learned early on how much of a story could be communicated through a single gesture. Today, in her studio, Davis casts friends, family members, strangers, and sometimes herself in plaster, developing characters and elaborate scenes that draw from her own life, mythology, and overlooked chapters of Black history. “I always look at each sculpture as an actor. What’s their background, where are they going, where do they come from?” she explains. In two concurrent exhibitions, Wishful Thinking at Salon 94 in New York and Not My Circus at the Seattle Art Museum, Davis is working through some of her most ambitious ideas yet. The former grew, in part, out of a recent trip to the Vatican, where, among centuries’ worth of sculpture, Davis was struck by the absence of figures that resembled her. In response, she developed her own mythology, taking cues from classical sculpture to depict Black intimacy, tenderness, and the beauty of the female nude. In Seattle, meanwhile, Davis has constructed a circus of her own, complete with a sinister ringmaster and a half-woman, half-lion confined to a gilded cage. Beneath the spectacle is an exploration of the mechanics of power and manipulation, from the domestic sphere to the political arena. For Thelma Golden, director of the Studio Museum in Harlem and a longtime admirer of Davis’s work, what the artist is doing extends beyond the question of representation. Her sculptures, at once fragile and formidable, give presence and power to people whose stories have been neglected by history, while expanding the possibilities of the medium itself. After a summer spent almost entirely in her studio, Davis joined Golden to discuss the paradoxes of plaster, the politics of the nude, and the joy of recovering stories that have long been untold.
THURSDAY 3PM OCTOBER 22, 2026 NYC
THELMA GOLDEN: Hello, Karon.
DAVIS: I’m good. I’m a bit exhausted. I locked myself in the studio all summer. I just finished, so I did a little staycation because I was really burnt out.
GOLDEN: Well, having had the chance to see images, it feels like your practice is just blooming and broadening in such profound ways.
GOLDEN: We can frame this around your exhibition at the Seattle Art Museum, Not My Circus. And soon, you have an exhibition opening at Salon 94 called Wishful Thinking.

GOLDEN: When I think about your practice, I think about how you’ve been expanding the vocabulary of sculpture. I also think about how you think about the body as a way to tell stories, to think about history, to evidence the way in which our lived experience exists in the body. Can you talk about the impetus of your figuration? What does it spring from?

DAVIS: I think definitely it springs from my youth, growing up in a family of dancers and performers that performed at a time when there was freedom. I saw a lot of nudity being backstage with dancers. The body to me has always been so natural. It’s nothing I shy away from. Watching dancers tell stories without words taught me that it’s all about the gestures and how I can capture that. Maybe it’s also my way of stepping into these other bodies that don’t belong to me and being able to express an emotion or tell a story, because my characters aren’t bodies. I don’t like to use “bodies” because it feels like it’s void of a soul, void of a history. I always look at each sculpture as an actor—what’s their background, where are they going, where do they come from? I want people to, in their mind, finish these steps, finish the story. Being a storyteller, growing up in theater and studying film at USC, it’s just part of my nature.

GOLDEN: Right. Your figures seem to carry histories that extend beyond a singular representation. Looking at the works in Wishful Thinking, these figures represent broadly what it means to think about the female form. How much are you creating in terms of form? What are some of the references you’re thinking about as you start a body of work?

DAVIS: I had a trip to Italy recently, and every time I go there, I’m totally inspired. This time, I went to the Vatican, which blew my mind. I had a revelation like, “Wow, everything is here.” They took so much. I’m going down these corridors of heads, and arms, and sculptures ,and all this history from around the world. But I don’t see myself in these forms, in these sculptures. I don’t see myself in this building. I’ve been wanting to do a nude show for a long time, because when I go into the Louvre, the Met, and all these museums, if I see us, it’s either contemporary or it’s the Blackamoors. So I wanted to create work that I want to see. I want to see myself when I walk in: the beauty of the Black female form, the folds. I have a sculpture of a couple that’s based on Paul et Virginie, which is a very tender moment. I’ve never seen a sculpture of a tender moment between a Black woman and a Black man. As I was making it, it was just going to be inspired by this sculpture, and they’re nude in all their beauty. And then all of a sudden I was like, “I’m going to make her an angel coming down to this man.” Then the story starts to build and he’s broken. I started treating the plaster a different way and sanding it so she looks like the old sculptures. I wanted to do something whimsical and full of mythology, and also bring our mythology into the conversation as well and our stories.
GOLDEN: So it’s really centering an idea of the Black figure and the Black presence, both in relation to its absences in art history, but also in relation to your own desire to represent who you are?
GOLDEN: Can you talk about your initial choice and your continuing commitment to plaster?

DAVIS: Actually, Noah [Davis, Karon’s late husband] introduced me to plaster. He was like, “Let’s experiment,” and I just fell in love with it. For me, the plaster wraps look ancient. There’s something about the wrapping of the bodies and holding time in that moment of preservation, and also my process of casting the bodies, bringing people in and laying my hands on them. It’s a spiritual experience for me. I work with plaster strips, but also plaster itself. You have to have faith in the process because it’s not like clay where you can go back to it. I’ve cut off arms and faces and gouged out eyes because it wasn’t right. But there’s something beautiful that happens when you’re working with something so fast, where there are these happy mistakes, and you learn so much about the process and yourself and what you can make. More and more, I’m learning how to mold the plaster in the ways that I want. This summer, I had it embedded in my nails and my hair, on my face, but everyone’s like, “You should dive into clay.” And maybe one day I will, but right now I’m loving the plaster. There’s this conversation about making Black figures using this white material.
DAVIS: One person said, “Well, if they’re Black, why don’t you make them Black?” And I’m like, “Well, it’s not a color, it’s void. It’s all about the figure and the form.”

GOLDEN: Exactly. It also feels like plaster is a bit of a paradox because it’s fragile. But quite often you are making sculptures which show your subjects with strength and a sense of true solid grounding. Can you talk about that aspect of your material and your mission, how these two work together to create what you hope we experience with your work?

DAVIS: Great question. I’m drawn to the fragility of plaster. When I’m making the figures, I think about certain societies that believe when you take a photograph of them, you’re taking their soul. I feel that way when I cast a person, that I’m capturing a little bit of their spirit and their soul. Plaster does break. When I make my work and it’s broken, I really want people to see that even though this person is strong, they’ve obviously gone through it—their spirit is broken, their body is broken, but they’re still standing. They’re still there to tap into that strength. I hope people feel that when they look at my work. A lot of people say to me, “Your work is so haunting.” They’re ghosts in a way. They’re there, but they’re not there. If it’s about the past, like Bobby Seale, or that moment of history, it’s there. It still lingers.

GOLDEN: Exactly. Can we talk a little bit about Not My Circus, the exhibition at the Seattle Art Museum? Because that forms itself as a full installation. You’re giving us the sculptures, but also context. What drew you to the circus, and can you tell us what Not My Circus means?

DAVIS: I’ve always been drawn to the circus because of the fantasy of it and the magic and the showmanship, because I come from that. I’ve always wanted to do a circus show. This show is about control from the top down, from the government all the way down to the mother, the woman that’s in a relationship and being controlled by her husband, an abusive relationship. It’s about control at home, in the workplace, and the government; how we deal with narcissists and manipulators. How do you find your strength to leave? For instance, I have this gilded cage with a half woman, half lion in it. I know a lot of women that have been like her before, where although the bars of your cage are open, you stay because of the gaslighting, the abuse, the manipulation, and the fear. But if you tap into that lion that’s inside you, you’ll have the strength to walk through those open bars. I’m so excited about the installation part, which comes from my filmmaking and theater background, because I really want people to walk into a space and feel like they’re in that.

DAVIS: Exactly. I have the paintings in this circus tent and the ringmaster, who has monkeys crawling all over him, holding the gaslight and whips. So he’s gaslighting and whipping you at the same time, with a smile on his face like most narcissists. Especially during COVID, a lot of people were separated from their workplace and their families, and it was a time to reflect on what and who they wanted in their life, and how to move on. I thought it was a subject that we can all relate to, where we find ourselves in this circus of emotions and people. It’s that moment when you say, “It’s not my monkey. It’s not my circus. I’m out.” Even in the paintings, I have these patches with these codes that, although you’re trapped in the circus, there’s always a way to be free. Not My Circus is that moment where you recognize what’s happening and it’s time to go.

GOLDEN: Seeing both these bodies of work, it feels like your work is broadening and deepening. What’s inspiring you? What are you looking at, thinking about, reading, watching? What is allowing you to think about your work in new and different ways?

DAVIS: I’ve been thinking about my work differently for years, but my capacity to produce what I want has been so limited. I am a single mother. I ran The Underground [Museum] and Noah’s estate. And slowly, as my son gets older and I prioritize certain things, I want to be able to take these shows to another level. Soon people will see some short films from me, some collaging. I’m making paintings. There might be a performance. So being able to not hide, not be scared, and really express myself and show people what’s going on in this crazy brain of mine. Did I answer the question?
GOLDEN: Absolutely. I was trying to get at how your own life and experiences are leading this moment of practice.

DAVIS: I can’t make work unless it’s coming from a deep place. I’ve been commissioned, and sometimes if I’m not feeling it, I just trash it. I can’t do it if it’s forced. But if it comes from an experience, like Not My Circus or even Wishful Thinking with my travels, definitely.

GOLDEN: But we feel that in your work, because it’s clear it comes out of a deep intellectual place, but also a very clear emotional place. When I encounter your sculptures, I know that you’re creating the possibility for these figures, these spirits, these people to be seen—that idea of not just representation, but visibility.
DAVIS: Exactly. Telling more stories. Actually, what I’m getting into now is a story of all the Black women that got on the boats between the two wars and went to Paris.
GOLDEN: The expatriates leaving the US and going to Europe between the World Wars.

DAVIS: And [Ada] “Bricktop” [Smith]. I don’t want to give too much away about that, but it’s a larger project that I’m working on. Also The Frogs of Harlem. I want to tell their story. History does inspire me a lot because I’m Black. Not a lot of people know about The Frogs and Bert Williams and their influence in Harlem being, I feel, the catalyst.
GOLDEN: So it’s about recovering the stories that have not been told.
DAVIS: Exactly. Unearthing.
GOLDEN: Embodying them with their humanity and with what we know is the foundation on which much of our work, our lives, our creativity, and even our own freedoms now exist because of.

DAVIS: Right now, it’s more important than ever that we tell these stories because they’re burning the books. They haven’t gone into museums yet and started burning, dismantling everything. So right now, the safest space for our stories are museums.

GOLDEN: Right. You’re making this work for a present and a future, but it also feels as if you’re thinking about where your works live within these longer and larger art histories. You are adding to an understanding of the human form through your practice, its materiality, but also through its broader meanings as you imbue each of these with a sense of the stories that each of your figures holds and tells.
DAVIS: I couldn’t have said it better.
GOLDEN: So now that these bodies of work are made, what’s going on in the studio right now?

DAVIS: I’m making these smaller maquettes for Wishful Thinking. Everyone’s like, “It’s such a big footprint and I can’t put it in my home.” So I’m making smaller works, collaborating with Sidney Garber on a jewelry line, and working on Not My Circus. When it leaves Seattle, it’ll go to Jeffrey Deitch and it’ll be a larger show with more circus freaks. I have my first show in Paris, so I’m just going to be in the studio collaging and making video work for the circus show. I’m looking forward to having time to experiment and push ideas I’ve been meditating on and marinating in.

GOLDEN: I know I’m not the only one who cannot wait to see it. So Karon, thank you. It has always been such a joy to engage with your work, to feel all of the power that you put into what it means to think about the human form and to think about it as a form of not just art making, but resistance to the ways in which there are stories not told, lives not honored. Your work lives as a monument, a way to meditate on these ideas in a form sometimes of a memorial, but always with this deeply felt sense of joy as well. I always feel so grateful here at The Studio Museum [in Harlem] when we have the chance to have your work on view and see the way in which it lives, for so many, as a deep and profound experience to be in the presence of the people that you make.

DAVIS: Thank you. Wow. That just fills my heart with so much joy. You have to be so vulnerable to be an artist, and be in the studio, and make your work. And although you love it, you never know how people are going to react or see it or understand it or what their gaze is going to be. So I appreciate you and all that you do.
GOLDEN: Many will have the chance now, in these coming months, to see your work on view in many places. So I know we all look forward to that.

items.title: Ambika Mod Can’t Stop Thinking About What She’s Eating Next
items.description: Ambika Mod Can’t Stop Thinking About What She’s Eating Next
items.author: Interview
paragraphs: Ambika Mod Can’t Stop Thinking About What She’s Eating Next

Ambika Mod can get a laugh and break your heart in the same scene. She came up through British sketch comedy, crossed into drama with I Hate Suzie and This Is Going to Hurt, and carried the romantic saga One Day as Emma Morley, a role that made her a name on both sides of the Atlantic. Now, the 31-year-old shows up in the second season of Netflix’s funny and violent spy thriller Black Doves as Laila, an operative with a sharp tongue and high body count. Here, she takes us inside her sleepless nights, Chipotle habit, and unpopular opinions about French cooking.
What’s something you’ll never get rid of?

The thing that comes to mind is lip balm. I have a really codependent relationship with it. Probably just means I’m not hydrated enough, but that’s not a problem that I’m able or willing to solve at this time.
What’s the last text you sent?

This isn’t the last text I sent, but the last message I sent to someone was replying to Anya Magliano, who sent me that American comedian who has that character called Chanty Beluga, where the joke is that she just introduces herself in different contexts as Chanty Beluga, and that’s the whole joke. But I was not familiar with her work, so that’s the last message I sent to someone. Is that interesting to anyone?
What’s the most expensive mistake you’ve made?

There was a short period of time when I was like nine or ten where I convinced my mom that I really wanted to play the saxophone. She was like, “Okay, but are you actually going to practice?” And I was like, “Yes.” So we hired a saxophone, I had the lessons, and obviously never practiced. But it’s just so insane that I decided out of nowhere that I wanted to play the saxophone, and she used money that she didn’t really have to help me achieve my dream, like the good immigrant mother that she is. All this to say, that was a monumental waste of everyone’s time and money and effort, mainly my mom’s, and I’m really sorry to her for that.
What’s a habit you’d love to break?

You are talking to the queen of bedtime revenge procrastination. All I want is to consistently get a good eight, nine hours sleep every single night, as I know that that is something that me and my body physically needs in order to function properly. And yet something just happens between the hours of 9 and midnight, 1:00 a.m. where I can just spend hours on my phone, watching TV, just sort of popping around the house, doing various administrative tasks that don’t need to be done, but yet I feel I must undertake in order to maintain some kind of control in my own life. If there’s a fix for that, someone get in touch because I’m so tired.
I think I’ve just told you that. I can kill so many hours with absolutely nothing of substance and that is why I’m worried about how the rest of the course of my life is going to play out.
What’s the best decision you made today?

I didn’t actually make this decision today, but it was something that happened today, which was there’s this girl I’ve known tangentially for a while through work and through Instagram, and we chatted very sparingly on and off over the years, but I messaged her a few months ago being like, “I always thought we’d get on and I’m looking to make new friends in my 30s. Do you want to hang out?” And she was like, “Oh my god, yes. I’ve always thought the same thing.” And we finally had lunch today and it was so wholesome and so nice and we really got on, at least I hope we did. And if she ever reads this and thinks differently, that’s utterly humiliating. But I just think it’s a really nice thing to know that there are so many amazing people out there that you’ve not yet met and there are so many amazing connections yet to come. Even at the ripe old age of 31.
What’s the pettiest thing I’ve done?
I didn’t actually do this, but someone suggested recently that I hire an Etsy witch to hex a man who did me wrong. I didn’t do it, but I thought about it really hard.
What song do I know every word to?

I know all the words to a lot of songs. Sorry to brag, but I have an excellent melodic and lyrical memory. But the most impressive song I know all the words to is Billy Joel’s “We Didn’t Start the Fire.” And actually last year, when I did a one man show on the West End, I found a way to shoehorn that song into the show and I just sang the first two verses of it on stage by myself and made everyone listen to me. And isn’t that the American dream?
What’s something you were wrong about?

I feel like I’m wrong about quite a lot of stuff. I’m a big catastrophizer. My mind will go there quickly and seamlessly and effortlessly. So often, the things that I’m wrong about are things going better than I anticipated.
What’s the best meal you’ve had this year?

It’s maybe not the best meal I’ve had this year, but it’s something that’s immediately sprung to mind. There was a week in, I want to say May, where I was going through a bit of a rough patch. I took a mental health week where I basically just stayed at home and canceled a lot of my plans, and in that week I ordered Chipotle like three times. I ordered the exact same burrito bowl, and those burrito bowls are quite big, so I had leftovers, so I ended up having leftovers an additional three nights that week. I ended up having the same Chipotle burrito bowl six nights in that week and it was absolutely delicious every single time. If you want a proper answer, I went to this restaurant called Rogues in February in Hackney that had a really good rep, and that food was actually delicious, but it was also part of just a much bigger, nicer day. So it’s like the meal enhanced the lovely day that was had. But if I think about the food in isolation, Chipotle’s winning every time.
What’s your most irrational fear?

This isn’t like a humble-brag. I don’t think any of my fears are irrational. All my fears, all my genuine fears are deeply existentially based. So I’m scared of regret. I’m scared of wasting my potential. I’m scared of stagnation over many, many years. These are the things that I’m afraid of in this mortal realm. I do have trypophobia. Actually, I can’t even talk about it. It’s so disgusting. I once Googled it and I almost was sick in my mouth. It’s actually like the thought, even visualizing small [inaudible]. Oh my God, I couldn’t even finish saying it. Good luck transcribing that to the written word.
Ooh. I am always jealous of people more or less successful than me, especially if they’re younger, which is becoming increasingly the case.
What have you waited in line for lately?

I’m a British person who lives in London, so I’m queuing all day every day. I don’t know why the instance of queuing that’s coming first and foremost to my mind is when me and my friends went to go see Hilary Duff in September at the O2, and we obviously queued to get into that, and that was a really good night. When she sang “What Dreams Are Made Of” at the end, it was genuinely the most euphoric three minutes of my entire life.
What do you talk to yourself about?

This feels like a trick. I could try and manipulate this answer to come off as really worldly and socially conscious, but aren’t we all just talking to ourselves about ourselves and how we’re perceived by others? Because that’s what I’m doing.
What can’t you stop thinking about?

This also feels like a trick, like a trap. I wish I could not say I can’t stop thinking about myself and how I’m perceived by others, but that is a major part of the narrative. I also can’t stop thinking about what I’m going to eat next. I feel like my days are just running on a routine of what am I going to feed myself? Having to eat three times a day is really exhausting and I love to eat. But my god, you always just have to be thinking about the next meal and you can’t always be getting Chipotle three times a week.
Who do you text first with good news?
Depends what the news is. The most consistent two are my family group chat or my best friend Abby. And then of course when the time is right, my therapist.
What’s my most unpopular opinion?

I feel like I have a lot of unpopular opinions that I don’t have the time or scope or breadth to go into now via this title or this medium. But I will say that the French don’t know how to cook. I’m not going to say anything more about that, I’m just going to leave that out there, let people do with that as they please. I might regret that later, but it’s what’s happening now.
What did you think of these questions?
I thought that there were a lot of them. Thank you.

items.title: Watch Wu-Tang Clan Perform ‘Triumph,’ ‘Bring Da Ruckus’ at NFL Thanksgiving Halftime Show
items.description: Wu-Tang Clan showcased a slew of classic hits during the NFL Thanksgiving Day Game Halftime Show.
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Wu-Tang Clan showcased a slew of classic hits during the NFL Thanksgiving Day Game Halftime Show.

The annual match-up pitted the Chicago Bears against the Detroit Lions at at Ford Field in Detroit, with the hip-hop group taking the field midway through. The game, which aired on CBS, also saw Broadway singer Antonio Cipriano performing the National Anthem.

The group, joined by Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith on drums, kicked it off with “Triumph” from their 1997 album Wu-Tang Forever. The rappers also showcased a medley that included “C.R.E.A.M,” “Da Mystery of Chessboxin,” and “Bring Da Ruckus.” Notably, Ol’ Dirty Bastard’s son Young Dirty Bastard performed his father’s lines off 1995 single “Shimmy Shimmy Ya.”

Wu-Tang Clan were recently inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame during a ceremony in Los Angeles. During the ceremony, all living members of the Staten Island group hit the stage to perform a medley of some of their biggest hits, including “C.R.E.A.M.” and “Wu-Tang Clan Ain’t Nuthing ta F’ Wit.” They got a spirited introduction from Chris Rock.

Earlier this year, the group celebrated the Knicks’ championship victory with a performance on The Tonight Show. The musicians showcased a medley of performed a medley of two songs, “Bring Da Ruckus” and “C.R.E.A.M.,” on the late-night show, with the help of the NBA team themselves.

Wu-Tang Clan played a small (but apocryphally pivotal) role in the team’s championship run. During Game Four, the Wu-Tang Clan provided the halftime entertainment, taking the stage when the Knicks were down a seemingly insurmountable 29 points. Had the Knicks lost, the Spurs would’ve tied the series at two games apiece. Despite the heavy deficit, Method Man ended the performance by declaring, “Knicks in five.” The team then rallied to win Game Four 107 – 106, then dispatched the Spurs in Game Five a couple of days later.

items.title: Ariana Grande’s Best On-Screen Roles
items.description: Ariana Grande may be one of the biggest pop stars in the world, but she’s also a true multi-hyphenate, known for her uncanny impressions and acting chops. Grande can hit a killer vocal run, produce a sleek beat, and steal a scene with terrific comedic timing.
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: Ariana Grande may be one of the biggest pop stars in the world, but she’s also a true multi-hyphenate, known for her uncanny impressions and acting chops. Grande can hit a killer vocal run, produce a sleek beat, and steal a scene with terrific comedic timing. (It’s called range.) Her Hollywood career has grown with her pop star status — she started as a Broadway baby, singing her heart out in the musical 13, and eventually became one of Nickelodeon’s most beloved airheads as she played Cat Valentine on Victorious.

Now, she’s starring alongside Robert De Niro in the new movie Focker-In-Law, which is out this week. So what better time to look back at the roles that have helped the megastar get to this point? Here are some of her most impressive moments both on the big and small screens.

- ‘Zoolander 2’ Part of what makes Grande’s acting career so much fun to watch is that she never does what anyone is expecting her to do — and she’s not above extreme silliness. That makes her Zoolander 2 performance particularly entertaining. It’s extremely brief, but she pops on-screen just in time to have a wild orgy with Hansel (Owen Wilson). The scene marked her first time meeting Ben Stiller, who she reunites with in Focker-In-Law. She looked back at their meet-cute fondly during a recent appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon: “He was directing me in an orgy scene in Zoolander 2 with a hippo and Susan Sarandon,” she shared. “So right off the bat, we had a comfortability.” —Julyssa Lopez

Grande is one of the best parts of Adam McKay’s 2021 satire Don’t Look Up. She plays Riley Bina, a major pop star who is out-of-touch with the world — and the fact that a humanity-ending comet is headed Earth’s way. Once people start believing PhD student Kate Dibiasky (Jennifer Lawrence) and her advisor Dr. Randall Mindy (Leonardo DiCaprio) about their chilling prediction, Bina performs her new song “Just Look Up” with her cheating boyfriend, DJ Chello (Kid Cudi). The scene finds Grande delivering killer one-liners like, “Listen to the goddamn qualified scientists, we really fucked it up this time” while suspended onstage and sporting a ridiculous get-up of white feathers. According to McKay, many of the song’s lyrics were improvised by Grande. —Maya Georgi

- ‘Swindle’ In 2013, Nickelodeon adapted Gordon Korman’s 2008 novel Swindle, shaping it into a made-for-television heist movie revolving around two friends who set out to recover a $1.2 million baseball card. They form an unlikely group with other kids from their school harboring secret skills, and Grande steps in as a cheerleader with an undercover geeky side. The film came during her Sam & Cat days, and teamed her up with co-star Jennette McCurdy, while also letting her go beyond her flaky Cat persona. —J.L.

- ‘Wicked: For Good’ When Grande reprises the role of Glinda for the second half of the Wicked tale, she’s planning her wedding to Prince Fiyero, all of Emerald City idolizes her, and everything is as she always wished — or is it? As Glinda reevaluates her life and decides to change paths to help her friend Elphaba (Cynthia Erivo), there are fewer of the rollicking comedy moments that made Grande’s performance in the first film so fun to watch. But with big songs like “I Couldn’t Be Happier,” “The Girl in the Bubble,” and the booming duet “For Good,” she makes clear why she was a natural fit for the iconic role. —Kate Storey

- ‘Scream Queens’ Guest-starring on the campy horror-comedy television show Scream Queens as Chanel #2 was Ariana Grande’s first adult role after leaving Nickelodeon’s Sam & Cat to focus on her music. Creator Ryan Murphy said in 2015 that initially, Grande “was just going to do one episode, but she loved the process so much that she wanted to do more.” Even though she played a corpse in a few of those episodes, Ari’s comedic skills shine through, especially in a scene where her character’s ghost visits Emma Roberts’ Chanel #1. Grande is hilarious when speaking about her afterlife in hell. Whether her character is that she’s in a bad mood because Adolf Hitler was motorboating her boobs or that Jesus broke into heaven and stole the dinosaurs, she steals every scene. —Alison Weinflash

- ‘Victorious’ Let’s look beyond the fact that Cat Valentine seemingly has a legitimate lobotomy in the middle of the Victorious run. There would not be an Ariana Grande without the exposure, preparation, and genuine war stories that the cast ofVictorious went through. While the will-they-won’t-they nature of Cat’s relationship with Robbie (Matt Bennett) was finally resolved in the apocalyptic music video for “One Last Time,” the most memorable musical moments of the series all involved Grande: from the karaoke bar rendition of “Give it Up” to the “They didn’t say I couldn’t sing” riff on the Victorious iCarly collab “Leave It All to Shine.” As Cat, Grande earned her place in the Hollywood Arts High School hall of fame and started her path toward becoming a household name. —C.T. Jones

- ‘SNL’ Ariana Grande has hosted SNL three times now, and she always makes her appearances memorable by leveraging her exceptional impersonation skills, showcasing her comedy agility, and refusing to shy away from being wildly silly.
