We’ve seen her play Jennifer Lawrence during a Family Feud recreation and playing a shy intern who saves her radio station with her ability to sound like everyone from Shakira to Celine Dion. But her most beloved contributions might be in an off-key bridesmaid in the famed Domingo skit and giving us a hilarious take on Home Alone. —J.L.

- ‘Focker-In-Law’ Grande’s character in Focker In Law, Olivia Jones, is a multi-hyphenate not unlike the actress who portrays her. Just swap the gold records for FBI credentials, throw in vegan cooking chops, and you have a future in-law (to grandpa Jack Byrnes, reprised brilliantly by Robert De Niro) hell-bent on entering the “circle of trust” in record time. Grande plays the ultra-competitive Liv with exacting comedic timing, offering the perfect foil for Ben Stiller’s goofball insecurity. —Shirley Halperin

- ‘Wicked’ It takes self-determination, drive, and a lot of pink to make the world’s most coveted role your own. Ariana Grande wasn’t the frontrunner when Universal first announced it would be making a Wicked film. But the Petal singer fought to claim Glinda’s glitter wand. “Oz has been my safe space for as long as I can remember,” she wrote in an open letter to fans before the film’s premiere. It’s hard to imagine a world where the gleeful shrieks of Grande’s “Popular” outro didn’t exist — and her participation in the John M. Chu duology is a career-defining moment, proof the former Nick star is never far from her musical theater roots. —C.T.J.

items.title: Snoop Dogg Teams Up With Feid for Thanksgiving Single ‘Gracias x Todo’
items.description: Feid and Snoop Dogg joined forces for a gratitude-filled single “Gracias x Todo.” The track, released in honor of Thanksgiving, celebrates “gratitude, perseverance, and the importance of appreciating life’s journey,” per a press release.
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Feid and Snoop Dogg joined forces for a gratitude-filled single “Gracias x Todo.” The track, released in honor of Thanksgiving, celebrates “gratitude, perseverance, and the importance of appreciating life’s journey,” per a press release.

The music video for the track highlights people and moments that have shaped Feid’s life, including members of his family. In the clip, Feid pays tribute to his grandparents, giving thanks for their influence. In its closing scene, he is joined by the Fundación Good Kidz children’s choir.
The musician shared the video on Instagram, writing, “Happy thanksgiving for you all!!”

Feid first previewed “Gracias x Todo” during the 27th Annual Latin Grammy Awards last week, where Snoop Dogg made a surprise appearance as part of the song’s debut alongside Divino, Lil Supa, Baby Ranks, and DJ Premier.

Feid was up for three awards at this year’s ceremony, including Best Urban Performance and Best Rap/Hip-Hop Song alongside Lil Supa. Surprisingly, he won Best Reggaeton Performance for “Verano Rosa,” his feature with fellow Colombian star and former partner, Karol G.

Feid will tour in arenas across North America and Mexico on his Ferxxo – The Green Star Tour 2027 next year. The trek kicks off Feb. 5 in Orlando, and will visit major cities throughout the United States, Canada, and Mexico, including two closing performances at Mexico City’s Palacio de los Deportes.
On Saturday, Feid will perform as part of the rescheduled Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, which originally scheduled to be held today in New York City.

items.title: Donald Trump Rants About ‘Radical Far Left,’ Ballroom Critics in Thanksgiving Post
items.description: Donald Trump celebrated Thanksgiving by posting a lengthy screed taking aim at the “radical far left,” critics of his ballroom project, and “murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors.”
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: Donald Trump celebrated Thanksgiving by posting a lengthy screed taking aim at the “radical far left,” critics of his ballroom project, and “murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors.”

The president, writing on Truth Social, opened the post with a sincere note: “HAPPY THANKSGIVING TO ALL AMERICAN PATRIOTS WHO HAVE WORKED SO HARD TO MAKE OUR COUNTRY GREAT!” He then launched into a rant-filled tirade that was far less grateful.

“Additionally, I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated,” Trump wrote. “Also, I would like to wish a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left, those that are looking to change our Court System to that of Sharia, those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work.”

He continued, “I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance. These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately, thereby saving the Great State of Minnesota, which has no chance if they are allowed to stay.”

He then shifted focus to the White House and his ballroom, which has yet to be completed. “I want to commiserate with those Reporters and Citizens who don’t understand filth, dirt, lack of maintenance, and corruption, and are upset with me because I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House,” Trump noted. “It hasn’t been properly painted, or taken care of, for years. I felt strongly that, after being built in 1792, it was time to fix up the White House which is, after all, a primary symbol of our Country. Today, it has never looked better, and will soon have the Ballroom that Presidents have sought for over 150 years.”

He concluded with a final thank you to “the murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors, who illegally entered our Country from other countries’ jails, prisons, mental institutions, and places unknown, to rape, plunder, and kill American Citizens in record numbers.”

“They are mostly gone now, brought back to their point of origin and, hopefully, living a beautiful and idyllic life, and promising, ideally, never to kill innocent people again, but we won’t have to worry about that, because they are GONE but, Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from Faraway Lands,” Trump affirmed. “We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!”

Trump’s Thanksgiving post followed another about his pal Russian president Vladimir Putin, explaining that he would “like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe.”

As per annual tradition, the president pardoned a Thanksgiving turkey earlier this week. During the event, Trump went so far as to joke he would send two turkeys receiving a presidential pardon to the same infamous Salvadoran prison where he sent undocumented migrants to be tortured — a classic act of gratitude in the holiday spirit.

items.title: Hoda Kotb Defends Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponement: ‘I’m Relieved’
items.description: After the announcement yesterday that the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed due to weather, the event’s co-host Hoda Kotb stopped by Late Night to express her relief that it has been rescheduled for Saturday.
items.author: Emily Zemler
paragraphs: After the announcement yesterday that the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed due to weather, the event’s co-host Hoda Kotb stopped by Late Night to express her relief that it has been rescheduled for Saturday.

“The people who have been preparing this 100-year parade have been working tirelessly for a year-plus,” Kotb told host Seth Meyers. “The musical acts are incredible. So imagine spending all that time painting every little bit of every float, wondering if the float is going to fly away somewhere. So the good news is, to me, I’m relieved. Saturday is going to be amazing. Everybody’s still hanging out. We’re going to watch it anyway.”
She added, “It’s going to be literally out of this world. It’s amazing.”

Weather experts have been warning U.S. residents about a rapidly approaching storm system making its way up the east coast, bringing with it high winds, heavy rains, and flood warnings. According to CNN, winds in New York City are expected to reach around 25 to 35 mph today — which would be dangerous for the parade’s famous floats and giant balloons.

“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said in a statement. “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”

This is the first time the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has been postponed because of inclimate weather. It was cancelled in 1942, 1943, and 1944 because the U.S. needed all excess helium and rubber for the World War II effort.

Kotb is set to co-host the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade alongside Savannah Guthrie and Al Roker. Grammy-nominated singer Raye is expected to open the parade with a holiday performance featuring her sisters, Amma and Absolutely; followed by floats and performances by Wyclef Jean, Smash Mouth, Natasha Bedingfield, Icona Pop, JoJo, Hunger Games star McKenna Grace, and Queen Latifah. No additional changes to the parade programming or lineup have been announced.

items.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade No Longer Happening on Thanksgiving Day
items.description: Christmas is canceled! Or at the very least, delayed. The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is reportedly moving from its titular Thanksgiving Day to Saturday due to inclement weather. Since Santa’s arrival at the end of the parade marks the end of turkey-lurkey
items.author: Bethy Squires
paragraphs: Christmas is canceled! Or at the very least, delayed. The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is reportedly moving from its titular Thanksgiving Day to Saturday due to inclement weather. Since Santa’s arrival at the end of the parade marks the end of turkey-lurkey time and the beginning of Christmas, the schedule change also cuts the holiday season two days short. Think of it as revenge for years of Christmas carols playing by Halloween.

“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” a rep from Macy’s told NBC News. Thanksgiving Day is predicted to bring a nasty nor’easter, and had the parade proceeded as usual, it would have been miserable for everyone involved. No balloons (not even the hippo one that got people so mad), marchers and viewers soaked to the bone, and the already-curtailed Broadway medley made all the more precarious with slippery ground underneath those character shoes. Plus think of the poor high-school marching bands! Have you ever felt how heavy a water-logged shako hat is? Hell on earth.

This is the first time the parade has been postponed. In the parade’s 100 years, the whole shebang has only been canceled three times — 1942, ’43, and ’44 were no-gos due to wartime rationing. The last time balloons were grounded due to wind was in 1971. The 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will begin Saturday, November 28, at 8:30 a.m. EST. In its place on Thanksgiving Day, NBC will air a rerun of last year’s parade. If you missed Mr. Fantasy in 2025, now is your chance to catch him.

items.title: The Hunting Wives Recap: No More Scissor Sisters
items.description: Six months ago: Brad is planning his promposal when Margo drops by. Jill should be back in a minute, but in the meantime, can he practice his promposal dance on her? Crazy of him to choreograph it to “Lose Control” by Teddy Swims. It’s crazier still for this w
items.author: Christina Grace Tucker
paragraphs: Six months ago: Brad is planning his promposal when Margo drops by. Jill should be back in a minute, but in the meantime, can he practice his promposal dance on her? Crazy of him to choreograph it to “Lose Control” by Teddy Swims. It’s crazier still for this whole performance to be working on her? They almost kiss, but Jill returns from the store in the nick of time.

In the present, Margo is trying to gently talk Brad down like he’s a spooked animal. It works well enough; she gets him to drop the gun and sit with her on the couch. She asks what’s wrong, and the dam breaks. He’s confused about his mother, and this thing his dad said about her not being a killer. He insists there is proof, but Margo reminds him that his mother did kill Starr, and that she was unwell. To say the least of it! She almost has him where she wants him, but Brad’s mind is working now. There were only four people at the lakehouse, and out of all of them, Margo is the only one who had motivation to kill Abby. “Did you care about me at all?” he asks plaintively, before both of their eyes fall on the gun. Margo is the faster draw, and despite Brad begging that he knows how to keep a secret, Margo shoots him. Damn, that is the second teenager she’s murdered. That’s a little nutty, no?

All of this happens mere moments before Sophie arrives, and Margo doesn’t even bother to sugarcoat it. He knew that Margo killed Abby, so she shot him. Sophie locks in. They have to call the cops, and they have to tell Jonny that Brad attacked Margo, so she shot him in self-defense. Sophie gives her a big old shiner to make the story believable, and Jonny buys it. Both because he’s kind of an idiot, but also because Brad killed Chase Brylan, shot his own father, and was on drugs. As far as Jonny is concerned, case closed!

In bed, Sophie is telling Margo that none of this is her fault (all of it is), and Margo is wondering if she is a sociopath. Hmm. I don’t know what you are, babe, but I am a little scared! Sophie insists that if Margo is, so is she. Well … yeah, I could see that. In the morning, Margo is gone, back to Alba to have some memories and a dark day of the soul.

Jed is PISSED to have to leave the campaign trail and deal with Margo and her usual dead body baggage. The fact that she is simply MIA is not helping her case at all! Lincoln Trout is in agreement, and even losing a touch of his trademark cool. “On one hand, voters love her. On the other, she keeps getting wrapped up in fucking murders!” Lincoln Trout wants that lady on a leash ASAP!

When Shopie drops Jack off from school, Graham has had enough. He is pissed upon hearing that she is wrapped up in yet another murder, and he’s not even hearing it from her. “If I had to set a meeting every time a body dropped in your orbit, we’d never get anything done!” You know what? Fair enough! He threatens her with full custody, and Sophie goes kinda Margo on his ass, if I’m being honest? She’s like Oh, you think I hang out with murderers? Go ahead, take my son, see what happens. Girl! This is not a compelling case to keep a child in your custody! Finally, Margo reappears, and the bonkers duo makes plans to meet at the Halloween fair.

Nadia goes to see Callie and explain herself. Starr was the one who called the network, like literally seconds before she died, and Nadia used that to get a deal with the network. Three months to crack the case, a budget, and clearance for a fake show. Damn, how much money does the Christian Network have? Probably troubling to discover the real answer, huh? Callie demands to know who really killed Abby, if everything they know is a lie. Nadia admits she doesn’t know, and Callie throws her to curb again … but it does kick her mind into gear. She bugs Jonny for more information, and finally comes back to Nadia, who properly apologizes for lying and manipulating, while also fully admitting that’s part of the job and a part of her personality. Callie wants proof that Nadia cares about her more than the show, and just when I start to think that Callie has gone too hard, Nadia goes harder. She sits down and whips up an email that says she resigns from her job and the show effective immediately, because she fell in love with the star. LOVE! Awwww, God bless lesbians, never change, my people! Callie stops her from sending the email because she’s not a fucking idiot, and even though she loves her man, she is aware that he might have fumbled the bag here. She wants everything Nadia has on this murder, now. The two of them put the motives and people in place REALLY damn fast, and by the time the scene ends, the two of them are sure Margo killed Abby. Bad news for Margo!

At the Halloween fair, the vibes are bad, immediately. Lincoln Trout calls Sophie on her way there, casually informing her that she will never see Margo again, and if she tries, Jack very well might go missing. Oh fun! She calls Margo to tell her about this new wrinkle in their lives, but Margo is about to find out what her new life looks like. A giant man grabs her at the fair and escorts her to Lincoln, who tells her there is a new world order: his. No more fun and games on this campaign trail; she is under 24/7 supervision, and her bodyguard, Kane, seems very comfortable with breaking fingers. This is all told to Margo seconds before she joins Jed on stage, and in the crowd, she and Sophie look at one another, two sets of big blue eyes quivering with tears and lesbian longing. Yikes!

• Margo’s trailer-induced flashback involves a teenage Margo begging her mother to wake up and help her sew a thrifted prom dress. Her mother comes to enough to help, but the mother-daughter bonding time is interrupted by a young Zelda, looking for money. She pistol-whips Margo’s mom, then takes Margo’s money, imparting some wisdom to a young, impressionable Margo. “She eats what she hunts; you eat what you hunt.” It’s a dog-eat-dog world, girlie — welcome to it!

• Jamie, so nice to see you again! I wish it were not because your best friend was killed, and I wish you were not sobbing in a server alley about it. Nadia comes to get information about the lake house night, but Jamie isn’t about to talk about it at work. They agree to meet at a hotel, but not before Jamie stops by Sophie’s place to give her a heads up. No matter how much stammering and panicking she does, this boy is not moved. He’s right! Sadly, the odds for teenagers on this show are really bad! Stay alive at all costs, Jamie! Not a great sign that Sophie ends up reporting this to Jed, is it?
• Love the little moment when Chet and Jonny agree on the hat. Rock those hats, boys!

items.title: Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Leads With $15 Million on Thanksgiving Eve, ‘Focker In-Law’ Earns $5 Million on Opening Day
items.description: “Sunrise on the Reaping” stuffed the box office competition ahead of Thanksgiving, generating $15 million on Wednesday. Fueled by positive word-of-mouth, Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” prequel looks to collect $85 million over the five-day holiday period, which wo
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: “Sunrise on the Reaping” stuffed the box office competition ahead of Thanksgiving, generating $15 million on Wednesday. Fueled by positive word-of-mouth, Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” prequel looks to collect $85 million over the five-day holiday period, which would push its domestic tally to $233 million.

Despite opening last weekend, “Sunrise on the Reaping” towering over two new releases. Disney’s animated “Hexed” earned $7.6 million from 3,725 theaters, and Universal’s comedy “Focker In-Law” grossed $5.3 million from 3,382 venues on their respective opening days. (“Focker In-Law” didn’t have Tuesday previews; showtimes began on Wednesday.) Although “Hexed” has pulled ahead on Wednesday charts, the fantasy adventure is projected to finish the weekend in third place behind “Focker In-Law.” Based on updated projections, “Hexed” is now targeting a five-day debut of $31 million to $35 million, while “Focker In-Law” is aiming for $35 million to $36 million over the same frame. Both films are falling short of pre-release expectations, which forecasted a $40 million to $45 million haul.

Elsewhere, Netflix’s Brad Pitt-led “The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” brought in $910,00 from 252 Imax screens on Wednesday. The sequel to Sony’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which isn’t getting a traditional wide release, is expected to earn $4 million to $5 million by Sunday.

In the case of “Hexed,” this opening weekend could spell trouble. That’s because the studio spent more than $200 million to produce the film, and theaters keep about half of ticket sales. So the studio needs the movie to resonate in international markets, and throughout holiday season, to justify the sizable prize tag.

Disney has long dominated the Thanksgiving corridor, and the studio’s animated sequels, namely “Moana 2” and “Zootopia 2,” are some of the holiday’s biggest earners of all time. Post-pandemic, however, Disney has struggled with original offerings, including 2024’s “Wish” ($31 million over its first five days) and 2022’s “Strange World” ($18 million debut over its first five days). “Wish” tapped out with $254 million worldwide on a $200 million budget, while “Strange World” left theaters with $73 million globally on a $180 million budget. What’s promising in this case, though, is that audiences seem to like “Hexed,” which was awarded an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. Positive sentiment should help the film’s box office longevity. The story follows a teen girl who discovers magical powers that take her from suburbia to Hexe, the world of witches.

“Focker In-Law” also carries a sizable budget; Universal and Paramount co-financed the film for $90 million. Although theatrical comedies have become a box office rarity, the three prior “Focker” movies were notable box office winners. The original comedy of errors, 2000’s “Meet the Parents,” starring Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro as mismatched in-laws Greg Focker and Jack Byrnes, generated $330 million worldwide. The 2004 sequel “Meet the Fockers” is the highest-grossing in the franchise with $522 million worldwide, while 2010’s “Little Fockers” amassed $310 million worldwide. In this installment, Ariana Grande joins in the festivities the girlfriend of Greg’s son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) who meets the family as they gather for Jack’s 80th birthday party. Critics panned the film (a 29% on Rotten Tomatoes) but moviegoers have been more receptive; “Focker In-Law” holds a “B+” grade on CinemaScore exit polls.

Despite the range of offerings, this Thanksgiving will fall short of cementing any box office records. Ticket sales are expected to hit $210 million to $215 million across all films in the marketplace. Thanksgiving 2024 was the holiday’s biggest on record with $422 million across all films, led by “Moana 2″ ($225 million debut), “Wicked” ($118 million) and “Gladiator II” ($44 million). Last year was among the top five with $293 million, boosted by “Zootopia 2” and “Wicked: For Good.” Theater owners aren’t discouraged because domestic ticket sales are already 20% above the same point in 2025. Plus, North American revenues are projected to surpass $10 billion for the first time since Covid upended the theatrical business.

items.title: BBC’s Antisemitism Crisis Represents an Unprecedented Chapter for the World’s Most Trusted News Organization
items.description: It is a dark day for the BBC.
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: It is a dark day for the BBC.

On Thursday, government adviser Lord John Mann announced he is launching an investigation into alleged antisemitism at the broadcaster. It is an unprecedented chapter for the corporation, long held up as one of the most venerable and reliable media institutions in the world.

For those who have been paying attention, however, the move is not surprising following a litany of public missteps dating as far back as 2021, when BBC News misreported an incident in which a group of Jewish students were attacked on a bus in Central London and then doubled down on it, despite eventually acknowledging the reporting lacked accuracy and impartiality.

Later, the broadcaster steadfastly refused to reprimand Gary Lineker, one of its most high-profile sports anchors, as he repeatedly breached its much-touted social media guidelines, which were instituted precisely because of Lineker’s increasingly political Twitter activity. Under the guidelines, high-profile presenters hosting flagship programs are expected to be impartial while the show is on air and for a two-week window before and after. At the time, he called the guidelines “very sensible.”

It was only when last year Lineker reposted an Instagram story about “Zionists” alongside a rat emoji that the BBC finally cut him loose. Even then, rather than a punitive measure, his exit was presented to the public as a mutually agreed decision for the host to leave after the final “Match of the Day” episode aired the following week. The BBC’s press release went on to call him a “defining voice in football coverage” and “thank him for the contribution he has made.”

Critics compared the BBC’s apparently favorable treatment of Lineker to that of former BBC Radio 5 Live broadcaster Danny Baker, who was sacked immediately in 2019 after tweeting an image of a chimpanzee with the caption “Royal baby leaves hospital” just days after Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, gave birth, with the BBC calling it a “serious error of judgment.”

The following month saw yet another incident when the BBC broadcast a little-known rapper’s rant about a former (apparently Jewish) boss, described alternately as a “fucking Zionist” and “bald-headed cunt,” before the crowd was engaged in a chant of “Death to the IDF.” It later emerged that producers had assessed the rapper as “high risk” and yet decided to broadcast his set live.

Even as he embarked on his rant, which BBC chair Samir Shah later acknowledged consisted of “unconscionable antisemitic views,” no one at the broadcaster thought to cut the Glastonbury feed. Shah apologized for the oversight, and the BBC’s director of music, Lorna Clarke, briefly “stepped back” from her duties, although it appears little other action was taken (she has long since returned to her post).

Then, last month, it was revealed that the BBC had reached an out-of-court settlement with one of its top factual producers, Lucie Kon, after she brought a legal claim alleging antisemitic discrimination. Kon, an Emmy and Oscar winner who exec produced “Mr Nobody Against Putin,” had worked for the corporation for 25 years but said that after Oct. 7, when Hamas murdered 1,200 people in Israel and kidnapped 250 more, the atmosphere toward her changed.

The BBC rejected those claims but agreed to pay Kon £400,000 ($520,000) to settle out of court. For health reasons, Kon accepted. By comparison, the average award handed down by courts for race discrimination in the U.K. is £29,532, according to the most recent statistics.

At the same time, the BBC’s reporting on Israel has been an ongoing source of contention. There was the Gaza documentary which failed to tell viewers the narrator was the son of a senior Hamas official, the report speculating Israel had bombed a hospital in Gaza which had actually been hit by a Hamas rocket misfiring and the news story in which an anchor misrepresented a Reuters story, saying the IDF was “targeting … medical teams as well as Arabic speakers” when in fact the medical teams and Arabic speakers were part of the IDF, there to assess patients on the ground.

A leaked internal report last year — the same one that led to BBC boss Tim Davie resigning when it revealed the BBC had doctored one of President Trump’s speeches — noted that BBC Arabic, a part of the corporation’s World Service, had made 215 corrections and clarifications in its reporting of the Israel-Gaza war since 2023, amounting to two a week. At the time, a BBC spokesperson told Variety: “BBC News Arabic strives for the highest standards of journalism across its services.”

(Incidentally, the BBC World Service currently operates in 45 languages, including Arabic, Amharic, English, Hausa, Kirundi, Marathi, Tigrinya, Ukrainian, Urdu and Yoruba. It does not include Hebrew.)
So how did the BBC find itself embroiled in yet another crisis?

Part of the problem stems from the fact that the corporation effectively marks its own homework. While British newspapers are regulated by an independent body, IPSO, the BBC operates the Executive Complaints Unit to investigate grievances about itself.

But there is also a sense that the BBC, even under its new director general Matt Brittin, is not interested in engaging seriously with the issue. Each time there is a public blunder, the BBC will roll out the same playbook: issue a cut-and-paste apology (usually with reluctance), defend its reporting and make a gesture to suggest it has learned a lesson. But the sheer frequency of incidents — only a handful of which even spin out into the public realm — suggests nothing is being learned.

Earlier this month, the corporation’s deputy director-general, Rhodri Talfan Davies, was asked during an on-the-record Q&A session with journalists whether he would support an internal inquiry into antisemitism at the BBC. His response was to deny there was a “deep-rooted issue” or any “institutional discrimination” at the broadcaster. Notably, he didn’t answer the second part of the journalist’s question, namely, if Talfan Davies didn’t think there was antisemitism at the BBC, “Why do you think many of your Jewish employees think there is?”

Even the corporation’s checkbox response to Lord Mann’s announcement on Thursday gives the impression, whether intended or not, that the threat of an investigation into its internal conduct is of little consequence. When approached for comment, a BBC publicist told Variety by email, “We’d also like to direct you to the below statement, that we’ve previously issued,” before copy-and-pasting it underneath.

In his speech announcing the investigation, Lord Mann said he is “not interested in targeting individuals. That would entirely miss the point. I am targeting the institution.” The biggest clue as to the depth of the BBC’s antisemitism problem will be whether the institution even cares.

items.title: Former Disney Boss Bob Iger ‘Got ABC Employee Pregnant’ During Affair, New Book Claims
items.description: Former Disney boss Bob Iger allegedly impregnated an employee in the 1990s, according to an explosive new book, per the New York Times.
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: Former Disney boss Bob Iger allegedly impregnated an employee in the 1990s, according to an explosive new book, per the New York Times.

The newspaper has published an interview with Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan, the author of a forthcoming and reportedly unflattering biography of the Disney big cheese titled “The House of Mouse.”

According to the NYT, the book documents a consensual extramarital relationship between Iger and an “ABC marketer” that took place in the early 1990s when Iger was head of ABC and resulted in a pregnancy. Whelan reportedly writes that the woman, who was at the time rungs below Iger on the corporate ladder, allegedly “suffered through a traumatic termination procedure.”

Iger’s 18-year-long reign (split across two tenures) as Disney CEO ended in March, when he was replaced by parks boss Josh D’Amaro. Iger is due to attend his final Disney board meeting next week – the same day “The House of Mouse” is published.

Whelan told the Times that neither Iger nor Disney spoke to him for the book but said his publisher, William Morrow, received legal letters from Iger’s lawyer raising concerns about the tome painting a “false and defamatory” picture.
“Their instinct was to bully me,” Whelan told the Times. He said he spoke to other sources, including former Marvel CEO Ike Perlmutter, who has a frosty relationship with Iger.

“A character having an ax to grind — or a motivation is a better way of putting it — just makes him a better character,” Whelan said of his sources’ possible agendas. “It doesn’t make them disqualified.”
Variety has contacted Disney and Iger’s legal representative for comment.

In a statement to the Times, the company said: “Bob Iger is one of the most respected CEOs of his generation” pointing to his “bold creative and strategic decisions” and that he leaves Disney “stronger and more innovative.”

items.title: Luca Guadagnino Wants Next Movie to Be a ‘Love Story,’ Confirms ‘American Psycho’ and ‘Separate Rooms’ Not Happening
items.description: Luca Guadagnino wants to return to romance.
items.author: Anna Tingley; Elsa Keslassy
paragraphs: Luca Guadagnino wants to return to romance.

Speaking to Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival where he’s presenting “Artificial,” the Italian filmmaker behind “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All” and “Queer” revealed that he hopes his next directorial endeavor will be another love story.

“I think a lot of inspiration could come from facts of history,” Guadagnino said when asked what he would like to explore in his next film. “I want to make another love story, so I have to think about it, but I want to make a kind movie, another love story.”

He also confirmed that two of his previously announced projects — a new adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ “American Psycho” and the gay romance “Separate Rooms” — are no longer moving forward with him.

“Separate Rooms” was set to be an adaptation of Italian writer Pier Vittorio Tondelli’s 1989 novel about a writer grappling with the death of his lover. Josh O’Connor, who previously worked with Guadagnino on “Challengers,” and Léa Seydoux had been linked to the project since 2024.
“I don’t think I’m doing a movie with Léa Seydoux, unfortunately. That’s not happening,” Guadagnino said. “But I would love to work with Léa, of course.”

The director also addressed the demise of his “American Psycho” adaptation, which was first announced by Lionsgate in October 2024. The film, penned by Scott Z. Burns, was intended to be a fresh interpretation of Ellis’ 1991 novel rather than a remake of Mary Harron’s 2000 cult classic starring Christian Bale. “That’s the job of a director,” he said of its dissolution. “You direct movies and sometimes it happens, sometimes it doesn’t. It’s very simple and linear and usual.”

The filmmaker also dispelled speculation that Robert Pattinson had been in contention to play Patrick Bateman, though he said “he’s a perfect choice for James Bond,” adding: “He’s an incredible star, he’s done so many great roles and I wish someday to work with him, of course.”
Would Guadagnino direct a Bond film? “I would say yes, yes, of course,” he said of the prospect. “I would like to play with icons.”

The director’s upcoming film, “Artificial,” marks another departure from the sweeping romances that have come to define much of his oeuvre. The Amazon MGM Studios feature dramatizes the turmoil at OpenAI surrounding the ousting and subsequent reinstatement of CEO Sam Altman, played by Andrew Garfield.
The film premiered at New York Film Festival and screens at Marrakech Film Festival on Thursday night.

items.title: All 17 Quentin Tarantino Movies, Ranked From Worst to Best
items.description: June, 1977. Cliff Booth runs the projector at the New Beverly Cinema, tends a couple bars, and drives a tow truck to a demolition derby. These are not his only day jobs, and they’re all at night. In his spare time, the ex-stuntman disappears blackmailers with
items.author: Darren Franich
paragraphs: June, 1977. Cliff Booth runs the projector at the New Beverly Cinema, tends a couple bars, and drives a tow truck to a demolition derby. These are not his only day jobs, and they’re all at night. In his spare time, the ex-stuntman disappears blackmailers with a payoff or a bullet. Something called Star Wars has taken over theaters, threatening a half-century of blockbuster family fun. Cliff inhabits an older world, gnarly yet noble, gory and shagadelic. He runs with blaxploitation macks, bored Malibu wives, underworld assassins, the snobby former critic of the Superfood Gazette and whoever that body in the trunk used to be. These are Cliff Booth’s people — and Quentin Tarantino’s, too. Once upon a time in the 1990s, Tarantino was the breakout bad boy of independent film, surf riding the crest of a youth tsunami. Now he’s our reigning entertainer-historian, overstuffing hard-R sensations with motion picture lore. He owns the real New Beverly in actual Los Angeles. So when Netflix agreed to make his Once Upon a Time in Hollywood follow-up, they paid him a fortune to advertise his theater. Franchises have been no-brainers since, well, Star Wars. But a sequel on a streamer is something new for Tarantino. And The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth marks the first time in 30 years that someone besides him has directed one of his screenplays. Let’s get rambling to find out where it ranks in his filmography.

- 17. Past Midnight (1992) He swears he will make only 10 films. We’re starting at 17. Is he lying, or is this list stupid? Probably both. However, this ranking seeks totality: his screenplays, his TV diversions, the simple fact that Kill Bill counts as two. Let’s count all his official writing and directing credits — plus this middling erotic thriller, which earned him a co-producer credit for doctoring the script. (He later polished Crimson Tide and The Rock.) A beautiful social worker with a bodacious lake house gets knocked up by an ex-con who maybe killed his pregnant wife. You hear trace Tarantino elements emerging in Past Midnight’s dialogue, especially when a cop says the phrase “natural born killer.” And a very minor character, the snarky physician, is named “Dr. Zastoupil.” Quentin Tarantino was Quentin Zastoupil through childhood, keeping his stepfather’s surname even after his mom’s second divorce. A teen dropout with acting ambitions, he snagged “Tarantino” back from his biological father. Not because he loved the guy, matter fact he barely knew the son of a bitch. It just sounded better.
- 16. Four Rooms, “The Man From Hollywood” (1995)

After Pulp Fiction won him his first Oscar, he hosted Saturday Night Live, got his head blown off in his buddy Robert Rodriguez’s Desperado, and played an animistic “god with a small g” named Johnny Destiny in the interminable Vegas comedy Destiny Turns on the Radio. Then came this dire anthology. Miramax must have hoped for generational showcase, with studio mascot Tarantino joining Rodriguez and their Sundance youngfriends Allison Anders and Alexandre Rockwell. Each filmmaker writes and directs their own New Year’s Eve farce, set on different floors on a Tinseltown hotel. Tarantino also stars in his entry, playing a fresh-minted shirtbird celebrity who complains if you call his Cristal mere champagne. It’s a wearisome (if admirably self-aware) snapshot of his peak overexposure, and a disastrous victory lap for the renegade age of indie cool.

- 15. My Best Friend’s Birthday (sometime in the 1980s) The rest of Four Rooms’ band of outsiders started directing the regular independent way, with little money and amateur pluck. Anders’ and Rockwell’s first features were black-and-white cheapos about arty goofs, and Rodriguez wrote a book about El Mariachi’s $7,000 budget. Reservoir Dogs looks insanely professional by comparison: soundtrack money, a prosthetic ear, Harvey Keitel. Tarantino’s missing link is this early unfinished comedy he directed about DJ pals on a manic night out. Acolytes peg My Best Friend’s Birthday as a True Romance beta test, though the fuzzy half-hour cut online suggests an alternate timeline where he made loosey autobiographical romcoms instead of meticulous profane epics. Pompadoured with earrings like some rockabilly nerdpunk, his character plainly admits he has a foot fetish.
- 14.75. CSI: Crime Scene Investigation, “Grave Danger — Volumes 1 and 2” (May 19, 2005)

He owns a couple theaters, co-hosts a movie podcast, and wrote a great book of film criticism. Still, deep down, I wonder if Quentin Tarantino is more of a TV guy. His work chases an old forever feeling of channel-surfing into some random weekly episode about characters walking from place to place, meeting people, and getting into adventures. In the 1996 biography King Pulp, author Paul A. Woods memorably quotes Steve Buscemi: “When I saw Pulp Fiction, the little boy watching this big TV, being alone in the room, the TV being his friend — to me, that’s Quentin.” Does that explain why, fresh off Kill Bill’s impressive exertion, he directed a couple hours of a hit procedural he adored? Wiliam Petersen’s brainiac cop Gil Grissom reveals an abiding fandom for Roy Rogers. Frank Gorshin and Tony Curtis play themselves. George Eads’ niceguy Nick hallucinates his own autopsy while buried alive.
- 14.5. ER, “Motherhood” (May 11, 1995)

CSI was already half-lame by 2005. This NBC hospital drama was still blazingly cool in its first season. And while Tarantino dutifully hits CSI’s CBS marks, he brings an exuberant kick (and some cool long takes) to ER’s Mother’s Day episode. One patient is newly earless. Julianna Margulies and Sherry Stringfield lay out on the roof, barefoot and sunglassed.
- 14.25. The best scene in Sin City (2005)

For one cultural millisecond, in the month between the third El Mariachi and the first Kill Bill, Rodriguez was awesomer than Tarantino. Actually, he came off like the real Tarantino: a legitimate peddler of anything-for-a-dollar gut thrills, not a devoted student expostulating the genre curriculum. Alas, Rodriguez early-adopted all the millennium’s annoying industry trends: 3D, CGI backlots, HiDef video, rigid adherence to sacred Comic-Con texts. A lot of hot shit gets fucked in his frantic adaptation of Frank Miller’s comic noir. The ensemble shot in a void; post-production filled in the cartoon cityscape. Tarantino was “Special Guest Director” for helming practically the only sequence without violence, when Clive Owen’s heroic goon drives Benicio Del Toro’s evil goon to the local tar pits. Del Toro’s already dead, which doesn’t stop him from having a very entertaining conversation. Easy to guess this greenscreen pit of hell was not Tarantino’s bag. He kept filming on film, and made celluloid his theaters’ mission statement.
- 14. Kill Bill: Vol 1 (2003) and 13. Natural Born Killers (1994)

Movies! Good for you, or bad? The first Kill Bill ornated Uma Thurman’s vengeance quest with samurai codes, Ennio Morricone needle drops, Shaw Brothers zooms, weeks of wirework, and fountains of bloodgush. When martial arts legend Sonny Chiba rhapsodizes about the sword he just made, it’s sheer religious ecstasy for a cultural obsessive. A decade earlier, director Oliver Stone adapted an early Tarantino screenplay into a screed against media obsession. Woody Harrelson and Juliette Lewis play Bonnie and Clyde plus MTV, sinners idolized into celebrities by our broken culture. Acclaimed cinematographer and psychedelic wizard Robert Richardson shot both Kill and Killers, blending multiple stocks and intense aesthetics. You don’t watch these films. You inhale.

To the straight world of 1994, Tarantino and Stone probably looked like identical madmen. There was no love lost. Tarantino disavowed Stone’s Killers and published his original script as a middle finger. Stone added activist Russell Means as a kind of shaman, declaring with moral authority that the whole problem is “too much TV.” I assume Tarantino thought Stone was a preachy boomer, and that Stone saw Tarantino as everything wrong with a Generation X. Who was right? Are we living in a dark dystopia of true-crime infotainment and mass-transmitted megalomania? Or a wonderworld of multicultural exchange, with no divisions between highbrow and lowbrow, where a “silly Caucasian girl” in Bruce Lee’s clothes becomes a feminist action hero? Actually, they both nailed it. And these Killfests only rank so low because I’m an old man who prefers 20-minute dialogues to 20-minute action scenes.
- 12. From Dusk Till Dawn (1996)

Rodriguez directed and Tarantino wrote this genre mash-up. The divide between their styles is clear as the Tex-Mex border. Dusk’s daylit first hour is pure rancid QT-inflected neo-noir. George Clooney — never meaner, never hotter — and Tarantino himself play the fugitive Gecko Brothers. Killers fatale Juliette Lewis and top Reservoir dog Harvey Keitel are RV-riding normals forced to drive the bros south to El Rey. Oddly, the fun falls off at the halfway twist, when surprise vampires lock the doors at the Titty Twister and trap the cast in a horror-comedy. Still, the closing lines pinpoint Tarantino’s unsteady moral code. “I may be a bastard,” says the last man standing, “But I’m not a fucking bastard.”

From Dusk Till Dawn also has the snake dance: Salma Hayek, wearing little except a Burmese python, pouring liquor down her leg so Tarantino can drink it off her toes. An astonishing scene, really, if you only care about desire. When he directs, Tarantino is comparatively chaste. He prefers a good flirt, with comfortable silences. He’s only filmed one sex scene — in Jackie Brown, in the kitchen, standing, 9/10ths clothed, loveless — unless you count a couple man-to-man assaults. I’m talking about sex because Grindhouse, the flop that ended his Rodriguez partnership, turned into their big sex movie: gauzy with the male gaze, an essential artifact from the dirtbag 2000s. They each made their own film, then released them together as a three-hour double-bill. (Never watch the split-off versions. For better and worse, the three-hour experience depends on too-muchness.)

Rodriguez’s kickoff feature, Planet Terror, is the more obvious HR nightmare: Produced by then-wife Elizabeth Avellán, starring eventual girlfriend Rose McGowan as a gun-legged go-go dancer, overseen by the studio boss who wound up disgraced for assaulting multiple women (including, allegedly, McGowan.) Tarantino’s Death Proof is smarter and safer, punctuating all-female convos with car-assaults by Kurt Russell’s ladykiller stuntman. The director later told the Church of Tarantino podcast that he based Tracie Thoms’ badass driver on a girlfriend and all the women onscreen reflect genuine female posses he rolled with. I dunno. The chicks’ habits mostly evoke novelist Gillian Flynn’s immortal line that “Cool Girls are above all hot.” Lotta booze-swilling daisy-duked dames here, who dig Zatoichi and keep finding new ways to put their feet up. You can’t be cynical when the climax is an act of friend-to-friend hero worship. Stuntwoman Zoë Bell was Thurman’s Kill Bill stunt double. Fascinated by her talent — and furious at the computers invading fast cinema — Tarantino cast Bell as herself to ride on top a Dodge Challenger for an all-time car chase. In her daffy stunt-action charisma, you spot the primordial Cliff Booth: genial, lusty for danger, more than a little insane.
- 10. Django Unchained (2012)

Since we’ve talked about sex, we should talk about race. Spike Lee was not the only one noticing all the n-words in Tarantino’s dialogue. To love his work, you do have to kinda think cultural appropriation is a good thing, that it’s okay for anyone — even a white kid from the South Bay — to melt the cultures he adores into one big pot. That may even be the conventional wisdom; Tarantino’s biggest success is his Blackest. Jamie Foxx stars as the freedman learning the bounty trade from Christoph Waltz’s cheerful German. Tarantino won his second Oscar for a baggy script, which runs an hour longer than Sergio Corbucci’s stupendously garish Django (source of Unchained’s name and theme song). Foxx’s gunslinger is too mythic for any personality, especially compared to Leonardo DiCaprio’s plantation tyrant Calvin Candie. But Tarantino has always been interested in performance as an act of self-preservation. (Track how many people on this list go deep undercover into a life-or-death con.) Foxx comes alive when Django playacts race betrayal as a Black slaver. As the head of Candie’s household, Samuel L. Jackson gives what amounts to a ferocious double role, plotting brilliantly behind a mask of loudmouth servitude.
- 9. Kill Bill: Vol 2 (2004)

After the Crazy 88 fight wraps the first volume on an operatic high, the deadliest woman in the world gets taken down by… Budd, a drunk with a shotgun. Tarantino regular Michael Madsen plays the ruminative assassin as the one person in the Billogy who lives anywhere close to reality. Working in an empty strip club and living alone in the desert, Budd is another proto-Cliff, a doomed killer basking in the slushy margarita of his decay. 2 is great fun — the showdown in Budd’s trailer is Tarantino’s best fight, period — until the talky finale veers baffling. Despite Thurman’s all-in performance, I’m not sure she (or anyone) can fully unpack the romantic-paternal Bill-Bride dynamic. Was the anticlimax purposeful? After months of martial arts training, David Carradine’s one big bit of choreography is a 12-second seated swordfight. Tarantino used to promise a third volume, possibly suspecting that 2’s happy ending left unfinished business.
- 8. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026)

I love it. I love it! You’re telling me David Fincher — the serious man, the hundred-take cyborg, the serial killer fetishist — you’re telling me that David Fincher directed a plotless meander about a dude in puka shells bopping around Los Angeles? Cliff Booth looks fuzzier than Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, because digital still can’t capture night like 35mm. The obvious CGI (and alleged AI) adds to the cut-rate effect — like some high-tech toupee the whole screen is wearing. With Leonardo DiCaprio’s sadsack Rick gone, Pitt’s good-timer Cliff mixes banana margaritas, plays tennis, watches TV with his pops, and walks the earth like Caine in Kung Fu. “I’m not that deep,” he tells Elizabeth Debicki’s tall drink of Aussie. Co-star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II has a specific line, “This don’t mean shit to me,” that gets repeated a couple times. Should we trust that carefree attitude? Is this Tarantino’s Walking Tall Part 2, a low-ambition cruise backward through pleasurable familiar territory? Don’t miss the elegiac resonance. Cliff’s a gig-economy freelancer juggling six or seven jobs, scamming friends out of cash, commodifying his own buff bod, living with a gainfully employed parent. The biggest movie of 1977 is about to bankroll the rise of Industrial Light & Magic, which will do for stuntmen what ChatGPT is about to do to me. From that perspective, Cliff’s commitment to joy isn’t just infectious. Motherfucker, it’s revolutionary. (Read The Hollywood Reporter’s full review here.)
- 7. Reservoir Dogs (1992)

Still his cleanest screenplay, especially when things get messy. A wild bunch of color-coded badmen congregate in a safehouse. Somebody’s dying, somebody’s lying, somebody’s crazy, and everyone’s armed. Skeptics noted similarities to Ringo Lam’s City on Fire. That Chow Yun-Fat thriller has romance, impressive heists, and a sincere cop-criminal friendship. Dogs’ robbery is unseen. The one woman is a doomed bystander. The most tender friendship aims toward oblivion. What a cast: Keitel’s gruff Mr. White, Madsen’s smirkish Mr. Blonde, Tim Roth’s gutshot Mr. Orange. Even pallid quirkster Steve Buscemi looks damn slick as Mr. Pink, nailing Tarantino’s caffeinated patter and the perfect SoCal deployment of “man” as a punctuation mark. Buscemi should have been in all these movies. At a minimum, he should have played any part Tarantino wrote for himself.
- 6. The Hateful Eight (2015)

Skeptics call him ironic or nihilistic, but Tarantino does believe in good guys. The Bride, Cliff Booth, Django, and even Zoë Bell are paragons, their violence justified by righteous vengeance. Django appeared in the original concept of this snowblood frontier mystery, until Tarantino realized his white hell had no place for an iconic moral compass. Django became Major Marquis Warren, plantation-raised Union veteran, brilliant sleuth, unrepentant killer, documented Friend of Lincoln — and the greatest Tarantino character, played by the greatest actor to ever spout a Tarantino monologue. What secret does Samuel L. Jackson understand about his longtime director? Is it just a Tennessee thing: One born in Nashville, the other raised in Chattanooga? Hateful Eight traps Jackson’s disgraced veteran in a stagecoach stop with seven other tough customers. Three hours in a blizzard would feel claustrophobic, if everybody wasn’t such a riot. Kurt Russell’s noose-happy bounty hunter comes off crude and naïve. Jennifer Jason Leigh’s captive looks on, watchful and feral. Walton Goggins chatters memorably as the jerky bigot who worships a Confederate husk played by Bruce Dern. At once statelier and more bugfuck than Django, this second Western of Racism luxuriates toward its nutty-in-ever-sense twist. Make of this what you will: In the High Obama days of liberal goodwill, Tarantino made three features looking back (and ahead) toward fascism and white supremacy.

Yes, Christian Slater is too pretty as Clarence, a Sonny Chiba-worshipping Quentinian comics clerk. Yes, the dark nonlinear screenplay got straightened out with a happy ending. Yes, the score has a lotta marimba. No, I don’t believe a sweet call girl like Patricia Arquette’s Alabama would ever fall for a geeky john her fourth day on the job. Director Tony Scott saw something in Tarantino’s writing, though, that nobody else ever found. Met-cute and insta-wed, Clarence and Alabama flee smoky Detroit for sunny California, with stolen coke in their bag and hell following after them. Gary Oldman, Christopher Walken, and James Gandolfini are all memorable baddies, even more impressive since they all only have a scene or two. A couple detectives come off like lunatics, because they’re played by Tom Sizemore and Chris Penn, men never known for their good behavior. It all works as glossy gutter pulp, set with comic precision in the chlorinated motels and rollercoasters of Los Angeles. But Scott was a true romantic. He makes Alabama and Clarence the greatest of Tarantino’s straightforward heroes, so stupid with passion that even colliding criminal underworlds can’t stop their love. Sound like a fairy tale? Fine. Pretend it’s called Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.
- 4. Inglourious Basterds (2009)

1978’s The Inglorious Bastards was a rude romp about semi-psychotic soldiers in Occupied France. That’s the sort of squad-on-a-mission plot Brad Pitt’s Aldo Raine seems to be arranging in this similar-titled war film. The Lieutenant assembles eight Jewish servicemen (and one Hugo Stiglitz) to scalp a hundred Nazis apiece. But Aldo and his Basterds only show up after a lengthy opening interrogation, which introduces Waltz’s Jew-hunting Hans Landa. Then the Americans mostly disappear for a whole middle hour. The action shifts to a Paris cinema, and a basement bar. Parallel plots converge. Mélanie Laurent’s moviehouse operator seeks revenge for her murdered family. Aldo and his allies devise an attack. Goebbels (that Goebbels) hopes Der Führer (dat Führer) loves his new movie. Basterds’ tavern setpiece marked a complete inversion from Kill Bill’s excess: Twenty dialogue-heavy minutes of twisted-nerve tension followed by 15 onslaught seconds. It’s the Inglourious experience in micro, full of vivid characters and fatal consequences.

After Pulp Fiction, everyone knew what “Tarantinoesque” meant: Funny, shocking, loquacious, retro, now. Then he returned with a marvelous, middle-aged, low-key caper about a desperate flight attendant and a bail bondsman sick of bonding bails. “Didn’t exactly set the world on fire, did you, Jackie?” a lout detective teases the title character, who makes a piddling $16,000 plus benefits before she gets popped smuggling cash with a sprinkle of cocaine. Tarantino was casting Pam Grier for talent, not just stuntcasting her ‘70s fireball persona. When Jackie lands in jail, the soundtrack cranks the song Grier sang for the 1971 prison-hottie wackfest The Big Doll House — but the look on her face tells you the wild days were a long time ago. She finds an unlikely ally in Robert Forster’s Max Cherry, a bond agent weathered by years of scum and bureaucracy. Jackie’s big problem (and biggest opportunity) is Ordell Robbie, a gun dealer astounded at his own cleverness. Add in Robert De Niro’s semi-verbal ex-con and Bridget Fonda’s pothead siren, and you’ve got a collection of misfits in the South Bay — the former home of Quentin Zastoupil. Jackie Brown is the director at his least Tarantinoesque and most Zastoupilian, uncovering surprising soul in a landscape of food courts, airplane-hotel bars, beach pads, delusional small time crooks, and the occasional oil derrick. Transplanting Elmore Leonard’s novel from Miami, Tarantino chopped a gunfight, unrequited the romance, turned a white woman Black — and added one last ambiguous kiss.

What’s your favorite chapter? The buzz in ‘94 fixated on Vincent Vega and Mia Wallace at Jack Rabbit Slim’s, that binary-star supernova of John Travolta’s comeback and Uma Thurman’s arrival. Me and my teen buddies, scared or baffled by love, preferred the middle segment, with a katana-wielding Bruce Willis. The final act of corpse disposal has the most questionable rep, depending whether you think Tarantino’s acting is serviceable or unforgivable. (He’s fine.) Yet it’s the last bit that reveals Jackson’s Jules Winnfield as Pulp’s moral core. Tarantino characters rarely change in the screenwriting-101 sense — he keeps casting Brad Pitt to specifically not do an emotional arc — but Jules is transformed after six point-blank bullets miraculously don’t execute him. In a moment of clarity, he starts wondering over Ezekiel 25:17, the Bible verse he’s been misquoting. Has he been his brother’s keeper? Or the tyranny of evil men? Heavy themes for a sensational quotefest, but Tarantino was always after more than his bratty referential imitators. His characters dress cool, talk cool, murder cool, and know cool things. It’s not enough to just be cool. So Jules becomes a killer who doesn’t kill — a Bad Mother Fucker trying real hard to be the shepherd.
- 1. Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019)

Brad Pitt exudes folkloric chill as convertible cowboy Cliff Booth. Whereas Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton is all hat and no cattle, a whiskey-soured mess with a nervous stutter. They’re near-nobodies in Hollywood’s Hollywood: A stuntman who can’t get stunt jobs, a fading TV star clutching guest parts. One memorable day, they both go to different fake Wests. Rick’s on a backlot doing a cowboy TV pilot. Cliff returns to the defunct western town at Spahn Ranch, where lurks doom. A fatal mood lingers, even if you don’t know the history. Rick got famous on Bounty Law for never bringing back his targets alive. Cliff maybe-definitely killed his wife. Zoë Bell is the stuntlady who refuses to work with a spouse-killer — hilarious, since Kurt Russell plays her stuntman husband, and they were the stuntpeople trying to kill each other four movies ago.

That’s just one way Tarantino Voltrons together his whole filmography into his magnum opus. Here’s a Los Angeles thriller, a meta-western, and an alternate history, with Grindhouse-worthy re-enactments and a whole society incapable of turning off the radio or the television. There’s even — call Oliver Stone! — a meditation on screen violence, with one wannabe murderer declaring “If you grew up watching TV, that means you grew up watching murder!” Is it weird the heroes are older men, while the Mansonites (Margaret Qualley, Sydney Sweeney, Mikey Madison, Austin Butler, Maya Hawke) turned out to be Gen Z’s top stars this decade? I think Tarantino was being honest about late midlife fears, with Rick in particular worrying that some whole rising generation of longhairs is coming for his ass. There’s always been so much you don’t see in Tarantino’s movies, though, like Dogs’ jewelry store or Pulp’s briefcase. The climactic awe in Hollywood is how magnificently one big nothing happens. Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate is a luminous mystery, worshipped yet unknowable. Manson himself barely appears. Tarantino resurrects an era that finished horrifically in the true 1969, then merrily twists the facts. Sadness embeds in that fantasy. We know the end came and will come again. Celluloid projection won’t return to the global multiplex, no matter how many repertory theaters Tarantino runs. Nobody lasts forever, in Hollywood or anywhere else. Good thing art is death proof.

items.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Devouring $85M Over Thanksgiving Weekend as ‘Focker-in-Law,’ ‘Hexed’ Launch
items.description: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is claiming the head of the table at the Thanksgiving weekend box office as Focker-in-Law and Hexed enter the arena.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is claiming the head of the table at the Thanksgiving weekend box office as Focker-in-Law and Hexed enter the arena.

Lionsgate’s sixth film in the dystopian Hunger Games franchise screens in 4,018 North American theaters for its sophomore frame, as it grossed around $15.1 million on Wednesday. Director Francis Lawrence’s adaptation of author Suzanne Collins’ 2025 prequel novel is looking at a five-day sum around $85 million to take its domestic cume to roughly $233 million through Sunday. The movie stars Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy, played by Woody Harrelson in the first four Jennifer Lawrence-led films.

After opening to the fifth-biggest launch in Lionsgate history last weekend with $119 million domestically and $225 million worldwide, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has continued its momentum. The $150 million-budgeted film, which earned an A- CinemaScore, grossed $15.98 million domestically on Tuesday to notch the franchise’s biggest first Tuesday, narrowly topping the $15.96 million for 2013’s Catching Fire. Sunrise’s Monday sum of $12.8 million also bested the series’ previous top opening Monday of $12.3 million for Catching Fire.

The East Coast has been impacted by a major storm stretching from the Midwest to the Eastern seaboard, leading the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to be moved to Saturday for the first postponement in its 100-year history. The inclement weather could slow down moviegoing throughout the weekend, including on Black Friday, which tends to be the biggest day for the box office over the Thanksgiving frame.

Disney released Hexed in 3,725 North American theaters on Wednesday, with the animated fantasy film collecting an estimated $7.6 million on opening day, including $2.1 million in Tuesday previews. Directors Jason Hand and Fawn Veerasunthorn’s movie, which carries a budget north of $200 million, could be heading for a five-day launch around $35 million. This looks to be down a bit from the $45 million opening that the studio had initially been projecting.

Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster lead the voice cast for Hexed, which centers on a mother and her teenage daughter grappling with the girl’s magical powers. The studio has been hopeful that it will continue to run throughout the holiday corridor and follow the lead of this year’s original animated features with pleasing performances, including Goat and Hoppers, although other recent originals like Forgotten Island have struggled.

Earning an A- CinemaScore, Hexed holds a 66 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes. The Hollywood Reporter critic Angie Han wrote in her review that it offers “more than enough to make for a pleasurably transportive trip to the theater.”

Universal Pictures’ Meet the Parents sequel Focker-in-Law launched in 3,382 North American theaters on Wednesday, grossing $5.3 million on its opening day. Director John Hamburg’s film appears to be in line for a $36.3 million opening over the five-day frame, also a bit below the initial projection in the $45 million range. Ariana Grande joins franchise returnees Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, as she plays a woman set to marry the son of Stiller’s Greg Focker.

Meet the Parents opened to $28.6 million domestically in 2000 (en route to its $166.2 million domestic cume). Sequel Meet the Fockers launched even bigger with $70.5 million over the five-day Christmas frame in 2004, while 2010’s Little Fockers dropped to $45 million for its five-day opening frame.

Focker-in-Law earned a B+ CinemaScore from audiences and holds a rough 29 percent critical score on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for THR, critic Frank Scheck wrote that the sequel “feels like the nadir in a series that recycles the same tired jokes in increasingly desperate manner.”

Disney animated features are known for debuting over Thanksgiving, as Moana 2 opened to a massive $225 million over the five-day weekend in 2024 to help that year’s holiday frame set the all-time record with $423 million across all titles. Last year, Zootopia 2 launched on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving and collected $158 million over the five days to help lead the frame to a combined sum of $290 million. The total for this year’s holiday frame is expected to rank below both of those.

In limited release, Netflix launched director David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth on 252 Imax screens in North America. The Brad Pitt-led follow-up to 2019’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood appears headed for around $5 million domestically over the five days before it begins streaming Dec. 23.

items.title: Thanksgiving TV: 26 of the Tube’s Best Turkey Day Celebrations
items.description: ‘Tis the season for Thanksgiving. While many can gather with loved ones or seek a delicious meal, a myriad of television shows offer episodes centered on the holiday to offer laughs and maybe even some drama.
items.author: THR Staff
paragraphs: ‘Tis the season for Thanksgiving. While many can gather with loved ones or seek a delicious meal, a myriad of television shows offer episodes centered on the holiday to offer laughs and maybe even some drama.

From Friends to Modern Family and New Girl, the Thanksgiving-themed episodes from a number of television shows deliver family conflict, laugh-out-loud moments — remember Friends‘ Monica having a turkey on her head? — and even may cause viewers to shed some tears all while battling the inevitable turkey coma nap.
Below, The Hollywood Reporter takes a look at 26 memorable episodes dedicated to the Thanksgiving holiday.

- ‘Gilmore Girls,’ “A Deep-Fried Korean Thanksgiving” (2002) The mother-daughter duo successfully fit in four Thanksgiving dinners, but the fun stops when Lorelai (Lauren Graham) finds out that Rory (Alexis Bledel) applied to more colleges than just Harvard.

- ‘Friends,’ “The One With All the Thanksgivings” (1998) With 10 Thanksgiving episodes, Friends mastered the holiday. But this one is especially memorable because Joey (Matt LeBlanc) gets Monica’s (Courteney Cox) turkey stuck on his head — a gag that Rowan Atkinson later noted had first appeared on his show Mr. Bean.
- ‘Family Guy,’ “Thanksgiving” (2011) Joe’s son (Kevin Swanson) unexpectedly appears during Thanksgiving dinner after supposedly going missing in Iraq, but something about his story doesn’t line up.

- ‘Grey’s Anatomy,’ “Thanks for the Memories” (2005) Izzie (Katherine Heigl) attempts the perfect Thanksgiving dinner, with Burke (Isaiah Washington) to thank. Instead of helping, Cristina (Sandra Oh), Meredith (Ellen Pompeo) and Alex (Justin Chambers) work.

- ‘Modern Family,’ “Punkin Chunkin” (2011) With the family gathered at the Dunphys’ house for Thanksgiving, a disagreement sends them to a football field where Cam (Eric Stonestreet) proves his “punkin chunkin” story.

- ‘Cheers,’ “Thanksgiving Orphans” (1986) The gang attempts the best Thanksgiving ever, but after invited guests never show and an unexpected guest makes an appearance, the plans don’t quite live up to their expectations.

- ‘Full House,’ “The Miracle of Thanksgiving” (1987) It’s the Tanners’ first Thanksgiving without Pam, Danny’s wife, and the result is a frozen turkey. Danny (Bob Saget) takes the less-than-perfect moment to teach his girls about the true meaning of the holiday: “Thanksgiving wasn’t about turkeys; it’s about family and about being thankful for what we have.”

- ‘How I Met Your Mother,’ “Slapsgiving” (2007) As Marshall (Jason Segel) and Barney (Neil Patrick Harris) continue their slap bet, Thanksgiving night marks the third one. Ted (Josh Radnor) and Robin (Cobie Smulders) sleep together the night before.

- ‘Mad Men,’ “The Wheel” (2007) Thanksgiving is near as Peggy (Elisabeth Moss) is given a new opportunity in the office, Betty (January Jones) discovers something that causes her to re-evaluate her marriage, and Don (Jon Hamm) chooses not to spend the holiday with Betty’s family.
- ‘Seinfeld,’ “The Mom and Pop Store” (1995) In the sitcom’s holiday special, Jerry (Jerry Seinfeld) accidentally takes out one of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade floats.
- ‘New Girl,’ “Thanksgiving” (2011) When Jess (Zooey Deschanel) invites Paul (Justin Long), a music teacher at her school, to her Thanksgiving dinner at the loft with the guys, the evening goes awry.
- ‘Brooklyn Nine-Nine,’ “Thanksgiving” (2013) In the freshman comedy’s first Turkey Day episode, Amy’s (Melissa Fumero) Thanksgiving meal at the precinct doesn’t go as perfectly as planned.

- ‘Parenthood,’ “Happy Thanksgiving” (2010) The chaos that family holidays bring is no stranger to Parenthood. In the end, however, the drama emphasizes the deep connection that exists between the families.

- ‘Raising Hope,’ “Meet the Grandparents” (2010) Jimmy (Lucas Neff) wants Hope (Baylie and Rylie Cregut) to experience a traditional Thanksgiving dinner for the first time, instead of his usual routine of ordering pizza. He invites her maternal grandparents (Greg Germann, Valerie Mahaffey) over, only to learn that the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.

- ‘The Goldbergs,’ “Stop Arguing and Start Thanking” (2013) Beverly (Wendi McLendon-Covey) wants to be appreciated for all her cooking on Thanksgiving, Adam (Sean Giambrone) beats his brother at something for the first time, and Murray (Jeff Garlin) wants Marvin (Dan Fogler) to be more responsible.

- ‘Boy Meets World,’ “Turkey Day” (1996) When Cory (Ben Savage) and Shawn (Rider Strong) attempt to merge their family Thanksgivings, the Matthews find themselves at trailer park for dinner with the Hunters. In spite of the differences between them, the boys’ relationship is only strengthened.

- ‘The O.C.,’ “The Homecoming” (2003) Kristen (Kelly Rowan) invites Caleb (Alan Dale) and Julie (Melinda Clarke) over for Thanksgiving dinner and Seth (Adam Brody) unsuccessfully plays both Summer (Rachel Bilson) and Anna (Samaire Armstrong).

- ‘This Is Us,’ “Pilgrim Rick” (2016) In the 1980s Thanksgiving, the Pearsons travel six hours to Rebecca’s (Mandy Moore) parents’ home for the holiday, only to run out of gas and have to celebrate in a hotel with convenience store snacks and Police Academy 3. Fast forward to present day and the family, who now have significant others and children of their own, is celebrating with those same traditions.

- ‘Gossip Girl,’ “Blair Waldorf Must Pie” (2007) Dan Humphrey (Penn Badgley) invites new girlfriend, Serena van der Woodsen (Blake Lively), over for Thanksgiving when her family has nowhere to go, unaware of the romantic history between his father and her mother. Elsewhere in NYC, Blair Waldorf (Leighton Meester) has a relapse of her eating disorder when she discovers her father isn’t coming home for the holiday.

- ‘Friends,’ “The One With the Late Thanksgiving” (2003) Monica (Courtney Cox) is tricked into making an elaborate Thanksgiving dinner for the group, who end up arriving an hour late after going to a hockey game. Joey’s (Matt LeBlanc) head gets stuck in the door until he breaks it down, ruining the meal, but all is forgiven when Monica gets a phone call that she and Chandler (Matthew Perry) have been selected to adopt a baby.
- ‘Black-ish,’ “Auntsgiving” (2016) Pop’s (Laurence Fishburne) sister shows up unexpectedly for Thanksgiving, causing family tension and drama with Ruby (Jenifer Lewis).

- ‘Everybody Loves Raymond,’ “The Bird” (2003) A bird hits the family’s home while they are celebrating Thanksgiving, and when Pat (Georgia Engel) kills it, the group gets into a big fight. The argument carries over into the family’s performance of “First Thanksgiving.”

- ’Gossip Girl,’ “The Treasure of Serena Madre” (2009) Serena van der Woodsen (Blake Lively) is exposed for her affair with married politician Tripp van der Bilt (Aaron Tveit) during Thanksgiving dinner with her friends and family and decides to run away with him, despite Nate (Chace Crawford) declaring his love for her.

- ‘The West Wing,’ “Shibboleth” (2000) President Bartlet (Martin Sheen) must make a decision about granting asylum to Chinese evangelical Christians who arrived by boat on Thanksgiving Day, when press secretary C.J. (Allison Janney) convinces him to pardon two turkeys instead of one.

- ‘Will & Grace,’ “Homo for the Holidays” (1999) Jack (Sean Hayes) finally comes out to his mother (guest star Veronica Cartwright) during Thanksgiving with the group, and in return she tells him that the man he thought was his father isn’t really his father.
- ‘The Simpsons,’ “Bart vs. Thanksgiving” (1990) After arguing with his family on Thanksgiving, Bart runs away, only to end up on the bad side of town and realize how good he had it at home.

items.title: How Amin Joseph Brought “Humanity” to Sonny Liston in ‘The Greatest’
items.description: Sonny Liston stood 6’1″ and, in his prime, weighed in at 218 pounds. For Prime Video‘s The Greatest, actor Amin Joseph (Snowfall) added the requisite 23 pounds to his 6′ (and ½”!) frame to perfectly match that of the former champ.
items.author: Tony Maglio
paragraphs: Sonny Liston stood 6’1″ and, in his prime, weighed in at 218 pounds. For Prime Video‘s The Greatest, actor Amin Joseph (Snowfall) added the requisite 23 pounds to his 6′ (and ½”!) frame to perfectly match that of the former champ.
Joseph proved to be a solid facsimile of Liston in other ways, too. For one, he can really throw hands.
“I grew up fighting,” Joseph told The Hollywood Reporter. “My dad got me into boxing when I was probably around 8 or 9.”
It was probably no coincidence that the formal lessons began shortly after the family moved to Harlem.

Either way, it stuck, and Joseph would box on and off into his college years studying theatre at Howard University. The natural southpaw (not that he told production before landing the role — Liston was a righty) says he had a “knack” for the violent sport, but ultimately was unwilling or unable to “slave [his] mind over” to a coach.

“If he says, ‘Run through a wall.’ If he says, ‘Eat sheetrock’ — you need to slave your mind over to that process,” Joseph said. “[My coach] saw that I already had self-confidence and that I was already shaped as a young man in a certain way, and it was just not worth the investment (for him).”

Boxing is a sport built on length, speed, power, mental fortitude, and in many cases, having an absent (or at least shitty) father. With a present dad at home, Joseph was not looking for what so many younger fighters subconsciously seek. His training had logical limits.

“If [a trainer says], ‘Run at 3 in the morning when it’s raining,’ you don’t need someone going, ‘Well, wait a minute — is that the smartest thing?'” Joseph explained. “You need someone that goes, ‘I’m running.’ Because it could be life or death if you’re in the ring and [a coach] says, ‘I need you to throw this combo.'”
The coach needs the fighter to throw that combo and never question his corner. Joseph, who describes himself as “a thespian through and through,” always saw past the ring.

Liston, for better or worse, was a boxing coach’s dream. Born into a poor sharecropping family, Liston was uneducated and basically tortured by his father. As a young teenager, he ran away from their Arkansas plantation and toward the streets of St. Louis, Missouri. By his early 20s (Liston never really knew his age), Liston was incarcerated.
Not that he minded much: inmates get three meals a day, every single day.
Liston “wanted to be accepted” like “a child” does, Joseph said. So he did as he was told. It was not a lifetime of great advice.

It was in the Missouri State Penitentiary that Liston found boxing. Or really, it was boxing that found Liston. Once more, that would be for better (he’d become World Heavyweight Champion in 1962) and for worse (Liston died under suspicious circumstances in 1970). Throughout his career, Liston was surrounded by unsavory characters.

Before reading Ben Watkins’ scripts, Joseph didn’t know more about Liston than your average… Joseph. He was tangentially aware of the man from the below-pictured infamous KO, which lived on as a mural on the wall of Joseph’s boxing gym (and surely hundreds of others).

Joseph got the education needed from those scripts. He also gained the confidence that he’d have the appropriate screen time to show Liston’s “thought process,” as well as his “humility” and “humbleness.” It is Joseph’s quietest moments in the series that speak the loudest to viewers — not an easy task when playing opposite the loudest and most relentless talker in boxing history.

(Cassius Clay/Muhammad Ali was portrayed with trademark bravado by Jaalen Best. Yes, “Best” was “The Greatest” in what THR TV critic Daniel Fienberg called “a star-making performance.” Fienberg said Joseph “makes Liston into a flawed but tragic figure, ferocious in the ring but eager to find acceptance outside of it,” and calls Liston/Joseph’s talk show-appearance scene “one of the series’ highlights.”)

As heavy as Joseph’s new (pure muscle) weight was, what weighed most on the real Liston was “the shame” of being illiterate throughout adulthood, Joseph said. For Joseph, the greatest selling point of The Greatest is that Watkins doesn’t portray Liston as “a dimwit,” as the media of the time certainly did.
“Literacy isn’t a direct correlation to your intelligence,” Joseph said. “[Liston] is a man that moves in the silence, but when he does talk, it’s so poignant.”
All episodes of The Greatest are currently available on Amazon Prime Video.

items.title: Two Menswear Darlings Just Made the Most Covetable Boots of 2026
items.description: Say you wanted to create the perfect pair of vintage-style military boots. First, you’d need a designer with impeccable taste and encyclopedic knowledge of vintage workwear; then you'd need a bootmaker with the requisite skills to produce it at the highest lev
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: Say you wanted to create the perfect pair of vintage-style military boots.
