First, you’d need a designer with impeccable taste and encyclopedic knowledge of vintage workwear; then you'd need a bootmaker with the requisite skills to produce it at the highest level. If everything went right, the result would be something like the Modèle 1917, a new collaboration between famed Parisian creative director Gauthier Borsarello and renowned Canadian bootmaker Viberg.

In basic terms, the Modèle 1917 is a pair of boots based on the French Army’s 1917 “brodequin,” a design used by soldiers in the trenches of WWI, available in soft brown suede (Mud) and glossy textured black leather (Pavement). But there’s nothing basic about them. The design comes courtesy of Borsarello, a top-tier collector of vintage workwear and the creative mind behind Gersaint Paris and L’Etiquette magazine. Viberg, a third-generation, family-owned boot specialist, got its start making footwear for forestry crews in British Columbia, and it still builds every pair in its Vancouver Island workshop. While it doesn’t make boots for smokejumpers and loggers anymore, old-school shoemaking techniques like a channeled insole Goodyear welt and stitchdown construction ensure their footwear retains its heirloom-level durability.

The backstory of the “brodequin” begins with the Mdl. 1893, a hobnail-soled marching boot created for French infantrymen in the late 1800s that remained in use until the 1950s. In the First World War, the brodequin’s iron-studded soles and sturdy uppers proved ideally suited to the muddy conditions of the trenches, and American troops soon adopted them in place of their inferior M1904 Marching Shoes. “To me, it’s the blueprint for many combat boots across different countries after WWI,” says Borsarello. “I love the idea that France inspired others after fighting side by side in the trenches. They’re very simple, yet instantly recognizable at the same time.”

For all of its strengths in the field, the original brodequin—whose nickname pays tongue-in-cheek homage to a medieval torture device—wasn’t what you’d call a comfortable boot, especially by modern standards. “They were so stiff that they were almost impossible to walk in,” Borsarello admits. This created something of a design challenge.

To stay as true as possible to the original, Borsarello and Viberg designed the boots on a period-correct “pied haricot” (bean-shaped) last, with a cotton twill lining, solid brass hardware, and reinforced panels that support the midfoot so the forefoot can move freely. To make the Modèle M1917 something you’d actually want to wear, they replaced the hobnailed soles with rubber ones and swapped the original roughout leather for supple American-tanned Horween. The result is a pair of boots that are as comfortable as they are durable, not to mention surprisingly versatile. In other words, exactly what you’d expect from a meeting of these formidable talents.

items.title: Jensen Huang Traded His Leather Jacket for a Humble Cotton Zip-Up During His Nvidia Return
items.description: Jensen Huang is back in. The leather jackets? They’re out. The disgraced former Nvidia CEO reclaimed the top job at the American tech giant yesterday, returning to a big welcome from employees and even the president himself. (Trump told CNBC that he “made the
items.author: Tyler Chin
paragraphs: Jensen Huang is back in. The leather jackets? They’re out. The disgraced former Nvidia CEO reclaimed the top job at the American tech giant yesterday, returning to a big welcome from employees and even the president himself. (Trump told CNBC that he “made the deal” to get Huang back in as CEO.) But as Huang returned to the office where he became a billionaire, something was noticeably different. His gray hair remained neatly side-parted as ever, but his usual standout outerwear was swapped for something a whole lot humbler: a navy cotton jacket.

Or, sort of humbler, anyway. Subtle as it may be, Huang’s zip-up appears to nonetheless hail from luxury designer Dior. (The label did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation or comment.) The $3,300 number is the brand’s zippered shirt, one that he’s actually worn in the past, notably when he landed at Gimpo International Airport in Seoul in June of this year. (That was the same trip during which he got memed for wearing a leather jacket on one of the city’s sweatiest summer days.)

The 63-year-old, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, wore high-end black leather jackets as his daily uniform for over a decade. In September, he told CBS News he owned between 30 to 40, from brands like Tom Ford, Burberry, Dior, and Dunhill. At a Stanford economic summit in 2024, Huang offered up a very practical, Silicon Valley-esque reason for his leather preference: They don’t make him itch. But they also felt like an intentional effort to use fashion to break beyond the tech industry’s traditionally geeky image, à la Mark Zuckerberg sitting front row at Prada or Adam Mosseri showing up at the Met Gala in Kartik Research.

Following the revelation of his extramarital affairs, however—most notably with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as with at least two Nvidia employees—the garments took on a new meaning. Rather than evoking the likes of James Dean or Marlon Brando, the lush outerwear instead began to suggest a man in the throes of a midlife crisis.

Huang’s return as CEO isn’t unprecedented. For example, OpenAI’s Sam Altman was reinstated after employees revolted against the board’s initial firing of the CEO. The move does, however, raise concerns about national security and Nvidia’s company culture.

The dismissal of the leather jacket marks a new chapter in Huang’s tenure at the helm of Nvidia. It had always been a talking point, and after becoming a symbol of his fall from grace, wearing it again would risk turning it into his own scarlet letter. By swapping out stiff leather for easy, approachable cotton, Huang seems to be signaling the desire for a reset. As he told his staff during his return: “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

items.title: APC Just Dropped a Pair of Incredibly Clean Casios
items.description: We’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japa
items.author: Josiah Gogarty
paragraphs: We’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japanese giant has just followed up its 2024 collab with APC. The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

The first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

What about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two new ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

Maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent new G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are big and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.
This story originally appeared on British GQ.

items.title: The Robot Vacuum I Refuse to Part With Is on Sale for Black Friday Already
items.description: Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Frid
items.author: Nena Farrell
paragraphs: Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Friday deals already kicking off, it's one of the best times to shop for one.

One of our favorite robot vacuum brands, Roborock, began its early Black Friday deals yesterday, and some of our favorite models we've tested are available for the best prices we've seen. Here's which models I'd snatch up while the prices are low.
- Roborock's best budget vac at its best price: Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro for $450 ($350 Off)
- A powerful, but still affordable roller mop vac: Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow for $600 ($400 Off)
- If you want Roborock's arm attachment: Roborock Saros Z70 with OmniGrip for $950 ($700 Off)
The Best Early Black Friday Vacuum Deals from Roborock

The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro launched in late summer as the newest addition to the brand's more affordable Qrevo line, and it quickly landed as a pick on my guide to the Best Robot Vacuums. It's often on sale for around $600, and thanks to Black Friday it's down to the lowest price I've seen it for: $450, nearly half off.

Overall, Roborock's vacuums are great, but I've been especially impressed by this one's corner cleaning, thanks to its extendable mop arm. It won't always spot cords, but it does a better job at navigating furniture and getting underneath my cabinets than more expensive robot vacuums I've tested.

If you'd rather have a roller-mop-style robot vacuum, the Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is another great option from Roborock's Qrevo line. This one came out in January of this year, and our reviewer instantly loved it.

The Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is a more expensive robot vacuum than the Qrevo 2 since it comes with the brand's SpriaFlow roller-mop. The internal roller spans nearly the entire width of the vacuum and can extend to edge-clean your home. It even has a built-in scraper to move dirty water into the tank instead of rolling it back onto the floor. If you're looking for an affordable mopping powerhouse, this is the one to choose. It's also nearly half off, down to $600 off the $1,000 price tag.

There's the affordable Qrevo line from Roborock, and then there's the higher-end Saros line. While both I and former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So weren't particularly impressed with the Saros 20, I've been much happier with the performance of the Saros 20 Flow. Like the Curv 2 Flow, it has a roller mop instead of spinning mop pads and did well in my mopping tests. It also didn't leave debris around, even with its high suction of 36,000 Pa.

It's one of Roborock's most expensive vacuums, and it comes across while using it—it feels very premium. I've been preferring it over the new Dyson robot vacuum I've been testing. Luckily, you can get it on sale right now for Black Friday. It still isn't cheap at $1,300, but it's one of my all-time favorites and one I have kept coming back to after trying other models.

If you're looking for something truly unique in a robot vacuum, Roborock's Saros Z70 might be what you're looking for. It has a mechanical arm built into it to pick up small items like socks while it vacuums, which feels handy, but didn't work as well as we'd hoped during testing. Still, maybe you feel that's the solution you've been dying for. If that's the case, it's available for a nice discount right now at $950.

It also packs 22,000 Pa of suction (not as powerful as the Saros 20 Flow, but still plenty of suction to clean carpets and rugs alike!) and still executes fast, effective cleaning. But the battery life on this vacuum isn't as long as that of other Roborocks we've tested. Again, you're mostly getting this one for the mechanical arm.

items.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
items.description: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.
Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 26, 2026
items.description: With the moon moving through emotional Cancer — and clashing with Neptune, the sun, Pluto, and Saturn throughout the day — your feelings might be erratic today. One moment, you might be sensitive and insecure, the next irritated by everyone around you, only to
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: With the moon moving through emotional Cancer — and clashing with Neptune, the sun, Pluto, and Saturn throughout the day — your feelings might be erratic today. One moment, you might be sensitive and insecure, the next irritated by everyone around you, only to finally conclude you were overreacting. Don’t take any of your passing moods too seriously just now: The conflict and frustration will blow over soon enough.

You’re likely to take everything personally today. Throwaway comments will feel like personal digs and lighthearted jokes could cut deep. Your feelings are valid, and you’re not required to give anyone a pass just because their intentions are good — but do your best not to be too reactive. If you can take a moment to breathe, you might realize that what you’re actually upset about is something unrelated to these comments or jokes. Try to avoid taking out your frustrations on people who don’t deserve it.

Usually, your opinions are firm and unwavering. Once you make your mind up about something, it takes a lot to make you change it. Today, though, you might find your convictions escape you; you’ll have a hard time figuring out what you think or feel about anything. For now, the best course of action is to review the available information without pressuring yourself to come to a final decision. There’s no hurry to make up your mind, so don’t commit to anything if you’re not convinced yet.

You know that nothing good comes from comparing yourself to others — but today, you might do it anyway. When you doubt that you’re “good enough,” or when you worry your life is lacking in some way, you’ll start to wonder whether observing other people’s lives might set your mind at ease. But comparison won’t provide the clarity you want; it’ll only become an added stressor. Focus today on how you are feeling, not how you stack up to some imaginary set of external standards.

You might be tempted to blame yourself for everything right now — not just your own problems, but your friends’ problems, too. You might believe that if you’d only had better judgment in the past or been a little kinder, everyone around you would be happier now. But there’s a thin line between taking accountability for your mistakes and making everything about you. Check that your self-reproach doesn’t veer back into self-centeredness. It helps nobody when you apologize for things that aren’t your fault.

You might have the feeling lately that nobody understands you. Even the people who love you most don’t seem to get you, and that’s making you lonely. But make sure you’re not expecting others to read your mind. If you make them guess what’s going on in your head, a sense of disconnect is almost inevitable. If you want to be understood, make the effort to explain what’s on your mind. People will get where you’re coming from if you give them a real chance to connect.

Other people’s emotions are likely to affect yours more than usual today. If someone around you is cranky, you’ll quickly become irritable, too; if they’re looking forward to the future, you might feel equally optimistic. So if it’s possible to surround yourself with the kind of energy you want right now, it’ll make a big difference. And if you don’t have control over who you’re spending time with at the moment, simply leaving the room during heated interactions can help you restore your equilibrium.

You’ll likely have a hard time today if people express disagreements with you. Even when you know that their approval (or lack thereof) isn’t necessary for you to move forward, you’ll still crave it. Acknowledge that you want others to think well of you, but try not to let it impact the actual decisions you make. You’ll never please everyone, no matter how hard you try. Right now, prioritize living up to your own principles rather than impressing anyone else.

Most of the time, you can be relied upon to make smart decisions: You have good judgment and a clear sense of your own limits. But today, boredom could scramble your usually clear thinking. The more restless you are, the more likely you are to take foolish risks. Make a point of slowing down and thinking your options through right now. You won’t regret taking your time.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You might convince yourself today that your decision-making is purely practical — you know how to assess every situation through a clear, objective lens! In reality, your thought processes are probably shaped by emotion much more than you realize. This isn’t necessarily a problem — in fact, relying on intuition will likely lead to good decisions right now — as long as you’re aware of it. Don’t try to convince anyone else (or yourself) that your desires are the only “right” ones.

You expect your close relationships to be a source of comfort and emotional security. Life is already full of drama, and you don’t see why you should spend time with people who only create more of it. But today, even your strongest relationships might challenge that expectation. Your closest friends and family members might come across uncharacteristically critical and demanding right now. Don’t read too deeply into it: Every relationship goes through stressful periods, and chances are good that things will get back on track if you can be patient.

Indecisiveness might prevent you from accomplishing as much as you’d hoped today. You’re facing a long to-do list, but you can’t decide what to do first — and the longer you hesitate, the more likely you are to end up doing nothing at all. So stop trying to make the perfect move. If you can release your desire to do everything just right, and instead settle on being good enough, you’ll have a much easier time moving forward.

You might feel more spontaneous than usual right now. Don’t be surprised if you want to live in the moment rather than plan every minute of your day. But be aware that your desires could change from one moment to the next, and what might initially seem like a great idea could quickly lose its appeal. Spur-of-the-moment decisions can sometimes turn out to be the best ones — but leave yourself room to change your mind, just in case.
Buy Claire Comstock-Gay’s book, Madame Clairevoyant’s Guide to the Stars, here.

items.title: Exclusive: The Unhinged ‘Hunger Games’ Look Mckenna Grace Couldn’t Pull Off On Tour
items.description: For Mckenna Grace, This Unhinged Hunger Games Look Was Her White Whale
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: For Mckenna Grace, This Unhinged Hunger Games Look Was Her White Whale
Her stylist reveals the viral scene that became “the one that got away” on the press tour — plus the Easter eggs fans missed.

If you thought Mckenna Grace’s dedication to The Hunger Games maxed out when she brought a binder of book notes to the Sunrise on the Reaping set, you clearly haven’t heard about her press tour mood boards. Over the past few weeks, the actor turned every red carpet into a Panem fashion tribute, serving up looks packed with deep-cut references and Easter eggs only superfans like herself could clock.

Though she left the binder at home this time around, Grace *did* show up to her fittings armed with visual inspiration. “Mckenna was very, very clear about what she wanted from the beginning,” her stylist, Molly Dickson, tells Bustle. The vision? Full-blown method dressing, a red carpet approach Dickson doesn’t typically take: “Her excitement and passion for the idea was honestly contagious, and that made me even more excited to bring it all to life for her.”

And deliver they did. Her homages ran the gamut, with Dickson transforming Grace into everyone from Rue to Lucy Gray. And since her character Maysilee Donner was the original owner of the mockingjay pin, Katniss was obviously a pillar reference — Grace even bookended her press run with Katniss’ unforgettable wedding gown *and* mockingjay dress. They didn’t stop at onscreen nods, either, pulling IRL inspo from the OG cast’s own red-carpet archives.
“As much as I wanted to make every one of Mckenna’s ideas happen, Peeta’s rock might be the one that got away.”

Still, there is one truly unhinged look Grace wishes they could’ve pulled off: Peeta’s infamous rock camouflage. If you’ll recall, Grace is a certified Team Peeta stan who used to make fan edits growing up. Naturally, Josh Hutcherson’s character was at the top of her vision board — particularly *that* scene.

“Mckenna actually really wanted to recreate that iconic moment,” Dickson says. Unfortunately, executing it proved to be a challenge. “We explored the idea, but I just couldn’t find a way to translate it into a fashion look that felt elevated rather than costume-y,” she says. “As much as I wanted to make every one of Mckenna’s ideas happen, Peeta’s rock might be the one that got away.”
Ahead, Dickson spills on the Easter eggs fans missed, the late-night text that sparked an archival Céline hunt, and the hardest look to bring to life.
Congratulations on the press tour! Was there an Easter egg fans might have missed on the carpet?

One of the most hidden ones was the white dress she wore to SiriusXM ahead of the premiere. It’s a reference to Johanna Mason’s white gown in the Capitol propaganda portraits for The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 1.
I actually remember seeing this white structured vintage Givenchy dress in 2011, and I knew it would be the perfect nod to that character.
You don’t typically lean into literal method dressing quite like you have on this tour. What made Mckenna and SOTR the exception to your usual rule?

It’s a very collaborative process with all my clients. My job as a stylist is to take my client’s vision and bring it to life. If they don’t necessarily have a clear vision, then it’s my job to help them discover and create one.

The most important thing is staying true to who my client is. In this case, method dressing felt so authentic to Mckenna and her excitement around this project that it made perfect sense to fully embrace it.
Mckenna famously brought a binder of book notes to set. Did she come to your first styling fitting with a master spreadsheet of Hunger Games references?

She didn’t come with a binder, but she definitely had Pinterest boards and mood boards ready for me, which I absolutely love. I’m such a visual person, so whenever a client comes to me with references or ideas, I get so excited. It gives me a great understanding of what they’re envisioning and makes the creative process that much more collaborative.

Mckenna knew the Hunger Games world so well, and I loved how much thought she had already put into what she wanted to reference. My job was to take those ideas and figure out how to translate them into fashion moments that still felt like her, rather than costumes.
You’ve referenced some of Katniss’ most elaborate looks. Apart from those, what was the most difficult homage to pull off?

One of Johanna Mason’s looks — the lumber look. Mckenna texted me one night and said, “I need to be a tree.” I was completely confused at first because I had no idea how to turn a tree into a fashion moment without it feeling too literal or costume-y.

After a major research rabbit hole, we eventually came across this incredible Céline by Phoebe Philo piece that almost resembled wood. We reached out to practically every vintage rental house and dealer we could think of, and after all that searching, we ended up finding the archival Céline piece on The RealReal of all places.

Method dressing walks a very fine line between chic fashion homage and looking like a costume. What was your personal rule for keeping these looks editorial so Mckenna was the one wearing the dress rather than the dress wearing her?
Fashion always has to come first. No matter how perfect a reference might be, if the look isn’t flattering or doesn’t feel like Mckenna, then it’s not the right look.

That’s one of the biggest challenges with method dressing. You can have the most incredible reference, but bringing it to life in a way that still feels fashionable and true to your client’s personal style is a completely different story. You can’t get so attached to a concept that you lose sight of the person wearing it.
At the end of the day, I want people to see Mckenna looking incredible, and then discover the clever reference behind the look. Not the other way around.
As a lifelong fan, Mckenna must have had a pinch-me moment during fittings. Which look made her the most emotional when she zipped it up?

Mckenna was just so incredibly grateful and genuinely excited about every single premiere look. We did multiple fittings for each gown, and somehow her excitement never faded. Every time she put one on, it felt just as special as the first time.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Forget Dinner Dates, Head To An NWSL Game
items.description: Rom-coms have been pushing the sporty date night agenda for years, whether it’s Jimmy Fallon obsessing over his beloved Red Sox in Fever Pitch, or Kate Hudson sending Matthew McConaughey to refill her Coke during the final seconds of the Knicks game in How to
items.author: Megan LaCreta
paragraphs: Rom-coms have been pushing the sporty date night agenda for years, whether it’s Jimmy Fallon obsessing over his beloved Red Sox in Fever Pitch, or Kate Hudson sending Matthew McConaughey to refill her Coke during the final seconds of the Knicks game in How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days. These movies, and many others like them, are marketed to women, and yet there never seems to be women on the field, court, or ice. The recent explosion in popularity of women’s sports, however, has changed the game. As more pro women’s teams grow their fan bases and sell out stadiums, National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) games are filling up couples’ social calendars.

For those who have been a victim of a spilled drink or a loose elbow at a rowdy men’s game, a female-leaning audience might sound like a welcome change of pace. But NWSL matches aren’t just an alternative to watching the boys play. The NWSL brings its own unique flair to date nights, where high energy and competitive sport meet an inclusive atmosphere. Basically, an NWSL date is the ultimate green flag.
Everyone’s Welcome At Women’s Sports Games

For Natali Espitia, 30, a merchandise manager from Houston, a feeling of acceptance is a major factor drawing her to an NWSL date night. She and her wife, Haley, first attended a Houston Dash game four years ago, when they were invited by friends with season tickets. Since then, they’ve become regular attendees, going for a couple’s night out, or with a local lesbian community group that frequently organizes outings.

In particular, Espitia gravitated toward the soccer league’s LGBTQ+-friendly reputation. The Dash invited their community group to hold the American flag on the field during the national anthem, and the players even frequent local queer bars. The result is a space where Espitia feels more than comfortable being openly affectionate — a key ingredient for a good date night, and one not always promised at men’s games.

“Put me on the kiss cam, I'm fine here,” Espitia says. “I’ll see in the press, ‘Oh, this sports team isn't doing a Pride night,’ or ‘This player refused to wear the Pride jersey.’ And it's like, my team is at the lesbian bar doing bingo night for their outreach. My team is wearing the jerseys, their 24/7 merch is Pride-themed. They're not afraid to wear a rainbow. That makes me feel really safe.”
A Dream Date For Soccer Fans, Old & New

You don’t have to know the entirety of every player’s stat sheet to have a good time at an NWSL game. While Espitia doesn’t consider herself a huge sports fan in general, she enjoys the energy of a good match. “I’m just a ‘woo’ girl. I love to go anywhere where I know who to cheer for,” she says.
For her, Dash games bring together both dedicated fans and people who are there for a good time in a way that feels more welcoming and less intimidating than men’s sports.

“I feel like men's games are the intro games that people default to,” she says. “The thing that I love about the women's games is that you also see so many younger girls there, or big groups who are really passionate about the team itself or just women's sports in general.”

Natalie Jones, 23, is one of those especially passionate fans. The environmental scientist grew up in Los Angeles and is currently based in Portland, Oregon. A soccer player all throughout her youth, she was a lifelong admirer of the women’s national team, and became one of Angel City FC’s original supporters when they joined the NWSL in 2022. She’s been regularly attending games ever since, along with her fiancé, Craig. The pair has been together for seven years, and had their first Angel City date night in 2023. Craig is also a soccer fan, particularly of the men’s national team, so getting him to hop on the Angel City bandwagon was easy.
While they’ve been on a handful of dates to men’s pro soccer games before, in both Los Angeles and Portland, she and her fiancé prefer the atmosphere at women’s games.

“At men's games, sometimes the crowds can be a little rambunctious. People might be throwing beers around or yelling or cussing,” Jones says. “At the women's games, there's a lot of kids there, young girls and boys.”
Take A Break From Your Regularly-Scheduled Programming

After a year of marriage, and eight of dating, Espitia says the games keep her and her wife from defaulting to an endless string of dinner dates. “I feel like the games are also the perfect length,” she adds. “You're not burning out like you are with baseball or football or something that's too long,” she says, comparing the NWSL’s average two-hour-long matches to the NFL’s three-hour average gametime, and MLB games that can stretch on for upwards of 10 innings.
“He was like, ‘Do you have anything pink?’ [Angel City’s color]. It was a green flag for me.”

That makes NWSL games great for the getting-to-know-you phase, too — not to mention an early indicator of a potential partner’s values. Ashley Johnson, 38, a Los Angeles-based healthcare tech auditor, experienced her first match as a welcomed change in pace. After going on a first date (a sit-down dinner) with a guy back in March, he invited her to an Angel City game for their second get-together. While there was never a third date, she saw the outing as an attractive signifier.

“His family has season tickets and it's like, out of all the sports they could have invested in and put their money into, I thought it was super cool that they chose a women’s team,” Johnson says. “He was like, ‘Do you have anything pink?’ [Angel City’s color]. It was a green flag for me, that he is secure in himself.”
Beyond setting her at ease with her date, Johnson’s first NWSL game was simply a great time. “It’s the perfect date, because you can go there, eat, have a drink, and watch some women kick *ss.”

items.title: Rob Lowe Explains Why Celeb Memoirs Need To Be “Honest, Unflinching, No B*llsh*t”
items.description: In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.
items.author: Charlotte Owen
paragraphs: In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.

Rob Lowe has been famous for more than four decades, but even starting out in the early 1980s meant he was too late for the days when the press could be kept on a leash — an era vividly captured in David Niven’s memoir The Moon’s a Balloon, one of the four books Lowe has chosen to discuss today. “The press would take orders,” he says. “I have a friend who was in the Blue Angels in the ’60s. He told me a story about being at a party. JFK invited the Blue Angels because he was an aviation enthusiast, and [a famous actress] apparently walked into the party nude, but with a mink and was like, ‘The president will be down in a few minutes, boys.’ And no one said a word.” He pauses. “By the way, for the record, I have no idea if that story is true, but that was directly from my friend who flew with the Blue Angels.”

Lowe may have come of age in a different media cycle, but his career speaks to his ability to stay ahead in an industry obsessed with what’s new and what’s next. His new documentary, Rob Lowe: The Outsider, spotlights the vicissitudes of the 62-year-old’s life, from his personal battles and eventual sobriety to his fight to break through as a young actor. “I’m so interested in the new James Bond reveal,” he says. “Robert Pattinson got it, and he’s the best. Like duh, Robert Pattinson, hello, sure… When I came up, it was like Tom Cruise and Patrick Swayze and Kevin Bacon, and they’re like your frenemy. You want them to win, but not at a cost to you.”

The documentary is one half of a Netflix double-header for Lowe, who also appears in the streamer’s festive rom-com In a Holidaze as an eccentric honorary uncle. Being the veteran on set made for a full-circle moment with his younger colleagues. “I remember when Hal Holbrook, the great character actor, was on The West Wing for a week,” he says. “I just wanted to hear every story from him. Now I’m sitting there and there’s Maddie Ziegler and all the kids going, ‘Tell me about this and that.’ I’m like, ‘I’m that guy. I’m that guy.’”

Surely top of the list were questions about St. Elmo’s Fire, the 1985 cult classic in which Lowe’s performance as Billy Hicks, opposite Demi Moore and Emilio Estevez, turned him into a star. A sequel is in the works. “We’re trying to get the script right,” he says of a possible reunion. “In St. Elmo’s Fire, my character has got his sax slung across his back [at the end] — not in a carrying case, of course — and he’s getting on the bus to New York. So he literally gets to New York almost a year before the sax solo is completely removed from every pop hit. Overnight, no sax solos. So my thing is he gets there and gets one big sax solo in Billy Ocean’s ‘Caribbean Queen,’ and then it’s curtains and [he] has to figure out what to do.”
Keep reading to discover four of Lowe’s favorite books.

Lowe’s first selection is The Killer Angels by Michael Shaara, a Pulitzer Prize-winning fictional account of the Battle of Gettysburg. “It’s soaring, emotional, inspirational, and patriotic,” he says. “That it really happened is amazing, but more than anything, it’s the subject matter and the prose.”

Throughout the book, Confederate leaders feel doubtful about Robert E. Lee’s choice of military tactic. Ultimately, many defer to the General’s authority, choosing not to raise red flags. Lowe likens that mentality to working with Peter Bogdonavich, whom he describes as “the General Lee of movie directors” on the 1988 film Illegally Yours. He was initially skeptical of the script but decided to trust the legendary director’s expertise. “I was like, ‘I don’t know. I kind of like the script, Lee…’ But I was young,” he says. “This is an analogy you never saw coming — Peter Bogdanovich versus Robert Lee and a rom-com versus the Civil War.”

Ultimately, the film was a box-office flop, grossing around $259,000 against a reported $13 million budget. “Like Lee and Gettysburg that day, I was decimated by the loss of that movie because the General definitely sent me on Pickett’s Charge,” he says. “The number one thing that anybody in life should do, but particularly as a creative, is trust your instincts.”

Lowe is also a fan of Gettysburg, the 1993 film adaptation featuring his West Wing co-star Martin Sheen as Robert E. Lee — except for one thing. “Worst beards you’ll ever see. I’m telling you, it’s Saturday Night Live-level beards,” he says. “Tom Berenger, I love him. He’s a great actor. But that beard. It’s like they took muskrats and just soldered them to their faces.”

The actor’s love of history runs in the family. “My son, Matthew, who's a military history major, recommended it to me,” he says. “When he got married three weeks ago, he walked down the aisle to ‘Ashokan Farewell.’”

His second pick is actor David Niven’s 1971 memoir The Moon’s a Balloon. Lowe says he turned to the book for inspiration while writing his first memoir, Stories I Only Tell My Friends. “It delivers on all of the things a memoir has to, but a lot of them don’t, particularly when they’re written by celebrities,” he says. “It has to be honest, unflinching, no b*llsh*t, warts and all, authentic. It has to name names. He has to give the people what they want, but in a way that’s not gratuitous and in a way that’s not taking shots or going for a pull quote.”

His third choice is The Year of Magical Thinking, Joan Didion’s 2005 memoir recounting the year following her husband’s death while her daughter Quintana was critically ill. “I love Joan Didion. Probably if I have to pick one, she’s my favorite writer,” he says. “Incidentally, I used to see her every morning at a drop-off in Malibu. My brother, Chad, was in Quintana’s class. I was too young to know her but I knew she was some kind of writer, and she had the famous Stingray.”

Throughout the book, Didion describes keeping mementos from her loved ones who have passed. Lowe says his family is less sentimental. “My version of it is, ‘Oh, well, I really need to keep this ill-fitting crew jacket from John Irving’s Hotel New Hampshire adaptation film that I made. It doesn’t really fit me, but for my kids,’” he says. “And then they’re like, ‘Nah, not interested.’"

During this interview, Lowe learned that Didion briefly mentioned him in her 1988 essay Insider Baseball. “What? I got mentioned by Joan Didion? You’ve made my day. She knew who I was!” he says. “That’s up there with having a star on the Walk of Fame.”

His final pick is What It Takes: The Way to the White House, a nonfiction account of the 1988 presidential election from Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Richard Ben Cramer. The author follows each politician from the moment they announce their candidacy through the general election. The theme that ties together the six men is persistence, a trait Lowe takes to heart.

“I’m just naturally resilient. My self-image is of those old toys that we grew up with — the inflatable clown, you punch it in the nose and it would go wink, and then it would slowly come back up,” he says. “If you don’t have that, then you are very easily one of the many people who have a couple of movies and are gone and never come back. You have to be able to keep coming back, and a lot of people aren’t built that way.”

items.title: ‘Hunting Wives’ Fans, These 5 Spicy Page-Turners Are For You
items.description: Happy Thanksgiving, indeed: The Hunting Wives Season 2 arrives just in time for the holiday season.
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: Happy Thanksgiving, indeed: The Hunting Wives Season 2 arrives just in time for the holiday season.

Based on May Cobb’s novel of the same name, the hit Netflix series follows a group of small-town Texas women who cultivate friendship — and sometimes a little more — against a backdrop of killer small-town scandal.

So buzzy is the series starring Malin Akerman and Brittany Snow that a third season is officially on the way. But if you’ve already breezed through the latest episodes and can’t wait for more, there’s no shortage of steamy page-turners that you’ll enjoy just as much in the meantime.

Whether you’re looking for small-town sapphic romance, friendship mysteries, or swoony country settings that make you want to slip into your cowgirl boots, here are five spicy books to read after The Hunting Wives.
Ribbonwood by Ruby Landers

Lara happily plays the part of Ribbonwood’s social pariah. But from the shadows, she uses her scandalous reputation as a cover for helping women break free from the bad men in their lives — cobbling together a close-knit group of friends who become family over bonfire nights. When her former high-school rival Ollie returns to their small Australian hometown, the women forge a steamy relationship that catches them both off-guard.

If the cowgirl trappings of The Hunting Wives have you craving further country spice, you’ll devour Wild Love. The first of Elsie Silver’s Rose Hill series (an adaptation is coming to Prime Video!) follows wealthy music executive Ford and his irresistible connection with his best friend’s sister, Rosie, all set in a charming small town nestled in the Canadian Rockies.
One of Us Is Dead by Jeneva Rose

From her exclusive salon, Jenny gets a front-row seat to the toxic drama afflicting the wealthy housewives of Atlanta’s Buckhead neighborhood. But she’s more than professionally invested in the lives of her clients, especially when one of them is murdered.
Bloom Town: Genesis by Ally North

Like Sophie and Margo, this sapphic love story plays out amid major criminal activity. Female outlaw Joey kidnaps preacher’s daughter Abby on a train ride out west in the 1850s, but before long, the mission gives way to a passionate and eye-opening romance.
Zetas Till We Die by Amber & Danielle Brown

A group of sorority sisters reunites 10 years after one of their own was killed. But as the novel hops between then and now, you realize with the Zetas that the truth of Lupé’s death is murkier than it first appeared.

items.title: There Are A Few Thanksgiving Movies, Actually
items.description: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
items.author: Lia Beck; R
paragraphs: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
Beautycon is a global platform that brings together beauty enthusiasts, brands, and industry leaders to explore the latest trends, innovations, and conversations shaping the future of beauty.

You can probably think of ten Christmas movies off the top of your head, but when it comes to Thanksgiving movies, that's not so easy. Even though, like Christmas, Thanksgiving is a holiday when people spend hours sitting around doing nothing but eating, but there aren't many feel-good Thanksgiving-specific movies to watch while you're doing all that sitting around. Make us some genuine Turkey Day rom-coms, Hollywood!

Until that happens, there are actually some Thanksgiving movies out there. We've rounded up 16 of them, ranging from movies that are actually Thanksgiving-focused to good movies that that merely contain Thanksgiving scenes, to one that is definitively not about Thanksgiving because it definitively is about the mob. We have our reasons; just hear us out.

But don't expect to get too many of the warm and cozy feelings with these Thanksgiving movies, like you do with Christmas films. A lot of them are about estranged family members and fights at the dinner table, whether they're dramas or comedies or some mix of the two. But, hey, maybe something a little emotional and relatable is what you need during this stressful time of year.
If not, there's also a superhero movie on this list. In case you didn't know, Spider-Man eats Thanksgiving dinner, too.

Hear us out. Sure, Addams Family Values isn't fully about Thanksgiving, but it does have one of the most iconic Thanksgiving scenes in movie history. During a Thanksgiving play at Camp Chippewa, Wednesday (Christina Ricci) and her friends go rogue and decide to adapt their counselor's script to more accurately depict the real events that led to Thanksgiving and in true Wednesday fashion, mayhem ensues. If you love Wednesday on Netflix, this season is the perfect time to revisit this classic.

Let's start with a movie that is explicitly about Thanksgiving. Katie Holmes stars in 2003's Pieces of April, a dramedy about a young woman who invites her estranged family to Thanksgiving dinner in her New York City apartment.

Holidate, which was dropped on Netflix this year, is a Thanksgiving movie because it's an every holiday movie. Emma Roberts and Luke Bracey star as two people who pretend to be dating at every holiday gathering that they're invited to in order to avoid questions about being single. Of course, they start to actually have feelings for each other. It's not great, but it's the closest we've got to a Thanksgiving rom-com right now.

Who doesn't love some romance and emotional manipulation over the holidays? Sweet November, starring Keanu Reeves and Charlize Theron, may have been panned by critics when it came out in 2001, but it's got a cult following of fans who love the sweet story of an overworked, selfish workaholic (Reeves) who falls for a free spirit (Theron) after moving in together for the month of November.

In She's Gotta Have It, Nola Darling is a young, independent Brooklyn artist who finds herself juggling relationships with three very different men, none of whom can quite give her everything she wants —and she invites them all over for a memorable Thanksgiving dinner, of course. As she navigates love, dating, and her own desires, Nola challenges the expectations placed on women and discovers the importance of staying true to herself.

Home for the Holidays stars Holly Hunter as a single mom who visits her family for Thanksgiving after losing her job. Her wacky relatives include Robert Downey Jr. as her brother and Anne Bancroft as her mother.

In Scent of a Woman, a young college student (Chris O’Donnell) agrees to look after a blind, retired Army lieutenant colonel (Al Pacino) over Thanksgiving weekend. But what starts as a simple job turns into an unforgettable adventure when the outspoken colonel takes him on a trip to New York City, where the two form an unexpected bond and learn a thing or two about life along the way.

A group of friends — and a sassy mom played by Jane Seymour — get together at a big, gorgeous house for a Thanksgiving full of drinking and innuendos. Malin Åkerman, Aisha Tyler, Kat Dennings, Chelsea Peretti, and more make up the ensemble cast.

Yes, Miracle on 34th Street is a classic Christmas movie, but it's also technically a Thanksgiving movie since it starts with the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The story about the parade's Santa (Edmund Gwenn) claiming to actually be the real Santa continues from there.

In Soul Food, the Joseph family comes together every Sunday for a family dinner hosted by Big Mama, where food, love, and laughter bring everyone closer. But when Big Mama falls ill, family tensions begin to surface, threatening to tear the family apart. As they navigate their struggles, they learn the importance of sticking together and keeping their family traditions alive.
Planes, Trains and Automobiles

Steve Martin stars in Planes, Trains and Automobiles as a man who is trying to get home to his family for Thanksgiving, but due to a flight issue, ends up stuck with a traveling salesman (John Candy). They set off on an adventure filled with hijinks as they try to make their way to Chicago.

If you're in the mood for something dark this Thanksgiving, look no further than Krisha. It stars director Trey Edward Shults actual aunt Krisha Fairchild as a woman suffering from addiction, who visits her family for Thanksgiving after years of being estranged.

1995's The Ice Storm features all sorts of drama taking place during one family's Thanksgiving weekend in 1973. There's young love, an affair, a key party, and more. Christina Ricci, Tobey Maguire, Kevin Kline, Joan Allen, and Sigourney Weaver star.

Spider-Man? A Thanksgiving movie? That's right. In 2002's Spider-Man (that's a Tobey Maguire one), there is a scene in which Aunt May (Rosemary Harris) holds Thanksgiving dinner and Willem Dafoe as Green Goblin very menacingly prepares to carve the turkey.

For Your Consideration is a mockumentary about the production of a horrible-looking movie and the Oscar buzz it generates. The melodramatic movie they're making ends up being titled Home for Thanksgiving. You see, it's a stretch, but the Thanksgiving theme is still there. Eugene Levy, Catherine O'Hara, Parker Posey, and Harry Shearer star.

Want a good holiday cry? Try Stepmom! In it, Isabel (Julia Roberts) is a career-driven photographer trying to find her place in the lives of her boyfriend’s two children, who are still struggling to accept her. Their mother (Susan Sarandon) is haboring a devastating secret. There's a memorable Thanksgiving play scene as tensions rise and everyone is forced to confront their changing family dynamics, learning what it means to love and support one another through difficult times.

items.title: 11 Candle Gifts For Your Most Stylish Friend, Curated By A Candle Connoisseur
items.description: 11 Candle Gifts For Your Most Stylish Friend, Curated By A Candle Connoisseur
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa; Jacqueline Kilikita
paragraphs: 11 Candle Gifts For Your Most Stylish Friend, Curated By A Candle Connoisseur
Flamingo Estate Prinsesstårta Candle

Inspired by NYC institution Sant Ambroeus' Swedish Princess Cake, this impossibly chic Flamingo Estate candle is a sweet treat for the senses. With notes of lemon peel, neroli leaves, toasted cinnamon, amber, and warm incense, it's the perfect gift for the gourmand fragrance lover on your list.
Nest New York Birchwood Pine

You’ll be hard-pressed to find another candle that captures the holiday spirit like Nest’s Birchwood Pine. Crisp notes of white pine and balsam fir meet comforting birchwood, musk, and amber to transform any space into an idyllic winter forest. Plus, the three-wick jumbo size will last well into the new year.
L'Occitane Veillée Pralinée Scented Candle

Capture the cozy magic of a kitchen filled with freshly baked treats with this deliciously warm, nutty candle. Notes of golden praline, creamy sandalwood, and sweet vanilla come together for an irresistibly comforting gourmand scent.
Glasshouse Fragrances Velvet Rhapsody Candle

Aussie candle brand Glasshouse is so underrated. The scent projection is just as good as any designer candle, and my favorite has to be Velvet Rhapsody. Creamy jasmine is spliced with zippy yuzu citrus and fresh waterlily, resulting in a scent that’s unmistakably floral but incredibly clean.
Sidia x Sofie Pavitt Face The Studio Candle

NYC-based facialist Sofie Pavitt is the ultimate “IYKYK” name on any skincare savant’s lips, so when she teamed up with Erin Kleinberg’s lifestyle brand Sidia, we knew we were in for a treat. The result between these two powerhouse founders is The Studio, inspired by Pavitt’s downtown hotspot. Featuring invigorating yuzu and neroli alongside an earthy base of blonde woods, rose water, and white musk, it’s the perfect candle for the beauty lover who’s always ahead of the curve.

You might know Jenni Kayne as the brand behind plush cashmere sweaters and elevated home décor, but word to the wise this year: Don’t sleep on the candles. Our choice pick for an unforgettable gift that’ll impress even the bougiest friend is Aspen, which juxtaposes crisp notes of balsam fir, eucalyptus, and cypress with bright, juicy grapefruit for a result that’s festive yet unexpected.

If you have a little less to spend, go for Cozy Earth’s Gather candle. Earthy cinnamon, warming bourbon, and smoked wood give it a leathery, brooding quality — perfect if they like deeper, more complex scents. It’s a soy and coconut wax blend, which also means better indoor air quality, if that matters to them.
Bath & Body Works Cypress + Cedar Candle

This is not your average Bath & Body Works Candle. With an elevated ceramic votive (which can be repurposed to house everything from makeup brushes to paper clips), these candles make an excellent gift for anyone with a soft spot for the iconic mall brand’s multi-wick candles. Cypress + Cedar is a grown-up take on your favorite Christmas tree scent, with wintry notes of warm roasted chestnut, pine, cedarwood, and tonka bean.
Loewe Tomato Leaves Candle

Loewe’s Tomato Leaves candle is oddly addictive, and the vessel is so undeniably chic, you’ll forgive them for not wanting to light it. It perfectly captures the sweet, green, spicy, and fuzzy scent of crushing tomato leaves between your fingers. If they’re into growing veg and plants on their porch or balcony, they’ll adore this.

Every cool girl owns a Diptyque Tubereuse candle, and if you ask me, it’s the brand’s best — and most compliment-worthy — scent. It’s a creamy, heady floral that feels intoxicating in the best way. It’s also one of Diptyque’s most popular wedding candles, so if they’re getting married this year and thinking about scenting their wedding, they’re likely to fall in love with this one.
Jo Loves Black Cashmeran & Tonka Candle

They’ll burn through this faster than you can strike a match — it’s that good. The initial notes of bitter orange, zippy ginger, and warming cardamom give way to a glug of rich rum, vanilla-esque tonka bean, and creamy cedarwood. It fills my entire apartment with a scent that’s as cozy as a cashmere blanket — which makes sense, considering Jo Malone (of fragrance fame) is the mastermind behind the dreamy brand.

items.title: The streets of Karachi scared me less than home did
items.description: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watch
items.author: Sadia Khatri
paragraphs: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watched me drive away – to another part of the city, where my childhood best friend Aesha and I had found an apartment for ourselves.

Salute to the girls who do this here, in Karachi: live outside of blood, family, marriage or whatever patriarchal bargain most women in my city use to seek their freedom. Anam was the first girl I saw who did this – who did not transfer, like property, from her father’s house to a husband’s, but instead lived with two others in this sprawling city of at least 20 million, but very likely more, home to every ethnic and religious group in Pakistan. Its indigenous communities were historically fisherfolk, pastoralists, and Sindhi and Baloch people, but modern Karachi was founded and funded by Sindhi Hindus and Parsis and Gujaratis. Post-partition, it became home to Muhajirs, who migrated from India, as well as millions of Pashtuns from northern Pakistan and Afghanistan. In the city’s mix are also migrants from Punjab and Balochistan, Burma and Bangladesh. Every kind of population has laid its stake to the city, so why not single women?

We might be one of the tiniest populations in Karachi’s history to fight for our right to the city. A friend from Bangalore visited and, after we’d walked the old streets of Kharadar and the shiny roads of Clifton, she said, baffled: ‘And I thought we in India had few women on the streets.’ Where were the akeli women? She meant unaccompanied women – not the rich-girl variety who outsource their lives to drivers and guards who shuttle them around the city in protective containers, but middle-class girls like us.

‘My family lives in another city,’ I’d told my landlord, nervously avoiding his gaze. In Karachi, respectable girls did this only under the pretext of majboori – some justifiable excuse grounded in necessity, like working or studying away from home. Otherwise, only sex workers and trans women typically broke away from their families to live an unconventional life, one far more difficult than mine. Turned out he hardly cared. The apartment was cheap and, given the neighbourhood it was in – Badar Commercial, an unruly stretch in an otherwise upscale residential part of town, where the lane was not well kept and the building did not have a lock – he wasn’t looking for respectability points. Most others, landlords and landladies alike, had looked at me and said: ‘Families only.’ They did not want to hand over their apartment to two girls, all akeli, all alone, by themselves. Potential blemishes. Danger.

When we moved into the building at Badar, we anticipated all kinds of eyes. The apartment opposite ours was a lawyer’s office, or posed as one. Upstairs lived a gruff old uncle, a retired policeman who fought with everyone and threatened to call the cops after arguments. All day, he slept with the rooftop keys, effectively controlling access to the building’s water tanks.

The two apartments below us belonged to a family that had bought both units and broken down the middle wall. There were lots of women and children and a little dog. The ‘man of the house’ was a 21-year-old boy, evidently a drug addict who was usually found by the entrance staircase, getting high and holding a gun. His 20-year-old wife, a decade younger than us, was friendly. She asked us how we managed, all akelay. Again that word. We got into the habit of saying: ‘Yes, God knows how we manage, all akelay, all saath saath.’ Alone-together.
Since she’d been over a few times, we told her that the gun made us feel queasy. Could her husband please put it away? Very calmly, she replied: ‘He has never pointed it at you, has he?’
The neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely

Our balcony faced the balcony of the building opposite ours. The grilles were close enough to talk to the person on the other side. We knew these neighbours only at this elevation: it was the COVID-19 pandemic era, so everyone was stuck inside. WhatsApp numbers were exchanged; regretted it instantly. Uncle A had an on-again, off-again relationship with his wife, which meant he sometimes rang me up in the middle of the night, sobbing. Aunty B, wonderful to chat with during the day, was obsessed with jinns at night. She loved sending us links to YouTube videos where such supernatural beings were summoned into a courtroom, and she wanted to know if we, too, had ever seen one.

Badar Commercial – with its cast of characters all breaking the codes of Pakistani respectability in some way – got used to us faster than we got used to it. But the neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely. We sometimes dressed respectably – shalwar kameez and saris – whereas other times I walked around Badar in knee-length shorts and tank tops. We spoke English but also Urdu, Kutchi and Memoni; one of us was a teacher and the other a psychologist, but was that really all we did? And were we really Muslim? Often, at home, or grocery shopping, or having chai at the streetside dhaba, or tea-shop, someone would ask: Hindu? Christian? Foreign?

This inability to categorise us reached its pinnacle after a Qawwali night at our apartment – a Sufi music performance. A neighbour who had invited himself midway through the performance after hearing it from his window later asked us with utter confusion: ‘Are you Sunni or Shia?’
We said: ‘It’s hard to explain…’
He leaned in uncomfortably close and whispered: ‘You are the Illuminati?’

Some men assumed we were sex workers and showed up at our door. This might have been my father’s deepest fear: if my family discovered I lived akelay, they’d think me a loose woman, and him a dishonourable man who could not keep his property in line. My extended family continued to believe I still lived with my parents. If an uncle visited, he was told I was out of town. ‘Sadia goes to Hyderabad a lot,’ my relatives noted.

Our time in that apartment was spent, really, undoing our lives. Aesha and I came from families where a room of your own was a luxury only richer relatives afforded their children. Until I was 16, I shared a room with my parents and four siblings; after that, there were two rooms, one for my parents and one for us. Now, Aesha and I each had a room, with a door we could close behind us and let nothing in for a while. At first, I did not know what to do with the emptiness. Just me and my friend, and a feeling of being untethered, unpropertied. We wanted others to feel it too, so our home was always filled with friends and women and anyone who needed a place to crash.

We set up the space with what little we had. Our mothers donated precious items from their kitchens. (When she came over, I introduced ammi to the neighbourhood women – trying to prove, I think, that it was possible to not live a double life, to have both my freedom and my mother by my side.) Our friends gave us our first furniture: a floor rug, a cupboard. We raised and killed too many plants, and washed our clothes by hand or sent them home when the water was out again. We learned to interact with the city in ways we never had before: comparing the vegetable vendors’ rates and learning who had been taking advantage of us, becoming experts at shortcuts on foot, especially during the rain, and knowing where to find rickshaws at 6 pm versus 9 pm.
For the first time, I prayed under the open sky while the city raged around me

Karachi is a logistical nightmare for anyone who lives here – and none of its systems are designed to include women in their public unfolding. Every bank vendor and dhaba server and home electrician is a man. This was another city that opened up to us: of everyday upkeep and haggling and bills. In this city, we learned to be less afraid of the men we had been taught to be suspicious of our whole lives: the electrician boys, the plumber uncles, the carpenter brothers. While any kind of man can turn uncomfortably friendly at a moment’s notice, there’s a way both patriarchy and capitalism benefit by insisting that the working-class man is the biggest threat to a woman’s safety. Under this ruse, the ‘good’ men in my life can surveil and control my movements, while a whole world of centrally airconditioned, securitised and gatekept enterprises can capitalise on this idea of keeping out the riff-raff.

In Badar Commercial, this lie came further undone. Plumber #1 was younger than us, fascinated by our women-only lives, and before leaving would help himself to swigs of whatever alcohol we had left over. Electrician uncle was popular among all the single girlies and slowly taught us how to drill the walls and reinstall ceiling fans. Plumber #2 was of a more conservative bent, refusing to look us straight in the eye but kindly and non-patronisingly telling us we had burned, nay destroyed, our new water heater.

At the roadside dhabas where I read books and people-watched, I often met men not from my world. M J, a rickshaw-wallah, learned my daily routines and routes, and knew exactly which friend lived where, and where I went and what I bought. I, in turn, learned about his life, one among thousands of Pashtuns who migrate from the northwest to seek a better life here. He had two jobs, sent money home to a family he maybe saw once a year, yet made less than our monthly rent. M J was beloved by everyone he met, punctual to a fault, and smoked two packs a day. He said: ‘Sadi, if you weren’t a girl, I’d invite you to Ludo nights with the boys.’ We went everywhere in his grand rickshaw that he’d decorated himself, every inch of it shiny and tasselled. I loved sitting amid all those colours. For the first time, with him, I prayed under the open sky in Karachi, touched the grass with my forehead while the city raged around me. We were by the sea; he rolled out his janamaz to pray and offered that yes, I could do it too if I wanted, why not?

I think we got away with living in that apartment because it was in a seedy neighbourhood where everyone knew everyone’s shit but collectively agreed not to meddle unless things got really out of hand. In close quarters, noise is not contained. Everyone knew when Uncle A and his wife were fighting, or whose side Aunty B took when her sons clashed over the eaten biryani. And when the retired officer upstairs sent cops after the drug-boy on the first floor, the whole neighbourhood knew, because men with guns were banging on our doors at 3 am.

There were conflicting accounts. One neighbour said the boy downstairs sold ice, others said he consumed it, yes, but did not sell. Everyone agreed he was high out of his mind when, middle of the day, in our tiny alley, he pointed his gun to the third floor where the police uncle lived and fired four times.
It was difficult to get to sleep; our bodies now jumped at the slightest noise
‘Motherfucker, wait,’ said the shaking retired cop from his balcony. ‘Motherfucker, you just wait, I’m gon get you fucked up.’
All this was relayed to me via WhatsApp by my best friend, who was watching it unfold. ‘Maybe don’t come home tonight,’ she texted me.

By that night, the boy had fled the scene, and police uncle was having it out in the alley with the boy’s wife. A chair was hurled, unclear who hurled it upon whom, and a few nights later, men with guns were at our door. When the story was pieced together over the following days, it was already too late: fear had lodged itself in our bodies; we now jumped at the slightest noise.
‘No one will enter your house just like that,’ the grocery store uncle said.
‘But if they come back…?’ I asked him.
‘That ice-boy needs to go,’ he said. ‘If nowhere else then to rehab.’
‘But his wife is pregnant,’ I said, and realised how deep I was in Badar Commercial gossip and lore.

Something I learned living alone-together in Badar Commercial, and that I want younger women to know, is that we are actually never guaranteed safety. Therefore, one way to collect the guts and energy to move out of your parents’ home and make a life alone in this city is to realise that the question is not whether we are safe but what the cost is, the violent cost, of trying to live a full life in this city and world.

At Badar, the cost for me was estrangement from my relatives, especially my aunts whom I loved but who knew nothing about my feminist life anymore. The other cost was a new edginess – always alert for the 3 am bang on the door. Then there were the men who tailed me while I cycled, who lurked outside our building, the officer who showed up with my full name at my door, who wanted me to know he knew I lived here.

Still, none of the fear these men instilled in us came close to the body-wreckage from the violence and betrayal we had known inside our own homes. Under our family’s so-called protection, we were surveilled and shamed in the same breath. Men, assigned as our guardians and teachers, hurt us. In my case, it was my cousin and my music teacher. The worst part was having to continue showing them respect. That kind of lying festers inside the body, when everyone knows that danger for women is two feet away, at home. It’s a trap to think we have ever overcome danger. As a result, I have spent my life watching men’s gazes for that livewire glint. The ones on the street I can usually recognise and quickly counter. The home gaze is tricker because I cannot anticipate when and where it might suddenly appear.

As the streets got to know me and I them, some knots in my body loosened, knots that had to do with the entanglement of class and gender politics, of who is portrayed as a threat versus where the actual danger lies. Other un-knottings had to do with feeling free in practice, not just theory, cycling around Badar in shorts and shalwar kameez.
I told my aunts the truth about my life. What was the point of all this public and street freedom if nothing changed in the hardest of spaces: at home?

As the knots loosened, other cities opened within us. A parent’s death; a friend’s secret abortion; walking away from a marriage; walking towards ourselves. We learned that it is possible to live within four walls that hold our grief, not just cause it – that can take it all, and more and more and more. I’d spent my 20s chasing freedom in the streets because I’d never imagined an inner space – the apartment, my room, but really, a space within – that could feel like home, where you don’t feel trapped or sealed or estranged. This indoor city opens up what you can do with your body in the cities outside, so that one day, in that same Badar Commercial, I chased a man away with a chappal because he was following me. I chased him away, wielding that slipper with a confidence that came from having lived in Badar for three years now. How familiar the streets felt; how I knew that they would not betray me.
Another time, however, I ran home breathless and called M J for help, worried I had been followed home. Limits of bravery differ day by day.
‘I’m coming to pick you up,’ he said. ‘Let’s get you some air by the sea.’

items.title: Feeling at home in a new country makes you a stranger in the old
items.description: The morning was warm when I left home. Under the bluest of skies, I was driven to Lisbon’s airport, where I bid my parents farewell. It was a departure that I imagined as a pause in our ongoing conversation rather than its reconfiguration. Hours later, as I st
items.author: Iuri Portalegre
paragraphs: The morning was warm when I left home. Under the bluest of skies, I was driven to Lisbon’s airport, where I bid my parents farewell. It was a departure that I imagined as a pause in our ongoing conversation rather than its reconfiguration. Hours later, as I stepped out of what was then Berlin’s Tegel airport, the first thing that struck me was the cold wind shallowing my breath. I had to go back inside and add layers I hadn’t imagined needing so soon. I relive that day often.

That day I crossed the city three times. I almost strayed on my way to the only place I knew: the university in Dahlem, where I would start my five-month Erasmus semester (an EU student-exchange programme). Waiting for the underground, I was taken by a language school advertisement at Samariterstraße, which asked: ‘Tired of speaking silly German?’ – a provocation that would imprint itself on me for years. Enthralled, I passed through streets that seemed unreal and insubstantial, as if venturing through a sea of meanings that meant nothing to me yet. I obsess over that day often.

I had read the Berlin sociologist Georg Simmel’s reflections about how the metropolis affects its dwellers, creating a certain ‘indifference toward the distinctions between things.’ This is a kind of protective numbness, an emotional flatness of the overstimulated urban denizen. More than a century ago, in this same city, he had named such numbness ‘the blasé’.

If the blasé, however, is overstimulated by familiarity, I was overstimulated by novelty. The novelty of a perceptual greyness. For the blasé, everything has been felt too often. For me, nothing had been felt at all. It wasn’t that I had become numb to distinctions between things; it was that I couldn’t perceive any distinctions at all. Meaning had not yet sedimented, no attachments had been formed. The cobbles would need to be well-trodden before they would tell me their stories. So, in time, I too would become indifferent.
How then do you compose meaning in a place that seems to refuse it? How do you become blasé in the place of arrival? And what about that place once called home?

In bars, waving my glass around, I would speak of these topics. I wanted to hear stories I hadn’t heard before. What about the others, my fellow travellers, who settled for unsettledness? I sought willing storytellers, other Portuguese migrants residing in Berlin. Across 2024 and 2025, I sat in cafés, kitchens, parks and bars where winding conversations returned textures of belonging. I asked few direct questions, in the hope that stories would find themselves.

I think of a moment from an interview with a girl who told me how, on one of her visits back to Portugal, her father, his eyes bright with welcome, asked if she was glad to once again sleep in her own childhood bed. She stuttered. One’s bed is usually at home. She understood the unsaid, the premise hidden behind her father’s loving eyes. And yet, when she thought about the bed she would like to sink into after a long trip, it was not that childhood bed she thought of. Instead, a riving sense of home was her answer.
Belonging, that elusive feeling, cannot simply bloom out of nowhere

This misalignment between parent and child, between what home means to those who stayed and what it means to those who left, is felt but seldom acknowledged. Maybe the people who love us most are often the least equipped to see what departure has done. Seeing it would mean accepting that we are no longer fully theirs, nor they fully ours. Home might be somewhere else now; it seems kinder simply not to point it out.

Home is not simply a matter of being in a place; it requires an entire world to be built, embodied, maintained. It is a peculiar way the body attunes itself to what’s at hand. Belonging, that elusive feeling, cannot simply bloom out of nowhere. It requires time and closeness to endow your world with meaning.

Somewhere in Berlin, there is a daughter with a bed she seldom thinks about. She notices it only from afar. Such is the quieter thing beneath Simmel’s numbness. The blasé’s indifference is not the absence of meaning, but its sediment. You grow numb to what you have thoroughly absorbed. To feel at home somewhere is to have earned the right to stop noticing it. This, perhaps, is how meaning is composed in a place that first refuses it. The blasé, then, might not be the opposite of belonging, but its symptom.

The first days can be the hardest. Grey skies, cutting cold. The weather appears as more than meteorology; it registers as a reminder that you are from elsewhere, that here even the sun seems to remind you of your strangeness.
