You look around, and others seem unaffected. ‘What am I doing here?’ becomes a refrain.

Unlike the cutting wind, there are changes that arrive gently, rehearsed before the greater drama. An exchange programme, perhaps, or a temporary job posting. Through promises of an escape from routine, departure seems a suspension rather than the story itself. You have institutional scaffolding and, most importantly, an end date. There will be a return, you tell yourself. But departure also begins the subtle labour of reconfiguration. The realisation that the first day of the next five months might have been the first day of the rest of your life.

Berlin had gifted Simmel more than the blasé. In the same streets I now inhabit, he observed another figure. The stranger occupies a more unsettling position. They are not simply the other, the foreigner looking in, but someone who is neither entirely ‘them’ nor entirely ‘us’. Someone familiar to the very spaces that make for their strangeness. To be a stranger is to be in medias res, obliged to feel at ease in a story that has already started.

Both of Simmel’s figures share something. They make for a dual condition. The unbothered blasé and the unsettled stranger are entangled in their need for familiarity. The blasé can only grow numb to what they have already absorbed. The stranger can only be strange to places they have come to know.
What should feel most stable may erode precisely when it’s reached for

What I didn’t understand then was that becoming a stranger is not a moment, but a process. What starts as a temporary detour ends up reorienting an entire cartography of possibilities. The body that returns, even from these limited departures, is not the same one that left. A slow unfolding arises the instant you step away from familiar rhythms. The migrant will not tread out of the airport a stranger; they become one, grain by grain, through the accumulated weight of the everyday’s pulse. That strangeness, however, is not confined to the new. It finds its way back, even to that place once called home.

Departure transforms perception itself. It means not merely learning new rules, but feeling differently, altering what appears meaningful, close or distant. This altered perception doesn’t overlay the old. It retroactively changes how the once-familiar appears. Whatever introduces strangeness here will do the same there. Simmel’s own last years were spent away from Berlin. His writings on the stranger predate that departure. I wonder what he would have added had he returned.

Returning ‘home’ for a visit is walking ghostly paths. Not wholly yours, just familiar. ‘Every time I go back,’ someone told me, ‘the whole process feels like small bouts of grief.’ You will tread old, acquainted streets as a testimony of change. Once the initial commotion eases, once routine reasserts itself, there comes a feeling that it is time to leave again. The feeling settles in that home is not fully there anymore. And yet it will always be. Grieving for a loss that can only be felt, never quite named. Stranger in the place of departure than in the place of arrival.

The stranger has often been evoked in the third person; rarely is the writer included in this strangeness. And rarely does the figure account for what happens upon return. But the stranger must have left somewhere. Strangeness then is not directional; it is recursive. It folds back upon itself. It makes us exiles from a former self. What should feel most stable may erode precisely when it’s reached for. Home is not something to simply return to. Such is a peculiar arithmetic of departure.

On one of those grey, wintry days that Berlin so generously offers, sitting in someone’s kitchen, I heard the remark: ‘I used to think a lot about what I could gain here, and I’ve gained, I’d say, but I hadn’t realised so much what I could lose, you know?’ These words brought up something in me. In that kitchen, I thought of how, with time, something had also shifted in me. A form of change that didn’t announce itself, that went years unnoticed, yet continuously accruing. Not a crisis, but a silent drift. A misalignment between the stories I tell myself and the body I feel. I’ve come to call it unbecoming: a tension between a lived self and its socially recognisable articulation. It doesn’t demand resolution, yet becomes noticeable in moments of hesitation. A tacit detachment from who I expect myself to be. A reaching for words that don’t quite fit, yet no better alternative presents itself.

To unbecome is not to come undone. It is the accretive awareness that something no longer fits as before. It is to feel the weight of change before one has the words for it. A transformation so gradual that you notice it only when standing at the place of departure, only to find that it, like you, has become something stranger than you remembered. It is neither tragedy nor triumph.
The sigh that follows so many failed attempts at articulating this says what words alone cannot

Others recognised this feeling. A stranger might feel more like themselves in their new milieu than they ever did at ‘home’. They nevertheless miss a version of themselves who existed only there. This gap between what is felt and what can be said is itself a measure of change. And these are stories of change, after all.

The sigh that follows so many failed attempts at articulating this says what words alone cannot. How do you paint the picture of who you see yourself to be when the very feelings contest the words available? Loss is not the opposite of gain, but is somehow produced by it. Every new capacity for feeling at home in the place of arrival might also be a small chipping away at the ability to feel at home in the place of departure. What if, at a distance, becoming implies a quiet unbecoming? A strange resolution for a strange arithmetic.

The morning was warm when I left home. What was supposed to be a short five-month stay will soon be nine years. Yet the bluest of skies still has a hold on me. What in the moment felt like the most ordinary of days is now a refrain. I relive that day often. On returning, I’m left with questions that seem to resist resolution altogether. Maybe this too is recursive. How could it ever be anything but?
Yet the bluest of skies does not soothe the strangest of feelings.

items.title: Falsely claiming Indigenous identity is a grave form of theft
items.description: What does it mean to belong to an ethnic community or group? And who gets to decide? From an Indigenous American perspective, people are ‘Indigenous’ because they have family and clan-based ties to the community. When those ties don’t exist, stories fill the g
items.author: Dina Gilio-Whitaker
paragraphs: What does it mean to belong to an ethnic community or group? And who gets to decide? From an Indigenous American perspective, people are ‘Indigenous’ because they have family and clan-based ties to the community. When those ties don’t exist, stories fill the gap. But what if those stories are unverifiable? Or what if people take on ‘identities’ based on ‘knowledge’ that turns out not to be true, what then? How do they benefit from those narratives, whether true or not? Self-indigenisation based on self-identification describes people who claim to ‘be’ Indigenous, even when there is ample evidence that they have no Indigenous ancestry or lived experience as Indigenous people. It is a growing phenomenon in the United States and Canada as well as in other countries. Explaining why people pretend to be Indigenous when they aren’t is complicated, especially in light of the fact that the United Nations accepts self-identification as one criterion for indigeneity. However, in places where self-indigenisation has become egregious, it usually comes down to the fact that they perceive benefits, both material and psychological. The way it plays out varies from place to place, but there are commonalities across difference.

I am an Indigenous studies scholar in the US, and I study and wrote a book about self-indigenisation. I am an American Indian person, someone who comes from a long line of people who have been colonised. So mine is in part an insider perspective. As Native people, our experiences and cultures are unambiguous to us, if not always well known to others. They are well recorded in our families’ oral histories and usually in mountains of documentation, given that Indians are arguably the most documented ethnic group in the history of the US. Beginning with the earliest European settlers, missionaries and colonists kept track of the lives of Indigenous people for reasons including religious conversion, treaty negotiations, and census enumeration.

Anthropologists also, of course, study Indigenous people. The kinds of knowledge produced from external perspectives can vary widely from that which Indigenous people produce about themselves. Sometimes they conflict, but on occasion anthropologists’ research has helped tribes to recover lost knowledge. Both have their place. Anthropologists who study Indigenous cultural identity use the term ethnogenesis to describe how the identities of ethnic communities are formed or understood, and how they can change over time. Even Indigenous studies researchers recognise that, contrary to popular thought, Indigenous communities don’t remain static and unchanged over vast expanses of time. A popular tendency to misconceive of Indigenous people as gripped in terms of ‘authentic cultures’ doesn’t account for historical processes, including colonisation. History has imposed seismic changes on all Indigenous peoples, especially those who were in the way of foreign invasion and conquest. Expectations of cultural authenticity, then, can be a trap that doesn’t allow for peoples to experience history, to change with changing times.

In our modern world, there are of course many ways that cultures have evolved, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous. This blending of cultures through intermarriage has resulted in a blurring of lines that has made it difficult to make distinctions based on social constructions of race and ethnicity. Around the world, the questions are about what Indigeneity is and who decides, and how those questions are answered will vary. Laws and custom vary by country, and people will also make their own determinations. That said, there is also the very real phenomenon of ethnic fraud, the wrongful claiming of Indigeneity by people without any demonstrable connection to a historical Indigenous community. In extreme examples, these claims are based on flagrant lying.

Some anthropologists have identified a phenomenon they refer to as neo-Indianism. It was first named by Jacques Galinier and Antoinette Molinié, whose book The Neo-Indians: A Religion for the Third Millennium (translated from French by Lucy Lyall Grant, 2013) examined the rise of a new kind of Indigenism in Latin America where New Age rituals were invented for tourist consumption at Teotihuacan in Mexico, Cuzco in Peru, and other archaeological sites. Misrepresented as traditional Indigenous religion, the general public was unaware of the ruse even as it became a global industry. Similarly, there are growing instances of fake Aboriginal individuals in Australia. The same is happening in Aotearoa (New Zealand) among the Māori. Nowhere, however, is the problem of ethnic fraud more prevalent than in the US and Canada, where it is called ‘pretendianism’.
The Boy Scouts of America blatantly relied on playing Indian to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people

Pretendianism is sometimes known by the more benign-sounding term cultural appropriation, which describes an array of offensive behaviours, such as sports mascots or events with inappropriate names and imagery, Halloween costumes, or the flagrant, unauthorised use of Native spirituality and culture, such as pipe ceremonies and sweat lodges, just to name a few. In Germany, for example, there is an entire subculture dedicated to the fetishisation of Native Americans, which perpetuates harmful, inaccurate stereotypes. If we understand Nativeness conceptualised as a spectrum, then cultural appropriation, ethnic fraud and pretendianism can be understood as existing on the extreme end, at which claims to Indigeneity are objectively illegitimate.

The noted American Indian studies scholar Philip J Deloria coined the term ‘playing Indian’ with his seminal 1998 book of the same name, in which he traced a history of Americans’ penchant for adopting the dress and cultures of Native Americans for a variety of reasons, ranging from frivolous to serious and even politically motivated. The Boy Scouts of America, an extremely popular hobbyist club for children that romanticised America’s frontier days, blatantly relied on playing Indian in the early 20th century to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people. More than a century earlier, the 1773 Boston Tea Party, in which colonists costumed in Indian garb, was clearly a political incident that contributed to the incitement of a revolution. Many, many examples can be given of how the cultures of Native Americans are claimed for reasons that most Native people find offensive.

Pretendianism takes cultural appropriation to the next level when it goes beyond playing Indian to becoming Indian. People ‘become’ Indian when they claim to ‘be’ Indian with no connection to a tribal community, or little to no evidence of Native ancestry. It often begins with an individual who at some point in life transforms their identity claims from white (but sometimes other races or ethnicities) into Native American, based on family folklore or nothing at all, hence ‘race-shifting’, the term used in Australia. When those people have children and raise them with that mythology, pretendianism becomes generational. Amid many legitimate tribes who wrongfully lack political recognition by the US federal government, there are also hundreds of fake tribes that sprouted up in the 20th century. The majority of them claim to be Cherokee, but there are numerous others claiming to be Chumash, Shawnee, and more.

The work of Darryl Leroux shows how in Canada pretendianism is most prevalent in the east with a proliferation of ‘Abenaki’ groups. Faux Abenakis are also a problem in the state of Vermont, with four groups whom the state politically recognises but who have virtually no documentation to back up their claims of Abenaki descent. There are also dubious Metis and Inuit groups in Canada.
Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry

There are many pretendians whose names or faces you may recognise, emerging predominantly from the film industry. Perhaps most familiar is Iron Eyes Cody, who became best known as the ‘Crying Indian’ in the 1971 anti-littering commercial. Cody was not just an American actor who played Native American characters, he was an imposter of the highest order with a detailed but wildly false story about being Cherokee and Cree, which he wrote about in a 1980 autobiography. In 1996, a New Orleans Times-Picayune article revealed his true identity as the son of Italian immigrants. Born Espera Oscar de Corti, his film career began in the 1920s and spanned eight decades, with more than 200 film credits.

In Canada, the early 20th-century ‘Apache’ conservationist Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry. Both Belaney and Cody married Native women, which doubtless helped legitimise their false claims. The same was true for James Young Deer, a silent-film actor, director and producer who rose to fame working for the Pathé Frères film company. Young Deer falsely claimed to be Winnebago/Ho-Chunk, and married the actual Ho-Chunk actress Lilian St Cyr.

More recent exposures include Sacheen Littlefeather and Buffy Sainte-Marie. Littlefeather is best known as the ‘Native American’ woman who rejected an Oscar on behalf of Marlon Brando at the 1973 Academy Awards, ironically in the name of accurate representation of Native people in the film industry. I knew her for a decade before she died in 2022, and I document this story in detail in my book. A year after Littlefeather’s death, a bombshell story broke in the Canadian media that the rock-and-roll legend Buffy Sainte-Marie – who had risen to fame for her fiery Indian activism upon which her music was based – had fabricated a story about being born to a Piapot Cree family, adopted out, and raised by a white family. The evidence was overwhelmingly convincing that none of it was true.

There are many other examples of high-profile people who long claimed Native identities but with thin or non-existent evidence. In Canada, they include the celebrated author Joseph Boyden, the influential children’s rights lawyer Mary Ellen Turpel-LaFond, the prominent academic Carrie Bourassa, and the filmmaker Michelle Latimer, to name a few. In some of these cases, awards and honorary doctorates have been rescinded after investigations revealed their façades. In the US, one example stands out for the attention it received in the political arena. In a dramatic misstep, the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren in 2018 released the results of a DNA test in response to a challenge by the president Donald Trump about her claims to being Cherokee. The test showed that there was ‘strong evidence’ that she had a Native American ancestor six to 10 generations in the past. The Cherokee Nation, however, responded as it had for many years about her claims, that it had no record of Warren’s kinship to them, and that DNA does not always translate to Native identity or tribal belonging.

Pretendianism tends to be concentrated in entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, environmentalism and, increasingly, social media. In the US, the high-profile academics Ward Churchill and Andrea Smith, who lost their tenured professorships, have sparked intense debates about what it means to claim Native American identities with little or no evidence of connection to a tribal heritage. In another high-profile case, the University of California Berkeley professor Elizabeth Hoover drew the ire of Native American scholars after confessing that she had been wrongly claiming to be Mohawk throughout her career.

It’s safe to say that, in the US and Canada, no other non-white ethnicity is as commonly falsely claimed as the Indigenous identity. Explaining why is not as simple, however, and researchers continue to offer compelling and sometimes provocative answers. There is no single explanation, and even in the cases of Canada and the US, both former British colonies and neighbouring North American countries, there are different factors and nuances. And there is likely more than one point of origin, historically and geographically, which would mean a potential variety of reasons for why people ‘became’ Indian at certain moments in time.

That said, there is an explanation that fits within the long history of the US’s colonialism and American Indian policy. This perspective can help us understand the motivations of those who fraudulently become ‘Indian’ and the social landscape of various eras. It shows us that, for example, pretendianism is not just a matter of personal and individual pathology – it’s systemic, which explains why it is continually perpetuated.

One point of pretendianism’s origin is in the late 19th century, when the US, under the ideology of manifest destiny, was engaged in the violent dispossession of Native Americans. With the 1887 passage of the General Allotment Act came the brutality of boarding schools, family separation, forced religious conversion, and the allotment of Native lands. The boarding schools were tools of forced assimilation. Land allotment accomplished these objectives by confining Native Americans to reservations, and encouraging a sedentary life of farming and industry.
Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it

All aspects of assimilation meant to move Native Americans into a cash-based capitalist economy. Boarding schools and land allotment forced a shift in their fundamental way of life, one in which everything is commodified, a concept previously unknown in Native life.

By the 1920s, federal policymakers had recognised that assimilation was a catastrophic failure because it produced widespread poverty and all manner of social ills in reservation communities. Farming and ranching often proved to be unviable on many reservations. But there was one way that Native people could earn a lucrative living in the late 19th century: performing in the Wild West shows that were sweeping the country. The majority of Native Americans who were recruited to Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West show and others were veterans of the Plains Indian wars. For decades, the US had been fighting wars of aggression against Plains and other tribes in the west to force them on to reservations, thus freeing up vast tracts of land for settlers. Militarily defeated and succumbing to the US’s policy of Americanisation, many Indians went from prisoner-of-war camps to the Wild West shows. For the first time, Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it. This is the historical moment when Nativeness became a commodity, a way to make money from who one was, ethnically.

The US film industry has deep roots in the Wild West shows. Westerns were a prominent thematic genre of the early films, at a time when the US was contemplating the closing of the frontier. No longer a military threat, Native peoples became highly romanticised as Americans lamented the ‘vanishing Red Man’ in film. It was a natural progression, then, when the Show Indians became Movie Indians. It wasn’t long before people of other races and ethnicities began passing themselves off as Native Americans to obtain roles. The War Paint Club was the first Native American advocacy group, formed in 1926 to combat problems like fair representation and Native American roles for Native Americans in the industry.

In this way, Southern California became ground zero for the normalisation of Native ethnic fraud. Throughout the 20th century, other circumstances arose expanding opportunities to falsely claim Native American heritage based on no more than a family rumour, or simply the desire to profit financially. They included loose land-claims processes; changes in census rules that allowed for self-identification, and the reduction of the negative stigma of being Native American. In addition, a US government federal relocation programme in the 1950s led to urban Native American population centres where people with false claims could blend in as Native without community accountability; and a budding New Age industry that capitalised on all things Native American. California was the centre for all of these.

People are often mystified when they learn about the pretendian phenomenon; why would someone want to claim a heritage they weren’t born into? Identity commodification, coincident with the growth of Hollywood, gives us a conceptual tool to understand its historical particularity. Over the previous century, the opportunities for material gain associated with this ethnic fraud have only grown, and they show up in several specific spheres: film and entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, and environmental activism.

It’s not difficult to see why film and entertainment would attract opportunists looking to capitalise on an ethnically ambiguous appearance, paired with a convincing story. Iron Eyes Cody and Buffy Sainte-Marie were of Italian ancestry, and performativity is a key aspect of pretendianism. The ability to pass as Native American can be a door-opener, especially in casting rooms, but in other spaces as well. Yet, even when one does not ‘look’ stereotypically Native, a good story can compensate.
Fraudulently obtaining government contracts not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion

Stories help how many academics and authors deliver a compelling performance, regardless of whether they can pass as Native based on looks. In higher education, the ability to use words convincingly gives a leg up in competitive job markets, sometimes at the expense of actual, verifiably Native people. In academia, there is always caution about violating anti-discrimination laws, so hiring committees steer clear of asking about a person’s Native heritage, even when entire careers are built on identity claims. Such was the case with Elizabeth Hoover, whose environmental research in Mohawk communities was facilitated by her supposed Mohawk heritage.

In the publishing world, a gifted storyteller can cash in on the experiences of Native people. There are many books on the market by authors who co-opt Native culture, Native aesthetics, even Native trauma as though they are their own. In Canada, Boyden won many top Canadian book awards, honorary degrees and prestigious teaching appointments for his novels and short stories about Native life, based on his supposed lived experience. But Boyden was another fraudster, not a First Nations person, and is one of many examples of people who absorbed valuable resources meant for legitimate Indigenous people. Thanks to deep investigative journalism, his lack of Indigenous heritage was exposed in 2016. Boyden has since unconvincingly defended himself as having a small amount of Indigenous ancestry.

Native identity fraud also occurs in government contracting. In 2019, the Los Angeles Times conducted an investigation revealing that, since 2000, more than $300 million had gone to 12 companies claiming membership in three fake Cherokee tribes under federal, state and municipal programmes for minority businesses. One of the businesses turned out to be owned by the brother-in-law of the then-Congressional representative for California, Kevin McCarthy. Fraudulently obtaining government contracts does a double harm. It not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion toward legitimate tribally affiliated businesses.

Since the rise of the environmental movement in the 1970s, there has been a marked surge in Native American cultural appropriation, including patterns of Native becoming. During the US presidency of Joe Biden, we saw an elevation in influence of Indigenous cultural knowledge related to climate change resilience strategies up to the highest levels of policymaking, including the White House. The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the Inflation Reduction Act and other legislation that privileged green energy, environmental justice and Indigenous knowledge in climate resilience projects brought material benefits to Native communities through unprecedented levels of funding for environmental and energy projects. But fraud dilutes its effectiveness.

The surge in funding coincided with a proliferation of Indigenous conservation and environmental nonprofit organisations. In many cases, Indigenous conservation groups were led by legitimately Indigenous people. But when grant programmes are opened up to groups who are not federally recognised tribes, there tends to be far less scrutiny about who the leaders are of an ‘Indigenous led’ group. The same is true in the philanthropy world. Private funders are often ill-equipped to make those kinds of determinations and sometimes fear that enquiring about them is rude or even illegal. Too often, the result has been the distribution of grants (in the environmental sector and beyond) to people or groups posing as Native, but with no verifiable Native American heritage.

There are other ways that posing as an Native American can be lucrative. Again in California, for example, where there is a proliferation of groups that call themselves ‘tribes’. Some are more legit than others, and there is no law prohibiting a group from calling itself a tribe. One group known as the Northern Chumash Tribal Council (NCTC) near San Luis Obispo, for instance, began as a ‘cultural monitoring’ group, overseeing the development of sensitive sites where there might be Native American human remains or other burial items. Contracts for cultural monitoring can command hundreds of thousands of dollars and, while laws allow only the ‘most likely descendants’ to monitor a site, they are notoriously lax. Fred Harvey Collins, the founder of NCTC, also went on to lead an effort to establish a national marine sanctuary, garnering significant attention and massive cultural and financial support. However, a legal battle involving his ancestry revealed in 2017 that he possessed no Native American heritage.
Claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past

Not everyone who dubiously calls themselves Native American does it for financial gain. In the US and Canada, it is wildly common to hear people talk about having ‘Indian blood’ or a mysterious Native American ancestor somewhere in the family tree, with no evidence whatsoever to back up the family lore. Sometimes, commercial DNA tests will suggest trace amounts of Indigenous ancestry in the distant past (recall Warren’s case), but as the scholar Kim TallBear has shown in Native American DNA (2012), from a Native standpoint, without a tribal community or family ties, DNA isn’t enough to legitimately call oneself Native American, and certainly not with any legal standing.
So what’s in it for them – what are the benefits of untruthfully claiming Native American heritage?

There are psychological, affective benefits to thinking one has a linkage, however distant, to the ‘original Americans’. Who, after all, is more ‘American’ than Native Americans? In another strand of reasoning, claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past. If one is the colonised, they must not be coloniser. Self-indigenising is a way to be absolved of responsibility for the crimes of colonialism and maintain the fiction of familial innocence.

Ultimately, though, in a country founded on the rights to private property and free speech, identity is perceived as a personal possession, something one can claim at will. In the US, there is a strong common belief that a person can be whoever and whatever they say they are, regardless of facts or evidence.

Native people have come to see the stakes of pretendianism as higher than ever. When university and entertainment jobs, contracts and grants meant for actual Native Americans are taken by people with no connection to legitimate tribal communities, it constitutes stealing resources from the descendants of people who have already been victimised by centuries of theft and loss. Money that is meant to help mitigate those patterns of erasure is unintentionally rendered a tool of more erasure.

At the same time, determining who is Native is not always a simple or easy task. There is a wide, grey area on the spectrum of Nativeness, where people can be legitimately Native American and not be an enrolled member of a federally recognised tribe. Confusion and fear about how to determine who is legitimately Native in our institutions has contributed to the perpetuation of pretendianism. There is growing recognition that something can and must be done to ensure that the resources meant for Native people go to Native people.

In the US, this has long been acknowledged in the art world. Since 1935, the Native American art market has been governed by the Indian Arts and Crafts Board, a US government agency within the Department of the Interior. It was originally set up to encourage the growth of the market, promoting economic self-sufficiency of ‘federally recognised American Indians and Alaska Natives (Indians)’. In 1990, US Congress passed the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, a truth-in-advertising law with strict requirements that anyone selling art as ‘Indian’-made should be enrolled in a federal or state-recognised tribe, or be a certified artisan of the tribe. It is meant to ensure authenticity, in turn guarding the commercial value of Indian-made art. While the law is widely viewed as deeply flawed for the ways it excludes documented Native people and simultaneously includes people from state-recognised groups, it does act as a bulwark against fraud.
Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when leveraged for financial or professional gain

The art world is virtually the only realm of social life with regulatory guardrails against Native ethnic fraud. Aside from this, those addressing the issue with the most urgency are in universities, particularly in Canada. There, a few colleges have implemented verification processes for admissions and scholarship applications. In the US, fears about violating race-based anti-discrimination laws present significant obstacles to implementing similar verification procedures.

Scholars push back against these fears by emphasising that Native Americans are more accurately understood as a political group than as a racial group by virtue of their sovereignty. Verification involves questions about relationships to claimed tribal communities, not questions about race. It’s not unlike asking for proof of military service for those who seek a veteran’s benefits. Wrongly claiming to be a veteran is called stolen valour and can lead to legal consequences. Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when it is leveraged for financial or professional gain. At the very least, it should not be rewarded.

The pretendian wars that Indigenous people are fighting in the US and abroad are aimed at spreading awareness that wrongful Native-claiming is not a harmless frivolity. Valuable resources are being diverted from those to whom they are intended. In some cases, it is a criminal offence, and more needs to be done to guard against it. It should be just as socially unacceptable to illicitly claim Native American heritage as it is to illicitly claim to be a military veteran. People with unsubstantiated stories about Native American heritage should seriously rethink those claims before perpetuating them. They should do the research to find out the truth, but if no evidence is found, they should stop repeating the story. They should also remember that DNA tests showing Indigenous ancestry do not substitute for kinship; this is how belonging is determined in most tribal communities. Until then, Native people are sounding the alarm bells with urgency and determination.

items.title: We need a language to name the grief that comes without death
items.description: I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say
items.author: Derek van Zoonen
paragraphs: I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say goodnight, her cheeks covered in thick layers of night cream. Then, out of nowhere, the image would flip into the raging woman who was so entangled in her own suffering that she turned her frustration on us. Over the years, that second woman slowly swallowed the first, as she got pulled into my brother’s addiction. It’s hard to say where her own unhappiness ended and my brother’s suffering began, but together they drifted into a parallel reality, cut off from the world beyond their heads. There was no funeral for this. No condolence cards. No flowers. No phone calls. No leave of absence. What was I supposed to mourn?

And yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning. Can there be grief without death? I have come to think that we grieve much more often than we realise, and that death is grief’s most visible occasion rather than its essence. If that doesn’t match your experience, it may be because we rarely call these other losses by their name. Most of our losses arrive without a funeral. That is the human predicament: we are creatures built to attach, living in a world where nothing stays. Sooner or later, we lose the things we care about. And since we are complex beings with a body, a mind, a community and an environment – beings who love many different things – there is a great deal we can lose, from our physical health to our sense of who we are, from relationships to homelands to the natural world we share with other species. For creatures like us, there is no way around heartbreak: to live is to lose. Grief is what love does when its object is gone. It is love with nowhere to go.

Over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses. There is the psychological loss of my father as I knew and loved him: a brutal stroke rendered him incapable of walking and cycling, and cycling was the only thing that could ‘make his thoughts liquid’, as he used to say. There is the loss of old friendships. First you are no longer part of each other’s lives – you just update one another about your life – and then, one day, it becomes awkward to reach out at all. There is the gradual softening of an academic identity I’d spent the most vital years of my life constructing. It was a genuine vocation, a life of the mind that taught me to think slowly and carefully. But it was also, as I came to realise, a way of living safely at one remove from where actual life takes place. What is slipping away is a future in which being an academic philosopher would be the whole answer to the question of who I am.

There was the woman whose calmness, clarity and silence embodied the qualities I have come to like so much about the Nordics since moving to Norway. Like a magical stranger, she entered my life unexpectedly, but at the same time her arrival felt so natural, her presence so obvious, that it was as if she had always been there. After our first meeting, which lasted almost 24 hours, I wrote in my journal: Ze is gekomen om te blijven. ‘She had come to stay.’ And she did, for nine intense months. She tried to teach me to ski. We listened to the music of Nils Frahm, which reminded her of melting snow. And she made me see that the deepest form of intimacy happens in the space between the words.

But despite the depth of our bond, she left, abruptly, as if she had never been there. She had fallen in love with another man. I was left behind, dazed and disoriented, and although my heart was broken, this kind of loss did not have a name that matched how shattered I felt. It was ‘just a breakup’, and it didn’t even deserve that name: we had been dating, but it never technically became a relationship. It was also a romantic connection that ran alongside another one, a long partnership that was open by mutual agreement and conscious design. Much about it wasn’t legible to most people around me. I faced the grief largely by myself. No scripts, no rituals, no recognised form, no legitimacy, no shared language, no way to make sense of what had happened to me.

Part of what made the experience so disorienting was a narrow idea of what grief is. In psychology, in philosophy and in our Western culture at large, grief has been treated almost exclusively as a response to the death of someone we love. It’s a neat, tidy understanding. The most celebrated grief memoirs – think of The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) by Joan Didion and A Grief Observed (1961) by C S Lewis – are concerned with the loss of a life partner. And Michael Cholbi’s Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) – one of the most extensive philosophical treatments of the emotion – focuses mostly on the grief we experience at the death of someone we love or who otherwise matters to us.
Restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches

Death is visible and final: it has a body, a date, a medical certificate. The other losses are blurrier: they have no physical object, no clear beginning or end, no tangible proof they happened. We also have an infrastructure for death: funerals, condolence cards, flowers, casseroles, bereavement leave – a whole social script. Perhaps the infrastructure defines what counts: if there is no social and cultural scaffolding to digest the experience, it must not be real grief.

The prime reason for the single-minded focus on death loss, however, must be that bereavement is simply the most striking instance of a broader emotional phenomenon that comes in degrees. But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.

If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.

Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.

What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):

Grief is thus distinctive insofar as it involves recognising and comprehending the implications of lost possibilities for the structure of one’s life or world, and – over time – coming to reorganise one’s life accordingly.

This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).
‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’

My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.

The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.

The case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.
They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience

‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.

Those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’

The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.

The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.

Sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.
If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves

But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):

Grief and love are sisters, woven together from the beginning. Their kinship reminds us that there is no love that does not contain loss and no loss that is not a reminder of the love we carry for what we once held close.

Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.

The tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.

Behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.

Christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.
The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder

Arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.

What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.

But the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.

Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.

I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting said what neither of us could.

items.title: AnOther Performance: Lewis Gribben
items.description: About to break out with his role in the new Blade Runner, the Glasgow-born actor tells us why he admires Eminem’s performance in 8 Mile
items.author: Jamie Dunn
paragraphs: About to break out with his role in the new Blade Runner, the Glasgow-born actor tells us why he admires Eminem’s performance in 8 Mile

When Lewis Gribben was growing up in Glasgow, he felt like an outsider. “I was a very antisocial kid,” he tells me. “I mostly liked to play video games and would imagine myself in those scenarios fighting against zombies or demons.” Gribben’s mum recognised that this love of imaginative play could break him out of his shell, so she enrolled him in the Citizens Theatre youth group when he was seven. “One of the first plays we did was superheroes trying to save Glasgow from a villainous invasion,” the actor recalls. “I played a character called Lizard Boy, and I remember thinking, ‘Wow, this is really fun. Maybe I’m not a weirdo.’”

Now, Gribben is returning to sci-fi on a slightly grander scale as one of the stars of Blade Runner 2099. The new show is set 50 years after the events of Blade Runner 2049 and seems to be a not-so-subtle window into humankind’s possible future. The social fabric of the world has flipped. Replicants now dominate society, and their creators, the humans, are the working underclass. As with any dystopia, a group of rebels are trying to break out of that system, including Gribben’s character Elias.

Despite having a CV that includes massive shows like Black Mirror and Masters of the Air, Gribben was taken aback by the scale of Blade Runner 2099’s production. “I’ve mostly done location work,” he says, “so I was amazed by the sets and the size of the crew, and just the details of the environments that were created.” The production designers seem to have taken their cues from Ridley Scott’s scuzzy cyberpunk original rather than Denis Villeneuve’s shinier sequel. “One [set] was a toolmaker’s apartment, so it was stuffed with all these different pieces of junk and metal. You’re on a sound stage, but it all looked so rustic and lived in.”

We haven’t lost Gribben to the grandeur of Hollywood quite yet, though. He may have fallen in love with acting because it allowed his imagination to run wild, but his heart belongs to the realism of British cinema. “I love stories about real life, that are grounded and have some grit,” says Gribben, who lists the likes of Molly Manning Walker (How to Have Sex), Luna Carmoon (Hoard) and Shane Meadows as directors he’d like to work with. But he seems haunted by one director who got away. “I auditioned for Ken Loach’s The Old Oak a couple of years ago and never got it, so if he ever does another film, I’m desperate to be involved.”
As he explains below, Gribben is also drawn to the grit of Eminem’s performance in 8 Mile, which shares parallels with the rapper’s own early years.

Lewis Gribben: “I was too young when 8 Mile came out initially, but when I got to finally see it on DVD, when I was 12 or 13, I was struck by how grounded Eminem was in that film. He’s great in all the rap scenes, obviously, particularly during that freestyle one near the end where he destroys himself to defeat his opponent. But there’s one scene where he just yells at his mum and it’s so impassioned. His mum is like, ‘My boyfriend’s left me, what am I gonna do?’ And he’s like, ‘What are you gonna do? Lily [his character’s younger sister] is out by herself right now. How could you do this to us?’ And I was like, ‘Fuck, that came from somewhere really deep.’ It’s a really small scene, but the anger is so real and sudden that it really stuck with me.

“Some people say, ‘Oh, well, he’s just playing himself’. But I think what’s so interesting about Eminem’s performance is that he’s playing a version of himself. It’s not technically him; it’s a characterised version. I identify with that. You can’t really escape yourself when you’re acting, because it’s still you at the end of the day. Even if you have to do a different accent or you’re in sci-fi clothing, like with Blade Runner, you’re still bringing a part of yourself to the character.”

items.title: Louise Giovanelli: Shimmering and Cinematic
items.description: As her third exhibition opens at White Cube Mason’s Yard, the painter tells us about her painting rituals, recurring subject matter and unsettling new directions
items.author: Sayori Radda
paragraphs: As her third exhibition opens at White Cube Mason’s Yard, the painter tells us about her painting rituals, recurring subject matter and unsettling new directions

“I usually paint beautiful, desirable things, so I wanted to challenge myself to paint something grotesque and make it beautiful,” says British painter Louise Giovanelli, of Aphros (2026), a painting based on a photograph she took during a visit to a slaughterhouse. It’s a departure from the shimmering theatrical curtains, lustrous wigs and glamorous female figures drawn from cinema that are now characteristic of her practice.

Rendered in crystalline greys and blues, the claustrophobic close-up of butchered meat initially resembles a geological formation, perhaps a seascape or a starry night. Only upon closer inspection might the viewer notice a meat inspection stamp in the lower-left corner, revealing the painting’s unsettling and grotesque subject. Presented in In the Light of False Suns, Giovanelli’s third solo exhibition with White Cube, Aphros was conceived as a kind of Trojan horse. Its carnal focus signals a new direction, “pushing me into new realms”, as she puts it. Yet the painting remains rooted in one of her central artistic concerns: the tension between beauty, seduction and the unsettling, and their combined power to captivate the viewer. “It’s very boring if it’s too nice,” she explains. “There has to be another element that grips and unsettles you.”

This tension takes another form in Ad Astra (2026), where two of Giovanelli’s longstanding motifs converge for the first time: the female cinematic figure and the theatrical curtain. Glistening female faces, their heads tilted back, lips parted and eyes closed in apparent ecstasy, evoke a sense of claustrophobia as they appear trapped within shimmering, spotlit curtains, their features dissolving into the folds of the fabric. Through this fusion, Giovanelli explores cathexis, the psychological investment of emotional energy in an image or object, as the female figures and theatrical curtains imbue one another with new meaning and intensity.

Drawing on Hollywood glamour and the archetype of the femme fatale, the Manchester-based painter (born in London, 1993) references figures ranging from Sissy Spacek in Brian De Palma’s Carrie (1976) to Sharon Stone in Basic Instinct (1992). These cinematic references intersect with the visual language of Catholic worship, blurring distinctions between bodily desire and religious devotion.

Despite studying at Manchester School of Art (BA, 2015) and Frankfurt’s Städelschule (2018–2020) under Amy Sillman, Giovanelli is largely self-taught in traditional Old Master painting techniques, maintaining that “no one really gets taught how to paint at art school these days.” On her own initiative, she travelled to European museums to study Northern Renaissance masters, particularly Jan van Eyck. Through this independent study, she developed her command of glazing and underpainting, and developed the characteristic glow of her paintings.
Sayori Radda How did you arrive at painting as your primary medium, and how has your approach evolved since the beginning of your practice?

Lousie Giovanelli I wasn’t exposed to much art growing up, as I didn’t come from an artistic family. At art school, I began visiting museums and galleries across the UK and Europe, studying Renaissance paintings and Old Master collections. I wanted to paint like the great masters who came before us. That’s essentially how I taught myself to paint, through looking and studying.

Initially, I appropriated excerpts from Old Master paintings, cropping small details and making my own versions. My work was more figurative and closer to its art-historical sources. Over time, those influences became more subtly embedded, and I developed my own recurring motifs: hair, drapery, fabric, film stills, women’s necks and light phenomena.
SR What does a typical day in your studio look like? Do you have particular rituals?

LG I treat painting as a discipline, almost like a job. I start at 6am and work ten to 12 hours, making use of all the available natural light. I have an image bank on my phone and computer containing thousands of images, which I constantly add to. Some remain untouched for years; others I use immediately.

I work on ten or 15 paintings simultaneously because oil is a slow medium. The paintings inform one another as ideas bounce between them. I also return to the same image repeatedly, adjusting the format, scale or colour each time. Sources range from film stills and the internet to my own photographs. For this exhibition, I staged a photoshoot using wigs from my studio.
SR How did you develop In the Light of False Suns, and how does it depart from your earlier work?

LG The title comes from parhelia, an optical phenomenon in which sunlight refracts through ice crystals, creating bright spots resembling additional suns. I became interested in light emanating from different sources, rather than the authentic one.

Light has always been crucial to my work, both as something depicted and something emanating from the canvas itself. People often describe my paintings as luminous, associating them with a feeling of worship. I’m interested in light reflecting off curtains, gold fabric or hair, but equally in how luminosity emerges through technique. I use Old Master methods of glazing and underpainting, revealing light through the white gesso beneath. The more paint you add, the deader the surface can become.

In this show, I’ve introduced thicker, textured gesso, pointillist techniques and impasto brushstrokes. These contrast with the thin washes and glowing surfaces of my earlier work, creating a different rhythm.
SR In Ad Astra (2026), female faces appear superimposed onto spotlit curtains, while Media Luna (2026) belongs to your series of large-scale paintings of wigs. How does cathexis connect these works?

LG I came across the term in a book and immediately thought it described what I was trying to do. It’s the first time I’ve fused two different series and introduced figures into the curtain paintings.

Cathexis involves investing energy in desirable objects, whether silk, marble or skin. In these works, the female figure takes on meaning from the curtain and vice versa. To me, their combination makes both images more powerful.
SR In Media Luna, the wig takes on an almost artificial, porcelain-like appearance. How did you develop this image?

LG I photographed a blonde wig, doubled and warped it, then added a celluloid sheen. I wanted luminous, artificial colours that remove its association with a real person. The enlarged wigs become closer to shrouds or drapery, with an uncanny quality. Media Luna means crescent moon, referencing the shape of a head and the moon’s changing phases. The celestial titles throughout the show encourage associations beyond the human world.
SR Curtains recur throughout your work, and Mark Fisher described their role in David Lynch’s films as thresholds between different realities. What do they represent to you?

LG Exactly, ‘thresholds’. Curtains are barriers but also entrances; they conceal and reveal. What fascinates me most is how they change people’s behaviour. At my exhibitions, people take selfies in front of the curtain paintings, as though they’re on stage or about to perform. Curtains give people a sense of permission to perform. That behavioural aspect is fundamentally why I’m interested in them.
SR With Aphros, you introduce an unexpected image: a meat carcass. What prompted this departure, and how does it relate to the exhibition’s wider themes?

LG Aphros refers to foamy seawater and connects to the root of Aphrodite. I’m exploring classical themes of sex and death. I usually paint beautiful, desirable things, so I wanted to challenge myself to paint something grotesque and make it beautiful.

The painting initially resembles a seascape, a ski slope or a starry night. Only later might viewers realise they’re looking at meat. I’m interested in that jarring moment, almost like a Trojan horse, where beauty draws you in before revealing something darker. I want that recognition to interrupt their enjoyment.

I’ve placed it beside a painting of a woman in a rapturous state, referencing associations between women and the sea in Greek mythology. The relationship between these works and the curtain paintings adds another dimension. It’s a departure for me, pushing my painting into new territory.
SR How do you approach pastiche? Is it a way of bringing together different references to create something new?

LG We’re living in an era of pastiche. I rarely see anything truly novel, including in my own work. We’re so saturated with images and what came before us that appropriation is almost inevitable. I’m comfortable with that. For me, referencing other art forms is a kind of reverence, a celebration of what came before. I’m less interested in cynical postmodern art that mocks or subverts the past.

SR Female figures recur throughout your paintings, particularly those drawn from cinema, such as Sissy Spacek in Carrie and Christina Ricci in Buffalo ’66. What draws you to these images, and how do you approach the representation of women?

LG I’m interested in female glamour, the femme fatale and actresses like Elizabeth Taylor and Sharon Stone. There’s a painting of Stone from Basic Instinct in this exhibition. People often ask whether my focus on women is political or feminist, but I don’t think it is. It’s something deeper, perhaps more ancient, that I haven’t fully understood. Painting is my form of research, and I hope one day I’ll understand why I felt compelled to make these portraits. It has something to do with reverence for female beauty and glamour, and their power to seduce in visual culture.
SR How do you represent these women physically? You often use close-ups.

LG I’m drawn to necks, tilted heads and lips. Their eyes are often closed, rarely looking directly at the viewer. I’m particularly interested in women appearing in ambiguous states of ecstasy, as though undergoing a transcendent experience. There’s a religious aspect to this, particularly Catholic imagery and representations such as The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa. I’m interested in bringing these spiritual depictions together with contemporary, bodily experiences of ecstasy.
SR How has your Catholic upbringing influenced your work?

LG It has definitely shaped how I appreciate religion now, particularly the opulence and sheer visual intensity of it, the rituals and the idea of worship itself, the weight of its idols and icons. I don’t practise, but I have a deep reverence for religion and am currently fascinated with tracing those impulses back in time, especially into pre-Christian and pagan traditions. That’s very much where my research sits at the moment.
Louise Giovanelli: In the Light of False Suns is open at White Cube Mason’s Yard until 16 January 2027

items.title: Pared-back but perfect gifts for the minimalist in your life
items.description: The festive season, typically one of excess, can be trying for the minimalist. All those adornments, trimmings and more stuff. So, if a physical gift really is in order, soothe your favourite minimalist’s sensibilities by offering something that in some way em
items.author: Bridget Downing
paragraphs: The festive season, typically one of excess, can be trying for the minimalist. All those adornments, trimmings and more stuff. So, if a physical gift really is in order, soothe your favourite minimalist’s sensibilities by offering something that in some way embraces the spirit of less but better. We’ve gathered a selection of refined and rarefied suggestions that will never feel de trop to a reductivist recipient, from transparent-framed sunglasses to floating diamonds, an understated hoodie and (a wild card) lip balm grown in space.
Sunglasses with a subtle difference

The subtraction of colour adds allure to these Cutler and Gross sunglasses. A strong silhouette is softened by the chamfered edges and transparency of the acetate frames (look for Sand Crystal or Neutral colourways). Meanwhile, the subtly tinted Zeiss LightPro lenses take away just enough of the sun’s glare for those who value clarity in all things.

Elevating an everyday routine into something more indulgent, Dior’s La Collection Privée Scented Ritual Duo – a soap and a lotion, both for hands and body, subtly scented with a choice of signature Dior scents – makes a gift that’s luxurious but still essential. And the simple packaging will look right at home in the sleekest of bathrooms.

Clean-lined and covetable in ‘Plaster’, Stone Island’s stripped-back hoodie in technical stretch jersey fabric retains thoughtful functional details, such as vertical zip chest pockets as well as side snap-fastening pockets, a drawstring hem and elasticated hood, that make it both stylish and utilitarian.

If you love your minimalist to the moon and back, Exist’s lip balm containing a bioactive complex grown at the International Space Station feels like a grand-ish gesture in a small and sleek package. The ultra-rich formula – vegan and cruelty free – promises smoother lips in three days and includes Lysate, good for ‘hydration and line reductions’, according to brand founder Lauren Bowker, ‘but because it was grown in space, it has 300 times more power than anything Earth-grown’. Choose from a spaceship-shaped vessel or a straightforward capsule container.

Designed in 1968 by Superstudio, the ‘Gherpe’ lamp for Poltronova is an interactive and irreverent piece of Italian Radical Design history that’s still mesmerising today. Breaking with rigid functionalism, the lamp’s Perspex layers can be drawn up to resemble a sea creature’s shell or folded down neatly for a more minimal form. Almost like an early fidget toy for design lovers. Available in red or white.

Pearls have classic, timeless appeal, but Tasaki’s ‘Balance Parallel Neo’ open ring, in white gold with pavé diamonds, offers a contemporary take. Two lines of three Akoya pearls rest either side of the finger, parallel and perfectly poised, like a mini sculpture.

Smart in every sense, Apple’s debut home assistant display is a polished step up from plasticky rivals, with a seven-inch Liquid Retina display and an aluminium finish that should please the aesthete. Integrating Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, with stringent privacy functions, it offers smart-home management (right down to home security, which Apple can also now take care of), streaming audio and making calls, facial recognition – useful in multi-person households with numerous accounts – and a lot more. It’s available on a domed speaker base or, to keep those immaculate surfaces clear, wall-mounted.
A luxurious take on the paper bag

There’s little more minimal than a paper bag. Issey Miyake gives the idea a playful but meticulous upgrade with paper-style totes in leather (sold out on the brand’s site, but there are a few remaining elsewhere), and also a pressed fabric version that includes yarn made from washi paper, giving a paper-like texture to a durable accessory.

Fine jeweller Christina de Kerpel pares back the love token with this lab-grown diamond ring. Set in pink or yellow gold, the gem appears to float on the finger thanks to the ring’s nylon-wire structure. Enquire via her website to order.

Monochrome often wins the day for the minimalist-leaning sartorialist. Which makes Hermès’ latest iteration of its sports-inspired H08 watch a bit of all-white. In Blanc Chantilly, to be precise, the model features a braided glass-fibre composite case with a delicately mottled finish, offsetting the sunburst, satin-brushed white ceramic bezel and white rubber strap. Available online in the US at the time of writing. UK and EU customers, check back at hermes.com or enquire in store.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

On the Wallpaper* staff since 2004, Bridget Downing worked first as production editor and then chief sub editor on the print magazine. Executive editor since 2017, she turned to digital content-editing in 2021 and works with fellow editors to ensure smooth production on Wallpaper.com. With a BA in French with African and Asian Studies, she began her career in the editorial research library at Reader’s Digest’s UK edition, and has also worked at women’s titles. She is the author of the (2007) first editions of the Las Vegas and Cape Town Wallpaper* City Guides.

items.title: Two designers met in Brazil with a pile of discarded hardwood and no Wi-Fi: this is what they made
items.description: One of the paradoxes of being a globally in-demand designer and maker is that long stretches of uninterrupted making time are surprisingly few and far between. For Max Lamb – whose 20-year career has included major commercial collaborations and seen his pieces
items.author: Ali Morris
paragraphs: One of the paradoxes of being a globally in-demand designer and maker is that long stretches of uninterrupted making time are surprisingly few and far between. For Max Lamb – whose 20-year career has included major commercial collaborations and seen his pieces enter permanent museum collections – it had been more than a decade since he’d had the chance to set everything else aside and focus on a single project. But in August 2026, he did just that, spending ten days on the fringes of the Atlantic Forest in Trancoso, Bahia, in the workshop of Hugo França. Here, for the past three decades, França has used a chainsaw to carve discarded tree trunks, roots and fallen timber into furniture and sculpture.

The project grew out of a longstanding interest in Brazil on the part of Gallery Fumi, the London gallery that represents Lamb. Its founders, Sam Pratt and Valerio Capo, have been travelling to the country for years. Meanwhile, Lamb’s own interest in França’s work goes back to 2007, when he saw a solo exhibition in Tribeca, New York. ‘I’d been dreaming of this opportunity for a long time,’ he told Wallpaper*.
