paragraphs: «Платежки — 40% от пенсии. Вот как тут выжить?» Жители разных регионов — о ценах на коммунальные услуги
Хоть кто-то понимает, за что вообще мы платим?

С 1 октября выросли тарифы на коммунальные услуги: где-то на 8%, а где-то сразу на 22%. Редактор «Мела» Надежда Тега попросила людей из разных городов России рассказать, сколько они платят теперь, на чем экономят и какую сумму сами считают справедливой. Оказывается, кто-то выбрасывает платежки не читая: тревог в жизни и так хватает.

В 2026 году коммуналка дорожала дважды. С 1 января тарифы выросли на 1,7% во всех регионах из-за повышения НДС с 20 до 22%. А с 1 октября прошла основная индексация: в среднем по стране около 9,9%. В регионах предельные индексы разные: в Москве — 15%, в Московской области — 12,8%. Самый высокий — в Ставропольском крае, 22%.

По подсчетам РИА «Новости», в 2025 году средняя российская семья тратила на жилищно-коммунальные услуги 6713 рублей в месяц — 9,3% всех потребительских расходов. У некоторых наших героев получается больше.
«Меньше чем за год газ подорожал в два раза, если не больше»
Артур и Татьяна, Подмосковье (15 тысяч рублей и 10 тысяч рублей)

Интересный факт: каких-то пунктов в платежках появляется всё больше и больше, а понимания, что это за пункты, становится всё меньше и меньше. Некоторые значения записаны в каких-то гигакалориях, всё как-то хитро. Нормальный человек, который МИФИ не оканчивал, разобраться точно не сможет.

Но вот что можно уверенно сказать: мы живем в частном доме, и меньше чем за год газ подорожал в два раза, если не больше. Честно, это просто треш какой-то. В среднем в течение года за газ и свет обычно выходит 13–15 тысяч. За воду мы не платим — у нас скважина.

А еще у нас простаивает трехкомнатная квартирка в Подмосковье, которую мы тоже оплачиваем. Последняя платежка пришла на сумму 10 тысяч 50 рублей. Ровно год назад эта же квартира стоила 7500 рублей в месяц. И это платежка без счетчиков на свет и воду.
Топовые позиции, которые всегда дорожают в первую очередь, — это капремонт, вода по счетчикам и отопление

Разумеется, мы как-то пытаемся экономить, но получается не очень. Единственное, нам сильно помогла элементарная замена лампочек на энергосберегающие, а потом — на светодиодные. Мы всегда много света жгли, и если бы не светодиодные лампы, то вообще бы вылетели в трубу.

Наша семья в состоянии оплачивать платежки с повышенными ценами, но это не значит, что мы с этими ценами согласны. Слава богу, в добром здравии живут наши пенсионеры — бабушка и дедушка. И у них прям совсем печальная история: последние платежки составляют порядка 40% от их пенсии. Вот как тут выжить? Что делают другие пенсионеры, у которых нет накопленных денег, ощутимой помощи от детей? Услуги ЖКХ не должны составлять больше 10% от среднего дохода семьи.

Если коммуналка действительно сейчас должна стоить 10 тысяч за среднюю квартиру в 50–60 квадратных метров, пусть хотя бы для пенсионеров цены минимум в 5 раз урежут. Жалкая льгота в 20% тут не поможет
И реформы ЖКХ все какие-то провальные. Например, зачем подняли цены за вывоз мусора в несколько раз? Да, поставили какие-то красивые контейнеры, но люди же не стали в 10 раз больше мусора выкидывать.

Нашей семье всегда удавалось оплачивать все платежки в полном объеме, долгов никогда не было. А вот знакомых с долгами полно. Людям приходится выбирать между тем, чтобы купить себе что-то крупное, съездить отдохнуть или оплатить квитанции за квартиру за несколько месяцев. Причем все эти траты обязательные — нельзя от чего-то отказаться.
В общем, наше мнение однозначно: повышение тарифов ЖКХ и всего, что касается обслуживания квартир, ничем не оправдано
Поддержите «Мел»: отметьте нас галочкой в Google — и классные, интересные, важные тексты будут появляться в вашей ленте чаще.
«Зарабатывать стали больше, а позволять себе — меньше»
Анастасия, Москва (11 тысяч рублей)

Мы с мужем и кошечками живем в двушке в 43 квадратных метра. Я оплачиваю сразу три квартиры: нашу, коммуналку дедушки и коммуналку за нашу квартиру в Воронеже. Честно, обычно я особо не отслеживаю, где какие цены: приходит счет в онлайн-банке — я сразу закрываю.

Сейчас я взяла квитанции из ящика, чтобы отправить «Мелу» фото. Потом они сразу полетели в мусорку. Я в них никогда не вчитываюсь, и так тревог в жизни хватает. Еще настроение портить… Зачем? Но понимаю, конечно, что в среднем за год цены выросли примерно на 20%: и за отопление, и за свет, и за газ, и даже за интернет.
Московская квартира обходится примерно в 11 тысяч — сумма с лета выросла на полторы тысячи. На мой взгляд, это очень дорого.
Мне сложно чисто психологически принять тот факт, что я должна платить по 11 тысяч за небольшую квартиру просто потому, что искупалась, выпила чай и включила свет

Больше всего энергии тратится на посудомойку и кофемашину, но кофе мы пить не перестали, как и стирать или мыть посуду. Да и как вообще можно экономить на коммуналке? Я преподаватель, работаю в основном вне дома: в офисе, в редакции, в университетах. А вот муж постоянно дома — у него удаленка.

Целыми днями у нас работают два компьютера, куча телефонов, модемы, роутеры. Всё, что можно сделать, — не лить лишнюю воду, выключать свет в комнате, если там никого нет, пользоваться многотарифным счетчиком. А еще мы регулярно меняем всю технику, поскольку новая более энергосберегающая.

Мне кажется, наша квартира должна обходиться в два раза дешевле — тысяч в 5. Мы с мужем тратим на коммуналку незначительную часть дохода, потому что у нас по две работы. И соседи все очень порядочные: во всем подъезде всего два неплательщика с задолженностью до 100 тысяч (узнала по объявлению). То есть они около полугода не платят.

Не знаю, как справляются люди с сильно ограниченным доходом. При этом вводить кредит на оплату коммунальных услуг было бы совсем жестоко. Но было бы неплохо хотя бы квитанции сделать более человеческими, сейчас они выглядят как выгрузка из какой-то программы 1С: какие-то строчки, аббревиатуры — ХОВ, ГВ и прочее.

Важно держать в уме, что коммуналка — это товар отрицательного спроса, нельзя выбрать себе коммунального поставщика. Я не могу отказаться от вывоза мусора или от света — всё это необходимо. Лучше я сэкономлю и не куплю платье, но оставлю деньги на коммуналку.

Я не люблю быть в должниках, поэтому некоторые коммунальные платежи оплачиваю даже авансом, но рост цен меня очень тревожит. Мы с мужем зарабатываем всё больше и больше, а позволить себе можем всё меньше и меньше.
Ипотека съедает настолько огромную сумму, что и подумать страшно

Молотый перец в маленькой баночке, которая сломается через два месяца, стоит 350 рублей, капучино в кофейне — 400 рублей, такси до работы не в час пик — тысячу рублей. Каждый раз я отдаю в магазине минимум тысячу рублей, а выхожу с пустым пакетом.

Печально, когда предлагают еще один проект, я соглашаюсь, а сама думаю: «Я же ничего на эти деньги не куплю». Жить сейчас тяжело — без планирования (планировать что-либо просто бесполезно) и в постоянной тревоге.
«12 тысяч при зарплате 50 тысяч — это уже практически одна четвертая дохода»
Виктория, Ставропольский край (6,2 тысячи рублей)
Мы живем втроем в частном доме. Коммуналку оплачиваю я — карточкой через СБП. Ровно год назад сумма была 5,9 тысячи, сейчас уже 6,2 тысячи.

Судя по коммунальным платежам, сильно выросла цена на воду: раньше она стоила примерно 84 рубля, сейчас 103 рубля. Мусор тоже заметно подорожал — раньше платили примерно по 184 рубля с человека, а теперь — 224.

В принципе, всё сильно дорожает. Летом мы много отдавали за кондиционеры, в холода будем разоряться на отоплении. В январе этого года мы платили около 12 тысяч. В 2027-м, наверное, получится гораздо дороже, учитывая рост цен. 12 тысяч при зарплате 50 тысяч — это уже практически одна четвертая дохода.

Конечно, мы стараемся экономить на воде, свете и отоплении — у нас свой котел, который мы отключаем в теплую погоду. Многотарифный счетчик в частных домах не предусмотрен. Все лампочки у нас энергосберегающие, как и у всех, наверное.
И, естественно, мы пользуемся душем вместо ванны, отказываемся от полива огорода. А еще приходится экономить на продуктах и на отдыхе

Платим мы всегда вовремя, чтобы не набежали пени. Пожалуй, повлиять на рост цен на коммуналку невозможно, поэтому нужно увеличивать доход. Жаль, не все работодатели это учитывают. По крайне мере, в Ставропольском крае, наоборот, стараются платить всё меньше и меньше: ни индексаций, ни премий.
«За пять лет оплата выросла с 5–6 тысяч до 8–9»
Катерина, Нижний Новгород (10 тысяч рублей)
Я живу в двухкомнатной сталинке размером 52 квадратных метра вместе с мужем и двумя кошками, для которых в межсезонье мы включаем масляный обогреватель.

Коммуналку я оплачиваю сама, через приложение банка или бумажные квитанции — на них для удобства печатают QR-код. Тарифы выросли от 10% до 20%. Газ сейчас стоит 270 рублей, свет — 750 рублей (или 2,5 тысячи, если включаем обогреватель), содержание жилья — отопление, домофон, вода — около 8 тысяч, капремонт — 500 рублей. Итого выходит около 10 тысяч — 5–10% от зарплаты. Причем счетчик у меня стоит только на электричество — знаю, что по счетчикам люди еще больше платят.
Вообще, я люблю экономить: свет выключаю везде машинально. Недавно выключила свет, когда выходила из кабинета на работе, хотя была там не одна.
Цены на коммуналку повышают минимум два раза в год, причем давно. За последние пять лет оплата выросла с пяти-шести тысяч до восьми-девяти.

Долгов у меня никогда не было: плачу сразу, как получаю заработную плату, иначе звонят из ДУК (ЖКХ). Но вообще среди моих знакомых много тех, у кого долги. Особенно поражает, как оплачивают коммуналку пенсионеры и люди с небольшой зарплатой — им же приходится отдавать по 25–50% от дохода. Очень грустно.
Было бы справедливо сделать коммуналку для всех разной: государство же не требует от пенсионеров платить налог на единственное жилье
Почему бы не снизить для них плату за коммуналку? Если бы все компании были только государственные, можно было бы регулировать цены. А так ничего личного — просто бизнес.
«Я не считаю рост цен неоправданным»
Гульфия, Казань (7,7 тысячи рублей)

Я живу одна в трехкомнатной квартире со счетчиками в панельном доме. Пару месяцев назад коммуналка выходила в 5–6 тысяч, сейчас 7,7 тысячи — примерно седьмая часть дохода. Не знаю, как на платежах отразились новые тарифы. Мне кажется, вот эта разница примерно в 2 тысячи возникла из-за отопления. Рост цен по тарифам уже кажется привычным, а из-за отопления каждый раз резко бьет. В Казани коммуналку за отопление платят только в период отопления, не весь год.

Я вроде всегда экономлю: где не нужно, свет не включаю. Зато водой пользуюсь в свое удовольствие — сколько надо, столько и лью. Если надо, в ванне полежу. Больше не на чем экономить. Если я буду подниматься на девятый этаж пешком, всё равно за лифт платить придется.

Я не считаю рост цен неоправданным. 5–7 тысяч — вполне нормально для трехкомнатной квартиры. Например, в подъезде убирается уборщица — она тоже хочет большую зарплату получать. А за свет, воду, газ цены всегда растут — не знаю, с чем это связано. По квитанциям всё равно ничего непонятно. Пишут какие-то пункты — что это такое?

- Владимир Кунаев В РФ большая беда в сфере психологии. Нет четких профстандартов, нет справедливых механизмов проверки компетенций. В добавок ко всему этому действительно толковые молодые специалисты не могут выйти на рынок из-за массивного пейвола (из личного опыта). Проблем столько, что на целый цикл статей хватило бы, если погружаться. Я редактор. Вот почему я не доверяю всем, кто называет себя психологом

- Светлана Плеханова Я Вас умоляю, по закону ничего нельзя сделать. Многие молодые люди себе не представляют, как достаются деньги! Им кажется, что булки растут на деревьях, а пироги падают с неба. Многое вокруг пропагандирует светский образ жизни, сидение на чужой шее, бездумное, безалаберное отношение к деньгам. Неуважение к чужому труду тоже в чести. Многие унижают тружеников сферы обслуживания. А эти люди делаю нашу жизнь комфортной. Их приветливая улыбка, вежливая речь дарят хорошее настроение! Дочь учится на платном и даже подработку не ищет – живет за наш счет, и ей нормально. Как с ней поговорить?

- Андрей Абсолютно согласен! Надо ещё и математику убрать, а то учат детей думать и раскладывать по полочкам! И читать и грамотно общаться сейчас не в моде. Есть же нейросеть! И комментарии поможет написать! Отправлять в школу только на физкультуру, труды и ОБЗиР. А все остальные предметы платно и по желанию! Хотя и эти три предмета требуют особой подготовки, поэтому их надо тоже по желанию, а лучше вообще платно! «Врачей жалко. А вас, тварей, нет». Честный монолог учительницы о том, что стоит за особым статусом педагогов

items.title: Football Practice and Red Dirt Music: On the Field With Oklahoma Band Keyland
items.description: There is arguably no better day for football — watching it or playing it — than the autumnal crispness of Thanksgiving. But on this particular late summer afternoon, despite triple-digit temperatures and the Oklahoma sun making it feel even hotter, football is
items.author: Josh Crutchmer
paragraphs: There is arguably no better day for football — watching it or playing it — than the autumnal crispness of Thanksgiving. But on this particular late summer afternoon, despite triple-digit temperatures and the Oklahoma sun making it feel even hotter, football is the sweat-drenched task at hand: Coach Kyle Ross is putting me through practice. It’s not lost on either of us that Ross’s primary job is coaching high-energy junior-high athletes in the state’s flagship football program, at Bixby, and I’m an out-of-shape journalist in his late 40s. If I finish Ross’s drills upright and healthy, we’ll declare it a success.

“What are you? Three-for-three or four-for-four catching passes here?” Ross — who is also the founder and frontman of the band Keyland — asks me. My football career ended in high school, 30 years ago, but I was a slot receiver with a reputation for catching anything thrown my way. What would my parents say if I started dropping passes now? “I will throw my body on this turf to not miss a pass,” I promise him.

Over the next few months, Ross will attempt to strike a rather unique balance as coach and touring artist. He’ll headline and sell out the Mercury Lounge in Tulsa, 30 minutes north of Bixby, open an East Coast run for Morgan Wade, and announce a series of 2027 dates supporting Kaitlin Butts. And while he’s ostensibly promoting Knuckle Sandwich, Keyland’s third studio album, Ross will always have football season in the back of his mind.
“I haven’t found anything better to do,” Ross says of why he continues to coach. “Except for maybe, get paid to play guitar and drink beer.”

Few pastimes are as all-encompassing in Oklahoma as football. Its two largest college programs — Oklahoma and Oklahoma State — play their home games in modern stadiums to sold-out crowds on most Saturdays in the fall, but it’s the high-school version of the sport that unites the state. Students, fans, and parents fill stadiums in the state’s urban cores and rural farm towns every Friday night, and for the past decade, no program has dominated this landscape like Bixby’s. The varsity Spartans are eight-time defending champions in Oklahoma’s largest class and this season were ranked No. 1 again by the state’s largest media outlet.

This is Ross’s program. He’s an assistant coach for Bixby’s eighth-grade team and a junior-high English teacher. He grew up in rural Missouri, playing football through high school. Shortly after graduating college, Ross befriended Tyler Schneider — Bixby’s longtime offensive coordinator. The two hit it off, and within weeks, Ross joined the Spartan’s staff. Seven years later, Ross is throwing passes to me on the same turf that those Spartans play their home games. We’re here to talk about music, but I am here to experience what it’s like being one of Ross’s players.
“Let’s go!” he shouts as I haul in another pass. “And he scores!”

As it happens, that particular end zone is where I scored my last touchdown as a player. Before Bixby became the state’s juggernaut program, it was a mid-sized school in the same conference as my hometown team, the Okmulgee Bulldogs.

When he’s playing as Keyland — Ross uses the moniker interchangeably for his solo and full-band shows, named for a duck club he and his father used to hunt near his Chillicothe, Missouri, hometown — he wears an infectious smile that’s integral to his show. He describes the irreverent Knuckle Sandwich, which Keyland recorded at the Sonic Ranch studio outside of El Paso, as a product of pals hanging around for several days and finding music at the end of it.

“This album is about taking what you do seriously, but not taking yourself seriously,” Ross says. “That kind of embodies the whole creative process in recording it. It’s more of a hang than anything, and we get music at the end of it.”

It’s a microcosm for his entire music career. He had a guitar growing up, but played it sparingly. It was not until he was in college and caught a Chris Stapleton gig that he decided to give music a try. “I fell in love with Chris Stapleton, and that was the entry way to the long rabbit hole I fell into,” he says.

Landing a full-time job right in the heart of Tulsa’s music community was a bout of good fortune. Ross befriended Brandon Clark, frontman of the Red Dirt outfit BC & the Big Rig and highly respected in Red Dirt circles. Clark has a weekly gig at Mercury Lounge, and in 2022, he suggested that Keyland get booked at the bar.

Keyland’s first Mercury Lounge show was opening for the Big Rig. Shortly afterward, venue general manager Ashley Kirkley booked Keyland as a headliner. The show sold out, and Keyland have been a regular since.

“Keyland is a great band, no doubt, but the energy and charisma that emanates from Kyle is palpable at every show,” Kirkley says. “Beyond being an incredible performer with a distinctive voice that is unlike anything I’ve heard, he is also one of the most down to earth, kindest people I have ever met. Kyle is always striving for greatness in everything he does. He’s an incredible human, and we are incredibly lucky to have him as a part of our music family.”

Keyland have since gone on to, at least, regional notoriety. Ross has been booked multiple times at nearby Cain’s Ballroom, playing alongside the likes of Johnny Mullenax and opening a sold-out show for Josh Abbott earlier this year.

“Everyone’s at different levels of what they’re doing,” Ross says of the Tulsa music community. “I have friends who have sold out a place like Cain’s. I’m friends with people who are doing house shows for ten people. It almost seems like everyone has a very similar mindset of, ‘We’re almost there.’”

Ross knows better than anyone that Keyland is growing at a fast clip. He is likely to come to a crossroads between coaching and making music before too many more gigs or summer practices pass. But until then, he’s happy to pull double duty. And even at Bixby, where the focus is annually on another state championship, he has found support. He had a fan from the start in Schneider, but he’s brought most of the Spartans’ coaching staff onto his bandwagon — and even a few players.

“There’s a huge Venn diagram of coaches’ interests outside of football, and one of them is music,” Ross says. “All the coaches are super supportive. We have over 20 coaches, and a huge number of them have been to more than one concert. It’s just a community-oriented place to work. The kids, as they get older, they start to appreciate it.”
And on that note, practice is over. Ross’s actual players are starting to trickle in to Bixby’s behemoth of a training facility. Ross gives me a Bixby Spartans shirt for surviving his drills.
“Didn’t die. No passes dropped,” he deadpans.
Josh Crutchmer is a journalist and author whose upcoming book, Sonoran Sounds, is set for release in March 2027 via Back Lounge Publishing.

items.title: The 200 Greatest Rock Songs of the 21st Century So Far
items.description: “Rock & roll can never die,” Neil Young sang deep in the 20th century. Guess what: Neil wasn’t lying. Nearly 50 years later, rock is thriving the way it always has — by mutating, diversifying, evolving into the future. Now that we’re deep into the 21st century
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: “Rock & roll can never die,” Neil Young sang deep in the 20th century. Guess what: Neil wasn’t lying. Nearly 50 years later, rock is thriving the way it always has — by mutating, diversifying, evolving into the future. Now that we’re deep into the 21st century, it’s a perfect time to celebrate the songs that have made this a golden age for rock fans. But as always, rock & roll keeps moving too fast to get pinned down, which is why it remains defiantly, unrepentantly vibrant a century after Chuck Berry was born.

That’s the spirit behind this list — the 200 best rock songs of the 21st century so far. It’s a companion piece to our recent Reasons to Love Rock feature. The list is a wide-ranging mix of different rock styles, different generations, different voices. Some of these tunes are universally beloved classics, known and sung worldwide; others are deep cuts or underground cult faves. But from Bruce to Boygenius to Bombino, from Dylan to D’Angelo to Deftones, from Wilco to Wednesday to the White Stripes, we’ve got artists from around the world and all over the stylistic map.

This is an era when rock can’t be contained — it travels everywhere. In our Top 10 alone, we’ve got the blues, we’ve got dance-floor glam, we’ve got gritty punk and psychedelic jams and high-tech dystopia and acoustic storytellers, along with loads of air-guitar riffs. We’ve got metal warriors from Black Sabbath to Mastodon. We’ve got pop-punk and emo. We’ve got sex and drugs and black leather jackets. We’ve got riot grrrls, rock en español, indie upstarts, rootsy twang, African desert grooves, virtuoso guitar heroes, garage bands, electro experiments, grunge, deep soul. We’ve got Nineties legends from Fiona Apple to Sonic Youth. We’ve got the grizzled veterans who learned new tricks instead of going quietly: David Bowie, Prince, even Neil “Time Fades Away” Young himself.

We’ve got country rebels. We’ve got hip-hop headbanger anthems from OutKast and Jay-Z. (You know, the guy who called himself “rap’s Grateful Dead.”) We’ve got ambitious pop rockers from Olivia Rodrigo to Harry Styles to Taylor Swift, who’ve kept their unabashedly rock moves at the top of the charts. We’ve got the skinny-tie postpunk club commandos of the Meet Me in the Bathroom era. We ramble from the U.S.A. to Colombia, Tokyo, Versailles, Niger, Dublin, CDMX, and YYZ. Some of these songs are innovative and complex; others are three-chord bangers to make you jump up and down. Their only thing in common is that they rock. You can listen to it all here.

It’s a list of songs, not artists, so we mostly avoid repeating songs by the same artist. But a handful of legends simply had too many classics to deny. (How could you pick just one Radiohead song from this century?) The toughest part was cutting it down to a mere 200, with so many more worthy artists than we could cram into one list. But it’s a tribute to the vitality, diversity, and energy of rock in our modern age. There will always be folks asking why it can’t stay like the old days, but that question has been around since Buddy Holly’s plane went down, and the answer is the same as it ever was — rock keeps growing because rock keeps changing. The only way to deny the music’s irrepressible health is to stop listening, and what fun would that be? Keep reading for 200 excellent reasons to pump up the volume and let it blast.

- Yellowcard, ‘Ocean Avenue'(2003) Yellowcard managed to capture the ephemera of teenage summers of yore — and the angsty yearning for those days — in this violin-driven pop-punk classic. It wasn’t an easy feat. As the band finalized recording its debut, Ocean Avenue, lead singer Ryan Key couldn’t find a melody for the title track’s chorus. “One day I walked in, exhausted and almost defeated … and I sang, ‘if I could find you now, things will get better,’” Key told Rolling Stone for Ocean Avenue’s 20th anniversary. It was just what producer and pop-punk architect Neal Avron was looking for. “I tracked it on the spot, and our lives were changed forever.” —Maya Georgi

- Noah Kahan, ‘American Cars’ (2026) On his 2026 album, The Great Divide, Vermont songwriter Noah Kahan broadened his palette beyond the indie-folk magic of “Stick Season.” On “American Cars,” he dug deep into heartland rock, channeling Bruce Springsteen, John Mellencamp, and the War on Drugs. He likens drinking to a profession (“If drinkin’ was a day job/I’d be askin’ for more money”), while begging his sister to come fix the latest kerfuffle in the family. “The song was basically like, ‘You’ve got to get your ass home, we really need you this time,’” Kahan told us in his Rolling Stone cover story. It’s a propulsive stunner unlike anything in Kahan’s catalog — and proves he’s a genuine rock star. —Angie Martoccio
- Speedy Ortiz, ‘The Graduates’ (2015)

Sadie Dupuis’ pen was never sharper than on this 2015 song, which spins an alt-rock anthem out of a complaint about feeling overlooked: “I was the best at being second place, but now I’m just the silver you dread.” Her witty, literate lyrics and her twist-and-turn chords somersault over one another until she hits the bridge and flies even higher. (“Someone tweeted that I looked bored onstage,” she told RS. “I’m like, ‘I’m just focusing so I don’t fuck up this guitar part!’”) It’s a gem from a moment when indie rock was heating up again, and it seemed like all you needed was a distinct perspective and a distortion pedal to get the world’s attention. —Simon Vozick-Levinson

- Mogwai, ‘2 Rights Make 1 Wrong’ (2001) Thirty years in the noise game, and the Scottish punk lads in Mogwai have yet to go stale. They rose up in Glasgow, after getting their minds blown by My Bloody Valentine and Slint, blasting their own massively emotional — yet ear-bleedingly loud — style of worshipful feedback devotionals on their 1997 debut, Young Team. “2 Rights Make 1 Wrong” is their apex, from the 2001 gem Rock Action, around the time Stephen Malkmus was declaring them “the best band of the 21st century.” It’s a swirl of banjos, a vintage 1970s Vocoder, heavy guitar fuzz, distorted strings and horns, barking dogs — a psychedelic hymn, building for nearly 10 cathartic minutes. —Rob Sheffield

- Incubus, ‘Circles’ (2001) Incubus broke through in the final breath of the 20th century with Make Yourself in the fall of 1999 — a cosmic rock odyssey that featured their meditative acoustic hit “Drive.” They carried that momentum into the 2000s with Morning View, an ultra-chill California masterpiece that glistened with rockers like “Wish You Were Here” and “Mexico.” The album’s hardest-rocking moment was the head-banging kiss-off “Circles,” complete with guitarist Mike Einziger’s fiery riffs. When they rerecorded Morning View in 2024, the songs were less an exact replica of the originals and more a reflection of how they’d evolved in live settings over the years. Unsurprisingly, “Circles” sounded more ferocious than ever. —Angie Martoccio

- The Mountain Goats, ‘This Year’ (2005) Singer, songwriter, and guitarist John Darnielle’s look back at “playing video games in a drunken haze” when he was “17 years young” and acting out against an abusive stepfather brims with the sort of warts-and-all autobiography that feels uncomfortably intimate. And then you get to the chorus, in which the Mountain Goats founder vows that “I am going to make it through this year/if it kills me.” This track from the Goats’ stellar The Sunset Tree has long been a fan favorite before becoming an unexpected viral hit in 2020, when the notion vowing to make it through a shit time became unexpectedly resonant. —David Fear

- Old 97’s, ‘Rollerskate Skinny’ (2001) Dallas’ Old 97’s were initially lumped in with the alt-country scene, but by 2001’s Satellite Rides, they had turned into something else: an ace pop-rock band. Inspired by a brief romance with Winona Ryder, “Rollerskate Skinny” finds frontman Rhett Miller piling up lines both boyishly endearing (“You’re pretty as a penny”) and caustic (“Wouldn’t be here if the Athenia hadn’t sunk”). It’s joyfully buoyant, but with an ache at its center, summed up by its final line, which Miller stretches out till it sounds almost like an affirmation: “I believe in love, but it don’t believe in me.” —Jon Dolan

- Momma, ‘Speeding 72’ (2022) The Brooklyn-by-way-of-Los-Angeles band Momma was born out of the tight-knit friendship between childhood pals Etta Friedman and Allegra Weingarten, who met in grade school. Their longtime connection is all over the group’s wistful melodies, often hidden in under blankets of distortion, as no song might be as reflective of what they’re good at than “Speeding 72,” off their 2022 album, Household Name. It’s a dreamy, riff-heavy joy ride that brings in more and more overlapping guitars, swelling into a bit of chaos that sounds like the whole band moving around each other without ever stepping on each other’s toes. —Julyssa Lopez

- Juanes, ‘Es Por Ti’ (2002) Back in the late 1990s, Medellín, Colombia native Juanes left Ekhymosis, his heavy metal band, and decamped in Los Angeles in search of pop-rock stardom. He found it almost immediately thanks to a superlative ear for comforting hooks, and the guidance of producer Gustavo Santaolalla, By the time his second album, Un Día Normal, dropped in 2002, Juanes was a Latin Grammy winner and concert favorite. “Es Por Ti” sums up the Zen beauty of his spiraling, guitar-based melodies, the supple comfort of his guy-next-door vocals, and a sunny cosmovision of disarming sincerity. —Ernesto Lechner

- Wolf Parade, ‘I’ll Believe in Anything’ (2005) Spencer Krug’s baroque and surprisingly hopeful rock anthem has had a few lives now, the most recent being the endlessly charming needle drop from HBO’s Heated Rivalry. Krug actually wrote the first version of the song, a low-fi take on an upright piano, for his side project Sunset Rubdown back in 2005, calling it a “kooky” experiment. “For me, it was a scrappy little love song about two people willing to take a chance on their young relationship,” Krug said. He eventually rerecorded it into the billowing version that’s become the enduring Wolf Parade classic that saw a 2,650 percent steaming jump and peaked at Number Seven on the Billboard U.S. rock chart 20 years later. —J.L.
- Alex G, ‘After Ur Gone’ (2014)

Alex Giannascoli was a college kid making music in between term papers when he wrote, recorded, and produced this two-and-a-half-minute stunner. Released as the first track on his breakthrough album, DSU, it has all the qualities that would make him a star — the haunting falsetto, the piercing guitar lead, the cryptic words alluding to an unnamed loss. “I guess some kids do model cars or skateboarding,”  Giannascoli told Rolling Stone at the time, describing how he developed his DIY methods. “I’d go to the basement after everyone was asleep and record all fuckin’ night.” Many years later, he’s still doing more or less the same thing, for an audience so huge you can hardly call it a cult anymore. It all starts here. —S.V.L.

- Baroness, ‘Isak’ (2007) A surface read of the lyrics to “Isak” makes this song seem to be about living an unfulfilling existence on a farm. But singer-guitarist John Baizley hollers couplets like, “Isak, tender the swine, carry the hare and barrow home,” in a way that suggests there’s something deeper going on. Ultimately, it’s the overall feel of this Red Album standout that made “Isak” an instant classic. Baizley and Brian Blickle play swinging blues-metal riffs, each guitarist dutifully stacking his part over the other’s, with two great solo breaks — the first echoing Pink Floyd space rock, the second summoning Tony Iommi–like metal miasmas. And drummer Allen Blickle somehow holds them together with unusual, jazzy rhythms.—Kory Grow

- The Raconteurs, ‘Steady, As She Goes’ (2006) “Steady, As She Goes” was the first song Jack White and Brendan Benson wrote together before forming the Raconteurs in 2005 with Patrick Keeler of the Afghan Whigs and Jack Lawrence of the Greenhornes. They had an alt-rock hit with “Steady, As She Goes,” a catchy garage-blues tune with a bassline that recalled Joe Jackson’s 1979 hit “Is She Really Going Out With Him?” This song has two very different videos, each directed by notable filmmakers. The first was more traditional, directed by Jim Jarmusch, with the band playing in a barn, and another directed by the Malloys that featured Paul Reubens as a cartoonish villain. —Alison Weinflash

- Slipknot, ‘People = Shit’ (2001) “I’m in this band because of everything that I hate about everything in the world,” Slipknot drummer Joey Jordison told Rolling Stone in 2000. Actual children of the corn, the nine mutants of Slipknot came out of Iowa in the late Nineties with their scary masks and bone-breaking live shows, and made their eye-popping extremism the most explosive attraction on Ozzfest. They summed up their hate-everything worldview with succinct fury on the nu-metal maelstrom “People = Shit,” an undeniable statement of tribal misanthropy and outcast self-determination. —J.D.

- Tame Impala, ‘Elephant’ (2012) On “Elephant,” Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker took some of rock’s most familiar pleasures — fuzzed-out Sabbath chug, high-heeled glam stomp, mind-melting psychedelia — and fused them into a sonic funhouse of his own. The lead single from his sophomore album, Lonerism, builds a whole world around Parker’s supersized riff. The song’s wonderfully wiggy midsection — a fantastic voyage of proggy synths, heavily distorted guitar, and burbling electronics — blasts into the cosmos before snapping back into its big dumb riff, showing Parker’s knack for indulging headphone listeners without losing the arena crowd. —Jason Roth

- Velvet Revolver, ‘Slither’ (2004) Unlike so many other Frankenstein bands, the mashup of Stone Temple Pilots and Guns N’ Roses known as Velvet Revolver wasn’t a cringey lark. The group actually turned out kick-ass, relevant hard rock songs, and “Slither” is chief among them. Driven by the river-bottom bass of Duff McKagan, the song twists and turns like its serpentine title, with Scott Weiland’s keening vocals cutting through the din. It climaxes with an eruptive Slash solo that ranks right up there with the guitarist’s best. Even Axl Rose seems to like the song: It’s become a staple of the reunited GNR’s set list. —Joseph Hudak

- Mudcrutch, ‘Crystal River’ (2008) After an incredible run of in the 1990s, Tom Petty hit a creative rough patch in the 2000s, with underwhelming albums like The Last DJ and Mojo. But he rediscovered something in 2008 when he made the unlikely decision to reform his pre-Heartbreakers band Mudcrutch and record a new album with them. Unlike Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, this was a democratic unit where all members wrote songs and even sang lead. But their best song, “Crystal River,” was a Petty original that clocked in at nearly 10 minutes. (In concert, it stretched out to 15.) Though considerably longer than just about anything else in Petty’s catalog, it’s a mellow journey that never gets boring or repetitive. —Andy Greene

- Bombino, ‘Amidinine’ (2013) A member of the nomadic Tuareg people, singer and guitarist Omara “Bombino” Moctar traveled from Niger to the Nashville studio run by Black Keys frontman Dan Auerbach and recorded the searing 2013 album Nomad. It kicks off with the anthemic “Amidinine,” which bridges West African “desert blues” and the pyrotechnics of Jimi Hendrix, whom Bombino discovered as a child living in exile with his family in Algeria. As he told Rolling Stone, “The freedom that Jimi expressed through his guitar sent me to another world, where I was also free.” You can hear that freedom in every note he plays.—J.D.

- Avril Lavigne, ‘My Happy Ending’ (2004) Following the spunky one-two punch of breakout hits “Complicated” and “Sk8ter Boi,” Avril Lavigne had something to prove on her sophomore effort, 2004’s Under My Skin. Though barely 20 years old, the Canadian pop-punk star had already seen her share of challenging relationships, channeling her disappointment into a singular line — “So much for my happy ending” — at the top of the album’s breakup ballad. She’s a co-writer on the song, with producer Butch Walker, and Lavigne’s lament is achingly felt in the bridge, “It’s nice to know we had it all/Thanks for watching as I fall/And letting me know we were done.” The success of “My Happy Ending” confirmed the opposite, as Lavigne’s star continued to rise.—Shirley Halperin
- Yungblud, ‘Hello Heaven, Hello’ (2025)

While he hadn’t yet turned 30 when his fourth album, Idols, came out in 2025, British agit-rocker Yungblud had already blazed a singular career path by the time of its release, and he used its opening cut to reintroduce himself to the world. The nine-minute, three-part rock opera, he told Rolling Stone, was inspired by him realizing the parallels between stadium rock and concert-hall classical; Yungblud added a dollop of 21st-century angst to the mix, cementing the song as his own. “Hello Heaven, Hello” veers from propulsive rock to swaggering post-glam to cavernous neo-power-balladry; it’s audacious and triumphant, with Yungblud’s tightly wound yawp sounding ready to conquer the world. —Maura Johnston

- Downtown Boys, ‘Monstro’ (2015) Providence, Rhode Island’s Downtown Boys combined refreshingly confrontational left-wing politics and a refreshingly confrontational punk attack on their excellent second album, Full Communism. The album’s peak cathartic moment was “Monstro,” a roaring critique of sexist, racist stereotypes and celebration of revolutionary power. With a blaring Lora Logic-style sax leading the charge, the song builds and builds until it combusts, as frontwoman Victoria Ruiz repeats the line “She’s brown! She’s smart!” like a battle cry. It’s political punk rock primed for the DSA era. —J.D.

- Moses Sumney, ‘Virile’ (2019) Moses Sumney is no stranger to challenging our expectations, whether he’s making your jaw drop with his ocean-deep, sky-high vocal range or creating spellbinding visual worlds to complement his otherworldly music. On “Virile,” a standout from his 2020 album, Græ, Sumney raises his glass to masculinity and smashes it on the ground. Sumney does rock music his way, alchemizing cavernous drums with spritely harp, industrial rock with classical music, heaven with hell. “Dear son,” he screeches to the stars, before slinking into his lower register, “We pick our own prisons.” “Virile” is evidence that we’re only confined to the boxes we lock ourselves into. —Jaeden Pinder

- Sleigh Bells, ‘Rill Rill’ (2010) A band birthed both in the belly of MySpace and peak-hipster Williamsburg, Sleigh Bells became a huge hit with blog-era tastemakers. This breakout track — off 2010’s Treats — sounds like your heart beating its way out of your chest, a tidal wave of guitars, booming drums, and electro sleaze, all showcasing Alexis Krauss’ almost too-sweet vocals. If you ever saw them perform live, you’ll know the feeling of all those amps buzzing in your chest as the crowd pogoed along. The track just sounds like 2010: languid and hopeful, a party before the world burns. —Brenna Ehrlich

- Alejandro Escovedo, ‘Castanets’ (2001) No one is better at merging the worlds of country-roots and punk than Alejandro Escovedo, and no song of his embodies his New York Dolls meets Austin roadhouse sound than “Castanets.” Escovedo storms and stomps his way through his deceptively nuanced tale of “a woman people don’t understand,” as he later explained. When George W. Bush was reported to have liked the song in 2005, Escovedo retired it from his set lists for several years, even though it was his most well-known tune. Then, more than two decades later, Escovedo deconstructed his cowpunk anthem with an entirely new arrangement and Spanglish lyrics on 2024’s “Castañuelas.”—Jonathan Bernstein
- King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, ‘Rattlesnake’ (2017)

The marvelously prolific Australian psych-punk shredders King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard have released a slew of songs that could potentially be on this list, but the opening track from their 2017 exploration of alternate guitar tunings Flying Microtonal Banana has taken on a life of its own. Chugging guitars and huge gales — as well as a Vibraslap that echoes the titular serpent’s warning sound — give “Rattlesnake” an ominously windswept, while lead Gizzard Stu Mackenzie’s constant repetition “rattlesnake” (he says it 54 times on the album version, according to fans) and the microtonal tuning make it feel like a fever dream that won’t — and shouldn’t — end. —M.J.

- Red Clay Strays, ‘Wondering Why’ (2022) Though ostensibly a country band from Alabama, the Red Clay Strays sure can rock: Songs like “Ramblin’” and “Down South” have all the punch of Lynyrd Skynyrd. In the case of their breakout song, “Wondering Why,” however, they display more of a slow burn. There’s no big riff, no bombastic intro — just Elvis-adjacent frontman Brandon Coleman’s smoldering croon, which blazes near the song’s end as drummer John Hall plays an understated beat with a few choice cymbal hits. For the really ferocious version of “Wondering Why,” check out the band’s Live at the Ryman album.—Joseph Hudak

- Future Islands, ‘Seasons (Waiting on You)’ (2014) The idiosyncratic Baltimore indie band had a surprise hit with the high-drama synth-pop of “Seasons (Waiting on You),” a song about how time may pass but some people remain frustratingly the same. Singer Samuel T. Herring delivered his heartbroken lyrics with an uncanny emotional force, going from a forlorn croon to an overwrought rasp that was hard to shake once you heard it. His ungainly dance moves were unforgettable too; when the band performed on The Late Show With David Letterman, the host’s floored reaction helped seed the song’s viral success. —J.D.

- Blondshell, ‘Salad’ (2023) “Gonna get big,” Blondshell’s Sabrina Teitelbaum declares. She accomplishes all that and more on “Salad,” the deliciously dark centerpiece of her 2023 self-titled debut. It’s the indie-rock version of “Goodbye Earl,” as Teitelbaum sets out to get revenge on a guy for abusing her friend — specifically by poisoning his greens. She lays out her plan across thrashing, restless riffs, inspired by Hole’s “Doll Parts” and Nirvana’s “You Know You’re Right,” a move that proved she was carrying the furious torch of the Nineties into a new generation. “Look what you did/You’ll make a killer of a Jewish girl,” she sings. It was one of the first startlingly great Teitelbaum lines — and certainly not the last. —A.M.

- The Monkees, ‘Me and Magdalena’ (2016) The idea of a brilliant new Monkees album in 2016 seemed about as likely as the Archies making a major musical comeback. But for their 50th anniversary, Monkees superfan Adam Schlesinger recruited an incredible slate of songwriters, including Noel Gallagher, Paul Weller, and Rivers Cuomo, for the comeback LP Good Times! Dead Cab for Cutie’s Ben Gibbard contributed the gorgeous ballad “Me and Magdalena,” which Schlesinger arranged as a duet between Micky Dolenz and Michael Nesmith. Their voices blended as seamlessly as they did back in the 1960s, finally giving them a new classic they could play in concert alongside “I’m a Believer” and “Pleasant Valley Sunday.” —A.G.

- Mdou Moctar, ‘Afrique Victime’ (2021) Equally inspired by Eddie Van Halen as he is by the Tuareg guitarists of his native Niger, Mdou Moctar is one of the 21st century’s greatest guitarists — and his hypnotizing solo on the desert blues track “Afrique Victime” is a perfect example why. Across the song’s seven-minute run time, the tempo rises and rises as Moctar laments French colonialism’s eternal scar on Niger. He plays the song’s guitar solo as if he’s vehemently typing away on a computer, sliding back and forth and drumming along the strings, warping the instrument’s tones to mimic a wailing siren. “Afrique Victime”’ is frenetic yet liberating — it’s no wonder he’s often called the Hendrix of the Sahara. —J.P.

- Sum 41, ‘Fat Lip’ (2001) “Fat Lip” is so immaculate, you’d never know Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley cobbled it together from disparate parts: a monster riff, a howl-along chorus, a tender bridge, and, most daringly, a rap-rock verse with the pass-it-off stylings of the Beastie Boys and Run-D.M.C. By Whibley’s admission, the demo stunk, but producer Jerry Finn saw the vision. “Fat Lip” remains one of the great achievements of the early-aughts pop-punk boom: an undeniable hit that’s sneakily inventive in construction and execution; a brilliant loser anthem that’s defiant, deprecating and degenerate, funny and furious. Still, to this day, it’s guaranteed to get the pit going. —J. Blistein

- The Rolling Stones, ‘Whole Wide World’ (2023) At the start of the 2020s, Rolling Stones fans had resigned themselves to the idea that they were simply a touring band at that point. Fortunately, producer Andrew Watt didn’t share this viewpoint and managed to coax them into the studio for 2023’s revitalized Hackney Diamonds. The LP’s climax is “Whole Wide World,” where Mick Jagger sings about a broke-down Londoner convinced his best days are long behind him: “When the whole wide world’s against you/And that’s got you on the run/And you think the party’s over/But it’s only just, only just begun,” he sings. The song was also a tribute to the Stones themselves, who managed to extend the party longer than any rock band in history. —A.G.
- Electric Six, ‘Danger! High Voltage’ (2002)

All together now: “Fire in the disco! Fire in the Taco Bell!” (Yes, it rhymes with “gates of hell.”) “Danger! High Voltage” was an insanely catchy floor-filler in the indie-sleaze days of the early 2000s — if you were a drunk girl and this song came on in the scuzzy rock bar at 2 a.m., you were legally required to dance on a table and kick the DJ’s drinks over. Detroit conceptual mastermind Dick Valentine groans about the agonies and ecstasies of physical love for a global left-field hit. But he gets a big assist from his duet partner: Jack White, uncredited but unmistakable, wailing “danger, danger!” in his high-pitched sex yelp. —R.S.

- Jason Isbell and the 400 Unit, ‘Cumberland Gap’ (2017) Before his name became synonymous with the best in detail-rich Americana songwriting thanks to albums like his 2013 opus, Southeastern, Jason Isbell was one of the three singer-guitarists in this century’s top literate bar band, Drive-By Truckers. On this rocker from his 2017 LP, The Nashville Sound, Isbell showed how hard he could still bring it, singing about working-class angst and desperation in the heart of coal country over the roaring backing of his band the 400 Unit. “Maybe the Cumberland Gap just swallows you whole,” he wonders. That sense of fatalism is deep in his bones, but so is the dream of punching your way out. —J.D.

- At the Drive-In, ‘Arcarsenal’ (2000) At the Drive-In’s third album, Relationship of Command, truly felt like a band firing on all cylinders. Their sound was sharper, crisper, and more adrenaline-surged than ever — some of that a result of producer Ross Robinson finding ways to capture the musicians at their most heightened state. And the first song, “Arcarsenal,” offers the best introduction to the power coursing through the album, functioning as a forceful call to action to break from societal conformity. It’s also a solid example of Omar Rodríguez-López and Cedric Bixler-Zavala’s almost telepathic connection, with Bixler-Zavala howling out the lyrics (“I must have read a thousand faces”) to Rodríguez-López’s blistering riffs. —J.L.

- Louis XIV, ‘Finding Out True Love Is Blind’ (2005) Deliciously sexy and sleazy, this track epitomized why Louis XIV were once banned in Alabama. What other band can make “carrot juice” sound dirty? The standout on 2005’s The Best Little Secrets Are Kept, this song encapsulates a truly horny era replete with flat-ironed bangs, that first foray into skinny jeans, and a solid lacquering of eyeliner. The song may have an STD or two, but singer Jason Hill is an equal opportunity letch: smart girls, short girls, tough girls, girls of all races and creeds, he’s down to wind you up and make you crawl to him — even 20 years later. —B.E.

- Deerhunter, ‘Desire Lines’ (2010) On their space-rock epiphany “Desire Lines,” the Atlanta band Deerhunter found a happy place somewhere between moody Velvet Underground drone poetry and languid, stretched out, eat-a-peach transcendence. The peak moment on their great LP Halcyon Digest, the song begins as a hesitant reflection on twentysomething coming-of-age ambivalences, then lifts off into a mind-meld monster jam between guitarists Lockett Pundt and Bradford Cox, who make like shoegaze ninjas for three dazzling minutes. It’s a modern psychedelic bounty that brilliantly undercut trippy escapism with real-life ambivalence. —J.D.

- Sturgill Simpson, ‘Call to Arms’ (2016) After the release of his breakthrough album, Metamodern Sounds in Country Music, it was clear that Sturgill Simpson was in a category all his own, far beyond just the bounds of traditional country. He cemented that on 2016’s A Sailor’s Guide to Earth, which ends with the furious “Call to Arms,” where Simpson, alongside a wailing horn section, bemoans our modern discontents. “They serve up distractions and we eat ‘em with fries, until the bombs fall out of our fucking skies,” he sings. When Simpson appeared on Saturday Night Live, he finished the song with the ultimate rock star move: smashing his guitar.—Marissa R. Moss
- Ought, ‘Beautiful Blue Sky’ (2015)

The Montreal post-punk rebels Ought racked up a string of cerebral records in the 2010s, eventually evolving into the new band Cola, which put out one of 2026’s finest rock statements with Cost of Living Adjustment. “Beautiful Blue Sky” is a life-affirming staccato guitar groove, building under Tim Darcey’s acerbically witty voice, as he narrates another boring no

items.title: Introducing: Castmaster
items.description: It’s almost Thanksgiving, and maybe you’re traveling to see friends and/or family for the holiday. Maybe instead you’re preparing for the arrival of friends and/or family who are traveling to see you. Maybe you’re not going anywhere and spending the holiday al
items.author: Vulture Editors
paragraphs: It’s almost Thanksgiving, and maybe you’re traveling to see friends and/or family for the holiday. Maybe instead you’re preparing for the arrival of friends and/or family who are traveling to see you. Maybe you’re not going anywhere and spending the holiday alone. Regardless of the scenario, you’re about to either have some time for yourself or carve out some time for yourself, and what you’d love to do during that time is play a movie trivia game. But there’s only one Cinematrix each day, and you’ve already exhausted the archives, so you need a new game — ideally one that’s challenging and infinitely replayable. What are you to do?

We anticipated that you’d have this problem, so we decided to help. We’re happy to present Castmaster, a new Vulture movie trivia game that you can play whenever you’d like, as often as you’d like. The objective is simple: A movie title is presented, and a player is tasked with naming an actor from that film. For each correct answer, a player gets 100 points; if a correct answer is entered within ten seconds, bonus points are awarded based on the speed of the entry. No more worrying about “exhausting the archives” — you can play to see how long of a streak you can string together, how high of a score you can manage, or both, as much as you desire. If you’re signed in to your New York Magazine log-in, your high scores will be recorded, and you’ll be able to see how your scores stack up against other players for a given day, week, and month.

This is just the first iteration of Castmaster; more features and game modes will be coming soon. Stay tuned, tell your friends and family, and please share any feedback you have with us on Discord. We’ll see you on the leaderboards.

items.title: The Hunting Wives Recap: Good Evening, Ms. Banks
items.description: While I admit I have been a little annoyed at the many moving pieces and timelines of this second season, I do have to admit it is all rather tidy and all stems from one event: Margo sleeping with Brad. Abby’s murder, Sophie getting caught up in it, Sophie kil
items.author: Christina Grace Tucker
paragraphs: While I admit I have been a little annoyed at the many moving pieces and timelines of this second season, I do have to admit it is all rather tidy and all stems from one event: Margo sleeping with Brad. Abby’s murder, Sophie getting caught up in it, Sophie killing Kyle, Nadia’s involvement — none of it would have happened if Margo had not, you know, raped a teenager. So it makes sense that this episode culminates with Brad waiting for Margo in her house with a gun, doesn’t it? But it takes us a minute to get there, so here we go!

It’s a good night to get down to business in Maple Brook! Sophie and Margo are enjoying their newfound domestic bliss, Jonny and Chet are keeping it #professional by fucking at work, and Callie is strapping Nadia down, my actual word! My girl is a born top, I’ll tell you what! It’s also nice to see her with someone who actually likes her, as Nadia clearly does. She confirms that they are dating, and it’s very sweet to see Callie all giggles and stars in her eyes. We all know the show is about the Abby Jackson murder, and boy, I am not looking forward to Callie finding out! But there is no time for that, cause Nadia has to run and meet up with Chet in the park for some light blackmail. Look, if you are gonna fuck the sheriff in his office, perhaps turn off the mics?

Chet has the missing piece Nadia has been searching for. She’s never bought the theory that Jill killed Abby, so getting traffic cam photos of Jill on her way home ten minutes before the murder has her feeling quite good. I imagine the orgasms also didn’t hurt. Chet seems kind of hilariously (and troublingly?) unconcerned about this huge piece of evidence that went missing? The case is CLOSED, and that’s all he has to say about that! Nadia just rolls her eyes before confirming he is gonna stay on her blackmail list until this is all sorted out. For now, she’s gotta get to the Married Justice photoshoot, where she picks out a sexy blazer for her new gf. Said GF is feeling a little nervous to see Margo, as Callie hasn’t seen her since she drove over to call her a cunt. But the two of them manage to have a bonding moment about their new significant others, and it seems all signs are pointing towards a renewed friendship.

After the photo shoot, Nadia takes Callie to see the proofs, bragging about how hot and cool she is. “He protects … but she serves.” They celebrate by making out, but before they can get to the good stuff, Nadia’s phone rings. She steps out, and Callie uses her moment of privacy to click on the VERY prominent and very tempting item “MARRIED JUSTICE SIZZLE.” Of course, it’s all about Abby’s murder, and ugh, my heart hurts for poor Callie! Can one person just tell her the truth, please? Nadia insists that she never meant to hurt Callie; she’s desperate to explain, but Callie wants her out, and I think that’s fair. Nadia, how else did you think this was gonna go?

Meanwhile, our two murderers are just as happy as can be, taking giant baths in Margo’s house while Jed is out campaigning. Sophie has decided she doesn’t mind Jed and Margo’s relationship, as long as Margo isn’t fucking other women; she’s as happy as can be. Kind of a wild turnaround from “your husband is a creep who wants to fuck me,” but Sophie is not known for making smart choices, now is she? In tougher news, Graham is not being cool about their divorce; in fact, he has repossessed the Tesla, and now Sophie is stranded with a Halloween costume in one hand and no car to drive. One little call to her girlfriend later, and she’s at the dealership. Sophie mostly needs to pick up her son and go to the grocery store, but before you know it, Margo has her in a gorgeous little green sports car. Shoutout to Porsche for the sponsorship; I hope you were listening to all the details about the car! But if it takes Porsche money to get a better wig on Malin Ackerman, well, it was all worth it! Also, Margo reallllly wants Sophie to come to church with her, and because she is #downbad, Sophie agrees.

And finally, we have Brad. He’s gone from hanging with Chase at parties and photoshoots to doing a guided ayahuasca trip, and I hope you are ready, because it’s quite a trip! After ingesting (and then throwing up) the drugs, he “wakes up” in his house, set to “Crazy.” Jill is there to welcome him, but it turns nasty very quickly. One moment she is talking about how much she loves him, and the next she is calling every other woman in his life a whore. Finally, she insists that he have a snack, unbuttoning her blouse so he can breastfeed. Brad tries to push her away, and she tells him that she gave him “everything he ever wanted.” Brad screams that he didn’t want it, and there is our confirmation that Jill sexually abused him. This is a logical place to take this storyline, and season one laid enough groundwork for it to feel earned. And though this show tends to trend toward “silly and on the nose,” this storyline has been pretty well handled. It is clear that Brad is not well, and his mother’s actions are clearly being condemned, not used for titillation. My problem is that the show treats his relationship with Margo like a sexy secret instead of a straight-up crime! You can’t have it both ways!

Deep in his hallucination, Brad kills his mother, and then immediately comes to the real world to discover that he has, in fact, killed Chase Brylan. Pants around his ankles, so we can guess that the combination of real-life attempted assault and memories of abuse led the boy to snap. R.I.P. John Stamos, and just wondering, player to player, what was your day rate for this? Worth it??

The next morning at church, everyone is just holding on for dear life. Callie is fighting back tears as the girls ask her about the photoshoot and the show; Nadia is trying to talk to the Reverend about the fact that his wife was not a killer, but he doesn’t want to hear it. He gets maybe three sentences in for the sermon before Brad appears, in a hospital gown and jeans. Brad begs his father for help, and the Reverend promptly ends services for the day. Maybe the first time in his life he put his kid before work, but does it count if he’s only doing it because his kid embarrassed him at work? I submit it does not! Also, Brad has a gun! It doesn’t really matter, but I am curious about how Brad got from Austin back to Maple Brook and also saw a doctor and grabbed a gun? Busy kid! The Reverend tries to talk him down, even telling him that his mother did not kill Abby, but it’s too late for Brad. When the Austin PD calls, Brad knows the jig is up. He begs his father not to answer the phone, but his father clearly doesn’t believe his son is a killer and picks up. Brad shoots him, then leaves.
Margo and Sophie are planning another grand night of romance, but instead, Margo comes home to Brad and gun in her living room. Ruh-roh!

• HUGE development for Wanda and Walter: they slept together! Weeks ago, right before Wanda came back from her injury. In the flashback, we can tell Walter is clearly hoping for a relationship, but Wanda doesn’t want it to get messy since they work together. In the present, at Walter’s bedside, Wanda thinks she might have made a mistake. “What is the point in caring if you don’t have anyone to care about?” Good point, my friend!

• Jonny has, of course, assigned the John Doe case to Wanda, and she is intrepidly digging into it, as she is wont to do. Dr. Bob in the morgue senses something is off with her, and her many lingering glances at Walter’s desk make me think she is missing her buddy! John Doe has been nibbled on by too many creatures to make an ID, so she’ll just have to rely on the bag of items on the body. Her one stroke of luck? The set of keys that she finds. They turn on the truck that she has been insisting is Kyle’s, and with this one piece of evidence, she might have figured out the whole Kyle Burkett mess. Can I get a “hell yea, Wanda?”

items.title: Gérard Depardieu to Stand Trial for Rape Charges After Failed Appeal
items.description: French actor Gérard Depardieu will face a criminal rape trial after an appeal from his lawyers failed.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: French actor Gérard Depardieu will face a criminal rape trial after an appeal from his lawyers failed.

According to Reuters, on Thursday the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that a trial would go ahead regarding rape charges that stemmed from accusations made by actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018. She alleged that in August of that year, Depardieu raped her twice at his Paris home. He was indicted in December 2020 and has denied any wrongdoing. Last year, his lawyers appealed the prosecutors’ decision for the case to go to trial.
Though the court rejected his appeal, it ruled that Depardieu will only be tried for the first alleged rape, and not the second. If convicted, the 77-year-old could face 15 to 20 years in prison.

The news comes just 10 days after Depardieu’s withdrawal of a separate appeal regarding his conviction last year on sexual assault charges. He was given an 18-month suspended prison sentence for sexually assaulting two women on the set of his 2021 film “Les Volets Verts.”

In a statement to French newspaper Le Monde, he said: “Justice has spoken. I have been found guilty. I accept this and take responsibility for this conviction,” offering his “deep and sincere apologies” to those who “may have suffered as a result.”

Last week, a new complaint alleged further rape and sexual assault allegations against Depardieu during the filming of Guillaume Nicloux’s “Thalasso” in 2018. His lawyers told French radio station RTL that they were unaware of the complaint, which was filed in May 2025, shortly after his first sexual assault trial.

items.title: Ben Affleck Negotiates With a Duck as Artists Equity Kicks Off Thanksgiving Campaign for Aflac
items.description: Ben Affleck’s Artists Equity and the insurance company Aflac are using Thanksgiving to launch a new installment of their campaign starring the actor and the namesake duck.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: Ben Affleck’s Artists Equity and the insurance company Aflac are using Thanksgiving to launch a new installment of their campaign starring the actor and the namesake duck.

The new spot, dubbed “High Stakes,” is set to debut on the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on NBC Thursday, and will see Affleck serving as a translator between a team of negotiators… and the Aflac Duck.

Artits Equity and Aflac unveiled their campaign in September via a viral marketing effort that saw Affleck vandalizing Aflac billboards. It’s expected to run through next summer, leaning on tentpole events (like, say this week’s parade) to move it along.
Affleck himself frequently directs commercial spots from Artists Equity

“Sure, it’s funny to have Ben Affleck translating for the Aflac Duck. But the idea is rooted in a simple truth,” said Aflac senior VPand CMO Garth Knutson. “Every year, millions of Americans turn to Aflac agents and HR professionals to help them understand their benefits and make informed decisions about their coverage. In this commercial, Ben does it for 60 seconds. They do it every day.”

“As we explored the bond forming between the Aflac Duck and the Affleck Human, it became clear we needed to show audiences that Ben was gaining a deeper understanding of Aflac and its brand icon,” added Brandon Pierce, co-president and ECD of Artists Equity Brand Studio. “And what better way to prove it than through a high-stakes negotiation where Ben could simply and boldly declare, ‘I speak Aflac.’”

items.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed as Storm Descends on Northeast
items.description: In an unprecedented move, the 100th edition of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City will be postponed until Saturday Nov. 28, Macy’s and NBC announced Wednesday.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: In an unprecedented move, the 100th edition of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City will be postponed until Saturday Nov. 28, Macy’s and NBC announced Wednesday.
The decision comes as a powerful nor’easter storm is bearing down on the northeast, with potential wind gusts north of 60 miles per hour alongside heavy rain.
It’s also a major headache for the broadcast partner NBC, with last year’s parade drawing over 34 million viewers between NBC and Peacock.

The parade is now expected to kick off on the Upper West Side at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, with the floats, balloons and performers making their way down to Macy’s flagship store on 34th Street. NBC confirmed that it will broadcast the parade Saturday at 8:30 a.m. to all time zones; it will also stream on Peacock.

“Due to the extreme weather conditions, the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC have decided, in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators, to move the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, Nov. 28,” an NBC spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter. “More details to follow. In addition, NBC will telecast the 2025 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade tomorrow at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones.”
It’s also a logistical nightmare, with many performance groups and musical artists coming into town for the parade, and which may need to find alternative travel plans.

The parade has never been canceled in its 100 years, though some of the iconic giant balloons have been grounded when there have been high winds. Balloons are supposed to be grounded if wind gusts top 34 miles per hour.
In 1993, a Sonic the Hedgehog balloon was pushed into a lamppost amid high winds, injuring multiple people, and a similar incident occurred in 1997 with a Cat in the Hat balloon.
This year’s postponement is also a first. New York City officials and Macy’s executives are expected to address the postponement later on Wednesday.

items.title: NBC Uses Thanksgiving TV to Kickstart 2028 LA Olympics Marketing Push
items.description: It’s still 2026, but NBC Sports is using a stacked Thanksgiving TV lineup to tee up the 2028 summer Olympics, which will be held in Los Angeles, California.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: It’s still 2026, but NBC Sports is using a stacked Thanksgiving TV lineup to tee up the 2028 summer Olympics, which will be held in Los Angeles, California.

The network is debuting a pair of spots on today’s (surprise rebroadcast of last year’s) Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, and they will re-air on the National Dog Show Presented by Purina and in Thursday night’s national NFL game between the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills.

The spots star Olympic track & field gold medalists Sydney Levrone and Rai Benjamin encountering enormous Olympic rings at famous L.A. locations, like in Griffith park overlooking the city, or on the coast at sunset.

“For LA28, the city itself is going to be one of the stars of the Games, and we wanted this creative to capture what it will mean to welcome the Olympics back to the United States,” said Jenny Storms, CMO of NBCUniversal Television & Streaming. “Sydney and Rai have delivered unforgettable moments for Team USA and seeing them discover the Rings in iconic Los Angeles settings is the perfect way to remind America that the Games are coming home. Thanksgiving is annually one of NBCUniversal’s biggest days and an unmatched platform to continue building excitement for the Olympics.”

NBC officially kicked off its 2028 Olympics marketing at the end of the 2026 winter games in Milan-Cortina in a spot featuring actress Kate Hudson and set to the tune of The Mamas & The Papas’ 1966 classic “California Dreamin.’”
The new spots build on that, teeing up what is sure to be aggressive 2027 push ahead of the 2028 games.

items.title: Специальный показ фильма «Вершина»
items.description: Специальный показ фильма «Вершина»
items.author: Ольга Скворцова
paragraphs: Специальный показ фильма «Вершина»

29 ноября в кинотеатре «Каро 11 Октябрь» состоится специальный показ триллера «Вершина». После сеанса зрители смогут обсудить картину с ее режиссером Юрием Быковым и кинокритиком Никитой Демченко. Приглашаем членов клуба «Сноб» посмотреть фильм, поговорить с его автором о режиссерском замысле и задать свои вопросы.

В лагерь альпинистов с опозданием на два дня приезжает Дмитрий Зорин (Артём Быстров). Вместе с группой любителей он собирается подняться на высоту 5200 метров. Погода портится, но гиды решают вести группу к вершине, чтобы не потерять заработок.

Идея фильма возникла у Быкова после восхождения на Эльбрус. Сценарий он написал вместе с Саввой Минаевым. Перед съемками исполнители главных ролей тренировались в предгорьях Эльбруса с профессиональными альпинистами. Часть съемок прошла в Архызе на высоте около трех тысяч метров. В картине также снялись Александр Робак, Анна Банщикова и Андрей Смоляков. В прокат «Вершина» выйдет 3 декабря.

items.title: Молодые люди с синдромом Дауна познакомились с работой гостиничной сети
items.description: Вместе с педагогами и сотрудниками отеля ребята побывали за стойкой регистрации, узнали, как готовят номера к приезду гостей, учились сервировать стол и приняли участие в кулинарном мастер-классе. Они с интересом брались за незнакомые задания и уверенно справл
items.author: Благотворительный фонд «Синдром любви
paragraphs: Вместе с педагогами и сотрудниками отеля ребята побывали за стойкой регистрации, узнали, как готовят номера к приезду гостей, учились сервировать стол и приняли участие в кулинарном мастер-классе. Они с интересом брались за незнакомые задания и уверенно справлялись с поручениями.

Для фонда «Синдром любви» такие встречи особенно важны. Молодые люди с синдромом Дауна, как и их сверстники, задумываются о будущем и ищут дело по душе. При этом возможностей найти работу у них по-прежнему мало. Многие работодатели сомневаются, какие обязанности можно поручить человеку с синдромом Дауна и как поддержать его на рабочем месте. На стажировке в AZIMUT Отель Аэростар Москва ребята попробовали себя в разных ролях и смогли понять, что им ближе. А сотрудники отеля увидели, как уверенно участники справлялись с поручениями, получая понятные инструкции.

«Одна из важных задач инклюзивного общества — создавать условия, в которых каждый человек может раскрыть свой потенциал, получить необходимые навыки и почувствовать себя частью команды. При этом знакомство с профессиями и практический опыт должны быть доступны всем. Крайне важно дать ребятам эту возможность. Мы рады стать для участников проекта наставниками и проводниками в сферу гостеприимства», — отметил Владислав Святной, генеральный менеджер AZIMUT Отель Аэростар Москва.

В тот же день специалисты фонда провели тренинг для сотрудников гостиницы. Они обсудили, как общаться с гостями с синдромом Дауна и другими ментальными особенностями, как предложить помощь и что сделать, чтобы гостям было комфортно в отеле.

«Для фонда „Синдром любви“ такие встречи — возможность больше рассказать о людях с синдромом Дауна. Они могут приехать в отель как гости, и важно, чтобы сотрудники понимали, как с ними общаться и при необходимости помочь. Возможно, в будущем кто-то из наших ребят станет сотрудником гостиницы, поэтому знакомство с её работой — ценный опыт. Сегодня мы провели тренинг для персонала, а ребята прошли экскурсию-стажировку и попробовали себя в разных ролях. Спасибо команде AZIMUT Hotels за открытость и такую возможность», — сказала Юлия Лентьева, руководитель направления «Сопровождение подростков и молодых людей с синдромом Дауна» фонда «Синдром любви».

Московский «День добра» стал первым мероприятием совместного проекта фонда «Синдром любви» и гостиничной сети. AZIMUT Hotels планирует масштабировать инициативу и проводить экскурсии-стажировки на базе других отелей в российских городах.

items.title: Экскурсия по выставке «Случаи и характеры»
items.description: Экскурсия по выставке «Случаи и характеры»
items.author: Ольга Скворцова
paragraphs: Экскурсия по выставке «Случаи и характеры»

3 декабря «Сноб» приглашает членов клуба в Центр культуры «Солодовня» на экскурсию по выставке «Случаи и характеры». Её название отсылает к статье Николая Карамзина, который в 1802 году предложил художникам сюжеты из русской истории. Участники экскурсии увидят, как Иван Айвазовский изобразил переправу Александра II через Дунай, а Константин Вещилов — Стеньку Разина перед походом на Астрахань. В экспозицию также вошли эскизы Ильи Репина, миниатюры и предметы декоративно-прикладного искусства.

Центральное место на выставке занимает «Иван Сусанин» — последнее большое полотно Константина Маковского. Художник написал его в 1914 году. Современники ожидали, что картина попадёт в Русский музей, но после смерти Маковского она осталась во Франции. В 1976 году внучка художника продала полотно в частное собрание в США. Сорок лет спустя российские коллекционеры приобрели картину и привезли её в Россию. Теперь у «Ивана Сусанина» постоянное место в «Солодовне».
