items.title: Ученые обнаружили тренировку, которая позволяет терять жир, но не мышцы после 65 лет
items.description: При снижении веса важно не только то, сколько килограммов уходит, но и за счет чего меняется масса тела. Вместе с жиром организм может терять и мышечную ткань. С возрастом это особенно важно: мышцы постепенно слабеют, и человеку становится сложнее ходить, подн
items.author: Ксения Зернова
paragraphs: При снижении веса важно не только то, сколько килограммов уходит, но и за счет чего меняется масса тела. Вместе с жиром организм может терять и мышечную ткань. С возрастом это особенно важно: мышцы постепенно слабеют, и человеку становится сложнее ходить, подниматься по лестнице и сохранять равновесие. Исследователи из Университета Саншайн-Кост в Австралии сравнили три режима тренировок и выяснили, что высокоинтенсивные интервальные занятия могут помочь уменьшить количество жира, сохранив безжировую массу. Результаты опубликованы в журнале Maturitas.

В исследовании участвовали 123 здоровых человека в возрасте от 65 до 85 лет. Средний возраст составил 72 года. На протяжении шести месяцев они трижды в неделю занимались в спортзале под наблюдением специалистов. Каждое занятие длилось около 45 минут.
Ученые сравнивали то, как организм реагирует на разную интенсивность нагрузки. Для этого участников случайным образом распределили на три группы по типам занятий:

В начале исследования, через три месяца и по окончании программы ученые измеряли состав тела участников с помощью двухэнергетической рентгеновской абсорбциометрии (DXA). Этот метод позволяет оценить количество жировой и безжировой массы, а также распределение жира в организме.
И интервальные, и умеренные тренировки помогли участникам уменьшить жировую массу. В обеих группах снижение было заметнее, чем у людей, которые занимались с низкой интенсивностью.

Однако изменения безжировой массы различались между группами. У участников, которые выполняли умеренные непрерывные тренировки, этот показатель немного снизился. В группе HIIT такого сокращения не обнаружили. Более того, через шесть месяцев только в группе интервальных тренировок было зафиксировано снижение доли жира в общей массе тела.

Обе программы — HIIT и умеренные тренировки — также помогли уменьшить количество висцерального жира. Он накапливается глубоко в брюшной полости, вокруг внутренних органов, и при избытке связан с повышенным риском инсулинорезистентности, сердечно-сосудистых и метаболических заболеваний.

Безжировая масса — это все ткани тела, кроме жировой: мышцы, кости, органы, соединительная ткань и вода. Ее снижение не всегда означает, что человек потерял именно скелетные мышцы. В этом исследовании ученые измеряли состав тела, но не проверяли силу мышц или их способность выполнять повседневную работу.

Тем не менее сохранение безжировой массы особенно важно для людей старшего возраста. Постепенное уменьшение мышечной массы и силы может привести к саркопении — состоянию, при котором человеку становится сложнее двигаться, удерживать равновесие и сохранять самостоятельность. При изменении веса имеет значение не только количество потерянного жира, но и то, удается ли сохранить ткани, необходимые для нормальной работы организма.

Авторы предполагают, что HIIT может лучше поддерживать безжировую массу благодаря более сильной нагрузке на мышцы. Во время интенсивных интервалов им приходится активнее работать, а периоды восстановления позволяют повторять усилие несколько раз за тренировку.

Высокоинтенсивные интервальные тренировки могут быть хорошим вариантом для людей старшего возраста, которые уже готовы к достаточно серьезной нагрузке. Но начинать с них после долгого периода малоподвижности не стоит. В исследовании все занятия проходили под наблюдением, а интенсивность нагрузки для каждого подбирали индивидуально.

HIIT может стать частью вашей программы, но не заменяет силовые тренировки. А вот сочетание аэробной нагрузки, упражнений с сопротивлением и работы над равновесием помогает поддерживать выносливость, силу и самостоятельность с возрастом.
Низкоуглеводные диеты, интервальное голодание и подсчет калорий: какие стратегии действительно помогают снизить вес и сохранить мышцы

items.title: 7 основ счастливой жизни: как расслабиться и отказаться от бесконечного самосовершенствования
items.description: Счастье несложно превратить в очередной проект по самосовершенствованию: нужно и выстроить идеальный режим дня, и завести полезные привычки, больше зарабатывать, путешествовать и постоянно работать над собой.
items.author: Ксения Зернова
paragraphs: Счастье несложно превратить в очередной проект по самосовершенствованию: нужно и выстроить идеальный режим дня, и завести полезные привычки, больше зарабатывать, путешествовать и постоянно работать над собой.

Британский философ Эндрю Копсон предлагает взглянуть на хорошую жизнь с другой стороны. В своей новой книге How to Be a Happy Human: Seven Humanist Foundations for a Better Life он перечисляет семь принципов, которые помогают ценить время, поддерживать дружбу, замечать красоту природы, быть добрее к окружающим и находить смысл в повседневности.

Как современная культура предлагает нам добиваться благополучия? Постоянно работать над собой, повышать продуктивность, осваивать новые практики и искать способы обмануть возраст и даже смерть — здесь Копсон вспоминает биохакера Брайана Джонсона. В попытках все контролировать люди могут забывать о самых простых составляющих хорошей жизни — отношениях, общении, интересе к миру и времени, которое проводят с близкими.

В гуманистической традиции, как утверждает Копсон, человек сам отвечает за то, чтобы придать своей жизни смысл, и может опираться на разум, знания и отношения с другими людьми. Придерживаться религиозных убеждений или искать готовые ответы на вопросы о предназначении для этого не обязательно. Важно научиться ценить единственную жизнь, которую мы имеем, и находить в ней поводы для радости.
Копсон также критикует привычку относиться к себе как к проекту, который нужно бесконечно улучшать. Он предлагает остановиться и обратить внимание на то, что составляет суть человеческой жизни:

Среди авторов, на чьи идеи он опирается, — философ Джон Стюарт Милль, писательница и публицист Маргарет Найт, писатель и ученый Айзек Азимов, писательница Зэди Смит. Историческую философскую традицию автор дополняет современной наукой и психологией.

Важную роль в написании книги сыграли и разговоры с учеными, психологами и людьми, которые регулярно сталкиваются с вопросами жизни и смерти в своей работе. Это, например, специалисты, оказывающие поддержку пациентам в больницах и заключенным в тюрьмах.
В книге Копсон формулирует семь идей, которые читатель может исследовать и применять по-своему. Он специально подчеркивает: это не обязательные инструкции и не набор лайфхаков для достижения счастья.

Осознание конечности жизни может вызывать тревогу — и это нормально. Но Копсон предлагает взглянуть на вопрос с другой стороны. Мы обладаем ограниченным количеством времени, и именно это делает его ценным. Признание собственной смертности помогает сконцентрироваться на том, как мы живем в настоящем, и противопоставляет это бесконечной погоне за молодостью и попыткам отсрочить неизбежное.

Мы не можем существовать отдельно от окружающего мира, поскольку зависим от среды вокруг нас и сами являемся частью живой природы. Копсон предлагает чаще проводить время вне стен и уделять внимание окружающему миру. Для этого необязательно ходить в многодневные походы: это могут быть прогулки в парке, комфортные поездки за город или время у воды. Контакт с природой — одна из самых простых составляющих хорошей жизни, но ей легко пренебречь в повседневной суете, напоминает философ.

То, что может быть приятным для одного, может оказаться неудобным для другого. На презентации своей книги Копсон привел пример с вечеринкой-сюрпризом: для одного человека это будет неожиданной радостью, а для интроверта, напротив, может стать источником стресса. Проявлять заботу означает не только хорошо относиться к окружающим, но и учитывать их желания и особенности.

Копсон предлагает обращать внимание на привычные способы рассуждения и проверять, всегда ли они помогают нам принимать решения. К примеру, человек может продолжать смотреть неинтересный ему фильм только потому, что уже потратил на него час своего времени. Это пример ошибки невозвратных затрат: прошлые усилия влияют на решение продолжать, хотя это их уже никак не компенсирует. Автор призывает относиться к своим ошибкам спокойнее и даже радоваться, когда становится ясно, что вы были неправы. Это дает возможность пересмотреть свою позицию и сделать выводы.

Любопытство — очень важный ингредиент счастья, и его нужно стараться сохранять на протяжении всей жизни. Осваивайте новые навыки, знакомьтесь с непривычными идеями и будьте готовыми пересматривать собственные взгляды, советует Копсон. Развитие не обязательно должно сопровождаться большими достижениями или измеряться продуктивностью. Порой достаточно просто попробовать то, чего вы раньше не делали, или взглянуть на знакомую ситуацию по-новому.

Можно десятилетиями искать свое единственное предназначение или ждать какого-то поворотного события, после которого и начнется настоящая жизнь. Но все это может так и не наступить, а смысл тем временем может складываться из повседневных вещей: близких отношений с теми, кто рядом, любимого дела, заботы о других и занятий, которые приносят удовольствие. Замечайте то, что делает жизнь значимой уже сейчас, и уделяйте этому больше внимания.

Мы не всегда можем повлиять на обстоятельства, но можем осознанно выбирать отношение к происходящему. Это не означает, что нужно сохранять позитивный настрой при любых событиях. У вас всегда есть возможность решать, на что опираться в трудные моменты, каким ценностям следовать и как поступать в соответствии с ними.
Низкоуглеводные диеты, интервальное голодание и подсчет калорий: какие стратегии действительно помогают снизить вес и сохранить мышцы

items.title: The Middling State of the Sitcom
items.description: These are dire days for TV comedy. In the past few years, entire genres that once anchored the network lineups have become endangered: late night, sketch shows, sitcoms. Of these, the last has probably been the most mourned. The internet can deliver topical jo
items.author: Inkoo Kang
paragraphs: These are dire days for TV comedy. In the past few years, entire genres that once anchored the network lineups have become endangered: late night, sketch shows, sitcoms. Of these, the last has probably been the most mourned. The internet can deliver topical jokes and parody skits faster and more cheaply than television can, but the soothing rhythms and aspirational relationships that audiences crave from traditional sitcoms are harder to replicate online. And they remain a reliable draw: “The Big Bang Theory” is one of HBO Max’s most watched titles, seven years after airing its final episode. Its long tail is hardly unusual among the popular comedies of the first two decades of the millennium, which saw the generation-defining runs of “Arrested Development,” “The Office,” “30 Rock,” and “Parks and Recreation.”

And yet, despite obvious viewer interest, the twenty-twenties have seen a precipitous drop in new sitcoms. By one estimate, the genre accounts for less than two per cent of the shows produced since the start of the decade. As with so many of Hollywood’s current ills, streaming deserves much of the blame: the binge model incentivizes serialized arcs over self-contained stories, and short seasons of six to thirteen episodes over the broadcast networks’ customary twenty-two. The streaming wars also prioritized prestige programming with conventional markers of quality, which caused the multi-cam setup to lose out to the single-cam approach, and comedies to grow increasingly sad (“BoJack Horseman”), sometimes to the point where humor became an afterthought (“The Bear”).

Such doldrums ought to spur television comedy’s next evolution, and perhaps they still will. But, save for a few outliers (“Adults”), contemporary sitcoms offer little hope for the genre. Two recent projects from single-cam veterans, the Amy Poehler vehicle “Dig” and the Tracy Morgan-led “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins,” exemplify the middling state of TV comedy today—less for their own shortcomings than for what they reveal about the staleness and timidity of the genre’s reigning conventions. The streaming age promised that a fragmented landscape would make room for experimentation; instead, it has bred a self-sabotaging cautiousness.

“Dig” débuts in the shadow of Poehler’s last sitcom, the government-workplace comedy “Parks and Rec,” which cemented the comedian’s onscreen persona as an ostensible normie never too far from wild-eyed obsession. The new series, a ten-episode mystery-comedy on Peacock, adapted from Kate Myers’s novel “Excavations,” reunites Poehler with the “Parks and Rec” showrunner Mike Schur. Poehler stars as Elise, an archeologist stationed in the fictional Greek town of Simantikos. After stumbling upon an eight-foot statue of Hera, a career-making discovery, the oft-overlooked Elise schemes to conceal it from her self-promoting boss, Neville (Hugh Laurie), who’s sure to take the credit. In order to unearth the statue, Elise is forced to let others in on the secret—a circle of trust that keeps widening until the artifact goes missing.

Like so many recent half-hour series, such as the romance-comedy “Nobody Wants This” and Schur’s detective dramedy “A Man on the Inside,” “Dig” fuses two genres and shortchanges both. Compared with the humor that typified the Obama-era heyday of the sitcom, “Dig” ’s jokes are derivative and sparse. And the mystery is not particularly engaging, since the characters who give it stakes get lost in heavy plotting. They include Clare (Antonia Thomas), a passionate technician whose stuffiness rankles her colleagues, and Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), a gadabout who returns to the dig site after an abrupt departure five years before. A gaggle of undergraduates flock to Simantikos to sift for shards under Neville’s light supervision, but the only one with any real characterization is Patty (Fina Strazza), a mythology buff who relates to the world mostly through Disney movies.

It’s hard to invest in any of the characters, least of all Elise, who self-deprecatingly says that her life motto is “Work hard and never have fun.” (Work was Leslie Knope’s idea of fun; Elise, whose devotion to archeology is never explained, comes across simply as a sullen deputy.) Poehler’s magic as a performer surfaces during bursts of mania, when she enters that liminal space between human and cartoon, but here she’s hemmed in by such a dour character. Only the silver-tongued Neville, whose dread of obsolescence lends Laurie some poignant moments, escapes the thin sketching that defines the rest of the ensemble: Clare needs to loosen up, Dylan needs to commit to something, Patty needs a friend. Each character inches from stunted to healed without surprise or spontaneity. The propulsion that serialization is meant to provide leaves no breathing room to explore, say, Elise’s genuine inadequacies as Neville’s potential successor, which form a gray cloud over the students’ summer break, or archeology’s reliance on a vanishing breed of benefactors. The result is less a find than a fragment, suggestive of a richer show that never emerges.

On a joke-by-joke basis, few current series can match the pace or the wit of “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins,” which rarely sags in the way of so many streaming originals. The show, an NBC mockumentary that returned for a second season this month, hails from the “30 Rock” writers Robert Carlock and Sam Means, and it may as well have been pitched as recalibrating the earlier sitcom’s signature style—zippy, sketch-based, pop-culture-savvy—for a broader audience. The title character, played by Morgan, another “30 Rock” alum, is a would-be N.F.L. legend who was run out of the league in the mid-two-thousands over a gambling scandal. (The amiable Reggie notes the irony of his continued infamy now that sports betting has become inescapable.) To rehabilitate his public image, Reggie hires Arthur (Daniel Radcliffe), an Oscar-winning documentarian who has experienced his own flameout, to give him a rebrand. But, since neither has a plan for Reggie’s redemption, they have a camera crew follow them around the ex-athlete’s New Jersey mansion, trusting that a story will take shape.

“Reggie Dinkins” proves that serialization needn’t overwhelm a sitcom. In the first season, the show fills in the details of Arthur’s professional derailment, while his growing attachment to his subjects chips away at his artistic pretensions. Arthur is also our entry point into the Dinkins home, which has been knocked gently off-kilter by fame and money. Reggie remains on friendly terms with his ex-wife and manager, Monica (Erika Alexander), who kept him from squandering his football fortune. The rest of his family life, forged after his time on the field, is even less conventional: his teen-age son, Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), treats him like “a bro with a Black Card”; his live-in best friend, Rusty (Bobby Moynihan), is always free for a hang; and his video-vixen fiancée, Brina (Precious Way), was a random hottie tracked down from an Instagram photo. As on “30 Rock,” the characters navigate an absurdist entertainment industry that supplies the show’s sharpest gags: Arthur idolizes a documentary mentor who “spent six months living as a corpse to expose corpse abuse,” and Monica’s search for a new assistant turns up the freshly unemployed—food inspectors, CBS News producers, vaccinated country singers.

But, like “Dig,” “Reggie Dinkins” can’t quite overcome the gap between archetype and character. The show is an exactingly crafted joke machine, but most members of the ensemble feel like setups for one-liners. The inevitable comparison to “30 Rock” underscores the vision that helped make that series a masterpiece; its creator and star, Tina Fey, gave her protagonist, Liz Lemon, an autobiographical urgency and an unexpectedly resonant friendship with her hyper-confident yet frantically neurotic boss, Jack Donaghy. Liz and Jack were regularly tipped into lunacy by their high-pressure jobs, but “Reggie Dinkins” shies from making its leads too weird, or even too selfish, leaving a disconnect between the geniality of the characters and the strangeness of their circumstances. In the end, the show gives its disgraced hero the puff piece he asked for, by seldom letting him fumble. ♦

items.title: How Offline Should a Person Be?
items.description: So far in this series, I’ve written about how we might collectively organize against Big Tech and how we might ward off the fear of rudeness that compels us to reply to every text message we receive. We’ve established that we should smash our devices and walk
items.author: Jay Caspian Kang
paragraphs: So far in this series, I’ve written about how we might collectively organize against Big Tech and how we might ward off the fear of rudeness that compels us to reply to every text message we receive. We’ve established that we should smash our devices and walk off into the field of not knowing, or whatever, but, given that we’re not actually going to do that, we should probably try to set a more realistic standard for how much time we can safely spend online. What is acceptable for someone who wants to be as offline as possible while remaining employed and “connected” enough to know, for instance, that your daughter’s soccer practice has been cancelled? Is two hours a day too much? What about thirty minutes? Should we get it down to the eight minutes it might take to read vital text messages from your child’s school or your mother or your boss?

I don’t think we need to put a precise number on it; nor do I think we need to buy the snake oil of every wellness entrepreneur selling a revolutionary app that will track our eyeballs to tell us the exact amount of time we should be spending online. But one statistic I found genuinely illuminating comes from a large survey conducted across fourteen different countries by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The O.E.C.D. found that people who reported between one to three hours of personal screen time per day also reported a higher “life satisfaction” than those who spent more time online. That figure excludes time spent on a screen for work or school but includes television and video games. The peak happiness for work-related screen time landed somewhere between three to five hours per day. If you do a little bit of extrapolating, then, it does seem possible to spend upward of six or seven hours a day in front of a screen and still report that you’ve got a high level of “life satisfaction.”

I think I could get my daily screen time down to around five hours without resorting to absurd affectations like, say, purchasing the print edition of the Times and reading all my news in a café with a tight yet self-satisfied frown on my face. And the reduction, I’m sure, would help. Maybe I would sleep a little bit better; maybe my relationship with my family would improve. But I’m not sure that such a gentle weaning would solve the core discontent I feel about online life, even if it made the symptoms mild enough for me to ignore the underlying sickness. It’s true that I still feel some “satisfaction” with my life, but I remain certain that we are all doomed if we don’t get off the internet in a real way. Changing my habits so that I fit within the band of O.E.C.D. high-satisfaction reporters is not a radical enough solution.

To put it more simply: If we believe that online life is, on balance, horrible, and that smartphones are destroying the minds of the youth, is some incremental adjustment to the current situation really sufficient?

Nearly everyone who hates the internet is an incrementalist, largely because it’s hard to go into true dropout mode. Unless you move to the woods, like the Unabomber, you will likely need some connection to the internet to survive. Full-blown opposition to technology is not a new affliction born from our addiction to phones but a way of thinking that has been around for hundreds of years. It is monastic, antisocial, and usually quite vague. The Unabomber, for instance, writes in his manifesto about the need for an “ideology that opposes technology,” but he does not explain what that opposition might look like outside of the example he set through his murderous actions. The goal of the bombings, he seems to suggest—albeit not very clearly—is to place stress on “the system” and somehow open up the possibility of revolution. He does not tell us what will happen when mankind finally breaks through the barricades; nor does he spend much time explaining how the revolution will be won. The manifesto, which continues to find an audience, is mostly a lot of buzzwords. Most anti-technology screeds similarly suffer from grandiose rhetoric and slippery prescriptions.

Incrementalism wins, then, because there’s no good alternative. Unfortunately, technology continues to replace many of our brain functions. In recent months, I’ve noticed my recall failing much more than it has in the past. At least a few times a week, a name gets stuck at the tip of my tongue; even if I can picture the person’s face and think of several details about them, the name remains behind an impermeable wall. Much of this, I’m told by my doctors, can be explained by a lack of sleep, but I still wonder if part of my memory simply up and quit after being repeatedly bypassed in favor of Google searches and A.I. prompts.
The Unabomber, despite his general fuzziness, was quite prescient when it comes to this kind of dependence. In his manifesto, he writes:

This, of course, is a description of today, when we have major outages that ground planes and grind businesses to a halt and yet nobody in charge can entirely explain what went wrong—or, when they do, people dismiss the official record and assume that the robots are either messing up or acting up. We now assume the machines make the decisions. This, it should be said, is a bit different from the machines actually making all the decisions. It’s quite possible that the nationwide ground stop that happened this past week did come from faulty network equipment, but the conspiratorial, A.I.-centric explanations that immediately surfaced online betray the public’s extreme suspicion and rank dislike of this new technology and how quickly it has begun to shape our lives. On any trip to the hospital, for example, we will likely be screened by A.I., talk to a nurse who has been scheduled by A.I., and then have our conversation with the nurse recorded by A.I. If any part of that system breaks, the recourse will almost certainly be more A.I.

This overreliance is why the anti-tech side can speak only in the language of general imperatives rather than specific actions. How could you describe a society without technology and not sound like a monk or a transcendentalist who’s lost his way from the nineteenth century? I’ve tried and failed. Can you do it?

But, if incrementalism is our only option, then how do you turn a call for moderately less screen time into a political movement? In an earlier column, I mentioned the Luddite Club, a group of young people trying to put down their phones. I expressed some skepticism about whether anyone, young or old, could really break free, which prompted Lucy Jackson, one of the early members of the Luddite Club, to send me an e-mail; we later spoke on the phone. Jackson, who is now in college, talks with a slow, careful confidence. In the past couple of years, she has helped expand the Luddite Club to seventy chapters across the country.

“I started as an incrementalizer, because that’s the easiest thing to do,” Jackson told me. “I’ll delete Instagram today and then, tomorrow, I’ll see how I feel. And then I had this dream where I was talking to somebody who was my mentor. And they said, ‘You never do anything unless you do the thing.’ ”

Jackson’s time online increased sharply during the pandemic lockdowns, as it did for so many of us, and doing the thing meant trading in her iPhone for a flip phone, taking periodic “cold-turkey” breaks from all screens and internet time, and, most importantly, spreading the gospel of this modern, piecemeal Luddism to anyone who would listen. She has made peace with the fact that Luddism will preclude her from many future jobs—basically, anything that requires her to be on Slack or e-mail. She says that she wouldn’t want to do those jobs anyway, because such a close connection to technology would feel unbearable to her.

For Jackson, deleting an app or two and otherwise going about your days as usual is not enough. Still, she is wary of being too prescriptive about what Luddism means. She told me that there had been an internal fight within the Luddite Club community concerning just how offline someone should be, and whether a dropout existence was the only way to free oneself from what she called “techno-fascism.” Many people, she said, felt an almost ascetic desire for deprivation, and would “buy two hundred acres and build a self-sustaining cabin” if they could, but Jackson believes in a big-tent version of Luddism that meets people where they are. “I want it to be mainstream,” she told me. “We like civilization—we like this exposure to diversity and culture and media, generally. Why can’t we make this livable for everyone? Why do people have to be forced into this alcove of peace?”

But despite her insistence that even people who merely set a screen-time limit for YouTube are welcome, and her belief that a more drastic retreat from society will never yield a sustainable movement, she does see a value in people showing us alternative ways to live. She told me about a friend who had started renting out rooms in a screen-and-internet-free house. “She gives you a typewriter and dinner and arts-and-crafts supplies and all this stuff—and you pay her when you arrive, so she doesn’t need to access anything online anymore.”

I was most interested in how Jackson thought about change. The dropout vision, she said, drew people to Luddism and has a powerful symbolic appeal, but would, she believed, limit a fight against the tech oligarchs. “I’ve been taking some classes and learning from people who are decades older than me,” she said. “The main thing in movement-building is you have to have a slot for everyone.” The Luddite Club is decentralized; the members of each individual chapter have to define their terms and their goals. “It’s not like church where you have an overarching religious framework,” she said. “You try to foster this space and create a new social norm and help other people find how they can do that, too, and how they can live that. And you don’t discriminate against people because they haven’t been on this road as long as you have.”

This openness was necessary, she explained, because it was quite difficult, at the beginning of the club, to get people to commit to even the slightest reduction in online life. “The group was founded out of loneliness,” she told me. “It was, like, ‘I can’t do this alone. I need somebody else to hold me accountable.’ ”

What she described sounded like a movement of friendly monks who led by example, refused to judge one another, and tried to uphold an admittedly vague ethos. They believed in “human rights” and “how we attain equality in this digital sphere that is entirely dictated by algorithms and a few select people who are coding these things.” The goal, she said, was to create a “livable world for everyone where you don’t need these things and where everybody on the planet can live without them.” When I asked her how many hours I should spend online, she said that I should figure out for myself what would work for me. She apologized for being vague.

Jackson’s theory of change does not require violent revolutionary action à la the Unabomber or hostility for everyone who ever picks up a device. Instead, change can come from simply using a flip phone and reassuring others who hate their digital lives that they will be fine if they swap out a SIM card and stop texting all the time. Happy abstinence can change the world. I understand why some people might see this as soft or, at the very least, naïve. But, in the Luddite Club’s defense: How many people do you know without a smartphone? And, if you swapped out your iPhone for a flip phone, would that constitute a radical change in your life?

“Your digital footprint is forever,” Jackson said. The sense of self and permanence that comes from this makes it hard, she explained, for people to get off their phones, which is something I certainly understand. If I stopped posting and replying, I feel as though I would simply cease to exist. Jackson preaches a modest weaning for people like me. “You can get a flip phone for a week,” she said. “That’s O.K. Who is gonna tell you that’s wrong?” ♦

items.title: Raye’s Theatrical Pop Nostalgia
items.description: The British singer and songwriter Raye presents her retro big-band act through a mesh of knowingness, often breaking the fourth wall to provide a meta-text. “I had hoped you’d find your way to this piece of music / And that would mean, oh my friend, we have ma
items.author: Doreen St Félix
paragraphs: The British singer and songwriter Raye presents her retro big-band act through a mesh of knowingness, often breaking the fourth wall to provide a meta-text. “I had hoped you’d find your way to this piece of music / And that would mean, oh my friend, we have made it to the end,” she sings, in the final song on her sophomore studio album. Never does she allow her listeners to feel anything like abandon; she is always reminding them, as she is always reminding herself, of the intractable frame of entertainment, that we are all plodding through our private dramas on a public stage. Although she is deep in a phase of mid-century drag, with her banana-curled bouffant and her corseted silhouette, she is as painfully contemporary as they come, by which I mean, preoccupied with being understood. Her breakthrough mini-album, “Euphoric Sad Songs,” released six years ago, when Raye, born Rachel Agatha Keen, was twenty-three, was, as its postmodern title ironically suggests, competently produced generica, a collection of mid-to-up-tempo dance-pop melodies that served as vessels for her melancholy. The music she has made since then—two albums, “My 21st Century Blues” and “This Music May Contain Hope,” the latter of which has just garnered her the most nominations of any artist for the 2027 Grammys—only deepens the impression that this is a musician trapped in her idea of what it means to be a musician.

But another fact persists: everybody loves Raye. Why wouldn’t they? She’s got that city charm. She provides the comfort of the legacy act, and the light perversity of the theatre kid. She can do what Sabrina Carpenter does, make us succumb to camp and humor, as in her enormous hit “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!” She is a Christian, but she knows what it is to have lost one’s faith.

Born in South London to a Ghanaian Swiss mother and a white English father, she grew up with three sisters, two of whom are also professional musicians who sometimes join her onstage, and all were trained in the way of praise singing in the church. Jazz—the scatting of Ella Fitzgerald, the blowing of Louis Armstrong—was an early obsession. As an adolescent, Raye had a clear view of pop success and how to attain it; she dreamed of attending the BRIT School, an institution that had been a way station for many singers, including Adele and Amy Winehouse, idols whose extraordinary presence Raye sought to emulate. She got in. And then she dropped out, at sixteen, perhaps feeling creatively stifled. (She was one year ahead of another British star, Olivia Dean.) The disillusionment with the institution introduced Raye to the general disillusionment experienced by the female singer, who is confronted again and again with the cold reality of the industry, its hostility to her art.

A teen-aged Raye entered a limbo. At seventeen, she signed with Polydor Records, a sub-label under Universal. She released a body of work on SoundCloud, called “Welcome to the Winter”; it tried out lo-fi, Rihanna-esque vocals, set against gothic beats that call to mind the Weeknd. You can hear, too, the stamp of Lily Allen. (She is not ready, at this stage, to bring out the full influence of Winehouse, but you can feel it under the surface.) Raye was forced to divert her songwriting skills to other artists, a soul-killing kind of ventriloquism for some, that also had the effect of teaching her versatility. Her credits include work for Beyoncé, John Legend, and her cultural peer Charli XCX. Memorably, in 2021, Raye—who was becoming a darling among the keen-eyed observers of her evolution, from the development of her performer’s armor to the stylized stage name—posted on X, “I have been on a 4 ALBUM RECORD DEAL since 2014 !!! And haven’t been allowed to put out one album. ALL I CARE ABOUT is the music. Im sick of being slept on and I’m sick of being in pain about it this is not business to me this so personal.”

To my ear, the extraction from that bad deal hasn’t exactly facilitated freedom for Raye. “My 21st Century Blues,” released in 2023, is a likable record choked by its music-student stridency, the compulsion to prove she is the inheritor to any number of blues women. It’s in the title of the album. It’s in the titles of the songs, all of which are punctuated with a period, as if to say that there is nothing up for discussion. In the tradition of Brits who have molded themselves in genres born across the Atlantic, Raye is an acolyte; she isn’t a raider, the sort of nostalgist who picks diamonds from corpses and pretends as if they were hers all along. She wants to pay her respects—to Sarah Vaughan, to Fitzgerald, to Dionne Warwick. She has to, as this album addresses her past addiction, and how it nearly destroyed her, along with her experience of sexual assault, by a music producer, and how it fed a season of self-abnegation. This is personal and exhibitionistic songwriting, on subjects that mid-century singers could have only found expression for through metaphor. Raye sings it straight, hyperverbal, multisyllabic, like she’s a bad-bitch Sondheim: “Codeine / silent, marvellous codeine.” But genuflection creates a stasis, which we feel on “The Thrill is Gone.,” and “Mary Jane.,” with its overwrought guitar. The album is torn, seesawing between nostalgia play and up-to-the-minute “issues” music. (There is a song on it called “Body Dysmorphia.”) Vocally, Raye is most interesting when she is playing sedate, closer to rapping than belting, like on the viral single “Escapism.,” a nocturnal track about desire and regret, featuring the crooner 070 Shake. She is most interesting when she is of her time.

Then again, what is her time but the age that the British cultural theorist Mark Fisher called “the slow cancellation of the future”? I kept asking myself that question while listening to Raye’s most recent album, the international crowd-pleaser “This Music May Contain Hope.” In spoken interludes throughout, Raye is the maestra, nesting explanations and analyses about the album’s four-season structure, which she has, of course, borrowed from Vivaldi. The twenty-twenties are beginning their slow end, and Raye’s recombinant maximalism—her need to be vaudeville and to be Fosse and to be dance hall and to be trip-hop, to feature Al Green, to feature Hans Zimmer, to know everything—is the picture of a present rushing pathologically into the bosom of the past. Fifteen years ago, the music critic Simon Reynolds provided a term for this condition: “retromania.” At the time, I had many issues with Reynolds’s thesis: the Freudian undertone, the inadequate engagement with hip-hop and sampling. These days, I have fewer. ♦

items.title: The Former Trump Official Who Thinks Trump’s Staff Has Let Him Down
items.description: In his new book, “The President Deserves Better: Leadership and Accountability to Keep America Great,” John Ullyot argues that President Donald Trump’s advisers and appointees have let him down in his faltering second term. As Ullyot, a former deputy assistant
items.author: Isaac Chotiner
paragraphs: In his new book, “The President Deserves Better: Leadership and Accountability to Keep America Great,” John Ullyot argues that President Donald Trump’s advisers and appointees have let him down in his faltering second term. As Ullyot, a former deputy assistant to Trump at the White House who has held several government jobs during Trump’s Administrations, including as chief spokesman for the National Security Council, writes “The bottom line is this: The President deserves better.” He adds, “And it’s not just from his Cabinet Secretaries. Many individuals and groups work behind the scenes to block or slow-roll Trump’s reform agenda. You often hear about how liberal media outlets and the foot-dragging, antireform, bureaucratic Deep State try to stop Trump. This book provides a first-hand account of how that happens on a day-to-day basis.”

Recently, in The Atlantic, Ullyot called for the resignation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whom he had advised at the Pentagon in 2025, saying that Hegseth had mismanaged the Iran war and was becoming an embarrassment to the President. (In April of that year, Ullyot detailed the chaos at the Pentagon under Hegseth in Politico.) I recently spoke by phone with Ullyot about his time working with Trump, and the source of the problems in the President’s Administration. Our conversation, edited for length and clarity, is below.
I read your Atlantic piece calling for Hegseth’s resignation. What is it that you think he has done wrong?

Hegseth has done a lot of damage to the Pentagon and to the military. I volunteered to stand up his press operation just for a short period of time at the start of his term last year, and he and I got along very well. When I left, as planned, after standing up his operation and turning it over to his friend—a friend of his that he had selected to run the operation—he thanked me for doing a good job, et cetera. And then it was after that that things got very crazy. I didn’t notice a lot of crazy things going on when I was there, but it was after that point, after I left, that I decided to write that op-ed in Politico. And that was because things had gotten so crazy that he had two of my friends marched out of the building by security, and he accused them of leaking material to the press, and he just had become very paranoid about the leaks.

Hegseth is the least qualified and most polarizing Defense Secretary in modern memory. And as a Marine veteran, and as someone who has spent a lot of time in both the Senate Armed Services Committee and at the National Security Council working with senior members of the military and senior Pentagon leaders, I felt the need to speak out, because he was doing real damage and it was hurting the President as well.
He was appointed to the job by President Trump, right?
So how do you understand President Trump’s decision to appoint him, and also to keep him in the job, even as he’s doing this tremendous damage that you referenced?

So, the President hired him. In his first term, President Trump hired people based on recommendations from many people who were outsiders. And he felt, I believe, that he was not well served by several of them. In his second term, it has been different. He’s hired more on loyalty and hired more people who are going to pursue his agenda rather than those who have a résumé.
So is Hegseth pursuing Trump’s agenda?

I think he is in a lot of ways. The President decided to go to war in Iran, and the Secretary reportedly pushed him into that. I do not think that the President has paid attention to the damage that Hegseth has done on either the cultural front or the self-promoting front, or to the damage that he’s done in taking out very good leaders of the military. I think that the President is mainly briefed on what’s going on at the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, and doesn’t have people around him who have apprised him of the job that Hegseth’s doing and the damage that he’s done.
If Trump could focus a little more, sit down, read a briefing book on what Hegseth was doing, it might be easier to get him to come around to what you’re saying.

Yeah, I think that’s right. But I really do think that the President hired Hegseth without really looking under the hood. He watches Fox News a lot, and Hegseth, he’s very bombastic, outspoken; he really shouts into the camera on Fox News. And I think President Trump said, “Hey, this guy must be a real military hero. He’s a man’s man, et cetera.” I doubt that he looked at his résumé much, because a lot of people are surprised that Hegseth was not a SEAL Team Six door-kicker or something like that. But he has a persona, and he wrote three books about lethality in the military. I read all three of them before going to work for him.
Yeah, and basically they all say the same thing, and they can be summed up with one page: The military’s gone woke. And, No beardos, no weirdos, no trannies, no fatties, this type of thing.

Did that message appeal to you when you first joined the Administration, but then you thought, Oh, maybe the “no beardos, no weirdos” thing is not actually the way to carry out the running of the Pentagon?

I wrote an op-ed back when Hegseth was still in high school, when I left the Marine Corps, about the need to keep high physical standards, because that was going out, particularly with integrating women into Marine units. Anyway, so I’m not agreeing with him. He’s not the person who invented the idea of high physical standards. And then, in terms of his criticism of how identity politics were woven into the military, I agreed with that. But I wouldn’t make it a big deal. I would just get it done. So I didn’t think you needed to beat your chest about restoring . . . whether it’s in any government position, I agree with eliminating identity politics or identity-based hiring. So I was on board with both of those, but I wasn’t screaming about it.
“Talk softly and carry a big stick” kind of thing.
Yeah, just make the changes and don’t make a big deal about it.

It does occur to me that people who write books that, as you say, can be summarized by lines like “No beardos, no weirdos” might not be so laser-focussed on really running the department as well as they should, and might be more focussed on being obnoxious and things like that. I don’t know. I’m just speculating.

Yeah, I think that’s right. I mean, with his résumé and his bombast, I think that he was probably qualified to be the Pentagon spokesperson, or since he spends a lot of time P.T.ing with the troops, he could have been head of the Presidential physical-fitness council, like Arnold Schwarzenegger was. But, actually, you need a manager or somebody with real management experience to run the largest department in the federal government.

Let’s just go back to President Trump, because your book is very interesting on this idea that Trump has been let down by the people around him in his second term. Is the problem Hegseth, or is the problem more that Trump didn’t do his due diligence?
I don’t think he did due diligence. I think President Trump just saw him on Fox News, liked what he saw, and didn’t say, O.K., let’s look into his background.

Is that then the fault of people around Trump, or is it more Trump’s fault? Because your book is saying that Trump himself is a very effective leader, but that he’s been let down. So I’m curious how you think that through.

So I think that ultimately the buck stops with the President. So, when I say the President deserves better, yes, he deserves better from his staff, but above all he deserves better from himself. Let’s say you’re a friend of a pro golfer and the pro golfer knows that he can do better. You would say, “Hey, look, I think you deserve better than that. You deserve to train a little more or to work on your swing with a swing coach,” et cetera. It’s not a great analogy.

Like any C.E.O., the President is the steward of his own brand. And his brand has slipped badly. But he needs to have staff that are not yes-men. He never did this in the first term, but if you look at these scripted or televised Cabinet meetings where they’ll go on for an hour, the Cabinet meetings with the cameras rolling, they’ll just go around while all the Cabinet members are trying to outdo each other. Each Cabinet member’s trying to outdo the others in praising the President. And that’s not serious. The President doesn’t need that, but ultimately he’s responsible.
Trump’s first Cabinet meeting, in 2017, five months into his term, included a lot of praise, if I remember correctly.

Well, I mean, that could have been the case, but now every Cabinet meeting is televised. I mean, in the first term there were some serious people there who were supporters of the President, but they were not seal clappers the way you see a lot in this Administration.

I am looking now, and in June of 2017, at that first Cabinet meeting, they did go around the room praising him. But, as you say, there’s going around the room and praising him, and then there’s going around the room and really praising him. So you have to draw distinctions, which I think is what you are trying to do.

That’s right. I’ve been in and out of the private sector and advise C.E.O.s, and I say a good C.E.O. surrounds himself with people who are strong enough to tell him what he doesn’t want to hear. And one of them that I worked with was Alan Mulally, when he was C.E.O. of Ford, and they were doing the auto-bailout hearings, back in December of 2008. Mulally was great to work with, and, famously, when he took over Ford, he had his first review of the business units and all the charts, and he said, “Put a green, yellow, or red chart based on how your business unit is doing.” So it was all green while the company was losing billions. And then one executive finally put up a red slide, and Mulally just started applauding him, and later that executive became C.E.O. and replaced Mulally. Mulally wanted to hear the bad news, probably before the good news.
Does it seem to you that Trump wants to hear the bad news before the good news?
No, I don’t think so. I think he deserves better from himself on that. He deserves to look under the hood much more than he has been doing in his second term.

Your book is about how the President deserves better from his staff, but it seems like one of the things you’re saying in this conversation is that the President deserves better from himself, which is a little different.

Yes, that’s right. He made three promises when I worked for him as a senior adviser on the 2016 campaign: no more forever wars, drain the swamp, and put America first. In his first term, when I worked for him in the White House, he was new to Washington and very laser-focussed on delivering on those priorities.

When I remember the first term, it was a lot of tweeting in the middle of the night. It was a lot of staying in the residence to watch Fox News. It was a lot of golfing. I’m not saying things are exactly the same as this term, but when you say the President was laser-focussed on his priorities, I’m trying to remember that.

No, you’re right about his tweeting and his watching TV and staying up late. That hasn’t changed, but what I think has changed in this second term is that he has lost focus on implementing his promises.
I think the ballroom is distracting him. Honestly, I think that’s one of the problems.
Yeah, exactly. So, anyway, things slipped in the second term. Now you’ve got former aides who are cashing in on his name.
Is he cashing in, too, do we think?
I don’t think he is, but certainly there are allegations that his family is. I mean, I think that he’s not personally—
Oh, so you think it’s more his family than him?

Well, it’s his family, but it’s also, let’s look at the ballroom or the library. He is building these big projects that need a lot of money, and so any donor to any President does not contribute to their projects five years after they’ve been President. They’re all lining up to contribute when the President has the power. But, in draining the swamp, that was his promise to be a different President, and now you’ve got his aides.

But do you think that flows from the top? Maybe this gets back to what you say about the fact that he himself deserves better. Maybe he should tell himself to tell his family not to focus on business deals.

Right. This was not a visible embarrassment in the first term. Now it’s a visible embarrassment, and, in fact, he’s reportedly surprised by some of these revelations. So, when we come back to “the President deserves better,” he should have set the tone in the second term and said, “No more of this B.S., I’m different. That’s why I was elected in 2016, because people wanted me to drain the swamp, and I don’t want to have anybody, whether it’s my family or anybody else, riding on my name.”
I think one important thing about your book is getting the message out there that he needs to do this.

Yeah. I appreciate that. That’s what I was trying to do in writing the book. And I had no idea when I started writing it a year and a half ago that the Republican Party would take the shellacking that it did. I mean, nine Senate seats. I worked in the Senate for seven years, and nine seats is seventeen per cent of all the senators. I looked it up—seventeen per cent of the entire collection of senators in the chamber.
Wouldn’t nine Senate seats be nine per cent of the Senate?
Of the Republicans. Republicans had fifty-three. If you divide nine out of fifty-three—
Of course, yeah, my mistake.

Yeah, no worries. So, anyway, nine seats is a lot of seats. Anyway, when I started writing this book, I was saying it is maybe intended for future Presidents, but now it has become a lot more relevant to this President.

Well, honestly, if there’s a theme to this conversation, I think it’s that if Trump had read Hegseth’s books, or if he reads your book now, things could be better. Maybe Trump reading more books is the solution here.
Yeah, maybe that’s the solution.

Last question for you: What if someone said, “Look, this Donald Trump, he’s got a little older, he’s surrounded by more loyalists, but fundamentally, this is the guy who, from the start, talked about Obama’s birth certificate, and then he talked about ‘Mexican’ judges, and then he insulted people all the time, and there are all these accusations about how he assaults women, and then there were all these things that he said about Haitians, and January 6th, and then you go to the second term, and he’s posting the video of the Obamas as apes, and actually he is just the same guy who never really had any sense of how to run the country or a sense of the national interest”? I’m not saying there’s any merit to this idea, but what do you think of it?

Well, no, I think that’s a very good point. What I would say is he’s the same man, but, politically, voters were once willing to overlook this pugilistic, crude character tweeting about the Obamas as apes and all of that business.

It seems as if you wish Trump would remind himself, and remind people, that fundamentally he was a businessman who came to shake up Washington. If he could get back to that, maybe he could get back on the right track.
Yeah, absolutely. There’s still a runway for him to get things done. ♦

items.title: Is Science Accelerating?
items.description: What was American life like a hundred years ago? The economist Robert J. Gordon offers a vivid picture in his book “The Rise and Fall of American Growth,” from 2016. In 1926, Gordon writes, there were almost no paved roads west of the Mississippi. Fewer than o
items.author: Joshua Rothman
paragraphs: What was American life like a hundred years ago? The economist Robert J. Gordon offers a vivid picture in his book “The Rise and Fall of American Growth,” from 2016. In 1926, Gordon writes, there were almost no paved roads west of the Mississippi. Fewer than one in ten homes had an electric refrigerator. (A typical one cost the equivalent of ten thousand dollars today.) If you lived in Muncie, Indiana, the odds were one in four that your house had no running water, and one in three that it had no sewer connection. Life was rough by our standards. And yet, Gordon shows, scientific and technological progress was obvious everywhere. Thousands of new hospitals were being constructed, many with cutting-edge X-ray departments. Ninety-three per cent of Iowa farmers owned automobiles, even though the automobile itself had begun to appear only three decades before. 1926 was the year it became possible for an ordinary person to travel on an airplane; it was also when an inventor named Clarence Birdseye perfected frozen food, making the consumption of fish affordable in landlocked places. The way people lived was clearly better than how their parents had lived.

This rapid “epochal transformation,” Gordon writes, actually continued for a whole century, stretching from 1870 to 1970. It was powered by five “Great Inventions”—electricity, urban sanitation, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, internal-combustion engines, and signal transmission. The Great Inventions, in turn, were based on foundational discoveries in physics, biology, medicine, chemistry, math, and other fields. “What makes the period 1870–1970 so special is that these inventions cannot be repeated,” Gordon writes. The germ theory of disease, which Louis Pasteur advanced in the eighteen-eighties, led to sweeping changes in pretty much every aspect of life, and yet it could be discovered only once. The principle of electromagnetism unlocks everything from engines to radios, but there aren’t infinite, similarly powerful principles to uncover and apply. The staircase of science—or at least this flight of it—appears to have only so many steps.

What happens after the biggest discoveries have been made, explored, and put to use? Arguably, the rate of progress slows, and dramatic transformation becomes harder to achieve. The practice of science itself also changes. In recent decades, economists and other researchers have explored a field that they call “metascience”—the study of why the pace of scientific discovery increases or decreases. They point out that, although more scientific papers are being published, fewer are truly disruptive; more patents are granted, but a smaller number are for “breakthrough” inventions. Increasingly, science is conducted inside enormous bureaucracies that favor cautious, incremental research. Grants are awarded mainly to sure bets; power concentrates among august institutions and scientists. In a 2020 paper, the economists Nicholas Bloom, Charles I. Jones, John Van Reenen, and Michael Webb asked, “Are ideas getting harder to find?” They observed that the number of researchers required to double the speed of computer chips was eighteen times larger than it had been in the early nineteen-seventies. For a long time, they concluded, progress had emerged from “a constant flow of new ideas.” Now that flow has slowed.

Is this how life feels in 2026? Does it seem to you that scientific and technological progress has plateaued? It’s true that the iPhone Duo is only somewhat exciting. But, on the other hand, there is now a pancreatic-cancer pill and a melanoma vaccine. In Massachusetts, a man named Tim Andrews lived for the better part of a year while relying on a gene-edited kidney grown inside a pig. Norwegian salmon farms now use underwater A.I.-controlled laser robots to kill sea lice; in France, a startup has made tiny drones that can do the same for mosquitoes in your back yard. “Technological evolution is still accelerating,” the computer scientist John von Neumann wrote, in a 1955 essay, toward the end of Gordon’s spectacular century. In that particular essay, von Neumann was thinking mainly of nuclear power, machine automation, and climate control—technologies that have progressed slowly or fizzled out. And yet computer science, a field to which he made foundational contributions, has made steady—and now startling—new advances. The question of whether science is slowing or accelerating is complicated by its essential unpredictability. And because science is an interpersonal, interwoven enterprise, progress in one area can enable it in others, in ways that might not be easy to foresee.

A cartoon equation for science might go like this: B (brainiacs) + M (money) x T (technology) = D (discovery). Needless to say, it isn’t that simple. The brainiacs can be arranged in all sorts of organizations and hierarchies; the money can flow to the right ones or the wrong ones. The technology can be employed correctly or incorrectly; the discoveries can result in smarter brainiacs, more money, and better technology, or they can die on the vine. Fields and methods, meanwhile, can be young or grown-up, flexible or ossified, fashionable or passé. “At the time I was starting, lots and lots of things were just opening up,” Eve Marder, a neuroscientist who began her career in the nineteen-seventies, told me. “I started just after the time when someone could put an electrode anywhere in any nervous system and see something that no one had ever seen before—which is very, very different from the much more mature science that we have today.” For neuroscientists now, she went on, “what constitutes ‘success’ or ‘new knowledge’ has changed, and the incentive structures have also changed.” Marder recalled going to her first neuroscience conference, which had around five hundred attendees, allowing her to meet many of the most important figures in the field. Today, the big annual meeting put on by the Society for Neuroscience typically hosts around twenty thousand researchers.

Marder is now an eminent scientist: her lab, at Brandeis University, studies how individual neurons connect to create stable circuits that can survive and function over time. She has won major awards, supervised large numbers of scientists and graduate students, and participated in research projects of varying sizes. “We have a very complicated challenge in science today, which is that there are some things that can only be done by ‘big science,’ ” she said. “If you’re doing ‘small science,’ with small groups of people, then the ones who make mistakes can be very easily corrected or can self-correct. But, if you do big science poorly, somebody can make a bad decision and take everyone down a bad path.”

In a big-science world, researchers often work in large consortia that cross institutional and disciplinary lines. They collaborate to gather vast quantities of data, hoping that it will be amenable to analysis now and in the future. Young scientists can find themselves assimilated, Borg-style, into these expansive projects and the institutions that make them possible. “A student who goes into a field is captivated by ideas,” Marder said. “They want to discover something, to create something, just like a philosopher wants to think something no one’s ever thought. And then they are socialized by having to get to the next step, or get the next fellowship. They start worrying about who they have to please—and that can flow down and change the science that they’re willing or able to do.” Some young scientists “are very stubborn, and will continue to be independent and innovative, and become leaders in their fields,” Marder went on. But “a lot of very creative people get driven out.”

If the scale of modern science can dwarf individual scientists, it can also sideline their contributions. “Right now, on my desk in my office, I have a huge pile of really important papers by brilliant people that I don’t have time to read—there’s too many of them,” Michael Levin, a biologist at Tufts, told me. “I conclude, by symmetry, that nobody has time to read my papers, either. That raises the question: Who the hell am I writing all this for?” Levin, who studies bioelectric computation—the process through which cells communicate and make collective decisions—believes that science is, in fact, accelerating: one sign is that “it’s becoming more and more difficult to stay apprised of the important things.” In a 2005 paper titled “The Burden of Knowledge and the ‘Death of the Renaissance Man,’ ” the economist Benjamin F. Jones explored this paradox. Since “knowledge accumulates as technology progresses,” he wrote, there is ever more to know, and so the “educational burden” on researchers increases; eventually, it becomes harder not just to know everything but to know what’s needed for you, in particular, to push knowledge forward. Ironically, science may be slower precisely because it’s moving quickly in too many directions.

Organizational and communicative challenges exist alongside what might be called problems of ambition: science can be slow simply because, at this point, its aims are Olympian. Kristin Persson, a materials scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, explained one overarching goal in her field: predicting how different arrangements of atoms will behave under different conditions, so that they can be combined into new and useful materials. “For a very long time, we’ve been trying to do what some people call multi-scale modelling,” she said. “You start out with atoms and electrons, and you have an equation for behavior on that length scale and time scale. Then you take those properties and you feed them into higher-scale equations.” The approach, she said, has “never really taken off, because of what’s lost in translation every time you move from one set of equations to the next.”

It’s hard, in other words, to precisely predict the behavior of matter at every scale. The theoretical basis for such predictions was established a century ago—in 1926, as it happens—by the physicist Erwin Schrödinger, who devised a single equation describing how electrons interact under the laws of quantum mechanics; it’s relatively simple to solve for small numbers of electrons, but becomes unwieldy as atoms add up. If you want to use it at a large scale, you can solve it only approximately, unless you want your computer to calculate for billions of years. Science is full of such bottlenecks: places where dramatic insights, some long-standing, can’t yet yield practical results.

Today’s computers may not be fast enough to effortlessly apply Schrödinger’s Equation—but they are, apparently, fast enough to read and think. Accordingly, Levin told me, scientists are using artificial intelligence to respond to the burden of knowledge. “They take that stack of papers and put it through an A.I., and say, ‘Summarize this for me,’ ” he said. Levin regards it as a useful innovation, wielded by experts, that might itself be accelerated. “If all my work is going to get filtered through an A.I., then why am I putting out a traditional paper, with all of this stuff we do for each other—with the freaking grammar, and the PDFs, and the figures, which the A.I. has to take apart?” he asked. He anticipates a near future in which the form of the scientific paper becomes A.I.-ready, with old knowledge ably surfaced by artificial intelligence alongside new work. “There are amazing authors with amazing sets of papers from twenty, thirty years ago that nobody knows today,” he said. “Theoretically, that information is there somewhere, but, if nobody knows it and nobody uses it, then do we really have it?”

It could be that some version of this transformation is already under way. Scientists are increasingly using large language models not just to read papers but to write them: studies from last year, when A.I. was less capable, found that many researchers had experienced writing-productivity boosts of between thirty-three and fifty per cent, and submissions to journals and to conferences are up, in some cases dramatically. Meanwhile, in a study titled “AI Article Reviews Dominate Human Peer Reviews at Their Best,” two Harvard researchers, Gary King and Steven Worthington, show that peer reviews performed by L.L.M.s “are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts”; they’re even “judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors.” It’s possible to discern, in these developments, a new rhythm of scientific communication.

L.L.M.s work with language: it’s not surprising that they can be used to process information. But what about the actual labor of science, which is concrete, empirical, and often outrageously time-consuming? “There’s a lot of ‘donkey work,’ ” Persson, the materials scientist at Berkeley, said. Experiments must be done painstakingly, over and over, for years, and even then they can produce unpredictable results; a brilliant young researcher might spend her whole postdoc on the creation of a statistical model that’s immediately bested by someone else’s. Scientific progress is slow, in part, because there aren’t that many passionate, hyper-educated people willing to devote themselves to hands-on, detail-oriented, ruthlessly competitive, and often fruitless labor.

It’s clear, at this point, that A.I. can automate some of the donkey work. “We have a bunch of computational neuroscientists in my lab, and every last one of them says, ‘I can now do in a week what would have taken me six months,’ ” Marder, the neuroscientist at Brandeis, told me. Materials scientists use computer simulations that can easily run off the rails. “When I was a graduate student, I logged in late at night to see if my simulation had worked out,” Persson said; she’d then spend untold hours troubleshooting. Now, she explained, “L.L.M.s are learning from errors in the simulations and applying their corrections autonomously to keep them on track.” This leaves time-constrained researchers free to focus on higher-level questions.

The advantages may go beyond vibe coding. A.I. systems “are so helpful at solving problems because they can try lots of things,” Michael Brenner, a professor of applied math and physics at Harvard who also helps direct A.I. science efforts for Google, told me. At Google, Brenner led the development of a system called Empirical Research Assistance (ERA), which scientists can use to create data-analysis tools. In many ways, ERA also addresses the burden of knowledge: researchers pose questions to it, and provide it with data, and it responds by trying and mixing different extant methods of analysis in numberless combinations, discovering new paths to progress. (Researchers have used ERA to create improved disease-forecasting models, for example.) “It’s like swapping and flipping, flipping and swapping the pieces, and trying to figure out something that actually works,” Brenner said. The power of the system, he went on, was “not Einsteinian but Edisonian”: it consisted in the novel application of known ideas.

Could A.I. offer even more in the way of novelty, contributing to the automated production of new data, new knowledge, and new theories? Both Levin and Persson described automated laboratories as a logical next step. Currently, Persson said, the creation of new experimental data is extraordinarily expensive and time-intensive—but robots, she argued, could be used “to produce data at scale,” which could then be analyzed by existing A.I. models or used to train new ones. (This data, she noted, might also have the advantage of being unusually consistent and free from human error.) “We’re going to get lab automation,” Levin said. “Then there’s going to be no more concern with hallucination or confabulation—the A.I.s are going to try stuff, and it either works or it doesn’t. At that point, once they have the ability to actually test out the consequences of their hypotheses, the loop is going to accelerate, and all this is going to go exponential.” This vision—in which A.I. speeds up not just the collection and analysis of data but the generation of hypotheses and the design of experiments—represents one of the more radical acceleratory possibilities for science. Levin suggested one major obstacle: “A.I. has been obviously trained on human output where conventional theories are overrepresented,” he said. To arrive at “unconventional ideas”—the kinds that lead to full-throttle acceleration, and to world-changing invention—it would have to become less consensus-driven.

If dramatic scientific acceleration occurs, it will be significant on at least three levels. First, there’s the question posed by John von Neumann, the computer scientist, in his 1955 essay: “Can we survive technology?” Today, the concept of a technological “singularity” is easily taken to refer to a single Promethean moment, such as the invention of superintelligent A.I. But the concept, which is often credited to von Neumann, can have a simpler meaning. New technologies are frequently hard to manage; as more of them pop up, their management gets more and more difficult, until they become, in aggregate, unmanageable. How many simultaneous “upgrades” can society withstand? This problem concerned von Neumann precisely because he was writing toward the tail end of the century of invention described in “The Rise and Fall of American Growth.” If we are entering such a period again, we need to be as concerned as he was with the problem of technology management. We need to shift from a fetishization of disruption to a fascination with control.

Second, there’s the question of growth. In his book, Gordon shows how much life can improve when Great Inventions are changing the world. During the hundred years he describes, people got healthier and ate better; worked less and travelled farther; moved into bigger, more comfortable houses; and grew increasingly educated while exercising more personal freedom. The economy expanded because lives were expanding. But today, the United States, along with most of the Western world, is facing a crisis of growth. Populations are aging, and the ratio of workers to pensioners is falling. The costs of housing, food, education, health care, and other necessities are rising, as are our debts. “What are we going to do?” the economist Tyler Cowen asked, recently. “Plan A is that A.I. will help us grow more quickly, and we will manage to pay our bills. . . . There is no Plan B.” We need some new Great Inventions; an acceleration in science, enabled partly by A.I., is our most promising path to getting them.

Finally, there’s the not-unimportant matter of human knowledge. Progress in science is good—but it doesn’t always feel good. Often, it centers not on the arrival of answers but on the proliferation of difficult questions. The same may be true for progress in the practice of science. Sudden advances in mathematics have led some mathematicians to say that their field has been “broken” by artificial intelligence. “I don’t think math is broken,” Brenner told me. “It’s hard for the community, and some of my math colleagues might disagree with me, but I think it’s a very exciting time in mathematics, a time to really rethink things and break new ground.” Persson agreed: “Maybe the mathematicians are having a rough time, but honestly I would congratulate them,” she said. “You should talk to some of my students: They see a lot of their mundane work going away. They can focus on fun things; they can do simulations they could never do before.” It was, she suggested, a great time to become a scientist. ♦
