items.title: Hit the right note with 12 fragrances and home scents to give this Christmas
items.description: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long winter evenings, here is Monocle’s pick of the best scents to gift this Christmas.
Discover a Homeric fragrance from To My Ships

Named after a line in Homer’s Iliad, To My Ships launched in what its founder, Daniel Bense, calls an “uninspiring” category: deodorant. The Aesop and Sunspel alumnus has since worked with celebrated nose Céline Barel to develop the brand’s bestselling Of the Gods perfume around polygonum, a herby ingredient that’s usually only used in trace amounts.
“It’s a fragrance discovered by those near the wearer, rather than announced to a room,” says Bense. Backed by 18 investors, the label has grown by word of mouth and will soon expand to Japan.
Toast the wool mill with Zegna’s Il Lanificio

For its latest foray into perfume, luxury menswear house Zegna drew inspiration from the life of founder Ermenegildo Zegna and his Italian Alpine homeland. The brand’s fragrance collection includes six scents and we’re particularly taken by Il Lanificio, which means “wool mill” in Italian.

The perfume’s heady mixture of suede, vanilla and sandalwood pays tribute to its namesake and is a celebration of Zegna’s ability to take raw material and transform it into something unique. Simultaneously urbane and rustic, this is a scent to savour.
Pair Italian fig with American cedar in Bottega Veneta’s Balliamo

Bottega Veneta expanded its fragrance offerings this year with Alta, a new collection of 10 scents. Each combines an ingredient from Italy with a far-flung counterpoint (think blood orange with North African neroli or plum with Spanish labdanum).
We’ll be wearing Balliamo – a heady combination of Italian white fig with American cedarwood – to the aperitivo.
Head into the woods with Documents’ Inter Cedar

Documents is one of a handful of Shanghai-based, high-end fragrance brands that is proving popular with Chinese consumers and poised to go global. Its premium scents are inspired by Eastern culture, featuring notes from ylang ylang and sichuan pepper to incense and black tea.
The brand operates more than 40 shops across 20 cities. We recommend its Inter Cedar eau de parfum, a tree-inspired scent with a woody profile and aromas of cypress, cardamom and mugwort.
Try Monocle and Claus Porto’s own Soleil Zeste

Crafted by French perfumer Daphné Bugey, this fragrance and body wash are the result of an exclusive collaboration between Portuguese beauty brand Claus Porto and Monocle, with packaging designed by our in-house art team.

The Soleil Zeste scent features notes of bergamot, lemon and lime, alongside green aromas of galbanum, petitgrain and cypress, and a refreshing base of white musk and lavender. Plus, the perfume bottles are made by Vista Alegre, an Aveiro-based heritage manufacturer of porcelain and crystal.
clausporto.com; monocle.com
Start a conversation with Jijide

Milan-based fragrance brand Jijide – meaning “positive” in Mandarin – emerged from a conversation between Italian and Chinese friends Adam James Cavallari, Andrea Alessandri and Fanqi Guan. Perfume, they decided, was the ideal language through which to explore their cultures.

The Riso scent layers notes of kumquat and rice with the salty intensity of soy sauce, while Dentro evokes an Italian morning through aromas of coffee and fig. It’s proof that perfume can be a talking point.
Count down to Christmas with Diptyque’s advent candle
The countdown to Christmas is celebrated in many ways. Some unwrap the gold foil of a small chocolate each morning or acknowledge Advent by fasting in advance of a seasonal feasting.

Parisian maison Diptyque has chosen to mark the days ahead with a Danish tradition. The kalenderlys candle burns down bit by bit, a simple reminder of coming festivities. This edition is scented with pine, cedar and moss, bringing the scents of the fir tree to warm the darker nights.
Bring the forest indoors with Deux Frères

Owners of gin distillery Deux Frères, Gian and Florian Grundböck, tend to think outside the box. Producing thousands of bottles of their signature gin in their Zürich-based distillery leaves several hundred litres of fragrant botanical remnants, known as tails.

“We wanted to turn the tails into something meaningful,” says founder Gian. Enter Forêt, a characterful room scent with notes of juniper, pink pepper and sandalwood. “For us, the fragrance is an example of how a by-product can become something distinctive in its own right,” says Gian. We’ll drink to that.
Escape to the Himalayas with Be Boundless

Beijinger Lydia Wang turned her personal interest in Tibetan medicine, meditation and yoga into a business in 2020 when she established incense brand Be Boundless. The label’s all-natural sticks are shorter than traditional incense from Lhasa, so they fit easily into a carry-on.

Wang tapped one of China’s leading graphic designers, Li Xibin, to create the branding, which features block colours and a bold typeface. A box set comes with 60 sticks in three scents, as well as a small, wooden pull-out tray. The Nighty Night scent – made from dong quai, clove, narra safflower and myrobalan – is a popular pick.
Light up winter evenings with Ffern

Somerset-based perfumer Ffern’s winter candle burns with comforting notes of coffee, frankincense and Peru balsam. Set into the lid of the attractive steel vessel is enamel artwork by South Korean-American illustrator Cory Feder.
Drawing from Scottish folklore, it depicts an ethereal woman swimming alongside a seal. The candle is both a covetable design object and an indulgent scent for the season.
Indulge in a slow burn from Astier de Villatte

Paris-based Astier de Villatte, a design house known for its elegant and lightweight ceramics, has found inspiration in the island nation of São Tomé and Príncipe for the latest addition to its incense line.

The new scent draws on São Tomé’s plentiful cocoa reserves, blending notes of roasted cocoa with Atlas cedar, labdanum, sandalwood and musk, making for a luxurious room filler to accompany the workshop’s delicate ceramics.
Channel the silversmith with Georg Jensen’s Home Scent

Seeking inspiration for its first foray into scent, Danish heritage design house Georg Jensen turned to its own silversmith. The result is a trio of candles that pays tribute to the materials found in the brand’s Copenhagen workshop: silver, steel and quartz.
As you might then expect, the candles emit scents with an intriguing metallic edge, balanced with olfactory layers taken from the Danish countryside – think moss, ivy leaf and pine.

items.title: How Marc Grebler turned a family workshop into a maker of bespoke Land Rover Defenders
items.description: Born in Barcelona and raised in Geneva, Marc Grebler studied finance in the UK before deciding to take his career off-road. Back in Spain, he turned his boyhood passion for four-wheel-drive vehicles into a small family business that restores, customises and mo
items.author: Ed Stocker; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Born in Barcelona and raised in Geneva, Marc Grebler studied finance in the UK before deciding to take his career off-road. Back in Spain, he turned his boyhood passion for four-wheel-drive vehicles into a small family business that restores, customises and modernises Land Rover Defenders.

“My grandfather on my mother’s side had a workshop just outside Barcelona that specialised in servicing Saabs,” says Grebler. “But Saab stopped making cars in 2015. Shortly afterwards, my grandfather died and there wasn’t much for the mechanics to do.” After a period of inactivity at the workshop, he approached his aunt, who had been running the business for her father, and suggested trying something new.

“I was always a car fan and fell in love with Land Rover Defenders in my teens,” he says. “At the time, you could pick them up for very little in Spain. My idea was to renovate Defenders in my grandfather’s workshop. I was still at university and the family thought that I was crazy, so we decided to start with one vehicle. When it sold, we began to see the idea’s potential and Costa Motor found its second wind.”

Then the coronavirus pandemic hit. Though Grebler initially saw this as a setback for the company, it allowed him to spend more time in Spain with his aunt and the cars. Plus, the period had an unexpected bonus. “There was an explosion of interest in Defenders during that time,” he says. “People were buying them, painting them and selling them on for two or three times what they had paid. But we decided to double down on quality. That’s how you build trust and a loyal customer base.”

Costa Motor’s clients are predominantly wealthy European car enthusiasts who appreciate Grebler’s personal approach. No two builds are the same and the process begins with a personal consultation. “First, I ask them what they want it for,” he says. “Do they have children? Dogs? Will they drive it in the city? Is it going to Mallorca? Will they head to the beach every weekend?” Once Grebler understands his clients’ intentions, he can build the concept and source an original Defender shell. The finished models typically sell for about €160,000, plus tax.

“If it’s a businessman who wants a fun car for his holiday home in the Med, we recommend technical upholstery,” says Grebler. “He can jump in wearing a wet swimsuit, his kids can spill drinks in the back and everything is easy to clean. Someone else might want a 200TDI because that’s what his father drove. He’s looking for authenticity. For him, we recommend real leather that will age beautifully over time. It starts with a conversation.”

Grebler restricts Costa Motor’s workload to no more than 12 projects a year. A team of craftspeople – including mechanics, leatherworkers and paint specialists – spends an average of 900 hours on each car. The approach is uniquely Iberian. “They’re incredibly committed,” he says. “Most of them have families so we have found a rhythm that works for everyone. We start at 07.00, work until 10.00, then there’s a pause for breakfast. After that, they work straight through until 15.00, then head home. There’s a flexibility in Spain that you don’t find everywhere.”

As well as Grebler’s hands-on approach, what sets Costa Motor apart is its focus on materials. Leather is a key element for Grebler. “You can have the most incredible engine in the world but if the leather feels cheap, the whole experience is ruined,” he says. “We’re obsessed with how the car feels. Everything your hands touch should feel substantial. We replace plastic with aluminium wherever we can. We cover surfaces in leather. We want to keep the original character of the Defender but give it a premium feel.”

This approach extends beyond materiality. Costa Motor recently delivered a Defender 90 to a client who loves his dog so much that the team incorporated its likeness alongside the company’s wolf logo throughout the interior. Once the cars are finished, they will be sent to their new owners; so far, their destinations have included Saint-Tropez, Verbier, Andorra and Comporta.

So, with Costa Motor’s order book full until well into 2027, what’s next for the company? “I would like us to become less dependent on Defenders,” says Grebler. “We’re finally at a stage where we have almost a year’s worth of work, which gives us peace of mind. There are so many possibilities. What I really want is for a client to come to me and say, ‘I loved what you did with my Defender. I also have a Porsche 911. Can we do something equally special with it?’ That would be the dream.”

Launched in 1948 as the Land Rover Series I, the original vehicle evolved through successive models before becoming the Defender in 1990. Renowned for its rugged aluminium body, four-wheel drive and go-anywhere capabilities, it became a staple among those working in farming, exploration, military service and humanitarian work across the globe. Built largely by hand at Solihull in the UK, the original Defender remained in production until 2016, with only minor updates. Stricter safety and emissions regulations brought almost seven decades of continuous production to an end and Land Rover tapped out at two million sales.

items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the countries where they work to produce objects and buildings that enhance our lives.

Europe’s architectural and design landscape has a rich history, from ancient castles and cathedrals to modernist masterpieces. Contemporary designers are using this as a foundation for cutting-edge adaptive reuse and the establishment of circular economies, setting global industry standards.
The country’s contemporary designers build on a foundation of secessionist art and early modernist rigour.
This Vorarlberg-based studio’s practice draws on the region’s timber-building traditions and exacting craftsmanship.
+43 5574 44440, bernardobader.com

Schottenfeldgasse 62/2/22, Vienna
+43 1 890 8921, mostlikely.at

items.title: The Hunting Wives’ Showrunner “Get[s] Real” About the Inspiration for Netflix’s Steamy MAGA Parable
items.description: In 2021, at the recommendation of a film producer, the writer and showrunner Rebecca Cutter read a pulpy murder-mystery novel on a flight from her native Massachusetts to her current base in Los Angeles. By the time she landed, Cutter had finished the book and
items.author: Dan Adler
paragraphs: In 2021, at the recommendation of a film producer, the writer and showrunner Rebecca Cutter read a pulpy murder-mystery novel on a flight from her native Massachusetts to her current base in Los Angeles. By the time she landed, Cutter had finished the book and was already mapping out the TV adaptation in her head.

The plot heavily involved a Texas abortion clinic, and the state had just passed SB 8, one of the country’s most restrictive abortion bills until Roe v. Wade was overturned the following year. As she contemplated bringing The Hunting Wives to life, Cutter saw the political stakes come into focus as well.
“I started thinking about the ‘red state, blue state’ of it,” she tells Vanity Fair ahead of the show’s season two premiere on Thursday. “What if…we really play this culture war?”

The result was one of Netflix’s biggest breakout hits in recent years, sent up in a Saturday Night Live sketch as the “straight but lesbian, horny Republican murder drama.” As a show, Hunting Wives amps up the noirish aspects of the suspense thriller written by May Cobb, a native of the East Texas Piney Woods, and adds a heaping dose of MAGA-adjacent camp. Cutter finishes the mix with plenty of sex scenes, particularly between Malin Akerman’s Margo, a femme fatale partly inspired by Melania Trump who is married to a Republican gubernatorial hopeful, and Brittany Snow’s Sophie, a liberal do-gooder who, like Cutter, arrives in town from a blue corner of Massachusetts. (Cutter was raised in Cambridge and graduated from Wesleyan University, the Connecticut liberal arts college known for its progressive politics and pipeline to Hollywood.)

Hunting Wives executive producer Erwin Stoff told Cutter he’d pay for her to go to Texas to meet Cobb and breathe the Piney Woods air herself. She met Cobb’s father and her best friend from high school. She shot skeet with the women—she even got it in three, just as Sophie does in the first season. At a high-end Dallas shopping area where the likes of Gucci can be found, Cutter got a better sense of the hair, clothes, and bodies of her eventual characters. “I understand the notion that Sophie could be amused and entertained and intrigued by these women,” Cutter says, “and eventually seduced.”

Cutter thinks of the show primarily in terms of its tonal mash-up: “I think we managed to wrangle it into one piece of art,” she says, “but there’s comedy, there’s violence, there’s noir, there’s soap, there’s earnest emotion.” To the extent that she assigned any political beliefs to the rich white women of Cobb’s novel, it was in the spirit of grounding her characters in the specifics of their world. Still, as we speak, Cutter decides “to get real with it.”

“The whole thing was a little bit of a parable, in my mind, of how you could fall for someone like [Donald] Trump,” she admits. “Sophie has her principles, but they only go so far. They end right where something starts to make her feel good.” Cutter was as curious as anyone else from her educated milieu about the quirkier aspects of Trump, like the Diet Coke button he had installed on the Resolute Desk. How liberating must it feel to embrace a movement so openly untethered from the pieties of politics and taste?
“Not that my show is a deep dive on Trump,” Cutter says, “but maybe there is an element that’s sort of looking under the hood.”

The twisted love story between Margo and Sophie entangles all of the wealthy, hard-drinking, gun-toting women in their orbit, and its central killing—one of several propelling the show forward, with a third season slated to begin filming this year—stems from an effort to cover up Margo’s abortion as her NRA-loving husband plots his political ascent. (In this proudly oversexed town, he has his own share of affairs.) Hunting Wives is the rare Netflix soap to receive steady coverage from mainstream national outlets; the fascination undoubtedly has something to do with the impression that, like Yellowstone or Morgan Wallen before it, the show unlocks something about MAGA’s cultural staying power. In a New York Times guest essay this month that evaluated the post-2024 Hollywood landscape, Sharon Waxman, the editor in chief of The Wrap, wrote, “From Melania on Amazon’s streaming service to The Hunting Wives on Netflix to the ever-expanding Taylor Sheridan universe on Paramount+ to Bari Weiss’s being put in charge of CBS News, the vibe shift was visible on all our screens.”

Cutter says she had no particular agenda nor any “ultra-evil villain plan of how it was going to be received or how it would be culturally relevant.” But Hunting Wives is sprinkled with enough proper nouns—a Peter Thiel mention here, a Walmart reference there—and distinctly modern aesthetics that she can acknowledge its appeal as something of a Rosetta stone for the moment in MAGA femininity. Even in the ostensibly waning days of the movement, the plastic surgery and soaring heels continue to captivate and horrify coastal elites. Cutter says that Callie (Jaime Ray Newman), another of Margo’s lovers, has a bit of Kristi Noem and Marjorie Taylor Greene in her: that “sort of slightly butch, real gun, real ‘back the blue’ [element]…the toughness of those women.”

The second season of Hunting Wives maintains the slipperiness that keeps the show from veering into moralism; it stands apart from other Trump-era art in its refusal to take sides. “I think I remember, in the pitch, someone saying, ‘But will red-state people like it too?’” Cutter recalls. “I was like, ‘I think so.’” Both Margo and Sophie are awash in their respective red and blue stereotypes, but neither is more admirable than the other. Their sordid union is a testament to the flexibility of both their principles and their preferences. From one vantage, it is, in the end, all about sex.

“Margo is the symbol of freedom and sexuality and feminine power and empoweredness and selfishness that [Sophie] feels she’s lost,” Cutter says, adding that Akerman’s comfort in such a role helped drive her liberal use of physical intimacy. “The audience may disagree with me,” she says, but “I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes. I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.” Last year, though, when Netflix acquired Hunting Wives, which was initially ordered by Starz in 2023, Cutter had a more practical concern.
“I literally googled,” she recalls, “‘Does Netflix show boobs?’”

items.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed For Weather

items.author: CT Jones
paragraphs: While families across the nation gather to celebrate the Thanksgiving holiday, one tradition will look a little different this year. The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for weather, according to NBC News. The parade is now expected to take place on Saturday.

Weather experts have been warning U.S. residents about a rapidly approaching storm system making its way up the east coast, bringing with it high winds, heavy rains, and flood warnings. According to CNN, winds in New York City are expected to reach around 25 to 35 mph — which would be dangerous for the parade’s famous floats and giant balloons.

“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said in a statement. “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”

This is the first time the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has been postponed because of inclimate weather. It was cancelled in 1942, 1943, and 1944 because the U.S. needed all excess helium and rubber for the World War II effort.

But past windy parades might provide insight into the decision to postpone this year’s. During the 1997 parade, winds broke a Barney the Dinosaur balloon and pushed a Cat in the Hat balloon into buildings, injuring one bystander. In 1998, a “Where The Wild Things Are” balloon hit a lamppost during its debut parade and had to be removed. In 2006 and 2019, parade officials had to lower the height of the balloons to avoid aggressive wind and subsequent damage.

More than 3 million people were expected to watch the parade along its 2.5 mile route. Grammy-nominated singer Raye was expected to open the parade with a holiday performance featuring her sisters, Amma and Absolutely; followed by floats and performances by Wyclef Jean, Smash Mouth, Natasha Bedingfield, Icona Pop, JoJo, Hunger Games star McKenna Grace, and Queen Latifah. No additional changes to the parade programming or lineup have been announced.

items.title: The Hunting Wives Season-Premiere Recap: Madam Justice
items.description: Police sirens, lesbian sex dreams, and gunshots? That’s right, baby: The Hunting Wives is back in action for season two. Grab your best cowboy hat and the longest set of acrylics you have, because there is a lot to cover!
items.author: Christina Grace Tucker
paragraphs: Police sirens, lesbian sex dreams, and gunshots? That’s right, baby: The Hunting Wives is back in action for season two. Grab your best cowboy hat and the longest set of acrylics you have, because there is a lot to cover!

As is always the case with these shows, we begin with a flashback. Cops pouring into a driveway; Jonny the sheriff demanding that whoever is holding Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman) hostage come out with their hands up. Is anyone surprised to see Sophie (Brittany Snow) shaking and holding a gun before we cut back in time to one week ago?

Sophie’s trying to put her life back together in the wake of the events of last season, but you have to imagine it’s not super easy to do when you are still having (hot) sex dreams about the woman whose brother you killed. And sure enough, Sophie’s sex dream is rudely interrupted by a vision of bloodied and battered Kyle. She manages to shake it off long enough to remind Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) that they have couples therapy today. Oh GOD, she’s trying to make it work with that absolute bore of a man? Madam, denial is a river in Egypt; YOU are gay! Therapy is rough to watch as Sophie ties herself in knots trying to make it seem like she loves being in the “box” that is the life of a wife and mother. Yes, she used to party and drink a lot, and yes, there was a woman back then too, but she doesn’t want to be that wild person anymore! She wants containment and safety; who cares if that means feeling trapped? I have never done couples therapy, but I am kinda eyeing this therapist and hoping she will jump into Sophie’s rant about wanting to be back in a box and say, “Hey, so that sounds like repressing a lot of who you are to fit in this role; that could be bad!” Graham doesn’t understand why Sophie is going through all this work to fix their marriage, because he, like me, remembers last season when Sophie told him she didn’t see him in her future. What changed? Helpfully, Sophie has a flashback to killing Kyle, so we all remember why she wants to get back together. I don’t know how being with Graham will save her from getting caught, to be honest! Sounds like you’ll just be jumpy and scared for the rest of your life, plus you’ll live with a man. Bad!

Wanda and Walter, the only cops who actually work in Maple Brook, are trying to track down the pickup truck they found in the middle of the road next to a pool of blood. You know it’s Kyle’s truck; I know it’s Kyle’s truck; damn near everybody knows it’s Kyle’s truck but the cops themselves. Dramatic irony, hello! Wanda discovers the car was stolen eight months ago in Fort Worth, but hits a roadblock with the Fort Worth PD. No time to worry about that, for there is another dead body in the woods. They have nothing to help them identify this young woman, but Wanda spots a tattoo on her wrist. Aha! She would have had to show ID for a tattoo, and the shop should keep records. Off they go, lights and sirens blaring.

Surely Margo is having fun, though, right? It can’t all just be dead bodies and panic attacks! Jed (Dermot Mulroney) is running for governor, and she is playing the loving and doting wife, talking about coming from nothing and life with a mother who was addicted to drugs. The people love her; she and Jed hold hands and smile, everything is great! … until they get offstage and it becomes clear Jed is still pissed about the events of last season. Fair enough, my guy! Not only was your wife sleeping with a teenager, but she got pregnant by him and then killed his girlfriend. One of the tougher marital issues to overcome, I think. Jed leaves Margo quite literally in the dust, with his hands all over his campaign manager’s ass. All she can do is play her part and chain-smoke in the pool house while sending Sophie “thinking of you” and “can we talk” texts. When those go unanswered, there is only one person left to call: her ex, Callie.

Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) is possibly the only person for whom the events of last season led to something positive. We see assistants bustling around a new house, setting up lights and taking test shots of Jonny, who wants to be sure his boots are in frame. Callie’s “heroic” antics from last season (killing an innocent woman) have led to — what else — a reality show. Married Justice (perfect title, no notes) has its first shoot tonight! She’s got a fake house to live in for the shoot and, hold on a moment, what’s this? A super-hot brunette with a cunty bob, messy eyeliner, and a leather jacket? Hello, producer Nadia (Kim Matula)! She reminds Callie that she is the STAR of Married Justice, and honey? Stars get to ask for whatever they want. There is a gorgeous long pause after this while the two of them look at each other, and I am rooting for these two to start fucking, like, ASAP.

First, Margo has to check in with Nadia about this whole “law enforcement” angle the show is aiming for. She’s not particularly subtle with her questions, but Nadia assures her that this show is absolutely about this group of women, first and foremost. The law enforcement part is just the cherry on top, she chirps cheerfully, before getting Margo changed, wired, and onto the party bus. Things I am a sucker for: brunettes and women who lie to get what they want. I fear I may be in trouble! Nadia dazzles and delights all the women on the party bus — you can almost see their eyes get wide with dreams of having more Instagram followers. Everyone performs beautifully on-camera for her. If you can’t admit that a well-executed line dance whips, you are a loser! Them’s the breaks, sorry to report!

Sophie is chatting with Jack (her kid, you can go ahead and forget him now; he doesn’t matter) on FaceTime before Graham interrupts with a pressing question. $1,500 credit card charge to an auto-body shop? What’s that all about, guv’nor? Sophie, shocked that her husband checks their credit card statement, barely manages to stammer that she hit an armadillo, and she definitely told him about it, don’t be silly, of course she did! Graham is like, “… Okay, whatever, just send me the footage from the Tesla so I can get an insurance claim.” “What footage from the Tesla?,” Sophie wants to know, in a way that is not at all casual but rather obviously panicked. Graham tells her exactly where the USB is, and she puts that to good use by boiling it. In case you miss what she is doing, there is a helpful, absolutely added-in-post line: “Try recovering data from this now, Elon.”

To her credit, Nadia waits maybe a whole 20 minutes while the girls chatter on-camera before dropping that this feels like a really natural time to start talking about Abby Jackson. Margo flares up instantly, trying to insist that it’s too dark and macabre for a night out. There’s no need to dig all that old stuff up again, is there? Callie, who is down to do whatever it takes to ensure her show is a hit, drops something even juicier: Cops found another dead girl in the woods. What is happening to their perfect little town? Margo sits through it as long as she can stand, before dragging Callie to the bathroom. She’s got questions about Nadia and her inventions but also couldn’t help but wonder if Callie has heard from Sophie at all? No reason, juuuuust wondering! Not surprisingly, Sophie has not reached out to her ex’s ex, and faced with disappointment but a woman who wants her, Margo does what she does best: pulls Callie into a stall and gets fucked while Tanner Adell’s “Do-Si-Don’tcha” plays. Award-winning television, IMO!

Nadia is shooting Jonny in his office, briefing them about the body that they found in the woods. Her name was Elly Gates, and Wanda and Walter (sorry, it’s so, so dumb, but it’s sooo fun that their names start with W) are en route to talk with the foster mother right now. The little moment after Nadia calls “cut” and Jonny triumphantly slams his hand on the desk in satisfaction really made me laugh. We might as well get it out of the way now: I am kind of a sucker for Jonny’s big dumb gay ass! Nadia earns my love anew by dangling her hot cameraman for Jonny to take around the office to get some background shots. I laughed again when he suggested the showers, sorry! Is there anyone on earth who was surprised that Nadia immediately snooped in Jonny’s files for the Abby Jackson case?

Elly’s foster mother does not give a convincing performance of a woman who is concerned, and Wanda clocks it right away. To her credit, her foster mother doesn’t pretend and drops the mask almost instantly. Her rant about Elly getting hooked on pills by some loser gets to Wanda, who runs outside to weep. Walter is right by her side, nodding calmly as she rants about being fine. Things just get to her sometimes, okay? And that girl had no one, just a bitchy foster mom who didn’t even notice she was gone. Those things get to you; I get it! And let’s just shout out Karen Rodriguez for her performance as Wanda; I find her SO charming in this role.

Hey, was anyone thinking we were a little low on plot? Good news, here’s a new one! On her way to her “Stars, They’re Just Like Us” photo shoot at the Giant Penny, Margo gets run off the road by a motorcycle gang led by Zelda, played by the great and good Dale Dickey. They are also looking for Kyle; he owes them big money. Big enough that they are willing to take their pound of flesh from Margo, that’s for sure. Rattled, she still shows up for her photo op, dazzling the regular citizens of Maple Brook with her beauty. Also dazzled? Sophie, who is shopping and trying not to have a million panic attacks, only to be immediately confronted with the woman she can’t stop thinking about. It’s not surprising that she runs out of the store, but I was surprised when Margo flung herself at Sophie’s still-moving vehicle! I can only imagine how Sophie must have felt, what with all that “recently killing someone via car” trauma she’s got running through her. Honestly, it’s kind of surprising that she manages to yell at Margo for Kyle threatening to kill her, and tell her that she has not confessed anything to the cops before having a panic attack. She makes it home amid flashes of killing Kyle and ringing cell phones, finally going full “Tell-Tale Heart” and ripping up her floorboards. Kyle’s phone lies there silently, totally taken apart. Ohooo, mama, you are in for a tough week!

• Jed swings by Graham’s job site to threaten him in a variety of ways. Not only will he fire Graham if he doesn’t get his house in order, but he might also just fuck his wife while he watches. It’s not the best day for Graham, but Jed, on the other hand? Well, he got to threaten someone, fuck Jia-Yi, and meet Lincoln Trout, the man who is going to take him to the Governor’s Mansion. Can we all let the name Lincoln Trout really sink in? Because he’s about to be Jed’s campaign manager, so we are gonna hear it a lot.

• Lincoln. Trout. He’s got an evil gay-guy vibe to him, which I love, to be honest. He gets the job after insulting Jia-Yi (“cocksleeve” is wild work, my guy) and proving that he is ruthless and connected to a lot of money. “Believe it or not, being presidential is still a real thing, and you have ‘it,’ whatever ‘it’ is.” Yes, he has something called “Being Dermot Mulroney,” and it really works for him! Hired and raring to go, Lincoln Trout skips over to the pool house to bend Margo’s ear about how good she’ll be for the campaign. Margo, lounging in a towel, naturally, wants Jia-Yi gone and to be on Married Justice. In exchange, she’ll happily go shop at the grocery store for broke normies, right after she makes Lincoln Trout hand her a thong. She’s gotta big-dog someone, and it looks like it’s your turn, buddy.

• Also, for some reason, we have to pay attention to Brad, son of Jill (RIP), boyfriend of Abby (RIP). He is at Baylor, and he is not doing well. He is getting into fights, getting kicked off the basketball team, and generally is filled with rage and sorrow. His dad is NOT HELPFUL, encouraging him to “forget” about his mom and move on. If times get tough? Well, pray! Yes, that feels like a foolproof plan, Reverend!

items.title: The Lowdown Season-Finale Recap: Stay a Little Longer
items.description: What would it mean for Lee Raybon Jr. to grow all the way up? He’s fifty-something years old and suddenly an orphan. He’s an adoring father but not a conventional one. Since he asked Vickey to raise chickens with him in the season premiere, there’s been the ru
items.author: Amanda Whiting
paragraphs: What would it mean for Lee Raybon Jr. to grow all the way up? He’s fifty-something years old and suddenly an orphan. He’s an adoring father but not a conventional one. Since he asked Vickey to raise chickens with him in the season premiere, there’s been the running suggestion that what Lee needs to move beyond this stalled version of himself — “Maybe you’re really running from you,” Chilli Franks intuited in episode two — is another person. The love of a good woman, as his ex-wife put it last week.

In “The Tower,” he nearly gets her. Whatever faint and twisted hopes Ginger may have been harboring for a future with Mekko are extinguished when he rips off the Fresh Start bagman and absconds again, this time with his wife and son. Without Mekko’s eyewitness account of Nathan’s death, Lee’s forced to spike his own story — the one he believed would bring Oklahoma’s nefarious elite to its knees. Both are awash in their respective disappointments, but they’re also freer to be together than ever before.

Lee is all in, or at least he thinks he is. After they sleep together for the second time, he invites Ginger to his father’s funeral, a quirky but sweet first date. From the shower, he shouts to Ginger about their future: a house in the country with chickens and fresh eggs and a pack of Border Collies. A life beyond the limits of the block Hoot Owl Books shares with Sweet Emily’s diner and Abel’s failing record shop. (Personally, I would banish people who talk to me while they bathe in Room 101.)

But what if Mekko was never the real obstacle between them? And what if the tension between Ginger’s public defender disillusionment and Lee’s savior complex was just an excuse? While Lee waxes about buying a place on the Oklahoma prairie, Ginger leaves him a note: “Write the story, Lee.” The story that threatens Mekko’s safety. The story that may reveal her affair with a client. Ginger’s not tempted by the one-size-fits-all vision of the future that we first heard Lee peddling to Vickey, nor does she want to restrain his ambition in turn.

On her way out, Ginger runs into Francis. They’ve never met before, and Ginger can’t resist the chance to introduce herself to the cool girl reading Eve Babitz outside her dad’s old bookstore. She tells Francis that she was sorry to hear about Frog’s passing, and Francis tells Ginger that Lee didn’t like Frog, offering up the information eagerly. Ginger had a flawed dad, too, she reveals, and his incarceration is why she became a lawyer in the first place. She leaves Francis with some revealing advice: Don’t get so good at pushing love away that you can’t accept it later. Ginger’s feelings for Mekko aren’t the obstacle between Lee and Ginger, but a symptom of it. For a woman who can’t accept a loving future, what boyfriend is safer than a man behind bars who can’t really offer one?

Lee doesn’t chase the girl. He calmly removes Mekko and Ginger’s pictures from his murder wall and tries to think it all through again. Yesterday, Ginger accused Lee of caring only about the story — the mythic battle between the Light and the Dark side — and not the real lives of the people involved. It’s a brutal admonishment, and yet, I don’t think it goes far enough. Because Lee does care about one person: Himself. His mission to save the world is, perhaps paradoxically, ego-driven.

Still, even Lee has to admit that without Mekko going on the record, the only proof he has of misconduct is an old lamster’s cell phone footage. It’s stark and terrifying, but it’s also a long walk from Nathan Spence’s death to Sallsman’s front door. Lee shows the video to Cyrus, who reminds him that there’s purpose in bringing down Fresh Start even if he can’t bring down the judge with it. A story like this needs more support than the Tulsa Beat or the Heartland Press can offer. How does Lee Raybon Jr. grow all the way up? By realizing that the world needs the truth more than it needs Lee as its renegade truth-teller.

Lee visits Alejandro, the reporter who first decked Lee outside the Tulsa Journalism Awards, and tells him what he knows. He hands dossiers of evidence over to other Establishment journalists, too — even softies like Dale Slater, who finally deems the corruption in Woodrell fit to print. Lee’s long told himself he’s a lone crusader in the war on evil, but Nathan Spence’s death and potential corruption at Fresh Start make the evening news almost immediately after Lee discloses them to the reporters he called “sellouts” a few weeks earlier.

From there, the dominoes fall fast. Vela cuts ties with McMann, who kills himself rather than allow Lonnie to arrest him. Vela herself is arrested as Robert Thorne dies in a violent standoff with the FBI. Judge Sallsman denies any knowledge of a cover-up, but his diversion program gets suspended, so at least his cash cow dries up. He visits Lee at Hoot Owl to threaten him against reporting out the story any further.

Then, it’s time for Frog’s funeral. Ginger doesn’t attend, but everyone else we know — Marty, Ray, Sam, Johnny, Vickey, etc. — comes out and dresses up. Lee’s a good son. In the end, he doesn’t deny Frog his expensive pink coffin or his folk bagpiper or even the all-Black choir. Instead of a eulogy, Wendell, now sober, delivers a loud and livid version of “Do not go gentle into that good night,” a poem so Frog-coded I’m surprised its reading wasn’t on the old man’s list of funeral demands. I’ve never heard it read like Peter Dinklage does it, the distinctive way he clips the ends of every line. Even Lee, who isn’t sure he likes his dad, cries.

The repast at Sweet Emily’s gives other cast members a chance to show off their talents. Obie-winner Rachel Crowl, who plays Sally, leads the ensemble in a rendition of “Stay All Night,” while Unhoused Jack — played by Scott Mason— accompanies her on the spoons. Later, Jacob Tovar, who plays the funeral director, sings “Red River Valley.” The centerpiece of the episode comes from a journal entry Frog wrote the week Lee was born, read by Frances in the context of the episode but performed by Tommy Lee Jones, who sits in a vacant diner booth just beyond the party being thrown in his honor.

For a few minutes, we’re watching something that feels more like a great American stage play than an episode of television, not to mention something far more elegiac than the actual funeral. Beginnings can be as nostalgic as endings. Frog writes about wanting to be a better father than his own, about wanting his son to have a good and true life. “I hope he ain’t scared of nothing,” he says. Lee Sr. was by all accounts a lousy dad, and somehow his dreams for his only kid came true.

What do you do when you lose the father you never had, the girl of your dreams, and the best lead of your career all in a matter of days? You sleep with Vickey, naturally. Lost as we’ve ever known him to be, Lee asks her to reread his tarot, hoping perhaps for a new future. Vickey draws The Tower card from the deck — the card of calamity, catastrophe, and chaos, which is to say, Lee’s default setting. He took The Cup, just like Vickey told him to in the season premiere, and now he’s going to raze the Tower.

Again, Lee confronts his murder wall, looking for strings in need of pulling. Shorty Henderson, the bagman. Lee’s never talked to him. He’s preparing to knock on the guy’s door when Marty appears from nowhere to wave Lee off. It turns out Marty is staking out the same house at the same moment. Jimmy — the tall guy with the “weird” eye from season one — hasn’t been seen or spoken of since Lee and Marty visited the One Well congregation, but recently he paid Marty a menacing visit. He threatened Marty over his investigation into the archeological black market, and Marty tailed Jimmy to Shorty’s.

What a small, sordid world. We’ve seen the veritable Native American museum that Jed Sallsman keeps at Tall Grass; any story about Oklahoma’s illicit artifact trade is likely to implicate him. Suddenly, it doesn’t feel so random that Dan could have ended up in possession of Lonnie’s gun, which Lee stole from the Woodrell deputy sheriff, and the owl-shaped gorget, which Lee Sr. stole from a secret auction. Without knowing it, father and son have been on the same side of the same story, as have Marty and Lee.

So Lee starts working his sources. Jeff, the dirty public defender, agrees to talk to the Heartland Press. Vela, widowed and imprisoned, can’t say enough when Lee comes to visit. Lonnie, never suited to a life of crime, cooperates. Jed Sallsman survived the implosion of Fresh Start, but Lee hasn’t followed the money as far as it goes. Yet. In the episode’s final scene, we learn that Lee has catfished the judge’s ex-wife — Juliette Lewis, always captivating — into a date with his smarmy alter-ego, Dallas. His journalistic integrity is questionable, his tactics veer toward the nasty, but let no one say that Lee Raybon Jr. doesn’t have a nose for the story.

Not to mention a flair for the dramatic, which he probably got from his dad. “The Tower” opens with a scene from a few weeks earlier, in Palestine, Texas, in the days before Frog hoofs it back to Tulsa. He’s working at a fireworks stand when the electric panel at his feet starts to spark. No hesitation, Frog grabs the petty cash from a tackle box behind the counter and runs while the owners are still busy putting out the flames. Frog was watching Paris, Texas on an old TV when the place burned itself to the ground.

On his way to Oklahoma, Lee Sr. must spend some of that stolen money on a light suit. At a rest stop, he buys a red hat and a bottle of water, not unlike Harry Dean Stanton’s in Paris. (Frog also asks the girl behind the till if she’s selling the secret cure for cancer.) These references aren’t simply Sterlin Harjo’s homage; they belong to Frog, who has cast himself as the lost man in need of redemption. What would it mean for Frog to grow all the way up? Maybe he walks to Tulsa believing it’s not too late to put the world back together, just like in the movie.

But The Lowdown is TV, and TV implies a world that exists over time — that doesn’t end when the credits roll. Satisfying as it may be to see next season’s mystery teased, there’s a trade-off, I think. As “The Tower” comes to a close, Ginger dips into an alley to have her Tarot read in a city we’ve never seen; we can’t know what it means. Will Juliette Lewis turn out to be a source or a victim or a villain? One problem with previewing the future is that it reduces the current story to a preamble. The season before the season. The tarot reading before the tarot reading. Mekko was once the emotional center of our story, but by the end of the episode, he feels more like a red herring.

And maybe that’s for the best. Because if Mekko is ancillary to what’s happening in The Lowdown, then he has a real chance of escaping this dark corner of Oklahoma. Wherever he and his family are headed, I hope they make it and that season three never finds them.

items.title: Survivor Recap: God Save the Queen
items.description: Tribal Councils these days are all about players not really saying anything, so they have to use complicated metaphors to discuss how they’re playing the game without giving anything away. While it is rhetorically stunning, it is a bit narratively deadening. W
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Tribal Councils these days are all about players not really saying anything, so they have to use complicated metaphors to discuss how they’re playing the game without giving anything away. While it is rhetorically stunning, it is a bit narratively deadening. We hear about bands playing music despite the members having different tastes, and then Green Day members, of all people, catch some strays. But it was one metaphor that really hit on the narrative of both of these eviction cycles. At the second of this episode’s Tribal Councils, Thien An uses a metaphor about chess and says that while some people see a pawn, other people see a queen. Or they see themselves as a queen, but they’re really a pawn. This resonates with Sharonda, who grunts in agreement and nods along. It should resonate because this is exactly her game. She is playing a pawn but is clearly the queen.

This episode was like the clouds over Fiji parted, the sun-damaged hands of Jeffrey Lee Probst reached out from the sky like a mythical being in an old master’s painting, and placed a crown squarely on Sharonda’s head. It was all about her moves, her manipulation, her mastery of staying in the shadows. At one point, she asks, “How can I get my way and keep everyone on my side?” That’s the distillation of her strategy, and she provided a master class.

The episode starts with the aftermath of Lewis being voted out by one person: Mr. Beast. Since there was no vote to talk about, there isn’t any discussion on the beach. The coin flip has truly broken the cadence of the episode. Devin says, “My weaponized honesty got him to flip the coin. The problem is he told everyone at Tribal tonight. Honesty is dangerous out here.” He says this like “weaponized honesty” is somehow different from regular honesty, but when no one is being honest, any true statement is basically a toothbrush whittled into a shiv.

Devin also has a problem with dishonesty because Maggie fully catches his fake idol and confronts him. I can’t do a better job describing the showdown than Devin does: She says it’s like lying to your parents after they have all the evidence to catch you. He really plays this part, and Maggie, clearly someone who has caught a kid lying more than once, plays every single mother in the world, nodding along, pretending to believe him when she knows that he is doing the world’s worst Elizabeth Holmes impersonation, blinking in her face and flattering her while telling fibs. This makes Maggie want to get him out, but Sharonda is what we Real Housewives fans would call a “bone collector.” She has all the information, and she decides how and when to distribute it to maximum effect for herself. She tells Devin he better win this immunity challenge or he’s gone.

They get to the challenge, and Thien An says, “We’re perplexed. This is new!” Yes, a new challenge on Survivor is not something we see often these days. In this challenge, they have to hold two ropes, balancing a ball on a piece of wood while standing on a balance beam that gets smaller and smaller. You’re perplexed? We’ve seen every permutation of this exact challenge, like where they balance a little ball on a stick, where they balance a ball on a bow-shaped object, or where they balance a ball between two sticks. Just three episodes ago, Mike won an immunity challenge balancing an (adorable) whale statue at the end of a pole while standing on a balance beam. You’re trying to tell me this is new? It’s sort of like when Dick Wolf went into NBC with a pitch for an entirely new drama, something they’ve never seen before, something that will perplex them. “No, it’s not Law &Order, it’s Law & Order: SVUUuuuuUUUuUuuuuuu [jazz hands].”

The best part of the challenge is that Maggie and Devin, sworn enemies, are standing next to each other nattering on about their fast food orders and being so loud that they’re drowning out Jeff, who is nattering on with his usual play-by-play. They eventually tire out, and Maggie starts dedicating each minute to someone: “This minute is for my dad,” “This minute is for teachers,” “for Jesus,” “for Nadine whose fish tacos are da bomb,” “for my high-school friend Jenny Smith who taught me how to paint my nails in study hall,” “for Lizzo, just cause,” “for that guy who once complimented me on my hair in line at the supermarket after I just got in a fight with my husband.” (I made up, but they were still funny.)

Devin tries his best to get to the end and comes close, but Mike wins once again. I’ve started to think of Mike as the epitome of corporate America, and after his win he goes full corporate jargon in his confessional, saying, “I’m the first two-time individual immunity winner in the open era of Survivor.” That’s like an earnings call where the CEO says, “We’re the most profitable Fortune 2000 company in East Texas whose name starts with the letter V.” Mike, you are just the first two-time immunity winner this season. Let’s not turn a minnow into a whale that you can balance on a pole.

Back at camp, there are two different camps. Maggie, Cristian, Carter, and Thien An want to get rid of Devin because Maggie hates that he lied to her and because he and Jelly are a power couple that they need to take out. They also say his social game is great because he teaches them TikTok dances when they’re bored. However, Devin, Jelly, Eric, and Mike want Maggie gone because Devin knows he lied to her, and Mike knows that she wants him out next and would be voting for him if he hadn’t won the most revolutionary and innovative immunity-slash-reward challenge on an episode of Survivor that aired on November 25, 2026.

Sharonda wants to keep another member of the helicopter alliance safe while making everyone think she’s still working with them. She uses the most common weapon on Survivor: weaponized dishonesty. She tells Cristian that Maggie and Thien An want to come after Cristian and Carter, and she’s been hearing his name all afternoon. When he supposes that it’s Thien An leading this charge, she says, “No, I think it’s Maggie.” As they go off to Tribal Council, I thought the reason this plan got short shrift was that it wasn’t going to come to fruition, that Sharonda would do the smart thing and vote out another member of her squad to stay under the radar.

To my utter shock, she pulls it off, Cristian and Carter believe her, and everyone votes for Maggie, which is a clear misdirection that ultimately pays off. Maggie, surprisingly, is delighted and gets more and more excited with each vote. She goes out with dignity and grace, and I hope that Brody Brady is watching, because this is what sportsmanship looks like. Thien An is the only one left out of the vote and goes to cry in a boat. Christian does come to comfort her, but they both better get used to being left out of votes because it is about to come for them once again.

Before the second challenge, Mike and Carter sit down on the beach and have a complete bro-down where they decide that they’re going to be each other’s No. 1s for the rest of the game and come up with a full strategy for how they’re going to win. They both seem elated.

The challenge is not a new one. It’s Law & Order: WikiFeet (don’t search that up!), where they all have to arrange blocks using only their little tootsies. Cristian is shockingly adept at this because when he was younger, his father used to make him do chores only with his feet, like one night his father had a prophetic dream where a wise monkey in a papaya tree told him, “Teach them how to use their feet. It will change the trajectory of their whole lives.” If Cristian wins the $1 million, he better burn $100 of it for that spirit monkey.

Mike and Carter’s plan is to get Thien An out, save Devin and Jelly for a couple more votes as smoke screens, and then go all the way to the end. The problem is, no one else wants this to happen. Mike is talking to Sharonda, Devin, and Jelly, who he voted with the last tribal, and they all want to get rid of Carter because he has an idol that that all know about because the spirit monkey did not tell Cristian’s father to teach him not to tell other people’s secrets.

As they’re talking about it, Mike says that he’s worried that Carter will catch wind of the plan; he’ll play his idol, and then one of them might go home, and Carter will know they’re after him. “Why would he get wind of it, Mike?” Sharonda says, spitting out his name like it’s a poison dart. “Do you not trust this group?” Mike is as caught as Devin was earlier in this episode, and he starts smiling and dissembling and trying to convince them that he’s in with them when he’s really not.

This is what I mean when I say that Mike is a product of corporate America. What he knows how to do is locate centers of power, get in their slipstream so he’s protected, and then last as long as possible until there is another center of power that emerges. He thought that was Carter, who had the power of an idol, but now he’s realizing the real power is Sharonda, who is running this game like Beyoncé dancing at the front of a tight formation of backup dancers. What Sharonda keeps doing is figuring out how to keep the people she wants to work with, even if they’re unpopular. Mike has no loyalty to anyone as long as he’s as close to power as he can possibly be, and that’s why no one trusts him. Mike could have tried to save Carter. He says he could have gone “nuclear” and told Carter that he knows he had an idol and to play it. That would have been the best move. He, Carter, and Cristian (and maybe Thien An) could have chosen who went home, and he would have solidified that No. 2 deal with Carter. He does not do this. He cowers to save himself. That is the difference between his game and Sharonda’s. Mike is cowardice dressed as caution, whereas Sharonda’s is forward momentum. Mike is playing to keep his job. Sharonda is playing to win.

To do that, she goes to Thien An and tells her that maybe they should get rid of Mike, fully getting her off the scent that anything might happen and getting her to keep aligning with Carter and Cristian. Though Mike does tip off Carter a little, Carter doesn’t take the bait. Mike says going into Tribal Council that it’s him versus Sharonda and we’ll see who comes out on top, but Mike totally rolls over, knows he doesn’t have the votes, and sends Carter packing with an idol in his pocket after allying with him that morning.

The image that I’m going to take away from this episode is at the end of the first Tribal Council, once Maggie was voted out, where Sharonda has her hands in front of her face trying to hide the smile that her plan worked. All of her plans are working; everything is going in her direction. The only way her game gets blown up is if Cristian, Thien An, Mike, Eric (who is becoming increasingly irrelevant as Sharonda’s pawn), and Devin and Jelly can get together and tell that she’s playing all of them. But at that point, will they even care? If she has Mike, Eric, Devin, and Jelly in her pocket, she’s definitely making it until the final five. The hardest part of her game is yet to come, when she has to keep convincing them that she is not the one who is pulling all the strings. But right now, she seems untouchable. Sandra Diaz-Twine says the queen stays queen, but she better look out because Sharonda is coming for her crown.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City Recap: Rat Race
items.description: Against all odds, Mary is no longer mad at Angie. She traded in that ire for being mad at Quai instead, for telling Angie about why she was mad at her. Once Quai apologized, Mary was no longer mad at her either and traded in that ire to instead be mad at the p
items.author: Tom Smyth
paragraphs: Against all odds, Mary is no longer mad at Angie. She traded in that ire for being mad at Quai instead, for telling Angie about why she was mad at her. Once Quai apologized, Mary was no longer mad at her either and traded in that ire to instead be mad at the person denying that they told her what Quai did. Thank God you guys are also watching this because I wouldn’t know how to even begin trying to explain this without context; none of what I just wrote sounds like real sentences. Now the mystery, at least for most of the group, is who ratted on Quai to Mary?

When Whitney pays Quai a visit in her two-bedroom apartment — which is so packed with miscellaneous accessories and overflowing clothing racks that it looks like a T.J. Maxx that’s been firebombed — she tries to get to the bottom of it. She’s sure that Quai must have let it slip to Meredith or Lisa, who in turn told Mary, but Quai completely denies this. Since they would have been betraying her in this scenario, she has no reason to cover for them, so unless Quai truly forgot, I believe that she didn’t tell them.

Luckily for Whitney, she won’t have to sleuth much harder, because across town Lisa is shopping with Mary for Diet Coke-branded sweatshirts when she asks Mary outright who told her. “Bronwyn told me,” Mary says matter-of-factly, adding that she thought Bronwyn was going to own it in the moment but instead was offended that she wouldn’t cop to it. Her silence felt like a betrayal, so now Mary’s mad at Bronwyn. The cycle continues.

Speaking of Bronwyn, she’s setting up her new house when something truly shocking happens. In walks a cheery Todd, wearing a mic pack and wielding a coffee for Bronwyn, as if his previous scorched-earth blow-up never happened. It’s one of the most haunting things I’ve ever seen. He apologizes for the terrible things he said, and it sends a shiver down my spine. In both of these scenes, he clearly entered with a mission to rehabilitate his image and leave the show on a positive note. The last time went unbelievably poorly, so this time he has to be on even better behavior — as if being kind in the last shot we see of him will cement his reputation on the show as such. Luckily, things don’t devolve this time, so hopefully he’s satisfied with his performance, and we never need to see him on our screens again. Go eat your cherries somewhere else, old man.

This episode also sees the women heading off on their cast trip to Hawaii, all convening at the airport in the same cream-toned getups like a cult, save for Angie looking like a highlighter in neon yellow and Heather dressed like Zara Larsson. In one of the strangest itinerary moves I’ve ever seen, they hop off the plane in Hawaii and almost immediately then get into a helicopter to sightsee. After a flight over the Pacific Ocean, I wouldn’t give a shit where they filmed Jurassic Park; I would just want to enjoy being back on the ground.

And for as bumpy as that ride was (I thought this was about to turn into a series finale), things only got bumpier when Heather and Bronwyn got to talking at the hotel. We’re told by Heather that after Mary and Angie’s big blow-up, Angie, Meredith, and Lisa went back to her house without cameras (not wanting to leave Angie alone). While I’m normally against anything at all ever happening on these shows without the presence of cameras, I will say that I loved hearing this because it signals the existence of real friendships — which many try to deny exist on this show. Heather thought it was a moment of closeness, but Bronwyn is now telling her that it’s getting spun as Heather trying to turn everybody against Mary. Bronwyn got texts from Mary alleging as much, and being the masterful Housewife that she is, Heather asks to see those messages for herself. Bronwyn was characterizing them accurately, but on a show like this it’s always best to cut out the middleman.

Clearly, Meredith and Lisa told Mary about this pow-wow, which convinces Heather that they also were the ones telling her about what Quai said. This show makes me feel like I need to invest in a cork board and red string to keep all of these conspiracies straight.

When the women all begin arriving at their luau that night, my body starts to have a fight-or-flight reaction. Much like a sprinter van, nothing good ever happens when these women are dining al fresco on a cast trip. Well, to be fair, good television happens; it’s just at the cost of the friend group. But before we get to that inevitability, things are looking positive as they’re all handed real coconuts filled with coconut water. “I put some vodka in hers,” the bartender says about Heather’s coconut when Mary asks what’s in them. The first betrayal of the night. Heather is aghast to be thrown under the bus like this, citing a broken “bartender’s code.” It was ultimately wise of Heather to start drinking, no matter how stealthily, because that bartender was only the first rat getting exposed this evening.

Lisa wastes no time the second they sit down, and delivers a little poetic preamble about loving the truth and wanting to know who it was who told Mary. In other cities, the cast may be addicted to fame, plastic surgery, or alcohol — but in Salt Lake this cast is addicted to solving whodunnits. It’s such an epidemic that I really believe they think they’re contractually obligated to solve a mystery at least once per season, and we even get a dramatic montage of mysteries past, from Jen Shah to Reality Von Tease. Granted, that montage (and the length for which it goes on) does make me understand their obsession with whodunnits a little more. They’ve collectively been through some truly insane circumstances, which I think is both the glue that binds them together while also being what stokes the flames of their paranoia. They’ve been conditioned to believe that anything and everything might be a vast conspiracy that they need to uncover.

And now the subject of that paranoia is Bronwyn, whom Lisa outright accuses of being the rat, with Mary co-signing. You can feel her wanting to disappear into an inflatable shark costume, because it’s hard to imagine a way for her to get out of this one. Nonetheless, she maintains that by the time she spoke to Mary about Whitney’s party, Mary already knew the details of what was said from somebody else. So she’s not denying telling Mary; she’s denying being the first to do so.

But her real rebuttal — which was locked and loaded in a way that, to me, proves at least some guilt — was bringing up Lisa and Meredith ratting on Heather, to demonstrate their history of ratting. All this talk about rats, I feel like I’m writing about Lisa Rinna’s house. In any case, when Bronwyn brings up Mary’s texts about Heather, Mary cops to that instantly with no apology. She considers Heather to be “multi-faced,” and to Heather’s credit, she admits that she is too much of a people pleaser and she’s been trying to work on that for years, noting that she wants everybody at the table to like her. It’s one of the realest things I’ve ever heard on one of these shows.

But now Heather is angry with Bronwyn, who’s trying to write this off as a misunderstanding about how much Mary knew and when. But Mary, who seemingly has to have her ire directed at one castmate at any given time, is not buying it and says she’s disappointed in Bronwyn as a friend. That’s the part that is bothering Bronwyn, who says that this was a deliberate move from Meredith and Lisa to try to put distance between her and Mary, and it’s working.

While I do think Bronwyn incorrectly thinks she’s able to control any narrative, she’s not dumb enough to fall into this trap this easily. More likely than not, the truth is somewhere in between all of this back and forth. Mary probably said something in passing about Quai leaving Meredith’s that made Bronwyn think Mary had more information than she did, and used that as a free pass to blab. She didn’t consider that to be ratting until it got brought to the group, at which point it may have occurred to her that Mary learned more from her than she realized. That’s when she launched this proactive campaign, not only reiterating over and over that she wasn’t the rat — but launching a counterattack by showing those texts to Heather, thus making Lisa and Meredith look like they have a history of ratting. But the grey area is not a space that these women are particularly equipped to live in.

One thing is for sure: Quai must be thrilled by this turn of events. Somehow the big scandal here wasn’t her action, but rather who told Mary about that action — a classic case of it being the cover-up, not the crime. And a classic case of these women all being beautifully insane.

items.title: The Rings of Power Season-Finale Recap: The Last Temptation of Gandalf
items.description: “Your Majesty, the board has changed,” Elrond tells Pharazôn in the opening moments of “The Doom of Men,” the third-season finale of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. Some time has passed since we saw Númenor’s forces setting sail and their arrival at
items.author: Keith Phipps
paragraphs: “Your Majesty, the board has changed,” Elrond tells Pharazôn in the opening moments of “The Doom of Men,” the third-season finale of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. Some time has passed since we saw Númenor’s forces setting sail and their arrival at Umbar, time enough for word of Sauron’s forging of the ring to have spread to at least this pocket of Middle-earth. As anticlimactic as the previous episode’s forging scene might have been, the moment clearly has already had profound implications. His advice: Hook up with the Elves lest they get slaughtered. Not only is Pharazôn deaf to that advice, but he’s extremely rude with his rejection, telling Elrond he’s not there to help Elves; he’s there to “slay a god.”

That, as the subsequent shot of the forces gathered outside Barad-dûr makes clear, won’t be easy. It’s Sauron’s Triumph of the Will moment. He gets his followers — a diverse bunch of orcs, Pallando cultists, at least one troll, and who knows what else — pumped up about repelling the invaders and telling them the One Ring will assure their victory. Then it’s up to Theo, now seemingly fully back in the fold, to keep the energy up with a chant in the Black Speech. None of this looks good for the good guys (if we want to lump Pharazôn in with the good guys, that is). That Sauron now has Gandalf in his clutches isn’t encouraging either. The outcome of this finale looks like it might be decided before we even reach the credits.

Still, the arrival of Celeborn and Galadriel at Pharazôn’s camp suggests all is not lost. Galadriel and Celeborn still seem to be in an awkward phase, though it’s not clear how much this has to do with their relationship and how much it has to do with Galadriel’s glumness at having removed her Ring after sensing the existence of the One Ring — a tough but necessary move — and having to share some bad news of their failure and Arondir’s death with Elrond and Gil-Galad once they arrive. The Elf leaders are happy, if a little surprised, to see her and even more surprised that she’s brought the long-lost Celeborn with her.

Galadriel and Celeborn keep the bad news coming when they meet with Pharazôn, explaining that Sauron has them surrounded and there’s no one they can turn to for help. In fact, this has been Sauron’s plan all along, and they’ve fallen into his trap. Undaunted, Pharazôn declares that if Sauron wants a fight, he “will serve him up one for the poets.” It looks like we’re in for a clash of supremely confident leaders, although only one has a magical ring, overwhelming numbers, and a superior position.

It seems like Sauron has every advantage now. But does he? It turns out he doesn’t plan to hurt Gandalf, at least not yet, because he wants something from him. Specifically, he wants Gandalf to bend the knee and makes a pretty tempting offer to bring Gandalf to his side. Pallando (or “the dark wizard,” as Sauron still calls him) will rule over Rhûn, while Gandalf can take Middle-earth in the West, which Gandalf can rule with all the kindness and gentleness he wants. Pallando sees it as a chance to do good, like they always planned, but Gandalf sees it as being against the followings of the Secret Fire. To Sauron, this is nonsense. If the Secret Fire weren’t on his side, how could he make the Rings of Power? What’s more, Sauron tells his guest that there’s a ring waiting for him, too. In fact, Gandalf’s already chosen one.

In an instant, Gandalf finds himself in a cell with Nori. Hey, it’s Nori! Except it’s not really Nori, as Gandalf discovers before long. As “Nori” tells it, she voluntarily went with Sauron’s forces to save Poppy and her family when they threatened the Harfoot caravan. That’s the first sign that something’s off, since the last time we saw Poppy and Nori, they were nowhere near the Harfoot caravan. What’s more, Nori seems a little, well, off, though the ordeal she’s been through might help explain this. Still, she sounds pretty reasonable as she describes how hard it is for the “small folk” these days. Maybe Gandalf could help? If he doesn’t know already, Gandalf confirms that he’s talking to a fake Nori after tricking her into talking about a brother he knows she doesn’t have.

The illusion shattered, Sauron lets the mask drop and brings Sauron before what appears to be the Secret Fire and asks him to call upon the One — as in the Supreme Being, not the One Ring — to help him. But that’s not how the One and the Secret Fire work, Gandalf explains. He refuses by tossing his staff to the ground, at which point the episode smash-cuts back to reality — or at least what appears to be reality — where Pallando stops Sauron from beheading Gandalf at the last possible moment, arguing, “Why would Sauron the Wise waste the power of an Istari?” What’s more, Pallando believes that Gandalf can be broken and volunteers to do the breaking himself.

After Gandalf’s taken away, Pallando and Khamûl, who’s dropped the Naznagôl outfit for the moment, get into an argument about what’s just happened and what’s to happen next. Khamûl’s already pissed that Sauron has offered Rhûn to Pallando and suggests that putting these two wizards together is a bad idea. (We’ll see about that.) Pallando’s counterargument: Sauron spared Gandalf because he knew he’d return in an even more powerful form. (Which will eventually be true, as we know.) This seems to convince Sauron, who sends Khamûl away.

But does Sauron trust Pallando? He seems to when the two speak privately after Khamûl’s departure. In fact, he seems to trust Pallando enough to offer him a ring that will make him the “greatest of the nine, a witch-king no man can slay.” That sounds like a tough offer to refuse, and despite Gandalf being convinced that the secret fire has shown him that Pallando can be brought around, the dark wizard doesn’t refuse it. When he visits Gandalf in his cell, he shows off his new ring with the pride of a newlywed. Maybe Sauron really does hold all the marbles now.

Even Pharazôn looks spooked as he gazes at Sauron’s forces — and Theo atop the winged beast — through a spyglass. They’re outnumbered two to one, Gil-Galad tells him, and the threat of an imminent battle has rattled everyone in the camp, whether they have a spyglass or not. Gil-Galad understands just how grim the situation is and, without telling Elrond and Galadriel to get out while the gettings’ good and go help the Elves, he throws it out as a suggestion and asks that they search their hearts before deciding what to do next.

This is even harder than it sounds. After Elrond suggests that Galadriel and Celeborn take the chance to slip away, Galadriel shares that their marriage isn’t quite working these days, that it feels like something from the past. (Centuries add up even for elves, it seems.) Galadriel gets the big picture, arguing that failing to acknowledge the passing of time — the “frailty of elves,” as she puts it — is what led to the creation of the rings in the first place. The world has changed, and it’s changed her. She’s not sure that Celeborn belongs by her side anymore.

Separately, Gil-Galad offers his own counsel to Celeborn, reminding him that things change, as elves know better than anyone, and that while “always is a long time,” as Celeborn says, “never” is even longer. With that, something clicks. Outside, husband and wife approach each other in slow motion on their way to an emotional reunion that’s interrupted by Pharazôn’s summons. They decide to answer this call together and head to Pharazôn’s tent. It’s not exactly a romantic night out, but it’s something. Successful couples need common interests, after all. They find Pharazôn humbled? Is this even possible? What’s more, he asks for their help.

Outside, the alliance between men and elves appears kind of shaky. Asked if he’d truly fought Sauron before at Eregion, Elrond demurs. What they really want to know is if they’re all fated to die in battle the next day. Elrond sidesteps this a bit by saying “many will live,” which reveals that the Men, or some of the men at least, resent the elves’ immortality. In response, Elrond (after reminding them he’s a half-elf) offers a phrase in Quenya that his brother Elros used to say that he translates as “Death is the gift of men.” But isn’t it more like a curse, one of his listeners asks? It’s the fate Elros chose for himself because he found the idea of death noble. Dread allows men to call on hidden reserves of strength in order to survive. This becomes a full-on “once more unto the breach” moment with Elrond taking the Henry V part and rallying the troops for the fight to come. By the end, they’re all chanting in Quenya, ready to fight (though the look on Elrond’s face makes it seem like he has some mixed feelings about what’s to come and his role in it).

If anyone feels like all is lost, it’s Gandalf. Until, that is, he remembers that Tom Bombadil once told him Gandalf could summon him with a song. As silly as that sounds, Gandalf commits to it and begins singing and dancing around. He’s still at it when some of Pallando’s followers show up to bring him to their leader, a development that makes it seem as if his efforts will come to naught. Then several dramatic developments arrive in rapid succession. First we witness a hand grabbing Gandalf’s staff after a strange noise calls Pallando away. This will become a big deal in short order, but only after the two wizards have a heart-to-heart.

After tricking Pallando into believing he’s escaped, Gandalf grabs his friend turned foe by the wrist and removes his ring. After warning Gandalf of just how evil Sauron is, Gandalf delivers a pep talk of his own. “Our task here,” Gandalf tells him, “has never been to destroy evil, but to inspire good.” That does it, too. Pallando first reclaims his name, then recommits himself to fighting the good fight.

He doesn’t have to wait long. While attempting to return Gandalf’s staff to him, Pallando discovers it’s been taken. The thief soon reveals himself: It’s one of the Naznagôl. Pallando is sorely wounded in the ensuing fight, but not so sorely that he can’t summon his last reserve of strength to toss the Naznagôl off the balcony and to the fiery depths below. (Is he dead? Which Naznagôl is it? These questions will have to wait.) Pallando then dies in Gandalf’s arms, a redeemed wizard who fades away, describing a vision of being surrounded by lilies. RIP Pallando. He did a lot of bad stuff but eventually saw the light.

Pallando’s death causes others to see the light, too, literally and figuratively. An aurora borealis-like astral phenomenon ripples through the skies as his followers drop their weapons and walk away from the fight. When Sauron meets Theo the next day, Theo explains that Khamûl and the other Gaudrim, sensing which way the wind was blowing, have left with Pallando’s followers. (Sauron is unsurprisingly not happy to hear any of this.)

As Gandalf, wandering alone, stumbles upon a lily, it becomes clear that calling to Tom Bombadil wasn’t so silly after all. Tom Bombadil appears out of nowhere; then, after Gandalf offers his ring to him, he magics it away to parts unknown, saying that his wife Goldberry wouldn’t care for it. He turns down Gandalf’s offer to return his hat, too; then the pair set out west after Tom Bombadil notes that they’re heading in the same direction and wouldn’t mind Gandalf’s company along the way.

As dawn breaks, Pharazôn, Galadriel, Gil-Galad, and Celeborn ascend to the top of a hill with their forces behind them only to find an abandoned plain below. Might this battle not happen after all? Hidden behind the treeline, Theo estimates that though they’ve lost the overwhelming advantage they once had, they’re about evenly matched.
