He advises Sauron that they go forward with the attack, only for the arrival of a fresh wave of troops led by Elrond to reveal that they don’t seem to have a chance. Pharazôn takes this moment to deliver a taunting message telling him to fight or crawl back to the shadows because there “can only be one king of men, and his name is Númenor.” Emboldened, the men begin chanting Elrond’s Quenya phrase as we learn that not a single soldier has deserted overnight. Maybe death really is a gift to men.

That’s not how Sauron reads it, however. If they want death, he decides, he’ll give it to them. Then, in what seems like an odd choice, he removes the One Ring and begins walking toward Pharazôn and the others. This is, Gil-Galad declares, the “Doom of Men,” but that description doesn’t stop Pharazôn, followed by the others, from riding to the fore to meet him, with weapons ready. Then Sauron kneels before them in surrender, Pharazôn begins laughing, the soldiers cheer, the Elves look deeply concerned, and Sauron almost cracks a smile as the season ends.

This is more like it. It’s been an odd season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. It opened well and felt like it had fully found its footing by the fourth episode. But the back half, especially the fairly dreadful penultimate episode, turned into kind of a slog. Yet the finale plays like an episode in which the series remembers everything it does well. Sauron doesn’t play edgelord torture games. The Gandalf scenes feel not just purposeful but essential and, with both the visit from “Nori” and the fight with the Naznagôl, generate a lot of tension. The confrontation between Númenor’s forces and Sauron seems mammoth, even if it never breaks into battle. And the final scene suggests anything could happen next.

Something will, too, as Amazon just renewed it for a fourth season with the same creative team. Will The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power find its consistency when it returns? We’ll have to wait and see. But at least this finale suggests it will be worth tuning in to find out.

• It’s sometimes lost in all the plot machinations just how good this cast can be. Check out the emotions that ripple over Morfydd Clark’s face as she delivers the bad news with a “forgive me.” And while the Gandalf/Pallando branch of the series has heretofore been this season’s weakest element, both Daniel Weyman and Ciaran Hinds, given meatier material, deliver terrific performances here.
• Speaking of Pallando, will he, as an Istar, also be returning in another form?

• Other unanswered questions: Who was the Naznagôl who fought Gandalf and Pallando, and what became of him (and his ring)? Where did Pallando’s ring end up? Will we ever see Marnûkh, one of the season’s best new additions again?
• Nori’s back! But not really. Though we did get a glimpse of the (presumably) real Nori in one of the montages, so maybe we’ll see more of the halflings next season.

• Though it’s used differently in the final scenes, the episode’s title, “The Doom of Men,” is from Tolkien, who used the word doom as synonymous with “fate,” not necessarily meaning “the awful thing that will destroy everyone,” which makes it closer to Elros’ Quenya saying.

items.title: Jesse Eisenberg Says Fans Aren’t Crazy With Him Because ‘There’s No Sexuality to My Work’: Life Is ‘Different’ When People ‘Want to Sleep With’ You
items.description: Jesse Eisenberg recently told the New Yorker that fans of his are “mostly fine” when he’s in public, a fact he attributes to his generally sexless resume.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Jesse Eisenberg recently told the New Yorker that fans of his are “mostly fine” when he’s in public, a fact he attributes to his generally sexless resume.

“People are mostly fine,” he said to reporter Rachel Syme when asked if strangers ever interrupt him when they spot him working on scripts. (The “A Real Pain” actor told Syme that his typical schedule revolves around sitting at a branch of the New York Public Library, where he writes from nine to five). “It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work,” he continued. “I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.”

Though, despite Eisenberg’s assertion, his “Fleishman Is in Trouble” co-star Claire Danes told Syme that people began to “rubberneck” when the two had a coincidental run-in on the street and stopped to chat. “People are very aware of him as a figure, even though he is so determined to be invisible,” she said.

Elsewhere in the lengthy profile, Aaron Sorkin, who directed Eisenberg as a young Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Network,” told the outlet that “I hardly know him at all,” noting that the actor reminds “me of Holden Caulfield, if that makes any sense. He has absolutely no patience for phonies.”

Eisenberg earned an Oscar nomination for the part, but has since been outspoken about his decision not to reprise the role in the director’s follow-up, “The Social Reckoning,” released earlier this year. “I’d be out at a bar, and a drunk guy would say, ‘Hey, I love your website,’” he told the New Yorker. “And as I’m pretending to laugh, I’d just wish all of the oxygen would leave my lungs, and that I would collapse on the floor in front of this guy and show him what he’s doing to me.”

The actor-turned-director, who is currently promoting “The Debut,” his latest project, also spoke about creating “nonhierarchical” environments on his sets. “How could you be making a movie about a woman who’s an underdog, who no one notices, and then have a set where the people walking around feel like that?” he said. “You’d have to be so stupid and blind and compartmentalizing, in a psychopathic way, to write a movie about that and then perpetuate it.”

“The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, stars Julianne Moore as Mona Friedman, a New Jersey housewife who auditions for a part in her local theater’s production of a fictional musical. After she’s cast as Miss Danielle, Friedman’s life begins to unravel as she becomes more consumed with the role and falls under the spell of director Jerry Blankenbuehler (Paul Giamatti).
“The Debut” opens from A24 in theaters on Dec. 11

items.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed to Saturday Due to Storm
items.description: Thanksgiving morning will not feature the Macy’s Parade this year due to extreme weather in New York, as the annual event — celebrating its 100th anniversary this year — has been moved to Saturday for the first time in its history.
items.author: Jazz Tangcay; Emily Longeretta
paragraphs: Thanksgiving morning will not feature the Macy’s Parade this year due to extreme weather in New York, as the annual event — celebrating its 100th anniversary this year — has been moved to Saturday for the first time in its history.

“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration. Due to the expected severe weather, the 100th March of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, Nov. 28,” Macy’s said in a statement to NBC News on Monday. “Our team is working through the operational logistics for this change and will share details as they are finalized. We expect the Parade to kick off at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday. Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”
The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will now air live on Saturday, Nov. 28 at 8:30 a.m. ET/CT/MT and 7:30 a.m. PT. Peacock and Telemundo will also carry the delayed parade at that time.
On Thanksgiving Day, NBC will instead rebroadcast the 2025 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones.

Meanwhile, NBC is keeping plans to run a preview special, “Countdown to Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade,” on Wednesday night at 8 p.m. ET, hosted by Jack McBrayer (“30 Rock”). But newly added is a just-taped segment with NBC meteorologist and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade co-host Al Roker, who will “discuss the extreme wind conditions that led to this historic decision.”

“Due to the extreme weather conditions, the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC have decided in the interest of safety for both the participants and the spectators, to move the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, Nov. 28,” an NBC spokesperson said.

New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani held a press conference and said, “Tomorrow we are expecting severe weather, including winds up to 60 miles per hour, heavy rain, and coastal flooding. To protect every New Yorker and keep our city safe, we have made the decision with @Macys and @NYPDnews
to reschedule the 100th Annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to this Saturday, November 28th.”

Ahead of the postponement, organizers behind the parade had been monitoring the weather situation all week, worrying that strong winds in New York City would ground the iconic balloons. Parade rules prohibit giant balloons from flying if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or if gusts are 34 mph or stronger.

Over 100 balloons and balloon handlers were set to be on display in celebration of the parade’s 100th anniversary. Buckaroo Bob the Minion, Joe Cool, Mickey’s Sorcerer’s Apprentice and Billie Brightpaw were among the balloon characters that had to be grounded.

Preparations for the parade balloons take months, with a village of creatives working behind the scenes to bring everything together. As early as July, the parade’s concept artist begins working on both balloon and float designs. By September, the parade’s costume designer, Kimberly Montgomery, starts piecing together over 5,000 costumes and collaborating with partners to ensure she has the right colors for the balloon handlers and accurate designs.
Float performances on the schedule include Natasha Bedingfield, McKenna Grace, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Queen Latifah and a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty.

“Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade brings the extraordinary together: iconic entertainers and emerging talent, artistry and imagination, hometown pride, cherished traditions and the thrill of discovering something new,” said Sharon Otterman, Macy’s chief marketing officer. “For our 100th Parade, we’re creating a celebration of unprecedented scale and will deliver an unforgettable Thanksgiving for millions across the country.”

items.title: ‘The Pitt’ Sets Season 3 Release Date at HBO Max
items.description: “The Pitt” has set its Season 3 premiere date at HBO Max.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “The Pitt” has set its Season 3 premiere date at HBO Max.
The third season of the smash hit medical drama will debut on Jan. 7. That is in keeping with the other season premieres of the series, which aired on Jan. 9, 2025, and Jan. 8, 2026 respectively.

The official series logline describes “The Pitt” as “a realistic examination of the challenges facing healthcare workers in today’s America as seen through the lens of the frontline heroes working in a modern-day hospital in Pittsburgh.”

The cast for Season 3 includes: Noah Wyle (Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch), Patrick Ball (Dr. Langdon), Katherine LaNasa (Dana Evans), Fiona Dourif (Dr. McKay), Taylor Dearden (Dr. King), Isa Briones (Dr. Santos), Gerran Howell (Dr. Whitaker), Shabana Azeez (Javadi), Ayesha Harris (Dr. Ellis), Sepideh Moafi (Dr. Al-Hashimi), and Shawn Hatosy (Dr. Abbot).
As Variety exclusively reported earlier this year, Supriya Ganesh, who played senior resident Dr. Samira Mohan, has exited the series ahead of the third season.

R. Scott Gemmill created the series and serves as an executive producer along with John Wells via John Wells Productions (JWP), Wyle, Michael Hissrich, Erin Jontow of JWP, Joe Sachs, Simran Baidwan, and Eli Attie.

“The Pitt” has proven to be a massive hit with both audiences and critics as well as the awards community, with the show having nabbed 12 Emmy Awards across its first two seasons out of 38 total nominations. That includes back to back wins for outstanding drama series and outstanding lead actor in a drama series (Wyle).

items.title: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran Guitarist, Dies at 65
items.description: Guitarist Andy Taylor, whose tenure in England’s glammy, pop-savvy rock band Duran Duran coincided with the group’s commercial pinnacle of the early ‘80s, died of prostate cancer at his home on Monday while surrounded by family. He was 65.
items.author: Chris Morris
paragraphs: Guitarist Andy Taylor, whose tenure in England’s glammy, pop-savvy rock band Duran Duran coincided with the group’s commercial pinnacle of the early ‘80s, died of prostate cancer at his home on Monday while surrounded by family. He was 65.

In a statement shared with Variety, Taylor’s wife Tracey said on behalf of their family, “To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather. He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”

Duran Duran added, “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”

Taylor, who was diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, had opted out on appearing at the group’s November 2022 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, citing a decline in his health in a statement.

He said, “Although my current condition is not immediately life-threatening there is no cure…. Recently I was doing OK after some very sophisticated life-extending treatment, that was until a week or so ago when I suffered a setback, and despite the exceptional efforts of my team, I had to be honest in that both physically and mentally, I would be pushing my boundaries.”

Duran Duran had been in existence for two years in the Midlands city of Birmingham when Taylor — then a 19-year-old Northumberland native seeking new opportunities after successfully touring British army bases in Europe with cover bands — spotted a April 1980 Melody Maker classified ad seeking a “Live Wire Guitarist.”

He wrote in “Wild Boy,” his candid and frequently sensational 2008 autobiography, “[The ad] cited Mick Ronson of the Spiders From Mars and Steve Jones of the Sex Pistols as musical influences so I thought it looked worth a call.”

After a successful audition, Taylor became a member of the quintet, which became a popular fixture at the Birmingham club the Rum Runner. Sporting extravagant coiffs and makeup — “We’d end up discussing cosmetics with the girls,” Taylor later wrote — the band was lumped in with Britain’s New Romantic movement of the early ‘80s. After only eight months with Taylor in the lineup, the act was signed by EMI.

Duran Duran — whose early compositions were credited to all five group members — became a nearly instant success in the U.K. Its third single “Girls on Film” (No. 5) helped push its self-titled debut album to No. 3. The 1982 follow-up album “Rio” spawned the hits “Hungry Like the Wolf” (No. 5) and the eponymous single (No. 9). Its first No. 1 single “Is There Something I Should Know” was issued in 1983.

The band was among the first beneficiaries of Stateside exposure on MTV, the then-new cable network that broke through with wall-to-wall airing of videos; their lavish clips, handsomely directly by former 10cc members Kevin Godley and Lol Creme and the prolific Russell Mulcahy, captured eyes with their lush cinematography, scantily clad models and expensive location shoots in exotic locales like Sri Lanka and Antigua. Three Duran Duran singles reached the U.S. top five in 1982-83.

Taylor noted in his memoir that those videos often found the band members risking life and limb: “They were enormous fun to make — even if it nearly killed us at times. I’m not joking! Several of us risked being drowned, we narrowly escaped being trampled by a crazed elephant, and we were forced to flee one shoot after being threatened by four thousand angry monks.”

Unsurprisingly, Duran Duran’s only Grammy Awards, both presented in 1986, were for best short form music video and (for “Duran Duran,” a compilation of their first 12 clips) best long form music video.

By 1983, the act was big enough in England to headline a London charity benefit attended by Prince Charles and Princess Diana, who told its members, “I don’t need any introductions to these boys. I know exactly who they are.” Their album of that year, “Seven and the Ragged Tiger,” shot to No. 1 in the U.K. and No. 8 in the U.S.

However, by 1984, when the singles “The Reflex” and “The Wild Boys” reached No. 1 and No. 2 respectively in both the U.K. and the U.S. (thanks in no small part to the participation of Chic cofounder and David Bowie/ Madonna producer Nile Rodgers), the band’s hard-partying, notoriously debauched lifestyle was beginning to shred their reputation; a story in the Fleet Street tabloid the Sun detailed stories of extreme cocaine abuse — later verified by Taylor, who, with bassist John Taylor (no relation), was the drug’s most enthusiastic user. Additional turmoil came into the guitarist’s life that year after his wife Tracey suffered a postpartum psychotic episode following the birth of their son Andrew.

Wrung out from a grueling recording and touring schedule and increasingly debilitated by their drug habits, Andy and John Taylor made a lateral move into a new quartet, the Power Station, which also featured British R&B singer Robert Palmer and Chic’s drummer Tony Thompson. Produced by Thompson’s bandmate Bernard Edwards, its self-titled 1985 debut reached No. 6 in the U.S. and No. 12 in the U.K. (A long-delayed 1996 sequel, with Edwards standing in on bass for John Taylor, then in rehab, failed to chart.)

By the time Duran Duran appeared at the U.S. incarnation of the transatlantic, internationally televised benefit concert Live Aid in July 1985, the original lineup of the group was reaching the end of its tether. Taylor wrote in his memoir, “John and I were in a dark place….[W]e were dying inside. We were tired of twenty-four-hour attention, tired of drinking and taking drugs, haggard from the lifestyle we had once aspired to.”

Exiting the band in 1986, Taylor attempted to clean up his life in Los Angeles and began working with Steve Jones, the former guitarist for the Sex Pistols and himself then newly in recovery. The fruits of their collaboration included “Take It Easy,” a No. 24 pop hit heard on the soundtrack for the film “American Anthem,” and the tough “I Might Lie,” which rose to No. 17 on Billboard’s mainstream rock chart. His 1987 solo set “Thunder” reached No. 46 domestically.

Following occasional work behind Rod Stewart, Taylor rejoined Duran Duran, after an absence of 14 years, for a full reunion of the original band. A successful world tour and a new album, 2004’s “Astronaut” (No. 3 in the U.K., No. 17 in the U.S.), followed. But the guitarist soon became discontent again, and exited a second time in 2006; material he had worked on for a new album was shelved.

“I was tired of going over and over the same old creative difficulties and financial tensions,” he later wrote, “and I was fed up with having blazing rows with our management over what I perceived to be our lack of clear direction….We’d ceased to function as a band; it was seriously dysfunctional. We’d returned to being five individuals pulling in different directions, just as we’d become in the eighties. When it came to sorting out our problems, just like before, we failed to connect.”

He then entered a long hiatus from music that ended in 2019, when he toured and released a solo single. He produced a 2022 album by the band Reef, and then reunited with Duran Duran for their 2023 album, “Danse Macabre.” That Halloween-themed album, which featured the original lineup and, on one song, a reunion with Nile Rodgers, combined three new originals with covers of their own songs as well as covers of songs by artists ranging from the Rolling Stones and Billie Eilish to Siouxsie & the Banshees and the Specials. Also that year, Taylor released a final solo album, “Man’s a Wolf to Man.”
He is survived by wife Tracey and his children Andrew, Isabelle, Bethany and Georgina.

items.title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Season 35 Finale Attracts 9.2 Million Viewers
items.description: “Dancing With the Stars” aired its Season 35 finale live coast-to-coast for the first time on Tuesday, and the results were big. A season-best 9.2 million total viewers watched Paralympic track and field athlete Ezra Frech and partner Daniella Karagach take ho
items.author: Michael Schneider
paragraphs: “Dancing With the Stars” aired its Season 35 finale live coast-to-coast for the first time on Tuesday, and the results were big. A season-best 9.2 million total viewers watched Paralympic track and field athlete Ezra Frech and partner Daniella Karagach take home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, according to Nielsen live+same-day preliminary, panel-only program ratings.

According to ABC, the finale posted a 2.38 rating with adults 18-49, which made it the best number in the demo since Nov. 25, 2014 (coincidentally, the season when now-host Alfonso Ribeiro won the trophy with partner Witney Carson). The finale was also up 11% in the demo vs. last year’s telecast (2.15 rating).

That 2.38 rating makes it TV’s top entertainment telecast with adults 18-49 since the Oscars in March and the highest-rated regularly scheduled entertainment telecast in 18-49 since the April 1, 2020, episode of Fox’s “The Masked Singer.”
In total viewers, the 9.2 million viewers matched last year’s finale.

In other demos, the finale averaged a 2.86 rating with adults 18-34 — the best performance since the Season 12 finale on May 24, 2011. With women 18-34, “Dancing With the Stars” posted a 4.46 rating, which is the best series telecast number in the demo for any network broadcast since the Season 3 premiere of Fox’s “Empire” on Sept. 21, 2016. And the show posted the best teens 12-17 rating (1.18) since “The Masked Singer” on Feb. 27, 2019.

ABC said the finale attracted more than 86 million votes, a new high (up 19% from 72 million in 2025) — the most ever for a single episode. The finale was the No. 1 most social program on television across broadcast and cable on the night and the No. 1 most social episode of any broadcast primetime series, year-to-date.

“Dancing with the Stars” aired live in every U.S. time zone for its special three-hour finale on Tuesday; the finale also re-aired in primetime in the Pacific time zone and started streaming the next day on Hulu.
The five final couples also included Amber Glenn and partner Pasha Pashkov, Maura Higgins and partner Mark Ballas, Connor Wood and partner Rylee Arnold and Tatyana Ali and partner Jan Ravnik.

The three-hour event included an instant dance challenge, where the couples were tested on their ability to improvise; a “judge’s choice” round and a freestyle round. The finale kicked off with an opening number to “One More Time” by Daft Punk. The “Dancing with the Stars: Live!” 2027 tour pros performed a routine to “It’s Not Right but It’s OK (Thunderpuss Mix)” by Whitney Houston, and then all Season 35 couples returned for multiple performances. Season 34 champs Robert Irwin and Witney Carson danced to “Free Bird” by Lynyrd Skynyrd.
“Dancing with the Stars” is co-hosted by Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough. Ballroom judges are Carrie Ann Inaba, Bruno Tonioli and Derek Hough. BBC Studios produces.

“Dancing With the Stars” Season 35 had been building to its finale with some of its strongest ratings in years. For its penultimate episode on Nov. 17, the show hit season highs with 7.64 million total viewers and a 1.68 rating in adults 18-49, based on preliminary Live + Same Day Panel Only data. It was the best ratings for a semifinal telecast in nine years, since Season 25 on Nov. 20, 2017 and Season 24 on May 22, 2017.

Season to date, “Dancing With the Stars” is primetime’s No. 1 entertainment series in adults 18-49 (1.59 rating in live+same day) for the third year in a row. It’s 86% above the No. 2 show, CBS’ “Survivor” (0.86), which ABC said is the largest advantage in Nielsen electronic measurement history.

items.title: 36 Thanksgiving Movies to Feast on This Season
items.description: There are certain ingredients without which Thanksgiving dinner is incomplete, beginning with the traditional fixins such as turkey, dressing and macaroni and cheese, and ending with some version of friends, family and fun. The latter can take on many forms, f
items.author: Brande Victorian
paragraphs: There are certain ingredients without which Thanksgiving dinner is incomplete, beginning with the traditional fixins such as turkey, dressing and macaroni and cheese, and ending with some version of friends, family and fun. The latter can take on many forms, from playing card games around the dinner table to putting up Christmas decorations and stringing lights around the tree before the next major family holiday. And while for some there’s nothing better to watch on turkey day than football, we’ve rounded up a few additional options for everyone who might find themselves in your home, from the little ones seated at the kids table to the adults seeking a respite from weeklong food preparations and the stress of Black Friday shopping that’s to come.

Thanksgiving movies don’t typically get the same attention as spooky Halloween flicks and feel-good Christmas films, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t plenty of options when it comes to stories about one of the biggest family gatherings of the year. In fact, the entries on our list run the gamut of genres, from rom-coms and road-trip comedies to horrors, fantasies and, of course, (family) dramas. So, if you’re not already planning to head to the theaters to catch Wicked: For Good, Zootopia 2 or Now You See Me: Now You Don’t with your loved ones, here are 36 movies that are worth a watch from home this Thanksgiving and throughout the holiday weekend.

- ‘Addams Family Values’ This is far from the most traditional Thanksgiving movie on the list, but the scene in this 1993 dark comedy in which Wednesday is cast as Pocahontas in the Thanksgiving play at Camp Chippewa and decides to enact revenge on her fellow camp peers who are portraying pilgrims makes this worth the watch alone.

- ‘Black Friday’ In this 2021 horror comedy starring former teen heartthrob Devon Sawa, Michael Jai White and Bruce Campbell, a group of toy store employees have an even worse night than expected when they show up to work the night of Thanksgiving and find themselves fending off throngs of Black Friday shoppers who’ve been infected by a parasitic organism.

- ‘The Blind Side’ The story at the center of this 2009 biographical sports drama is well known, but there’s something extra special about watching Sandra Bullock’s Leigh Anne Tuohy take in 17-year-old foster kid “Big Mike” Oher the night before Thanksgiving on the actual holiday. (However, there has been real-life drama over this film: Oher has said he doesn’t like the movie, and he and the Tuohys have engaged in legal action since it was released.)

- ‘A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving’ A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving, based on Charles M. Schulz’s Peanuts comic strip, is a tale of two Thanksgiving dinners that finds Charlie Brown making new traditions with friends Peppermint Patty, Marcie, Franklin and Snoopy. The special originally aired on Nov. 20, 1973.

- ‘Dutch’ Ed O’Neill stars in this 1991 comedy as Dutch Dooley, an average Joe who endures a series of mishaps on a road trip with his girlfriend’s snooty son, Doyle, whom he agrees to pick up from his private school in Georgia and bring home to Chicago for the Thanksgiving holiday.

- ‘A Family Thanksgiving’ In this 2010 Hallmark Channel Original Movie, a high-powered attorney reconsiders her life as a single career woman when a mysterious older woman introduces her to an alternate reality on Thanksgiving Day where she’s a happily married wife and mother.

- ‘Four Brothers’ When an older woman is gunned down in a convenience store while shopping for Thanksgiving dinner, her foster sons, played by Mark Wahlberg, Tyrese Gibson, André Benjamin and Garrett Hedlund, decide to take matters into their own hands and avenge her murder.

- ‘Free Birds’ In this 2013 animated comedy, two turkeys, voiced by Woody Harrelson and Owen Wilson, travel back in time to the first Thanksgiving to change the course of history and stop humans from domesticating and eating their kind.

- ‘Friendsgiving’ Based around the Thanksgiving trend that’s become a tradition of its own for individuals wanting to celebrate with their found family, Friendsgiving is a bit of a cautionary comedy about two friends whose plans for a low-key holiday dinner get turned upside down when one too many guests show up at the dinner table. The 2000 film stars Kat Dennings, Aisha Tyler, Chelsea Peretti, Jane Seymour and Wanda Sykes.

- ‘Funny People’ The Thanksgiving scene in this otherwise non-holiday flick is what lands this 2009 Judd Apatow film on the list. The black comedy-drama stars Adam Sandler as a retired comedian who tries to fix his relationships with the people in his life after he’s diagnosed with a terminal illness. It features an all-star lineup of talent including Seth Rogen, Leslie Mann, Eric Bana and Jonah Hill.

- ‘Garfield’s Thanksgiving’ In this 1989 animated special based on the Garfield comic strip, the famous food-loving orange cat is none too pleased when he’s forced to go on a diet the day before Thanksgiving.

- ‘Grumpy Old Men’ Next-door neighbors John Gustafson and Max Goldman’s longstanding feud is taken to higher levels when they find themselves competing for the affection of a woman who’s new to the neighborhood after they find out their mutual friend has had Thanksgiving dinner with her.

- ‘Hollidaysburg’ In this 2014 coming-of-age comedy-drama starring Rachel Keller, a group of high school friends reunite in their hometown of Hollidaysburg, Pennsylvania, during Thanksgiving break following their first semester away at college.

- ‘Home for the Holidays’ A single mother whose daughter opts to spends Thanksgiving with her boyfriend returns to her childhood home alone for a holiday dinner with her dysfunctional family. The 1995 film stars Holly Hunter, Robert Downey Jr., Claire Danes and Dylan McDermott.

- ‘The House of Yes’ In this 1997 dark comedy, Parker Posey plays a woman obsessed with Jackie-O who, recently released from a psychiatric hospital, plots to break up her twin brother’s engagement over the Thanksgiving holiday.

- ‘The Humans’ In this 2021 American psychological drama starring Richard Jenkins, Amy Schumer and Steven Yeun, Thanksgiving takes a dark turn when three generations of the Blake family gather together for holiday dinner in a rundown New York City apartment.

- ‘The Ice Storm’ Set during Thanksgiving 1973, The Ice Storm is a story about two upper-class Connecticut families who use alcohol and sexual experimentation to escape the social changes of the early ‘70s. The ensemble cast includes Tobey Maguire, Christina Ricci, Elijah Wood, Katie Holmes and Sigourney Weaver.

- ‘Instant Family’ Another entry whose Thanksgiving dinner scene lands it on the list, 2018’s Instant Family stars Mark Wahlberg and Rose Byrne as a couple who become a mom and dad of three overnight when their plans to adopt one child are thwarted upon meeting siblings in need of a home.

- ‘Jim Henson’s Turkey Hollow’ The Emmerson family occupies their internet-free time chasing a monstrous legend in the quaint town of Turkey Hollow where they’ve come to visit their Aunt Cly for the holidays in this 2015 Lifetime Original Movie.
- ‘Krisha’ In this 2015 psychological drama, a 60-something recovering addict attempts to reconcile with her family on Thanksgiving Day.

- ‘Kristy’ When a college student can’t afford to fly home during Thanksgiving break she finds herself terrorized by a cult while on campus alone in this 2014 horror starring Haley Bennett and Ashley Greene.

- ‘Miracle on 34th Street’ George Seaton’s Miracle on 34th Street is as much a Thanksgiving Day tradition as cranberry sauce. The Academy Award-winning film begins on the morning of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade and tells the story of an old man who’s hired to play Santa Clause at the iconic department store on 34th Street in New York City and claims to be the real thing.

- ‘Pieces of April’ This 2003 comedy-drama starring Katie Holmes centers on eldest daughter April Byrnes as she attempts to prepare what’s expected to be her estranged family’s last Thanksgiving dinner together following her mother’s breast cancer diagnosis.
- ‘Planes, Trains, and Automobiles’ Steve Martin and John Candy encounter hilarious misadventures on their unexpected three-day journey back home for Thanksgiving dinner in this road trip comedy.
- ‘Prisoners’ The abduction of two young girls following a Thanksgiving dinner in Conyers, Pennsylvania, is the subject of this 2013 thriller starring Jake Gyllenhaal, Hugh Jackman and Viola Davis.

- ‘Rocky’ Rocky isn’t a Thanksgiving movie per se, but the date does hold significance in the original 1976 sports drama, even if it doesn’t mean much to the film’s lead Rocky Balboa, played by Sylvester Stallone, who, in the film, delivers the famous line, “To you it’s Thanksgiving, to me it’s Thursday.”

- ‘Scent of a Woman’ In 1992’s Scent of a Woman, Chris O’Donnell stars as a preparatory student who takes a temporary job as an assistant to a blind and depressed retired Army lieutenant colonel, played by Al Pacino, ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
- ‘She’s Gotta Have It’ This 1986 Spike Lee joint makes the list for its scene where Nola Darling invites three of her male suitors to her Brooklyn apartment for Thanksgiving dinner.

- ‘Son in Law’ A South Dakota farm town valedictorian brings an unlikely free spirit from her Los Angeles college home for Thanksgiving in this 1993 cult classic starring Pauly Shore and Carla Gugino.

- ‘Soul Food’ Large Sunday dinners are the norm for the Josephs — and the place where family drama unfolds in 1997’s Soul Food staring Nia Long, Vanessa Williams, Vivica A. Fox, Michael Beach and Mekhi Phifer.
- ‘Sweet November’ Keanu Reeves and Charlize Theron star opposite each other in this 2001 romantic comedy about a couple who engages in a one-month trial courtship that has an unexpected outcome.
- ‘Thanksgiving’ In this 2023 Eli Roth slasher film starring Patrick Dempsey, a small Massachusetts town is terrorized by a killer during the Thanksgiving holiday.

- ‘A Waltons Thanksgiving’ Actor Richard Thomas, who played John-Boy Walton in the original CBS historical drama The Waltons, stars in this film which follows the Walton family as they prepare for Thanksgiving and the annual Harvest Festival Fair.

- ‘The Weather Man’ In Gore Verbinski’s The Weather Man, Nicholas Cage stars as a Chicago meteorologist who, amid a mid-life crisis, reconnects with his estranged family during the Thanksgiving holiday.

- ‘What’s Cooking?’ In this 2000 comedy-drama starring Mercedes Ruehl, Kyra Sedgwick, Julianna Margulies, Alfre Woodard and Dennis Haysbert, four ethnically diverse families — Vietnamese, Latino, Jewish and African American — share a Thanksgiving meal, each having their own take on the traditional holiday dishes.
- ‘You’ve Got Mail’ The Thanksgiving scene is what lands this nostalgic 1998 rom-com about two strangers who fall in love via email, starring Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks, on the list.

items.title: Peak Halftime Show: The A-List Machine Eventizing Pro Games
items.description: Nearly 73,000 fans inside Rio De Janeiro’s Maracanã Stadium rocked out to Ricky Martin and Brazilian DJ Pedro Sampaio on Sept. 27, when the duo performed their song “pikito pikito” live for the first time. But they weren’t headlining a concert — they were play
items.author: Alex Weprin; Ethan Millman
paragraphs: Nearly 73,000 fans inside Rio De Janeiro’s Maracanã Stadium rocked out to Ricky Martin and Brazilian DJ Pedro Sampaio on Sept. 27, when the duo performed their song “pikito pikito” live for the first time. But they weren’t headlining a concert — they were playing a halftime show.

The NFL has long held global ambitions, but this is the year it leaned into music to serve as a sort of cultural diplomacy. The Rio game, between the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys, may be the best example, combining a global superstar in Martin with a local talent. “There was a lot of preparation and many hours of rehearsals leading up to the performance,” Martin tells The Hollywood Reporter, “but it was one of those experiences where everything came together beautifully.”
He adds, “These are memories I’ll carry with me for a long time.”

In fact, the NFL has seven halftime shows planned this season, kicking off with the Jonas Brothers in Melbourne on Sept. 10, running through The Warning in Mexico City on Nov. 22. It’s also part of a concerted effort to elevate games into cultural events. Just look at Nov. 25, when U2 will perform during a halftime show for Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve game at SoFi Stadium between the L.A. Rams and Green Bay Packers. “There’s really this gathering momentum about how we can further eventize some of the parts on our schedule and our calendar,” Hans Schroeder, executive vp and chief media officer of the NFL, told reporters in October.

The league is leaning into halftime shows as the sports world overall has been more heavily embracing music programming in games. FIFA for instance, had its first World Cup Final halftime show this summer, with Coldplay’s Chris Martin curating a lineup that included BTS, Madonna and Justin Bieber. The NCAA, meanwhile, tapped EDM act The Chainsmokers to play a “bridge show” between the two Final Four games. The NHL has dug in, too, tapping Benson Boone to headline the first intermission during this year’s Winter Classic on New Year’s Eve.

“The NFL and all these leagues understand that to grow the game internationally and even domestically for the younger generation, they need to find organic ways to get those eyeballs,” says Tyler Stimmel, a booking agent in UTA’s music brand partnerships division. He handled booking on many of the NFL’s international events this year, including Jonas Brothers, Burna Boy in Paris, The Warning and Drew Baldridge in Munich.

“It all stems from the younger generation,” Stimmel says, pointing toward a recent USC Annenberg study that suggested nearly 80 percent of Gen Z respondents in a survey suggested they’d go to a sporting event because of concerts and other brand activations rather than because of the game itself. It’s beneficial to the talent, too, with international acts getting a shot to play before a wide swath of stateside NFL fans who otherwise likely wouldn’t have been exposed to their music. The agent adds, “We live in a highly saturated pop culture ecosystem the NFL wants more ways to cut through. “Music is the most natural way because we already know where to put the show, and you can pick a booking to tap into a version of culture that people within the region can easily relate to.”

In the U.S., that means working with such partners as Netflix to create more event-sized moments, like having U2 perform. “Netflix has leaned in because they see the success of Super Bowl and the Super Bowl halftime show, and it draws more eyes and it brings more attention and it brings more people, and not necessarily all avid football fans,” says Jon Barker, senior VP of global event production and operations for the NFL. “Now we’re tapping into casual fans, now we’re tapping into new fans, and it’s just one more element that opens another door for somebody to walk into the ecosystem of football and participate.”

Unlike the Super Bowl, which is booked by Jay-Z’s Roc Nation (next year’s headliner is Jay-Z himself), the league books its other halftime shows itself, though Barker notes that there is close coordination with its media rights partners. “It gets a little complicated, to be honest with you, in trying to find the right balance,” Barker says of the booking process. “Who is touring and is available? Who can put on a show that can fill a stadium? Who will translate well and do well on television? Who is the right act for the audience that’s inside this area, and who is the right act that will attract new fans that will be interested in what we’re doing?”

Stimmel, for his part, describes the process as sophisticated, saying the NFL has heavily relied on its regional offices throughout the world, identifying artists who are a major draw in each market but who can pull viewers from several verticals. “Burna Boy in Paris in particular is one that checks off a lot of those boxes,” he says. “He was one of the first Nigerian artists to sell out Stade de France, so we know he is popular there, but he can draw from Africa, North America.”

While the increased bookings may bring in more younger viewers, they may not always be a popular offering to older fans, who might prefer to see just a traditional halftime report with pundits rather than a concert. Stimmel acknowledges that critique but adds that “they want this to appeal to everyone, but the leagues are recognizing that in order to sustain the sport, it has to appeal to younger fans.”

NFL exec Barker says the league isn’t done expanding its halftime ambitions, noting that while “there’s probably a limit and the right balance, I don’t think we’re there yet,” even if it maintains the Super Bowl as the ultimate showcase.

From the league’s point of view, the performances are ultimately about growing the game — and reasserting the league as the most culturally relevant piece of American pop culture. “The way that we think about music is the same way we think about art, the same way we think about fashion,” says Barker, adding that the more ways “we can open to bring somebody in and show them the sport, the better off we all are.”
This story appeared in the Nov. 17 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: Francis Lawrence Signed On for One ‘Hunger Games’ Movie. Five Films Later, He’s the Keeper of Panem
items.description: The morning after the New York premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Francis Lawrence is still taking in the view from the night before.
items.author: Lexy Perez
paragraphs: The morning after the New York premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Francis Lawrence is still taking in the view from the night before.

On one red carpet stood nearly every era of Panem. There were the newcomers: Joseph Zada, Whitney Peak and Mckenna Grace, along with franchise first-timers Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes and Glenn Close. Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Josh Andrés Rivera who starred in Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes prequel, were in attendance. And there were the originals, Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Woody Harrelson, Elizabeth Banks, Jena Malone and Willow Shields assembled like the franchise’s own Avengers.

“Last night at the premiere, for the first time, we had three generations of cast,” Lawrence tells The Hollywood Reporter of the Nov. 16 event. “There’s something really special about the time we’ve all spent together and the quality of people I’ve gotten to work with.”

Lawrence has been a constant across all of them. Since taking over from director Gary Ross with 2013’s Catching Fire, he has directed every Hunger Games film that followed, working alongside producer Nina Jacobson to turn Suzanne Collins’ dystopian saga following teenagers forced into fatal combat into one of Hollywood’s most dependable franchises. The original four films grossed roughly $2.98 billion worldwide, and Collins’ five books have sold more than 100 million copies globally, growing into one of the most successful young adult publishing franchises in history.

Still, the scale didn’t fully hit him until the final Mockingjay films. Around the release of the films, The Hunger Games: The Exhibition opened to fans, and Lawrence walked through it with his stars.

“Walking through it for the first time with Jen and Josh, and I think Liam [Hemsworth] was there, we were all just stunned that we had made something museum-worthy, with our music, our costumes, our props, pieces of our sets and the lore,” he recalls. “There’s something really special in that, knowing these stories have connected with people in a certain way.”

Amid the success, it’s easy to forget that Lawrence arrived in Panem as an outsider. He had never made a sequel to someone else’s first film, and on Catching Fire he was “joining an existing family,” with a cast “so big and so seasoned” that he felt he had a lot to prove. He also assumed it would be a one-time job.
“The weird thing is, when I signed on to Catching Fire, I thought that was going to be the only one I did,” he says.
Instead, the studio asked him to stay for the two-part Mockingjay. “A huge part of me is very appreciative of being invited to keep making these movies and be part of this team.”

That invitation, however, came with a nerve-racking stretch. A few weeks into shooting Mockingjay, production paused for a month so Lawrence and the team could promote and release Catching Fire. He would face its box office verdict with most of the next film’s shoot still ahead of him.

“Man, what if this thing bombs?” he remembers thinking of the pressure for Catching Fire success amid filming the third installment. “I now still have like 125 days of shooting with all of these people that are going to be looking at me like, ‘We just made a movie with this guy that bombed.'”

He needn’t have worried. After its 2013 release, Catching Fire became the franchise’s highest grossing film, and the once outsider became the keeper of the series. “The series was quite popular at that point, and there was a lot of excitement and confidence at the studio, so that was nice,” he says.

When Lawrence and Jacobson returned eight years later with 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, the odds felt less certain. The prequel had no Katniss and centered on the rise of the tyrant Coriolanus Snow, played by Donald Sutherland in the original films with Tom Blyth taking on the role for a younger version.

“A bunch of time had gone by, and you wonder if there’s still an appetite for Hunger Games, especially Hunger Games without Katniss,” he says. “It had a very different structure, and it was a story about the person everybody hates, so a lot of things made me a little nervous.”
Sunrise on the Reaping, which traces the origins of the fan-favorite mentor Haymitch Abernathy, felt different.

“Weirdly, this one I kind of felt less pressure,” Lawrence says. “I felt much more confident that this was one that fans really wanted to see, and it felt like a return to form for movies like Catching Fire and the original.”

There being a new Hunger Games book came as a surprise to Lawrence, who assures he, along with Jacobson, are just as in the dark as everyone else. After more than a decade of working together, Lawrence and Collins have a routine. She keeps quiet while she writes, and only once her publisher confirms she has a book does she bring in Lawrence and Jacobson, always with the same modest question of whether the story is a movie. Lawrence and Jacobson always say yes.

For Sunrise, Lawrence and Jacobson got word of the novel earlier than ever, and the secrecy was tighter as a result. The manuscript was kept at Collins‘ agent’s home, and then then moved to a locked safe kept with Jacobson. Screenwriter Billy Ray wrote on an offline laptop in Jacobson’s office, while Lawrence stayed busy making secret trips to meet with Collins.

“This one we got further in advance, while she was still going back and forth with her editors,” he says. “I had read it a couple of times, Nina had read it a couple of times, and I went to New York to work with Suzanne on breaking down the book into what we thought the movie would be. We hired [original screenwriter] Billy Ray. He was already writing and we were having calls about the draft. So a lot of work was done before the book was even announced, and I couldn’t talk to anybody about it.”

The book and its film adaptation were announced together in June 2024, which brought “a lot of relief,” he says. “At least then people knew we were working on it and that it was the Haymitch story. We just had to keep quiet about the storyline itself.”

That left the biggest challenge: finding a young Haymitch, the carefree kid from District 12 long before he became the drunken, broken mentor Harrelson made iconic. The search led to Zada, the breakout from Prime Video’s We Were Liars and Netflix’s East of Eden. Lawrence put him “through the wringer” in auditions before landing on the actor to carry the beloved character’s origin story. The seeds for the origin story were “planted over twenty years ago” when Collins began the original trilogy, the author reflected in a letter shared on social media amid the release of Sunrise.
Collins praised Zada’s performance as “remarkably powerful and moving.”

Long before he was steering a multibillion-dollar franchise, Lawrence spent years making some of the most memorable music videos of the MTV era for artists like Britney Spears, Lady Gaga, Justin Timberlake and Jennifer Lopez. He doesn’t think much about those days when he’s making a movie, he says, but their influence is still there nearly 20 years later.

“Having done maybe around 120 videos, it gave me a playground to learn the toolkit I have for making things look a certain way,” Lawrence says. “I got to create different worlds, try different things, learn about visual effects and learn about working with performers. So in terms of visual style, I just had confidence in the image in general: if I imagine something, how can I actually make that happen? Because of videos, that became second nature, so I could focus more on performance and story. That’s probably the biggest way it’s affected my moviemaking in general.”

It’s fitting, then, that music runs through Panem. The films have long used it to amplify their themes of resistance. Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss sings “The Hanging Tree,” which became a rebel anthem. In the prequels, Zegler’s Lucy Gray Baird and Peak’s Lenore Dove are both musicians who capture the hearts of Snow and Haymitch.
Lawrence approaches that music the way he approached his videos: “much more music-forward than lyrics-forward.”

“I take the mood, tone and feel of a song, and most of the ideas I built for my videos were based on the mood of the song rather than the lyrics. Not always, but I’d say 90 percent of the time. It’s the same here: I’m primarily thinking about the mood, tone and emotional value of music and what I want something to feel like,” he explains.

Music is also common ground with Collins. “She’s a real music aficionado with a library in her head, and I had long conversations with her and with [executive music producer and songwriter] Dave Cobb about the creation of songs. She [Collins] usually has a historical background for why and how she wrote certain things, and I would talk to Dave, our music producer, mostly about how I wanted songs to feel. So whether it’s ‘The Hanging Tree,’ a Covey song or ‘The Old Therebefore,’ it’s really about mood,” he says.

The music doesn’t stop when the cameras roll. “I also listen to a lot of music when I shoot,” Lawrence says. “Often I’ll be watching a scene with music I have as inspiration playing in my ear, whether it’s score from our movies or from other movies, because I’m evoking a mood, a tone and an emotional value I want to feel in the scene. So sometimes I’m listening to dialogue and to music on my phone at the same time.”
His usual choices: The franchise’s scores, of which there are five movies worth, and “Lily’s Theme,” Alexandre Desplat’s piece from Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2.

“That has always felt very Hunger Games-ish to me,” he says of the Potter score. “I also listened to some more disturbing stuff for this one, because I thought of it as a bit scarier. Instead of listening to action-oriented music during fight sequences, I’d listen to things that are a little more disturbing and scary. So it was kind of all over the place.“

Building worlds became Lawrence’s calling card when he made the leap to features. His 2005 debut, Constantine, was a dark take on the DC Comics antihero, and he followed it by envisioning a New York City post-plague for the Will Smith hit I Am Legend (2007). Then came the Great Depression-era romance Water for Elephants (2011), a reunion with Jennifer Lawrence on the spy thriller Red Sparrow (2018), and more recently Slumberland (2022) and the Stephen King adaptation The Long Walk (2025).

The genres vary, but in hindsight, the dystopian streak running through several of them looks a lot like a rehearsal for the road to the Panem Capitol. Amid revisiting Hunger Games in the prequels, the director says he’s “trying to” return to where it all began with his first feature, Constantine. It was announced in 2022 that Lawrence would helm a sequel with star Keanu Reeves reprising his role and Akiva Goldsman writing the script. “We have a script,” Lawrence confirms.

Part of the appeal of a sequel is getting the band back together. The other part is unfinished business with the ratings board, and this time Lawrence wants to lean into the R rating he once tried to avoid.

“We got saddled with an R rating even though we followed all the PG-13 rules, and that was a tough blow,” he says. “On Hunger Games, every time I turn in a cut, it’s an R, we go back and forth a little, and we get to PG-13. With Constantine, they said, ‘We’ve stopped taking notes. There’s no getting a PG-13 on this movie.’ So we were stuck. Part of it was: let’s make another one because we enjoyed it, but this time let’s make the hard-R version. If we’re going to get an R, let’s make the R-rated Constantine.”
However, the road to a sequel has been anything but smooth.

“We’ve been trying, and we’ve hit roadblock after roadblock,” Lawrence says. “The character was given to somebody to make a network television show, which I never watched, and I don’t think it lasted long.” He continues, “Then J.J. [Abrams] somehow had the rights, or control of the character, for a while and was going to do something with Constantine. But he switched over, and he’s now involved in our project too. He’s a great guy, and he’s pro making this Constantine movie, which is fantastic.”.
The other obstacle, Lawrence says, is “there were new people running DC with their own plans for the characters.”

Though he doesn’t name anyone, Lawrence notes there has since been a regime change at DC. It was announced on Nov. 9 that James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-CEOs of DC studios four years after taking the job. Skydance, which now oversees the division following the acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, has appointed former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham to the post of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios.

With new leadership in place, and with relationships of his own among the executives now running Warner Bros., Lawrence sees an opening. “Maybe there’s some renewed hope to get Constantine through,” he says.

“I’m a believer that we could make a sequel to our Constantine with Keanu, and if people at DC wanted to do a different version of Constantine in some sort of shared universe, they could do that, and the two could coexist.”

Constantine isn’t the only long-gestating project on his plate. With Sunrise now in theaters, Lawrence is also turning his attention to Red Rising, Pierce Brown’s bestselling sci-fi book series, which he has been developing with the author, a friend, for about eight years.

Development of an adaptation first began as a series at Netflix, with two pilot scripts he calls “fantastic,” but it stalled. “There’s just regime changes, and it was an expensive buy-in for them,” he says. “We kept getting shifted around to different departments.”
“They never really pulled the trigger,” he adds. “Now there’s a renewed excitement because we’re at Paramount and it’s theatrical again. We have a screenwriter working on it, so I’m very excited.”

All roads seemingly lead back to Panem, with Lawrence acknowledging how Red Rising can have a clear thread back to Hunger Games character Plutarch Heavensbee, the Gamemaker turned rebel played by Plemons in Sunrise and the late Philip Seymour Hoffman in the original films. “One of the things that I love about Plutarch is that Plutarch is a bit of an infiltrator,” Lawrence says. Red Rising is an infiltration story too. The story follows Darrow, described as “a rebel forged by tragedy, battling to lead his oppressed people to freedom.”

“It allows characters to really question themselves, cross weird moral boundaries and question the people around them. What happens when the people you hate suddenly become more relatable than some of the people that you’re fighting for?” he says. “I’ve always been fascinated by those kinds of stories.”

Also on deck is BioShock, an adaptation of 2K Games’ 2007 first-person shooter. “We’re doing a rewrite on a script now,” Lawrence says. “I think that’s getting closer and closer.” In fact, he had a call about the project scheduled for shortly after his conversation with THR.

Thirteen years after the Hunger Games franchise began, the odds remain firmly in Panem’s favor. In its opening weekend, Sunrise on the Reaping grossed $120 million, becoming its fourth-best debut in franchise history, besting 2015’s second Mockingjay movie ($102.6 million) and 2023 prequel The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($44.6 million) but behind 2013’s Catching Fire ($158 million), 2012’s series-launching The Hunger Games ($152.5 million) and 2014’s first Mockingjay ($121.8 million).
For Lawrence, who has lived in this world for more than a decade, the prequels have done more than extend the franchise. They’ve changed how he understands it.

“Going through each of these books page by page with Suzanne over time has given me a pretty deep knowledge of the world and the lore. But now that she’s writing these prequels and reframing characters, I’m also learning more each time she releases a book,” he says.

He counts himself a fan, but perhaps not the biggest one on set. “I’m sure there are super fans, even people like Mckenna Grace [Maysilee Donner in Sunrise], who is a super fan of these stories, who know more about all the little nooks and crannies than I do,” he says with a laugh.

After so many years of working side by side with Collins, the page and the screen have started to merge in his mind. “The lines between the book and the script start to blur, and you forget what’s just in the movies and what’s exactly from the book,” he says.

Plenty of dystopian YA series followed in The Hunger Games‘ wake, Divergent and The Maze Runner among them, but none has lasted the way Panem has. Lawrence credits Collins’ finger on the pulse of the world as the reason for the story maintaining its popularity.

“Part of what originally separated these books from other YA publications: they had real meat on the bone thematically,” Lawrence says of the story’s lasting appeal. “She also created a world, a narrative and characters people fell in love with: Katniss, Peeta, Effie Trinket. But if they didn’t have the ideas underneath them, they would feel a bit empty and surface-level, and they wouldn’t land the same way. That’s one of the things I feel really lucky about, honestly: we get to make movies that lots of people go to see, but that really have something to say about the world we live in. For me, that’s why they endure.”
Does telling this story in today’s climate feel different than it did when the original films came out? “A little bit,” Lawrence says. But the ideas, he argues, have always been built to last.

“Suzanne’s original inspiration was watching war footage, then switching channels and seeing reality game shows, and she decided to write this series about the consequences of war for teens. At the time, it was about an idea that was relevant in the moment but also timeless. That’s what she does: she looks at the world and finds ideas that are relevant but weirdly still timeless,” he says.

Whether Collins has more to say in Panem is a question only she can answer. In the meantime, the world she built keeps showing up in the real one. Fans dress as the characters at premieres, Lawrence notes, and the films’ songs and three-finger salute have even appeared at protests, “whether it’s Hungary, whether it’s Paris.”
“So much of what is created is so disposable,” he says, “and I feel like luckily Hunger Games is not.”

items.title: Former Disney Boss Bob Iger Got Employee Pregnant During Extramarital Affair, New Book Claims
items.description: Bob Iger‘s compensation frustrations and an extramarital affair with an ABC employee that resulted in a pregnancy are some of the revelations laid out in an upcoming tell-all book.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: Bob Iger‘s compensation frustrations and an extramarital affair with an ABC employee that resulted in a pregnancy are some of the revelations laid out in an upcoming tell-all book.

The House of Mouse, written by longtime Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan, is an unauthorized biography and corporate history of the former Disney CEO that releases Dec. 1. Iger reportedly declined to be interviewed for the book.

In the book, Whelan claimed Iger had an extramarital affair with an ABC marketer in the early 1990s while he was running ABC Entertainment at the time, according to The New York Times, which obtained an advance copy. The relationship was consensual. (Iger was previously married to Susan Iger from 1977 to 1994 and married his current wife, Willow Bay, in 1995.)

The woman, who wasn’t identified, became pregnant and “suffered through a traumatic termination procedure,” Mr. Whelan wrote. The Times noted that Whelan contrasts Iger’s personal relationship with his public support for the #MeToo movement in the late 2010s.

Elsewhere in the book, it also claimed the former Disney boss was irritated and vindictive when it came to money. In 2025, Iger received a total compensation package of $45.8 million from the company, an increase from his $41.1 million in 2024, The Hollywood Reporter previously reported.

“I am frustrated about compensation! I had a nasty and distasteful negotiation to extend my contract this last time,” Iger allegedly wrote in a private email in 2014 that was sent to Ike Perlmutter, then Marvel’s chairman and a major Disney shareholder, that Whelan obtained. In 2014, Iger earned $46.5 million, a 36 percent increase from the year prior.
Iger served as Disney CEO twice, first from 2005 to 2020 before he returned in 2022 when Bob Chapek was ousted. Josh D’Amaro took over in March of this year after Iger stepped down.

In The House of Mouse, Iger wasn’t the only Disney exec facing scathing accusations during their time running the company. Whelan also accused Chapek of mocking fans at a Marvel movie premiere in 2022.
The author recounted Chapek gesturing toward fans cosplaying as superheroes and asked, “Did you get a look at the freaks?”
THR reached out to Disney and Iger for comment. The Times reported that Chapek did not respond to their request for comment.

items.title: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?
items.description: Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents bei
items.author: Will Knight
paragraphs: Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree.

As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai.

Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
WILL KNIGHT: Why sell to Nvidia?

CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source.
We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before.
Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning?

It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs.
Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents?

At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating.
And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate.

I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem.
Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen?

Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models.
Do you think that will happen?
There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed.

The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do.
Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement?

You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate.
Can we talk about the Microduck? I’m a bit obsessed.
Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year.

We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up.
At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

Think of a world where two or three companies could write software and nobody else. That would be incredibly scary. It would mean that the whole world would be controlled by two or three companies. And unfortunately, that's kind of the direction that AI is taking right now.
Can open-source AI compete with something as capable as Claude or ChatGPT?

Yes, especially with agents. Many companies have shown that when you post-train your own model for your own use case, you get frontier—or even better than frontier—performance at a fraction of the cost.
Do you think we are getting close to AGI?

I struggle a little bit with the meaning of that. Obviously the technology is progressing incredibly fast, and it’s more and more capable. I just don’t necessarily find it super useful to always compare AI to human capabilities. But if we’re getting to AGI or to superintelligence, it’s incredibly important that it’s as distributed as possible. The last thing you want is to have it concentrated in a few corporations.
What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

items.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
items.description: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a woo
items.author: Matthew King
paragraphs: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.

The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”
