Dexter explains that Harrison tried to kill him to avoid turning into his father, while JJ killed his dad because he wanted to be the JawSplitter. As I said at the start, this is a dark moment for Dex, whose reasoning strikes me as flimsy. Yes, JJ should be locked up, but surely he deserves some mercy given the role his dad played in all this. Dexter doesn’t give him an easy death, either, eschewing the standard knife in the heart so he can strangle the boy with a tourniquet instead. “Monster born or monster made, you’re still a monster,” Dex growls. “Takes one to know one.” Now there’s the Bay Harbor Butcher I’ve been missing.

After dumping JJ’s body and snagging a fancy bottle of wine, Dex sends Charley a pretty blatant “you up?” text. He heads to her hotel and even checks his appearance in the mirror just before he gets to her room. This is really happening! Clearly, Dexter has every intention of consummating the relationship, and as an unabashed Dexter-Charley shipper (Dexley? Charter?), I’m all for it. But Charley has no time to celebrate, whatever that entails — she’s got a plane to catch. It feels a little mean that she lets him come all the way there just to return the brownstone keys, and I’m really hoping this isn’t a permanent good-bye. It sure looks like one, though. When Dexter bids farewell with “Until next time,” Charley answers, “Thanks to you, there won’t be one.” The dynamic between the two has been the most exciting part of this season, and I was looking forward to watching it play out over the next six episodes. Instead, we get Dex looking sadder than he has in ages and Harry offering some half-hearted comfort. “Partnerships never end well for you,” he consoles.

Maybe because he’s in such a vulnerable place, Dexter makes the exact wrong choice during a meal with his son. Harrison feels so dejected about FBK that he’s now reconsidering his earlier plea for Dex to leave the New York Ripper to the cops. “You are the only person that can actually stop these monsters,” Harrison tells his dad. “You’re necessary.” He now wants him to take out Framt, which will at least help take Dex’s mind off his heartbreak. The real problem is that he wants to help gather information, even as Harry warns Dexter to keep his worlds separate. Against his better judgment, he’ll let his son play double agent. Back at home, Dex is considering his next move against the Ripper when he’s again interrupted by a knock at the door. We don’t see who’s on the other side, just Dexter’s shocked reaction. “You’re alive?” he gasps. Now who could that be?

• It’s gotta be Hannah, right? This isn’t just about my own desire to see Yvonne Strahovski again — I’ve never been convinced she died. Off-screen deaths don’t stick on shows like this! I’m open to other theories, though.
• It certainly won’t be Deb, but hearing Dexter and Quinn reminisce about her did make me miss Jennifer Carpenter. She got to be a ghost on Dexter: New Blood. Why can’t she pop up again here?

• Whoever this familiar face is, I hope they make up for Uma Thurman’s absence. I will say, when Dex was headed to Charley’s hotel room, I did worry she was about to turn on him, so I guess I can be grateful they ended on good terms.
• Not much more intel on FBK this week, though Wallace concludes he has been planning these crimes for eight years. What could have happened then for him to break bad?

• Harrison and Fiona have sex again, but I continue to have zero interest in the younger Morgan’s love life, sorry. Yet it’s probably not a great idea to get this close to a fellow cop while working for your serial-killer dad.

items.title: The Altruists Recap: Overdraft Protection
items.description: Who is giving the best performance on The Altruists? I suspect most viewers would agree on Julia Garner, who’s doing a good job anchoring Caroline Ellison in something concrete and real, no matter how much the writing lets her down. Aside from her and Anthony
items.author: Ben Rosenstock
paragraphs: Who is giving the best performance on The Altruists? I suspect most viewers would agree on Julia Garner, who’s doing a good job anchoring Caroline Ellison in something concrete and real, no matter how much the writing lets her down. Aside from her and Anthony Boyle, though, Alex Lawther deserves some kudos. Yes, his English accent slips through every once in a while, and sometimes he goes a little too big with the expressive monologuing and compulsive fidgeting. But in his screen time, Lawther has managed to create a vivid, real-feeling character — someone nerdy and socially unaware but often funny and charming in his own sparkly way.

So in some ways, I’m inclined to view “The Duck” as the best episode of the show thus far. It’s sort of the climax of the whole story, seemingly filling in all the remaining pre-2022 details and depicting the central act of fraud that wrecked everything Sam and Caroline had built. That clears the way for two more streamlined final episodes unpacking the fallout, which is a good thing; the series could certainly benefit from less timeline hopping. But it’s also a standout episode because it puts the spotlight on Sam Trabucco, one of the show’s strongest characters and performances. Lawther is just watchable.

That’s not to say this episode actually indicates some big jump in quality. After all, I’m still keeping this at three stars. Filtering the established narrative through Trabucco’s perspective lends the episode some focus, but it also raises even more confusion about culpability instead of putting the full blame where it should probably lie. I try not to pay too much attention to the fact-versus-fiction discrepancies on this show, but even without knowing exactly what went down, most of the specificities of Trabucco’s involvement are pretty difficult to believe.

His tale begins at Cambridge in 2011, where his friend Sam has recently earned a little rubber duck to symbolize his place at Epsilon Theta, a nerdy fraternity at MIT. Sam shows early klepto tendencies, stealing some liquid nitrogen from Trabucco’s lab so that Epsilon Theta can make instant ice cream — and so that Trabucco can earn the cred to get him his own duck. Trabucco doesn’t mind, though. He doesn’t realize that Sam will be replicating this little incident on a much larger scale a decade later.

Here’s where we start to see how much of a role Trabucco has actually played in the story we’ve been watching. He was the one who advised Sam to simply laugh at Todd’s jokes to get by at Jane Street; more importantly, he was the one who introduced Sam to the multipart arbitrage idea that made Alameda Research an early success. And it doesn’t take much convincing for him to abandon his stable finance job and move to Hong Kong, where he is the one to suggest the company mint its own FTT coin.

That last move is pretty important, because Alameda can now take out loans against FTT, whose value will rise if tied to trading on FTX. This creates a sort of infinite moneymaking loop, or a “hack” in Trabucco’s words — a trick they can use in times of emergency, though Sam immediately starts abusing it and even using the hack to buy out CZ. Trabucco, who pivots to becoming the cautious one around this point, tries to fix things by joining Caroline as co-CEO at Alameda, rather than joining Sam at FTX, but it’s impossible for him to convince her to look at Sam more critically. At this juncture, they’re too wrapped up in each other. We see that when Trabucco tries to warn them about the danger of making an exception for Alameda and disabling the safeguards: If the fund takes a big loss on a trade and goes negative, it will draw from customer money as overdraft protection.

It’s becoming clear how this fraud came together. As always, though, the scheme needs a romantic angle. In this case, Trabucco starts really dedicating himself to breaking up Sam and Caroline, sowing seeds of discord by pointing out their issues to each other and encouraging miscommunication. The pandemic and resulting Chinese crypto crackdown help: Sam ultimately decides to move FTX to the Bahamas while Caroline holds down the fort with Alameda here in Hong Kong, forcing the lovebirds into a long-distance relationship.

It’s pretty easy to guess what happens next: In 2022, Trabucco discovers the $8 billion shortfall while going through the master ledger, a massive error that went undetected due to a lack of an accounting department at the company. Sam and Caroline were both paying for everything out of Alameda’s account, including naming rights to the Miami Heat stadium and private jets, so each has a reason to blame the other.

Surprisingly, “The Duck” doesn’t actually depict the conversation that follows, when Sam and Caroline break up for good. But both react in predictable ways, with Sam pushing for more growth instead of shrinking the company down to fill the hole. His stubbornness leads to a huge, friendship-ending fight with Trabucco, during which each of them delivers some low blows. They’re pretty deserved, though, especially the ones aimed at Sam. Maybe Trabucco was a coward who benefited by letting his friend take the risks he didn’t feel comfortable taking himself, but Sam is a spoiled brat relying on the safety net of his parents and the assurance of a bailout.

Honestly, there’s enough established history between these two now that this conversation works pretty well. It’s a tad silly that Trabucco’s biggest betrayal is telling Caroline that Sam was a virgin, but most of the dialogue is stronger and more cutting than usual. The fight is a solid enough way of transitioning Trabucco out of the main story, and the frame narrative, with Trabucco describing all of this to a worried, pissed-off Lily, adequately sets up the biggest threat going into the next episode: CZ, who sees the leaked balance sheet and now knows he could send the company into free fall by off-loading the FTT used to buy him out.

It’s all fairly entertaining, as far as this show goes, and the script does a nice job filling in background details that influenced most of the major events throughout the show. But it’s still difficult not to think of how much of this material is fabricated for the series, including the sheer level of Trabucco’s involvement in Sam’s major ethical compromises. Why is The Altruists so keen on letting Sam partially off the hook when there’s every reason to believe he made most of these decisions with full awareness of the likely ramifications? Sam blaming Caroline is true to reality, but he didn’t need to be delicately manipulated by Trabucco to go that route.

Kevin T. Dugan’s own reporting for New York acknowledges the more likely reality: “[Bankman-Fried] told biographer Michael Lewis that he learned Alameda was borrowing from FTX customers only after it was too late to do anything about it, and he has chalked up the problem to an $8 billion or so accounting error. Throughout the trial, former FTX and Alameda executives have testified that the opposite was true: Bankman-Fried directed a fraudulent crypto empire in which his hedge fund was secretly and purposely able to take money from unwitting customers, and he got caught when it was too late to stop it from crashing.” This is the real story here, but The Altruists only occasionally seems interested in telling it.

• I actually kind of like the scenes of Trabucco and Caroline becoming close friends. I doubt they had this type of dynamic in real life, but it felt believable here, and it adds a little bit of stakes for what’s to come. That said, he remembers her as “the girl with the glasses” at a Math Olympiad final?

• Caroline creates a spreadsheet detailing her hopes for the relationship, many sexual in nature, and Trabucco suggests she forward it directly to her boyfriend. Not gonna lie, I’d be in shambles if I were Sam, too.

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: World’s Worst Proposal
items.description: Hello, it’s me, your recapper, just sitting over here completely disturbed by what goes down in “Another Man’s Shadow.” Listen, those of us who’ve been watching Outlander from the beginning have seen some shit. We should be used to how unapologetically dark th
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Hello, it’s me, your recapper, just sitting over here completely disturbed by what goes down in “Another Man’s Shadow.” Listen, those of us who’ve been watching Outlander from the beginning have seen some shit. We should be used to how unapologetically dark these shows can get. And yet, watching how Colum and Letitia handle the birth of their son with deformities on top of Grace getting assaulted — it’s too much, Blood of My Blood. Perhaps my tolerance is gone; perhaps it’s that we’re constantly bombarded with equally dark images from the real world, but whatever it is, this episode was hard to stomach.

Well, Letitia has her baby. Scholars of Outlander already knew something was going to go wrong here because, if you recall, one of the worst-kept secrets in the mothership series is that Colum can’t have children, and he eventually enlists Dougal to impregnate his wife. (We also meet the child Letitia and Dougal have, and he’s way too young to be born at the moment.) So when the baby is born, and Mrs. Fitz and Letitia look on in horror, it’s not completely shocking. The baby, a boy, has deformities in his legs and head, and it’s clear he won’t live very long. Instead of mourning that, when Colum walks into the room, Letitia tells her husband that this simply is not their child. The Fair Folk must have replaced their son with a changeling, and she wants Colum to go leave the baby — he’s referred to as “the creature” at one point, should you need your blood boiled any further — out in the forest overnight in hopes the faeries will switch them back.

And sure, you can argue that these are beliefs of a certain people from a certain time if you want. Mrs. Fitz does genuinely believe that her choice to open a window in the room during the birth is what brought this bad luck on. Letitia is so bereft that, of course, she’s reaching for any bit of hope that could turn this situation around. But like Claire Fraser when she comes across this practice of leaving sick children in the forest for the faeries in season one of Outlander, I’m going to refuse to accept any of this. Could someone just hold that poor baby while he dies? Moreover, if Outlander already tackled the “changeling” of it all, did we really need to retread this idea in Blood of My Blood? I don’t need to see it. We’re all suffering enough here. It’s also frustrating because this whole point of this story line could’ve been made without the changeling aspect. It’s about grief and denial, and it’s also very much about Colum adding yet another thing to that internal list he’s been running through his head of his failings as both a man and a laird. I’d argue you can still get to that without us needing to watch a child left out in the forest, but maybe I’m old-fashioned.

Colum has really been taking L’s all over the place this season, and realizing that he must have passed on his disease to his son, realizing that he can never give his clan an heir or his wife a child, brings him to his lowest low. Has he ever looked so defeated? The best scene of this episode is the emotional conversation shared between Colum and Dougal after the baby dies. Colum rails against himself and his failings — and opens up to Colum about how the problems with his legs are from more than a horse accident — while Dougal tries to lift his brother up. (Colum offering himself up to Redcoats instead of turning Dougal in has really turned the tide on their relationship, it seems. For now.) But Colum tearfully insists that the only reason he can do anything as laird is because of his brother, who has become his legs and his sword. His son wouldn’t have had anyone to do that. But even when Dougal promises that he would be his son’s shield, too, Colum won’t hear it. He is a failure, and that’s all there’s to be said about it — and so he makes a drastic, and rather dramatic, move. He walks into Letitia’s room and tells his wife that he’ll never have sex with her again, that they will never have a child together. Yikes, I get that Colum is in the throes of a shame spiral, but he couldn’t have waited, like, a week to drop this on this woman who is still actively trying to put her body back together after pushing a human out of it? It’s not all about you, my guy.

The fact that Colum is clearly unable to pick himself back up after this latest tragedy is going to affect Dougal a lot, too. Surprisingly, Dougal seems quite sympathetic toward his brother and loyal, too. It’s Maura who is pushing the other MacKenzie brother to use this moment to make a move and prove to the clan that he should’ve been laird all along. She praises him after he has a great showing in the Hall when he fills in for Colum attending to clan business. And sure, she feels bad for Letitia, but when she tells Dougal she’s pregnant, she frames it as “a way to mend what’s broken” — she and Dougal will provide the heirs for Clan MacKenzie. The romance between these two has never been hotter — Dougal really has it bad for his wife, what a thing to see! — but something tells me it’s about to get super awkward in Castle Leoch. Having these two brothers share leadership responsibilities was the only way to keep their family in power at the time, but I don’t know if anyone really thought about the long-term ramifications of this agreement.

You’d think nothing could be bleaker than current events at Leoch, but the shenanigans over at the Cameron house are giving them a run for their money. It’s no secret: John Cameron sucks the big one. He’s awful and abusive to Jocasta and mostly just mocks her when she expresses legitimate fear at being left alone with John’s cousin Hugh while John heads off to the West Indies. Then, he promptly strolls into Grace’s bedroom just as she’s supposed to be meeting with Murtagh in the barn and demands she get on the bed. (Again, this is something that’s been heavily enough implied; we did not need to see it. Think of our mental health, please.) Mercifully, Murtagh walks in and rips John off of Grace, but during their tussle, John falls, hits his head on a bedpost, and dies. The relief of this development is short-lived since Jocasta walks in and everyone has to figure out how they’re going to explain this.

I’m glad Blood of My Blood has decided to make Jocasta, much like her brothers, so morally gray. When she comes upon something so harrowing, she doesn’t have sympathy for Grace or even Murtagh; she doesn’t even have a real reaction to her husband being dead — she mostly looks angry and jealous that Murtagh would kill a man for Grace, that he would choose to love her lady’s maid over her. All of her next moves are motivated by this jealousy that the guy she likes doesn’t return those feelings.

She and Murtagh move John’s body to the bottom of the stairs so it looks like that head trauma was an accident, but when Hugh gets a look at the scene and sees how thick Jocasta is laying on the tears over the death of a man everyone knows she hated, he remains unconvinced. He susses out pretty quickly that this wasn’t an accident, but he doesn’t blame Grace (even though he knows what John was doing to her) or Murtagh; he thinks Jocasta killed John. He saw them fighting earlier in the day, and he knows the inner workings of their marriage. Jocasta tries to turn it around on him, reminding him how obvious it is that he wants John’s money, but Hugh is unbothered — he’s going to get a magistrate involved.

Meanwhile, Jocasta goes to Grace, hands her a bunch of money, and tells her that she needs to leave Scotland and never come back. Hugh suspects her; she lies, and if Murtagh were to be seen with Grace, he, too, would be implicated. They would both be hanged. The fact that Jocasta is using this situation to help her break up a couple is fucking diabolical. The MacKenzies are so unhinged; how did Ellen make it out of that family partially normal? The worst part is watching Grace stand there and thank Jocasta for her generosity and help. She also asks her former employer to tell Murtagh she loves him, but babe, there’s no way she’s doing that.

And she doesn’t. Well, okay, she does tell Murtagh that Grace loved him enough to leave so as not to implicate him, but when Murtagh, beside himself and wanting to go after her, asks if Grace left any message for him, Jocasta tells him no. Grace is gone, and it’s best for everyone if they just let this be. And is it just me, or when Murtagh grabs Jocasta’s hand OUT OF HEARTBREAK, does it look like she is waiting for him to kiss her? Jocasta, girl, go on a vacation and get a fucking grip.

All of Jocasta’s scheming does her no good with Hugh anyway. He decided not to get a magistrate involved at all — they are going to tell everyone that John got ill and died and keep everything else between the two of them. In return, Hugh demands Jocasta marry him so he can inherit all John’s money. Jocasta makes one last-ditch effort to blame this on Grace, but Hugh doesn’t bite. She will marry him, or he’ll turn her in, and they both know who people will believe. Jocasta’s stuck, and she knows it. “I hope John smites you from the grave and you fall down dead at the altar,” she tells him. Hugh’s response? “Best acceptance I’ve ever heard.” These people are freaks.

• I do love that amid all this bleakness, we get tossed a scene of Ellen giving Brian a bath in their new home as if that’s supposed to balance out everything else going on. It doesn’t work — these two don’t even look particularly happy. They seem lonely! At least they’ve decided to attend the Twelfth Night masquerade next week along with all of our other main characters. Drama is afoot, no doubt.

• I laughed so hard when, during that bath scene, Ellen started going on about the fear of having “too much good at once.” Sister, what show have you been watching? Too much good?! A man just poisoned you and killed your unborn child! Are these people out of their minds?

• Henry and Julia are mostly sidelined in this episode, but rest assured they will have a major part to play in next week’s finale: We get a scene at the Grant house in which Uncle Grant asks Henry to draw up a marriage contract for Lord Lovat and Margaret. Uncle Grant and Lovat play it off like this is all hypothetical, just in case this should happen in the future, but Henry knows this is bad news for Julia.

• There’s also bad news for the MacKenzies: Uncle Grant declares that he, Henry, and Arch Bug will be attending Twelfth Night so that he can finally get his vengeance for his nephew’s death. That masquerade is going to be popping off, it seems.

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: Baba Black Sheep
items.description: I feel a little bit like Mo, who watched three hasty TikToks to figure out how to make all of his recipes for Patisserie Week. I’ve been to plenty of Parisian dessert shops, as Paul always likes to allude to during this week, but I’m still not sure exactly wha
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I feel a little bit like Mo, who watched three hasty TikToks to figure out how to make all of his recipes for Patisserie Week. I’ve been to plenty of Parisian dessert shops, as Paul always likes to allude to during this week, but I’m still not sure exactly what they’re looking for. Are these just really ornate desserts? There seems to be little throughline in what these three challenges are looking for. Is that a problem with the challenges or a problem with the theme of the week? Like Mo and Moyin hearing about the Concorde, I have absolutely no idea.

What I do know is that I hate a baba, a booze-soaked dessert that I associate much more with summer in Italy than I do with pastry shops in France. Maybe it’s a south of France thing? Which I hear is a very Nice place. (Noel would love that joke.) I also feel like Mo because he says that it’s just like “soggy bread,” and I fear that he is right. Maybe it’s because neither Mo nor I drink alcohol, so we’re missing out on one of the key ingredients, or maybe it’s because Italians, while they have perfected other cuisine, are shit at desserts. Baba, tiramisu, and panna cotta are three of the most disgusting confections ever to come out of a forno. Sorry to a whole country, but stick to pasta.

Our four young men all do a mixed job on their babas. Maybe it has something to do with the extreme heat in the tent, where the bakers aren’t even using the shabby-looking proving boxes that have returned to their benches and instead just leaving their dough to rise on the countertops. That’s because it’s 34 degrees in the tent. That’s like 94 American degrees. (I’m sorry, the only thing worse than Italian desserts is Celsius — the scale, not the beverage.) Actually, that’s not true that they’re all mixed. Moyin gets high marks for his hibiscus and orange liqueur concoction that turns the dessert beet red. They think they’re maybe too boozy, which is a compliment. Nigella does have one quibble: that a baba “should squirt in your mouth when you eat it.” Luckily, she also leaves us with a “Boys behave!” as she walks away, making us aware that she knows what she just said.

The rest of the bakers don’t do so hot. Mo’s non-boozy lemon babas are overbaked and crunchy on the outside. Tom’s are underproofed and falling apart. Gabe’s look cute with little hazelnut shards on the top, but Nigella says they need more drenching and bigger holes. As those words left her mouth, both of Gabe’s boyfriends popped up from behind his bench and said, “Boys behave,” in a sing-song voice and then laughed to the tune of Kylie Minogue’s “Can’t Get You Out of My Head” until they got simultaneous Grindr notifications.

I’m beginning to think that it’s time to cancel the technical entirely. It never served much of a purpose in judging, but it was a nice time to see who had the baking skills and who didn’t. It was also fun for the audience to see our bakers not know how to do something, figure it out, and unexpectedly triumph. I don’t know if the caliber of bakers has changed or the challenges have changed, but this is no longer the case. So many times this season, they were given something, and everyone failed at it. This time it was to make a Gateau Concorde, which is the name of a Parisian drag queen who dresses like cabin crew and then makes you puke in an air sickness bag. The trick to making this meringue and chocolate mousse cake is something called a pâte à bombe, which is the name of a Parisian drag queen who dresses like duck liver and then explodes. No, it’s pouring a sugar syrup into whisked egg whites that makes a mousse set. The only one who knows how to do it is Moyin, but then he messes it up, takes too long trying to fix it, and comes in last in the technical. This whole challenge is basically testing one skill, and the one person who even knew what it was flubbed it, and Mo, who did not have TikTok to look up how to do this, came in first just out of dumb luck. Is that even technical, or is that just like [shrug emoji]?

The showstopper is the only thing that felt like patisserie to me. They have to make 12 highly decorated little cakes in an ornate, edible stand. These are the kinds of little cakes with polished exteriors or things made to look like other foods that Mo has watched on TikTok more times than he’s ever been excited about anything. (That means he’s seen three.) All of them decide to make more than one kind of cake, and they all look absolutely delicious even if some of them are a little wonky and two of them use the dreaded nougatine.

Three of them also make desserts that look like fruits. Mo had the brilliant idea of bringing back his mango mousse from episode five and made them look like mangos. What was weird is he also made raspberries and blueberries, which contained white chocolate mousse and mixed berry and blueberry compote, respectively. The mangoes are life-sized, but then the blueberries and raspberries are absolutely gigantic, like Willy Wonka hit them with some kind of super-sizing ray. The judges love all of them, and Paul says it’s a “resounding success.” We know that he’s going to be Star Baker and in the finals. It is so.

Next, with a drive-by fruiting is Moyin, who makes apples and oranges in a surprisingly delicious nougatine basket that Paul Hollywood ruins trying to pick it up with his sausage fingers, and Nigella shoots him a sideways look that says, “Sigh. Men.” Nigella says his orange is like a cloud, and they just love the cremeux and the baked element that Paul heavily hinted he should include. The apple, which was full of apple chunks, Paul isn’t sold on, and Nigella says it lacks a little bit of refinement.

Gabe says that his creation is going to be a little greenhouse like the one he had as a kid and that there are going to be tomatoes and radishes inside. However, the desserts, obviously, aren’t going to taste like tomatoes and radishes. As soon as I heard he was making fruits that tasted like other fruits, I knew he was in trouble. (The only time a fruit should taste like another fruit is if he was just making out with another fruit. That was a gay joke. I’m sorry.) In this case, the tomatoes are going to be strawberry and basil, and the radishes are apple and pink peppercorn.

Tom, once again, is going to pop culture for his inspiration, which, honestly, I love, even if his inspiration is Wicked, which seems a little two Oscar seasons ago. He’s making a biscuit yellow brick road, a nougatine Emerald City, and one dark green dessert that is pistachio sable and jaconde sponge, and one pink dessert that is white chocolate mousse and a cherry insert. While Tom’s ode to Judy Garland is pretty, Paul says that the desserts, particularly the pink one, were forgettable. Nigella says the white chocolate is a “blunt instrument” that takes over the whole thing. The green one has a biscuit base that is far too thick and, I don’t know, both of them look really gloopy on the fork.

I was worried that Tom was going to have rocked the whole competition and then lagged when it matters the most. Luckily, he just sneaks through to the final. That’s mostly because Gabe made foods that tasted like other foods. It’s too much of a mindfuck, like trying to part your hair on the other side of your head. While his greenhouse was more adorable than a kitten going out on a first date with a puppy, they didn’t like the biscuit and the cake in the tomato, and in the radish they couldn’t taste the peppercorn and, once again, the white chocolate took over everything. (White chocolate, the fart in the elevator of the baking world.) Gabe is the one who is sent home, and he gets a consolation handshake from Paul on the way out. Only one handshake? How is he supposed to share that with both of his boyfriends?

Next week is going to be a very interesting finale with three young men all vying for the crown. Tom was the early favorite but has been flagging in the final laps. Moyim has been on the rise for the past few weeks, boosted by his success and his love of Connie. Mo has been as erratic as his FYP feed throughout the competition, but is one day away from taking it all. Honestly, I’d be happy with any of the winners and can’t wait to see what wonderful things (and a stupid technical) they make them do next week.

items.title: ‘Hexed’ Review: Disney’s Not-So-Wicked Witch Tale Is Cheery Enough, but Not Terribly Crafty
items.description: Thank goodness for Aunt Gladys. If it weren’t for last year’s fright-wigged “Weapons” villainess — a bracing figure of pure, malicious evil amid cinema’s recent run of goody-two-shoes witches, sparkling up the likes of “Wicked” and “Practical Magic 2” — you’d
items.author: Guy Lodge
paragraphs: Thank goodness for Aunt Gladys. If it weren’t for last year’s fright-wigged “Weapons” villainess — a bracing figure of pure, malicious evil amid cinema’s recent run of goody-two-shoes witches, sparkling up the likes of “Wicked” and “Practical Magic 2” — you’d begin to worry that screen sorcery has altogether lost its edge. Not that there’s anything wrong with humanizing witches per se, but surely we can all agree that the bad ones have more fun. The new Disney animated feature “Hexed” splits the difference. Its suburban teenage heroine Billie is about as wholesome a witch as witchery has ever seen, but at least she enjoys her powers, instead of moping about them: After the “Wicked” films spent nearly five hours telling us it’s not easy being green, the chief takeaway of the bright, chipper “Hexed” is that witchin’ is bitchin’.

There’s not a whole lot more to it than that, however, even as Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand‘s film attempts to squeeze a mother-daughter bonding tale in amidst all the magical hijinks. “Hexed” is ostensibly the first original animated film from the Disney stable since 2023’s swiftly forgotten “Wish,” but it certainly doesn’t feel that way: Quilting together story elements from any number of previous, occult-tinged coming-of-age tales, it’s about as familiar as, well, a witch’s right-hand cat. Even its lurid violet-and-jade color palette looks secondhand so soon after “Wicked’s” ubiquitous green-and-pink branding.

From its cookie-cutter characterization to its throwback design elements to a soundtrack embellished with well-known pop songs, the film is altogether too risk-averse to threaten classic status. That its narrative, about an ordinary American girl stumbling into an enchanted realm and discovering her hidden supernatural genes, bears some resemblance to that of the recent stop-motion stunner “Wildwood” — down to the flocks of malevolent ravens flapping about the place — can be only be coincidental, but “Hexed” isn’t especially flattered by the comparison. It is, however, an emphatically more kid-friendly enterprise, and with “The Cat in the Hat” fizzling at the box office, the Disney pic should make hay with families over the Thanksgiving weekend.

A tone of chatty irreverence is struck by the opening prologue, which lays out a fairytale backstory in jagged, collage-style animation: a witch-ruled queendom, a power struggle, the loss or misplacement of magical powers that our blasé narrator describes as “a real bummer.” She doesn’t sound that invested, so neither are we.

But as we begin the story proper in modern-day Salem, our interest is sparked in adorable, saucer-eyed newborn Billie — seemingly a typical baby girl, doted on by her single mom Alice (Rashida Jones), until one night in her crib, she demonstrates literal, lightning-like magic in her fingertips. Sadly the intriguing prospect of a telekinetic infant is quashed when, following a near escape from an otherworldly portal accidentally opened up by the tot, Alice neutralizes Billie’s powers with an unprepossessing bracelet, and leaves Salem for Blahville, Ohio.

Sixteen-odd years later, Billie (now peppily voiced by Hailee Steinfeld) is a strong-willed high-schooler wholly unaware of her powers, and chafing against her mom’s constant, chiding attempts to control her. When the latest of Billie’s rogue escapades gets her expelled from school, Alice decides again to leave town — at which point Billie, who has somehow never removed her safety bracelet until now, finally does so, and is immediately whooshed away into the magical realm of Hexe, where she is soon shown the strength of her witchy capabilities.

Those include flying — rare even among her newfound kind, and an immediate threat to Queen Celeste (a silky-toned Jodie Foster), the silver-coiffed sorceress who rules over Hexe with chic cruelty. Soon exasperatedly following her through the portal is Alice, who it turns out knows Hexe — and Celeste — all too well. No surprise that Billie’s powers are hereditary, and that it falls to mother and daughter to save the embattled queendom, with some crotchety assistance from Beef Roger Crummchuck (Walton Goggins), a three-eyed, Southern-drawled feline familiar who looks a little like Disney’s Cheshire Cat as misremembered by ChatGPT.

Accounting for pretty much all the humor on offer in a mostly earnest affair, Goggins’ ripe vernacular delivery is the most pleasingly unexpected element here. (There’s some sprightly sidekick potential in a live, four-legged cauldron with a wordless, puppyish demeanor, but the film oddly forgets about the cast-iron critter about halfway through.) Everything else runs pretty much entirely according to studio-blueprinted plan, down to the breakneck, back-and-forth chase of a finale in which the real duel for dominance plays out on the soundtrack: Demi Lovato’s “Confident” battles composer Kris Bowers’ busy orchestrations to a cacophonous draw.

The absence of original songs in “Hexed” feels like a concession to modernity on the studio’s part — the Dua Lipa banger “Levitating” gets not one but two prominent spins — but contributes to the film’s general air of corner-cutting, as if this patchwork story wasn’t quite deemed worthy of the full, classic Disney treatment. And it isn’t, even if the results are pleasant enough. For a tale that rests on the thrill of opening up new worlds, every dimension of “Hexed” feels already explored, likely to enchant only those young enough not to have seen it all before.

items.title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Crowns Season 35 Winner After Emotional Record-Breaking Finale
items.description: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the Nov. 24 finale of “Dancing With the Stars.”
items.author: Emily Longeretta
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the Nov. 24 finale of “Dancing With the Stars.”

Season 35 of “Dancing With the Stars” is officially coming to an end. On Tuesday, Nov. 24, the five remaining celebrities — Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins and Connor Wood — compete one last time for the mirrorball trophy. Each finalist will perform three routines: the instant dance, a freestyle, and judges’ choice.
Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik (82/90)

For judges’ choice, the duo kicked off the night with a sexy salsa to “Jamaican (Bam Bam),” directed by Carrie Ann Inaba, scoring a 27/30. When it came time for the instant dance, the duo drew the jive card, even though she preferred the foxtrot. Carrie Ann called the impressive routine “beyond insane,” and they earned a 27/30. They ended the night with a powerful freestyle to a mashup of Cab Calloway’s “Minnie the Moocher” and Judy Garland’s “Over the Rainbow.” Jan also may have forgotten he was on live TV, blurting out, “She fucking killed it” after the routine. They scored a 28, bringing their total to 82.
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov (90/90)

The pair’s judges’ choice dance, with direction from Derek Hough, was a quickstep to “Sing, Sing, Sing,” and they scored the first perfect score of 30 of the night. For the instant dance, they were given a cha-cha, dancing to Sabrina Carpenter’s “Tears.” They scored another perfect 30 after leaving Derek speechless. Their Madonna-inspired freestyle to “Like a Prayer” and “Music” was super emotional, with Amber crying midway through. She was also joined by Team USA’s Madison Chock and Evan Bates on the dance floor. Afterward, Derek said, “The queen of the ice is now queen of the ballroom.” The pair earned a perfect 30.
Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold (82/60)

Carrie Ann suggested the Viennese waltz for the judges’ choice dance, and they danced to Noah Kahan’s “Willing and Able.” The emotional number earned the pair a 28/30. For the instant dance, they were given a cha-cha to The Pussycat Dolls’ “Buttons” — their third cha-cha of the season. Carrie Ann called it their best cha-cha so far, despite a small mistake. They scored a 25/30. Taking a page out of Tom Hollland’s lip-sync battle, the pair danced their freestyle to Gene Kelly’s “Singin’ in the Rain” and Rihanna’s “Umbrella.” The routine featured Connor ripping off his outfit midway through to reveal a corset, short shorts and tights, as they then danced in the water. They earned a score of 29/30, bringing their total to 82.
Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas (90/90)

Assigned a tango by Bruno Tonioli, Team Tink danced to “Gallo Ciego” by Orquesta Color Tango, scoring the second perfect score of 30. For the instant dance, the pair were scared after choosing a quickstep and being assigned Little Richard’s “Tutti Frutti” — a song Maura had never heard of. Bruno complimented her “gorgeously spot on” footwork and Julianne Hough joked Mark had never looked happier than he did after the routine, which earned them a perfect 30. They then performed a powerful freestyle to Marilyn Monroe’s “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend” and traditional Irish folk songs “The Parting Glass” and “Flowers of the Red Hill,” honoring her roots. The pair “exceeded all expectations,” Bruno said, and earned a third perfect score.
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach (90/90)

Going last in the judges’ choice dances, Bruno assigned Ezra and Daniella a steamy salsa to  “Danza Kuduro” by Bruno; their routine earned a perfect score. For the instant dance, they were assigned the tango to Avicii’s “Levels.” Derek thanked Ezra for educating the audience to show what’s possible and complimented his “top-notch” artistry. The pair earned another perfect score. Ezra and Daniella performed the last freestyle of the night, dancing the most emotional routine of the night to Linkin Park’s “Numb,” along with other professional dancers in wheelchairs. He began the routine without his prosthetic leg; while he put it back on, it fell off. However, he recovered flawlessly, delivering one of the most incredible routines in the show’s history. It wasn’t surprising that the pair earned rave reviews and a perfect score.
At the end of the episode, Alfonso Ribeiro said that 87 million people voted in the finale, with 687 million votes over the course of the season.
The results revealed that Maura came in fifth, Tatyana came in fourth and Connor came in third. The new mirrorball champions are Ezra and Daniella, with Amber and Pasha coming in second.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried Reveals ‘You Can See Everything’ Script Required ‘Five-Factor Authentication App’ to Access
items.description: Amanda Seyfried not only appears in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” but her winning turn as Holmes (and herself) may make history as the first doc performance to win an acting Oscar (and perhaps the f
items.author: Marlow Stern
paragraphs: Amanda Seyfried not only appears in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” but her winning turn as Holmes (and herself) may make history as the first doc performance to win an acting Oscar (and perhaps the first to win an Oscar and an Emmy for playing the same person, since Seyfried previously depicted Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout.”) Distributor A24 kept Seyfried’s participation in the film a secret so as not to spoil the surprise — demanding press outlets not mention it in their reviews — and the “Mean Girls” actress lends a layer of candor and relatability to the otherwise odd and opaque proceedings.

Now that the film is a bona fide cultural phenomenon — becoming the first documentary in decades to cross $100 million at the global box office, pushing the genre’s boundaries, inspiring countless memes, and cementing Seyfried’s status as an awards contender — she’s been making the press rounds. Her latest stop was Jimmy Fallon’s “Tonight Show” Tuesday evening.
“At first, they had just done their whole documentary, and then I just jumped in kind of at the last-minute, and it turned into something else,” Seyfried told Fallon.

Once Holmes is sent away to prison, Fielder tapped Seyfried to take her place, with the actress reenacting scenes as Holmes. Seyfried told the host that she had a wealth of research at her fingertips to draw from since Holmes was a “very public-facing person,” but the “only footage I had of her in the present-day, or at that point when they were living with her, is the documentary itself, and I couldn’t watch the footage until I got to set.”

Seyfried alluded to the “You Can See Everything” script being kept under lock and key, revealing, “I didn’t know what the script would be until I got to set, or it would be, like, a five-factor authentication app where I could maybe read it the night before.”

items.title: Tidal Bans AI-Generated Music
items.description: The music streaming service Tidal said Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated starting next month, a move its leader believes “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”
items.author: Corbin Bolies
paragraphs: The music streaming service Tidal said Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated starting next month, a move its leader believes “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”

The service will remove the AI tracks starting Dec. 9, making Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely. It comes nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted and ban AI songs that were associated with “fraudulent activity,” a category that includes songs impersonating established artists and efforts to “deceive listeners.”

“But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” wrote Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, in an X thread on Tuesday. “We’ll begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from our catalog, and you’ll see them completely gone by the beginning of the year.”
Andersen said that 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. The move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks, he added, and have it reject between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day.
“We encourage our peers to follow suit,” he wrote.

The move comes as competitors such as Spotify and Apple Music continue to test approaches to combat the rise of AI-generated tracks proliferating on their platforms, many of which the services have labeled some version of “slop” or “spam.” Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform, while Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an “AI Persona.”

Spotify said in a blog post last month it also removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users’ recommendations this year, which came after it removed 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. The revelation came among a number of updates regarding Spotify’s efforts to combat AI spam.

“This work isn’t finished,” Spotify added. “AI moves fast, and bad actors adapt just as fast. But as AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more. Our job is to make Spotify the place they find it.”

items.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Review: A Bloody, Boundary-Shifting Reclamation of the American Dream
items.description: “Whereas the beautiful is limited, the sublime is limitless.”
items.author: William Earl
paragraphs: “Whereas the beautiful is limited, the sublime is limitless.”

Philosopher Immanuel Kant published this in his seminal 1781 text “Critique of Pure Reason,” and it’s amazing he had such insight 245 years before he could throw an iguana in the face of a disorderly driver in “Grand Theft Auto VI.”

The game, now available from Rockstar, approached $4 billion in sales on its launch day and has already had a seismic impact on pop culture. It presents an absolutely enormous open and free world, making Leonida, a lightly fictionalized version of Florida, a playground for murder, chaos and carjacking.

The primary narrative is the love story of Jason and Lucia and their descent into the local crime scene. It’s compelling and emotional, with action-packed missions coming from the jump. Consider the first proper challenge, “Gone Fishing”: After boating around to pick up dropped packages, you must rescue your contact from the clutches of hillbillies who live on a “Tiger King”-esque compound. You can either stealthily move through the patchy foliage and quietly knock out your foes, or come in guns blazing, stealing vehicles and running folks down on the property. A brilliant score, courtesy of French electronic duo Justice, punctuates the most stressful moments, and only once you escape in a seaplane does your heart stop beating. This is all before you’re fully taught the function of the buttons on your controller.

It evokes a thrilling set-piece from a Michael Bay movie, and it’s one of over 90 main missions, ranging from death-defying ambulance hijackings and shark attacks to rogue excavator demolitions and ticking-clock armed robberies.

Not only is the scale vast, but the specifics are treated reverentially. Be it the swampy backwoods or the neon-drenched city lights, Leonida is unmistakably built around the lore of the “Florida Man.” Scores of non-playable characters swarm the neighborhoods, with unique body shapes and quips alike. The radio is filled with retro hits, original music that evokes “Miami Vice”-era swagger, and endless talk from a murderer’s row of comic minds like Janelle James, Sarah Sherman, Jason Sudeikis and “Weird Al” Yankovic.

Even the mild modifications from “GTA 5” add challenges that don’t disrupt the fun but rather urge the player to be a bit more clever. Not every car can be hot-wired instantly; some take time to create a spark with the wires, while newer models won’t budge without a fob. How needlessly violent you are influences the story tree and might lead to dire consequences for the lovebirds. Even a slightly tougher shooting system encourages patience and skill over blind mayhem.

Beyond the brilliantly staged missions, it cannot be overstated how the freedom to do anything on the colossal open map allows for astounding adventures and fun. Crime sprees aside, Jason and Lucia can work out, play basketball, putt at mini golf, shoot pool, race drones, go parachuting, shop, go hunting, fire at the shooting range and dozens of other activities. Your life is a movie, and you’re the auteur. Sure, AI can spit out a junky-looking scene from a prompt, but “GTA 6” truly democratizes a cinematic canvas.

Spend the day doing upkeep on your home and punctuate it with stabbing, à la Chantal Akerman’s masterpiece “Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles.” Fending off an outrageously large crab attack feels like a surreal, Southern-fried homage to Denis Villeneuve’s “Enemy.” The most destructive can engage in their own “Purge.” Hell, stage a sequel to Harmony Korine’s “Spring Breakers” well before Bella Thorne gets hers off the ground.

But what does this limitless gameplay add up to beyond a choose-your-own-adventure for rifle-toting louts? In the 13 years since “Grand Theft Auto 5” was released, we’ve had a cultural sea change wherein the “greed is good” ethos of the ’80s has come roaring back: Billionaires are deified, even as workers jockey for bathroom breaks; politicians advocate for eschewing societal norms and conduct in order to get ahead; and AI anxiety has made it unclear if a waning job market will ever recover.

Yet the world of “Grand Theft Auto VI” offers unique control. The American Dream seems increasingly distant, as you pull yourself up by your bootstraps and never prosper, but there’s a draw in living out your dreams in a pristine simulation of real life. As the scales get tilted, taking destiny into your hands — legal or not — becomes increasingly appealing.

Conservative commenters dinged the game for inspiring people to skip work and glorifying violence to kids. Yet the storytelling serves a purpose. The fantasy of being the king of your block is alive in “GTA 6.” Call it a societal pressure valve, but time will tell if the adventures of Jason and Lucia will inspire real-life attempts to take the power back.

items.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ to Dominate Thanksgiving Box Office as ‘Focker In-Law,’ ‘Hexed’ Join Fray
items.description: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is expected to continue feasting at the box office as Focker In-Law and Hexed join the festivities over the Thanksgiving weekend.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is expected to continue feasting at the box office as Focker In-Law and Hexed join the festivities over the Thanksgiving weekend.

After opening in first place last weekend with $119 million domestically and a global haul of $225 million, Lionsgate’s sixth film in the Hunger Games franchise is expected to continue its reign atop the box office. Playing in 4,018 North American theaters, Sunrise on the Reaping is expected to earn north of $60 million and could hit upwards of $80 million and beyond. The $150 million-budgeted film hopes to build on solid word of mouth, earning an A- CinemaScore and holding a 94 score from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes, along with a 68 from critics.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is already off to a killer start this week, notching the highest-grossing opening Monday domestically in the history of the franchise that kicked off with 2012’s Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games. Sunrise on the Reaping collected $12.8 million on Monday, topping the $12.3 million for 2013’s Catching Fire. Over the weekend, Sunrise debuted with the fifth-biggest launch in Lionsgate history, which also ranked No. 5 among 2026 domestic openings for all studios. Its $56 million domestic sum on Friday gave the new prequel film the third-best debut Friday in franchise history, behind Catching Fire and The Hunger Games.

“I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call,” Lionsgate film chief Adam Fogelson told The Hollywood Reporter in a recent conversation about his hopes to work with author Suzanne Collins on bringing the franchise back to the big screen. Joseph Zada stars in the new movie as Haymitch Abernathy, whom Woody Harrelson portrayed for the first four titles.

Disney releases animated offering Hexed in 3,725 North American theaters on Wednesday, with the studio projecting a five-day opening around $45 million. Directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand’s movie, which carries a hefty budget north of $200 million, is expected to draw females and families, with the coming weeks clear of new animated competition until Paramount’s Angry Birds 3 in a month.

The studio feels optimistic about opening an original animated property following the bows for Sony’s Goat and Pixar’s Hoppers. But there have also been recent ones to have struggled, such as DreamWorks Animation’s Forgotten Island, while Laika’s Wildwood has faced a formidable path to profitability, given its budget.

Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster lead the voice cast for Hexed, which centers on a mother and her teenage daughter grappling with the girl’s magical powers. The film holds a 66 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, with critic Angie Han writing in her review for THR that Hexed offers “more than enough to make for a pleasurably transportive trip to the theater.”

Universal Pictures revives its Meet the Parents franchise with Focker In-Law, marking the fourth feature in the series that kicked off with the original 2000 release. As the series’ first installment in 16 years, Focker In-Law launches in more than 3,350 North American locations on Wednesday, with the studio projecting around $45 million for the five-day frame. Universal split the $90 million budget with Paramount Pictures — which co-produces and handles international distribution — as the film is projected to collect an additional $30 million from 62 international territories. Given the challenges for theatrical comedies in recent years, the budget — down from the reported $100 million for the most recent franchise entry, 2010’s Little Fockers — could present a high bar for profitability.

John Hamburg, a franchise vet who worked on the scripts for all three previous features — including 2004’s Meet the Fockers and 2010’s Little Fockers — takes over in the director’s chair. He follows Jay Roach, who helmed the first two titles, and Chris Weitz, who directed Little Fockers. Meet the Parents opened to $28.6 million domestically in 2000 (en route to its $166.2 million domestic cume), with Meet the Fockers launching even bigger with $46.1 million ($279.1 million domestic cume). Little Fockers slipped a bit with its $30.8 million opening ($148.4 million domestic cume).

Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro reprise their franchise roles alongside newcomer Ariana Grande, with all three stars being central to the global marketing. Grande, who becomes a Thanksgiving mainstay after dominating the frame for the past two years with the Wicked features, plays the potential daughter-in-law to Greg Focker (Stiller) as she gets to know their family. Critics haven’t needed a lie detector test to share their honest opinions on the latest sequel that holds a challenging 28 percent critical score from Rotten Tomatoes, far below the original’s 85 score but thankfully above Little Fockers’ painful 10 rating.
In his review for THR, critic Frank Scheck wrote that Focker In-Law “feels like the nadir in a series that recycles the same tired jokes in increasingly desperate manner.”

Also hoping to whet appetites at the multiplex over the holiday frame are Angel Studios’ biographical Hershey, starring Finn Wittrock as chocolate pioneer Milton S. Hershey and Alexandra Daddario as wife Catherine. Director Mark Waters’ movie launches in 2,275 theaters, with Scheck calling it “a blandly sanitized biopic that’s as sickly sweet as the candies the company sells.”

Debuting exclusively in Imax is Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, which sees Brad Pitt reprise the titular role he originated in Sony’s 2019 hit Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. After helming the original film, Quentin Tarantino penned the script for the follow-up that David Fincher stepped in to direct.

Set to begin streaming Dec. 23, the new movie hits 550 Imax screens worldwide and focuses on Pitt’s stuntman and fixer navigating Hollywood in the late 1970s. THR chief film critic David Rooney deemed it “sexy, seductive and chaotic in mostly fun ways.”

items.title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Names Historic Season 35 Winner: See All the Scores, Who Won
items.description: [This story contains spoilers for the season finale of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]
items.author: McKinley Franklin
paragraphs: [This story contains spoilers for the season finale of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]
Season 35 of Dancing With the Stars is officially over, and the show has crowned a new winner.

The finale episode of DWTS saw couples compete in three rounds of competition as Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins and Connor Wood battled it out for a chance to win the season 35 Len Goodman mirrorball trophy.
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach were ultimately named the winner’s of DWTS season 35; his win makes him the first amputee winner of the series.

The Paralympian previously told The Hollywood Reporter it would be “very, very special” to become the first amputee winner of DWTS. “Of course, getting the opportunity to make the finale, to win the show, to get to represent the disabled community in that way and become the first amputee to win Dancing With the Stars would be very, very special, and would mean a lot to myself and hopefully to all people with disabilities and the community as a whole,” he said.
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov placed second. Maura and Mark Ballas came in fifth, with Tatyana and Jan Ravnik in fourth, and Connor and Rylee Arnold in third.

First, contestants competed in the judges’ choice round, as each judge selected a dance style for one of the contestants to perform. Second was the instant dance challenge, which tasked them to perform a number without knowing the dance style or the song until only minutes before performing it live.
The final performance was the beloved freestyle round, where all rules are out the window, leaving contestants with one final dance to wow the judges and fans.

During the judges’ choice, three couples tied for the top of the leaderboard, earning perfect scores. Those duos were Amber and Pasha; Maura and Mark; and Ezra and Daniella. Connor and Tatyana trailed closely behind, respectively scoring a 28/30 and 27/30 each.

Amber, Maura and Ezra all earned perfect scores during the instant dance round, keeping the competition neck-and-neck. Tatyana matched her first-round score with a 27/30 for her instant jive; Connor received a 25/30 for his instant cha cha.

After Tatyana and Jan performed their freestyle, a medley of “Minnie the Moocher” by Cab Calloway and “Over the Rainbow” by Judy Garland, the duo was both tearful. A piece of the professional dancer’s comments after the dance were cut out due to him saying an explicit (“She fucking killed it!” Jan reportedly said). They scored a 28/30 for their last dance of DWTS season 35.

Amber and Pasha’s freestyle was set to Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” and “Music,” a tribute to her figure skating routine performed at the 2026 Olympics. She earned a perfect score, while also dancing alongside fellow Team USA members Madison Chock and Evan Bates.

Connor and Rylee referenced Tom Holland’s iconic performance on Lip Sync Battle, set to “Singin’ in the Rain” by Gene Kelly and “Umbrella” by Rihanna. Connor even wore a recreation of Spider-Man actor’s outfit in the number equipped with fake rain on the ballroom floor, earning them a 29/30.

Maura and Mark’s final number was another high spot, earning them a 30/30 for their glamorous performance to Marilyn Monroe’s “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend,” and “The Parting Glass” and “Flowers of the Red Hill.”

Ezra and Daniella performed a touching freestyle set to “Numb” by Linkin Park. Ezra began the number without his prosthetic on, and after putting it back on, it suddenly slipped off him mid-dance. The duo recovered swiftly, though, and were joined by wheelchair dancers, and finished the dance with another prosthetic in hand, paying tribute to the amputee’s wider journey. They scored a 30/30.
Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough serve as co-hosts while Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli judge.

Also during the finale, season 34 champion Robert Irwin was on hand to announce the renewal of Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro, which will feature a cast of prospective male pro dancers who will compete for a chance to join the season 36 cast. Robert also revealed that the men will dance with fans throughout the competition, teaching them how to dance.

Alfonso and Julianne further revealed that Jackson Olson, Taylor Hanson, Tyler Cameron and all five finalists and their pros would be joining the DWTS tour in select cities. In more news, the co-hosts also announced 86 million votes had been cast in the finale alone.

For the first time, the DWTS finale aired live coast-to-coast, allowing fans in any time zone in the U.S., its territories and Canada to vote for the season 35 winner. (The show typically only airs live for the East coast, with voting taking place only during the East Coast airing of each show, leaving West Coast and Mountain time viewers unable to vote live.)

The couple with the lowest combined total of judges’ scores and viewer votes is typically eliminated at the end of each DWTS episode; the winner is determined by combining the judges’ scores and viewer votes in the finale episode.

Each viewer is allowed up to 10 votes per couple, per voting method (via ABC’s website and by text). Live voting takes place during the live airing of each show and ends shortly after the final performance.
