items.title: My Chicken Shop Breakup
items.description: Growing up, I had two ambitions: to become famous and to fall in love. At 17, I figured out the perfect way to fuse both of my dreams: an interview series called Chicken Shop Date, where I’d invite celebrities on a date with me to a local chicken shop. As it t
items.author: Amelia Dimoldenberg
paragraphs: Growing up, I had two ambitions: to become famous and to fall in love. At 17, I figured out the perfect way to fuse both of my dreams: an interview series called Chicken Shop Date, where I’d invite celebrities on a date with me to a local chicken shop. As it turns out, one of those goals was a lot easier to achieve than the other.

After the school bell rang, boys did enter the picture and it became clear that I, small and awkward Amelia, was not someone they were interested in. (The boy I shared my first kiss with denied it ever happened to a room full of people.) I developed a strong sense of sarcasm to defend myself against their disinterest and occasional cruelty. It worked: I was able to create a barrier that meant I couldn’t be hurt, but that also prevented anyone from getting through. I didn’t know it at the time, but this was the genesis of my Chicken Shop Date character.

I am now famous after spending the past decade interviewing my heroes and celebrity crushes. Billions of views and millions of subscribers later, an idea that started as a column in a youth publication has grown into quite the online sensation. I have built a show and crafted a charmingly awkward unlucky-in-love persona that makes the series uniquely its own. But I have recently started to wonder if the show’s success is tethered to why I am still single.

There’s an art to teasing a man, puncturing his ego, and reeling him in while keeping him strictly at arm’s length. I’ve always loved flirting — especially the kind where you’re a little bit mean. I am playing a game entirely on my own terms, and only a few people I’ve interviewed have seen through it. Andrew Garfield was one of them. “I don’t like games, Amelia,” he told me during one of my most viewed episodes of Chicken Shop Date, trying to dismantle my persona. “But it’s fun!” I smiled back. “It’s fun for the person pulling the strings,” he replied. “I’m cutting them.” For over a decade, those strings held me up, protecting me from revealing too much of myself. What would happen if I let them go?

I knew my perspective on Chicken Shop Date was changing around 18 months ago, when I had my first and then second panic attack ever in the space of a week. Granted, the second one was at an insanely overstimulating karaoke bar called the K-Hole, but still, I knew something was up. I had stopped drinking at the time because I was trying to pinpoint exactly why I felt so unlike myself. All of my emotions felt so much more visceral; I figured that’s what happens when you cut out a sedative. I had started seeing a therapist a few months earlier in the hope that they might provide an answer as to why I was feeling so flat, so low, so confused. The last time I felt like this, it led me to break up with a boyfriend. But now I was single, and unfortunately, I couldn’t pin this all to a man who was dragging me down.

Naturally, questions started coming up around work. I was at the helm of a job I had created for myself — I was in complete control of every aspect of it. For over ten years, I had assembled a show, a brand, an identity with such care and detail — how could it be something I wanted to free myself from? It became clear I was in a relationship more all-consuming and self-defining than any I’d be in previously. But when a relationship must come to an end, your body might tell you first, then your brain. Then you just know.
Damn it, I thought. I need to break up with Chicken Shop Date.

As the sadness hit me, a heartbroken montage of me crying in the shower, sitting at the end of my bed in a towel staring blankly at the wall, and lying on my mattress wanting it to swallow me up ensued. As with every breakup, every realization that a relationship has run its course, I felt torn. On the one hand, I knew physically, viscerally, that the sun was setting on this chapter. But I also had to understand why I felt so compelled to move on and who I would be without it.

When I started the show, part of me genuinely believed I could fall in love with someone on-camera. Yes, really — the delusions of my career ambitions grew into a delusion that I might actually find the love of my life in a chicken shop. Why wouldn’t a hot celebrity want to be with me? I wondered. I started this show when I was a teenager, so of course I’ve had crushes on guests. I have gone through every emotion a 20-something woman might experience: fear that they might not like me back, overthinking if and how I should reach out to them again, wondering if they will be at the same glamorous awards show. My mother even has a shrine to my past dates, framed photos of us laid out in her home as if they were her actual sons-in-law. There is a truth and realness to the show that has kept me at it for so long. At the same time, I know that even if it feels authentic to me, that does not make it real for everyone else.

To actually date a guest would have been transgressive and implausible in this constructed reality. Nevertheless, this belief has been what kept me going and I think kept the audience believing too. Now that the prophecy has gone unfulfilled, a new one must take shape.

It took me a while to realize how much of my identity is bound up in Chicken Shop Date. For over half my life, I have been tied to not only the concept but the persona, one I crafted at first because I thought it would make for a funnier, more unique conversation (and it did). But recently, I have seen it more as a shield, a way to hide the real essence of me in case I wasn’t interesting enough. I remember filming the first episodes of the show, thinking there was no way I could do this if I didn’t have an exaggerated identity to perform.

When it comes to performance, it’s fair to say the girl nibbling on chicken nuggets and rolling her eyes isn’t a character so far removed from myself; I’m not Andy Serkis transforming into Gollum. I can be deadpan and sarcastic, I am not afraid of awkwardness, I am witty and charming (I’m told!). Yet as the years have gone on, it feels as if this persona has been causing a block. I have had little room for the more sincere side of myself on the show, the grown-up I am now. I wanted to evolve but couldn’t see a way to shift the dynamic within the confines of the show. For it to continue in perpetuity, I would have to sever a big part of myself — the innie and the outie, as it were — and as much as I loved my date with Ben Stiller, I’d rather my life weren’t comparable to an episode of Severance.

Over the years, social media has both distilled and amplified my persona and my attention to detail when it comes to my personal brand. It’s led to a type of success that has meant I now get recognized every time I leave the house. “It’s the chicken-shop girl,” people either whisper to their friends or call at me from across the street. I have hosted the red carpet at the Oscars and played myself in the Devil Wears Prada sequel, and Sir Paul McCartney knows who I am! I am truly living out my teenage dreams, but it would be dishonest to say it hasn’t affected the way I view myself — and warped the views of some of those around me. Having “Chicken!” shouted at you in the street is both a blessing and a curse.

When you are a child who desires fame, you are really a child who yearns for connection. I thought the more famous I became, the more likely it was someone would fall in love with me. If anything, playing a decadelong role of the serial dater has made my real dating life challenging. People often meet you with a preconceived idea of who you are, their curiosity misplaced. I am so proud of my success, but it has isolated me in some ways. I work … a lot. Does that leave room for someone else to enter the picture? Perhaps not. I also earn more money than the majority of men I meet, and that has been difficult to navigate. I have yet to find a man whose ego can sit proudly next to mine, but I know it’s possible.

I now have a new ex — a relationship I am proud to say I’ve left lovingly and one I’ll cherish forever. Like any past love, Chicken Shop Date will accent and haunt my work and life as long as I live. And I’m so grateful for that. I’ve built narratives and worlds; I’ve told stories to audiences far beyond those I ever imagined. It is my love for storytelling that I will take with me in my work to come. I always thought I would find the love of my life through the show without realizing that the love of my life might have been the show itself. I have created pop-culture moments I know will live on long after I’ve eaten my last nugget. But as daunting as it can be to end a relationship that has been so good to me, I want to leave before the party is over, before I start resenting it.

I was speaking to a school friend recently who was talking about the seismic shift one can feel reaching 30. We stop performing the identity of our 20s or simply start to understand we were performing in the first place. The coping mechanisms we teach ourselves — to fit in or stand out — begin to feel out of date. I think this is what has been happening to me: I am outgrowing both the persona of my 20s and that of Chicken Shop Date. And maybe they are one and the same.

So now, a new, less greasy vision for my future is taking shape, and it feels both intimidating and liberating. Self-reflection accomplished, I am changing my ambitions from finding love and fame to realizing I do not need either of those things to complete me. I no longer want to hold so tightly on to the puppet strings or to the persona I devised for myself as a teenager. I will excavate the inner computer-science scholar, the child who thought she wanted fame but really just craved connection, and make space for her to sit next to all of my many personas entering this next decade. And if that honest pursuit fails … I could always produce a rom-com where I’ll star as myself and fall in love with the gorgeous lead actor.

items.title: Looks Like Julianne Hough Is Dating a Peloton Hunk
items.description: Here’s some fun news that you can bring to your Dancing With the Stars finale watch party tonight: Former DWTS pro and current cohost Julianne Hough is apparently dating a super hunky Peloton instructor. How amazing is that? E! News reported on Tuesday that Ho
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Here’s some fun news that you can bring to your Dancing With the Stars finale watch party tonight: Former DWTS pro and current cohost Julianne Hough is apparently dating a super hunky Peloton instructor. How amazing is that? E! News reported on Tuesday that Hough is in a relationship with Adrian Williams, who you might recognize from your at-home HIIT classes.

It’s unclear how long the two have been dating, but the signs have been there for anyone to see. On the Emmys red carpet in September, Hough alluded to being in a relationship. “I might not be single,” she told E! host Justin Sylvester. “There’s a lot to discuss off-camera.” Earlier this month, Williams posted a series of photos from a trip to Los Angeles, the last of which was from the DWTS ballroom. Then, over the weekend, Williams posted a photo of Hough holding her dog on his Instagram Story, which she in turn posted to her own Story. To do some relationship calculus, I’d guess they’ve been dating for about four months.

Hough was previously married to the hockey player Brooks Laich. After three years of marriage, they announced their separation in 2020 and finalized their divorce in 2022. In 2024, she told People that her heart was “open” but that she wasn’t “actively looking for anything.” As a result of an open heart, she’s now dating a very handsome fitness instructor who keeps up a regular newsletter, meditates, and lists photography and long drives among his hobbies. Success!

items.title: Anna Camp Has Big Ideas For A ‘True Blood’ Reboot
items.description: Anna Camp Has A Ghost Story For You
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: Anna Camp Has A Ghost Story For You

The Pitch Perfect and True Blood actor, starring in the thriller play 2:22: A Ghost Story, is soaking up the animated audience reactions — and embracing her own spooky encounters with the theater’s resident spirits.

When Anna Camp signed on to star in Danny Robins’ thriller play 2:22: A Ghost Story at the Lucille Lortel Theatre, she didn’t expect to have ghost encounters of her own. “I had one onstage the other day,” she says. “I saw, no joke, a white orb of light facing upstage [moving] from stage right to stage left, all the way to stage right in front of my face. My brain started to rationalize: ‘Did something fall from the ceiling?’ And I became very alert.”

Camp became convinced it was the ghost of the theater’s namesake, actor-producer Lucille Lortel. (“We know the Lortel is haunted by Lucille herself,” she says. “And I’ve heard the lore and the tales about it.”) In 2:22’s next scene, there’s a fire onstage, and on this particular night the flames went off early while Camp had her back to it. “I think Lucille was warning me to stay alert so that I didn’t back myself into the fire. I told everybody backstage, ‘I think she was protecting me,’” she says. “And then Richard [Abel], our house manager, was like, ‘Oh, this is the time of year where she starts to show up — when it gets to be a little chillier.’”

It’s a fitting experience for 2:22. The show follows a young couple and new parents, Sam (Finn Jones) and Jenny (Jasmine Cephas Jones), the latter of whom hears odd noises coming from their daughter’s bedroom every night at 2:22 a.m. while Sam is away on business. Jenny begins to believe that their new home is haunted, and when Sam returns, she convinces him and their two friends to stay up until 2:22 to prove that the supernatural occurrences are indeed happening. Camp plays Lauren, a booze-loving psychotherapist and college friend of Sam’s who, like Sam, is initially skeptical of Jenny’s claims.

“She’s trapped between the rational and the irrational thoughts,” says Camp. “She’s going back and forth in this conflict that she’s playing throughout the play, being torn and then on top of it, and dousing herself in alcohol to not feel things.”

The suspense and jump scares that ensue make for a collective audience experience similar to seeing horror films in a movie theater — and Camp would know, having starred in Scream 7 along with other spooky or supernatural projects like True Blood and You. “It’s just really cool to hear the audience react,” says Camp. “It’s so much fun to be scared in a group of people because somehow you feel safer.”

My first Broadway play, I was really young. Mike Nichols directed it, and I was acting onstage with Morgan Freeman and Frances McDormand. I was like, “What am I doing here?” I would be talking to him, and he’d just casually be talking about being in Glory or Driving Miss Daisy. I would have so many butterflies. He would just keep talking and talking, and then it would be time for his cue and he would just walk out onstage casually and the place would erupt in applause — right? Because it’s Morgan Freeman.
On the roles she’s drawn to now:

I’m 44 now, and there’s so much stress and pressure on a woman to look young and be young and be an ingénue — “Don’t play a mother yet until you really have to” and all that stuff. And I’m like, “Well, those are the meatier roles.” I’ve grown a lot as an actor and as a woman. So much has changed in my life that I feel more comfortable with who I am. And it’s exciting to get to come onto a stage more fully realized as an adult, without all that self-consciousness and fear, and see how that translates to being in front of an audience eight shows a week. I feel really excited to get out there, so much more than I used to, when the nerves would sort of overtake the confidence. Now, I’m like, “Oh, I’m a woman.”

It’s really nice to be able to see that my work is affecting people in a positive way, because when you’re in Los Angeles, you don’t get that fan reaction, that one-on-one time. And sometimes you’re in this bubble of, like, “Is my work reaching people? Do people really respond to it?” It’s also been really cool to see fans of Pitch Perfect coming. A girl wanted me to write “Aca-excuse me” on her Playbill because it was going to be her tattoo. I go, “So wait, this is going to be your tattoo?” And she goes, “Yes, my first one.” And I went, “Oh, my God, the pressure — do you want it big or small?” And the parents behind her go, “Small.” I went over to the wall and was like, “Nobody talk to me for a second — this has to be perfect.” But she seemed really happy.

I like to get as grounded as possible and usually light a candle. There’s this brand Kai Rose, and I absolutely love them — it smells like roses and fills up the entire space. I’m not one of those actors who can just be in their dressing room and just go to the stage. There’s a certain stool that I have a lot of emotional moments on, so I like to go out and sit on the stool for a minute, look at the lights, and say hi to Lucille, because I feel like she’s looking out for me. And I go to her portrait sometimes and just say, “You’re beautiful, you know — thank you.”

And then we’re all backstage together. So we laugh and play music, and me and Jas riff and do our makeup together and talk about girl stuff. Jasmine and I love to play Enya — this show is scary, and your heart is racing. We’re fighting for things. We’re crying. We’re screaming a lot. So we love putting on Enya — we’re like, there’s our girl. We just vibe and chill and listen to Enya. It’s literally the best thing ever.
On her post-show cocktail hour:

I have a glass of rosé that’s waiting for me in the refrigerator, so that the minute I come off stage I can have a little sip of wine. I’m a rosé girl, and I have three bars in the West Village that I kind of rotate through: Little Owl, which is so great; Buvette, which makes an amazing dirty Tito’s martini — I was there just last night with Constance Wu, because she came to see the show, so we had a little martini moment; and then Jeffrey’s Grocery, where I do my oysters and orange wine. So when friends come, I pick one of those three spots, and we all just go and talk about the show. That’s the other beautiful thing about doing a play in New York — I’m seeing people I haven’t seen in years.
On soaking up other NYC theater:

On my day off, I stay horizontal and in bed for as long as humanly possible, and then I go see a play. It’s great. I’ve been seeing lots of plays because I don’t live in New York anymore, so I’m craving theater. It’s so nice to be in the audience and have someone else perform for me, because I’m doing it every day.

I’ve seen Other Desert Cities, which is great. Downstate — blown away. So incredibly good. What a dangerous play. I’m going to see Inter Alia on my day off, and I really want to see Much Ado About Nothing, which just opened.
On manifesting a True Blood reboot:

Sarah Newlin, the character I played, is not dead. The last time we saw her, she’s hanging up in the basement of Fangtasia, and she’s curing all the vampires. At the very end, I was just begging the writers, like, “Please make me a vampire.” So I would love to play a vampire in it and obviously get the whole cast back. Come on, let’s get Alex Skarsgård back. Anna Paquin, I love her so much.

It still has such an amazing fan base. I’ve also noticed younger people, like some Gen Zers, watching it for the very first time, which has been really exciting. They’re coming up to me even at the stage door being like, “I just started watching True Blood. I love the show. Why is it gone?”

items.title: Broken Records, Epic Returns, & 8 Other Moments That Defined The 2026 NWSL Season
items.description: 10 Moments That Defined The 2026 NWSL Season
items.author: Jessa Braun
paragraphs: 10 Moments That Defined The 2026 NWSL Season
Broken records. Epic returns. One groundbreaking season.
The 2026 NWSL regular season wasted no time making history.

Just three days into the season, the league broke its single-game attendance record. By the end of opening weekend, it also set a new league-wide attendance record, with 129,202 fans showing up across eight games. There were 19 goals scored, five multi-goal games, and — in exciting, atypical soccer fashion — zero ties.

That same weekend, North Carolina Courage midfielder Ashley Sanchez scored her first professional brace, while the Portland Thorns FC kicked off with a 1-0 clean sheet against Washington Spirit — two moments that evolved into bigger milestones that ultimately became defining moments of the season.

If that was any indication, fans were in for a very good year. The last seven and a half months of professional women’s soccer across the U.S. were full of records set by individuals and teams, taking the league to a whole new competitive level. From top scorers to franchise accolades, here are the standout moments from the 2026 NWSL regular season.
Jan. 22: Trinity Rodman Became Highest-Paid NWSL Player Ever

Being a top athlete comes with a historic paycheck. Trinity Rodman became the highest-paid player in league history — and the highest-paid women’s soccer player in the world — after she signed a record contract with the Washington Spirit. The three-year deal is worth over $2 million annually, including bonuses.
“It feels amazing,” the 2024 Olympic gold medalist said after signing the contract. “I’m very happy. I’m very blessed. I think it’s a monumental and game-changing moment right now.”

The deal was made possible by the league’s new High Impact Player (HIP) rule, made effective in July, allowing teams to spend up to an additional $1 million above the salary cap to attract and retain elite talent. In October, the league and union reached a settlement to allow any player to qualify, beginning in January 2027, subject to a salary threshold.
March 28: Denver Summit Set The Single-Game Attendance Record

The league welcomed two new kids on the block this season: the Denver Summit and Boston Legacy FC — both of which immediately set new bars for NWSL attendance, starting with the Legacy on opening weekend.

Bringing soccer back to Beantown for the first time since 2017, Boston played their home opener against Gotham FC at Gillette Stadium in front of over 30,200 fans on March 14. The match broke the previous single-game attendance record of 23,000.

That record almost doubled two weeks later when Denver Summit threw their own party, drawing over 63,000 fans at their home opener at Empower Field at Mile High. They tied 0-0 with the Washington Spirit.

“Boston and Denver have had that time to build out their team, build out their front office to be in such a way they can connect with their fans, and build up that hype,” soccer writer and host of the Gal Pal Sports podcast Lesley Ryder tells Bustle.
Turns out, people loved spending their afternoons with the Summit. Denver averaged the second-highest attendance in the league this season (behind the Portland Thorns) at over 16,600 fans per game.
Just Women’s Sports writer Claire Watkins is optimistic Denver and Boston will be able to keep their momentum, due to their quality on the field.

“Even though they didn’t make the playoffs this year, I think they are playing pretty good soccer right now,” she tells Bustle. “That is the key… are they making you proud to be a fan of theirs by putting it together on the pitch?”
April 21: Columbus Got Its Own Team

The NWSL is adding two more teams to the group chat by 2028. In two years, the league will have 18 clubs in the regular-season schedule. Columbus was awarded a franchise in April, led by the Haslam Sports Group and Nationwide, set to start play in two years. They reportedly set the new expansion fee record of $205 million.
Atlanta City FC will also begin playing in 2028, paying an expansion fee of $165 million — a record at the time of their announcement in November 2025.
That’s not all: the league is opening its financial data room for prospective ownership groups as it looks toward having 20 teams.
July 15: Rose Lavelle Led The Historic Queens Classic
The inaugural Queens Classic set the second-highest NWSL attendance record in league history with 42,175 fans.

Gotham FC and Washington Spirit faced off in a rematch of the 2025 NWSL championship, with Gotham taking the 1-0 regular-season victory. Rose Lavelle scored the lone goal on her "bobblehead night,” a match that had been marketed as her and the Spirit’s Trinity Rodman going head-to-head. But the real star of the Classic? Her English Bulldog, Wilma Jean Wrinkles, who was right next to Lavelle on her bobblehead.

The game was one to be remembered. A pre-match festival was held outside Citi Field featuring a World Cup watch party, live music, and activations. The night marked the largest crowd for a women’s sporting event in New York. This previewed Gotham’s upcoming move to Etihad Park in Queens, New York, planned for 2028.
Sept. 27: Ashley Sanchez Tied The Single-Season Scoring Record

Before 2026, Ashley Sanchez of the North Carolina Courage had never scored a brace in a professional match. But she’s not one to be underestimated. This year, the midfielder recorded four braces, a hat trick, and 20 goals total — tying the NWSL's single-season scoring record.
“She is incredible,” Courage head coach Mak Lind told reporters following North Carolina’s final regular-season match on Nov. 1. “What she has been doing for us this season is outstanding.”

Sanchez earned Player of the Month honors three times during the 2026 campaign. “I think good things happen when you put a lot less pressure on yourself,” the 27-year-old said after her first career hat trick in September. “I have incredible staff and teammates behind me and I think that’s helped me improve my game and enjoy what I’m doing.”

Sanchez is the first player since 2016 to win the Golden Boot while playing for a team that didn’t make the postseason. The Courage finished ninth, missing the quarterfinals by one spot, which makes Sanchez’s feat that much more impressive.
Oct. 3, March 15: Savannah DeMelo & Savy King Returned To The Pitch

Some of the season's most notable moments didn't involve trophies. For Savannah DeMelo and Savy King, simply returning to the field was a major achievement. Racing Louisville’s Savannah DeMelo made a return on Oct. 3 after collapsing on the pitch in September 2025 due to an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia. Over a year later, the midfielder subbed into a match against Utah Royals FC during second-half stoppage time.
“After everything that happened, it’s a huge perspective shift,” she told reporters ahead of her return. “Being able to do what I love again has brought me a newfound love and appreciation for it.”

In May 2025, Angel City FC’s Savy King also collapsed on the field due to an undiagnosed congenital heart defect while playing the Utah Royals. During Angel City’s home opener on March 15, she returned to the field in the 63rd minute as a substitute for the first time since. In her 27 minutes on the pitch, she had a shot on goal and made a key slide tackle in the 80th minute, helping her team secure a 4-0 victory over the Chicago Stars. By the end of September, she’d received her first international call-up to the U-23 U.S. national team.
“It’s one of those things where you’re so grateful they’re even still on this earth,” Ryder says of King and DeMelo. “The soccer is secondary. It’s the cherry on top.”
Oct. 23: Thorns FC Earned 100 Clean Sheets

Portland Thorns FC has proven that defense helps win games just as much as the attackers. As the team with the most championships in the league, they became the first NWSL team to play 100 regular-season matches with no goals conceded. They reached the milestone with their 10th clean sheet of the season in a 1-0 home victory against North Carolina Courage on Oct. 23.
In the post-match press conference, Thorns head coach Robert Vilahamn said his team “nailed the game plan.”

He added, “It’s a team effort and the tactical pieces were there and we made it very hard for North Carolina to do something.” The win also clinched the Thorns a playoff spot, marking their league-leading 10th consecutive postseason streak.
Oct. 25: Croix Bethune Broke The Single-Season Assists Record

In a true full-circle moment, Kansas City Current's Croix Bethune broke the league's single-season assists record against her former team, the Washington Spirit. As a rookie with the Spirit in 2024, she'd tied the previous record of 10. Simply poetic.
Her record-breaking 11th assist this season went to Vanessa DiBenardo, who scored in the 17th minute against the Spirit on Oct. 25.
“You can’t focus on [trying to break the record] too much or it won’t happen,” Bethune told reporters after the match.

“The assist record is an amazing individual accomplishment for Croix,” added Current head coach Chris Armas in the same press conference. “I think it’s also a team award in many ways. She has to get the ball to someone. Someone usually has to get the ball to her. She’s been a great addition for our team this year.”
Nov. 1: Gotham FC Won The NWSL Shield For The First Time
Three titles. One year. On Nov. 1, defending NWSL champions Gotham FC secured their first NWSL Shield, an honor awarded to the team with the most regular-season wins.

“We set up a target at the beginning of the year to be consistent, to be always ready to win, to play our way,” head coach Juan Carlos Amoros said after clinching the title. “Against everything, against everyone, we were able to do that.”

The team also won the Challenge Cup in June with a 2-0 victory over Kansas City Current, crowning them champions of all NWSL titles within a year: the league championship, the Challenge Cup, and the NWSL Shield. Talk about a masterclass.
League Surpassed All-Time Season Attendance Record
Just as they started, the NWSL finished with a bang. With 2.65 million fans attending throughout the regular season, the league has made it clear its audience isn’t going anywhere.

Between averaging more than 11,000 spectators per match, surpassing 2 million attendees for the third consecutive year, and a record 39 sellouts, the NWSL has no shortage of momentum heading into the next season.
Watkins, who has seen the league through multiple phases since she started covering it in the mid-2010s, has hopes for its future.

“Now that the business side is less of a concern, how can the powers that be really focus on just the best soccer product as possible,” she says. “Are the proper things being done to make sure the sport that people are falling in love with is being supported to the best of its ability?”

items.title: Hailey Bieber Launched Her First Matte Blush & I’m Fully In Love
items.description: A girl can never have too many blushes, I tell myself as I add yet another one to my Sephora cart. It’s become a bit of a problem, actually. I was late to the blush craze, but trust me, I’ve made up for lost time.
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: A girl can never have too many blushes, I tell myself as I add yet another one to my Sephora cart. It’s become a bit of a problem, actually. I was late to the blush craze, but trust me, I’ve made up for lost time.

My blush crush started this summer, when I went to a makeup master class with a group of beauty editors and influencers and got, well, influenced. Watching everyone swipe and dab away, it dawned on me that I’d been seriously underestimating the power of a little extra color on the cheeks.

As a beauty writer, I’m particularly susceptible to peer pressure — whether it’s trying a new trend, like blush blindness, or buying the products that go along with it. So it took very little convincing for me to become obsessed with Rhode’s Pocket Blush. (Specifically, the shade Tan Line — IYKYK.) For starters, it’s wonderfully dewy and melts right into my skin. But also, I’m the type to eat sushi while wearing a face mask — Hailey Bieber could sell me on anything.

All that to say, when I heard that Rhode was launching a brand-new Pocket Plush — a matte version in two limited-edition berry shades — I figured I could make space in my collection for a couple more. (In the name of journalism, of course.) I got my hands on both to see if they could live up to the hype, and spoiler: It’s a great day to be easily influenced. Ahead, my full review.
- Best for: A windswept flush with a soft-matte finish.
- What I like: It has better staying power than the OG Pocket Blush, but is just as easy to blend.
- What I don’t like: Nothing so far! I just wish it came in a full size because I know I’ll be using it all the time.

Bieber is turning 30, and yet we’re the ones getting presents. (A woman of the people!) On Nov. 20, Rhode released a limited-edition birthday collection, with a navy color scheme to mark the occasion. There’s a snap-on lip case for your phone, cherry-vanilla Peptide Lip Boost, newly designed Eye Preps, and even a reversible windbreaker — the brand’s first foray into merch. (May the fastest checkout win.) But for my fellow blush lovers, there’s one launch in particular to watch.

Meet: Pocket Plush, Rhode’s first-ever matte blush. Like the OG dewy formula, it contains peptides and tamanu oil to help keep your skin feeling hydrated — however, it delivers a velvety, soft-matte finish. You can apply it to both your lips and cheeks for a monochromatic look.

There are two shades in the collection: Baldwin, a rosy berry, and Tucson, a rich burgundy. Both come in navy packaging that contains 0.08 oz of product (less than half the size of the Pocket Blush, for reference). Whether you prefer a little flush or a lot, the pigment is designed to be buildable and promises at least six hours of wear, according to a clinical study conducted by Rhode.

I’ll admit: I wasn’t sure how I was going to feel about a matte blush. That’s pretty much the only gap in my collection, and it’s there on purpose. But I should’ve known better than to think Rhode would make something chalky. Instead, Pocket Plush is pretty much my ideal version of matte: creamy to apply and soft-focus without looking flat.

I started with Baldwin, a raspberry shade that’s more pink than my beloved Tan Line but deeper than Teacup. I swiped it directly onto my cheeks, blended it out with my fingers, then softened the edges with a brush. Immediately, I was surprised by how buttery it felt going on — and even more so by how well it melted into my skin. It left behind a velvety finish without tackiness, blurring my pores while also letting a little glow peek through.

After one layer, you better believe I was far from done. It already gave me a perfectly pretty watercolor finish, but I was trying to emulate Bieber’s look on that French TV show with the good lighting (yes, she was wearing Baldwin). Maybe I got a little carried away — I was just excited, OK? But three layers later, I can confirm: the color built beautifully, didn’t look streaky, and still felt *extremely* lightweight.

Sufficiently rosy, I decided to turn my attention to Tucson — the deeper, bruised-berry shade that looked much more intimidating to me in the packaging. Once I blended it out, though, I ended up really digging the vibe. Where Baldwin gave me that fresh-from-Pilates flush, Tucson looked more like I’d spent the afternoon skiing in Aspen. It’s a little redder, a little more windburned, and very just-came-in-from-the-cold. (With a frosty eyelid, it’s basically my dream winter makeup.) To play up that effect, I liked swiping some blush across the tip of my nose — and the smaller applicator actually came in handy for keeping the color exactly where I wanted it.

The finish caught my attention, and the shades made me stick around — but what really sets Pocket Plush apart is its staying power. As much as I love the original Pocket Blush, Tan Line usually needs a touch-up a couple of hours after I put it on. This one, however, seemed to set into my skin almost like a stain. Once it’s on, it’s really on — even without layering a powder blush on top to set it in place. Around the six-hour mark, the color had faded, but there was still rosiness around my cheeks (beyond the usual). What’s more, when I reapplied it over my setting powder at the end of the day, the formula was just as creamy and easy to blend as before — read: no patchiness.

I wish I could deinfluence you (and myself), but Mrs. Biebs has done it again: Pocket Plush is well worth the hype. For starters, it lasts longer than the original Pocket Blush, which is reason enough to give it a try even if you already have a few shades in your makeup bag. Plus, Baldwin and Tucson are different enough from the existing shade lineup to justify another purchase, IMO. And if you’ve been holding off on trying Rhode’s blush because you prefer something more blurring than dewy? Well, you’re in luck.

My only complaint? I wish it came in a full size. Sure, the smaller applicator makes it easier to control where the color goes, but I have a feeling I’ll be blowing through these minis. Oh, and while we’re at it, can we please make the formula permanent and get a few more shades? Maybe I’m being greedy, considering the state of my blush collection, but I’ll happily buy every single one.

items.title: “Dusty Denim,” Black Cherry, & More Trends Giving Your Toes A Winter Glow-Up
items.description: It goes without saying that, come winter, pedicures aren’t exactly at the top of the priority list. Your toes are tucked into boots, buried under a couple layers of socks, and unlikely to see the light of day until spring. So why bother getting one?
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: It goes without saying that, come winter, pedicures aren’t exactly at the top of the priority list. Your toes are tucked into boots, buried under a couple layers of socks, and unlikely to see the light of day until spring. So why bother getting one?

Aside from the fact that your feet could use a little extra TLC this time of year, “there's just something about having a fresh pedicure, even when nobody else sees it,” says nail expert and Sally Beauty ambassador Juli Russell. In other words, the stakes are low — meaning you can get away with just about anything. “Keep your manicure classic and let your toes have a little more fun,” Russell says. “A pedicure is such a fun place to experiment with colors you might not normally wear.”

Maybe you’re test-driving new nail shades for summer — try cobalt blue or tomato red, both of which happen to pop against a dark winter wardrobe. Or, if you’ve been tempted by this year’s maximalist manicure trends, bedazzled designs are making their way to your toes. Partial to pastels? Lavender, baby blue, and mint are all fair game this season — with a frosty update, of course. And if you’re looking for a new neutral, consider yogurt white or mocha brown.
Whatever your vibe (or your stance on open-toed shoes in cold weather), it’s never a bad idea to treat yourself. Ahead, the biggest winter 2027 pedicure trends to try, according to the experts.
Much like your favorite pair of jeans, a denim blue pedicure never really goes out of style — but to make it feel especially wintry, opt for a shade with slightly smoky undertones.

“Denim blue brings a cool, muted feel that looks modern and understated,” says Sandra Wei, nail artist and founder of Peach Bling. “While people naturally gravitate toward warmer colors during the colder months, it offers a refreshing alternative.”
If you’re partial to a white pedicure (same), there’s no need to wait until summer. “Instead of bright white, softer milky finishes are becoming popular,” says nail educator Vikki Swan.

Celebrity nail artist Elle Gerstein co-signs the milky takeover, particularly “yogurt white.” Her polish picks? Essie’s sheer white Waltz layered over Ballet Slippers, a pale pink. “It looks clean and gives a nice contrast to dark winter clothes,” she says.

For those already planning their New Year’s Eve pedicure, meet purple gunmetal. Less overtly festive than champagne but with plenty of shimmer and shine, it’s a shade you’ll want to wear well into January.

To get the look, layer silver chrome over a deep purple polish or reach for a multidimensional metallic like Sally Hansen’s Catch My Shift — a favorite of Russell. “The purple hue gives the industrial shade a sophisticated, feminine edge,” she says. “I especially love shades like this on toes because you get that little flash of unexpected color when the light hits.”

“Brown has been growing for a few seasons,” says nail artist and educator Viktoriia Voloshyna — but a rich, chocolatey mocha feels particularly “warm and expensive” this time of year. If black or burgundy is your go-to winter pedicure shade, consider this another contender for the season’s deep neutral. Just be sure to finish it off with an ultra-glossy top coat to really bring out the depth, according to Wei.

Even if you’re sticking to a darker color palette for your manicures this winter, you can have a little fun with pastels on your toes. “You can play with lighter, fresher colors because they’re your own little surprise under your boots,” says Voloshyna.

To make shades like baby blue, smoky lavender, and pale mint feel less springy, celebrity nail artist and ENailCouture founder Max Estrada likes to lean into their frostier vibes. “When you add shimmering finishes, delicate crystals, or platinum-colored detailing, they suddenly feel like a winter palace,” he says.

On the vampier end of the spectrum, Voloshyna expects black cherry to take off this season. “It looks rich on winter skin tones and feels more interesting than a classic red,” she says. Compared to cherry on its own, the purple-leaning shade is a great alternative for those who want something that feels more wintry without being holiday-specific. It’s also a particularly pretty color for a micro French tip — another trend Voloshyna predicts will be big.

With toe rings back in the mix, it only feels right to match your pedicure to your jewelry. “I think we’re moving beyond the soft glazed finishes and into something a little more bold, almost like your toes have been dipped in molten metal,” says Russell, whose go-to “liquid silver” polish is Nails.INC’s Mirror Chrome Nail Polish in Silver Served.

For a fun contrast, you can also add some dainty nail art on top, like tiny polka dots or thin stripes. “There’s something so unexpected about mixing softer, feminine details with a futuristic look,” Russell says. “It’s the perfect balance of playful and edgy.”

Tomatoes may be out of season at your local farmer’s market, but as a source of nail inspiration, they’re surprisingly ripe. “We’re so used to retiring our bright colors once fall rolls around, but I think that seasonal rule is becoming less relevant, especially for a pedicure,” says Russell. Look for a vivid red with a slightly orange undertone, like China Glaze’s Flame-Boyant Nail Lacquer — it not only looks fresh, but it also “warms up the skin,” according to Russell.

Another color to brighten up your winter pedicure rotation? Cobalt, which Russell calls “a power blue.” Though it typically calls to mind Mediterranean summers and glistening oceans, “there’s something so striking about a saturated blue against winter’s more muted wardrobe,” she says.

Voloshyna is also a fan of electric cobalt for the colder months, nothing that it “gives toes personality without being too loud.” In other words, think of it as the happy medium between neon and navy.

For a matchy-matchy moment between your hands and feet, Estrada suggests going all in on bedazzled nail art. He sees the big toenail as “a compact canvas for miniature jewelry-inspired artwork,” whether that means a cluster of tiny crystals, a few pearls, or gemstones paired with metallic detailing. Even a single rhinestone accent can dress up an otherwise plain pedicure.

If you are going the maximalist route, though, one thing to keep in mind: You’ll want to stick to flatter embellishments that won’t press against your winter boots, Estrada adds. Save the three-dimensional designs for nights when you’re breaking out your open-toed heels.

When you think of green this time of year, your mind probably goes straight to Christmas trees — but deep emerald is a different story. “It’s a more refined alternative to brighter holiday greens, with deeper undertones that make it feel elegant rather than seasonal,” says Wei.
Go for a cat-eye polish, and the vibe becomes “the velvet upholstery of an extravagant European palace,” as Estrada puts it. In other words, less Christmassy, more opulent.

items.title: The First Super Full Moon Of 2026 Is Here — & It's Time To Create The Life You Want
items.description: The Beaver Super Full Moon In Gemini Is Here — & It’s Time To Create The Life You Want
items.author: Lisa Stardust
paragraphs: The Beaver Super Full Moon In Gemini Is Here — & It’s Time To Create The Life You Want

The Full Moon focuses on our need to see the big picture after analyzing the facts. The Sun in Sagittarius is lofty, and the Moon in Gemini is concise. This pairing is known as “sister signs” because they're opposites but share similarities. Sagittarius and Gemini both have a thirst for knowledge and are inquisitive. They are also buoyant and optimistic by nature, which gives us the stamina to stay positive. They feed off each other — Sagittarius is the philosopher, and Gemini is the mind. They need each other to thrive — a sentiment that feels eerily true during this lunation.

Pallas in Aries fuels the Full Moon. For those who don't know, Pallas is one of the four major asteroids between Mars and Jupiter, known for its strategic, organized approach to problem-solving. Pallas gives us the common sense to apply logic with intuition; we can see patterns and contemplate how to resolve matters because of the themes that keep recurring. Pallas is wise and sharp-witted, so when it's in Aries, it isn't docile but a warrior that comes to win. We have the sense to work through dilemmas and issues with this asteroid, so use it as a tool to reconcile and stay the course toward achieving goals.

Having necessary conversations with those we are connected to will strengthen our feelings. Don't hide from speaking from the heart; in fact, it helps us find peace with ourselves and the relationship after we've said everything that needs to be said. If we aren’t in the mood to communicate, consider journaling out emotions. Doing so helps to recenter and recalibrate our thoughts through reflection. This is a spiritual moment to let go of anything troubling, so try to release it to honor the Moon. Starting fresh might not happen overnight, but we are on our way to rebuilding relationships that need improvement and attention after Mercury and Venus retrograde — now is the perfect opportunity to start again, or even forge a different path in a better direction that leads to happiness.

items.title: The house my father built was resilient and rickety, like him
items.description: I watched the excavator eat into my childhood home one bright fall. Its steely fangs bit into the cedar my father had nailed in more than four decades earlier. Windows burst inward. A slanted roof buckled. One wall heaved before folding into another, disappear
items.author: Henrick Karoliszyn
paragraphs: I watched the excavator eat into my childhood home one bright fall. Its steely fangs bit into the cedar my father had nailed in more than four decades earlier. Windows burst inward. A slanted roof buckled. One wall heaved before folding into another, disappearing in plumes of sawdust, glass and sheetrock.

I expected grief. I awaited a distinctive pain that comes only from watching the place that held your formative memories disappear into a pile of timber and insulation. But instead, I felt relief. Watching the structure come down meant seeing the building that organised my inner life begin to fade.

My father called the house a refugee. He meant it as a joke, though not entirely. Like him, it appeared foreign in a town where families had lived for generations. Built on pilings above the marshes of Broad Channel, a narrow island in Jamaica Bay on the edge of New York City, it looked as though it landed there by chance.
He built it in the early 1980s after spotting a burned-out lot on his way to Rockaway Beach. Where others saw a charred garage and overgrown, wheat-coloured grass, he saw possibility.
Soon, he recruited fellow eastern European immigrants and paid them in cash, six-packs of Coors Extra Gold and Marlboros. Together, they built a three-storey house with a slanted roof.

Nothing was quite straight. Tiles never lined up. Rain always found a way inside. During winter, without central heating, rooms warmed only with space heaters while elsewhere you could see your breath. The house squealed in high winds and shivered through nor’easters.
We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings
The birdhouse-like structure was never beautiful, but it was well-constructed and refused to surrender to its surrounding elements. Whenever a big storm hit, it proved its strength.
My father fit this same resilient archetype.

He’d spent his earliest years moving through refugee camps in postwar Germany after his family fled what is now western Ukraine. His six brothers and sisters moved through seven refugee camps in five years. They slept in divided classrooms as ‘displaced persons’. My father grew used to hunger while his parents struggled to survive. My grandmother, Kunegunda, would smuggle her silverware into each camp while my grandfather, Ignacy, would cradle his vodka-bootlegging gear as a moveable business. They both held on to what little they could, convinced they might have to leave again tomorrow.

The United States promised a stability my father’s family had never known. Yet he never trusted this belief. Ever since arriving in the US, he relied on chaos over peace, endurance instead of comfort. The house he built reflected this mindset.

During one nor’ easter in the early 1990s, bay water flooded the first floor of the house while wailing winds rattled the windows so violently I thought they would implode. We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings. Long after the storm passed, I lay awake listening to the building judder in the darkness.
Looking back, the house came with two competing realities: it showed me wonder while teaching me to expect instability.

I remember the seasons most. In summer, the home became a treehouse hovering over the lapping water. My sister and I fed swans, netted blue crabs, and learned to windsurf. In winter, we laced on skates and crossed the frozen channel to the nearby Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge where we spotted greater snow geese with our golden retriever, Blondie, slipping and sliding his way along the ice.

When my sister and I returned from our winter adventures, my mother made us hot chocolate while my father poured himself a vodka. My mom drank wine and played Simon and Garfunkel’s live concert from Central Park on the tape deck as we sat thawing by the fireplace.
The place felt alive and I loved it severely. It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry
‘This is Xanadu,’ my father liked to say. On the rickety, water-warped dock overlooking the bay, he would insist: ‘You can travel anywhere from here.’
The entire place felt alive and I loved it severely.
It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry.

Years later, the writer Andrew Solomon put words to what I felt. ‘Nirvana occurs when you not only look forward to rapture, but also gaze back into the times of anguish and find in them the seeds of your joy,’ he wrote in Far from the Tree: Parents, Children and the Search for Identity (2012). ‘You may not have felt that happiness at the time, but in retrospect it is incontrovertible.’

My mother tried to make the house feel steadier than it was. She’d grown up in Montreal, had studied art, travelled widely, and met my father by chance in Mexico while sailing from Portugal. She filled the crooked rooms with colour, music and food from places my father only imagined visiting. She introduced me to Nina Simone, French, and Campari. She rolled sushi on the kitchen counter, and painted the walls in vivid shades while my father disappeared with his brother to hunt in Connecticut. Whenever he embraced disorder, she responded with a cool serenity.

On Friday nights, after I started university, I would take the A-train from Manhattan to see my father. We’d sit by the fireplace drinking vodka while the cherry wood snapped over old newspaper in the fire. A cigarillo rested between his fingers, filling the room with its sweet and bitter scent.
One winter evening, he stared into the flames longer than usual.
‘My father wanted to get rid of me,’ he said.

A story followed about him being sick on a train in Germany while transferring camps. His father thought an unhealthy child would end their chances of emigrating, but his mother saved him from being thrown off the train. It was the closest I ever saw him to crying.
Compared with his childhood, mine was easy. But kids don’t compare their lives with history they didn’t live through. They compare it with their homes.

My family’s breaking point came during that first year of college. My mother had been diagnosed with breast cancer. On Christmas Eve, an argument erupted that ended with a shattered glass table. Pierogies slid across the floor. Wine-hued borscht bled into the carpet. Before midnight, my mother packed her things and left.
I knelt on the floor gathering shards of glass while my father sat near the fire, a cigarillo glowing between his fingers.
Without looking at me, he said: ‘Your mother wanted to throw you in the garbage when you were born.’
The words felt pent up and and arrived like a gut punch.

Pain like this can change form but often carries import for years. Psychologists now recognise that trauma can even extend beyond a single lifetime. This transmission occurs through emotional patterns and parenting styles. It can happen in the way a man treats his home and those who reside within it. It can transpire in how he transfers pain to his own child.
I didn’t recognise I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house

Looking back, I’m not sure if he was trying to wound me as much as connect. The rejection he felt as a child had become part of a dialogue through which he was forced to understand love, disappointment and family. He handed me a pain that voyaged across generations. It journeyed through wars, triumphs and tragedies until it landed near a shattered dinner table in Queens that Christmas Eve.

I visited, I awaited the worst, even when nothing happened. I mistook frenzied caution for astute awareness. I thought staying alert could prevent the next disaster. Over time, such experiences can produce what psychologists call hypervigilance, a heightened sensitivity to threat. The neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett has described the brain as a prediction organ, continually using past experiences to anticipate what will come next. Environments play a central role. At home, I was always on the lookout for the next calamity or volatile indiscretion. This habit would follow me for years after leaving Broad Channel. I expected relationships to fracture, success to dissolve, good fortune to reverse. Moments of happiness often carried a wary mistrust. I assumed this was a clear view of the world. What I didn’t recognise was I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house.

Wedged between Howard Beach and the Rockaways, Broad Channel existed in a perpetual negotiation with its surrounding waters that acted as both a threat and a neighbour. Every storm seemed capable of redrawing the map; every stunning sunset promised a celebration for the eyes.

When Hurricane Sandy tore through the island in 2012, things changed. Five feet of saltwater poured into my father’s house. The dock splintered. Furniture floated before setting into a thick grey sludge. I drove to the island first as a journalist covering the storm and then as a son trying to salvage what remained, carrying waterlogged boxes to the curb, and rescuing family photos.

The house had survived again but there was a shift. Around the same time, my father’s health began to fail. A quintuple bypass became stents that turned to medications he resisted taking. Slowly, a frailer version of the man who’d once built an impossible house with his own hands would greet me when I visited.
The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was

Buckets appeared beneath new leaks, instead of caulking. Shingles went unreplaced. Whenever I did work on the house, I would come back to see more leaks and more lost shingles to replace. Both the house and the man seemed engaged in a battle with time and its environmental pressures. Both refusing to surrender, and each losing more ground each day.

My father died of heart failure in late 2023. The house sat empty through a lengthy probate while vandals stripped the home of copper wiring, smashing windows and looting what they could. After years of storm damage, the city deemed it unsafe and ordered an emergency demolition.
Two years later, the house still stood, hovering defiantly over the bay even as it was getting torn down.

I gripped a cigarillo like the ones my father smoked. While the house broke off in pieces, I saw Blondie barking at the snow geese. My mother laughing at the bright yellow she painted the kitchen. My sister and I balling bagel dough to feed swans. My father shirtless telling stories of Germany from his water-logged Xanadu.

By late afternoon, there was nothing left of the structure except industrial trash heaps full of memories. The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was. The marsh had grown peaceful. Without the house, Jamaica Bay seemed larger, as if the horizon zoomed in.

I waited for the familiar tightness in the chest, the racing of the mind. I lit the cigarillo. The tide was about to rise again across the marsh. Planes climbed into the chalky blue sky from JFK. I paused for heartache but something else came. I rolled my shoulders, exhaled a cloud of smoke, and felt an unexpected release.
As the sun hovered, for the first time I could remember, I wasn’t bracing for the next storm.
