items.title: 100 граммов мяса в неделю и горсть орехов в день: ученые впервые за шесть лет обновили рекомендации по здоровому питанию
items.description: Международная комиссия EAT–Lancet, объединившая более 70 ученых с шести континентов, впервые за шесть лет пересмотрела знаменитую «планетарную диету». Диета получила свое название потому, что решает сразу две задачи: помогать людям сохранять здоровье и сокраща
items.author: Ксения Зернова
paragraphs: Международная комиссия EAT–Lancet, объединившая более 70 ученых с шести континентов, впервые за шесть лет пересмотрела знаменитую «планетарную диету». Диета получила свое название потому, что решает сразу две задачи: помогать людям сохранять здоровье и сокращает нагрузку на планету.

Исследователи пересмотрели данные о связи питания со здоровьем, уточнили рекомендуемое количество разных продуктов и оценили, как изменение рациона может повлиять на окружающую среду. Мы изучили доклад комиссии и разобрали, что теперь рекомендуют есть.
Большую часть меню должна составлять растительная пища. Комиссия предлагает ежедневно съедать около 300 г овощей и 200 г фруктов. Вместе это примерно 500 г — больше пяти порций в день.

В рационе также должны быть цельнозерновые продукты: овсянка, гречка, бурый рис, цельнозерновой хлеб. Их рекомендуемое количество — около 210 г в день. В таких продуктах сохраняются оболочка зерна и зародыш, в которых содержатся клетчатка, витамины и минералы.
Еще несколько групп продуктов, которые комиссия рекомендует регулярно включать в ежедневное меню:
Ориентировочно половину тарелки должны занимать овощи и фрукты. Остальную часть можно распределить между цельными злаками, бобовыми и другими источниками белка.

Планетарная диета допускает употребление продуктов животного происхождения. В нее входят рыба, птица, яйца и молочные продукты. Однако красного мяса — говядины, свинины и баранины — рекомендуется есть значительно меньше.

Среднее рекомендуемое количество красного мяса составляет всего 15 г в день. Если пересчитать на неделю, получится около 100 г — примерно одна небольшая порция. Такой ориентир связан с данными о рисках для здоровья при частом употреблении красного и особенно переработанного мяса.
Для остальных продуктов комиссия предлагает следующие количества:

Разнообразие источников белка поможет не выстраивать свой рацион вокруг одного продукта. К примеру, в течение недели можно чередовать блюда из чечевицы и фасоли, рыбу, птицу, яйца и молочные продукты, а если уж очень хочется поесть говядины или свинины, оставить их на один прием пищи.

Жиры нужны нашему организму: они участвуют в работе клеток, помогают усваивать некоторые витамины и служат источником энергии. Вопрос в том, какие именно жиры преобладают в вашем рационе. Комиссия предлагает получать большую часть жиров из растительных масел, богатых ненасыщенными жирными кислотами. К ним относятся оливковое, рапсовое и подсолнечное масла. Их рекомендуемое количество — около 40 г в день.

Сливочное масло, сало, животный жир, а также пальмовое и кокосовое масла стоит употреблять в меньших количествах. В рекомендуемом рационе на них приходится всего около 5–6 г в день. В этих продуктах больше насыщенных жирных кислот, избыток которых связан с повышением уровня «плохого» холестерина — одного из факторов риска сердечно-сосудистых заболеваний.
Есть рекомендации и для сахара и соли:

Сладости и продукты с большим количеством соли не стоит делать основой своего повседневного меню. Кроме того, комиссия также учитывает степень обработки пищи: предпочтение стоит отдавать цельным и минимально обработанным продуктам.

Все количества продуктов рассчитаны для условного взрослого рациона примерно на 2400 ккал в день. Ученые приводят и возможные диапазоны: например, овощей можно съедать от 200 до 600 г, фруктов — от 100 до 300 г, а бобовых — от 0 до 150 г. Конкретное количество зависит от энергетических потребностей, возраста, физической активности и пищевых предпочтений.

Отдельно исследователи учитывали, что одни и те же принципы питания можно реализовать с помощью разных продуктов. В одной стране основой рациона могут быть чечевица и другие бобовые, в другой — цельные злаки, местные овощи и рыба. Отказываться от пищевых традиций ради следования предложенному меню не нужно.

Комиссия изучила не только то, что происходит с организмом человека, но и то, какой след в экологии оставляет производство тех или иных продуктов. Производство продуктов питания и содержание животных требуют значительных земельных и водных ресурсов, а также приводят к выбросу парниковых газов. Разные пищевые продукты создают разную нагрузку на окружающую среду.

Состав самой диеты комиссия определяла на основе данных о влиянии питания на здоровье. Экологические последствия оценивали отдельно — с помощью моделей, которые показывают, как изменение рациона и производства продуктов может повлиять на состояние планеты.

В одном из сценариев ученые объединили три изменения: переход к планетарной диете, более рациональное сельское хозяйство и сокращение пищевых потерь и отходов вдвое. По расчетам комиссии, такой комплекс мер потенциально мог бы предотвращать около 15 млн преждевременных смертей ежегодно.
Как выйти из бесконечного потока плохих новостей и научить алгоритмы показывать больше искусства, природы и вдохновляющих историй
Низкоуглеводные диеты, интервальное голодание и подсчет калорий: какие стратегии действительно помогают снизить вес и сохранить мышцы

items.title: Trump Shouts About Corrupt Huang Intervention From the Rooftops
items.description: President Trump personally strong-armed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO.
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: President Trump personally strong-armed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO.

This seems like the kind of thing we’d learn days after the fact, from some bombshell report featuring half a dozen anonymous sources. After all, the case against Huang was pretty strong. He resigned less than two weeks ago after it was reported that he was having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence had identified as a Chinese spy. Since then, he’d also been accused of having extramarital affairs with at least one subordinate executive at his company, and of engaging in a wide variety of abusive behavior in the workplace. Oh, and the American people just signaled quite clearly that they don’t love what Silicon Valley is up to these days:

But the source for this wild story about the president’s intervention is actually Trump himself. He’s gone to absurd lengths to make sure everyone knows that he was personally involved in getting his pal reinstated.

Trump began publicly reveling in this almost immediately. On Monday morning, just moments after the news broke that Huang was back at Nvidia, Trump took to Truth Social to praise the company’s board for making the “correct and proper decision.” He also shrugged off concerns about Huang’s involvement with Chinese spy, saying, “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security”:
Less than an hour later, Trump posted a second, more succinct note of congratuations:

Then Trump called in to CNBC to take credit for this “absolutely GREAT decision.” In a 50-minute interview, Trump revealed that he contacted Nvidia’s board directly and urged them to bring back Huang.
“I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way, and I convinced them,” Trump said. “I made the deal.”
Trump went on to say he “felt very strongly that he should come back” because “we have to protect our geniuses, and he’s clearly a genius.”

As for whether Huang could face criminal liability for his relationship with the alleged spy, Trump said he’d been “exonerated.” He explained that “a very thorough investigation” by his administration concluded that Huang “did nothing wrong,” aside from having “bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents.”

For those who prefer their presidential bragging administered via meme, Trump then posted this image, which manages to simultanously belittle concerns about Chinese spying, inappropriate workplace relationships, and his own near-assassination:
Huang’s reinstatement was quickly denounced by both Democratic and Republican lawmakers. So why was Trump eager to shout about his involvement from the rooftops?

There are multiple possible explanations. Trump and Huang have forged a close personal and professional relationship over the past two years (it probably didn’t hurt that the CEO donated $25 million for Trump’s White House ballroom). Trump also owns Nvidia stock, and probably profited from the surge in the company’s shares on Monday — though as the New York Times reported, we don’t know by how much:

At the end of last year, Mr. Trump owned at least $12 million worth of Nvidia shares, according to his financial disclosure report, and his brokerage accounts have continued to buy and sell Nvidia shares as recently as September.

It is impossible to determine the current size of President Trump’s position in Nvidia, or any company, because there is a lag between when trades occur and when they must be disclosed under federal law.
During his CNBC interview, Trump seemed excited to see another powerful man succeeding despite his illicit affairs:
Trump explained that the midterm elections left him little choice but to pressure Nvidia into reinstating Huang.
“I’m doing it for the country,” he said. “After the election, I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election. And I wasn’t on the ballot, but it was still a bad election.”

Maybe the election was the primary motivating factor — but not because our benevolent leader wanted to save us from the consequences of our poor choices three weeks ago. Trump’s about to lose a lot of power, and nothing says “I’m still in charge here” like proudly shouting out your corruption.

items.title: Vance Wants Credit for Reinstating Huang, Too
items.description: Remember J.D. Vance? The vice-president was once President Trump’s would-be successor, at least until the chances of that dropped precipitously this year after American voters wholesale rejected Trump and the GOP, and Vance tried to blame it all on Trump’s fav
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: Remember J.D. Vance? The vice-president was once President Trump’s would-be successor, at least until the chances of that dropped precipitously this year after American voters wholesale rejected Trump and the GOP, and Vance tried to blame it all on Trump’s favorite war. That hasn’t gone over well for him. A year ago, the prediction markets rated Vance’s odds of being the 2028 Republican presidential nominee at better than 50 percent. Now it’s down to 30 percent, and Trump is clearly entertaining the idea that Secretary of State Marco Rubio would make a better standard-bearer.

Regardless, J.D. Vance is still trying to get everyone to remember J.D. Vance. There are reports about how he’s humbled but resolved to win back everyone’s good favor. He’s doing rhetorical gymnastics to back away from his own comments criticizing Trump’s Iran war. He even inserted himself into one of last week’s terrible AI-generated Grand Theft Auto political memes.

This morning, Nvidia shockingly (or not shockingly at all, depending on how cynical you are) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO following a pressure campaign from Trump and Huang’s Silicon Valley buddies. It’s blot-out-the-sun tech, business, and politics news. Nvidia’s stock price is surging. Elon Musk is psyched. And we know Trump was instrumental in this because he’s going on and on about it, talking about how he convinced Nvidia’s board to reverse course, and how this was the best thing for America, and posting stuff like this:

A lot of people are thrilled, including those who hero-worship Huang, and/or back American AI dominance, and/or don’t care about wealth-creator misconduct, and/or love red-bra theft, and/or think Trump is just the best. So it may come as no surprise that by midday in the news cycle, we had suddenly learned that J.D. Vance helped too!
Reports Semafor’s Shelby Talcott:

VP JD Vance was deeply involved in the process to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia. He and POTUS were “personally engaged” over the weekend to resolve the situation, a source familiar tells me — Vance used his relationships in Silicon Valley + business community to help move the Nvidia board along. Vance and Trump believe that Huang is an effective counterbalance against the incredible and increasing power of OpenAI and Anthropic, as the administration seeks to diversify model providers and support open source models.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. … In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley.
Take it from sources familiar with how integral and important J.D. Vance still is: J.D. Vance is still integral and important. Take that, Rubio!
This post has been updated with more information about how integral and important Vance is.

items.title: Trump’s Huang Games Show the Midterms Meant Nothing to Him
items.description: Whatever else they meant, the 2026 midterm elections were a direct and unmistakable signal to Donald Trump that he needed to change his priorities, his policies, and most of all, his ways. We know this from almost too many sources to count. Midterms are always
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Whatever else they meant, the 2026 midterm elections were a direct and unmistakable signal to Donald Trump that he needed to change his priorities, his policies, and most of all, his ways. We know this from almost too many sources to count. Midterms are always principally referenda on the president currently occupying the White House. It’s the only way Americans can register a demand for a course correction for the ship of state, particularly when the captain ignores or denies other signs of discontent. Moreover, Trump did everything within his power to personalize the election, imposing his will and his brand on the Republican Party constantly, and even personally insisting that voters imagine his own name was on the ballot. In addition, every bit of evidence we have about why the GOP suffered such a debacle on November 3 indicates that a lot of 2024 Trump voters felt he broke repeated promises to lower living costs, avoid wars, and limit mass deportations to violent criminals, while also defying popular concerns about AI and data centers in order to lead cheers for both.
So how has the 47th president, so often described as a “populist” with an uncanny eye and ear for what Americans want, responded to this direct rebuke? The term that comes to mind is “with contempt.”

There has been no course correction at all. Trump’s major moves since being slapped around by the midterm electorate have been to place the living symbol of MAGA extremism and the father of indiscriminate mass deportations and ICE violence, Stephen Miller, in charge of the White House; to double down on the Iran war and defend Pete Hegseth; and to illustrate his continuing indifference to domestic tranquility by consorting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in a manner that was both grandiloquent and obsequious.

And now, the president has capped off midterm election month by personally intervening to protect preeminent tech baron Jensen Huang for the consequences of his own terrible behavior. That this behavior might have included compromising U.S. national security has not given Trump a moment’s pause. Indeed, in the bizarre assassination-survival meme he posted on Truth Social today, he both proclaimed and at the same time dismissed as insignificant the idea than Huang was just another Epstein-era horndog whose indiscretions were nothing as compared to his great contributions to the NASDAQ.

You don’t have to attribute great political skill to Trump’s advisers to imagine that this latest power move must have horrified them. Of all the people on the planet for Trump to have conspicuously embraced in the wake of the midterms, he has chosen Miller, Hegseth, Xi, Putin, and Huang. Each maneuver seems calculated to insult the voters who repudiated him so recently, along with the newly empowered Democrats and the duly chastened Republicans, who must wonder if Trump is determined to sink their odds in 2028 as well. Has the president who is so emboldened to lecture the board of Nvidia on its leadership lifted a finger to help make people’s lives more affordable, head off a possible government shutdown on December 11, or to address the many challenges he will face in dealing with a Democratic Congress in the remaining two years of his tenure in office? If so, it’s hardly apparent, and Trump’s conduct since November 3 has not rewarded any hopes that he was paying attention.

items.title: Jensen Huang Returns With a Huge Target on His Back
items.description: On November 12, Nvidia’s board of directors announced that founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who had admitted to an affair with an outside executive who is also an Nvidia customer and possible Chinese intelligence asset, would resign, “effective immediately.” Elev
items.author: John Herrman
paragraphs: On November 12, Nvidia’s board of directors announced that founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who had admitted to an affair with an outside executive who is also an Nvidia customer and possible Chinese intelligence asset, would resign, “effective immediately.” Eleven days later, on the Monday after a deep late-week market sell-off, the board shared more news. Jensen is back, baby! Per Nvidia’s statement:

The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

Some industry figures had rallied around Huang in recent days, but the justifications for his resignation had been obvious. Huang had admitted to his affair with Alice Huang, the outside executive. Additional reporting had suggested a pattern, including an affair with an Nvidia executive and direct report as well as another relationship with an Nvidia employee. Combined with a brutal management style and news of an SEC investigation into the company’s accounting practices, it was easy to make an argument that keeping Jensen Huang around was an intolerable risk.

But his reinstatement makes clear that there are larger forces at play. The initial leaks about Alice Huang, which first appeared in the New York Times, concerned intelligence assessments that were overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, alongside Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, had advocated for stronger export controls on Nvidia chips. That put them at odds with Jensen Huang, who is eager to sell to Chinese firms, as well as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and the president himself, who had called for Huang’s return yesterday:

Donald Trump loves to take credit for things, and we don’t have a full account of the board’s thinking here. But it’s worth spelling out plainly what the president is claiming. A couple of weeks ago, one hand of the administration reached down, holding incriminating documents, to nudge Huang out of his role. On Monday, after a bad week in the markets, another picked him back up and put him back in his chair and took credit for this. Two competing impulses from within the administration — hawkish China policy and numbers-go-up market pumping — fell out of alignment, and the temporary health of the NASDAQ, as well as the president’s ego, won.

Huang now joins a small group of contemporary American leaders for whom accountability has been suspended almost entirely, a class of ultrapowerful figures for whom nothing can be permitted to matter. In government, we have the character of Donald Trump, whose most consistent belief seems to be in the impunity of himself and people like him, “when you’re a star, they let you do it” extrapolated to a government philosophy. We also have a superlative example in Elon Musk, who has, among many other things, enlisted his own subordinates into his campaign to have as many children as possible. Huang hasn’t started any wars, or gleefully liquidated any massive, life-saving aid operations, but he has comprehensively violated the norms and expectations of his position. Now we are told that this does not and, for the good of the nation, cannot matter:

Huang is joining this club a little bit late, however. The midterm blowout marked a point at which Trump’s grip over the machinery of the state, as well as his own party, was weakening. Musk, facing not just a blue Texas but the prospect of a national and possibly vengeful Democratic trifecta in a couple of years, is now claiming that, actually, he was never really MAGA MAGA. (A claim so facially absurd that even Donald Trump is shrugging it off.) Nvidia’s troubles predated Huang’s affair — the company’s stock price had peaked in early October and been falling ever since, dropping 37 percent by November 18 in a sell-off first triggered by worries about debt-funded AI spending, interest rates, and broader changes in the political environment. Today the stock surged dramatically on Huang’s reinstatement but remains far below its highs.

There was plenty of uncertainty ahead for an Nvidia run by an interim CEO or new hire, and the loss of the AI industry’s most effective and flamboyant hype man, who had made his company not just a lynchpin in the AI supply chain but structurally important in its increasingly elaborate and risky financing arrangements, was clearly understood by shareholders as both a corporate and systemic worry. But he will return with an enormous target on his back and a lot to answer for. Huang may be insulated from federal investigations for the time being, but state AGs and lawmakers are gearing up for war. Huang is set to testify in front of three House committees in December as well as the Senate Banking Committee at a future date TBD. He will do so as someone who, in the president’s own telling, has been reinstated to his role by Donald Trump, an Nvidia stockholder whose ballroom fund received a $25 million contribution from the company and whose dwindling public support is contingent on avoiding a market wipeout.

Huang’s return won’t settle the deeper concerns surrounding the trajectory of the AI business. And while it answers the narrow question of who will lead the company, it muddies the matter of who is really in charge. Huang left Nvidia under vague suspicions that he had been compromised by a foreign government. He returns beholden to the haggard and unpredictable man who is still in charge of his own, but not for long.

items.title: Bringing Austen, Wharton, and Steinbeck Into the iPhone Age
items.description: It’s a balmy late-September day in London, and Dolly Alderton is explaining to a befuddled Emma Frost what “iPhone face” means. Frost has never heard the term; her fellow showrunners Alderton and Zoe Kazan have.
items.author: Hillary Busis
paragraphs: It’s a balmy late-September day in London, and Dolly Alderton is explaining to a befuddled Emma Frost what “iPhone face” means. Frost has never heard the term; her fellow showrunners Alderton and Zoe Kazan have.
“You know [how] you look at some faces, like Rosamund Pike’s face—it looks like it’s never seen an iPhone? It looks like it’s seen a lute and a loom,” Alderton tells Frost.
“So actors who look like they’re comfortable in a period show, rather than feeling inherently modern,” says Frost, as understanding dawns. Alderton and Kazan affirm her: “Yes, yes. Exactly.”
Now that Frost gets it, she turns back to the group’s Zoom screen. “Sorry, what was the question?”

Kazan began her career as an actor, while Alderton started out as a dating columnist and Frost was a sculptor and painter. Now all three are overseeing vastly different but comparable Netflix period dramas, each based on a classic work of literature: East of Eden (Kazan’s, which was released October 1), Pride and Prejudice (Alderton’s, out December 3), and The Age of Innocence (Frost’s, coming February 18). They’ve gathered in a London conference room at Netflix headquarters for a roundtable discussion about art, work, the unique experience of adapting a beloved book—and, apparently, iPhone face.

Though this is the first time the trio has met face to face, their conversation flows so easily and naturally that interrupting them with questions sometimes feels impolite. Early on, I note that all three of these novels are, on some level, about unconventional women. Alderton, Frost, and Kazan pause for a moment, considering this Lit 101–level observation.
“I’d say that,” says Alderton.
“That’s true, I think,” agrees Frost.
And then they’re off to more interesting topics.
Vanity Fair: Have you read each other’s books?
Dolly Alderton: No, I haven’t read either of your books.
Emma Frost: I’ve read both.
Alderton: Did you read them at school, or did you read them for fun?
Frost: Pride and Prejudice I read when I was a teenager at school. East of Eden I read first about 15 years ago, I think.
Alderton: So Em already wins the round table.
Frost: And for both of you, was it the thing you most wanted to adapt?

Alderton: I would never have dared to dream to. I was so overwhelmed when I was first approached. I just thought, it’s such a precious IP. It would be way too much, and I wouldn’t be the right person. But then when I was asked to pitch for it, at that point there’s no other answer but yes.
Kazan: First of all, was it the Austen you liked the most?

Alderton: Yes. It was the one that I’ve always loved because of Lizzie Bennet. I’ve always been obsessed with Lizzie Bennet. She was my hook. But how about you two? Did you ever dream of adapting these texts?

Frost: I was at a place where I said, “I want to do anything except period, because I’ve done so much period.” Netflix asked me to do The Age of Innocence, and it was, I think at that moment, the one book that made me just go, “Oh my God, okay, let me go back and revisit it.” Because I know I love it, but you have to know what the reason is [to adapt it again]. And the thing that totally blew me away on a reread was how relevant and resonant it is. It is about the freedom of the individual versus the conformity of the pack. It has so many themes in it that are really resonant with social media, the bullying of the group.
Alderton [turning to Kazan]: Tackling Cathy, how did you begin? What was your way into that?

Kazan: I think of adaptation as an advanced form of reading. For me, everything I’ve ever written has come from a feeling of “I have to write this specific thing.” When I was 15 and I read the book for the first time, I felt like it literally grabbed me by the throat and wouldn’t let go. And then I just kept coming back to it. And specifically her character, I felt like I had never read anyone like that before or since.
[to Alderton] The BBC’s Pride and Prejudice—is that the one that you—
Alderton: No, that wasn’t my Pride and Prejudice.
Frost: That’s the Joe Wright.

Alderton: Yeah, the Joe Wright one was the one that I was more familiar with. But I’m so interested in what you were saying about getting to know Cathy. I was kind of nervous about doing press for a book that’s so beloved, and I’m finding it’s actually been really easy so far because I just know the people so well. So much of it has been basically like, putting Mr. Darcy and Elizabeth, all the Bennet family and Bingley through therapy. That psychological interrogation of these very well-known characters has been the thing I’ve just really, really enjoyed.
Frost: Have you both had to change points of view from the novel? Do you feel like you’ve had to make a specific choice about who you are foregrounding? I think I know the answer in your case, Zoe.

Kazan: No, I actually don’t. I’m aware that the way that I read a book is different from the way that anyone else reads that book. When I read East of Eden, I feel like I see Steinbeck becoming enthralled by this character, finding her as curious as I do. I think he starts out a real place of judgment and over the course of the book, really moves towards love and understanding.

Alderton: I have a similar thing in that for the majority of the book, one of the lead characters is completely unknowable. Not just to Elizabeth, but to the audience as well. So you have to honor that to make it satisfying. That’s kind of frustrating when you’re writing a romantic lead for the first three and a half episodes. None of us, least of all the female protagonist, can see who he is, and we misunderstand him. There is no other option I think than staying with Lizzie.
Frost: I think you’re right.
Alderton: But how about you?

Frost: It’s very different because the book is entirely from Newland’s point of view. The thing that I wanted to do, and that Netflix were really excited for me to do, was to open it up to find out who the women were.

I think in the book—rightly, because she’s writing from Newland’s point of view—both May and Ellen are sort of constructed as his other. One is the thing to be won, and one is effectively the antagonist. It’s so interesting, because it’s a female author—and [Wharton herself], she’s part Newland. That's who she was growing up. And she’s part Ellen, this woman who now lives in Europe, who's become really cosmopolitan, who is even based on her own love triangle.
The impossibility of that love triangle is the thing I want people to feel. It’s not like one of them is wrong. They're all just feeling what they’re feeling.
Alderton: And how do you feel about bringing that new perspective and analysis to the story? For a book that's so beloved, did you feel excited by that? Or did you feel kind of daunted by it?

Frost: Maybe I should have felt daunted. I didn’t. I think Edith Wharton—it’s so based on her own personal experience of when she was 45, she had this sexual awakening. She was in this really dull marriage. She’d never had an orgasm. When she was 45, she fell in love with this journalist and had this passionate affair.
Kazan: Quite aspirational.

Frost: She had this big affair, then he ghosted her. But she was trying to make sense of it through this love triangle. When she wrote it, she couldn’t possibly have written herself as a female character in the center of an illicit love triangle because we were still in time of censorship, and she was being published in a very commercial magazine. So she had to make herself the man that has more agency.
Alderton: With any script, you have a relationship with the characters. But with what we are doing, you have this relationship with the writer.
Kazan to Alderton: You’re also a novelist. How are you thinking about bisecting yourself—using both parts of your brain, the novelist part and the dramatist part?

Alderton: I’ll tell you how I felt about it. I’ve written two novels, both of which I’ve tried to adapt. I found it really, really hard. I found adapting Pride and Prejudice incredibly effortless. When I went from Pride and Prejudice to my novel, I was like, "Why is this so much harder? I hate this novelist. Jane Austen is so much easier."

What amazed me is just, it’s like she wrote it to be adapted. It’s like her agent had said to her, “I know you’re going to write this novel about this family of five women, but remember, we could get a great movie deal off the back of it. So try and make it as adaptable as possible.” It has literally been written for TV in this totally perfect six-part structure. I just wish she was around to have written screenplays.

Kazan: This is how I feel about Tolstoy too. When I read War and Peace, I’m like, “Oh, he’s seeing it as if it’s a movie.” It’s very strange to read that so far ahead of the technology to make that possible.
Where was each of your point of entry? What was the first scene that you wrote?
Frost: I always break the whole thing in quite a lot of detail to feel like I understand where the story's going. I think when I actually started writing, I probably wrote from the beginning.
Kazan: So you outlined her therapy?
Alderton: I do the same. It’s the only thing that gives me freedom and confidence to write.
Kazan: And did you know how many episodes you wanted from the start, or did that change?
Frost: At one point it was longer, and at one point it was shorter. It’s eight in the end. What about you?
Kazan: I wanted eight originally, and then for budget and logistical reasons, I had to boil it down to seven quite late in the process. I had been four years into adapting it.
Kazan: Yeah. And we were a month away from production, and I had to restructure everything quite late in the game.

Kazan: Yeah, but you know what? It was actually this enormous gift. I had this writing teacher in college, a poetry teacher who talked a lot about constraints. And I don’t know if you've ever seen the... What’s his name? He’s a nightmare, but forgive me—the guy who directed Melancholia.

Kazan: There’s this beautiful Lars Von Trier film called The Five Obstructions, a documentary. He challenges his filmmaking teacher to remake this perfect short film that he made in the 1960s with five sets of obstructions to help him break open his creative process again. And that, combined with what my poetry teacher was always saying—which is the form gives you freedom.

Kazan: I feel like having to... Every time I’ve received, “Okay, we don’t have the money for X, or we don’t have the location for Y, or you have to boil eight episodes down to seven,” that it made me think again about, okay, what’s important here? Seeing the instruction as a gift rather than as an obstacle really just helped me over and over again. I actually gave myself one night to be really mad about it, and then the next day I was—

Kazan: A lot of showrunning, for me at least, has been about learning how to manage my emotions on my own time so that I can go to work and help manage everything. The next day, as soon as I started reworking it, I discovered all of the gifts that it would give me.

Alderton: That lesson is one that you only learn with the privilege of experience. This is only my second TV show. My first, Everything I Know About Love, was an adaptation of my memoir. But I remember now the moments where I said, “If we have to lose this scene, there’s no point shooting the whole show.” Things like that.
Kazan: And then you’re in the edit and you’re like, “Actually, that’s better.”

Alderton: Totally. Or I think back on these things that we couldn’t afford or practically couldn’t work that I really thought would rip out the heart and soul of the show. And now I never dream of an alternate version of that show where those things were put in.
I don’t think I would’ve been as zen as you. I think I would’ve been a petty, grouchy bitch for three days, rather than one.
Kazan: At that point, I was still trying to get my greenlight. I want to hear Dolly’s answer to the first scene question.

Alderton: Oh, sure. So the opening of Pride and Prejudice in the book is obviously setting up the central drama, which is “we need a man. There's a new man in town.” We decided to put Darcy at the very, very top of the show. There is so much in Pride and Prejudice to delight in. What is easy to forget is that it is the best love story of all time. And I’m just like, “We should land that. The first thing we should land is this intrigue between these two characters.”

So Elizabeth is walking around Netherfield Park being kind of nosy and breaking the rules, and she’s intrigued by this man. So much of their attraction to each other, which everyone finds so delicious to read, is that they’re just fascinated with each other, and it takes them a while to work out why. So we wanted to establish that.
Kazan: I love that. I loved her spying and the sort of misunderstanding of who he is.
Dolly, were you wrestling at all about what to do with “it’s truth universally acknowledged,” the most famous line in literature?

Alderton: Andrew Davies gives that line to Elizabeth Bennet, but for me, it felt like it’s the Mrs. Bennet line. The reinterpretation, I suppose, that I’ve done on my Pride and Prejudice is a bit of a justice for Mrs. Bennet. I’m working so hard in this adaptation to really understand why she is the way she is, why she’s so hysterical, why she's seemingly such a social climber. So to give her that line, it felt like we were just off to the races. This is a woman whose preoccupation in life is making sure her daughters are safe. So yeah, it felt like it was an easy line for Olivia [Colman].
When it comes to casting, can you articulate what makes somebody feel appropriate for a period show, versus somebody who seems too contemporary?
Kazan: Or maybe that’s not a concern.
Frost: I think for me, casting is really instinctive. Ben Radcliffe, right from his first tape, I was just, “He is Newland Archer. That is the end of the conversation. We are having him.”
Kazan: Did you audition all of them?
Frost: All of them did tapes or auditions. It’s so hard to explain, isn’t it? You see somebody and you just go, “That’s what I have in my head. That’s what we need.”

Alderton: We kind of knew who we wanted Lizzie and Darcy to be, and we had to do chemistry. We did a chemistry [read] with Emma and Jack, and Emma’s an EP on the show. So the minute Jack left, Emma and I looked at each other, and we were like, “That’s totally Darcy.”

But it’s interesting that you were saying that thing about chemistry. I don’t know about you guys, but every time I do casting, I’m amazed how much it feels like falling in love. You go away and you find yourself Googling them and thinking about them and dreaming about them. It’s so wonderful if then they want to do it, and it’s so heartbreaking if they don’t.
Kazan: You fall in love, and then sometimes your love affair doesn’t work out.
Alderton: What was your process like?
Frost: Florence [Pugh] was involved really early, right?

Kazan: She was. I had always had this feeling about East of Eden, and I had sort of tried to ignore that feeling because of my grandfather’s relationship to the material and my relationship to coming from this family. And about a year and a half before this call came, I had written my agent saying, “This is so embarrassing, but if the rights to East of Eden ever come up, can you please let me know so that I can pitch on it?” So they did me a solid. I got an appointment to meet, but I didn’t have a lot of time to prepare.

They asked, “Do you have any actors in mind?” I think I had walked into the room not thinking that I had any actors in mind, and then Florence came out of my mouth. I had seen Midsommar, and I felt like I was witnessing the birth of a genius. And Cathy Ames is such a challenging part that I needed an actor of that caliber. But then we didn’t do any more casting for four years after that.
Frost: But she stayed faithful.

Kazan: She did. The whole reason this show came together when it did was that there was a window that she had in her schedule. We didn’t have directors yet, and we didn’t have any other cast yet. Her window was starting in October, and between April and June, we put everything together.

So much of it is alchemical. But once you have that central pole that all the spokes are going to come off of, then you start going, “Okay, well if it’s this Lizzie Bennet, it has to be that Mr. Darcy. If it’s this Newland Archer, it has to be this Ellen.”

On the page, East of Eden is the only one of these three novels that has a protagonist who isn’t white. But that isn’t true of your series. I’m curious, Emma and Dolly, if you can speak to that—casting actors who aren’t white in these stories that are largely about white characters.

Frost: Yeah. Edith Wharton came from such a privileged, elite white bubble. That is completely what her life was. But the story is about a man who is chafing against that, and these rules are killing him. So having the contrast of the world inside and outside of that elite white bubble felt crucial to telling this story. And Ellen is part of this really exciting wave of immigration that’s coming into New York at the time, and it’s blowing this old world to pieces. And it’s so much more exciting than this kind of decaying, crusty world that he’s been trapped by.

So for me, it felt like a very organic thing to have non-white characters as well that provide that contrast. They are the new ideas, they are the exciting conversations, they are the music that’s coming in. So he was one foot in each, and it was a very organic thing to do.

Alderton: I think there are so many different ways that you can look at diversity with period work. Bridgerton’s a great example of a specific thing. Colorblind casting is a specific example. We decided that we wanted our Pride and Prejudice to be very rooted in historical reality, but we also didn’t want to make an all-white Pride and Prejudice. We wanted to be inclusive and representative. So we just did our homework, and we found cases of families much like the Bingleys who had roots in trade where there were mixed-race families.

Was it the most common thing in Regency England? No. But it’s not the most common thing that a man like Mr. Darcy would’ve married Elizabeth Bennet. It’s so simple in my mind. It’s all made up anyway, and those actors were the best actors for those roles.

Kazan: Can I also say—we have white-presenting actors in East of Eden who have Caribbean roots, and Chinese American people that present as white in our series. I think the idea of whiteness, it can be a weapon. I think it can be weaponized: who we say is white and who we say isn’t white. I just think it’s a funny thing of who we agree is allowed to be in these things and who isn’t.

I do always think it’s a hard thing, because racial identity is such an important part of how people go through the world. And what both of you are saying about finding the logic within your stories for the casting that you want to make, I think, is really important. But I also think it's important to think about how there are identities that are not visible.
Was there one moment from each of your novels that you were the most nervous about getting right?

Frost: I don’t know if it’s one piece of the novel per se, but what gave me pause was trying to find a way into Ellen, Countess Olenska. I wanted to find a way to stay completely true to the spirit and intention of her as a character, but make her emotionally legible to a 21st-century audience. As framed in the novel, there is an element of her being beaten by her husband, and now she needs another man to rescue her. That isn’t this sort of independent, forward-looking woman that I felt I needed at the center of the show.

But Edith Wharton, as ever, is so brilliant that she sort of provided this solution partly through me drawing on her own life, which I used to infuse Ellen. Also, without giving spoilers, there are things that are said about Ellen in the novel that Ellen never confirms. We are in a world of rumor and reputation, and it suddenly became clear to me that what is said about her isn't necessarily true. Once I felt I understood who she was, the whole thing just sort of opened up for me. What about you guys?
Alderton: My take is not so much because of the text—it was because of a previous adaptation.
Kazan: I was going to ask you guys about this.
Alderton: About these adaptations that live in your head.
Kazan: All three of these books have multiple—if not multiple, at least a beloved adaptation.

Alderton: Totally. And on the whole, I feel very comfortable being in this great tradition of every 20 or 30 years, there's a Pride and Prejudice. I like that. I don't want to pretend like there are no other adaptations.

But the one thing that was in my head from the very beginning was the wet-shirt moment. Because it’s such a pivotal moment in the story when we see Darcy for who he is the first time. We understand why he’s been so guarded. We understand why he grips to these social structures so strongly. We understand that he’s a deeply honorable, protective, very recently wounded man.
Kazan: And hot as hell, too.

Alderton: And hot as hell. That’s why the wet shirt was so brilliant, because there’s something about literally seeing the skin of him—literally seeing underneath his carapace for the first time. So I was like, “How are we going to do that?” And I think where I got to in the end is that each generation gets the Darcy that they need, whether it’s Laurence Olivier or Colin Firth or Matthew Macfadyen. The ’90s was a very sexually charged, erotic time in culture, so that’s why we got that Darcy. Matthew, there was something that was kind of cooler about his Darcy.

Alderton: And more indie, which represents his time. And where we are now is a time where masculinity is in crisis. And where Jack instinctively went with his Darcy, it’s quite an honorable place and quite a tender place. So that moment in Pemberley, we actually chose to do it over a series of micro moments that show the softness of Darcy. Which I find very deeply erotic in its own way.
What are your own favorite adaptations, not counting the works we’re speaking about?
Alderton: Mine’s the 1995 Sense and Sensibility. The Emma Thompson Sense and Sensibility.
Kazan: That’s a perfect movie. I love another Ang Lee adaptation, The Ice Storm.
Kazan: Thinking of plays, too—Cabaret is unbelievable, [Liza Minnelli’s] performance and what [Bob Fosse’s] doing with film that he couldn’t do in any other medium.
Alderton: But it still retains the theatricality somewhat.

Kazan: Yeah, completely. I have to shout out to my parents—my parents adapted a lot of films. [Editor’s note: Among other films, her mother, Robin Swicord, wrote Practical Magic and the 1994 Little Women; her father, Nicholas Kazan, wrote Reversal of Fortune.] I just showed my kid their Matilda. When my parents wrote their adaptation, we did a table read when they had their first draft around their dining room table, and I read Matilda.
Kazan: Now my kid is eight, which is about the age that I was then. I got, in that same house, to show her their Matilda. That was really special.

items.title: See Noah Kahan Captivate Audiences With Extended ‘Orbiter’
items.description: Video of Noah Kahan performing “Orbiter” on a stop through Queens shows him plucking arpeggios from an acoustic guitar as he sings about looking exhausted and feeling stiff and awkward. But those are just lyrics, as he mostly looks awed by being able to sing t
items.author: Kory Grow
paragraphs: Video of Noah Kahan performing “Orbiter” on a stop through Queens shows him plucking arpeggios from an acoustic guitar as he sings about looking exhausted and feeling stiff and awkward. But those are just lyrics, as he mostly looks awed by being able to sing to stadiums of fans who sing along with his lyrics, flashing their phone lights at him. He even looks unbothered by the fan blowing up on him from below, set to a gentle “medium,” rather than the hair-raising “high” setting bands like Whitesnake used to prefer. It’s enough to ruffle his sleeves and the bottom of his shirt but not distract him from the raw emotion of the song.

The video heralds the release of a new live album, Live From the Great Divide, out Dec. 11. The album collects 16 songs Kahan recorded along the Great Divide World Tour, which supported his recent album, The Great Divide. It will serve as a souvenir of the singer-songwriters’ star-making year before he heads out next year’s Last of the Bugs World Tour. North American dates for that run begin in April; many are already sold out.

The Queens concert where Kahan recorded the extended version of “Orbiter” almost didn’t happen. The artist had booked a two-night run at Citi Field but had to cancel the first night due to rain, severe thunderstorms, and strong winds. “We’ll do everything we can to come back and make this right,” Kahan wrote in a statement. From the sound of the recording, he delivered.
