items.title: Bebe Rexha Burns Down the Asylum
items.description: “You’re going to gag,” Bebe Rexha says, squinting in the glare of late afternoon sunshine as she scrolls through her phone.
items.author: Joan Summers
paragraphs: “You’re going to gag,” Bebe Rexha says, squinting in the glare of late afternoon sunshine as she scrolls through her phone.

A moment earlier, the singer was juggling her laptop as she flipped over the edge of her hot pink bikini top to proudly show her publicist her tan lines. Bebe has brought her computer out onto a balcony overlooking Ibiza — a work from home setup fit for a pop star. Now she’s on her phone, hunting down a photo she took on set the day of her PAPER magazine shoot. It’s taking her a minute, but she’s determined. Then her face lights up as she finds what she’s looking for. Bebe holds her phone up to her computer camera. “I have a picture of me burning down the asylum,” she beams.

The proverbial in-patient program in question is The Khia Asylum, named perhaps unfairly after the rapper Khia, whose 2003 hit “My Neck, My Back (Lick It)” peaked just outside top 40 but lives on in infamy via this piece of pop terminology, used to describe any whiff of commercial under-performance. Since pop fans started using the term a couple of years ago, prior residents like Sabrina Carpenter, Charli XCX and Zara Larsson have all graduated from perceived flopdom, thus breaking out of the asylum. Could Bebe Rexha be next?
Bodysuit: Noscenegirls, Gloves: Wing & Weft, Shoes: Jean Paul Gaultier x Lotta Volkova courtesy of Gabriel Held Vintage

The 36-year-old Brooklyn-born, Staten Island-raised singer and songwriter has an unlikely CV for a flop: she’s written megahits, including Eminem and Rihanna’s enduring smash “Monster,” plus songs for Selena Gomez and Nick Jonas. She’s collaborated with everyone from Dolly Parton to Snoop Dogg, Cardi B, Doja Cat and Pitbull. And she’s got her own hits, too – four top 10s and five songs with more than one billion streams, including her most recent to join the billions club, a 2022 EDM smash with David Guetta, "I'm Good (Blue)."

But Bebe’s often been seen more as a voice on a hook than a superstar in her own right. Now she’s trying to change that. Early this year, Bebe announced her exit from Warner Records after three albums and more than a decade, instead striking a deal with an independent label and distributor, Empire. Then she started dropping dance floor fillers like “New Religion,” a searing EDM song built around a sample from the nineties dance classic “Insomnia” by Faithless and the propulsive “Çike Çike,” which sees Bebe embracing her roots by singing in Albanian. Finally, in June, she dropped her fourth studio album, Dirty Blonde, complete with a music video for every song.

So far, Bebe’s bet on herself has paid off: Dirty Blonde debuted atop the Billboard Top Dance Albums chart, having moved 19,000 album equivalent units its first week. On Spotify, she currently has 43 million monthly streams and not long after the album release she was one of the 100 most streamed acts on the platform. And she’s in Spain for a major moment — she joined David Guetta to sing their latest collab together, “Sad Girls” for 80,000 screaming fans.

PAPER catches up with Rexha shortly afterwards, fresh out of burning down the asylum for this very cover story. The pop phenom talks to PAPER about Dirty Blonde, going independent and having a party girl moment in her thirties.
Read our latest cover story below.
Dress, Corset, Blazer: Jane Wade, Shoes: Gianvito Rossi

It’s gorgeous. It’s amazing. I performed with David Guetta the other night and I got to watch his show. I was on stage with him mid-way through the show, so I got to go into the crowd to watch after. I was like, wow. This motherfucker is amazing. The whole show was amazing, like top to bottom, wow.
Congrats on Dirty Blonde topping the Billboard dance chart.
Thank you. I was like, “Oh, shit. That’s cool!”
You were with your old label for more than a decade. How does it feel to be independent?

It feels great. It feels refreshing being with a group of people who believe in me and want the best for me and see my vision and help me execute it. It’s a rebirth. Music feels exciting again and for a long time it didn’t feel exciting.
You recently said you were mourning the way your career had drifted. What had been frustrating you?

I was always scared of making the wrong decision. I was always worried about making everyone else happy and chasing what could be a hit. I feel like I lost my DNA. I wanted to be successful for everyone around me, you know? But what I learned is, even when I did have success on some songs, it didn’t even make me happy. I was like: this is not who I am. I am really grateful for “Meant To Be” and the way the country community accepted me, that was really nice. I was happy and I love “Meant To Be” but I didn’t feel like it was a reflection of my artistry even though I wrote it.
Bodysuit: Noscenegirls, Gloves: Wing & Weft, Shoes: Jean Paul Gaultier x Lotta Volkova courtesy of Gabriel Held Vintage
I thought your last album, 2023’s Bebe, was underrated. It was kind of slept on. “Call On Me” should have been a hit.

I love that album too. But you know what a lot of people say to me about that album? They’ll be like, “I didn’t even know you had an album out.” I was like, damn. Maybe I should have pushed it more. But I was also in a funk. I knew where I stood with my label and I knew I wasn’t a priority. I had kind of already given up.
Earlier this year, you posted that video of you running on the treadmill, joking about trying to exit the Khia Asylum. Do you feel like you’ve now broken out?

I’m the type of person who just likes to create music. I’m such a Virgo – I’m trying to celebrate that the album went number one on the dance chart, but I’m the type of person who is like, “Oh my god, I could still write better songs. I could do more.” More, more, more.

Every day, I don’t wake up being like, “Did I break out of The Khia Asylum?” I’m doing my thing. Once I hit a stride, I’ll know and it will feel good, but I still feel like I’m in the building stages of what I’m trying to build.
In terms of your stats, your streams are way up, Dirty Blonde moved 19,000 album equivalent units in its first week. The response to this record feels good. Does it feel good to you?

It feels good to me. Look, compared to where I was at, for a long time I was – I don’t want to say dead in the water, because that’s very dramatic – but I didn’t feel the energy. With this album, Dirty Blonde, the energy is different this time. It hasn’t felt like this in a long time.
Corset & Skirt: Andrew Curwen, Necklace: Stylist's own Gas Bijoux
The industry has changed so much and now you can get a big moment years into your career, like Charli XCX and Zara Larsson. What has it been like to watch those women have big moments?

It’s extremely inspiring. I’ve been in the industry for quite some time now and I’ve heard the things people have said about other artists and they’re not always nice. People always want to count women out, say “They’ve already had their chance,” or “They’ve already been signed before, they’ve had a certain number of singles.” What I’ve seen with Charli and Zara is they’re work horses. They never stopped.
To see them do what they’re doing is fucking awesome.
You chopped your hair off right before the start of this era. Did getting a blonde bob change everything?

Long hair is sexy. I get it. I love having a good extension in, you know what I mean? It makes you feel like Rapunzel. But for me personally, I’ve tried so many hair colours. I was trying to find my identity in hair colors and all these lengths. What I really like, when I feel the most me, is when my hair is a blonde bob. When I first dyed my hair, everybody said, “No, no, no.” I booked the appointment, went to the salon, spent 14 hours and everybody was like, “Oh my god, this looks unreal.”
I want to die blonde. Please, make sure my hair is blonde. No roots when I’m in my casket.
Let’s talk about “New Religion” with Faithless and what it took to get that sample cleared. I heard you had brunch with Sister Bliss.

I did. It took me a very, very long time to get that sample cleared. I didn’t know if I was going to get it cleared. I wrote some other songs with them. I spoke to Rollo, I spoke to Sister Bliss. I had brunch with Sister Bliss. I got to know her. She’s really cool, she’s very smart.
The original is such an amazing record. I feel really lucky they allowed me to use their sample.
Dress: Bach Mai, Shoes: Gianvito Rossi
You wrote and recorded this album while globetrotting from one nightclub to another, from Ibiza to London to Tokyo. What brought you out to the clubs?

I was never a party girl. Even though I’m in my thirties, I feel like it’s never too late. I feel like there’s a resurgence in partying in your thirties now. I was in Zurich and it was my birthday the next day…I went out that night and I went out the night after. I was up until like four in the morning. I was the last person in the club. Literally the last person. It was me, some random girl who was drunk and these two guys and I somehow ended up in the back of the DJ booth. It was so fun.
I love that your songs have big vocals. With so much pop music today, the vocals are restrained, they’re smaller. I love that you’re a singer’s singer.

I hope that actually comes back, because I agree with what you’re saying. We’ve gone into this world of small singing. It is beautiful, I actually love it, but I just feel like what I’ve noticed is that with my songs, they have big hooks and that’s what people love about me most. I guess maybe it makes them feel something. I’ve been noticing that more than ever at my shows and in my writing session, everybody always wants that big moment, they love when I hit the octave, it’s big, high choruses.

The only thing about that I don’t love is when I do it live, it’s like, you’re having all these songs that are super high. And I’m like, ah, shit, at the end of the show, I’m like “Why the fuck are the songs so high?” I literally had my music director look at me and go, “I guess talk to yourself?” I was like, shit. I need to start writing these songs a little lower.
You asked your fans on Twitter if they could find you a man. Were there any strong contenders?
Single as a Pringle! There’s nothing happening. I always think about Cher’s quote about her not needing a rich husband.

Ya! “Mom, I am a rich man.” I’m in Ibiza right now and I was trying to find somebody to get a yacht for me, just to be on the yacht. I was like, let me see what the vibe is. I came to a point where I was like, “I’m working so hard, I’m going to get the fucking yacht myself.” I did what I wanted to do with nobody else and that was so much more fulfilling than being on somebody else’s dime, on somebody else’s yacht.
I love how you embraced your Albanian heritage on, “Çike Çike.” Do you have any theories on why so many pop girls are Albanian?

There’s a hardness to Albanian women, but in the best way. We’re fighters. All the women that I’ve met who are Albanian, they’re crazy hard workers. They won’t take no for an answer. Insane work ethic. When I was getting to know Dua and Rita, they both had an insane work ethic. Not stopping, very hungry, focused energy.
You need a lot of tenacity to be a pop star.
I would say so. You have to be very strong mentally.
The lyrics for “I Like You Better Than Me” are very vulnerable. What type of experiences led to that song?

Being in the music industry and struggling, even when I was thinner, I always struggled with my image. Being on the red carpet, I always felt off or not good enough. And beyond the red carpet, it could be pictures people take of you on stage or being around other female artists in the industry who seem to always have it together. That gets to you. Comparison is the thief of joy, it really is.
Is it true you used to offer songs to artists but only if you could sing the hook?

Yeah, of course. I didn’t know that in the beginning. After I’d written a couple big songs for other artists, then I was like, “Sure, you can have this song but I have to stay on it.” I call it the power of the pen!
You clearly could stick to working behind the scenes, you have the talent to be a songwriter. Diane Warren has done it her whole career.
And she’s rich! What drives you to continue in the pop game, pursuing your own career as a pop star?
I really, really love performing live. I love feeling a crowd’s energy, I love when they sing along.
Are you still writing songs for other people?

I really want to but I really don’t have time. People ask me all the time. I’d love to write some more K-Pop songs, it’s really fun. What I love about K-Pop is there’s so many different melodies and you can be more fun and kitschy with the titles.
Do you have plans for live shows to support the album?
Yes. We’re working on it. Everybody keeps asking. Nothing is set yet but we’re working on it. I definitely want to tour Dirty Blonde.

items.title: Miley Cyrus Marries Maxx Morando at Frank Sinatra's Famous Palm Springs Mansion
items.description: It's official: After more than five years together and nearly a year of engagement, Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando have tied the knot. The couple were married in the desert hot spot of Palm Springs, California on Saturday, November 21, an outdoor ceremony held a
items.author: Diego Parrado
paragraphs: It's official: After more than five years together and nearly a year of engagement, Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando have tied the knot. The couple were married in the desert hot spot of Palm Springs, California on Saturday, November 21, an outdoor ceremony held at Frank Sinatra’s former mansion, with Wayne Coyne, frontman of The Flaming Lips and a Cyrus collaborator, officiating.

The 33-year-old singer and the 28-year-old musician—Morando is the drummer for the band Liily—had kept their plans a secret until Friday, when TMZ broke the news. Confirmation of the impending celebration emerged that same evening, during the dinner that capped off the rehearsal, when Miley’s half-sister, Lily-Rose Purcell, posted a photo on her Instagram Stories of a menu featuring the couple’s initials. This is Cyrus’s second marriage, following her alliance with actor Liam Hemsworth from 2018 to 2019.

According to images published in outlets including People, the ceremony venue was decorated with white flowers and large candles, with Sinatra’s pool in the background. Miley Cyrus wore a long-sleeved white satin dress with a plunging back and no veil, while the groom opted for a classic black tuxedo with a bow tie.

Among the guests were the bride’s mother, Tish Cyrus, accompanied by her husband, actor Dominic Purcell, and Miley's sister, Noah Cyrus. Also in attendance was the singer’s father, Billy Ray Cyrus, along with his rumored fiancée, British actress Elizabeth Hurley, and her son, Damian.

As the bride has recounted in past interviews, her relationship with her now-husband began in 2021 following a blind date organized by mutual friends. That same year, they went public by attending the singer’s New Year’s Eve TV special in Miami together. Their engagement came to light in December 2025, when, during another of those joint appearances, Miley Cyrus posed on the red carpet wearing a diamond ring that turned out to be her engagement ring.

One of the most emotional moments of the ceremony took place just before the couple exchanged their vows, when—according to multiple outlets— Dolly Parton’s “Love Is Like a Butterfly” began to play. The nod follows a similar one Miley made last month, when she broke down in tears over Parton's death during a performance at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles.

“Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart, and I’m gonna see her again,” Cyrus told the stadium crowd in October, per The Hollywood Reporter. “And I can’t fucking wait because I miss her,” Cyrus tearfully continued. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my Aunt Dolly."

items.title: Kate Middleton Announces Surprise Documentary About Her Cancer Journey
items.description: “Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton says, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a pu
items.author: Alessia Arcolaci
paragraphs: “Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton says, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a public event. Instead, they're the voice-over in a previously unannounced documentary about the Princess of Wales and her life since she disclosed a diagnosis of cancer in 2024.

According to Kensington Palace, which announced the film on Saturday, Heal is “a deeply personal new documentary from The Princess of Wales, exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.” It will air on the BBC in the UK on November 29, and in the US on NBCUniversal on November 30.

Heal follows Kate Middleton during her participation in one of the United Kingdom’s most demanding endurance events: The National Three Peaks Challenge, which she completed this summer. In less than 24 hours, the princess climbed the three highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales: Ben Nevis (4,413 feet), Scafell Pike (3,209 feet), and Yr Wyddfa–Snowdon (3,559 feet). The undertaking wasn't just a personal effort, as it was also in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization that supports people living with cancer before, during, and after the disease.

The documentary will also support that organization, Kensington Palace notes, saying “All funds received through the documentary's distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to help people living with and beyond cancer.” The Royal Marsden Hospital, at which Middleton received treatment, is also referenced in the film, as Middleton's brother, James, asks her “Isn’t it when you leave the Royal Marsden, you ring the bell?”

But while many patients participate in the bell-ringing ritual at the conclusion of treatment, Middleton says she missed out on that moment. “Yeah, but I didn’t ring the bell,” she replies. “So maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” James responded, suggesting her Three Peaks experience was that symbolic peal.

While Prince William is no stranger to documentary work, nor are Prince Harry and wife Meghan Markle, this is Kate Middleton's first venture into the format. Perhaps to ease her into the project, Heal's Director of Photography is a face quite familiar to the Princess: Will Warr, the filmmaker behind her video announcement marking the end of her chemotherapy treatments.

“Through this documentary, The Princess hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer and transform access to holistic cancer care which supports wellbeing, resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis,” Kensington Palace says of Heal, a message underscored by Middleton's words in the trailer. “You know, healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”

“It’s clear we're not meant to face life’s challenges alone,” the princess says as the trailer concludes. “Things can renew and grow. Often it is through pain that we realize that there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that."
Originally published by Vanity Fair Italy

items.title: Who Will Be The Next Bond Girl?
items.description: Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, new Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation
items.author: Valentine Ulgu-Servant
paragraphs: Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, new Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

The exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

In a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she said with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”

When pressed on who Pattinson's female lead might be, Seydoux expressed mixed feelings about the British spy's latest iteration. With the purchase of the Bond IP by Amazon, “It became American," Seydoux said. “But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”

The online megamart took control of the storied franchise in 2023, after which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos controversially sought feedback on the title character's casting via X. The announcement of Villeneuve as the next film's director brought things back from the brink.

Bezos, who confirmed that he was “very involved” in the film's casting process, also seems to give Seydoux pause. In an interview with Variety, she admitted “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.”

Denis Villeneuve, who directed Seydoux in Dune: Part Two, will release the final installment of this epic science-fiction trilogy will be on December 16. After that, he'll be free to focus on his next major project: reviving the world’s most famous secret agent. It remains to be seen who he will choose to star opposite Robert Pattinson as his female companion—but we know that despite her fondness for the director, Seydoux will not return: Just last month, the French actress told People “I really loved being on this franchise, but now it’s ... done.”
Originally published by Vanity Fair France

items.title: Victoria Monét Tells Toni Braxton How She Cooks in the Studio and the Kitchen
items.description: Victoria Monét Tells Toni Braxton How She Cooks in the Studio and the Kitchen
items.author: Toni Braxton
paragraphs: Victoria Monét Tells Toni Braxton How She Cooks in the Studio and the Kitchen

What better way to know you really made it then to be told by the very person who paved the way? Hours before the release of Victoria Monét’s latest album, Frequency of Love, R&B legend Toni Braxton hopped on a call to congratulate her on her 2024 Grammy win. Monét won the award for Best New Artist at the 66th Annual Grammy Awards—the same accolade received by Braxton exactly 30 years prior. But the two don’t define themselves by rhythm and blues alone. “By its name, rhythm and blues has always been more than one thing. The ‘and’ in R&B is like a culmination and combination of elements. We’ve had to really dig into who we are in order to pull to create something,” says Monét. While it first took the charts by storm in the 1990s and early 2000s, Monét proves R&B is still flourishing and growing today as she reinvents the genre through emotional storytelling, modern instrumentation, pop influences, and smooth vocals that glide through your headphones. As Braxton reminisces on the past and highlights her pride for Monét, the two gab about songwriting, collaboration, and how baking cookies led to “You Mean the World to Me.”
THURSDAY 1:30 PM OCTOBER 1, 2026 LOS ANGELES
TONI BRAXTON: Hey, pretty girl. What are you doing?
VICTORIA MONÉT: Hello, hello. I’m at Apple Music right now. There’s going to be an Apple Music takeover for the album release. Where are you?
BRAXTON: I’m in Atlanta. Are you excited? Tomorrow’s a big day.

MONÉT: I’m so excited. It takes so much time to get an album done and you finally get to this point where you’re like, “All right, it’s go time.” I’ve started celebrating already because Australia and Asia have it now. And then 9:00 PM, it’s on.
BRAXTON: I’m so excited. So proud of you.

BRAXTON: Seeing the younger artists doing their thing reminds me of when I was younger. Not as fun, but still just as hard work. So I’m just going to jump in. My glasses, I can’t see for pickles, so I’m going to have to put them on just a little bit.
MONÉT: I love “for pickles.” [Laughs]

BRAXTON: So congratulations on Best New Artist. I know you got that a couple years ago. I have that coveted award. It’s a wonderful award. It opens up so many audiences. I remember when I heard this song, “Hollywood,” I lost my mind like, “What is that? Who wrote that?” When you’re writing all these great songs, how do you know which songs are meant for you? You’ve written for so many incredible people. I mean, Ariana Grande, you’re just as grand as she is too. But how do you know, “This is for me or I’m going to give this to someone else”?

MONÉT: At first in my songwriting journey, it wasn’t easy to tell because I was writing songs in rooms with just me and a producer and then we would shop them. We’d get the “who’s looking” list from record labels, and anyone who would bite, I’d be like, “Okay, great. Amazing.” And then as my career developed, I was able to be in the room with the artist so it became easier to differentiate. And then when I made Jaguar and Jaguar II, sonically, it was a new space that I don’t think a lot of people were covering.
BRAXTON: Have you ever had some buyer’s remorse, like perhaps you wrote a song for someone else and thought, “God dang it, I should have kept that”?
MONÉT: Actually, no. I’m so happy and thankful for all the people who recorded my music because I felt like god made the choice and it was meant to be.

MONÉT: And a lot of them are really talented, big artists too. So while maybe I really loved the song and it may have been a reflection of my own life, it wouldn’t have reached the amount of people. And it’s always a joy to go to a concert where you’ve written a song and you look around and you’re like, “Wow, all of these people relate.” My voice and my story is still reaching people, but I don’t have to be the face of it every time, which is a gift too.

BRAXTON: Absolutely. Babyface has the same answer. When he wrote “End of the Road,” for himself and gave it away, he said, “I just know I’m going to be blessed. I’m going to have more music.” You’ve had success in your 20s writing for other people and being in the business. Sometimes it takes 10 years to get here overnight, and I think it happened to you.

BRAXTON: Sometimes it can be a collective mourning over the golden age of R&B during the ’90s and the 2000s, which is my generation. I’m telling my age. [Laughs] Everyone says things are missing from the R&B genre and that you’re bringing it back. I have to agree with that. But I think your music has a pop-soul and pop-R&B crossover. I don’t like when they put titles and genres on music. Music is music, and you love what you love, and it’s pop whoever likes it.

MONÉT: I have the same sentiment. When I think of the word “pop,” I just think popular versus a color of skin or a specific genre. R&B is pop because it’s popular, and so is hip-hop and country. All of these genres can really be mainstream so long as enough people popularize it. And R&B is no exception to that rule. By its name, rhythm and blues has always been more than one thing. The “and” in R&B is like a culmination and combination of elements. We’ve had to really dig into who we are in order to pull to create something. That’s just part of our nature.
MONÉT: It’s an old way of thinking.

BRAXTON: When you’re writing a song, I’ve heard you say the hook is most important. I agree with that. What inspires you to do the hook? I’ve heard you say you’re a chef. I think I’m a chef, too, sis, but you went to school for it. Do you think of cooking when you’re writing songs?

MONÉT: Sometimes ideas hit you at the funniest times. A melody of “You Mean the World to Me” on Frequency of Love came while I was baking cookies. There’s a kitchen down the hall in the studio I recorded at, and I brought my mixer to the studio and my little ingredients, and while I was making the cookies, the idea came. It wasn’t about cookies, but because I was free and not thinking too hard, my brain had the room. At random times like in the shower or while you’re driving and you’re multitasking with your brain, god blows these ideas with the wind and lands them into your brain. Sometimes it’s a melody, sometimes it’s a lyric. A lot of times, for me, it’s melody first.
MONÉT: I could hear you sing anything. You could mumble the dictionary and I would be like, “This is a smash.” So I’m not surprised about a melody coming to you super easy.
BRAXTON: Well, melodies have to matter to me, sis, because no one can understand what I say. [Laughs]
BRAXTON: When you’re writing the song, do you put it on your phone or do you just go to the studio and put it down? How does that part work?

MONÉT: There’s lots of ideas that I have missed the mark because I didn’t record them. Because it was catchy, I was so confident I would just remember it. Or it’ll happen in the middle of my sleep and I’m like, “I’m not picking up my phone right now. I’m going to remember this.” And it slips away.
MONÉT: So I’ve gotten better at just trying to record it as soon as possible in a voice memo. God forbid someone gets into my phone and finds those.

BRAXTON: I understand. Sometimes I do the same thing, “I’m going to remember,” and I completely forget. But of course something else comes to light. What’s your formula when you come up with a song idea?

MONÉT: When I’m first doing a song, I’m usually doing the first verse and hook, just for time’s sake so I can move on to another idea, unless it’s just so easily flowing out of me and we’re just in a vibe, I’ll finish completely. But most of the time I try to do scratch idea, scratch idea, and go back to the four or five I did and pick the ones that feel most special.

BRAXTON: Your engineer, are you guys like peas and carrots? You can tell them what to do and they do it or you go in the studio and he’s going to have it ready for you. Do you have that person, or are you all those people?

MONÉT: I always love to work with D’Mile and Camper. D’Mile’s all over this album, and Camper’s executive producing the album alongside me. For this album cycle, I have an engineer that I’m obsessed with now. His name is Luca [Zadra], and he came in when I was already one-third of the way done, but he really took it from 30 to 100 with me. I’m a repeat offender. I love going back to the same people that worked, like, “Don’t fix what’s not broken.” Most of the time, I’m going back to my comfort and adding new seasonings and ingredients from that foundation.

BRAXTON: Yeah. Music changes the trajectory of our lives. It’s like the playbook of life. I remember when I heard that song, who I was with, how I was feeling. I find your music so inspirational and beautiful. I can’t wait to see your live performances. Do you love performing live? That’s my favorite thing to do.

MONÉT: Oh my god. Can I tell you, when I got to see you, I was in tears. You are so captivating and your voice carries through the arena so beautifully. It’s not just when you’re standing there that we’re enamored by you, but when you start moving, you’re like, “Oh, shit.” You just do it all. I’m super inspired by you, and I do love live performances. Like a showgirl element, I love transforming from someone who’s in the house, cozy in sweatpants, into a whole new being on the stage. It’s really, really fun to express yourself in that way and project whatever character it is that the song calls for, and be of service to the energy of the crowd. And also perfect the live element, because every show is pretty unpredictable, but the more you practice, the better you are. I like the element of surprise too, because you don’t know how the audience will react. You may do something that surprises yourself, and then you integrate it into every show because you liked it. Or like an athlete, you watch the film and you’re like, “Okay, I’m not going to do that again.” It’s all constantly transforming.
BRAXTON: Tomorrow’s a big day. I’m so happy and so proud of you. What’s your favorite two songs to perform?

MONÉT: Honestly, right now it’s “Reach Out.” I did it on tour in Europe and it felt like a really great call-and-response song. I love for the crowd to be involved. You don’t have to sing to be able to sing it, you just yell it. “On My Mama” was fun for a long time because it was something that everyone got excited to see.
MONÉT: But now, I’m ready to move forward on the next album and people have different favorites.
BRAXTON: Well, my favorite is “Juicy.” I love the melodies. I love everything about it. It has a ’70s kind of thing about it, like Michael McDonald.
MONÉT: For a second, I was interested in doing yacht rock R&B, so I’m so glad you heard that.
BRAXTON: It’s fantastic. I think it’s so clever. You’re going to be fantastic tomorrow. I love you. The world loves you. You are a star.

BRAXTON: You’re the best new artist. You can pass the torch to the next artist in 10 years, in 15 years you’re going to be doing this. You were born great. You can’t help but be great. So go do what you’re supposed to do.

MONÉT: Oh my god, my heart. I can’t breathe. Thank you so much. I love you and I appreciate you for doing this, and I would love to see you and work soon and hug and hang out soon. So let’s make plans, please.
BRAXTON: Yes. Give me one or two of those leftover songs that didn’t make that incredible album. That works for me.
MONÉT: No, let’s work from scratch. Let’s do something fresh.
BRAXTON: Yes, I would love that. Take care, sis.

items.title: Los Javis and Penélope Cruz Agree the Kids Are Alright
items.description: Los Javis and Penélope Cruz Agree the Kids Are Alright
items.author: Penélope Cruz
paragraphs: Los Javis and Penélope Cruz Agree the Kids Are Alright

In Spain, they’re simply Los Javis. Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo started as actors, staged a small Madrid musical that became a film, then built a run of television hits that made them famous at home. Their latest, La Bola Negra, is on another scale entirely. Inspired by an unfinished Federico García Lorca play, the three-era queer drama about love and war won them Best Director at Cannes, set box office records in Spain, and has made them Oscar hopefuls. Few directors get a moment like this. Even fewer get Penélope Cruz, who appears in the film, to interview them about it.
FRIDAY 3:15 PM OCTOBER 9, 2026 LONDON
PENÉLOPE CRUZ: I have so many things I want to know, but we should start from the beginning because I’m a tiny bit older than you guys and I want context.
JAVIER AMBROSSI: Do you think so?
CRUZ: A tiny bit. You obviously have a shared obsession with cinema, but how did it start? At home on TV? Renting films? Going to the movies?

JAVIER CALVO: My father used to take me every weekend to the cinema, but also do you remember this DVD collection of Spanish films El País released? It included all the [Pedro] Almodóvar movies, it had—
CALVO: [Luis García]Berlanga, [José Juan]Bigas Luna, [Víctor] Erice. I was obsessed with that collection, and I would watch these films over and over in my room, on my little DVD player.

AMBROSSI: I started with an obsession for books and literature. From the time I was very young, I read every day, every kind of book. That stayed with me a long time before I switched to entertainment and television.

CRUZ: I watched everything. I wasn’t interested in going anywhere. I wanted to watch all the shows and all the movies. Whatever they were showing on television was fine with me. That was the happiest time of my life.
AMBROSSI: We are the same. I learned about entertainment from television before I discovered cinema.
CRUZ: And we all three have a shared crush on Almodóvar. Your experience of discovering him and his world was similar to mine, right?
AMBROSSI: Yes. As a kid, I saw the poster for Kika, the one that had the guy in a tank top. I was flushed, looking at that poster. So even the posters for Pedro’s films made a big impact.
CRUZ: I feel the same way.

CALVO: I went to the movies with my family, and I remember seeing you in Volver. It was shocking to see a reality similar to my own could be portrayed in the movies in such a beautiful, fun way. That was so inspiring for me—the way you talked, the way I recognized my culture and myself in there.

AMBROSSI: I went to a Catholic boys’ school and my mother knew I needed to see other things. Every week, she’d say, “Let’s go to the movies,” and everyone around was like, “Ah, but Spanish movies are not okay,” because I come from a very traditional family. But she was like—
AMBROSSI: “Let’s go, because I know it’s going to wake up something in you.”
CALVO: At a certain point, I discovered Gus Van Sant and other queer directors, but it was hard for me to find queer movies.
AMBROSSI: You had to go to a video store. It’s so funny when people say, “In Spanish cinema, there’s always gay people and civil war.” That’s not true.
CRUZ: And actually there are not so many films about the civil war.
AMBROSSI: No, it’s not true. I don’t know who said that, but some people think it’s a reality. This year, La Bola Negra is the only Spanish movie with a gay leading character.

CRUZ: That is incredible. Aren’t you looking forward to the day when a queer film is made and the first question in every interview is not, “How do you feel that this subject is being talked about?” It’s the same when you work with a female director and the first question is, “How is it different working with a female director?” It makes you realize how modern, important, and necessary the words of Federico García Lorca still are. I think that’s why everyone is connecting so much with your film, because you did something so brave without lecturing anybody.
CRUZ: You are reminding us what it is to be on the right side of things. It’s so heartbreaking to still hear that as almost the first question in every interview.
AMBROSSI: I understand why.
CRUZ: I also understand why they would ask, but in 2026, we are still like, “This is a big deal.”
AMBROSSI: I would love for it to be super normal to have leading gay characters, but it isn’t.
CRUZ: In the same way there are not so many female directors.

AMBROSSI: There are not. They can repeat it and repeat it and repeat it, but it’s not true. It’s a big thing now because our rights are being threatened. Fascism is growing. I think art comes when it’s needed, and it’s not a coincidence we’re seeing so many queer stories this year.

CRUZ: You’ve done something very huge. People are going like crazy to the theater to see this film, not only once, but two and three times. If you had done this from a place of, “I’m going to tell you what to think,” they would have rejected it, but what you did is so smart and so deep, and you did it from a point of view of no judgment. I don’t feel like we are giving enough credit to young people. Everyone is saying, “They’re so confused,” but they are seeing much more than we think. And you both knew that in the way you wrote this—you treated them as they deserve to be treated, as a smart generation, aware of the traps they are being served every day through social media. They are aware of the threats to democracy, the threats to freedom, the threats to respect. You are such old souls to have written something like this. You inspired teenagers to skip school on the day of the premiere because they wanted to be the first ones there. In the theater, you can see a 17-year-old and a 90-year-old man or woman hugging, strangers hugging. I don’t know if you realized how powerful it is.

AMBROSSI: I don’t realize yet, but when we did La Mesías, I was very surprised by young people because we were told specifically by everyone, “Young people are not going to watch this.” Everyone was worried because the first two episodes are so challenging, and everyone was like, “Guys, this time young audiences are not going to follow you,” but it ended up being the favorite show of a lot of young people.
CRUZ: That is my hope for the future, that these younger generations will say, “Wait, I also want to be part of this artisanal way of doing things, because the world wants to rob that from me.”
AMBROSSI: It’s happening. Young audiences know they want the real thing. They know better.
CRUZ: They also know so much about politics. We have to encourage them and make them feel seen and heard.

AMBROSSI: La Bola Negra is a movie specifically about Federico García Lorca, who was part of a free generation. He experimented a lot. He was a young, vibrant guy trying to understand what he wanted to do, mixing poetry with naturalism and family drama. Suddenly he wanted surreality, to experiment. Lorca represented young people very well because he was young, and that’s why people are connecting with his spirit.
CRUZ: There is hope for the world.
CALVO: There is hope. It’s beautiful to see young people from all over being interested in Lorca. Having a hit movie that talks about literature is amazing.
AMBROSSI: And about our Spanish literature.
CRUZ: This is like a revolution, and I’m so proud to be part of it because it’s huge and so necessary.
CRUZ: No. I’m very much aware how lucky I am to be part of this film.
AMBROSSI: But you being a part of this gave so much attention to the movie worldwide.
CRUZ: The movie would’ve gotten the attention anyway, because it’s a masterpiece.
AMBROSSI: Without you, it wouldn’t be La Bola Negra.
CRUZ: I know the two of you are very different, but it is amazing how life has put you together. This is not a coincidence.

CRUZ: You have been together so many years, and even now that you’re not a couple, you’re working together because you are best friends. The level of respect I see you have for each other is so inspiring.

CRUZ: It is beautiful to see people can continue to share things when a relationship is over. You told me a little bit about your writing process, the schedule. You wake up really early and exercise before you start writing?
CRUZ: I would like to spend a day with you both when you are writing. [Laughs]
CALVO: There’s a lot of silence, a lot of reading, a lot of thinking. There’s a lot of walking around the house, there’s a lot of music, and there’s a lot of talking.
AMBROSSI: At the beginning, it’s all about researching.
CRUZ: Together, or do you do that separately?
AMBROSSI: Together. I don’t know the words but it’s like “double body” or something. Hyperactive people work very well as couples.
CALVO: With someone next to you.
AMBROSSI: Is that the body double?
CRUZ: It’s because of ADHD?
AMBROSSI: Yeah. Body doubling.
CRUZ: I didn’t know it was called that.

AMBROSSI: It’s a strategy of productivity for people with ADHD that consists of realizing a task in the presence of another. I think both of us have that. If we are not in the presence of the other, we are not going to work.
CRUZ: I completely understand and relate to that. There’s so many things where I need somebody else there to be sharing that experience.
AMBROSSI: At the beginning of the process, we will be researching. Even though we are not talking, we are reading the same book and then we—

AMBROSSI: We will share thoughts. Or we’ll have a call with a historian for hours about Granada in the ’30s, then the civil war in the north of Spain for 10 days, and we will travel. But we have to be—

AMBROSSI: Very organized and really looking for research. Research is key in our work as creators. We work very well with reality. We need to anchor the script to something real, and after the research, we go with a structure. That’s where we do different things. I work well with the structures because my mind goes to big things, and I have a sense of the start, the middle, the end. Javi always starts from the beginning.
CALVO: I imagine the movie from the first shot and I go as far as I can, I go back, I try to imagine it again at night.
CRUZ: It’s exhausting. It also happens while I’m sleeping. I shoot my dreams and I do different takes of situations.
CRUZ: For many years, I shot my dreams. I go back, and back, and back, and back.
AMBROSSI: Take two, three, four.
CRUZ: The person has to react differently, but it’s a live sequence.
CALVO: We need to take a break.
CRUZ: But who cares? We wouldn’t change it for more stability.

AMBROSSI: I think I have something different than you both, but in a way it’s the same. For example, a conflict we always have is Javi will be obsessed with the first line for one month, and I will be building the rest of the movie. I’m always like, “Javi, at some point we need to talk about the next scene,” and he’ll say, “Oh, you’re always thinking about the future.” [Laughs]
CRUZ: I need to know what’s coming after.
CALVO: You’re a visionary. You think in the future and I think of the past.
AMBROSSI: I don’t care about the present or the past. I’m always in the future.
CRUZ: I imagine that writing this, you had to go through a huge crisis of trying to put together three stories in such a genius way.
CALVO: Yeah. At some point I said to Javi, “I don’t want to make this movie anymore.”
AMBROSSI: But you say that in every project.
CRUZ: I didn’t want to ask this, but now I want to.
CRUZ: What would you say to somebody who is maybe not going into the theater to see this film because they are afraid you will try to change the way they think?

CALVO: This is a movie about humanity and seeing the other, and acknowledging that the other exists. We shouldn’t be killing each other. I think it’s a really simple thing I hope everyone agrees on. It’s not trying to lecture anyone. It’s an emotional journey about humanity and the importance of life.
AMBROSSI: Yeah. I would say go, give it a try.
CRUZ: And that’s what is happening. Everyone is going!
AMBROSSI: Go to the theater, sit there for the movie, and I’m sure no one in the world will want Carlos, Sebastián, or Alberto to be unhappy.
AMBROSSI: Maybe they will think politically differently. Maybe they won’t agree with us, but I’m sure deep in their hearts, they won’t be able to wish bad things on the characters.

CRUZ: This is why the movie is conquering everyone’s heart. Your mind is so open and you don’t judge through your characters. You don’t judge anybody, which is the most important thing. The audience is very smart and they know that.
CALVO: You are the best interviewer ever.
AMBROSSI: The best sister, not mother.
CRUZ: I tell you, you and I are almost the same age.
CRUZ: And we love each other.
